examples.translation: As for his uncle Claudius, he spared him merely as a laughingstock.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Neminem exsulum nisi ex senatus auctoritate restituit.
examples.translation: He recalled no one from exile except with the approval of the senate.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Satis constat, Cn. Lentulum Augurem, cui census maximus fuerit, metu et angore ad fastidium vitae ab eo actum et ut ne quo nisi ipso herede moreretur;
examples.translation: All the world knows that he drove Gnaeus Lentulus Augur, a man of great wealth, to take his own life through fear and mental anxiety, and to make the emperor his sole heir;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: birth, descent, origin; and concr., a race, stock, etc. (cf.: familia, gens, stirps).
Latin: Natio, factum nascendi; familia, stirps

examples.original: Quot genera tibi in hac dabo, quibus peccetur?
examples.translation: In this department, what countless varieties of fault I can show you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Verrius Flaccus libertinus docendi genere maxime claruit.
examples.translation: Marcus Verrius Flaccus, a freedman, gained special fame by his method of teaching.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Erat et cupidus voluptatum et eius generis intellegens et copiosus;
examples.translation: His appetite for pleasures was only equalled by his taste and ingenuity in devising them.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: evil, wicked, injurious, destructive, mischievous, hurtful; of personal appearance, ill-looking, ugly, deformed; of weight, bad, light; of fate, evil, unlucky, etc.
Latin: Iniquae qualitatis, haud bonus
Latin: Arbor quae māla fert
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain.

examples.original: Malo te legas quam epistulam meam.
examples.translation: I prefer that you should read your own words rather than my letter;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si sit aliquis malus, puto improbabitur;
examples.translation: If any man is bad, he will, I suppose, be regarded with disapproval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nondum intellegis, quantum mali optaverint?
examples.translation: Do you not yet understand what evil they prayed for?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: then.
Latin: (illo tempore, illis temporibus, et cum cum respondens.)

examples.original: Terrebatur ad hoc evidentibus portentis somniorum et auspiciorum et ominum, cum veteribus tum novis.
examples.translation: In addition he was frightened by manifest portents from dreams, auspices and omens, both old and new.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Plerumque improborum facta primo suspicio insequitur, dein sermo atque fama, tum accusator, tum iudex;
examples.translation: The usual consequences of crime are, first suspicion, next gossip and rumour, then comes the accuser, then the judge;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In castris tiro etiam tum propter nimiam vini aviditatem pro Tiberio ”Biberius,” pro Claudio ”Caldius,” pro Nerone ”Mero” vocabatur.
examples.translation: Even at the outset of his military career his excessive love of wine gave him the name of Biberius, instead of Tiberius, Caldius for Claudius, and Mero for Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: in which place, in what place, where.
Latin: interrog. In quo loco
Latin: rel. In quo loco

examples.original: Ubique tanti quisque, quantum habuit, fuit. Quid habere nobis turpe sit quaeris?
examples.translation: All men are worth as much as what they own What is most shameful for us to possess?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is ita cum Caesare egit: Si pacem populus Romanus cum Helvetiis faceret, in eam partem ituros atque ibi futuros Helvetios, ubi eos Caesar constituisset atque esse voluisset;
examples.translation: He treated with Caesar as follows: If the Roman people would make peace with the Helvetii, they would go whither and abide where Caesar should determine and desire;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed adest defensor ubique Caesar et hos aditus gladiis, hos ignibus arcet, Obsessusque gerit—tanta est constantia mentis— Expugnantis opus.
examples.translation: But Caesar was present everywhere in defence, driving back some attacks with the sword and others with fire;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: any object composed of materials perceptible by the senses, body, substance
Latin: Res substantialis, praesertim animalis vel hominis (et vivus et mortuus)
Latin: Thesaurus librorum
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; perhaps from *kʷr̥p- 'body', but the reconstruction is not secure.

examples.original: Quae corporis bona sunt, corpora sunt;
examples.translation: The goods of the body are bodily;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Valitudo ei neque corporis neque animi constitit.
examples.translation: He was sound neither of body nor mind.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Laudare solebat Attalus culcitam, quae resisteret corpori;
examples.translation: Attalus used to recommend a pillow which did not give in to the body;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to the people, State, or community; that is done for the sake or at the expense of the State; public, common.
Latin: Qui ad populum pertinet

examples.original: Non privatim solum, sed publice furimus.
examples.translation: We are mad, not only individually, but nationally.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnium istorum felicitas in publicum spectat;
examples.translation: The prosperity of all these men looks to public opinion;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Orare eum collegamque ut capesserent rem publicam;
examples.translation: They begged him and his colleague to undertake the guidance of the state;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: before, in front of; and, transf., for, with the idea of protection, substitution, or proportion.
Latin: Ante
Latin: Indicans beneficium alicuius

examples.original: Quis de exceptione et formula perpetietur ilea immensa volumina quae pro M. Tullio aut Aulo Caecina legimus?
examples.translation: Would anyone endure the interminable arguments about pleas and procedure which we get in the speeches delivered in defence of M. Tullius or Aulus Caecina?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Femina canitiem Germanis inficit herbis, Et melior vero quaeritur arte color: Femina procedit densissima crinibus emptis, Proque suis alios efficit aere suos.
examples.translation: A woman stains her whitening locks with German juices, and by skill seeks a hue better than the real;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: In castris tiro etiam tum propter nimiam vini aviditatem pro Tiberio ”Biberius,” pro Claudio ”Caldius,” pro Nerone ”Mero” vocabatur.
examples.translation: Even at the outset of his military career his excessive love of wine gave him the name of Biberius, instead of Tiberius, Caldius for Claudius, and Mero for Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: only, single, sole
Latin: Sine alio; unus, unicus

examples.original: Quomodo hoc fiat, sapientia sola monstrabit.
examples.translation: And wisdom alone can show you how this may be done.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ne existimes nos solos generosa verba iactare;
examples.translation: But you must not think that our school alone can utter noble words;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cato grammaticus, Latina Siren, Qui solus legit ac facit poetas.
examples.translation: Cato, teacher of letters, Siren Latin-born, He, and none other, poets reads and makes.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: or, or whether
Latin: Particula quaestionis disiunctivae quae propositioni secundae anteponitur
Latin: Postclassice etiam num vel -ne

examples.original: An ille Ciceroni invideret, qui mihi videtur ne Caesari quidem invidisse?
examples.translation: Why, he does not seem to me to have felt any for Julius Caesar himself.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: An obliviscimur quanto opere in audiendo in legendoque moveamur cum pie, cum amice, cum magno animo aliquid factum cognoscimus?
examples.translation: Do we forget the strong emotion that we feel when we hear or read of some deed of piety, of friendship or of magnanimity?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed ut dicere institueram, deducuntur in scholas <de> quibus non facile dixerim utrumne locus ipse an condiscipuli an genus studiorum plus mali ingeniis adferant.
examples.translation: The place has nothing about it that commands respect—no one enters it who is not as ignorant as the rest;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a people, the people.
Latin: Vulgus, natio
entries.etymology: Origin debated; possibly borrowed from Etruscan.

examples.original: Sed nec populo aut moenibus patriae pepercit.
examples.translation: But he showed no greater mercy to the people or the walls of his capital.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hae sunt amicitiae, quas temporarias populus appellat;
examples.translation: These are the so-called ”fair-weather” friendships;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Scaptione hoc, contionali seni, adsignaturos putarent finitimos populos?
examples.translation: What grief it would cause the former, and what joy the latter!
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the earth, opp. to the heavens, the sea, the air, etc.; land, ground, soil (cf.: tellus, solum).
Latin: Solum siccum; materiae quod tellurem complectuntur
Latin: Noster planeta
entries.etymology: From PIE *ters- 'dry'; Latin torreō 'dry, roast' is related.

examples.original: Culcita in terra iacet, ego in culcita.
examples.translation: The mattress lies on the ground, and I upon the mattress.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Intellexi non inmerito nautis terram timeri.
examples.translation: I understood that sailors have good reason to fear the land.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Coit area belli: Hic alitur sanguis terras fluxurus in omnes, Hic et Thessalicae clades Libycaeque tenentur;
examples.translation: The field of war was now contracted; here is preserved the blood that will flow hereafter over every land;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a name, appellation (syn. vocabulum).
Latin: Vocabulum, quo singulae res appellantur et noscuntur
Latin: pars orationis declinabilis per casus
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁nómn̥ 'name'; Greek ὄνομα and English 'name' are cognates.

examples.original: Nomina ex ambitione aut ex iniuria nata.
examples.translation: They are mere titles, born of ambition or of wrong.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Flaccum iam adultum, cuius exitum sub nomine Daphnidis deflet.
examples.translation: Virgil grow up, and whose death he laments under the name of Daphnis.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Videlicet, quia res ipsa non recipiebatur a nobis nec in usu erat, nomini quoque repugnatum est.
examples.translation: This is natural, inasmuch as the thing itself has not been admitted to general use by us; the name, too, has met with opposition.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a walled town, a city.
Latin: Magnus grex aedificiorum, civitate culta, et praesertim muro cincto
Latin: → Roma
entries.etymology: Origin debated; possibly borrowed from Etruscan.

examples.original: Quid cognitio urbium aut locorum?
examples.translation: Or in surveying cities and spots of interest?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: I, caput obnube liberatoris urbis huius;
examples.translation: Go, veil the head of the liberator of this city!
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad eam multitudinem urbs quoque amplificanda visa est.
examples.translation: Eighty thousand citizens are said to have been registered in that census;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: because (usually, like quod, of the determining reason; while quonĭam introduces any casual circumstance).
Latin: Coniunctio causalis, quae significat ob eam causam, ea de causa

examples.original: Unde existimo nonnullos tradere ausos, suspectum eum Augusto revocatumque ex provincia et quia cunctaretur, interceptum veneno.
examples.translation: This I have mentioned, rather not to pass it by, than that I think it true or even probable;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Fecerunt enim et carmina et in bibliothecas rettulerunt, non melius quam Cicero, sed felicius, quia illos fecisse pauciores sciunt.
examples.translation: For they not only wrote poetry, but what is more they sent copies to the libraries.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Philologi appellationem assumpsisse videtur, quia sic ut Eratosthenes, qui primus hoc cognomen sibi vindicavit, multiplici variaque doctrina censebatur.
examples.translation: And that he was such is evident from his commentaries, though very few of them survive;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: all, all the (denoting a thing in its entireness), the whole, entire, total.
Latin: (Rarissime) tot
Latin: Omnes partes alicuius

examples.original: Per totam vitam opus eius extenditur.
examples.translation: His work goes on throughout his whole life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Totum autem id externum est, et quod externum, id in casu est.
examples.translation: But all the apparatus of pleasure is external, and what is external must depend on chance.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina.
examples.translation: And you aver that if a single letter be altered, the whole system will totter.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to cause to go, let go, send, to send off, despatch, etc.
Latin: efficere aliquid ire, ire iubere, allegare quempiam ad aliquem, rem ad alium preferendam curare
Latin: iacere, emittere, conicere, iactare, iaculari praecipue missile
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; perhaps from *meytʰ- 'exchange'.

examples.original: Mittuntur de his rebus ad Caesarem legati.
examples.translation: Deputies were despatched to Caesar to treat of this matter.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Missis ad Vitellium litteris auxilium postulat.
examples.translation: He wrote to Vitellius asking for help.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: O causam singularem! o defensionem miseram ac perditam!
examples.translation: What an amazing position, what a miserable and hopeless line of defence!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to clean, cleanse (in the lit. sense very rare; in the trop. very freq.).
Latin: Purum facere
Latin: falsa, superflua, infructifera in arboribus, fructibus et quacumque alia re, a veris et fertilibus purgare et resecare

examples.original: Si sit aliquis malus, puto improbabitur;
examples.translation: If any man is bad, he will, I suppose, be regarded with disapproval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est, quod putes magnum, quo dissidemus;
examples.translation: There is no need for you to suppose that our difference is great;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Leporem et gallinam et anserem gustare fas non putant;
examples.translation: They account it wrong to eat of hare, fowl, and goose;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a stranger, foreigner; afterwards transf., an enemy
Latin: Inimicus alienus

examples.original: Non diutius se in Hernico hostis continuit;
examples.translation: No longer did the enemy confine themselves to the country of the Hernici;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eodem die legati ab hostibus missi ad Caesarem de pace venerunt.
examples.translation: On the same day deputies sent by the enemy came to Caesar to treat of peace.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hic locus ab hoste circiter passus sescentos, uti dictum est, aberat.
examples.translation: The spot, as has been said, was about six hundred paces away from the enemy.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: before (syn.: prae, pro).
Latin: (indicans statum prae alia re)

examples.original: Tam bibit hunc avide, quam bibit ante merum.
examples.translation: He drinks it as greedily as he drank undiluted wine before.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Agere enim fortius iam et audentius volo, si illud ante praedixero, mutari cum temporibus formas quoque et genera dicendi.
examples.translation: I want to take a bolder line now, and to speak more resolutely, first premising however that the forms and types of oratory change with the times.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sed supervenientibus ab urbe nuntiis ut occisum Neronem cunctosque in verba sua iurasse cognovit, deposita legati suscepit Caesaris appellationem iterque ingressus est paludatus ac dependente a cervicibus pugione ante pectus;
examples.translation: But when some messengers came from the city, reporting that Nero was dead and that all the people had sworn allegiance to him, he laid aside the title of governor and assumed that of Caesar.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to write, draw, or otherwise make lines, letters, figures, etc. (cf. scalpo)
Latin: Litteras in superficiem alicuius rei scalpere
Latin: Verba in opus litterarium componere

examples.original: Quid fuit istic antea scriptum?
examples.translation: What was written there before?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De ipsa villa nihil tibi possum certi scribere.
examples.translation: I could not describe the villa accurately;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quattuor milia librorum Didymus grammaticus scripsit.
examples.translation: Didymus the scholar wrote four thousand books.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: so, so much, as.
Latin: Adverbium demonstrativum (comparativum), indicans eodem modo, cum quam respondens; et significat adeō, tantum, ita
Latin: Apud veteres pro tamen

examples.original: Tam bibit hunc avide, quam bibit ante merum.
examples.translation: He drinks it as greedily as he drank undiluted wine before.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Atque hic tam docilis ad cetera natare nesciit.
examples.translation: And yet varied as were his accomplishments, the man could not swim.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: In extructionibus praetoriorum atque villarum omni ratione posthabita nihil tam efficere concupiscebat quam quod posse effici negaretur.
examples.translation: He built villas and country houses with utter disregard of expense, caring for nothing so much as to do what men said was impossible.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: plant (freq. and class.; syn.: planto, semino, consero).
Latin: Concinnare, redimire
Latin: Semina dispergere

examples.original: Egentes in locupletes, perditi in bonos, servi in dominos armabantur.
examples.translation: You say the senate was on my side. It was;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non vixit iste, sed in vita moratus est, nec sero mortuus est, sed diu.
examples.translation: A person like him has not lived; he has merely tarried awhile in life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a hand.
Latin: Pars corporis quae componitur digitis et quae comprehendit res
Latin: bonus, benignus
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain.

examples.original: Ad manum est, quod sat est.
examples.translation: That which is enough is ready to our hands.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nullum laborem recusant manus, quae ad arma ab aratro transferuntur;
examples.translation: The hand which turns from the plough to the sword never objects to toil;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum M. Valerio, Mani filio, Volesi nepote quaestor erat T. Quinctius Capitolinus, qui ter consul fuerat.
examples.translation: Marcus Valerius, son of Manius, and grandson of Volesus, shared the magistracy with Titus Quinctius Capitolinus, who had thrice been consul.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the other of two
Latin: Secundus duorum

examples.original: Nullum animal alteri par est.
examples.translation: And no two living things are equal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Est alter, qui annos adulescentiae cludit.
examples.translation: The next circle limits the period of our young manhood.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Unum est sine dolore esse, alterum cum voluptate;
examples.translation: To be without pain is one thing, to feel pleasure another;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To consider, reflect, deliberate, take counsel, reflect upon, consult.
Latin: consilium quaerere
Latin: consilium habere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; lŭi, ltum, 3

examples.original: Lucretio consuli ea provincia evenit.
examples.translation: To Lucius Lucretius the consul fell the command in this affair.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea ita facta sunt ex senatus consulto.
examples.translation: By decree of the senate these things were done.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: P. Volumnius consularis vidit cadentem.
examples.translation: Publius Volumnius, a former consul, saw him fall.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: you (plural)
Latin: Pronomen secundae personae

examples.original: At minus habeo virium quam vestrum utervis.
examples.translation: But it may be said that I have less strength than either of you;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Orcus vobis ducit pedes senatum gestu notarat.
examples.translation: Orcus guides your steps, he indicated the senate by a gesture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Etiam si exclamaveritis, non aliter audiam, quam si ad tactum vitiorum vestrorum ingemescatis.
examples.translation: Do you wish to bear witness that you are attentive, that you are stirred by the grandeur of the subject?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to take in hand, take hold of, lay hold of, take, seize, grasp
Latin: Sumere
Latin: căp|ĭō, -ĕre, cēpī, captum

examples.original: Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lugerent.
examples.translation: The relatives of the victims were forbidden to mourn for them.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Temptata res est si primo impetu capi Ardea posset.
examples.translation: An attempt was made to capture Ardea by assault.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Multis hominum milibus captis perterriti Bituriges;
examples.translation: The capture of many thousand persons struck terror into the Bituriges;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to live, be alive, have life (syn. spiro).
Latin: Vitam in se habere; nondum mortuus esse

examples.original: Sapiens facilis victu fuit, quidni?
examples.translation: The wise man was easy-going in his way of living.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vives, inquit Aristo, magnifice atque praeclare;
examples.translation: O, says Aristo, you will get on splendidly, capitally;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque sapiens vivit, quantum debet, non quantum potest.
examples.translation: For mere living is not a good, but living well.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to call; to call upon, summon, invoke; to call together, convoke, etc. (cf.: appello, compello).
Latin: Appellare, nuncupare, nominare
Latin: Clamare cum sonis oris ad aliquem

examples.original: Ille, quem tu minus beatum vocas, non est beatus;
examples.translation: He whom you maintain to be ”less happy” is not happy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare noli me ad contentionem vestrum vocare, Laterensis.
examples.translation: Do not, therefore, Laterensis, challenge me to institute a comparison between you.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid est tamen, quare tu istas Epicuri voces putes esse, non publicas?
examples.translation: But is there any reason why you should regard them as sayings of Epicurus and not common property?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to lead, conduct, draw, bring forward, in all senses; very freq. passing over into the signif. of the compounds abducere, deducere, adducere, producere, etc
Latin: Facere ut aliquis aut aliquid moveatur
Latin: ducem esse, praeesse

examples.original: Suo enim quisque studio maxime ducitur.”
examples.translation: For we are all specially influenced by our own favourite study.”
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Orcus vobis ducit pedes senatum gestu notarat.
examples.translation: Orcus guides your steps, he indicated the senate by a gesture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Legionem Caesar, quam equis devexerat, passibus ducentis ab eo tumulo constituit.
examples.translation: Caesar stationed the legion which he had brought on horseback two hundred paces from the mound.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to know, in the widest signif. of the word; to understand; perceive; to have knowledge of or skill in any thing, etc.
Latin: Percipere vel apprehendere clare et certe; comprehendere

examples.original: Is qui scit plurumum, rumor.
examples.translation: It was that most knowing of persons,—gossip.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vis scire, quam dubium adhuc sit?
examples.translation: Do you wish to know how uncertain it still is?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae scribis, unde veniant, scio;
examples.translation: I understand the feelings which prompt your words;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: how great.
Latin: Quam magnus (cui tantus respondet, et interrogative)

examples.original: Quanta esset cum gratia auctoritas!
examples.translation: What a wonderful combination of sweetness and power!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At quanto ego de illis melius existimo!
examples.translation: But how much more highly do I think of these men!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O quantus risus inter ista tollendus est!
examples.translation: O what laughter should such things draw!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to give as a loan, to loan, lend, make or loan to any one: (vilicus) injussu domini credat nemini
Latin: Fidei alicuius commendare
Latin: Committere alicui rem ut mutuum

examples.original: Quia nos posse non credimus.
examples.translation: It is because we refuse to believe in our power.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non ignovit, mihi crede, non.
examples.translation: No, believe me, she has not forgiven you;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non est tamen molestus creditor;
examples.translation: And yet it is not a troublesome creditor;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: magic, magical

examples.original: Quo magis hoc philosopho faciendum est;
examples.translation: All the more is the philosopher compelled to do likewise;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Neque enim tantum arte et scientia, sed longe magis facultate et <usu> eloquentiam contineri, nec tu, puto, abnues et hi significare vultu videntur.”
examples.translation: To this view I am sure you will not demur, and our friends here, to judge by their looks, seem to indicate concurrence.”
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nihil ex eo tempore praetermissum est ad maiestatem eius augendam ac multo magis, postquam Agrippa abdicato atque seposito certum erat, uni spem successionis incumbere.
examples.translation: From this time on nothing was left undone which could add to his prestige, especially after the disowning and banishment of Agrippa made it clear that the hope of the succession lay in him alone.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a ruler of a country, a king.
Latin: Vir qui nationem regit
Latin: Vir qui nationem regit. Leo est rex animalium
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₃rḗǵs 'king'; Sanskrit rājan and Celtic rīx are related.

examples.original: Iam regi leges, non regere.
examples.translation: The laws were no longer in control, but were themselves controlled.
examples.author: Livy

examples.translation: This Lucius Tarquinius—whether he was the son or the grandson of King Tarquinius Priscus is uncertain;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nomine enim tantum minus invidiosum, re ipsa prope atrocius quam regium esse;
examples.translation: For it was only in name, he said, that it was less hateful than that of a king;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: life.
Latin: Status inter nativitatem et mortem
entries.etymology: Derived from vīvō 'live'; the same PIE root *gʷeyh₃- underlies English 'quick' in the old sense 'living'.

examples.original: Ordinem vitae hunc fere tenuit.
examples.translation: This was in general his manner of life.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: His enim rebus detractis negat se reperire in asotorum vita quod reprendat.
examples.translation: Eliminate those passions, he says, and he cannot find anything to blame in a life of profligacy.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed vobis voluptatum perceptarum recordatio vitam beatam facit, et quidem corpore perceptarum;
examples.translation: But with you it is the recollection of pleasures enjoyed that gives happiness;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: keep from some one: "qui pecuniam dissolvit, statim non
Latin: Aliquid alicui agendum esse; esse necesse alicui

examples.translation: But now I ought to close my letter.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Interdum populus est, quem timere debeamus;
examples.translation: It is sometimes the people that we ought to fear;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed quae perspicua sunt longa esse non debent;
examples.translation: But there is really no need to labour what is self-evident;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to order one to do something, to bid, tell, command (syn.: mando, impero, praecipio).
Latin: Mandare
Latin: Imperare

examples.original: In utram ire partem iubes?
examples.translation: Which party would you have me follow?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qua re impetrata arma tradere iussi faciunt.
examples.translation: Their request was granted, and they proceeded to deliver up their arms as ordered.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Dicebant antiqui ”si iusso,” id est iussero.
examples.translation: The ancients used to say iusso, instead of iussero, in conditional clauses.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a word; plur., words, expressions, language, discourse, conversation, etc. (cf.: vox, vocabulum).
Latin: Dictio, vocabulum; signum vocale quod rem vel ideam significat, vel eius forma scripta
Latin: Sententia, dictum
entries.etymology: From PIE *werdʰh₁om 'word'; English 'word' and German Wort are cognates.

examples.original: Simplicis illius verbi usus amissus est.
examples.translation: The plain word has become obsolete.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Verbum tamen facere non audebant, ne forte ea res ad Dolabellam ipsum pertineret.
examples.translation: However, they dared not say a word, fearing that Dolabella himself might be concerned in the outrage.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Deiectus verbo qui potest esse quisquam, nisi in inferiorem locum de superiore motus?
examples.translation: And how can anyone be literally ”ejecteda” unless he has been removed from higher to lower ground?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the other, that which exists besides, can be added to what is already named of a like kind with it; the other part
Latin: alius, reliquus

examples.original: Ceterum multae eius species sunt.
examples.translation: But there are many aspects of it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atque hic tam docilis ad cetera natare nesciit.
examples.translation: And yet varied as were his accomplishments, the man could not swim.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Simili superbia violentiaque ceteros tractavit ordines.
examples.translation: He treated the other orders with like insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

Latin: Factum rendi

examples.original: Atque haec ratio late patet.
examples.translation: And this is a principle of wide application.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam cum similes rationi sint, similes et inter se sunt.
examples.translation: For since they resemble reason, they also resemble each other.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Itaque sensibus rationem adiunxit et ratione effecta sensus non reliquit.
examples.translation: Thus she added to sensation reason, and after creating reason did not discard sensation.
examples.author: Cicero

Latin: Tempus a bruma ad brumam dum sol redit
Latin: Tempus a bruma ad brumam dum sol redit. Circuitus; praesertim, telluris circum solem, spatium CCCLXV dierum

examples.translation: Tell me, Damoetas, I pray, is ’cuium pecus’ really good Latin?
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Insignis hic annus est nuntio Tarquini mortis.
examples.translation: This year was marked by the announcement of Tarquinius’s death.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Decessit autem vitio stomachi anno aetatis XXX.
examples.translation: He died of a stomach trouble in the thirtieth year of his age.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English:  (so obsol.)

examples.translation: And I beg and pray you to proceed in this course;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc a magno animi malo oritur.
examples.translation: This is the result of great evil in the soul.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et si esse vis felix, deos ora, ne quid tibi ex his, quae optantur, eveniat.
examples.translation: And, if you would be happy, entreat the gods that none of their fond desires for you may be brought to pass.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

Latin: Duo et alius. Numerus III

examples.translation: The depth of the river was about three feet.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.translation: A third species consists of the ure-oxen so-called.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.translation: The first and second line he ordered to keep under arms, the third to entrench a camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: work
Latin: Labor
Latin: Id quod fit operando, quod labor produxit

examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.translation: I never receive a letter from you without being in your company forthwith.

Latin: In modo qui ad numerum maiorem pertinet; numerus maior

examples.translation: I reckon a benefit at a higher rate than an injury.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Consentire in hoc plures insignes et spectabiles viri debent, ut claritas sit.
examples.translation: In order to constitute renown, the agreement of many distinguished and praiseworthy men is necessary.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to seek.
Latin: Dare operam, ut res amissa, vel qua utcumque caremus, recuperetur, inveniatur
Latin: Interrogāre

examples.translation: It takes trickery to win popular approval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.translation: We give you the kingdom, to be yours without bloodshed;

examples.translation: Not to keep you in suspense, I will ask—Was that resolution agreed to?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: long.

Latin: Magnum tempus durans

examples.translation: But that kind of merriment does not last long.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.translation: There is no need to enlarge upon or illustrate this point;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.translation: For no great pain lasts long.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.author: Suetonius

examples.author: Tacitus

Latin: Non ante; ad dorsum
Latin: Ad tempus posterius

examples.author: Suetonius

examples.translation: While emperor he constructed no magnificent public works, for the only ones which he undertook, the temple of Augustus and the restoration of Pompey’s theatre, he left unfinished after so many years.

Latin: Significans locus prope rem vel ad rem, praesertim alicuius domum

examples.author: Suetonius

examples.translation: Then his mother was banished too, and he was brought up at the house of his aunt Lepida almost in actual want, under two tutors, a dancer and a barber.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.translation: Very likely you will not relish what I am saying, Maternus, or what I intend to state in the course of my argument;
examples.author: Tacitus

Latin: Sonum auribus accipere
Latin: Aures praebere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; īvi or ii, itum, 4

examples.translation: I ask what the matter is, and they say he is exercising his voice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Diodorus, eius auditor, adiungit ad honestatem vacuitatem doloris.
examples.translation: Diodorus, his pupil, couples with Moral Worth freedom from pain.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Audire enim debet non tantum, quid sibi praecipiatur, sed etiam quare.
examples.translation: For he must be told, not only what he is being instructed to do, but also why.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

Latin: Littera quinta alphabeti Romani, quae inter D (de) et F (ef) stat

examples.translation: These plays he viewed from the top of the proscenium.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.translation: Then Livia, in a rage, drew from a secret place and read some old letters written to her by Augustus with regard to the austerity and stubbornness of Tiberius’ disposition.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Puteolis dedicatione pontis, quem excogitatum ab eo significavimus, cum multos e litore invitasset ad se, repente omnis praecipitavit, quosdam gubernacula apprehendentes contis remisque detrusit in mare.
examples.translation: At Puteoli, at the dedication of the bridge that he contrived, as has been said, after inviting a number to come to him from the shore, on a sudden he had them all thrown overboard;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: that is above, upper, higher: inferus an superus tibi fert deus funera, Liv. And. ap.

examples.original: Color egregius, integra valetudo, summa gratia;
examples.translation: He had excellent health and a sound constitution.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et Parin Oenone summos tenuisset ad annos, Si non Oebalia paelice laesa foret.
examples.translation: Oenone had kept Paris till life was o’er, had she not been harmed by her Oebalian rival.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Inviti summae spei adulescentes Eporedorix et Viridomarus Vercingetorigi parent.
examples.translation: Unwillingly, for they were young and very ambitious, Eporedorix and Viridomarus obeyed Vercingetorix.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: Of these the most celebrated, C.Julius Caesar, distinguished as general

examples.original: Hic locus aequo fere spatio ab castris Ariovisti et Caesaris aberat.
examples.translation: The place was about equally distant from the camps of Caesar and of Ariovistus.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: An ille Ciceroni invideret, qui mihi videtur ne Caesari quidem invidisse?
examples.translation: Why, he does not seem to me to have felt any for Julius Caesar himself.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Magnam Caesarem iniuriam facere, qui suo adventu vectigalia sibi deteriora faceret.
examples.translation: Caesar was doing him a serious injury, for his advance was damaging his revenues.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: In partic.: filius familias, or, in one word, filiusfamilias, v. familia.—
Latin: Progenies masculina
entries.etymology: From PIE *dʰeh₁ylios, from the root *dʰeh₁- 'suckle'.

examples.translation: Let Verginius decide what to do about his daughter, when he comes;
examples.author: Livy

examples.translation: Ascanius, Aeneas’ son, was not yet ripe for authority;
examples.author: Livy

examples.translation: He left a son Orbilius, who was also a teacher of grammar.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to hold, keep
Latin: Habere in manu vel ut in manu

examples.original: Ordinem vitae hunc fere tenuit.

examples.translation: Mantua gave me the light, Calabria slew me; now holds me Parthenope.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.translation: There, too, the enemy kept within his walls, and the Romans laid waste his fields.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a soldier.

entries.etymology: Etymology debated; possibly connected with mīlia 'thousands', but this is uncertain.

examples.translation: The bravest soldier comes from rock-ribbed regions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.translation: The work involved was strange to the town troops and broke their spirit.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.translation: I merely wished to test myself and to give myself practice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.translation: The mind must be exercised both day and night, for it is nourished by moderate labour;

examples.translation: On all these days Ariovistus kept his army in camp, but engaged daily in a cavalry encounter.

examples.translation: When the trumpet sounds, the poor man knows that he is not being attacked;

examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hoc Epicurus in voluptate ponit, quod summum bonum esse vult summumque malum dolorem;
examples.translation: This Epicurus finds in pleasure; pleasure he holds to be the Chief Good, pain the Chief Evil.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: manliness, manhood, i. e. the sum of all the corporeal or mental excellences of man, strength
Latin: Vīs rōburque virīle
Latin: Aliqua proprietas bona

examples.original: Illic est individuus ille comitatus virtutum;
examples.translation: There is the whole inseparable company of virtues;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnis est enim de virtutis dignitate contentio.
examples.translation: For the whole dispute turns on the true worth of virtue.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Callipho ad virtutem nihil adiunxit nisi voluptatem;
examples.translation: Callipho coupled with virtue pleasure alone;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to follow
Latin: Ire vel venire post; movere post, eodem itinere vel cursu

examples.original: Hos secuti M. Genucius et C. Curtius consules.
examples.translation: It was a year of quarrels both at home and abroad.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad haec et quae sequamur et quae fugiamus refert omnia.
examples.translation: These he maintains lie at the root of every act of choice and of avoidance.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum aspexeris, quot te antecedant, cogita, quot sequantur.
examples.translation: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: new, not old, young, fresh, recent, etc.
Latin: Qui non longe exsistit; recens; haud antiquus
entries.etymology: From PIE *néwos 'new'; Greek νέος and English 'new' are cognates.

examples.original: Quid incredibile, quid novum evenit?
examples.translation: What can happen that is beyond belief?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Librum autem, quem Sulla novissimum ”De Rebus Suis” imperfectum reliquerat, ipse supplevit.
examples.translation: He himself completed the last book of Sulla’s ”Autobiography,” which the dictator left unwritten.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Cum maxime agmen e castris explicaretur, Volsci, ut eodem signo excitati, novissimos adoriuntur.
examples.translation: At daybreak he caused the signal for departure to be sounded on the trumpet.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: As contemporaneous, or
Latin: Eodem tempore quo
Latin: donec

examples.original: Eorum enim omnium, multa praetermittentium dum eligant aliquid quod sequantur, quasi curta sententia;
examples.translation: They pick and choose, pass over a great deal and fasten on a single aspect;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dumque illi effusam longis anfractibus urbem Circumeunt, Arruns dispersos fulminis ignes Colligit et terrae maesto cum murmure condit Datque locis numen;
examples.translation: While the long procession winds its way round the wide city, Arruns collects the scattered fires of the thunderbolt and hides them in the earth with doleful muttering.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: In voluptate corporis (addam, si vis, animi, dum ea ipsa, ut vultis, sit e corpore) situm est vivere beate.
examples.translation: Bodily pleasure (and I will add if you like mental pleasure, so long as this, as you hold, is understood to have its source in the body) constitutes happiness.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: proceeding from or
Latin: Igitur, qua de causa, propterea
Latin: Alicuius rei causa, propter aliquid; significans causam actionis aut status

examples.original: Quid ergo hoc loco intellegit honestum?
examples.translation: What therefore does he understand by ’moral’ in this passage?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ergo et avarus erit, sed finite, et adulter, verum habebit modum, et luxuriosus eodem modo.
examples.translation: He will be a miser—within limits; an adulterer—in moderation;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Potius ergo illa dicantur, turpe esse, viri non esse debilitari dolore, frangi, succumbere.
examples.translation: If that be true, are you not guilty of a crime in advising him to end his life?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: What is fitted to the body for its protection, defensive armor, as the shield, coat of mail, helmet, etc.
Latin: Apparatus belli, vel defensivus vel nocivus

examples.original: Qua re impetrata arma tradere iussi faciunt.
examples.translation: Their request was granted, and they proceeded to deliver up their arms as ordered.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Primam et secundam aciem in armis esse, tertiam castra munire iussit.
examples.translation: The first and second line he ordered to keep under arms, the third to entrench a camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Tum victi victoresque in lacrimas effusi, sortem civilium armorum misera laetitia detestantes;
examples.translation: Then vanquished and victors alike burst into tears, cursing, amid their melancholy joy, the fate of civil war.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: gerund. fandi, fando

examples.original: Ordinem vitae hunc fere tenuit.
examples.translation: This was in general his manner of life.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hospitem violare fas non putant;
examples.translation: They do not think it right to outrage a guest;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid C. Caesarem in sua fata pariter ac publica inmisit?
examples.translation: And what impelled Gaius Caesar to the combined ruin of himself and of the state?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: in comparison with; hence, over against, fronting, in front, opposite, in opposition to, against, contrary to, opposed to, etc.
Latin: Opposite
Latin: Oppositus

examples.original: Nec vero alia sunt quaerenda contra Carneadiam illam sententiam;
examples.translation: Nor need we look for other arguments to refute the opinion of Carneades;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: A falsa autem assensione magis nos alienatos esse quam a ceteris rebus quae sint contra naturam, arbitrantur.
examples.translation: The mental assent to what is false, as the Stoics believe, is more repugnant to us than all the other things that are contrary to nature.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Statuam habet Praeneste, in inferiore fori parte contra hemicyclium, in quo fastos a se ordinatos et marmoreo parieti incisos publicarat.
examples.translation: His statue stands at Praeneste in the upper part of the forum near the hemicycle, on which he exhibited the calendar which he had arranged and inscribed upon its marble walls.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: thereafter, thereupon (for syn. cf.: dein, exinde, inde, deinceps, post, postea, porro).—
Latin: Ad locum subsequens
Latin: Ad tempus subsequens

examples.original: Cur deinde Metrodori liberos commendas?
examples.translation: And secondly, why do you provide for the children of Metrodorus?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Deinde ”Catalepton” et ”Priapea” et ”Epigrammata” et ”Diras,” item ”Cirim” et ”Culicem,” cum esset annorum XVI.
examples.translation: Then he wrote the ”Catalepton,” ”Priapea,” ”Epigrams” and the ”Dirae,” as well as the ”Ciris” and the ”Culex,” when he was sixteen years old.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Aurelius Opillus, Epicurei cuiusdam libertus, philosophiam primo, deinde rhetoricam, novissime grammaticam docuit.
examples.translation: Aurelius Opilius, freedman of an Epicurean, first taught philosophy, afterwards rhetoric, and finally grammar.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: the condition or privileges of a (Roman) citizen, citizenship, freedom of the city
Latin: Status civis, vel praerogativae civium
Latin: Communitas civium; urbs vel urbes et terra suae

examples.original: Peragit concilium Caesar equitesque imperat civitatibus.
examples.translation: Caesar closed the convention, and made requisition of cavalry upon the states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Deinde ad civitatis vitam reductus ex bene coeptis pauca servavi.
examples.translation: For I had planned my whole life with great resolves.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo die L. Mamilio Tusculano adprobantibus cunctis civitas data est.
examples.translation: On that day Lucius Mamilius the Tusculan was granted citizenship, with the approval of all.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: then, therefore, thereupon, accordingly, in these circumstances

examples.original: Me igitur ipsum ames oportet, non mea, si veri amici futuri sumus.
examples.translation: So you must love me myself, not my possessions, if we are to be genuine friends.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Suscepto igitur civili bello ac ducibus copiisque in Italiam praemissis interim Alexandriam transiit, ut claustra Aegypti optineret.
examples.translation: Therefore beginning a civil war and sending ahead generals with troops to Italy, he crossed meanwhile to Alexandria, to take possession of the key to Egypt.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Prius igitur quam ultra progrederetur, praeventus est ab Agrippina, quam praeter haec conscientia quoque nec minus delatores multorum criminum arguebant.
examples.translation: But before he could go any farther, he was cut short by Agrippina, who was being accused besides of many other crimes both by her own conscience and by informers.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: Water, in its most gen. signif.
Latin: Hoc liquidum quod e nubibus descendit ut pluvia, et qui flumina, lacus, maria, etc. format; chemice, H₂O. (materialis)
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₂ekʷ- 'water'; Gothic ahwa 'river' is a related form.

examples.original: Ap. Claudius censor aquam perduxit;
examples.translation: Appius Claudius the censor completed an aqueduct;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Possum, quamvis in aqua sim, non natare;
examples.translation: It is possible for me, though being in the water, not to swim;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quantum aquarum per gradus cum fragore labentium!
examples.translation: And what masses of water that fall crashing from level to level!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: death in every form, natural or violent (syn.: letum, nex).
Latin: finis vitae
entries.etymology: From PIE *mer- 'die'; Latin mortālis and English 'mortal' are related.

examples.original: Quod enim morti tempus exemptum est?
examples.translation: For what season of our life is exempt from death?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Incertum est, quo loco te mors expectet;
examples.translation: You do not know where death awaits you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In nulla re magis quam in morte morem animo gerere debemus.
examples.translation: There is no occasion when the soul should be humoured more than at the moment of death.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Physically.
Latin: Sēnsibus percipere

examples.original: Haec non nego sentire sapientem;
examples.translation: I do not deny that the wise man feels these things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Effugit avaritiam, sed iram adhuc sentit;
examples.translation: They have escaped avarice, for example, but still feel anger;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nulla virtus est, quae non sentiat se perpeti.
examples.translation: There is no virtue that fails to realize that it does endure.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be valued, esteemed at so much.

examples.original: Adest ad tabulam, licetur Aebutius;
examples.translation: Aebutius attends at the sale.a He does the bidding.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Neque tu hoc dicere audebis, nec, si cupias, licebit;
examples.translation: You will not dare to say that; nor can you if you would;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nihil praeter arma et quod cocti ad manum fuit cibi ferre militi licuit;
examples.translation: The soldiers were allowed to take nothing but their arms and such bread as happened to be at hand;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To leave behind (cf. desero, omitto).

examples.original: Timere relicta ab suis plebes violentiam patrum;
examples.translation: The plebeians, having been abandoned by their friends, feared violence at the hands of the senators;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea qui conficeret, C. Trebonium legatum relinquit.
examples.translation: He left Gaius Trebonius, lieutenant-general, to carry out these orders.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Reliquit filium Orbilium, et ipsum grammaticum professorem.
examples.translation: He left a son Orbilius, who was also a teacher of grammar.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: broth, soup, sauce (class.)
Latin: Quod iustum est

examples.original: In mores fortuna ius non habet.
examples.translation: Fortune has no jurisdiction over character.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tectis ac parietibus iura dicturi estis?
examples.translation: Is it to roofs and walls you will render judgment?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quanta notitia antiquitatis, scientia iuris auguri!
examples.translation: What a knowledge of ancient history! What skill in augural law!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Often
Latin: Crebrō, frequenter

examples.original: Ibidem saepius et per complures cantavit dies;
examples.translation: In the same city he sang frequently and for several successive days.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Accepta itaque res saepiusque usurpando excitata.
examples.translation: And so the amusement was adopted, and frequent use kept it alive.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Videtisne, ut apud Homerum saepissime Nestor de virtutibus suis praedicet?
examples.translation: Do you not observe in Homer how, time and again, Nestor proclaims his own merits?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: any fortified place; a castle, fort, fortress (more rare than castellum)
Latin: Castellum, sive aedificium munitum
Latin: castra tant. | Locus ubi exercitus assidet; collectio tabernaculorum militarium

examples.original: Coloniae deductae sunt Castrum Sena Hadria.
examples.translation: Colonies were established at Castrum, Sena, and Hadria.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Primam et secundam aciem in armis esse, tertiam castra munire iussit.
examples.translation: The first and second line he ordered to keep under arms, the third to entrench a camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar Locus erat castrorum editus et paulatim ab imo acclivis circiter passus mille.
examples.translation: The position of the camp was on high ground, with a gradual slope from the bottom of about a mile.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: of a wound, Pollio ap.
Latin: vitam finire

examples.original: Vivere noluit, qui mori non vult.
examples.translation: He who does not wish to die cannot have wished to live.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Recto tibi invictoque moriendum est.
examples.translation: You must die erect and unyielding.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam vita, si moriendi virtus abest, servitus est.
examples.translation: For life, if courage to die be lacking, is slavery.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to bear about with one, to bear, carry, to wear
Latin: Portare, ferre
Latin: Agere, facere

examples.original: Consulatus super pristinum quattuor gessit;
examples.translation: He held four consulships in addition to his original one.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Orcus vobis ducit pedes senatum gestu notarat.
examples.translation: Orcus guides your steps, he indicated the senate by a gesture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Non opinor ex eis rebus, quae gestae sunt, rem ullam potuisse mutari.
examples.translation: I hold that of the actual facts of the case no single item can have changed.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a judge (class.).
Latin: Qui litigantium causas cognoscit, et sententiam fert

examples.original: De praesentibus facile iudicium est;
examples.translation: As to things present, the decision is easy.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis in meum locum iudicem subdidit?
examples.translation: Who substituted another name on the list of jurymen for my own?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed quid opus erat ad eam rem iudice sequestre?
examples.translation: But what need, for such a purpose, of a juror as go-between?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to like, to love
Latin: Sentire amorem pro aliquo
Latin: Existimare cum affectione vel bona voluntate
entries.etymology: Etymology debated; perhaps from *h₂emh₃- 'take hold of', but the connection is not certain.

examples.original: Huius te amor contra durissima armabit.
examples.translation: The love of reason will arm you against the greatest hardships.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Siquis amas, nec vis, facito contagia vites;
examples.translation: If you love, nor wish to love, see that you shun contagion;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Me igitur ipsum ames oportet, non mea, si veri amici futuri sumus.
examples.translation: So you must love me myself, not my possessions, if we are to be genuine friends.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be driven or carried by one's weight from a higher to a lower point, to fall down, be precipitated, sink down, go down, sink, fall
Latin: Prōcumbō, dēcidō
Latin: Morī, intereō

examples.original: Bonum omne in easdem cadit leges;
examples.translation: The good, in every instance, is subject to these same laws.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si quos Orbilius ferula scuticaque cecidit.
examples.translation: Whomever Orbilius thrashed with rod or with whiplash of leather.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Multi utrimque cadunt, plures volnera accipiunt;
examples.translation: At length the knights began to rail at one another.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: whoever or whatever it be, each, every, every body, every one, every thing
Latin: Omnes pluris quam trium rerum gregis, separatim tractatae

examples.original: Sed quoto cuique habere se contigit?
examples.translation: But how few men are blessed with ownership of self!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Suo enim quisque studio maxime ducitur.”
examples.translation: For we are all specially influenced by our own favourite study.”
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ut quamque adtigeris, fabula turpis erit?
examples.translation: As you touch upon each, shall there be a tale of shame?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: deliberation, consultation, a considering together, counsel (cf. concilium; very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
entries.etymology: Derived from cōnsulō 'consult, deliberate'.

examples.original: Quid ergo mei consili est?
examples.translation: What, then, is my counsel?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: At barbaris consilium non defuit.
examples.translation: But the natives were not lacking in resource.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ille dat consilia magnifica et erecta.
examples.translation: He it is that gives noble and upright counsel.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to India, Indian

examples.original: Post Dareum et Indos pauper est Alexander.
examples.translation: Alexander was poor even after his conquest of Darius and the Indies.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed Vergilius a Cremona Mediolanum et inde paulo post transiit in urbem.
examples.translation: Virgil, however, moved from Cremona to Mediolanum, and shortly afterwards from there to Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Studuit Flaccus usque ad annum XII. aetatis suae Volaterris, inde Romae apud grammaticum Remmium Palaemonem et apud rhetorem Verginium Flavum.
examples.translation: Flaccus studied until the twelfth year of his age at Volaterrae, and then at Rome with the grammarian Remmius Palaemon and the rhetorician Verginius Flavus.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: to bear, carry, bring, draw, or give back (very freq. and class.; cf.: reduco, reporto, retraho).
Latin: Vehere vel portare rem rursum
Latin: De rebus vel eventibus dicere, res describere

examples.original: Frumentum omne ad se referri iubet;
examples.translation: He ordered all the corn to be brought in to his headquarters;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quam bene vivas refert, non quam diu;
examples.translation: The point is, not how long you live, but how nobly you live.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: De cuius spatio atque cultu suffecerit haec rettulisse.
examples.translation: Its size and splendour will be sufficiently indicated by the following details.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: ever, always, at all times, forever (cf. usque).
Latin: In omnibus temporibus; per aevum totum
entries.etymology: From sem- 'one, whole' + -per, an old adverbial ending.

examples.original: In principatu maturius semper ac de nocte vigilabat;
examples.translation: While emperor, he always rose very early, in fact before daylight;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Mihi quidem Scipio, quamquam est subito ereptus, vivit tamen semperque vivet ;
examples.translation: For me, indeed, though he was suddenly snatched away, Scipio still lives and will always live;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dolet heu semperque dolebit, Quod scelerum, Caesar, prodest tibi summa tuorum, Cum genero pugnasse pio.
examples.translation: Grievous alas! is it, and ever will be, that Caesar profited by his worst crime—his fighting against a kinsman who had scruples.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that is in the middle or midst, mid, middle (class.).
Latin: Centralis, inter alia situs, ab aliis rebus circumdatus, inter ambo partes situs

examples.original: Infert pavidos fuga in mediam caedem;
examples.translation: In their panic they fled into the middle of the carnage.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed tolli me de medio puta et post mortem nihil ex homine restare;
examples.translation: But suppose that I am utterly annihilated, and that after death nothing mortal remains;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Miramur animalia quaedam, quae per medios ignes sine noxa corporum transeant;
examples.translation: We marvel at certain animals because they can pass through fire and suffer no bodily harm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: trust in a person or thing, faith, confidence, reliance, credence, belief (syn.: fidelitas, fiducia, confidentia).

examples.original: Quibus adductis eos in fidem recepit.
examples.translation: He therefore ordered them to furnish a large number of hostages;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ab hoc discede iudicio; non pietas constabit, non fides.
examples.translation: Dissent from this judgment, and duty and loyalty will not abide.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aeque enim contingit omnibus fidibus ut incontentae sint;
examples.translation: All the lyres equally are out of tune;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: In negative declarations (so most usually)
Latin: Ad minimum unus

examples.original: Non enim ullo honestamento eget;
examples.translation: For virtue needs nothing to set it off;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Negabat igitur ullam esse artem quae ipsa a se proficisceretur;
examples.translation: He then pointed out that no science or art can supply its own starting-point;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non sumus in ullius potestate, cum mors in nostra potestate sit.
examples.translation: We are in the power of nothing when once we have death in our own power!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to bear, support, undergo, suffer, endure (syn.: fero, tolero).
Latin: mala sustinere, ferre

examples.original: Deinde etiam tormentorum fortis patientia optabilis est.
examples.translation: And, lastly, because a brave endurance even under torture is desirable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ut fortiter amissorum desideria pateremur praecepimus nobis;
examples.translation: We have taught ourselves to endure bravely the loss of those we love;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae res illum non patitur ad imum devolvi, retinet in summo.
examples.translation: That which prevents him from rolling to the bottom, keeps him at the summit.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: strong, powerful.
Latin: Qui corporis robore pollet
Latin: audax

examples.original: Et fortior miles ex confragoso venit;
examples.translation: The bravest soldier comes from rock-ribbed regions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic autem est exercitationis etiam fortissimis finis.
examples.translation: And weariness is the aim and end of exercise, no matter how strong one is.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Deinde etiam tormentorum fortis patientia optabilis est.
examples.translation: And, lastly, because a brave endurance even under torture is desirable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: under.
Latin: (c. abl, indicans locationem ad partem inferam aliquis)

examples.original: Decessit aetatis exactae sub Tiberio.
examples.translation: He died at an advanced age under Tiberius.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Flaccum iam adultum, cuius exitum sub nomine Daphnidis deflet.
examples.translation: Virgil grow up, and whose death he laments under the name of Daphnis.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Et subinde matre etiam relegata paene inops atque egens apud amitam Lepidam nutritus est sub duobus paedagogis saltatore atque tonsore.
examples.translation: Then his mother was banished too, and he was brought up at the house of his aunt Lepida almost in actual want, under two tutors, a dancer and a barber.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: chance
entries.etymology: Derived from fors 'chance, lot'.

examples.original: In mores fortuna ius non habet.
examples.translation: Fortune has no jurisdiction over character.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc unum ad pristinam fortunam Caesari defuit.
examples.translation: This one thing was lacking to complete the wonted success of Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Illud fortunae indulgentiam rexit, hoc violentiam domuit.
examples.translation: The one controls the favours of fortune; the other overcomes her onslaughts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: each (of two), either, each one, one and the other, one as well as the other, both
Latin: omnis (quando sunt tantum duo)
Latin: ambo

examples.original: In utroque finis dolendi est.
examples.translation: In either case there is an end of pain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod paulo minus utrumque evenit;
examples.translation: And both predictions were all but fulfilled;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Pugnatum est ab utrisque acriter.
examples.translation: The fighting was fierce on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: any body, any thing, something (cf.: aliquis, ullus, quispiam).
Latin: (pronomen indefinitum substantivum)

examples.original: Quid per se peregrinatio prodesse cuiquam potuit?
examples.translation: What benefit has travel of itself ever been able to give anyone?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Negat oportuisse quidquam uni extra ordinem decerni.
examples.translation: He denies the propriety of decreeing any extraordinary function to an individual.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Tu autem negas fortem esse quemquam posse qui dolorem malum putet.
examples.translation: You however say that no one can be brave who thinks pain an evil.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a letter, a written sign or mark signifying a sound.
Latin: Signum scriptum per quod sonus significatur et verbum componitur

examples.original: Orbilius ubinam est, litterarum oblivio?
examples.translation: Where is Orbilius, pray, great learning’s tomb?
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Et ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina.
examples.translation: And you aver that if a single letter be altered, the whole system will totter.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: His rebus gestis, ex litteris Caesaris dierum viginti supplicatio a senatu decreta est.
examples.translation: And for these achievements, upon receipt of Caesar’s despatches, the Senate decreed a public thanksgiving of twenty days.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: equal (cf.: aequus, similis).
Latin: Aequus, similis
Latin: Homo par

examples.original: Non pono utrique par pretium.
examples.translation: I do not set an equal value on benefits and injuries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si rectae sunt, et pares sunt.
examples.translation: If they are right, they are also equal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Item equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt.
examples.translation: The horsemen of Ariovistus halted at an equal distance.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: light upon a thing; to find, meet with (cf.: reperio, offendo).
Latin: Reperīre; et dicitur de rebus omnibus, quae vel data opera quaesita, vel casu oblata, quocumque modo comperimus
Latin: Excōgitāre, comminīscī

examples.original: Animi remedia inventa sunt ab antiquis;
examples.translation: The cures for the spirit also have been discovered by the ancients;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod auxilium invenis inbecillitati humanae?
examples.translation: What succour can you discover for man’s helplessness?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid ergo adversus has amissiones auxili invenimus?
examples.translation: What resource do we find, then, in the face of these losses?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to cast or fix one's eyes upon
Latin: ( ) Membrum visus. Oculus
Latin: Facultas visus

examples.original: Pleraque ante oculos posita transimus.
examples.translation: We miss much that is set before our very eyes.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His imperitorum feriuntur oculi omnia subita, quia causas non novere, mirantium.
examples.translation: The eye of the inexperienced is struck with amazement by these things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Oculorum, inquit Plato, est in nobis sensus acerrimus, quibus sapientiam non cernimus;
examples.translation: The sense of sight, says Plato, is the keenest sense we possess, yet our eyes cannot behold Wisdom;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to turn a thing to or toward a place
Latin: Dirigere aliquid versum aliquod
Latin: dirigere aliquid versum aliquod

examples.original: Eadem nunc mea adversum te oratio est.
examples.translation: I take the same line now against you.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et adversus mortem tu tam minuta iacularis?
examples.translation: Are you, then, hurling petty weapons like yours even against death?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec secundi quicquam singulis est nec adversi;
examples.translation: There is no such thing as good or bad fortune for the individual;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a male person
Latin: Homo mas

examples.original: Quorum nihil sapienti viro potest evenire;
examples.translation: But none of these things can happen to the sage;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ac ne principum quidem virorum insectatione abstinuit;
examples.translation: He did not even refrain from gibes at men of distinction;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Vir fortis ac sapiens non fugere debet e vita, sed exire.
examples.translation: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: like, resembling, similar (cf. par); constr. with
Latin: Paene eandem formam habens

examples.original: Nam quid illi simile bello fuit?
examples.translation: For wherein was that war like this?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: His rebus fugae similem profectionem effecit.
examples.translation: By this means he made his departure like a rout.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Simili superbia violentiaque ceteros tractavit ordines.
examples.translation: He treated the other orders with like insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: the chisel or burin of the sculptor or engraver, a graver
Latin: Atmosphaera aut partes superiores atmosphaerae, quae sunt caeruleae (nocte nigerae)
Latin: etiam Paradisus, regnum Dei

examples.original: Magnus erat labor ire in caelum;
examples.translation: It would be a great task to journey heavenwards;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aequaliter splendebit omne caeli latus;
examples.translation: The whole expanse of heaven will shine evenly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Negant fas esse agi cum populo, cum de caelo servatum sit.
examples.translation: These assert that proceedings in assembly are sacrilegious when observation of the heavens is in progress.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to stand, in opposition to sitting, walking, or lying prostrate, to stand still, remain standing, stand upright.
Latin: Esse erecte positus

examples.original: Sic huius, ut caelestium, stata magnitudo est.
examples.translation: Her stature, like that of the stars in the heavens, is fixed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In edito stat admirabilis, celsus, magnitudinis verae.
examples.translation: He stands in a high place, worthy of admiration, lofty, and really great.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non enim minus secundum naturam est sedere quam stare aut ambulare.
examples.translation: For sitting is an act that is not less according to nature than standing or walking.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: easy to do, easy, without difficulty.
Latin: Qui sine opera fieri potest

examples.original: Quid huic optes nisi deos faciles?
examples.translation: What does he mean by such womanish and indecent verse?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cui non faciliora apparuere in actu?
examples.translation: To what man did they not seem easier in the doing?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et harum quidem rerum facilis est et expedita distinctio.
examples.translation: These cases are perfectly simple and easy to distinguish.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: friendly, kind, amicable, favorable, inclined to, liking; constr. with
Latin: vir amans vel socius
Latin: amans
