examples.original: Quis enim tibi potest amicus esse?
examples.translation: But who can be a friend to you?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Venit ad me pro amico blandus inimicus.
examples.translation: An enemy comes to me full of compliments, in the guise of a friend.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et saepe incidunt magnae res, ut discedendum sit ab amicis;
examples.translation: Often, too, important duties arise which require the temporary separation of friends;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: since now, since then, since, seeing that, because, whereas (quoniam gives a ground or reason, quod and quia give the determining cause or reason).
Latin: Quia, quod

examples.original: Quoniam autem omne quod est bonum primum locum tenere dicimus, necesse est nec bonum esse nec malum hoc quod praepositum vel praecipuum nominamus;
examples.translation: But since we declare that everything that is good occupies the first rank, it follows that this which we entitle preferred or superior is neither good nor evil;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Caesar Quoniam ad hunc locum perventum est, non alienum esse videtur de Galliae Germaniaeque moribus et quo differant hae nationes inter sese proponere.
examples.translation: Since I have arrived at this point, it would seem to be not inappropriate to set forth the customs of Gaul and of Germany, and the difference between these nations.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod efficitur hac etiam conclusione rationis: Quoniam enim videmus esse quiddam quod recte factum appellemus, id autem est perfectum officium, erit etiam inchoatum;
examples.translation: The same thing is also proved by the following argument: We observe that something exists which we call right action; but this is an appropriate act perfectly performed;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to see into, perceive, understand.
Latin: Videre, cognoscere, mente capere

examples.original: Quid ergo hoc loco intellegit honestum?
examples.translation: What therefore does he understand by ’moral’ in this passage?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Atque hoc quidem omnes mortales et intellegunt et re probant.
examples.translation: And indeed this is a statement which all men not only understand but also approve.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Erat et cupidus voluptatum et eius generis intellegens et copiosus;
examples.translation: His appetite for pleasures was only equalled by his taste and ingenuity in devising them.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a race or clan, embracing several families united together by a common name and by certain religious rites; orig
Latin: Plures familiae, quae non modo nomine, sed sacris quoque et politico vinculo inter se iungebantur
Latin: Tribus collectiove familiarum sub nomine et ritibus communibus

examples.original: Cuius populi ea cuiusque gentis classis fuerit nihil certi est.
examples.translation: To what people or race their fleet belonged is uncertain.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eius testamentum erat nullum; lege hereditas ad gentem Minuciam veniebat.
examples.translation: Before he became praetor, a man named Minucius died.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nero I. Ex gente Domitia duae familiae claruerunt, Calvinorum et Ahenobarborum.
examples.translation: Nero Nero I. Of the Domitian family two branches have acquired distinction, the Calvini and the Ahenobarbi.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: heavy, weighty, ponderous, burdensome; or
Latin: Magni ponderis
Latin: Cum opera coniunctus, molestus, laboriosus

examples.original: Haec poena apud eos est gravissima.
examples.translation: Those that are so banned are reckoned as impious and criminal;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Graviora vectigalia aut abolevit aut minuit.
examples.translation: The more oppressive sources of revenue he either abolished or moderated.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Leve aes alienum debitorem facit, grave inimicum.
examples.translation: A trifling debt makes a man your debtor;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: such, of such a kind, nature, or quality, such like; with a corresp.
Latin: pronomen substantivum, et cum qualis respondens

examples.original: Talem animum nostrum esse volo;
examples.translation: I would have my mind of such a quality as this;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pars vestrum tali munere magna caret.
examples.translation: A great part of you lack a gift so precious.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Qualis ratio est, tales et actiones sunt;
examples.translation: As reason is, so also are actions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a mark, token, sign, indication
Latin: Id per quod ulla res agnoscitur vel indicatur; id quod significat; indicium; insigne

examples.original: Crescere posse inperfectae rei signum est.
examples.translation: The ability to increase is proof that a thing is still imperfect.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eum impetum non tulerunt Etrusci versisque signis fuga effusa castra repetunt.
examples.translation: Their onset was too much for the Etruscans, who faced about and fled headlong towards their camp.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid signorum, quid vestium quidve tabularum raptum incensumque atque proiectum est!
examples.translation: What a vast quantity of statues, garments and pictures was carried off, burnt, and thrown away!
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to get a knowledge of, become acquainted with, come to know a thing (syn.: scio, calleo).
Latin: Spiritualiter videre, in animo invenire
Latin: scire, notum habere

examples.original: Nos ex illa prima nota non sumus;
examples.translation: We ourselves are not of that first class, either;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil novi facio, nihil novi video;
examples.translation: I do nothing new; I see nothing new;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non avaritia, non crudelitas modum novit.
examples.translation: There are no limits to our greed, none to our cruelty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to drive, move or bring a person or thing to or toward.
Latin: Pellere aliquid ad aliquam rem
Latin: naut. (Navem) terrae ducere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; pŭli, pulsum, 3

examples.original: Sunt item, quae appellantur alces.
examples.translation: There are also elks so-called.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Id ex similitudine floris lilium appellabant.
examples.translation: Eight rows of this kind were dug, three feet apart.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hae sunt amicitiae, quas temporarias populus appellat;
examples.translation: These are the so-called ”fair-weather” friendships;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the city of Rome, founded in the second year of the seventh Olympiad (B. C. 753)
Latin: Urbs in Italia meridionali et caput Italiae

examples.original: Missus tamen ab Roma consul in Volscos C. Nautius;
examples.translation: Nevertheless a consul, Gaius Nautius, was sent from Rome against the Volsci.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Stante potest mundo Romaque superstite Magnus Esse miser.
examples.translation: The world may remain and Rome survive, though Magnus is doomed.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Drusum fratrem in Germania amisit, cuius corpus pedibus toto itinere praegrediens Romam usque pervexit.
examples.translation: He lost his brother Drusus in Germany and conveyed his body to Rome, going before it on foot all the way.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: pain, smart, ache (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: aegrimonia, maeror, maestitia, luctus, plangor, tristitia, angor, anxietas, cura, sollicitudo).
Latin: Acerbus corporis sensus

examples.original: Adicio dolores continuos et graves;
examples.translation: I add afflictions which are unceasing and severe;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: De vacuitate doloris eadem sententia erit.
examples.translation: As regards freedom from pain her decision will be the same.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Unum est sine dolore esse, alterum cum voluptate;
examples.translation: To be without pain is one thing, to feel pleasure another;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: night.
Latin: Tempus inter occasum ortumque solis

Latin: Pars diei quando sol sub horizone est, vel tempus ab occasu ad ortum; praesertim tempus a crepusculo ad diluculum, quando lux solis non adest, sed solummodo lux lunae stellaeve, vel lux artificialis
entries.etymology: From PIE *nókʷts 'night'; Greek νύξ and English 'night' are cognates.

examples.original: Res disputatione ad mediam noctem perducitur.
examples.translation: The matter continued in dispute till midnight.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In principatu maturius semper ac de nocte vigilabat;
examples.translation: While emperor, he always rose very early, in fact before daylight;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Audio circa horam sextam noctis clamorem concitatum;
examples.translation: I ask what the matter is, and they say he is exercising his voice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to speak, talk, say
Latin: lŏqu|or, -ī, lŏcūtus vel lŏquūtus sum
Latin: ore verba emittere cum sensu

examples.original: Iterum ego tamquam Epicureus loquor?
examples.translation: Am I speaking again in the guise of an Epicureana?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Turpe est aliud loqui, aliud sentire;
examples.translation: It is ignoble to say one thing and mean another;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non enim ex praeparato locutus est, sed subito deprehensus.
examples.translation: For he spoke not from forethought, but was suddenly caught off his guard.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to care for, take or have care of, to be solicitous for, to look or attend to, trouble one's self about, etc. (very freq. in every period and species of composition); constr
Latin: (Generatim) in aliqua re elaboro, curam studium, diligentiam adhibeo, studeo, operam do, laboro
Latin: curam habere alicujus rei, parare, purgare, colere, administrare, conficere

examples.original: Quis medicus aegros in transitu curat?
examples.translation: What physician can heal his patient on a flying visit?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Exploratores, ut mos est, longius curabant.
examples.translation: His scouts, as usual, watched the country still further from camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Non ut diu vivamus curandum est, sed ut satis;
examples.translation: We should strive, not to live long, but to live rightlyb;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: skill in joining something, combining, working it, etc., with the advancement of Roman culture, carried entirely beyond the sphere of the common pursuits of life, into that of
Latin: Industria, solertia, atque adeo dexteritas in re aliqua agenda et perficienda, usu quotidiane acquisita

examples.original: Alias quidem artes sub dominio habet.
examples.translation: You see in her the skilled artisan of life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nulla sine motu ars, nulla mutatio est.
examples.translation: There is no art without motion, no change of any kind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Malis artibus popularis favor quaeritur.
examples.translation: It takes trickery to win popular approval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to give back, return, restore
Latin: Retro dare
Latin: Referre seu repetere quae audita sunt

examples.original: Unus tamen ex omnibus redditur;
examples.translation: Yet out of the many only one voice results.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Redditus Cadio Rufo, Pedio Blaeso, Saevino P .
examples.translation: Cadius Rufus, Pedius Blaesus, and Saevinus P. . .
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ingratus est, qui beneficium reddit sine usura.
examples.translation: A man is an ingrate if he repays a favour without interest.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the heads or presidents of the ten decuriae which usually formed the senate in an Italian city or Roman colony (afterwards called decaproti, v. h. v.)
Latin: Novem et alius. Numerus X
Latin: Novem et alius

examples.original: Quinctius sexto decimo die dictatura in sex menses accepta se abdicavit.
examples.translation: On the sixteenth day Quinctius surrendered the dictatorship which he had received for six months.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Septimam decimam cohortem e colonia Ostiensi in urbem acciri Otho iusserat;
examples.translation: Otho had given orders that the Seventeenth cohort be brought from the colony of Ostia to Rome.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Vixit annis viginti novem, imperavit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.
examples.translation: He lived twenty-nine years and ruled three years, ten months and eight days.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: near, hard by, at hand

examples.original: In castris tiro etiam tum propter nimiam vini aviditatem pro Tiberio ”Biberius,” pro Claudio ”Caldius,” pro Nerone ”Mero” vocabatur.
examples.translation: Even at the outset of his military career his excessive love of wine gave him the name of Biberius, instead of Tiberius, Caldius for Claudius, and Mero for Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ex quo intellegitur nec intemperantiam propter se esse fugiendam, temperantiamque expetendam non quia voluptates fugiat sed quia maiores consequatur.
examples.translation: This clearly proves that Intemperance is not undesirable for its own sake, while Temperance is desirable not because it renounces pleasures, but because it procures greater pleasures.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Qui cum propter siccitates paludum quo se reciperent non haberent, quo perfugio superiore anno erant usi, omnes fere in potestatem L. Labieni pervenerunt.
examples.translation: The enemy had no place of retreat, by reason of the dryness of the marshes, their refuge in the previous year; almost all of them, therefore, came and surrendered to Labienus.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: no man, no one, nobody: quem nemo ferro potuit superare nec auro, Enn. ap.
Latin: Nullus homo

examples.original: Quem libenter cenasse nemo negat.
examples.translation: No one will deny that he dined pleasantly.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Neminem exsulum nisi ex senatus auctoritate restituit.
examples.translation: He recalled no one from exile except with the approval of the senate.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ait enim Ennius neminem potuisse Scipioni neque civem neque hostem reddere operae pretium.
examples.translation: For Ennius must mean that neither friend nor foe could pay Scipio a reward worthy of his efforts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: earlier, before, previously, first
Latin: (indicans ante aliquam rem)

examples.original: Ceterum et prioribus civium bellis par scelus inciderat.
examples.translation: And yet a similar crime had happened in civil war before.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Tenetur in priore animali, in aliud animal transire ei non licet;
examples.translation: The soul is kept within the first-named being, and cannot cross over into another;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ut levior labor iudicantibus foret, ad quattuor prioris quintam decuriam addidit.
examples.translation: To lighten the labour of the jurors, he added a fifth division to the previous four.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: first in time or order (syn. primus).—
Latin: Primus
Latin: Homo primo statu

examples.original: Quid sibi istud principium velit quaeris?
examples.translation: Do you ask me what this preamble means?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sedulius, dux et princeps Lemovicum, occiditur;
examples.translation: Sedulius, commander and chief of the Lemovices, was killed;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ac ne principum quidem virorum insectatione abstinuit;
examples.translation: He did not even refrain from gibes at men of distinction;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: the mind, disposition; the heart, soul (class.).

examples.original: Quid autem id erit, nisi ut te exhorter ad bonam mentem?
examples.translation: And what shall this ”something” be, if not an exhortation to soundness of mind?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie.
examples.translation: The evil joys of the mind,c his words are eloquent, but not strictly appropriate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Prodigii ea res loco habita captisque magis mentibus quam consceleratis similis visa;
examples.translation: Their act was regarded as a prodigy, and suggested madness rather than felonious intent.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to feed, to nourish, support, sustain, maintain
Latin: Alimenta praebere
Latin: Nutrire
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; ălŭi, altum, and ălĭtum, 3

examples.original: Non avis utiliter viscatis effugit alis;
examples.translation: The bird cannot make good its escape when once its wings are limed;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid ista, quae nos circumstant, alunt, sustinent?
examples.translation: What becomes of all these things that surround us, support us, sustain us?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Colle tumet modico lenique excrevit in altum Pingue solum tumulo;
examples.translation: The fertile land rises in a hill of moderate height and ascends with easy slope;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: territory, district, domain, the whole of the soil belonging to a community
Latin: Fundus
Latin: Terra

examples.original: Hernicis ipsum agerque dono datus.
examples.translation: The town itself and its territory were given to the Hernici.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Volscis devictis Veliternus ager ademptus;
examples.translation: The Volsci, having been conquered, were deprived of the Veliternian land;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Agrorum atque vicorum populatione non contentus in ipsa Numidiae capita impetum fecit;
examples.translation: Not content with laying waste the fields and villages, he attacked the principal cities of Numidia.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: hope (the predom. signif. of the word; syn. exspectatio).

examples.original: Ne nimium in metu alieno spei ponerent;
examples.translation: Let them not trust too much to other men’s fears;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: His ac talibus inter spem metumque iactatum spes vicit.
examples.translation: These considerations and others like them made him waver between hope and fear;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ab hac spe repulsi Nervii vallo pedum ix et fossa pedum xv hiberna cingunt.
examples.translation: Foiled of this hope, the Nervii encompassed the station with a rampart nine feet high and a trench fifteen feet wide.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a brother.
Latin: Vir qui eosdem patrem matremque quam quisquam habet (frater germanus), vel solummodo aut matrem (frater uterinus) aut patrem (frater consanguineus)
Latin: fratrum nomine veniunt etiam sorores, quum simul enumerantur
entries.etymology: From PIE *bʰréh₂tēr 'brother'; English 'brother' is a cognate.

examples.original: Hoc mihi cum tuo fratre convenit.
examples.translation: On this your cousin and I are agreed.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sosippus et Philocrates fratres sunt Agyrinenses.
examples.translation: There are two brothers belonging to Agyrium, named Sosippus and Philocrates.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vitelliis Aquiliisque fratribus primo commissa res est.
examples.translation: The brothers Vitellii and Aquilii were the first to be entrusted with the project.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: at the same time, together, at once, as soon as.
Latin: Eodem tempore, una

examples.original: Etiam per provincias edicta dimisit, auctor in singulis universisque conspirandi simul et ut qua posset quisque opera communem causam iuvarent.
examples.translation: He also sent proclamations broadcast throughout the province, urging all men individually and collectively to join the revolution and aid the common cause in every possible way.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Huius belli gesta multi memoriae prodiderunt, sed ex iis duo, qui cum eo in castris fuerunt simulque vixerunt, quam diu fortuna passa est, Silenus et Sosylus Lacedaemonius.
examples.translation: Hannibal’s deeds of arms have been recorded by many writers, among them two men who were with him in camp and lived with him so long as fortune allowed, Silenus and Sosylus of Lacedaemon.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

examples.original: Gaio et Lucio intra triennium defunctis adoptatur ab Augusto simul cum fratre eorum M. Agrippa, coactus prius ipse Germanicum fratris sui filium adoptare.
examples.translation: When Gaius and Lucius died within three years, he was adopted by Augustus along with their brother Marcus Agrippa, being himself first compelled to adopt his nephew Germanicus.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to assent
Latin: Ita dicere

examples.original: Et ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina.
examples.translation: And you aver that if a single letter be altered, the whole system will totter.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ex ea difficultate illae ’fallaciloquae,’ ut ait Attius, ’malitiae,’ natae sunt.
examples.translation: This is the difficulty that gave birth to those ’base conceits deceitful-tongued,’ as Attius has it.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Scholam eius claros quoque viros frequentasse aiunt, in iis M. Ciceronem, etiam cum praetura fungeretur.
examples.translation: They say also that distinguished men attended his school, including Cicero even while he was praetor.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: a command, order, direction.
Latin: Imperatum; quod imperatum est
Latin: civitas (apud Benedictum de Spinoza)

examples.original: Si imperio proficitur, et admonitione;
examples.translation: If commands are helpful, so is advice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is A. Postumium Tubertum, socerum suum, severissimi imperii virum, dictatorem dixit;
examples.translation: He appointed Aulus Postumius Tubertus, his father-in-law, a man of the sternest authority;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hominem esse barbarum, iracundum, temerarium: non posse eius imperia diutius sustinere.
examples.translation: He is a passionate, a reckless barbarian: we can endure his tyrannies no longer.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to strike down, strike to the ground; to beat, smash, crush.
Latin: Cadere; obire; perdi

examples.original: Turnus Herdonius per Tarquinium occisus.
examples.translation: Turnus Herdonius killed by the machinations of Tarquinius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Angustissimum habet dies gyrum, sed et hic ab initio ad exitum venit, ab ortu ad occasum.
examples.translation: The smallest circle of all is the day; but even a day has its beginning and its ending, its sunrise and its sunset.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ceterum id quoque ad gloriam accessit quod cum illo simul iusta ac legitima regna occiderunt.
examples.translation: But there was this to enhance his renown, that just and lawful kingship perished with him.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: start

examples.original: Caesarem arbitrari profectum in Italiam;
examples.translation: He believed that Caesar had started for Italy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Negabat igitur ullam esse artem quae ipsa a se proficisceretur;
examples.translation: He then pointed out that no science or art can supply its own starting-point;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ipse ad vastandos depopulandosque fines Ambiorigis proficiscitur;
examples.translation: He himself moved off to devastate and plunder the country of Ambiorix;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: as if, just as, as it were (cf.: veluti, sicuti, tamquam): modo introii.
Latin: sicut,veluti

examples.original: Capiti Papiae Poppaeae legis a Tiberio Caesare, quasi sexagenarii generare non possent, addito obrogavit.
examples.translation: He annulled a clause added to the lex Papia Poppaea by Tiberius, implying that men of sixty could not beget children.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Persius Lives of Illustrious Men ut quasi finitus esset. Leviter correxit Cornutus et Caesio Basso petenti, ut ipse ederet, tradidit edendum.
examples.translation: Cornutus made some slight corrections, and on the request of Caesius Bassus that he might publish it, turned it over to him for that purpose.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Expugnatus autem a quadam, quasi amore suo deperiret, cum perductae pro concubitu sestertia quadringenta donasset, admonente dispensatore, quem ad modum summam rationibus vellet inferri: ”Vespasiano,” inquit, ”adamato.” XXIII.
examples.translation: Being asked by his steward how he would have the sum entered in his accounts, he replied: ”To a passion for Vespasian.” XXIII.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: in that place, there, =
Latin: non hic, sed ibi
Latin: non hodie, sed ibi

examples.original: Sunt qui tradant, ob infamiam quandam eum in Sardiniam secessisse ibique diem obisse.
examples.translation: Some write that because of some disgrace he retired to Sardinia and there died.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Is ita cum Caesare egit: Si pacem populus Romanus cum Helvetiis faceret, in eam partem ituros atque ibi futuros Helvetios, ubi eos Caesar constituisset atque esse voluisset;
examples.translation: He treated with Caesar as follows: If the Roman people would make peace with the Helvetii, they would go whither and abide where Caesar should determine and desire;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Eo anno C. Furius Paculus et M. Geganius Macerinus censores villam publicam in campo Martio probaverunt, ibique primum census populi est actus.
examples.translation: In that year Gaius Furius Paculus and Marcus Geganius Macerinus the censors approved a public building erected in the Campus Martius, and the census of the people was taken there for the first time.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to cultivate, till, tend, take care of a field, garden, etc. (freq. in all per. and species of composition).

examples.original: Coluit ut patrem Servilium Nonianum.
examples.translation: Servilius Nonianus he revered as a father.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Primus est deorum cultus deos credere;
examples.translation: The first way to worship the gods is to believe in the gods;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed ut sit, etiamne post mortem coletur?
examples.translation: But even granting birthdays, is a person’s birthday to be observed when he is dead?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a speaking, speech, discourse, language
Latin: Compositum ex pluribus dictionibus, seu vocibus, quo homines animi sui sensa exprimunt
Latin: ōrāti|ō, -ōnis fem

examples.original: Hac oratione habita concilium dimisit.
examples.translation: With this speech he dissolved the convention.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Oratio me istius philosophi non offendit;
examples.translation: With your master’s style I have no fault to find.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ea scientia et verborum vis et natura orationis et consequentium repugnantiumve ratio potest perspici;
examples.translation: This sciencea explains to us the meaning of terms, the nature of predication, and the law of consistency and contradiction;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: fire
Latin: Evolutio lucis calorisque in combustione corporum; combustio

examples.original: Quod ubi animadvertit Camillus, ignem in obiectam saepem coici iussit;
examples.translation: On perceiving this, Camillus ordered his men to throw fire on the barrier.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Miramur animalia quaedam, quae per medios ignes sine noxa corporum transeant;
examples.translation: We marvel at certain animals because they can pass through fire and suffer no bodily harm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Infelix gemino cecidit prope Pergamon igni, Et paene est alio Troia cremata rogo.
examples.translation: All but twice in the flames unhappy Pergamum perished Troy on a second pyre narrowly failed of her doom.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: to keep straight or from going wrong, to lead straight; to guide, conduct, direct (freq. and class.; syn.: guberno, moderor).

examples.original: Iam regi leges, non regere.
examples.translation: The laws were no longer in control, but were themselves controlled.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Recto tibi invictoque moriendum est.
examples.translation: You must die erect and unyielding.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nobis aliter videtur; recte secusne, postea;
examples.translation: We think otherwise—whether rightly or wrongly, I will consider later;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a master
Latin: Erus, dux, princeps
entries.etymology: From domus 'house'; the master is literally the head of the household.

examples.original: Dominus omnium est, supra omnia est;
examples.translation: It is superior to all, monarch of all it surveys;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Reliqua vendita, quibus domini non exstitere.
examples.translation: That the consul had earned a triumph all agreed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quam stultum est aetatem disponere ne crastini quidem dominum!
examples.translation: O what madness it is to plot out far-reaching hopes!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Put once, preserving the conditional signif. of the si (cf., on the other hand, infra, II. B. 2.).
Latin: ( ) vel si (c. disiunctiva conditionalis)
Latin: Vel, aut (c. disiunctiva dubitativa)

examples.original: Sive enim non respuit, humanitate eius inritamur, sive contempsit, superbia accendimur.
examples.translation: If our love be not spurned, we are excited by its kindness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ergo et supra humana est et par sibi in omni statu rerum, sive secundo cursu vita procedit, sive fluctuatur et it per adversa ac difficilia;
examples.translation: He is therefore above earthly things, equal to himself under all conditions,—whether the current of life runs free, or whether he is tossed and travels on troubled and desperate seas;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec vero sive a meo sensu post mortem afutura est, sive, ut sapientissimi homines putaverunt, ad aliquam mei partem pertinebit, nunc quidem certe cogitatione quadam speque delector.
examples.translation: Be that as it may, now at any rate I find satisfaction in the thought and in the hope.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a way of thinking, opinion, judgment, sentiment; a purpose, determination, decision, will, etc.

examples.original: Inter hostes variae fuere sententiae.
examples.translation: The enemy were of several minds.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: De vacuitate doloris eadem sententia erit.
examples.translation: As regards freedom from pain her decision will be the same.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nec vero alia sunt quaerenda contra Carneadiam illam sententiam;
examples.translation: Nor need we look for other arguments to refute the opinion of Carneades;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be strong.
Latin: fortis esse
Latin: potestatem habere

examples.original: Nemo per se satis valet ut emergat;
examples.translation: No man by himself has sufficient strength to rise above it;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illo sano ac valente oratio quoque robusta, fortis, virilis est;
examples.translation: When the soul is sound and strong, the style too is vigorous, energetic, manly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non ultra paucos dies quamquam acribus initiis coeptum mendacium valuit.
examples.translation: A deception, which had a lively success at first, prevailed for only a few days.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a horseman, rider.
Latin: Homo qui equitat in equo
Latin: Miles eques

examples.original: Item equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt.
examples.translation: The horsemen of Ariovistus halted at an equal distance.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Peragit concilium Caesar equitesque imperat civitatibus.
examples.translation: Caesar closed the convention, and made requisition of cavalry upon the states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Omnibus idem oculi, par est concordia flendi: Funeris exequiis adsumus omnis eques;
examples.translation: All eyes are the same, there is an equal harmony of weeping;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Favor which one finds with others, esteem, regard, liking, love, friendship (syn. favor)
Latin: Favor

examples.original: Quanta esset cum gratia auctoritas!
examples.translation: What a wonderful combination of sweetness and power!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Gratiae intercessoribus ab senatu actae.
examples.translation: The thanks of the senate were voted the protesters.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Votorum tuorum veterum licet dis gratiam facias, alia de integro suscipe;
examples.translation: As for your former prayers, you may dispense the gods from answering them; offer new prayers;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to please, to be pleasing or agreeable, to be welcome, acceptable, to satisfy (class.).
Latin: Iucundus esse, gaudio esse
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n.; cŭi and cĭtus, cĭtum, 2

examples.original: Uni Fidenatium populo rebellare placuit;
examples.translation: Only the people of Fidenae voted to renew the war;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Placebat Valerium Horatiumque ire in Aventinum.
examples.translation: It was decided that Valerius and Horatius should go to the Aventine.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec est, quare hoc inter nostra placita mireris;
examples.translation: You need not wonder that this is one of our principles;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a. [mora].

examples.original: Alioqui quid in mora est?
examples.translation: At any rate, what is there to hinder?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed nunc quoque non moremur.
examples.translation: But even now let us have no delay.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In mores fortuna ius non habet.
examples.translation: Fortune has no jurisdiction over character.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to give up, hand over, deliver, transmit, surrender, consign (syn.: dedo, remitto).

examples.original: Has ille litteras ephoris tradidit.
examples.translation: This letter the young man handed over to the ephors.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Qua re impetrata arma tradere iussi faciunt.
examples.translation: Their request was granted, and they proceeded to deliver up their arms as ordered.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quem Dion adeo admiratus est atque adamavit, ut se ei totum traderet.
examples.translation: Him Dion so admired and loved that he devoted himself to him heart and soul.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Dion

definitions: English: approach a person or thing (syn.: accedo, aggredior, advenio, appeto).
Latin: Hactenus
Latin: Tantus, quoque
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ĭī, and rarely īvi, ĭtum; 4

examples.original: Habes aditum mansurae in saecula famae.
examples.translation: Here is your opportunity for undying fame.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Simul ac potestas primum data est, adeunt hi quos dixi.
examples.translation: As soon as they were allowed, the gentlemen I have named approached the woman.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mihi crede, Lucili, adeo mors timenda non est, ut beneficio eius nihil timendum sit.
examples.translation: Believe me, Lucilius; death is so little to be feared that through its good offices nothing is to be feared.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to make or get ready, to prepare, furnish
Latin: Cum consilio aliquid facere ut tempore futuro praesto adsit

examples.original: Si rectae sunt, et pares sunt.
examples.translation: If they are right, they are also equal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Poteram tecum hac Maecenatis sententia parem facere rationem.
examples.translation: This saying of Maecenas’s might have squared my account with you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: A quo enim non prope est, parata omnibus locis omnibusque momentis?
examples.translation: It is ready for us in all places and at all times.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to deceive, trick, dupe, cheat, disappoint (freq. and class.; syn.: decipio, impono, frustror, circumvenio, emungo, fraudo).

examples.original: Nullus enim terminus falso est.
examples.translation: The false has no limits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Primum quis coegit eos falsum putare?
examples.translation: In the first place, who has forced them to form a mistaken judgement?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non est autem libertas nihil pati, fallimur;
examples.translation: But not to put up with anything is not liberty;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: from which place, whence.
Latin: Indicat locum a quo aliquid venit

examples.original: Quae scribis, unde veniant, scio;
examples.translation: I understand the feelings which prompt your words;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Reliqui se in castra recipiunt unde erant egressi.
examples.translation: The remainder retired to the camp from which they had marched out.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Unde existimo nonnullos tradere ausos, suspectum eum Augusto revocatumque ex provincia et quia cunctaretur, interceptum veneno.
examples.translation: This I have mentioned, rather not to pass it by, than that I think it true or even probable;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a mother
Latin: Femina quae progeniem peperit
entries.etymology: From PIE *méh₂tēr 'mother'; Greek μήτηρ and English 'mother' are cognates.

examples.original: Iunxit parricidio matris amitae necem.
examples.translation: To matricide he added the murder of his aunt.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: At vestrae matres teneras peperere puellas.
examples.translation: But your mothers have borne delicate girls.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Omnia ea auctor fuit Cornutus matri eius ut aboleret.
examples.translation: All these Cornutus advised the poet’s mother to destroy.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: toil, exertion (cf.: contentio, opera).
Latin: Actio laborandi
Latin: Quod laborando efficitur

examples.original: Quare enim qui labi coepit, alicubi subsistat?
examples.translation: For how, if one has begun to slip, can one stop at any particular place?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nullum laborem recusant manus, quae ad arma ab aratro transferuntur;
examples.translation: The hand which turns from the plough to the sword never objects to toil;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam ibi sunt, unde non est retro lapsus, sed hoc illis de se nondum liquet;
examples.translation: They have already arrived at a point from which there is no slipping back, but they are not yet aware of the fact;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: honor; respect/regard; mark of esteem, reward

examples.original: Ei mihi, non multum carmen honoris habet.
examples.translation: Alas, a poem is not much honoured.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Memoriae Domiti patris honores maximos habuit.
examples.translation: He paid the highest honours to the memory of his father Domitius.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Tum imperatori exercituique honos suus redditus;
examples.translation: The general and his army then received their meed of honour;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: just so, in like manner, after the same manner, likewise, also

examples.original: Deinde ”Catalepton” et ”Priapea” et ”Epigrammata” et ”Diras,” item ”Cirim” et ”Culicem,” cum esset annorum XVI.
examples.translation: Then he wrote the ”Catalepton,” ”Priapea,” ”Epigrams” and the ”Dirae,” as well as the ”Ciris” and the ”Culex,” when he was sixteen years old.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Munera, quibus a Pompeia Sex. Pompei sorore in Sicilia donatus est, chlamys et fibula, item bullae aureae, durant ostendunturque adhuc Baiis.
examples.translation: The gifts which were given him in Sicily by Pompeia, sister of Sextus Pompeius, a cloak and clasp, as well as studs of gold, are still kept and exhibited at Baiae.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Achaiam, Lyciam, Rhodum, Byzantium, Samum libertate adempta, item Trachiam Ciliciam et Commagenen dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus, in provinciarum formam redegit.
examples.translation: He made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom, and likewise of Trachian Cilicia and Commagene, which up to that time had been ruled by kings.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a citizen
Latin: Homo liber, urbis aut oppidi incola, et eodem cum ceteris iure utens
Latin: incola civitatis

examples.original: Eodem anno census actus novique cives censi.
examples.translation: In this same year the census was taken and new citizens were assessed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ceterum et prioribus civium bellis par scelus inciderat.
examples.translation: And yet a similar crime had happened in civil war before.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Illa modo in ducibus culpa quod ut odio essent civibus fecerant;
examples.translation: The only fault of the generals was that they had made the citizens detest them;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to drive together to one point, to collect, compress, crowd, bring, or urge together, to assemble, gather together (class. and very freq.; syn.: colligo, congrego)
Latin: colligo verbi gratia pecus

examples.original: Quibus rebus coacti Menapii legatos ad eum pacis petendae causa mittunt.
examples.translation: This action obliged the Menapii to send deputies to him to seek for peace.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Itaque non ego vobis ut indicem praedas vestras, sed vos id cogendi estis ut in medium proferatis.”
examples.translation: And so it is not I that must be forced to tell of your plunder, but you that must be compelled to give it up.”
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Caesar rursus ad vexandos hostes profectus magno coacto numero ex finitimis civitatibus in omnes partes dimittit.
examples.translation: Caesar marched forth again to harass the enemy, and, collecting a great host from the neighbouring states, he sent them off in every direction.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to say no, to deny, refuse (opp. ajo, to say yes; v. ajo; cf.: abnuo, diffiteor, infitior).

examples.original: Quem libenter cenasse nemo negat.
examples.translation: No one will deny that he dined pleasantly.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sevius Nicanor Marci libertus negabit;
examples.translation: Sevius Nicanor, the freedman of Marcus, may deny this;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Negabat igitur ullam esse artem quae ipsa a se proficisceretur;
examples.translation: He then pointed out that no science or art can supply its own starting-point;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: at no time, never
Latin: nullo tempore
Latin: non

examples.original: Si enim ad populum me vocas, eum qui ita sit affectus beatum esse numquam probabis;
examples.translation: Call me before a jury of ordinary people, and you will never persuade them that the man so afflicted is happy;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nihil habent quo tegantur, ad ictum totis corporibus expositi numquam frustra manum mittunt.
examples.translation: They are exposed to blows at all points, and no one ever strikes in vain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erant Menapii propinqui Eburonum finibus, perpetuis paludibus silvisque muniti, qui uni ex Gallia de pace ad Caesarem legatos numquam miserant.
examples.translation: There were the Menapii, near the borders of the Eburones, defended by continuous marshes and forests; and they alone in Gaul had never sent deputies to Caesar to treat of peace.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a Carthaginian

examples.original: Haec poena apud eos est gravissima.
examples.translation: Those that are so banned are reckoned as impious and criminal;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Servatur poenas in aperta luce daturus;
examples.translation: So he was spared, to suffer in the light of day;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Atilius Regulus cos. victis navali proelio Poenis in Africam traiecit.
examples.translation: Atilius Regulus the consul, having beaten the Carthaginians in a naval battle, crossed into Africa.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: come back; to turn back, re turn, turn around (freq. and class.; syn revertor).
Latin: Quasi retro ire, reverti
Latin: Reverti

examples.original: Nec victoriam sperant nec reditum.
examples.translation: They have no hope of victory, no hope of returning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Excutit redeuntem natura sicut intrantem.
examples.translation: You may take away no more than you brought in;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et rediere omnes Bononiam, rursus consiliaturi;
examples.translation: They all returned to Bononia to take counsel together again there;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: blood
Latin: Fluidum vitale quae per systema vasculare animalium fluit
Latin: caedes et mors

examples.original: Non fuit illi opus ferro, non sanguine;
examples.translation: No need had he of sword or of bloodshed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Plus praedae ac sanguinis Caecina hausit.
examples.translation: Caecina gained even more booty and shed more blood.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Coit area belli: Hic alitur sanguis terras fluxurus in omnes, Hic et Thessalicae clades Libycaeque tenentur;
examples.translation: The field of war was now contracted; here is preserved the blood that will flow hereafter over every land;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to say something in the ear, softly or in secret, to whisper in the ear: in aurem Pontius, Scipio, inquit, vide quid agas
Latin: Membrum auditus

examples.original: Nulla ad aures nostras vox inpune perfertur;
examples.translation: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed ambitionem scriptoris facile averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur;
examples.translation: So between the hostility of the one class and the servility of the other, posterity was disregarded.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sassiam in matrimonium ducere, Habiti matrem, illam, cuius virum A. Aurium occiderat, concupivit.
examples.translation: He conceived the desire of marrying Sassia, Habitus’s mother, her whose husband, Aulus Aurius, he had murdered.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: keep together.
Latin: Constringere aliquid
Latin: Conservāre
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; tĭnŭi, tentum, 2

examples.original: Non diutius se in Hernico hostis continuit;
examples.translation: No longer did the enemy confine themselves to the country of the Hernici;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Naturales divitias dixit parabiles esse quod parvo esset natura contenta.
examples.translation: He said that natural wealth is easily won, because nature is satisfied with little.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et hi quidem ita non sola virtute finem bonorum contineri putant, ut rebus tamen omnibus virtutem anteponant;
examples.translation: And these, though holding that the End of Goods is not limited to virtue alone, yet rate virtue higher than all other things;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a male yolk, i. e. which would produce a male chick
Latin: Homo masculus
Latin: Bestia mascula, animal masculum

examples.original: Navis, quae in flumine magna est, in mari parvula est.
examples.translation: A ship which looms large in the river seems tiny when on the ocean.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Mancino deinde consule terra marique fervebat obsidio.
examples.translation: The harbours were blocked up;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Libidinis in feminas profusissimae, marum omnino expers.
examples.translation: He was immoderate in his passion for women, but wholly disinterested in male partners.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: O! (vocative interjection)
Latin: (interjectio vocativa)
entries.grammaticalClass: the fourteenth letter of the Latin alphabet
principalParts: the fourteenth letter of the Latin alphabet
entries.etymology: A natural exclamation of address, not derived from a lexical root.

examples.original: O lapathe, ut iactare nec es satis cognitus qui sis!
examples.translation: Dinner of herbs, how all the earth Derides thee and ignores thy worth!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: O quando ille veniet dies, quo nemo in honorem tuum mentiatur!
examples.translation: O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O felicem, qui sic aliquem vereri potest, ut ad memoriam quoque eius se conponat atque ordinet!
examples.translation: And happy also is he who can so revere a man as to calm and regulate himself by calling him to mind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A province, i. e. a territory out of Italy, acquired by the Romans (chiefly by conquest), and brought under Roman government; freq
Latin: Natio vel regio, plus minusve remotus a Roma, sub gubernatione Romana; natio victa extra Italiam
Latin: Divisio similis regni imperiive

examples.original: Tu nunc in provincia, licet contemnas ipse te, magnus es.
examples.translation: So you in your provinceb are really of importance, though you scorn yourself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quam provinciam tenuistis a praedonibus liberam per hosce annos?
examples.translation: What province did you keep free from the pirates during those years?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ad cuius spectaculum commeare in urbem non solum praesidibus provinciarum permisit, verum etiam exsulibus quibusdam;
examples.translation: To witness the sight he allowed not only the governors of the provinces to come to Rome, but even some of the exiles;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to look or gaze upon, to watch, view; hence, pregn.

examples.original: Fata vetant, murique vicem Fortuna tuetur.
examples.translation: Fate is against them, and Fortune performs the office of a wall.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quaesita enim virtus est non quae relinqueret naturam sed quae tueretur;
examples.translation: For we started to look for a virtue that should protect, not abandon, nature;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid tuti superest, cum nominis extat adulter, Et credi quod non contigit esse, cupit?
examples.translation: What remains secure, when the dishonourer of her name abides, and would have what ne’er befell believed?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: The head, of men and animals
Latin: Pars anterior vel superior animalis, qui cerebrum et os continet
Latin: Pars summa aut extrema rei, praesertim

examples.original: I, caput obnube liberatoris urbis huius;
examples.translation: Go, veil the head of the liberator of this city!
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sic a iudicio capitis maxima discessit gloria.
examples.translation: Thus from a capital charge he gained the greatest glory.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

examples.original: Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lugerent.
examples.translation: The relatives of the victims were forbidden to mourn for them.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to deserve, merit, to be entitled to, be worthy of a thing; constr. with

examples.original: Equites tum primum equis suis mereri coeperunt.
examples.translation: The cavalry began then for the first time to serve on their own mounts.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Primum stipendium meruit annorum decem septemque.
examples.translation: He served his first campaign at the age of seventeen.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Cato

examples.original: Ex quibus Appius, qui praecipuam poenam meruerat, in carcerem coniectus est;
examples.translation: Of these, Appius, who had been most guilty, was flung into prison;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a boundary, limit, border, = terminus
Latin: Terminus; linea, res, vel tempus aliquid definiens
Latin: regio quae certis finibus continetur

examples.original: In utroque finis dolendi est.
examples.translation: In either case there is an end of pain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc felicitatem suam fine designat.
examples.translation: Such are the bounds which he sets to his own happiness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Finisque ille tam effuse evagandi Etruscis fuit.
examples.translation: This was the last time the Etruscans roamed so far afield.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to promise a thing in return for something else; to offer or present in return. So, only in a few examples, the phrase par pari

examples.original: Ad haec quae visum est Caesar respondit;
examples.translation: To this Caesar replied as seemed good;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum Sabinus respondisset: ”Et quomodo possum?
examples.translation: Sabinus answered: ”How can I?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Adiuro te per Christum, ut ad ista respondeas.
examples.translation: I adjure you by Christ to reply to what I have written.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: whoever, whosoever, whatever, whatsoever, every one who, each, every, all: hostem qui feriet, mihi erit Carthaginiensis, Quisquis erit, Enn. ap.
Latin: Quem velis

examples.original: In integrum restituit quidquid erraverat;
examples.translation: He had wiped out all his previous mistakes;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quicquid ante pugnatum est, misericordia fuit.
examples.translation: The previous combats were the essence of compassion;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quisquis dixit ”vixi,” cotidie ad lucrum surgit.
examples.translation: When a man has said: ”have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: so as, just as, as.

examples.original: Edidit autem auctore Augusto Varius, sed summatim emendata, ut qui versus etiam inperfectos sicut erant reliquerit;
examples.translation: However, Varius published the ”Aeneid” at Augustus’ request, making only a few slight corrections, and even leaving the incomplete lines just as they were.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Prope est a timente, qui fatum segnis expectat, sicut ille ultra modum deditus vino est, qui amphoram exiccat et faecem quoque exorbet.
examples.translation: A man who sluggishly awaits his fate is almost a coward, just as he is immoderately given to wine who drains the jar dry and sucks up even the dregs.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ego autem oratorem, sicut locupletem ac lautum patrem familiae, non eo tantum volo tecto tegi quod imbrem ac ventum arceat, sed etiam quod visum et oculos delectet;
examples.translation: My own view is that the orator, like a prosperous and well-found householder, ought to live in a house that is not only wind and weather proof, but pleasing also to the eye;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: To take back, get back, bring back; to retake, regain, recover.
Latin: iterum Sumere

examples.original: Non potest recipere rationem, non potest nutrire.
examples.translation: He cannot receive reason, nor can he nourish it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Reliqui se in castra recipiunt unde erant egressi.
examples.translation: The remainder retired to the camp from which they had marched out.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ex plurimis maximisque honoribus praeter paucos et modicos non recepit.
examples.translation: Of many high honours he accepted only a few of the more modest.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: then, at that time; but in ante-class. and class. prose tunc is always emphatic, and generally refers to a point of time. In post-Aug. style tunc freq
Latin: Isto tempore

examples.original: Scire debet quid petat ille, qui sagittam vult mittere, et tunc derigere ac moderari manu telum.
examples.translation: The archer must know what he is seeking to hit; then he must aim and control the weapon by his skill.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potest et qui ebrius est, tunc primum esse nec habere hoc vitium, et qui ebriosus est, saepe extra ebrietatem esse.
examples.translation: He who is actually drunk may be in this state for the first time and may not have the habit, while the drunkard is often free from drunkenness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Scribonius mathematicus praeclara spopondit, etiam regnaturum quandoque, sed sine regio insigni, ignota scilicet tunc adhuc Caesarum potestate.
examples.translation: Tiberiusinfancy the astrologer Scribonius promised him an illustrious career and even that he would one day be king, but without the crown of royalty;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a number.
Latin: Summa numeralis (quantitatis personarum vel rerum); summarium, e.g. Unus, duo, tres etc
Latin: Magnitudo

examples.original: Numera quam multa in ista defensione falsa sint, Piso.
examples.translation: Count the flaws in that argument, Piso!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ab eis qui emerant capitum numerus ad eum relatus est milium quinquaginta trium.
examples.translation: The purchasers furnished a return to him of three-and-fifty thousand persons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Callimachi numeris non est dicendus Achilles, Cydippe non est oris, Homere, tui.
examples.translation: Achilles must not be told of in the numbers of Callimachus; Cydippe suits not thy utterance, Homer.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: that is above, upper, higher: inferus an superus tibi fert deus funera, Liv. And. ap.
Latin: Qui supra est

examples.original: Duo illa bona superiora diversa sunt.
examples.translation: The two kinds of goods which are of a higher order are different;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Milites e loco superiore pilis missis facile hostium phalangem perfregerunt.
examples.translation: Then after a speech to encourage his troops he joined battle.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Etiamnunc est aliquid superius quam corpus. Dicimus enim quaedam corporalia esse, quaedam incorporalia.
examples.translation: What, then, will be the term from which these things are derived?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: that extends or lies in a horizontal direction, plain, even, level, flat
Latin: Planus
Latin: Par, aequalis

examples.original: Omnes qui non sint sapientes aeque miseros esse;
examples.translation: That those who are not wise are all equally wretched;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Aequi se in oppida receperunt murisque se tenebant.
examples.translation: The Aequi retired to their towns and kept within their walls.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et hoc, quod dico ”possit,” tale est: amissum aequo animo fert.
examples.translation: When I say ”can,” I mean this: he endures the loss of a friend with equanimity.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Greek
Latin: Qui ad linguam Graecorum pertinet
Latin: De Graecia, populo vel lingua sua

examples.original: Cum Graecis a Camillo nulla memorabilis gesta res;
examples.translation: With the Greeks, Camillus fought no memorable action;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Atque hoc Sosylo Hannibal litterarum Graecarum usus est doctore.
examples.translation: And it was this Sosylus whom Hannibal employed as his teacher of Greek.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

examples.original: Eodem anno a Campanis Cumae, quam Graeci tum urbem tenebant, capiuntur.
examples.translation: In this same year Cumae, a city which the Greeks then held, was captured by the Campanians.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: from this place. hence.
Latin: E hic

examples.original: Hinc celeriter deiecti se in signa manipulosque coniciunt: eo magis timidos perterrent milites.
examples.translation: They were speedily hurled down from thence, and ran headlong into the company formations, scaring the soldiers into greater alarm.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum Ciceronis librum de Re Publica prendit hinc philologus aliquis,hinc grammaticus,hinc philosophiae deditus, alius alio curam suam mittit.
examples.translation: When Cicero’s book On the State is opened by a philologist, a scholar, or a follower of philosophy, each man pursues his investigation in his own way.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nationes aliquas occupavit Vitellius, imaginem quandam exercitus habet, senatus nobiscum est: sic fit ut hinc res publica, inde hostes rei publicae constiterint.
examples.translation: Vitellius has won over some peoples; he has a certain shadow of an army, but the senate is with us.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to teach, instruct, inform, show, tell, etc. (for syn. cf.: edoceo, perdoceo, erudio, praecipio, instituo).
Latin: Certiorem facere de rebus scientificis, de artibus

examples.original: Postquam docti prodierunt, boni desunt.
examples.translation: When savants have appeared, sages have become rare.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Docet quomodo nihil perdam ex finibus meis;
examples.translation: The mathematician teaches me how I may lose none of my boundaries;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed nec hae nec illae docent aluntve virtutem.
examples.translation: But neither the new system nor the old teaches or nourishes virtue.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a precious stone unknown to us

examples.original: Hoc denique tibi circa mortis diem praesta: moriantur ante te vitia.
examples.translation: Of this one thing make sure against your dying day,—let your faults die before you die.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Flaminius censor viam Flaminiam muniit et circum Flaminium exstruxit.
examples.translation: The censor Gaius Flaminius built the Flaminian Way and the Flaminian Circus.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ardet et adsuetas Circe decurrit ad artes, Nec tamen est illis adtenuatus amor.
examples.translation: Circe aflame has recourse to her wonted arts, yet not by them is her passion calmed.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a regular row, line, or
Latin: Series rerum in sua dispositione recta
Latin: taxon. Collectio familiarum similium, vicissim sub classe collecta

examples.original: Ordinem vitae hunc fere tenuit.
examples.translation: This was in general his manner of life.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Simili superbia violentiaque ceteros tractavit ordines.
examples.translation: He treated the other orders with like insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Haec rursus patienda manent, hoc ordine belli Ibitur, hic stabit civilibus exitus armis.
examples.translation: Those same woes we must endure again; through that sequence of warfare we must pass;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: tempp. perff. contr. cognosti
Latin: Persōnam vel rem aliquam nōscere discō, nosco, bene nosco, etiamsi id fiat experientia, sensibus vel quacumque alia externa ratione

examples.original: O lapathe, ut iactare nec es satis cognitus qui sis!
examples.translation: Dinner of herbs, how all the earth Derides thee and ignores thy worth!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum consules in contione pronuntiassent tempus non esse causas cognoscendi;
examples.translation: The consuls announced in the assembly that there was no time to consider excuses;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: His rebus cognitis Caesar summo studio militum ante ortum solis in castra pervenit.
examples.translation: On report of this, Caesar reached the camp before sunrise, by a supreme effort of the troops.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to praise, laud, commend, extol, eulogize, approve (cf.: celebro, praed co).
Latin: Celebrare, extollere

examples.original: O illam mirabilem laudem et singularem!
examples.translation: What wonderful and rare distinction!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nolo nolo laudes, nolo dicas: ”o magnum virum!
examples.translation: He has learned to despise all things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Saepe ab Aristotele, a Theophrasto mirabiliter est laudata per se ipsa rerum scientia;
examples.translation: Aristotle and Theophrastus often and admirably praised knowledge for its own sake;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal (for syn. v paternus).

examples.original: Sed nec populo aut moenibus patriae pepercit.
examples.translation: But he showed no greater mercy to the people or the walls of his capital.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et tua sic latos spargantur membra per agros, Tamquam quae patrias detinuere vias.
examples.translation: And may thy limbs be so scattered o’er the broad fields as those which stayed a father’s march.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: At postquam leges bello siluere coactae, Pellimur e patriis laribus patimurque volentes Exilium;
examples.translation: But now law has been silenced by the constraint of war, and we have been driven from our country.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: tempp. press. only a few times in the ante-class. period, and coepturus

examples.original: Aliter certe Claranum nostrum coepi intueri;
examples.translation: At any rate, I have begun to regard Claranus in a different light;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Deinde ad civitatis vitam reductus ex bene coeptis pauca servavi.
examples.translation: For I had planned my whole life with great resolves.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: I, qua ire coepisti et in isto te vitae habitu conpone placide, non molliter.
examples.translation: Proceed as you have begun, and settle yourself in this way of living, not luxuriously, but calmly.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: peace, concluded between parties at variance, esp. between belligerents; a treaty of peace
Latin: Publica tranquillitas et concordia
Latin: Indutiae; belli absentiae

examples.original: Assyriae paci finem, Fortuna, precamur;
examples.translation: We pray to Fortune that peace with Assyria may end;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Multi enim sunt ex his togatis, quibus pax operosior bello est.
examples.translation: For there are many of our toga-clad citizens to whom peace brings more trouble than war.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eodem die legati ab hostibus missi ad Caesarem de pace venerunt.
examples.translation: On the same day deputies sent by the enemy came to Caesar to treat of peace.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: per synaeresin as one syll.
Latin: quod necesse est, sed non adest

examples.original: At barbaris consilium non defuit.
examples.translation: But the natives were not lacking in resource.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Postquam docti prodierunt, boni desunt.
examples.translation: When savants have appeared, sages have become rare.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tibi des oportet istud bonum, a te petas.
examples.translation: You must give this good to yourself, and seek it from yourself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to lift or take up, to raise, always with the predom. idea of motion upwards or of removal from a former situation.

examples.original: Facilius sustuleris illa quam rexeris.
examples.translation: You can more easily remove than control them.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tollenda est atque extrahenda radicitus.
examples.translation: It ought to be destroyed, uprooted altogether.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quem timorem Caesaris adventus sustulit.
examples.translation: This terror was removed by the arrival of Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: The period of life, time of life, life
Latin: Spatium alicuius vitae, ut, pueritia, adulescentia, etc
Latin: Vita

examples.original: Nulla aetas vacavit a culpa.
examples.translation: No era in history has ever been free from blame.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erat illi et fessa aetate parens;
examples.translation: He had also his mother, who was bowed with years;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Decessit aetatis exactae sub Tiberio.
examples.translation: He died at an advanced age under Tiberius.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: it is necessary, needful, proper, becoming, or reasonable; it behooves; I (thou, he, etc.) must or ought

examples.original: Additum non est; tamen oportebit?
examples.translation: It was not added: shall the point be relevant still?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ideoque illam inplicari non oportet;
examples.translation: We should not, therefore, make that language intricate;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si esset additum, de eo quaeri oporteret.
examples.translation: Had the clause been added, your point would have been a relevant one.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a foot of man or beast.
Latin: Crūris pars terminalis, hominis animalisve; praesertim, pars sub talo; pars animalis in qua nititur dum stat vel movet

examples.original: Fluminis erat altitudo pedum circiter trium.
examples.translation: The depth of the river was about three feet.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Orcus vobis ducit pedes senatum gestu notarat.
examples.translation: Orcus guides your steps, he indicated the senate by a gesture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis.
examples.translation: Read Cicero: his style has unity; it moves with a modulated pace, and is gentle without being degenerate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: rather, more, preferably

examples.original: Potius ergo illa dicantur, turpe esse, viri non esse debilitari dolore, frangi, succumbere.
examples.translation: If that be true, are you not guilty of a crime in advising him to end his life?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cur enim potius Aedui de suo iure et de legibus ad Caesarem disceptatorem, quam Romani ad Aeduos veniant?
examples.translation: Why should the Aedui come to Caesar to decide a question of their own right and law, rather than the Romans to the Aedui?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nec vero audiendus Hieronymus, cui summum bonum est idem quod vos interdum vel potius nimium saepe dicitis, nihil dolere.
examples.translation: Nor yet can we listen to Hieronymus, whose Chief Good is the same as is occasionally, or rather only too frequently, upheld by yourselves, freedom from pain.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: little

examples.original: Pauca mutat, vel plura sane;
examples.translation: He makes a few modifications, or indeed a good many;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Taurus paucissimorum iugerum pascuo impletur;
examples.translation: The bull is filled when he feeds over a few acres;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex plurimis maximisque honoribus praeter paucos et modicos non recepit.
examples.translation: Of many high honours he accepted only a few of the more modest.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: aged
Latin: Magnam aetatem habens, multos annos natus

examples.original: Sic vetere instituto vitae effugit nova pericula.
examples.translation: Thus by the long-standing policy of his life he avoided the new dangers.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Votorum tuorum veterum licet dis gratiam facias, alia de integro suscipe;
examples.translation: As for your former prayers, you may dispense the gods from answering them; offer new prayers;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Corpora si veteres non sic coluere puellae, Nee veteres cultos sic habuere viros;
examples.translation: If women of old did not so cultivate their bodies, the women of old had not lovers so cultivated;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a fault, defect, blemish, imperfection

examples.original: Armis vicit, vitiis victus est.
examples.translation: He conquered with his weapons, but was conquered by his vices.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Decessit autem vitio stomachi anno aetatis XXX.
examples.translation: He died of a stomach trouble in the thirtieth year of his age.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Atqui hoc perspicuum est, vitia alia aliis esse maiora;
examples.translation: Now, that some vices are worse than others is certain;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: kingly government, royal authority, kingship, royalty
Latin: Potestas regis
Latin: Quod rex regit
entries.etymology: Derived from rēx 'king'; the suffix -num forms a noun of office or domain.

examples.original: Ascani regnum Albae et deinceps Silviorum.
examples.translation: Reign of Ascanius, and after him of the Silvii, at Alba.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Patrum interim animos certamen regni ac cupido versabat.
examples.translation: The senators meanwhile were engaged in a struggle for the coveted kingship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ceterum id quoque ad gloriam accessit quod cum illo simul iusta ac legitima regna occiderunt.
examples.translation: But there was this to enhance his renown, that just and lawful kingship perished with him.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: for what reason, wherefore, why, to what purpose, from what motive.

examples.original: Cur deinde Metrodori liberos commendas?
examples.translation: And secondly, why do you provide for the children of Metrodorus?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Tu autem, si tibi illa probabantur, cur non propriis verbis illa tenebas?
examples.translation: If you accepted those views on their merits, why did you not hold them under their own terminology?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et si turpitudinem fugimus in statu et motu corporis, quid est cur pulchritudinem non sequamur?
examples.translation: And if we avoid ugliness in bodily movement and posture, why should we not pursue beauty?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Neutr., to stay, remain anywhere (class.).
Latin: In loco continuare; morari
Latin: durare

examples.original: Reliquum anni quietum ab urbanis motibus et ab externis mansit.
examples.translation: The remainder of the year passed without disturbances in either domestic or foreign relations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad Romuleam urbem hinc eamus, ubi vos labor haud maior, praeda maior manet.”
examples.translation: Let us go from here to the city Romulea, where no greater toil awaits you, but greater booty.”
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Qua sua Penteliden proles est ulta Lycurgum, Haec maneat teli te quoque plaga novi.
examples.translation: As his own offspring was revenged upon Lycurgus, the Pentelid, so may the stroke of a strange weapon await thee also.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English:  particle, why not? wherefore not? (only in exhortation or remonstrance; not in inquiring for a fact; cf.: quidni, cur non).

examples.original: Quin etiam speciem libertatis quandam induxit conservatis senatui ac magistratibus et maiestate pristina et potestate.
