examples.translation: He even introduced a semblance of free government by maintaining the ancient dignity and powers of the senate and the magistrates;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec durare valuit quin de condicionibus continuo tractaret, etiam de Paetinae, quam olim exegerat, deque Lolliae Paulinae, quae C. Caesari nupta fuerat.
examples.translation: Yet he could not refrain from at once planning another match, even with Paetina, whom he had formerly discarded, and with Lollia Paulina, who had been the wife of Gaius Caesar.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nam si est artius, ut ita dicam, holocleros, quid est quod dubitemus, quin per eosdem articulos et gradus producendus sit, per quos frater eius productus sit?
examples.translation: For if he be sound and so to say complete, what reason have we for doubting that he ought to be advanced through the same grades and steps through which his brother has been advanced?
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a trial, experiment, attempt, proof, essay (class.; cf. disorimen).
Latin: quod audetur, experimentum
Latin: damnum pendens
entries.etymology: Probably derived from perītus 'experienced, tested'; the derivation is debated.

examples.original: Atqui pericula contemnit et provocat.
examples.translation: And yet bravery despises and challenges danger.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nullum terrorem externum, nullum periculum esse;
examples.translation: There was no fear of foreign foes, no danger;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ab eo de periculis Ciceronis legionisque cognoscitur.
examples.translation: It was he who brought the information about the dangers of Cicero and the legion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to fear, be afraid of a person or thing; to hesitate, not to venture, not to wish (syn.: vereor, formido, timeo); with

examples.original: Satisne est nobis vos metuendos esse?
examples.translation: Is it not enough that we must fear you?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid autem stultius homine verba metuente?
examples.translation: But what is more foolish than a man afraid of words?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis calcare tuas metuat, salpuga, latebras?
examples.translation: Who would fear to tread on the lair of the salpuga?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a ship (syn.: navigium).
Latin: Vehiculum super aquam navigandi

examples.original: Navis, quae in flumine magna est, in mari parvula est.
examples.translation: A ship which looms large in the river seems tiny when on the ocean.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Gubernaculum, quod alteri navi magnum, alteri exiguum est.
examples.translation: A rudder Which is large for one vessel, is small for another.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Navium magnam copiam ad transportandum exercitum pollicebantur.
examples.translation: They promised a large supply of boats for the transport of his army.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to turn, to turn round or about (syn.: verso, contorqueo).
Latin: Dirigere aliquid versum aliud
Latin: in aliam partem convertere

examples.original: Quod bene vertat, castra Albanos Romanis castris iungere iubet;
examples.translation: He then made preparations to perform, on the morrow, a sacrifice of purification.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Picentibus gratiae actae et magna pars curae patribus ab Etruria in Samnites versa est.
examples.translation: The Picentes were thanked, and the senate’s anxiety was diverted, in great measure, from Etruria to the Samnites.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Commisso proelio diutius nostrorum militum impetum hostes ferre non potuerunt ac terga verterunt.
examples.translation: When battle was joined the enemy, unable to endure for long the attack of our troops, turned and fled.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to conquer, overcome, get the better of, defeat, subdue, vanquish, be victorious, etc. (syn.: supero, debello).
Latin: (Intrans.) in certamine superior esse
Latin: aliquem superare
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; vīci, victum, 3

examples.original: Armis vicit, vitiis victus est.
examples.translation: He conquered with his weapons, but was conquered by his vices.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sapiens facilis victu fuit, quidni?
examples.translation: The wise man was easy-going in his way of living.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Usque adeo miserum est civili vincere bello?
examples.translation: Is it so wretched a fate to be victorious in a civil war?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to save, deliver, keep unharmed, preserve, protect, etc. (very freq. and class.; syn. salvo)
Latin: Salvum et incolumem praestare
Latin: Solicite et diligenter observare oculis

examples.original: Mundus eundem habitum ac modum servat.
examples.translation: The universe keeps the same character, the same limits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Servatur poenas in aperta luce daturus;
examples.translation: So he was spared, to suffer in the light of day;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tu tamen malo serves tua, et bono tempore incipies.
examples.translation: I advise you, however, to keep what is really yours;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: abundant power, wealth, riches, abundance (very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Latin: multitudo, rerum, (etiam pluralis) multitudo militum, massa
Latin: divitia, plenitudo

examples.original: Non facio mei tibi copiam.
examples.translation: I am not at your service.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cuius adventu ab hostibus cognito magnae ex finitimis civitatibus copiae convenerunt.
examples.translation: When the enemy had news of his coming a large force assembled from the neighbouring states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ac statim advenere litterae fusas apud Cremonam Vitelli copias, ipsum in urbe interemptum nuntiantes.
examples.translation: And immediately letters came with the news that Vitellius had been routed at Cremona and the emperor himself slain at Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a child, whether boy or girl
Latin: Mas inter infantiam et adulescentiam
Latin: Servus

examples.original: Puer ipse sororem, Sit modo liber, amat;
examples.translation: The boy himself loves his sister, if only he were free;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ista decent pueros aetate et amore calentes;
examples.translation: Such doings suit lads aflame with youth and love;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non amicam habes, non puerum, qui amicae moveat invidiam;
examples.translation: You have no mistress, no favourite slave to make your mistress envious;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a busying one's self about or application to a thing; assiduity, zeal, eagerness, fondness, inclination, desire, exertion, endeavor, study
Latin: Factum studendi

examples.original: Suo enim quisque studio maxime ducitur.”
examples.translation: For we are all specially influenced by our own favourite study.”
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Studia te tua clarum et nobilem efficient.
examples.translation: It is your own studies that will make you shine and will render you eminent.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Habuit et pingendi fingendique non mediocre studium.
examples.translation: He likewise had no slight interest in painting and sculpture.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a highway, road, path, street.
Latin: Quivis locus, qua hominibus ire licet
Latin: Quivis locus, qua vehicolo seu pedibus seu alia quacumque ratione ire licet
entries.etymology: Often connected with vehō 'carry, convey'; the exact derivation is disputed.

examples.original: Quid horum ad virtutem viam sternit?
examples.translation: But which of these paves the way to virtue?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omne quod est igitur nulla regione viarum finitumst;
examples.translation: The universe then is not limited along any of its paths;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Una ad hanc fert via, et quidem recta; non aberrabis.
examples.translation: There is but one path leading thither, and it is a straight path;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: well
Latin: Bono modo
entries.etymology: Adverb formed from bonus 'good'.

examples.original: Atqui melius fuisset non queri quam vindicari.
examples.translation: Yet surely it were better to have no grievances than to need to seek redress.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Video enim et magnos et eosdem bene longinquos dolores;
examples.translation: For I see pains that are at once severe and considerably prolonged;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De malis autem et bonis ab iis animalibus quae nondum depravata sint ait optime iudicari.
examples.translation: Creatures as yet uncorrupted are according to him the best judges of Good and Evil.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: towards, to (only ante-class.): IS TERTHS DIEBVS OB PORTVM OBVAGVLATVM ITO, let him go before his house to summon him, Fragm. XII. Tab. ap. Paul. ex Fest. s. v. portum, p
Latin: Ante
Latin: Indicans rem vel causam pro qua, vel rationem ab qua, aliquid fit

examples.original: Sunt qui tradant, ob infamiam quandam eum in Sardiniam secessisse ibique diem obisse.
examples.translation: Some write that because of some disgrace he retired to Sardinia and there died.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Cum utraque divortium fecit, sed cum Paetina ex levibus offensis, cum Urgulanilla ob libidinum probra et homicidii suspicionem.
examples.translation: He divorced both these, Paetina for trivial offences, but Urgulanilla because of scandalous lewdness and the suspicion of murder.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Melissus, Spoleti natus ingenuus, sed ob discordiam parentum expositus, cura et industria educatoris sui altiora studia percepit, ac Maecenati pro grammatico muneri datus est.
examples.translation: Nevertheless through the care and devotion of the man who reared him, he received a superior education, and was presented to Maecenas as a grammarian.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to fear, be afraid of, to dread, apprehend; to be afraid or in fear, to be fearful, apprehensive, or anxious; constr. with
Latin: metum aut pavorem cuidam habēre
Latin: metū afficī, haesitāre; verērī

examples.original: Hic, cum quo ludis, timet;
examples.translation: This friend, in whose company you are jesting, is in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non homines timere, non deos;
examples.translation: It means not fearing either men or gods;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non mortem timemus, sed cogitationem mortis.
examples.translation: We do not fear death; we fear the thought of death.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to make out, work out; hence, to bring to pass, to effect, execute, complete, accomplish, make, form (very freq. in all periods and sorts of writing).

examples.original: Quae cum ita sint, effectum est nihil esse malum quod turpe non sit.
examples.translation: The conclusion follows that nothing is evil that is not base.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Id facile effici posse arbitrati sunt, si principes eius ordinis pecunias contulissent.
examples.translation: They thought that their purpose could easily be effected, if the leading men of that order would contribute.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Et quantum quaeque ab nobis res absit, imago efficit ut videamus et internoscere curat;
examples.translation: And the image enables us to see and takes care that we distinguish how far each thing is distant from us;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: A long time, long while, long
Latin: Longum tempus

examples.original: Hominem esse barbarum, iracundum, temerarium: non posse eius imperia diutius sustinere.
examples.translation: He is a passionate, a reckless barbarian: we can endure his tyrannies no longer.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod sua victoria tam insolenter gloriarentur quodque tam diu se impune iniurias tulisse admirarentur, eodem pertinere.
examples.translation: Their insolent boast of their own victory, their surprise that their outrages had gone on so long with impunity, pointed the same way;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Qui diutissime impuberes permanserunt, maximam inter suos ferunt laudem: hoc ali staturam, ali vires nervosque confirmari putant.
examples.translation: Those who remain longest in chastity win greatest praise among their kindred; some think that stature, some that strength and sinew are fortified thereby.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: go under any thing

examples.original: Nihil enim est, unde non subeat.
examples.translation: For there is no quarter from which death may not approach.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Subita aliqua et universa voce feriuntur aures meae.
examples.translation: My ears are smitten with sudden and general cheering.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Subito Labienus duabus portis omnem equitatum emittit;
examples.translation: Suddenly from two gates Labienus launched forth all his cavalry;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: property, riches, wealth (cf.: divitiae, res, bona, etc.).

examples.original: Habet pecuniae cupiditatem, sed modicam.
examples.translation: He has a craving for money, although in a moderate degree.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Captivam pecuniam in aedificationem eius templi seposuit.
examples.translation: The money from the captured city he put aside to build this temple.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Id facile effici posse arbitrati sunt, si principes eius ordinis pecunias contulissent.
examples.translation: They thought that their purpose could easily be effected, if the leading men of that order would contribute.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

definitions: English: to come forth, appear, be visible, show one's self; to be present or at hand.
Latin: Se ostendere, apparere
Latin: Ad alicuius nutum vel imperium comparere, praesto esse

examples.original: Si rectae sunt, et pares sunt.
examples.translation: If they are right, they are also equal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erat illi et fessa aetate parens;
examples.translation: He had also his mother, who was bowed with years;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Durius tractandum est, ne animo male pareat.
examples.translation: The body should be treated more rigorously, that it may not be disobedient to the mind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a body of soldiers

examples.original: Caesar in Belgis omnium legionum hiberna constituit.
examples.translation: Then Caesar established the winter quarters of all the legions in Belgic territory.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ab eo de periculis Ciceronis legionisque cognoscitur.
examples.translation: It was he who brought the information about the dangers of Cicero and the legion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Legio classica nihil cunctata praetorianis adiungitur;
examples.translation: The legion of marines without hesitation joined the praetorians.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: Jupiter or Jove, a son of Saturn, brother and husband of Juno, the chief god among the Romans; corresp. to the Gr.
Latin: Deus principalis Romanus, deus caeli
Latin: Caelum ipsum

examples.original: Spolia opima Feretrio Iovi lata.
examples.translation: Spolia opima dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nondum dedicata erat in Capitolio Iovis aedes.
examples.translation: The temple of Jupiter on the Capitol had not yet been dedicated.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Post hunc Apollinem et Martem et Iovem et Minervam.
examples.translation: After him they set Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to flee or
Latin: A hostibus persecutus currere
Latin: Abesse improviso

examples.original: Non enim vitat, sed fugit.
examples.translation: For it does not avoid danger, but runs away.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad haec et quae sequamur et quae fugiamus refert omnia.
examples.translation: These he maintains lie at the root of every act of choice and of avoidance.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vir fortis ac sapiens non fugere debet e vita, sed exire.
examples.translation: The brave and wise man should not beat a hasty retreat from life;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a voice, sound, tone
Latin: Sonus animalium ore aut alia collisione corporum expressus
Latin: Verbum, dictum, sententia, oratio, sermo
entries.etymology: From PIE *wṓkʷs 'voice', from the root *wekʷ- 'speak'; Latin vocō is related.

examples.original: Haec vox significat voluntariam relationem;
examples.translation: The phrase implies a voluntary return;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non vides, quam multorum vocibus chorus constet?
examples.translation: Do you not see how many voices there are in a chorus?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Magno malo ulla voce interpellatum silentium luitur.
examples.translation: There is a grievous penalty for the slightest breach of silence.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: sharing, joining in, partaking, united, associated, kindred, allied, fellow

examples.original: Verum quod institui dicere, miserias cognoscite sociorum.
examples.translation: But let us return to what I began to tell you of our allies’ unhappy position.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Certare socii civesque, utri reciperatae arcis suum decus facerent;
examples.translation: The leader of each party urged on his followers.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eo alter consul Aemilius cum exercitu ad liberandos obsidione socios venit.
examples.translation: Thither the other consul, Aemilius, came with an army, to relieve the blockade of the allies.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To stand together, stand with some person or thing.
Latin: Quantum pecuniae solvendum est aliquam rem emendo
Latin: Verum esse, rectum esse

examples.original: Vita autem honesta actionibus variis constat;
examples.translation: For example, I desire a life of honour.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inbecilli fluvidique inter vana constitimus ;
examples.translation: We are weak, watery beings standing in the midst of unrealities;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Valitudo ei neque corporis neque animi constitit.
examples.translation: He was sound neither of body nor mind.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: dedicated or consecrated to a divinity, holy, sacred, =
Latin: Qui deo devotus est, vel pro bono vel pro malo

examples.original: De sacris loquimur et de templis;
examples.translation: We talk of sacred rites and temples;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tractentur volnera nulla Sacra manu.
examples.translation: No other hand should meddle with the wounds of gods.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Privatim quoque id sacrum celebratum est.
examples.translation: They also observed the rite in their homes.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to venture, to venture to do, to dare; to be bold, courageous (with the idea of courage, boldness; while conari designates a mere attempt, an undertaking; syn.: conor, molior)
Latin: Possidēre satis fortitūdinem ut aliquid agat; perīculum fortasse incurrere; perīclitārī
Latin: parārī proeliō

examples.original: Illud, ut non doleas, vix audebo exigere;
examples.translation: That you should not mourn at all I shall hardly dare to insist;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At Zeno eum non beatum modo sed etiam divitem dicere ausus est.
examples.translation: But Zeno dared to say that a wise beggar was not only happy but also wealthy.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Plus in eo dilectu Valens audebat, tamquam ipsum Caecinam periculo exemisset.
examples.translation: In organizing these bodies Valens put himself forward as having rescued Caecina himself from peril.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: as much as, so as, just as, like as, as if, as it were, so to speak, etc.

examples.original: Sic gerere nos debemus, non tamquam propter corpus vivere debeamus, sed tamquam non possimus sine corpore.
examples.translation: We should conduct ourselves not as if we ought to live for the body, but as if we could not live without it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atque ea in optima quaque indole maxime apparent, in qua haec honesta quae intellegimus a natura tamquam adumbrantur.
examples.translation: And these traits are most apparent in the noblest characters, in which the moral excellences, as we understand them, are already roughly outlined by nature.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam Cn. Pompeius legionem primam, quam ad Caesarem miserat, confectam ex delectu provinciae Caesaris, eam tamquam ex suo numero dedit.
examples.translation: For the First Legion, which he had sent to Caesar, as it had been raised from a levy in Caesar’s province, Pompeius gave as one of his own.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: even as, just as, like as.
Latin: (idem ut alicui)

examples.original: Libri XVII Periocha Cn. Cornelius consul a classe Punica circumventus et per fraudem, veluti in conloquium evocatus, captus est.
examples.translation: Summaries Summary of Book XVII The consul Gnaeus Cornelius was surrounded by a Carthaginian fleet and was made prisoner by fraud, having been lured out as to a colloquy.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ita dico: extrinsecus aliqua sunt incommoda, velut in corpore interdum robusto solidoque eruptiones quaedam pusularum et ulcuscula, nullum in alto malum est.
examples.translation: This is what I mean: there are external disadvantages, like pimples and boils that break out upon a body which is normally strong and sound; but there is no deep-seated malady.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quaedam vero procul arceantur ut iam oblitterata et olentia: nullum sit verbum velut rubigine infectum, nulli sensus tarda et inerti structura in morem annalium componantur;
examples.translation: There should be never a word of the rusty, mouldy tinge, never a sentence put together in the lame and listless style of the chroniclers.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: from any limit of space, time, etc. (cf.: fine, tenus); of place
Latin: Per intervallum totum inter locum et alium
Latin: Per intervallum totum inter locum et alium. hinc usque ad Romam

examples.original: Quorundam illustrium exsequias usque ad rogum frequentavit.
examples.translation: He attended the obsequies of certain distinguished men, even going to the funeral-pyre.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Drusum fratrem in Germania amisit, cuius corpus pedibus toto itinere praegrediens Romam usque pervexit.
examples.translation: He lost his brother Drusus in Germany and conveyed his body to Rome, going before it on foot all the way.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec tamen expers insidiarum usque quaque permansit, sed et a singulis et per factionem et denique civili bello infestatus est.
examples.translation: Yet he did not remain throughout without experience of treachery, but he was attacked by individuals, by a conspiracy, and finally by a civil war.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: place
Latin: Ponere aliquid ad aliquem
Latin: iungere vel copulare, sicut aliquid alicui, vel partes nonnullas, ut augmentare quantitatem, magnificare, vel aggregare

examples.original: Tribus propter eos additae Maecia et Scaptia;
examples.translation: On their account the Maecian and Scaptian tribes were added.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Magister equitum dictatori additus Q. Servilius.
examples.translation: Quintus Servilius was assigned to the dictator as master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ut levior labor iudicantibus foret, ad quattuor prioris quintam decuriam addidit.
examples.translation: To lighten the labour of the jurors, he added a fifth division to the previous four.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: the common people, the commons or commonalty, the plebeians
Latin: Ea pars populi Romani, quae a patribus, seu patriciis distinguitur

examples.original: Eo nuntio erecti patres, erecta plebes.
examples.translation: These tidings cheered the Fathers and encouraged the plebs.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tribuni plebem agitare suo veneno, agraria lege;
examples.translation: The tribunes roused the plebs to madness with their usual poison, a land-law.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mortuus consul Quinctilius, quattuor tribuni plebi.
examples.translation: Death took the consul Quinctilius, and four tribunes of the plebs.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a. [root pug-, to thrust, strike, whence pugil, pungo, etc.], to fight, either singly or in armies, to combat, give battle, engage, contend (very freq. and class.).

examples.original: Pugnatum est ab utrisque acriter.
examples.translation: The fighting was fierce on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Mihi autem de vocabulo pugna non est;
examples.translation: Now I am not going to fight about a word;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ibi Lucius Cotta pugnans interficitur cum maxima parte militum.
examples.translation: There Lucius Cotta was killed fighting, with the greatest part of the troops.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: coming after, following, next, ensuing, future.
Latin: ultimus

examples.original: Maior ista hereditas a me ad posteros transeat.
examples.translation: This inheritance shall pass from me to my descendants larger than before.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Fabii postera die arma capiunt; quo iussi erant conveniunt.
examples.translation: On the following day the Fabii arm and assemble at the designated place.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Bona autem corporis huic sunt quod posterius posui similiora.
examples.translation: For they contribute something worth an effort to obtain;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a sharp edge or point.
Latin: Pars tenuis secansque laminae instrumenti
Latin: Positio militium vel navium constituta in ordine usuale sine decursu determinato

examples.original: Nutantem aciem victor equitatus incursat;
examples.translation: When their line wavered, the enemy’s victorious horse suddenly attacked;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: In acie Quinctius dextrum cornu, Agrippa sinistrum tenuit;
examples.translation: In the battle-line Quinctius held the right wing, Agrippa the left;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum hostium acies a sinistro cornu pulsa atque in fugam conversa esset, a dextro cornu vehementer multitudine suorum nostram aciem premebant.
examples.translation: The left wing of the enemy’s line was beaten and put to flight, but their right wing, by sheer weight of numbers, was pressing our line hard.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: suum of the MSS., Com. Trag. p. 262; in
Latin: Esse ad locum vel prope locum

examples.original: Adest ad tabulam, licetur Aebutius;
examples.translation: Aebutius attends at the sale.a He does the bidding.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Huic quoque adversus servatores suos bello Campanus aderat.
examples.translation: In this war, too, the Campanians took part, against their preservers.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ligus non aderat. L. frater eius causam agebat: aderant amici, propinqui.
examples.translation: Ligus not being in Rome, his brother Lucius appeared for him, supported by his friends and relatives.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: A town
Latin: Locus munitus
Latin: Urbs (praecipue parva urbs rure)
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain; perhaps connected with ob + pedum, but this is not established.

examples.original: Quot oppida in Syria, quot in Macedonia devorata sunt?
examples.translation: How many towns in Syria, how many in Macedonia, have been swallowed up!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Caesar Ab his castris oppidum Remorum nomine Bibrax aberat milia passuum octo.
examples.translation: From this camp a town of the Remi called Bibrax was eight miles distant.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Venit eodem cum suis copiis postero die Gaius Fabius partemque oppidi sumit ad obsidendum.
examples.translation: Next day Gaius Fabius joined him there with his own force and took a part of the town to blockade.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a going, walk; way, road, journey
Latin: Actio īendi in cursū
Latin: Via īendi in cursū

examples.original: Drusum fratrem in Germania amisit, cuius corpus pedibus toto itinere praegrediens Romam usque pervexit.
examples.translation: He lost his brother Drusus in Germany and conveyed his body to Rome, going before it on foot all the way.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ipse tantum itinerum faciebat, quantum satis esse ad mutationem locorum propter salubritatem existimabat.
examples.translation: He himself marched as far as he deemed sufficient for change of stations, to keep the troops in health.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Re frumentaria comparata equitibusque delectis iter in ea loca facere coepit, quibus in locis esse Germanos audiebat.
examples.translation: Having secured his corn-supply and selected his cavalry, he began to march into the localities in which the Germans were reported to be.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to take, take up, lay hold of, assume (syn. capio).
Latin: Capere

examples.original: Et hoc quoque ex alienis hortulis sumptum est.
examples.translation: Let me share with you the saying which pleased me to-day.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ipsis permittimus, unde velint sumere exemplaria.
examples.translation: We allow the purchasers themselves to get their samples from anywhere they please.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Puta me non dicere, unde sumpturus sum mutuum: scis cuius arca utar.
examples.translation: And just assume that I am not telling where I intend to borrow the necessary sum;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: near, nigh (class.).
Latin: Alicui rei propinquus
Latin: Proprie de loco, apud

examples.original: Infelix gemino cecidit prope Pergamon igni, Et paene est alio Troia cremata rogo.
examples.translation: All but twice in the flames unhappy Pergamum perished Troy on a second pyre narrowly failed of her doom.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Et cum his quidem insperata pax erat: aliud multo propius atque in ipsis prope portis bellum ortum.
examples.translation: Thus with the Laurentians peace was preserved against all expectation; but another war broke out, much nearer, and indeed almost at the city gates.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sic enim mihi perspicere videor, ita natos esse nos, ut inter omnis esset societas quaedam, maior autem, ut quisque proxime accederet.
examples.translation: For it seems clear to me that we were so created that between us all there exists a certain tie which strengthens with our proximity to each other.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: cut down, fell
Latin: Secare atque ad terram prosternere (verbum causativum a cadō)
Latin: Interficere, occidere, necare

examples.original: Homicidia compescimus et singulas caedes;
examples.translation: We check manslaughter and isolated murders;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si quos Orbilius ferula scuticaque cecidit.
examples.translation: Whomever Orbilius thrashed with rod or with whiplash of leather.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Capitolium ab exulibus et servis occupatum caesis his receptum est.
examples.translation: The Capitol was seized by exiles and slaves; who were slain and the Capitol recovered.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the breast, in men and animals.

examples.original: Spongia pectori tegumentum et sinistrum crus ocrea tectum;
examples.translation: Their helmets were crested, to make their stature appear greater.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nulla recantatas deponent pectora curas, Nec fugiet vivo sulpure victus amor.
examples.translation: No hearts will lay aside their passion by enchantment, nor love flee vanquished by strong sulphur.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tum pectore verum Fugit, et ad Phoebi tripodas rediere futura, Vixque refecta cadit.
examples.translation: Then the truth vanished from her bosom, and knowledge of the future went back to the tripods of the god;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: light in weight, not heavy (opp. gravis).
Latin: Parvi ponderis
Latin: plānus, non asper

examples.original: Levium metallorum fructus in summo est;
examples.translation: The yield of poor mines is on the surface;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Leve aes alienum debitorem facit, grave inimicum.
examples.translation: A trifling debt makes a man your debtor;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed tua sors levior, quoniam mors ultima poena est Nec metuenda viris.
examples.translation: But your lot is easier, since death, the utmost penalty, is not terrible to the brave.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: of or belonging to man, human.
Latin: Qui ad homines pertinet, hominum

examples.original: Quod auxilium invenis inbecillitati humanae?
examples.translation: What succour can you discover for man’s helplessness?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Incredibilia nobis haec videntur et supra humanam naturam excurrentia.
examples.translation: These goods seem to us incredible and transcending man’s nature;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Multa dicta sunt ab antiquis de contemnendis ac despiciendis rebus humanis;
examples.translation: The ancients enlarged on the duty of rising proudly superior to human fortunes;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To come together, meet together, assemble (class. and freq.).

Latin: (Intrans.) simul venīre; convenire de loco seu spatio simpliciter usurpatur, diciturque de duobus pluribusve personis aut rebus, quae in unum eumdemque locum coeunt vel in uno eodemque loco accidunt
Latin: aliquem vīsitāre

examples.original: In hoc bonis malisque conveniet.
examples.translation: Upon this point good and bad will agree.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc mihi cum tuo fratre convenit.
examples.translation: On this your cousin and I are agreed.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In colloquium convenit, condiciones non convenerunt.
examples.translation: He had an interview with Scipio, but they could not agree upon terms.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

definitions: English: a mountain, mount.
Latin: Moles naturalis magna, sive elevatio terrestris prominens

examples.original: Quid tum claustra montium profutura?
examples.translation: In that case, what will the mountain barriers avail us?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Monte sub hoc lapidum tegitur Ballista sepultus;
examples.translation: Under this mountain of stones Ballista is covered and buried;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Fidenatium plurimi locorum notitia effugere in montes.
examples.translation: Large numbers of the Fidenates escaped, thanks to their knowledge of the ground, into the mountains.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: four: ter quattuor corpora, Enn. ap.
Latin: Tres et alius. Numerus IV
Latin: Tres et alius

examples.original: Quarta causa est faciendi propositum.
examples.translation: Now what is this purpose?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Consulatus super pristinum quattuor gessit;
examples.translation: He held four consulships in addition to his original one.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Pacem petentibus Samnitibus foedus quarto renovatum est.
examples.translation: The Samnites sought peace and the treaty with them was renewed for the fourth time.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a being safe and sound; a sound or whole condition, health, welfare, prosperity, preservation, safety, deliverance, etc. (very freq. and class.: cf.: valetudo, sanitas).
Latin: Valētūdō
Latin: Quod salvum facit

examples.original: Studia mihi nostra saluti fuerunt.
examples.translation: My studies were my salvation.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Agnosco Lucilium meum;
examples.translation: On Siren Songs Now I recognize my Lucilius!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: An cuiusquam tibi temporalis salus carior esse debuerat quam huius aeterna?
examples.translation: Or ought anyone’s temporal welfare to have been more precious to you than his eternal welfare?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: he that brings about the existence of any object, or promotes the increase or prosperity of it, whether he first originates it, or by his efforts gives greater permanence or
Latin: qui rei affirmatae vadimonium quoddamodo praestat
Latin: Progenitor; conditor; artifex

examples.original: Qui rem non tacuerit, non tacebit auctorem.
examples.translation: And he who tells tales will tell names, too.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si mala bonaque non populo auctore distinxeris.
examples.translation: Simply by distinguishing between good and bad things without patterning your opinion from the populace.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnia ea auctor fuit Cornutus matri eius ut aboleret.
examples.translation: All these Cornutus advised the poet’s mother to destroy.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: innate or natural quality, nature.
Latin: Natura, qualitas innata

examples.original: Quid ingenii iste habuit, quid animi!
examples.translation: So full of wit and spirit it was!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Da mihi adulescentem incorruptum et ingenio vegetum;
examples.translation: But give me an unspoiled and sturdy-minded young man;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hae sunt exercitationes ingeni, haec curricula mentis;
examples.translation: These employments are my intellectual gymnastics; these the race-courses of my mind;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: wine.
Latin: Potio fortis ex uvis facta

examples.original: Occidit Eurytion stulte data vina bibendo;
examples.translation: Eurytion fell by stupidly drinking the liquor set before him;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ii, quorum pedes dolor repetit, aut vino aut balineo abstinent.
examples.translation: Those whose feet are visited by pain abstain either from wine or from the bath.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad hoc panis usu carnisque coctae et dulcedine vini mitigatos Marius in tempore adgressus est.
examples.translation: When they had been further demoralized by the use of bread and cooked meat and the delights of wine, Marius opportunely approached them.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to seize and carry off, to snatch, tear, drag, draw, or hurry away, = violenter sive celeriter capio

examples.original: Tanta est fiducia ferri, Non rapuere nefas;
examples.translation: Such was their reliance on their swords, that they did not hurry on the crime;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec raptis aut spes de se melior aut indignatio est minor.
examples.translation: The stolen maidens were no more hopeful of their plight, nor less indignant.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Debellandae sunt in primis voluptates, quae, ut vides, saeva quoque ad se ingenia rapuerunt.
examples.translation: To be conquered, in the first place, are pleasures, which, as you see, have carried off even the sternest characters.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to taste, savor; to be wise

examples.original: Quorum nihil sapienti viro potest evenire;
examples.translation: But none of these things can happen to the sage;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quomodo hoc fiat, sapientia sola monstrabit.
examples.translation: And wisdom alone can show you how this may be done.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnes qui non sint sapientes aeque miseros esse;
examples.translation: That those who are not wise are all equally wretched;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: walk into, to enter (syn.: ingredior, introeo).
Latin: pro interiōre, pro interō
Latin: inīre, invādere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum; 1

examples.original: Excutit redeuntem natura sicut intrantem.
examples.translation: You may take away no more than you brought in;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae latebra est, in quam non intret metus mortis?
examples.translation: What hiding-place is there, where the fear of death does not enter?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic ne intrare posset, saltum in quo Ciliciae portae sunt sitae Datames praeoccupare studuit.
examples.translation: To prevent him from entering the country, Datames wished to occupy the wooded gorge in which the Cilician Gates are situated;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

definitions: English: a battle, combat (class.; syn.: pugna, dimicatio).
Latin: pugna, duellum, pars belli

examples.original: Fit magna contentione diversum proelium.
examples.translation: In different parts of the field a fierce struggle began;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ita ancipiti proelio diu atque acriter pugnatum est.
examples.translation: Thus the engagement became twofold, and. the fight was fierce and long.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Multa secunda proelia fecit, aliquot urbes hostium vi cepit.
examples.translation: He engaged in many successful battles and took several hostile towns by assault.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: question, interrogate one about a thing.

examples.original: Subinde paedagogum suum rogat ut migret.
examples.translation: She keeps asking her attendant to change her quarters;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Coepi gubernatorem rogare, ut me in aliquo litore exponeret.
examples.translation: I began to ask the pilot to put me ashore somewhere;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum salvum esse flentes sui respondissent, rogavit essentne fusi hostes.
examples.translation: His weeping followers told him that it was. He asked, were the enemy routed?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a horse, steed, charger.
Latin: Quodlibet animal specie Equus caballus. Equus
Latin: Mas specie Equus caballus

examples.original: Hominis an equi an ferae?
examples.translation: Is it that of man, or horse, or wild beast?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non faciunt meliorem equum aurei freni.
examples.translation: A golden bit does not make a better horse.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Videtur autem species eius, equus et canis.
examples.translation: A particular animal, however, is seen, for example, a horse, a dog.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a judgment, i. e. a judicial investigation, trial; a judicial sentence (class.).
Latin: Quod iudicatum est, iudicis sententia

examples.original: De praesentibus facile iudicium est;
examples.translation: As to things present, the decision is easy.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sola ratio inmutabilis et iudicii tenax est.
examples.translation: It is reason alone that is unchangeable, that holds fast to its decisions.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ab hoc discede iudicio; non pietas constabit, non fides.
examples.translation: Dissent from this judgment, and duty and loyalty will not abide.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: for that reason, on that account, therefore (class.; esp. freq. in Quint.; cf.: eo, idcirco; ergo, igitur, itaque).

examples.original: Ideoque illam inplicari non oportet;
examples.translation: We should not, therefore, make that language intricate;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare non est quod existimes ideo parum bene conpositum esse te, quod in Campania non es.
examples.translation: For this reason you should not refuse to believe that your life is well-placed merely because you are not now in Campania.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Posthocproelium conlatum omne bellum est circa Corinthum ideoque Corinthium est appellatum.
examples.translation: After this battle the entire war centred about Corinth and hence was known as the Corinthian war.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Agesilaus

definitions: English: A swine

Latin: Animal artiodactylon corpore corpulento, rostro simo, caninisque dentibus magnis qui nonnunquam ex ore protrudunt. Taxonomice sub familia Suidarum dantur, et praecipue nomen ad Suem scrofam pertinet

examples.original: Ad honestatem enim illum omnem conatum suum referebat, non ad voluptatem.
examples.translation: For honour and not pleasure was the aim of that great enterprise.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Librum autem, quem Sulla novissimum ”De Rebus Suis” imperfectum reliquerat, ipse supplevit.
examples.translation: He himself completed the last book of Sulla’s ”Autobiography,” which the dictator left unwritten.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Caesar loquendi finem facit seque ad suos recepit suisque imperavit ne quod omnino telum in hostes reicerent.
examples.translation: Caesar made an end of speaking, and, withdrawing to his own men, commanded them not to discharge a single dart against the enemy in reply.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: your
Latin: Quem vos possidetis

examples.original: Privatae res vestrae quo statu sunt?
examples.translation: In what plight are your private interests?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed hic meus reditus, pontifices, vestro iudicio continetur.
examples.translation: But the reality of this restoration depends, gentlemen, upon your verdict.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et quando ego vobis pro tantis vestris in me meritis gratiam referam, si nunc cessavero?
examples.translation: And when shall I show gratitude for your great kindnesses to me, if I am backward now?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: gerund. abl. nolendo
Latin: Non velle

examples.original: Vivere noluit, qui mori non vult.
examples.translation: He who does not wish to die cannot have wished to live.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nolunt sine salebra esse iuncturam;
examples.translation: They would have jolts in all their transitions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Numerare eos noli, qui tibi metum faciunt.
examples.translation: Do not count the number of those who inspire fear in you.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to stretch out or spread before one; hence, to expose to view, to show, exhibit, display (syn.: monstro, exhibeo).

examples.original: Saevitiam ingenii per haec maxime ostendit.
examples.translation: The following are special instances of his innate brutality.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Ostendes morbum posse superari vel certe sustineri.
examples.translation: You will be showing that a disease can be overcome, or at any rate endured.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Maius malum est hoc, quod non possum tibi ostendere;
examples.translation: The abscess, or ulcer, is deep within my breast.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to draw, drag, or haul, to drag along; to draw off, forth, or away, etc. (syn.: tracto, rapio, rapto, duco).
Latin: Vi movere ad se vel secum

examples.original: Quid tractum in aestatem aliam bellum?
examples.translation: What profit shall we find in prolonging the war into another summer?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ille cum a lictoribus iam traheretur, provocavit;
examples.translation: The lictors were already dragging the man away, when he appealed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Multa enim sunt, quae in utramque partem trahere possunt.
examples.translation: For there are many arguments to pull us in either direction.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: worthy, deserving (in a good or ill sense), of things, suitable, fitting, becoming, proper (very freq. in all periods and kinds of writing).—Constr
Latin: cum auctoritate

examples.original: Dignus illa es, illa digna te est;
examples.translation: You are worthy of her; she is worthy of you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed laudare dignos honesta actio est;
examples.translation: But to praise worthy men is an honourable action;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil autem video ex istis voto dignum.
examples.translation: But I do not see that any of them is worth praying for.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: not at all, by no means; in class. prose most freq. with adverbs; rarely with adjectives, pronouns, or verbs
Latin: Non, minimē, nequaquam
Latin: Non, minime

examples.original: Hic exitus viri haud sane spernendi.
examples.translation: Thus died a man who was far from being despicable.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Isdem diebus a Martio Macro haud procul Cremona prospere pugnatum;
examples.translation: During these same days, Martius Macer had had a successful engagement not far from Cremona;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ut terrorem Italiae possessa Mevania ac velut renatum ex integro bellum intulerat, ita haud dubium erga Flavianas partis studium tam pavidus Vitellii discessus addidit.
examples.translation: While the occupation of Mevania had terrified Italy and had seemed to start a new war, it was also true that the timid retreat of Vitellius had increased the favourable feeling toward the Flavian party.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: imperat. orere
Latin: Nasci

examples.original: Hoc a magno animi malo oritur.
examples.translation: This is the result of great evil in the soul.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Crastino die oriente sole redite in aciem;
examples.translation: To-morrow at sunrise form your battle-line again;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ille enim habet suum finem, inania et ex libidine orta sine termino sunt.
examples.translation: For this has its bounds, but waywardness and the acts that spring from wilful lust are without boundaries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: vanquisher
Latin: Qui vincit (e. g. bello)

examples.original: Victorem autem se ipse pronuntiabat;
examples.translation: When the victory was won, he made the announcement himself;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Laetus fragor aethera pulsat Victorum;
examples.translation: A shout from his conquerors made the welkin ring;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nutantem aciem victor equitatus incursat;
examples.translation: When their line wavered, the enemy’s victorious horse suddenly attacked;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: ability, power of doing any thing (class.)
Latin: Facultas; qualitas rei qui aliquid agere potest

examples.original: Nunc flere potestas, Dum pendet fortuna ducum;
examples.translation: Do not delay your grief, nor keep it for the crowning sorrows.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Primum in nostrane est potestate quid meminerimus?
examples.translation: To begin with, have we the power to choose what we shall remember?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum bellum civitas aut illatum defendit aut infert, magistratus, qui ei bello praesint, ut vitae necisque habeant potestatem, deliguntur.
examples.translation: In time of peace there is no general officer of state, but the chiefs of districts and cantons do justice among their followers and settle disputes.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: that is left or remains, that is left behind, remaining, = relictus (freq. and a good prose word; not found in Cat., Tib., Verg., or Hor.).

examples.original: Reliqua vendita, quibus domini non exstitere.
examples.translation: That the consul had earned a triumph all agreed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Reliqui se in castra recipiunt unde erant egressi.
examples.translation: The remainder retired to the camp from which they had marched out.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hoc idem fit in reliquis civitatibus: in omnibus partibus incendia conspiciuntur;
examples.translation: The same was done in the other states, and in every direction fires were to be seen.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: wretched, unfortunate, miserable, pitiable, lamentable, etc. (cf.: infelix, calamitosus).
Latin: Infelix, infortunatus; haud beatus

examples.original: Nemo tantum praesentibus miser est.
examples.translation: The present alone can make no man wretched.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O te miserum, si contemnis hunc testem!
examples.translation: How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid fieri crudelius vel miserius potest?
examples.translation: What could be more cruel or more wretched?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to throw, throw about, scatter

examples.original: Consulatus super pristinum quattuor gessit;
examples.translation: He held four consulships in addition to his original one.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Crimen erit superis et me fecisse nocentem.
examples.translation: It will be a reproach to the gods, that they have made even me guilty.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Mulciber obscuros lectum circaque superque Disponit laqueos: lumina fallit opus.
examples.translation: Mulciber disposes hidden snares around and above the couch; the device baffles the eye.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to value, estimate, reckon, esteem, with

examples.original: Non est quod existimes paucos esse hos;
examples.translation: You need not think that there are few of this kind;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Statim a sapientia praeceps est?” Non, ut existimo.
examples.translation: Is there a sheer descent immediately below wisdom?” I think not.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc milia passuum octingenta in longitudinem esse existimatur.
examples.translation: The side is supposed to be eight hundred miles long.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to wonder (ante-class. collat. form of miror): quid miras? Varr. ap.

examples.original: Non est quod mireris animum meum;
examples.translation: You need not wonder at any genius of mine;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eius rei quae causa esset, miratus ex ipsis quaesiit.
examples.translation: He asked them, wondering, what might be the cause thereof.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Erat in proximo lucus; hunc asylum facit, et statim mira vis hominum;
examples.translation: There was in the neighbourhood a grove, and this he made a place of refuge;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: To pass away, come to nothing; to vanish, disappear, be lost

examples.original: Si hoc concesseris, omne honestum perît.
examples.translation: If you grant this, honour has wholly perished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nobis solvi perire est, proxima enim intuemur;
examples.translation: To our minds, this process means perishing, for we behold only that which is nearest;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quo die repulsus est, lusit, qua nocte periturus fuit, legit.
examples.translation: The day whereon he failed of election, he spent in play;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: anger, wrath, rage
Latin: Sensus malus, sensus malevolens contra rem aliquam vel hominem aliquem, vel contra res in commune

examples.original: Effugit avaritiam, sed iram adhuc sentit;
examples.translation: They have escaped avarice, for example, but still feel anger;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Auctae inde plebis ac militum in consulem irae.
examples.translation: This increased the enmity of plebs and soldiers towards the consul.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Amor enim, ira, cupiditas pericula depoposcerunt.
examples.translation: It is love, for example, anger, lust, which have challenged dangers.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be in motion, move, walk, go along.
Latin: ire, ambulare
Latin: locum dare, retro vadere, abire, retrahere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; cessi, cessum, 3

examples.original: In inritum cedit ista iactatio.
examples.translation: All your bustle is useless.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quomodo tamen hodiernum certamen nobis cesserit quaeris?
examples.translation: Do you ask, for all that, how our race resulted to-day?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nimius honos inter secunda rebus adversis in solacium cessit.
examples.translation: These excessive honours in prosperity presently became a solace in misfortune.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: infin. pass. parag.: defendier
Latin: (Generatim) omnia propulsare quae damnum vel dedecus afferunt

examples.original: Proximus a tectis ignis defenditur aegre;
examples.translation: A fire next door is ill repulsed;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fabius Vibulanus corona primum vallum defendit;
examples.translation: Fabius Vibulanus first manned the rampart with a cordon of defenders;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Deliberatur de Avarico in communi concilio, incendi placeret an defendi.
examples.translation: They deliberated in a general convention whether Avaricum should be burnt or defended.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a chieftain, commander, tribune.

examples.original: Certatum eo quoque anno cum tribunis est.
examples.translation: This year also there was a conflict with the tribunes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Stationem in castris agebat Iulius Martialis tribunus.
examples.translation: Julius Martialis the tribune was the officer of the day in the camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ita tribuni plebei creati duo, C. Licinius et L. Albinus.
examples.translation: And so they chose two ”tribunes of the people,” Gaius Licinius and Lucius Albinus.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Whoever, whatever, whosoever, whatsoever, every one who, every thing that, all that (class.)

examples.original: Ad quaecumque nos cogebat, instruxit.
examples.translation: For whatever she forced upon us, she equipped us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quibuscumque vires suppetebant ad arma ferenda praesto fuere.
examples.translation: All those who were able to bear arms were at hand.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Debeo hoc suburbano meo, quod mihi senectus mea, quocumque adverteram, apparuit.
examples.translation: I owe it to my country-place that my old age became apparent whithersoever I turned.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: at what time? when? Do. Venit Chaerea.
Latin: interrog. Quo tempore?
Latin: rel. Quo tempore

examples.original: O quando ille veniet dies, quo nemo in honorem tuum mentiatur!
examples.translation: O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Est sine dubio stultum, quia quandoque sis futurus miser, esse iam miserum.
examples.translation: It is indeed foolish to be unhappy now because you may be unhappy at some future time.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Probatos itaque semper lege, et si quando ad alios deverti libuerit, ad priores redi.
examples.translation: So you should always read standard authors; and when you crave a change, fall back upon those whom you read before.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to cover (syn. operio).
Latin: Superficiem alicuius rei altera re operire
Latin: Visui subtrahere, occulere

examples.original: Tectis ac parietibus iura dicturi estis?
examples.translation: Is it to roofs and walls you will render judgment?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Monte sub hoc lapidum tegitur Ballista sepultus;
examples.translation: Under this mountain of stones Ballista is covered and buried;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: At te Corfini validis circumdata muris Tecta tenent, pugnax Domiti;
examples.translation: But Domitius, eager for battle, lay behind strong walls in the city of Corfinium;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: name of a Roman gens. So the famous Cn. Pompejus Magnus

examples.original: Curtius Nicia haesit Cn. Pompeio et C. Memmio;
examples.translation: Curtius Nicias was an adherent of Gnaeus Pompeius and Gaius Memmius;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Ab amicitia Q. Pompei meo nomine se removerat, ut scitis, Scipio;
examples.translation: Scipio, as you both know, had severed his friendship with Quintus Pompeius on my account;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod enim par amicitiae consularis fuit umquam in hac civitate coniunctius quam fuimus inter nos ego et Cn. Pompeius?
examples.translation: For what bond between any friends of consular rank was ever closer in this state than that which bound Gnaeus Pompeius and myself one to the other?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: of immoderate size, vast, huge, prodigious, enormous; great, remarkable: magnas vero agere gratias Thais mihi?

examples.original: Ad haec visa auditaque clamor ingens oritur.
examples.translation: The sight of these things and the man’s recital produced a mighty uproar.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Utrumne ingentis multitudinis causa, quae nondum erat?
examples.translation: Is it because of the great number of people?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Haec inter duorum ingentium bellorum curam gerebantur.
examples.translation: These incidents occurred while men were preoccupied with two mighty wars.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: not to know, to be ignorant (syn. ignoro)
Latin: non Percipere vel apprehendere clare et certe; non scīre, non comprehendere

examples.original: Inter sapientiam et sapere quid intersit nescio;
examples.translation: What the distinction is between wisdom and being wise I do not know;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Solis nosse deos et caeli numina vobis Aut solis nescire datum;
examples.translation: (To them alone is granted knowledge—or ignorance, it may be—of gods and celestial powers ;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Artis opem vicere metus, nescitque magister, Quam frangat, cui cedat aquae.
examples.translation: The strife of the waters is helpful to the wretched sailors;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: bottle made of an animal's hide, a skin for wine, oil, water, etc.
Latin: Ambo, et hic et ille

examples.original: In utram ire partem iubes?
examples.translation: Which party would you have me follow?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Valerius Horatiusque consules sortiti uter dedicaret.
examples.translation: Valerius and Horatius the consuls drew lots to determine which should do it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Prospectu tenebris adempto multa utrimque vulnera accipiuntur.
examples.translation: As the darkness made it impossible to see far, many wounds were received on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: that belongs to another person, place, object, etc.
Latin: Qui ad alium vel ad aliam rem pertinet

examples.original: Hic est locus solvendi aeris alieni.
examples.translation: Now is the time for me to pay my debt.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aiunt homines plus in alieno negotio videre.
examples.translation: They say that men see farther in the affairs of others than in their own.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pudicitiae neque suae neque alienae pepercit.
examples.translation: He respected neither his own chastity nor that of anyone else.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: to the right, on the right side, right (opp. laevus, sinister).

examples.original: Manlius dextro, Decius laevo cornu praeerat.
examples.translation: Manlius commanded the right wing, Decius the left.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In acie Quinctius dextrum cornu, Agrippa sinistrum tenuit;
examples.translation: In the battle-line Quinctius held the right wing, Agrippa the left;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ille cruor meus est, illo maculata cruore Non profectura dextra lavatur aqua.
examples.translation: That is my blood: the hand that blood has tainted is washed in unavailing water.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: light.
Latin: Splendor; ea per quam res visibiles oculis efficitur esse, quae e sole, ignibus, et aliis rebus incandescentibus, procedit

examples.original: Luce prima inermos plerosque oppressere.
examples.translation: At daybreak they cut down many of them quite unarmed.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Lucis vobis huius partem, si liceat, adimant;
examples.translation: They would take from you, were it possible, a part of this daylight.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tempanius metu insidiarum suos ad lucem tenuit.
examples.translation: Tempanius feared an ambush and kept his soldiers close till daylight.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: near, to approach (class.).
Latin: Cedere ad rem; appropinquare

examples.original: Accedebat sententiae Paulini Marius Celsus;
examples.translation: Marius Celsus supported the opinion of Paulinus.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Et accesserunt maioris sollicitudinis causae.
examples.translation: He had besides reasons for still greater anxiety;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ad mortem dies extremus pervenit, accedit omnis.
examples.translation: The last hour reaches, but every hour approaches, death.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: glory, fame, renown, praise
Latin: Laus, fama

examples.original: Eo proelio praecipua equitum gloria fuit;
examples.translation: In this battle the cavalry particularly distinguished themselves.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: O quam ignorant homines cupidi gloriae, quid illa sit aut quemadmodum petenda!
examples.translation: On that day the Roman populace viewed the furniture of many men;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ceterum id quoque ad gloriam accessit quod cum illo simul iusta ac legitima regna occiderunt.
examples.translation: But there was this to enhance his renown, that just and lawful kingship perished with him.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to examine judicially, to judge, be a judge, pass judgment, decide (syn.: judicium facio, reddo; class.).

examples.original: Necessaria iudicat, quorum magna pars supervacua est.
examples.translation: At present it holds things to be essential of which the greater part is superfluous.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex quo, quantum boni sit in amicitia, iudicari potest.
examples.translation: From this it may be judged how great good there is in friendship.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nihil enim possumus iudicare nisi quod est nostri iudici;
examples.translation: We cannot decide any issue not within our jurisdiction;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: assess, rate, estimate.

examples.original: Census deinde actus et conditum ab Quinctio lustrum.
examples.translation: The census was then taken and Quinctius solemnized the concluding purification.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Triumviri capitales tunc primum creati sunt. Censu acto lustrum conditum est.
examples.translation: A board of three to deal with capital offences was then chosen for the first time.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Censuerunt etiam quidam ut Pannonicus, alii ut Invictus, nonnulli ut Pius cognominaretur.
examples.translation: Some also recommended that he be given the surname of Pannonicus, others of Invictus, others of Pius.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to this place, hitherto
Latin: Ad hunc locum, comprehendens finem et accessum; saepe cum usque; dictum de spatio
Latin: Ad hoc tempus

examples.original: Uxori ac filiae superstes fuit atque utramque adhuc privatus amisit.
examples.translation: He outlived his wife and daughter; in fact lost them both before he became emperor.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Munera, quibus a Pompeia Sex. Pompei sorore in Sicilia donatus est, chlamys et fibula, item bullae aureae, durant ostendunturque adhuc Baiis.
examples.translation: The gifts which were given him in Sicily by Pompeia, sister of Sextus Pompeius, a cloak and clasp, as well as studs of gold, are still kept and exhibited at Baiae.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Scribonius mathematicus praeclara spopondit, etiam regnaturum quandoque, sed sine regio insigni, ignota scilicet tunc adhuc Caesarum potestate.
examples.translation: Tiberiusinfancy the astrologer Scribonius promised him an illustrious career and even that he would one day be king, but without the crown of royalty;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: clean, cleanly, nice, neat, elegant.

examples.original: Mundus eundem habitum ac modum servat.
examples.translation: The universe keeps the same character, the same limits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pharsalia et Thapsos et Munda nusquam.
examples.translation: Pharsalia, Thapsus and Munda made no appearance;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Inde ruunt toto concita pericula mundo.
examples.translation: And now dangers, summoned from all the world, came rushing on.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: so many.
Latin: tam multī

examples.original: Ac sic accidit, uti ex tanto navium numero tot navigationibus neque hoc neque superiore anno ulla omnino navis, quae milites portaret, desideraretur;
examples.translation: And eventually, of all that number of ships and in all those voyages, not a single ship carrying troops in this or the previous year was missing.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid tibi, Torquate, quid huic Triario litterae, quid historiae cognitioque rerum, quid poetarum evolutio, quid tanta tot versuum memoria voluptatis affert?
examples.translation: What actual pleasure do you, Torquatus, or does Triarius here, derive from literature, from history and learning, from turning the pages of the poets and committing vast quantities of verse to memory?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Princeps neque opera ulla magnifica fecit—nam et quae sola susceperat, Augusti templum restitutionemque Pompeiani theatri, imperfecta post tot annos reliquit—neque spectacula omnino edidit;
examples.translation: While emperor he constructed no magnificent public works, for the only ones which he undertook, the temple of Augustus and the restoration of Pompey’s theatre, he left unfinished after so many years.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to stand before or in front.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ĭti; ĭtum, 1

examples.original: Surdum te amantissimis tuis praesta;
examples.translation: Be deaf to those who love you most of all;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Curam quoque solito exactiorem praestitit.
examples.translation: He also observed more scrupulous care than usual.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Aliquid nobis praestat geometriae ministerium;
examples.translation: We get some help from the service which mathematics renders;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a leader, head, chief, president

examples.original: Praetorum numerus ampliatus est, ut essent iiii.
examples.translation: The number of praetors was enlarged to four.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Atque id actum est praetore me, quinquennio ante quam consul sum factus.
examples.translation: And this took place while I was praetor and five years before I was elected consul.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Domi autem creant decem praetores, qui exercitui praeessent, in iis Miltiadem;
examples.translation: But at home they appointed ten generals to command the army, including Miltiades;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Militiades

definitions: English: a judicial decision, verdict, judgment; hence, transf., like the Gr.

examples.original: Si sortis, nullum crimen est in casu;
examples.translation: If you impute it to chance, then you have nothing to charge him with;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: His lacrimis contentus eris sine crimine mortis;
examples.translation: Those tears will content thee, free from the reproach of death;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ad hoc domi contionantis in modum sermones pleni criminum in patres;
examples.translation: Besides this he delivered in his house harangues that were full of accusation against the patricians;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: in the world
Latin: Res circularis

examples.original: Alter, si possis, orbis habendus erit.
examples.translation: If you can, you must live in another world.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ecce, parat Caesar domito quod defuit orbi Addere: nunc, oriens ultime, noster eris.
examples.translation: Lo! Caesar is preparing to add what was lacking to the conquered world: now, farthest East, shalt thou be ours.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non eadem belli totum fortuna per orbem Constitit, in partes aliquid sed Caesaris ausa est.
examples.translation: The fortune of war did not remain unchanged all the world over, but dared to strike one blow against Caesar’s side.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: sift (rare)

examples.original: Cernit tabe iecur madidum, venasque minaces Hostili de parte videt.
examples.translation: He saw the liver flabby with corruption and with boding streaks in its hostile half.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Oculorum, inquit Plato, est in nobis sensus acerrimus, quibus sapientiam non cernimus;
examples.translation: The sense of sight, says Plato, is the keenest sense we possess, yet our eyes cannot behold Wisdom;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Exanimati omnes tam atroci imperio nec aliter quam in se quisque destrictam cernentes securem, metu magis quam modestia quievere.
examples.translation: All were astounded at so shocking a command; every man looked upon the axe as lifted against himself, and they were hushed with fear more than with reverence.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: millet

examples.original: Ita omnis insula est in circuitu viciens centum milium passuum.
examples.translation: Thus the whole island is two thousand miles in circumference.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar Ab his castris oppidum Remorum nomine Bibrax aberat milia passuum octo.
examples.translation: From this camp a town of the Remi called Bibrax was eight miles distant.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ab eis qui emerant capitum numerus ad eum relatus est milium quinquaginta trium.
examples.translation: The purchasers furnished a return to him of three-and-fifty thousand persons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a speaking or talking with any one; talk, conversation, discourse
Latin: Colloquium; locutio

examples.original: Ad hoc domi contionantis in modum sermones pleni criminum in patres;
examples.translation: Besides this he delivered in his house harangues that were full of accusation against the patricians;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et cum iam pariter flevissemus, plenissima spe correctionis illorum finis sermonis mei factus est.
examples.translation: After we had thus wept together, I concluded my sermon in the full anticipation of their amendment.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Plerumque improborum facta primo suspicio insequitur, dein sermo atque fama, tum accusator, tum iudex;
examples.translation: The usual consequences of crime are, first suspicion, next gossip and rumour, then comes the accuser, then the judge;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that is common to several or to all, common, general, universal, public
Latin: Haud proprius; qui ad omnes vel multos pertinet

examples.original: In commune rerum natura fruebantur;
examples.translation: They enjoyed all nature in partnership.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Deliberatur de Avarico in communi concilio, incendi placeret an defendi.
