examples.translation: They deliberated in a general convention whether Avaricum should be burnt or defended.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Magna et generosa res est humanus animus: nullos sibi poni nisi communes et cum deo terminos patitur.
examples.translation: The human soul is a great and noble thing; it permits of no limits except those which can be shared even by the gods.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the talk of the multitude, like rumor, either as relating or as judging (v. rumor; cf. also: nomen, gloria, laudatio; clamor, plausus; honos, dignitas, honestas, laus, etc.).

examples.original: Id praecipuum alimentum famae erat.
examples.translation: Nothing furnished rumour with more food.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nihil sit illi cum ambitione famaque;
examples.translation: It should have nothing to do with ambition and reputation;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad famam obsidionis dilectus haberi coeptus erat;
examples.translation: On the rumour of a blockade they had begun to hold a levy;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: test, examine, inspect, judge of any thing in respect of its goodness, fitness, etc. (rare in class. Lat.; not in Cic. or Cæs.; in eccl. Lat. very freq.).
Latin: Cernere num aliquem aliquidve bonum sit
Latin: experiendo comperire

examples.original: Uni Crassicio se credere Zmyrna probavit;
examples.translation: Zmyrna will trust her fate but to Crassicius;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Quid enim me prohiberet Epicureum esse, si probarem quae ille diceret?
examples.translation: What should prevent me from being an Epicurean, if I accepted the doctrines of Epicurus?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Tu autem, si tibi illa probabantur, cur non propriis verbis illa tenebas?
examples.translation: If you accepted those views on their merits, why did you not hold them under their own terminology?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to run, to move quickly (on foot, on a horse, ship, etc.), to hasten, fly (very freq. in every period and species of composition).
Latin: Velociter ire

examples.original: Tam celer adsiduos explevit cursus honores;
examples.translation: So swiftly did thy career fill office after office;
examples.author: Claudian
examples.work: Panegyric On The Consulship Of Fl. Manlius Theodorus (A.D. 399)

examples.original: Quod ubi accidit, barbari vehementissimo cursu refugerunt.
examples.translation: When this occurred, the natives fled away at a most furious speed.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Possum pedes movere, ut non curram; currere non possum, ut pedes non moveam.
examples.translation: I can move my feet without running, but I cannot run without moving my feet.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: little, small

examples.original: Quod paulo minus utrumque evenit;
examples.translation: And both predictions were all but fulfilled;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Post quae dimotis omnibus paulum requievit.
examples.translation: After this he sent all away and rested for a time.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Varus perditas res eodem quo Cannensem diem Paulus et fato est et animo secutus.
examples.translation: Varus met disaster by the same fate and with the same courage as Paulus on the fatal day of Cannae.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: an evil deed; a wicked, heinous, or impious action; a crime
Latin: mala rēs, mala actio; crīmen, malum, iniūria

examples.original: Sed non diu latent scelera.
examples.translation: But crimes do not long remain undetected.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Atqui maximum scelerum supplicium in ipsis est.
examples.translation: And yet the worst punishment for crime lies in the crime itself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ceterum et prioribus civium bellis par scelus inciderat.
examples.translation: And yet a similar crime had happened in civil war before.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: five
Latin: Quattuor et alius. Numerus V
Latin: Quattuor et alius

examples.original: Dies colloquio dictus est ex eo die quintus.
examples.translation: A day—the fifth after that—was appointed for the parley.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quinta classis aucta; centuriae triginta factae;
examples.translation: The fifth class was made larger, and thirty centuries were formed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Apud Pythagoram discipulis quinque annis tacendum erat;
examples.translation: Pythagoras made his pupils keep silence for five years;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to command, order, enjoin (cf.: jubeo, praecipio, mando).
Latin: Iubere, mandāre
Latin: Regnāre
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Re nuntiata ad suos, quae imperarentur facere dixerunt.
examples.translation: They reported this to their tribesmen, and agreed to perform his commands.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Peragit concilium Caesar equitesque imperat civitatibus.
examples.translation: Caesar closed the convention, and made requisition of cavalry upon the states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Vixit annis viginti novem, imperavit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.
examples.translation: He lived twenty-nine years and ruled three years, ten months and eight days.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: all in a body, all together, the whole, all, entire

examples.original: Eo die L. Mamilio Tusculano adprobantibus cunctis civitas data est.
examples.translation: On that day Lucius Mamilius the Tusculan was granted citizenship, with the approval of all.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Arma cuncti spectant et bellum: en unquam futurum ut congredi armatis cum Samnite liceat?
examples.translation: Would ever the hour come, they asked, when they might encounter the Samnites, sword in hand?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed Asprenati cuncta ex fide nuntiata, cuius cohortatione expugnata navis et interfectus quisquis ille erat.
examples.translation: But they faithfully reported everything to Asprenas, at whose bidding they captured the pretender’s ship and killed him, whoever he was.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to cause to stand, put or lay down, to set, put, place, fix, station, deposit a person or thing somewhere (esp. firmly or immovably), etc.
Latin: Efficere aliquid consistere

examples.original: Lex de veneficio tunc primum constituta est.
examples.translation: A law about poisoning was then for the first time enacted.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Caesar in Belgis omnium legionum hiberna constituit.
examples.translation: Then Caesar established the winter quarters of all the legions in Belgic territory.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Orationibus instate horis et temporibus constitutis.
examples.translation: Be instant in prayerb at the appointed hours and seasons.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to move, to move away or from its place, to move to a place (rare)
Latin: movere de loco ad locum
Latin: Facere, ut res alio, atque antea, modo exsistat, aut in diversam vertatur

examples.original: Pauca mutat, vel plura sane;
examples.translation: He makes a few modifications, or indeed a good many;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid igitur voluit sibi qui illa mutaverit?
examples.translation: What then did he want by altering their old name?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non mutata feminarum natura, sed victa est;
examples.translation: This does not mean that woman’s physique has changed, but that it has been conquered;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Power, might, strength, ability, in abstr.: Romani scalis summā nituntur opum vi, Enn. ap.
Latin: Facultas, potestas
Latin: copiae, divitiae

examples.original: Adflictas opes equestri proelio Bellovacorum esse;
examples.translation: The power of the Bellovaci was crushed, they said, by the cavalry combat;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Adeo in uno omnibus satis auxilii fuisse, nullam opem in tam multis uni esse?
examples.translation: When one man had been quite able to help them all, was there no help in so many men for one?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quibus enim nihil est in ipsis opis ad bene beateque vivendum, eis omnis aetas gravis est;
examples.translation: For to those who have not the means within themselves of a virtuous and happy life every age is burdensome;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a sample.

examples.original: Nihil opus est exemplis hoc facere longius;
examples.translation: There is no need to enlarge upon or illustrate this point;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ex eodem tibi munere plura exempla promisi.
examples.translation: I have promised you, however, some more illustrations drawn from the same games.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vides autem, quid sequatur, ubi alicui vitium pro exemplo est.
examples.translation: So you see the results of copying another man’s vices.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to produce melodious sounds, whether of men or animals; later, with a designation of the subject-matter of the melody, as
Latin: Modulatum sonum edere
Latin: narrare aliquid versibus, pro laudare, praedicare, celebrare carminibus

examples.original: Cum classicum cecinit, scit non se peti;
examples.translation: When the trumpet sounds, the poor man knows that he is not being attacked;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Videtur autem species eius, equus et canis.
examples.translation: A particular animal, however, is seen, for example, a horse, a dog.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et Volumnius signa canere ac vexilla efferri castris iussit;
examples.translation: Volumnius, too, bade sound the signal and advance the banners from the camp.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: After this or that, hereafter, thereafter, afterwards

examples.original: Nobis aliter videtur; recte secusne, postea;
examples.translation: We think otherwise—whether rightly or wrongly, I will consider later;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed Asconius Pedianus adfirmat, ipsam postea maiorem natu narrare solitam, invitatum quidem a Vario ad communionem sui, verum pertinacissime recusasse.
examples.translation: But Asconius Pedianus declares that she herself used to say afterwards, when she was getting old, that Virgil was invited by Varius to associate with her, but obstinately refused.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Cadaver eius clam in hortos Lamianos asportatum et tumultuario rogo semiambustum levi caespite obrutum est, postea per sorores ab exsilio reversas erutum et crematum sepultumque.
examples.translation: His body was conveyed secretly to the gardens of the Lamian family, where it was partly consumed on a hastily erected pyre and buried beneath a light covering of turf;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: to value or esteem highly, to love

examples.original: Omnis enim est natura diligens sui.
examples.translation: For love of self is inherent in every species;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Plato ipse ad senectutem se diligentia protulit.
examples.translation: Plato himself, by taking pains, advanced to old age.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Superfluente multitudine curam dilectus in consules partitur;
examples.translation: On the senators he imposed a contribution of slaves and cash.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a wife, spouse, consort (syn. conjux).
Latin: Coniunx fēminea

examples.original: Uxor non habet potestatem corporis sui sed vir;
examples.translation: The wife hath not power of her own body, but the husband;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Uxori ac filiae superstes fuit atque utramque adhuc privatus amisit.
examples.translation: He outlived his wife and daughter; in fact lost them both before he became emperor.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Mandubii, qui eos oppido receperant, cum liberis atque uxoribus exire coguntur.
examples.translation: The Mandubii, whose town had received them, were compelled to leave it with wives and children.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: clear, bright (opp. obscurus, caecus; very freq. in all periods, and in all kinds of composition).
Latin: Lucem emittens vel repellens, lucidus
Latin: Celeber, bene notus
entries.etymology: From PIE *kelh₁- 'call'; Latin clāmō 'shout' is related.

examples.original: Studia te tua clarum et nobilem efficient.
examples.translation: It is your own studies that will make you shine and will render you eminent.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod igitur nomen umquam in orbe terrarum clarius fuit?
examples.translation: What name, then, in the whole world has ever been more famous?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Post pugnam ad Regillum lacum non alia illis annis pugna clarior fuit.
examples.translation: From the time of the fight at Lake Regillus no other battle of those days was more famous.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: consul, one of the two chief magistrates of the Roman Republic
Latin: Quidam magistratus Romanus. Confer: consulo

examples.original: Lucretio consuli ea provincia evenit.
examples.translation: To Lucius Lucretius the consul fell the command in this affair.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ab altero consule res gesta egregie est;
examples.translation: The other consul campaigned with great success.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Omnia iura, omnia insignia primi consules tenuere;
examples.translation: All the rights of the kings and all their insignia were possessed by the earliest consuls;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: A benefaction, kindness
Latin: Factum bonum in auxilio voluntario consistens

examples.original: Pluris aestimo beneficium quam iniuriam.
examples.translation: I reckon a benefit at a higher rate than an injury.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Idem immortali memoria percepta retinebat beneficia;
examples.translation: He had besides an unfailing memory for kindnesses received;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Nam cum beneficio par est iniuria, aliquid in animo benivolentiae remanet.
examples.translation: For when the injury merely equals the benefit, a certain amount of kindly feeling is left over.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: will, freewill, wish, choice, desire, inclination.

examples.original: Haec mihi dederunt voluntatem adiuvandi me et patiendi omne tormentum;
examples.translation: All these things gave me the inclination to succour myself and to endure any torture;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Venio nunc ad civitates Siciliae, de quibus facillime iudicium fieri voluntatis potest.
examples.translation: Let us now consider the Sicilian cities, the test of whose willingness may be applied very easily.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Perseverandum est et adsiduo studio robur addendum, donec bona mens sit quod bona voluntas est.
examples.translation: You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Italy
Latin: Natio in Europa meridionali; caput Roma est

examples.original: Caesarem arbitrari profectum in Italiam;
examples.translation: He believed that Caesar had started for Italy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum duobus ducibus de imperio in Italia est decertatum, Pyrrho et Hannibale;
examples.translation: Against two leaders we had bitter struggles for the empire of Italy—Pyrrhus and Hannibal;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nero in ultimum Italiae angulum summoverat Annibalem, Livius in diversissimam partem, id est in ipsas nascentis Italiae fauces signa converterat.
examples.translation: Nero had driven Hannibal into the uttermost corner of Italy, while Livius had advanced to the very opposite end of the country, the very entrance of the Italian frontier.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: satisfaction, enjoyment, pleasure, delight (whether sensual or spiritual; syn. oblectamentum).

examples.original: Callipho ad virtutem nihil adiunxit nisi voluptatem;
examples.translation: Callipho coupled with virtue pleasure alone;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Erat et cupidus voluptatum et eius generis intellegens et copiosus;
examples.translation: His appetite for pleasures was only equalled by his taste and ingenuity in devising them.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hoc Epicurus in voluptate ponit, quod summum bonum esse vult summumque malum dolorem;
examples.translation: This Epicurus finds in pleasure; pleasure he holds to be the Chief Good, pain the Chief Evil.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a service, whether of free will or of (external or moral) necessity (class.; cf.: studium, beneficium, meritum, munus).

examples.original: Nihil est enim remuneratione benevolentiae, nihil vicissitudine studiorum officiorumque iucundius. Quid?
examples.translation: For nothing gives more pleasure than the return of goodwill and the interchange of zealous service.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cingetorigi, quem ab initio permansisse in officio demonstravimus, principatus atque imperium est traditum.
examples.translation: The prerogative of chieftaincy was delivered to Cingetorix, who, as we have shown, had remained loyal from the beginning.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quis autem, vir modo et erectus ad honesta, non est laboris adpetens iusti et ad officia cum periculo promptus?
examples.translation: Who, moreover, if he is a man and intent upon the right, is not eager for reasonable toil and ready for duties accompanied by danger?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to loosen an object from any thing, to release or to loose, remove any thing which binds or restrains another.
Latin: Ligationem rumpere alicuius rei cum aliqua re
Latin: Pecuniam dare pro aliqua re

examples.original: Hic est locus solvendi aeris alieni.
examples.translation: Now is the time for me to pay my debt.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nobis solvi perire est, proxima enim intuemur;
examples.translation: To our minds, this process means perishing, for we behold only that which is nearest;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non dicimus ”reposuit beneficium” aut ”solvit”;
examples.translation: We do not say, ”He has ’restored’ the benefit,” or ’settled’ it;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: by or past, and hence, also, beyond, or rest outside a thing.
Latin: excepto
Latin: extra marginem alicuius rei

examples.original: In qua quid est boni praeter summam voluptatem et eam sempiternam?
examples.translation: But what good has everlasting life to offer beside supreme and never-ending pleasure?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ex plurimis maximisque honoribus praeter paucos et modicos non recepit.
examples.translation: Of many high honours he accepted only a few of the more modest.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Prius igitur quam ultra progrederetur, praeventus est ab Agrippina, quam praeter haec conscientia quoque nec minus delatores multorum criminum arguebant.
examples.translation: But before he could go any farther, he was cut short by Agrippina, who was being accused besides of many other crimes both by her own conscience and by informers.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: though, although, albeit; ante-class. always, and in class. prose regularly joined with
Latin: coniunctio concessiva, quaedam res aliter indicat, sed

examples.original: Quamquam quid est quod magis perspicuum sit quam non modo carum sibi quemque, verum etiam vehementer carum esse?
examples.translation: Yet what fact is more self-evident than that every man not merely of loves himself, but loves himself very much indeed?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque quamquam in eo sermone qui cum Torquato est habitus non remissi fuimus, tamen haec acrior est cum Stoicis parata contentio.
examples.translation: Hence although in our debate with Torquatus we did not spare our strength, nevertheless a keener struggle now awaits us with the Stoics.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod quamquam Aristippi est a Cyrenaicisque melius liberiusque defenditur, tamen eiusmodi esse iudico ut nihil homine videatur indignius.
examples.translation: This is the doctrine of Aristippus, and it is upheld more cogently and more frankly by the Cyrenaics;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a presiding over; hence, defence, protection, help
Latin: auxilium
Latin: milites qui personam sicut imperatorem custodiunt

examples.original: Is armata iuventute dispositisque praesidiis tuta omnia ac tranquilla fecit.
examples.translation: Arming the young men and disposing his defences, he made everything secure and tranquil.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Postridie eius diei Caesar praesidium utrisque castris, quod satis esse visum est, reliquit;
examples.translation: On the next day Caesar left what he deemed a sufficient garrison for each camp;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quinque cohortes, quas minime firmas ad dimicandum esse existimabat, castris praesidio relinquit;
examples.translation: He left as garrison for the camp the five cohorts which he regarded as least steady for action;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a producing, production, invention, cause

examples.original: Quanta esset cum gratia auctoritas!
examples.translation: What a wonderful combination of sweetness and power!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neminem exsulum nisi ex senatus auctoritate restituit.
examples.translation: He recalled no one from exile except with the approval of the senate.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quae sunt igitur voluptates corporis cum auctoritatis praemiis comparandae?
examples.translation: What physical pleasures, then, are comparable to the distinction which influence bestows?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that acts unlawfully, injurious, wrongful, unjust (mostly ante-class.): Scel. Quis igitur vocare? Phil.

examples.original: Nomina ex ambitione aut ex iniuria nata.
examples.translation: They are mere titles, born of ambition or of wrong.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pluris aestimo beneficium quam iniuriam.
examples.translation: I reckon a benefit at a higher rate than an injury.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Patietur plus inputari sibi. Invitus beneficium per conpensationem iniuriae solvet.
examples.translation: He will be unwilling to pay a benefit by balancing the injury against it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a proposition or motion for a law made to the people by a magistrate, a bill (cf. institutum).
Latin: Rogatio; regula seu ius propositum
Latin: Ius, regula, edictum

examples.original: Ad hanc legem natus es.
examples.translation: You were born to be subject to this law;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Lex agraria primum lata est.
examples.translation: For the first time a land-law was proposed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Bonum omne in easdem cadit leges;
examples.translation: The good, in every instance, is subject to these same laws.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be a hearer or beholder of something (v. arbiter, I.), to observe, perceive, hear, etc. (in this sense only ante- and post-class.)
Latin: Putare, opinari, censere

examples.original: Caesarem arbitrari profectum in Italiam;
examples.translation: He believed that Caesar had started for Italy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ea libera coniectura est, sed, ut ego arbitror, vana;
examples.translation: Here is freedom for conjecture, but in my opinion it is idle;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sunt multa quae Verres in me esse arbitratur, quae scit in te, Q. Caecili, non esse;
examples.translation: Verres believes me, Caecilius, to possess many qualities that he knows well you do not possess.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: very many, a very great part, most (anteclass. prim. form, for the class. plerusque, plerique): ager, campestris plerus, for the most part, Cato ap.

examples.original: Pleraque ante oculos posita transimus.
examples.translation: We miss much that is set before our very eyes.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Luce prima inermos plerosque oppressere.
examples.translation: At daybreak they cut down many of them quite unarmed.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit.
examples.translation: He commonly appointed consuls for a period of six months.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: full of honor, honorable.

examples.original: Quid ergo hoc loco intellegit honestum?
examples.translation: What therefore does he understand by ’moral’ in this passage?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ex honestiore causa coit turpis adfectus?
examples.translation: Can a cause which is more honourable produce a passion that is base?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vita autem honesta actionibus variis constat;
examples.translation: For example, I desire a life of honour.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: with difficulty, with much ado, hardly, scarcely, barely.

examples.original: Tum pectore verum Fugit, et ad Phoebi tripodas rediere futura, Vixque refecta cadit.
examples.translation: Then the truth vanished from her bosom, and knowledge of the future went back to the tripods of the god;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quodque vix auditu fas esse debeat, laudis et gloriae et ingenii loco plerique iactant cantari saltarique commentarios suos;
examples.translation: They make it their aim, by wantonness of language, by shallow-pated conceits, and by irregular arrangement, to produce the rhythms of stage-dancing;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nam illud quidem adduci vix possum, ut ea quae senserit ille tibi non vera videantur.” ”Vide quantum,” inquam, ”fallare, Torquate.
examples.translation: For I can scarcely bring myself to believe that you think his opinions untrue.” ”Let me assure you, Torquatus,” said I, ”that you are entirely mistaken.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: on the outside, outward, of another country, family, etc., foreign, strange (syn.: extraneus; alienus, peregrinus, adventicius).
Latin: peregrinus

examples.original: Venit ad extremum; haeret in salebra;
examples.translation: But when it comes to its conclusion, it finds itself in trouble;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Plura de extremis loqui pars ignaviae est.
examples.translation: To talk at length about the end is cowardice.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Extremi multorum tempus in unum Convenere dies.
examples.translation: What form of ruin will their anger assume?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: six
Latin: Quinque et alius. Numerus VI
Latin: Quinque et alius

examples.original: Frigere ac torpere senis consilia.
examples.translation: The old man’s strategy was cold and torpid.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit.
examples.translation: He commonly appointed consuls for a period of six months.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quaeris, quid doceam? Etiam seni esse discendum.
examples.translation: That even an old man should keep learning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: forth, to go away, depart.
Latin: (Intrans.) Extrā īre, aliquam rem relinquere in qua ante fueras
Latin: Praetergredī

examples.original: Nullum sine exitu iter est.
examples.translation: No journey but has its end.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nullus mihi per otium dies exit.
examples.translation: I never spend a day in idleness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic exitus viri haud sane spernendi.
examples.translation: Thus died a man who was far from being despicable.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: full all round; hence, great
Latin: Magnus; grandis magnitudine, capacitate, aut mole; spatiosus; late extentus

examples.original: Quaeris quod sit amplissimum vitae spatium?
examples.translation: And what, you ask, is the fullest span of life?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed virtutem ipsam inchoavit; nihil amplius.
examples.translation: But of virtue itself she merely gave the germ and no more.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et ita formatus est, ut illi nec amor vitae nec odium sit, patiturque mortalia, quamvis sciat ampliora superesse.
examples.translation: Bound, so to speak, to his oath of allegiance, he regards the period of life as his term of service.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: love, affection; the beloved; Cupid
Latin: trigesimus liber Bibliae, compositum novem capitula

examples.original: Hoc bene compositos, hoc firmos solvit amores;
examples.translation: This it is loosens loves that are well compact and strong;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hunc tam inmaturum amorem virginis ultus est ferro.
examples.translation: The maiden’s girlish affection he punished with the sword.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sese tamen et amore fraterno et existimatione vulgi commoveri.
examples.translation: For all that, I feel the force of brotherly love and public opinion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a flowing of water; and concr., a flood, stream, flowing or running water (syn.: fluvius, amnis, rivus).
Latin: Aqua fluens
Latin: Amnis
entries.etymology: Derived from fluō 'flow'.

examples.original: In eo flumine pons erat.
examples.translation: There was a bridge over the river;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Fluminis erat altitudo pedum circiter trium.
examples.translation: The depth of the river was about three feet.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In hos domandos Vinnium misit. Caesi sunt in utrisque fluminibus.
examples.translation: Caesar sent Vinnius to subdue them, and they were defeated on both rivers.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: The faculty of remembering, memory, recollection (class.)

examples.original: Valde enim bonae memoriae est, si meminit!
examples.translation: He must have a particularly good memory if he can remember that!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Calvisius Sabinus memoria nostra fuit dives.
examples.translation: Within our own time there was a certain rich man named Calvisius Sabinus;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O felicem, qui sic aliquem vereri potest, ut ad memoriam quoque eius se conponat atque ordinet!
examples.translation: And happy also is he who can so revere a man as to calm and regulate himself by calling him to mind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to disturb, agitate
Latin: turbas excitare, discordiam moliri
Latin: res confundere

examples.original: Is erat ex hac turba lucifugarum.
examples.translation: Papinius belonged to the tribe of those who shun the light.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quicquid ex tribus defuit, turbat et cetera.
examples.translation: If any of these three be defective, there is confusion in the rest also.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ab equitibus repente invectis turbati ordines sunt Sabinorum;
examples.translation: The cavalry made a sudden charge;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: what is out of doors, an outside space or place; in partic., as opp. the house, a public place, a market-place, market (cf.: macellum, emporium, velabrum)
Latin: fines aperti/publici
Latin: platea in urbe, locus mercaturae

examples.original: Faeneratorem non fugat a foro decoctor.
examples.translation: The banker is not frightened away from the forum by the swindler.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest quam forum?
examples.translation: Yet you can live quietly even there, if necessary.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec minore saevitia foris et in exteros grassatus est.
examples.translation: Those outside his family he assailed with no less cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to stretch out, reach, extend to a place; to arrive at a place (class., esp. in the trop. signif.); constr. with
Latin: Ad aliquem locum extendere
Latin: Alicuius interesse

examples.original: Hoc pertinet circiter milia passuum quingenta.
examples.translation: This side stretches about five hundred miles.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non enim prohibentur opera eius omnia, sed tantum ad alios pertinentia;
examples.translation: For all his functions are not checked, but only those which pertain to others;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dic Ciceronem, cuius libri ad philosophiam pertinentes paene totidem sunt, quot Fabiani;
examples.translation: Cicero, let us say, whose books on philosophy are almost as numerous as those of Fabianus.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the lower atmosphere
Latin: Gasium quod spiramus et terram circulat

examples.original: Hic est locus solvendi aeris alieni.
examples.translation: Now is the time for me to pay my debt.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aera non potuit Minos, alia omnia clausit;
examples.translation: The air Minos could not close, though he had closed all else;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Utque ferox Phalaris, lingua prius ense resecta More bovis Paphio clausus in aere gemas.
examples.translation: And like fierce Phalaris, thy tongue first severed with the sword, mayst thou bellow like an ox imprisoned in Paphian bronze.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a weapon used for fighting at a distance; a missile weapon, missile, as a dart, spear, javelin, etc.

examples.original: Nullum telum in corpore eius sedet;
examples.translation: No missile can settle in her body;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Magnis telis magna portenta feriuntur.
examples.translation: It takes great weapons to strike down great monsters.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qua sua Penteliden proles est ulta Lycurgum, Haec maneat teli te quoque plaga novi.
examples.translation: As his own offspring was revenged upon Lycurgus, the Pentelid, so may the stroke of a strange weapon await thee also.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: arrive at, reach a place.
Latin: Ad finem viae ire
Latin: In potestate alicuius ire

examples.original: Ad verum sine decretis non pervenitur;
examples.translation: But one cannot attain the truth without doctrines;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quando ad hoc gaudium pervenire continget?
examples.translation: When will it be your lot to attain this joy?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His rebus constitutis Caesar ad portum Itium cum legionibus pervenit.
examples.translation: When these matters had been settled Caesar proceeded with the legions to the Itian port.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: an open place for observation, marked out by the augur with his staff
Latin: Spatium patēns observātiōnī auguralī
Latin: Spatium dēdicātum deitātī; locus adōrātiōnī dīvīnae; sacellum
entries.etymology: From PIE *tem- 'cut'; Greek τέμνω 'cut' is related.

examples.original: De sacris loquimur et de templis;
examples.translation: We talk of sacred rites and temples;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haerentem dubiamque premens in templa sacerdos Inpulit.
examples.translation: When still she paused and hesitated, the priest thrust her by force into the temple.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Captivam pecuniam in aedificationem eius templi seposuit.
examples.translation: The money from the captured city he put aside to build this temple.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to look at, behold; to gaze at, watch, observe, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: adspicio, speculor, conspicor, contueor).
Latin: Oculis attentis aspicere
Latin: iacere, locatum esse

examples.original: Ipse te specta, ipse te lauda.
examples.translation: Be your own spectator; seek your own applause.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hos ludos spectavit e proscaeni fastigio.
examples.translation: These plays he viewed from the top of the proscenium.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Qui se spectat et propter hoc ad amicitiam venit, male cogitat.
examples.translation: He who regards himself only, and enters upon friendships for this reason, reckons wrongly.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a service, office, post, employment, function, duty (class.; syn.: officium, ministerium, honos).
Latin: Res, quae alicui datur et quam reddere illi necesse non est
Latin: Donum; res, quae alicui datur et quam reddere illi necesse non est

examples.original: Ex eodem tibi munere plura exempla promisi.
examples.translation: I have promised you, however, some more illustrations drawn from the same games.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam is gravis annis non militaribus solum sed civilibus quoque abscesserat muneribus;
examples.translation: This man, bowed down with years, had already withdrawn not only from military but even from civic duties;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Munus vigiliarum senatores, qui per aetatem ac valetudinem poterant, per se ipsi obibant;
examples.translation: The watchmen’s duty was performed by those of the senators themselves whose years and strength admitted of it;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to be silent, i. e. not to speak, to say nothing, hold one's peace (therefore more limited in signif. than silere, to be still, to make no noise)
Latin: Non loqui, nihil dicere, silere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; cŭi, cĭtum, 2

examples.original: Cornelii Taciti Dialogus De Oratoribus 1.
examples.translation: Cornelius Tacitus A Dialogue on Oratory 1.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Qui rem non tacuerit, non tacebit auctorem.
examples.translation: And he who tells tales will tell names, too.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Apud Pythagoram discipulis quinque annis tacendum erat;
examples.translation: Pythagoras made his pupils keep silence for five years;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be useful or
Latin: Pro aliquo esse (cum dativo)
Latin: habere vim salutarem in medicina

examples.original: Quid tum claustra montium profutura?
examples.translation: In that case, what will the mountain barriers avail us?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Remedia non prosunt, nisi inmorantur.
examples.translation: Remedies do not avail unless they remain in the system.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid per se peregrinatio prodesse cuiquam potuit?
examples.translation: What benefit has travel of itself ever been able to give anyone?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: as you will, as much as you will or like, ever so much, ever so; hence, to designate a very high degree, as much as possible, very much, exceedingly (class.)
Latin: coniunctio concessiva, quaedam res aliter indicat, sed

examples.original: Paupertas si malum est, mendicus esse beatus nemo potest quamvis sit sapiens.
examples.translation: If poverty is an evil, no beggar can be happy, be he as wise as you like.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ratio ista quam defendis, praecepta quae didicisti, quae probas, funditus evertunt amicitiam, quamvis eam Epicurus, ut facit, in caelum efferat laudibus.
examples.translation: The system you uphold, the principles you have studied and accept, undermine the very foundations of friendship, however much Epicurus may, as he does, praise friendship up to the skies.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et quamvis conscientia tibi tua fiduciam faciat, tamen quia multa extra causam valent, et quod aequissimum est spera, et ad id te quod est iniquissimum conpara.
examples.translation: Although your conscience makes you confident, yet, since many things have weight which are outside your case,a both hope for that which is utterly just, and prepare yourself against that which is utterly unjust.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to uncover, make or lay bare.
Latin: Pando, quod clausum erat, tollere operimentum
Latin: Reclūdere

examples.original: Omnia enim vitia in aperto leniora sunt;
examples.translation: For all unconcealed vices are less serious;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is terror obstructas mentis consiliis ducis aperuit.
examples.translation: This alarming danger opened their obstinate ears to the plans of their general.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sed quid attinet de rebus tam apertis plura requirere?
examples.translation: But what is the point of inquiring further into matters so obvious?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: comm., one who is in the flower of his or
Latin: Qui non diu natus est
Latin: Homo qui 20–40 annos natus est

examples.original: Non ira saltem, iuvenes, pietate remota Stabitis?
examples.translation: If duty be disregarded, will not rage at least make you stand your ground, ye soldiers?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Turpis et ridicula res est elementarius senex; iuveni parandum, seni utendum est.
examples.translation: An old man learning his A B C is a disgraceful and absurd object;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non ego per praeceps et acuta cacumina vadam, Nec iuvenum quisquam me duce captus erit.
examples.translation: I am not the man to go by precipitous paths and rocky heights; no youth under my leadership will be captured.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to measure, mete (lands, corn); also, to measure or mete out, to deal out, distribute by measure (class.).
Latin: Mensuram facere, longitudinem, latitudinem, ponderem etc. invenire

examples.original: Sed si sapis, omnia humana condicione metire;
examples.translation: If, however, you are wise, measure all things according to the state of man;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quia non ostrea illi Lucrina in ipsa mensa aperiuntur?
examples.translation: Or because he does not have Lucrinea oysters opened fresh at his table?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec ubicumque apparuit, omnia eiusdem mensurae ac pretii sunt.
examples.translation: For such critics think that whatever they themselves cannot do, is not done;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Moving in two directions alternately, vibrating to and fro, fluctuating (cf. ambiguus, anceps, incertus, perplexus, duplex).

examples.original: Id vero regnum haud dubie videri.
examples.translation: But this was unmistakable tyranny. Men mourned for liberty as for ever lost;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vis scire, quam dubium adhuc sit?
examples.translation: Do you wish to know how uncertain it still is?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haerentem dubiamque premens in templa sacerdos Inpulit.
examples.translation: When still she paused and hesitated, the priest thrust her by force into the temple.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a Roman cognomen in the gens Tullia.
Latin: Cognomen Romanum gentis Tulliae

examples.original: Nomen Attici perire Ciceronis epistulae non sinunt.
examples.translation: Cicero’s letters keep the name of Atticus from perishing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aptissimum tamen videtur mihi, quo Cicero usus est: cavillationes vocat.
examples.translation: But the word which Cicero used seems to me most suitable: he calls them cavillationes.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: An ille Ciceroni invideret, qui mihi videtur ne Caesari quidem invidisse?
examples.translation: Why, he does not seem to me to have felt any for Julius Caesar himself.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to pronounce a decision respecting something; to decide, judge, determine, decree; to vote for any thing (very freq. and class.).—Const. with

examples.original: Ad verum sine decretis non pervenitur;
examples.translation: But one cannot attain the truth without doctrines;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Negat oportuisse quidquam uni extra ordinem decerni.
examples.translation: He denies the propriety of decreeing any extraordinary function to an individual.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Caesar his de causis quas commemoravi Rhenum transire decreverat;
examples.translation: For the reasons above mentioned Caesar had decided to cross the Rhine;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: in, the simple

examples.original: Nullum telum in corpore eius sedet;
examples.translation: No missile can settle in her body;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Oportet me sedere: tunc demum sedeo.
examples.translation: Or suppose that I ought to seat myself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Lucretiam sedentem maestam in cubiculo inveniunt.
examples.translation: Lucretia they found sitting sadly in her chamber.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: short, little, of small extent, in space and time
Latin: Parvam distantiam inter fines suos habens, longitudine parvus
Latin: Parvum tempus durans

examples.original: Nulla vita est non brevis.
examples.translation: There is no life that is not short.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Brevissima ad divitias per contemptum divitiarum via est.
examples.translation: The shortest cut to riches is to despise riches.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His vivus furiis agitabere, mortuus isdem, Et brevior poena vita futura tua est.
examples.translation: Cruel thongs shall crack and twined serpents hiss, and torches smoke before thy guilty face.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Unavoidable, inevitable, indispensable, necessary (class.; cf.: opus, usus est)

examples.original: Quisquis enim sentit quemadmodum sit affectus, eum necesse est aut in voluptate esse aut in dolore.
examples.translation: A man who is conscious of his condition at all must necessarily feel either pleasure or pain.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Principio omnibus ab rebus, quascumque videmus, perpetuo fluere ac mitti spargique necessest corpora quae feriant oculos visumque lacessant.
examples.translation: In the first place, from everything that we see there must of necessity continually flow and discharge and scatter bodies which strike our eyes and excite vision.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Si nihil \[in eo quod perficiendum est\] praeter motum ingeni quendam, id est, rationem, necesse est huic ultimum esse ex virtute agere;
examples.translation: If it is a creature consisting solely of a certain operation of the intellect, that is, reason, its highest good must be activity in accordance with virtue, since virtue is reason’s consummation.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to pour, pour out, shed.

examples.original: Non vagatur, quod fixum atque fundatum est.
examples.translation: But that which is settled and solid does not wander from its place.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita fusi Volsci Antiates, Corioli oppidum captum;
examples.translation: Thus the men of Antium were routed, and Corioli was won.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ibi impedire opus conatos hostes fundit fugatque;
examples.translation: There, when the enemy sought to hinder the work, he defeated and routed them;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a seeing, sight, look, view
Latin: Aspectus, visus
Latin: Forma

examples.original: Rursus animalia in quas species seco?
examples.translation: They are either perishable or imperishable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non speciem agminis Gallorum per Tarpeiam rupem scandentis?
examples.translation: Could they not see the line of Gauls scaling the Tarpeian Rock?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: beloved, dear, acceptable, pleasing, agreeable

examples.original: His ego gratiora dictu alia esse scio;
examples.translation: I know that there are other things more pleasant to hear;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Omnia facienda sunt, ut quam gratissimi simus.
examples.translation: We should try by all means to be as grateful as possible.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Scilicet ut pudor est quaedam coepisse priorem, Sic alio gratum est incipiente pati.
examples.translation: In truth, just as there is shame sometimes in beginning first, so when another begins it is pleasant to submit.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: at any time, ever (opp. never; cf. aliquando); most freq. in neg. clauses, sometimes also in interrogations and in conditional clauses; but very seldom in affirmations.

examples.original: Immo contra nolo tibi umquam deesse laetitiam.
examples.translation: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Detrahendas praeteritorum dolorum conquestiones puto et illa verba: ”Nulli umquam fuit peius.
examples.translation: I hold that we should do away with complaint about past sufferings and with all language like this;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex hac fuga protinus, quae undique convenerant, auxilia discesserunt, neque post id tempus umquam summis nobiscum copiis hostes contenderunt.
examples.translation: After this rout the succours which had assembled from all quarters took their departure; and never afterwards did the enemy engage us at their full strength.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To bring, bear, or carry together, to collect, gather (freq. and class.).
Latin: Vehere vel portare res ad unum punctum
Latin: Ad pugnam ferre, portare

examples.original: Ad haec ergo remedia te confer.
examples.translation: These, then, are the remedies to which you should have recourse.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Latini ex fuga se Minturnas contulerunt.
examples.translation: The Latins fled to Minturnae.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed non multum ad tranquillitatem locus confert;
examples.translation: The place where one lives, however, can contribute little towards tranquillity;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: just, upright, righteous.
Latin: Cui rectitudo et ius ascribitur

examples.original: Acuebat hac moderatione tam iusta studia;
examples.translation: Such moderation but intensified the well-merited enthusiasm of his friends;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fortiorem fac iam, iustiorem, temperantiorem. Nondum exerceri vacat;
examples.translation: I have not yet the opportunity to make use of my training;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si nos tam iustum odium nihil movet, ne illa quidem, oro vos, movent?
examples.translation: If so just grounds of resentment have no power to move us, pray have the following considerations none?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: different, manifold, changing, varying, various (cf.: diversus, distinctus).

examples.original: Quam copiose ac varie vexavit antiquos!
examples.translation: With what readiness and versatility did he make war upon the ancients!
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sparsit et missilia variarum rerum et panaria cum obsonio viritim divisit;
examples.translation: He also threw about gifts of various kinds, and gave each man a basket of prepared food.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Pausanias Lacedaemonius magnus homo, sed varius in omni genere vitae fuit;
examples.translation: Pausanias the Lacedaemonian was a great man, but untrustworthy in all the relations of life;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: present; at hand; in person
Latin: Qui adest
Latin: Qui est in conspectu

examples.original: Nemo tantum praesentibus miser est.
examples.translation: The present alone can make no man wretched.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nisi praesentia prodesse non possunt;
examples.translation: And unless things are in the present, they cannot be helpful;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non potest ferre sententiam, nisi in rem praesentem perductus est.
examples.translation: They cannot record their opinion unless they are brought face to face with a fact;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: rub to pieces; to bruise, grind, bray, triturate (syn.: frico, tundo, pinso).

examples.original: Lustrum a censoribus ter conditum est.
examples.translation: The census was thrice taken by the censors.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non arma movendi Iam locus est pressis, stipataque membra teruntur;
examples.translation: The crowded soldiers have no longer space to ply their weapons;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Illa potest vigiles flammas extinguere Vestae, Et rapere e templis, Inachi, sacra tuis, Et dare mixta viro tritis aconita cicutis, Accepto venerem munere siqua negat.
examples.translation: That woman could extinguish Vesta’s watchful flame, and rob thy temple, Inachis, of its sanctities, and give aconite mixed with pounded hemlock to her lover, who receives a gift and then denies her favours.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to take or seize beforehand

examples.original: Sed ex praecepto quoque facies ;
examples.translation: But you will be acting according to their precept also;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aut augemus dolorem aut fingimus aut praecipimus.
examples.translation: We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quibus imperatum erat diligenter praeceptum curant.
examples.translation: Those to whom these orders had been given executed them to the letter.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: to occasion loss or damage to, to harm, damage = damno afficere

examples.original: Minucia virgo Vestalis incesti damnata est.
examples.translation: Minucia, a Vestal virgin, was convicted of unchastity.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Volscius damnatus Lanuvium in exsilium abiit.
examples.translation: Volscius was condemned and went into exile at Lanuvium.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lugerent.
examples.translation: The relatives of the victims were forbidden to mourn for them.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to mix, mingle, to intermingle, blend (for the difference between this word and temperare, v. below, II. A.; cf. confundo).
Latin: Simul res plures confundere

examples.original: Luna suis vicibus Tethyn terrenaque miscet;
examples.translation: The changes of the moon bring sea and land in contact.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quis sapiens blandis non misceat oscula verbis?
examples.translation: Who that is wise would not mingle kisses with coaxing words?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iam non excussis torquentur tela lacertis, Nec longinqua cadunt iaculato volnera ferro, Miscenturque manus.
examples.translation: No longer were weapons hurled from vigorous arms, no longer were the wounds of the hurtling steel inflicted at a distance;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to furnish with weapons

examples.original: Hae erant armata circiter milia lx.
examples.translation: These amounted to some sixty thousand men under arms.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ad contemptum nos doloris armavimus;
examples.translation: We have armed ourselves to scorn pain;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Huius te amor contra durissima armabit.
examples.translation: The love of reason will arm you against the greatest hardships.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the day seems too long for me.—In the

examples.original: Nihil perdis ex tuo tempore;
examples.translation: You are throwing away none of your own time;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qui se habet, nihil perdidit.
examples.translation: He that owns himself has lost nothing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sapiens autem nihil perdere potest;
examples.translation: But the wise man can lose nothing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to find, find out, discern; to get, procure, obtain

examples.original: Item Marcus Mettius repertus et ad eum reductus est.
examples.translation: Marcus Mettius also was discovered and brought back to Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quare aliud aliquod, Torquate, hominis summum bonum reperiendum est;
examples.translation: Therefore we are bound, Torquatus, to find some other Chief Good for man.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: His enim rebus detractis negat se reperire in asotorum vita quod reprendat.
examples.translation: Eliminate those passions, he says, and he cannot find anything to blame in a life of profligacy.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: not common with others
Latin: Qui non communiter habetur; ipsius; specialis

examples.original: Proprium autem est nocentium trepidare.
examples.translation: But it is the property of guilt to be in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie.
examples.translation: The evil joys of the mind,c his words are eloquent, but not strictly appropriate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnes species conplecti non possumus, atqui singulae propria exigunt;
examples.translation: We cannot include all the types, and yet each type requires separate treatment;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: iron.
Latin: Elementum chemicum cuius numerus atomicus 26 est
Latin: Ferramentum, instrumentum ferreum

examples.original: Non fuit illi opus ferro, non sanguine;
examples.translation: No need had he of sword or of bloodshed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non galea, non scuto repellitur ferrum.
examples.translation: What is the need of defensive armour, or of skill?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si furit aut, quod furori simile est, irascitur, turbatum esse corporis motum nec ire, sed ferri?
examples.translation: That madness in the soul, or anger (which resembles madness), hastens our bodily movements from walking to rushing?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: full, filled with any thing (class.; cf.: refertus, oppletus).
Latin: possibilem plurimum tenēns; complētus, implētus
Latin: esse implētus alicuius

examples.original: Haec bona non crescunt, si plena sunt.
examples.translation: These goods, if they are complete, do not increase;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quantum defuerat pleno post oscula voto?
examples.translation: After kisses how much was lacking to your vow’s fulfilment? ah!
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non facit nobilem atrium plenum fumosis imaginibus.
examples.translation: A hall full of smoke-begrimed busts does not make the nobleman.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: In partic.
Latin: ad terram planus esse, se extendere
Latin: esse aeger

examples.original: Culcita in terra iacet, ego in culcita.
examples.translation: The mattress lies on the ground, and I upon the mattress.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In uno iacetis, Non est vestrum ubicumque non estis.
examples.translation: No place is yours where you yourselves are not.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Solacia fati Carthago Mariusque tulit, pariterque iacentes Ignovere deis.
examples.translation: Carthage and Marius both drew consolation for their destiny ;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to go, walk; hence
Latin: Relinquere, ut disputationem argumenti
Latin: Locum relinquere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; cessi, cessum, 3

examples.original: Si hoc concesseris, omne honestum perît.
examples.translation: If you grant this, honour has wholly perished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: (quo quidem concesso, nihil opus est secundo;
examples.translation: (and if this be granted there is no need of the minor;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Concede nihil esse bonum nisi quod honestum sit;
examples.translation: It is like geometry: grant the premises and you must grant everything.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to long for a thing, to desire, wish

examples.original: Sabinus suos hortatus cupientibus signum dat.
examples.translation: Sabinus exhorted his troops, and gave the signal which they longed for.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ubi primum inluxit, abire sine certamine cupiunt;
examples.translation: As soon as it grew light they wished to retire without giving battle.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Qui multum habet, plus cupit; quod est argumentum nondum illum satis habere;
examples.translation: He who has much desires more—a proof that he has not yet acquired enough;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: soon, anon, directly, presently; mostly of the future (class.).
Latin: Paulo post tempus, cuius ratio habetur

examples.original: Statue sex et quinquaginta annos, quibus mox divus Augustus rem publicam rexit;
examples.translation: Count the fifty-six years in which the sainted Augustus thereafter held the helm of state;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Liberos ex tribus uxoribus tulit: ex Urgulanilla Drusum et Claudiam, ex Paetina Antoniam, ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.
examples.translation: He had children by three of his wives: by Urgulanilla, Drusus, and Claudia; by Paetina, Antonia;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hunc iuvenem Galba, quaestorem in Baetica impigre in partis suas transgressum, legioni praeposuit: mox compertum publicam pecuniam avertisse ut peculatorem flagitari iussit.
examples.translation: This youth Galba had put in command of a legion, for when he was quaestor in Baetica, he had not hesitated to join Galba’s party.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: help

examples.original: Quid ergo adversus has amissiones auxili invenimus?
examples.translation: What resource do we find, then, in the face of these losses?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Adeo in uno omnibus satis auxilii fuisse, nullam opem in tam multis uni esse?
examples.translation: When one man had been quite able to help them all, was there no help in so many men for one?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hisce ego auxiliis studentibus atque incitatis uti me, Laterensis, potuisse confiteor;
examples.translation: Of these helpers, Laterensis, so zealous and so enthusiastic, I admit that I might have availed myself.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a wound (cf.: ictus, cicatrix).

examples.original: Non opus est vasto vulnere dividere praecordia;
examples.translation: If you would pierce your heart, a gaping wound is not necessary;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Prospectu tenebris adempto multa utrimque vulnera accipiuntur.
examples.translation: As the darkness made it impossible to see far, many wounds were received on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Vidi ego, quod fuerat primo sanabile, vulnus Dilatum longae damna tulisse morae.
examples.translation: I have seen a wound, that at first was healable, by tarrying suffer the penalty of long delay.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: After that, after, as soon as, when (class., but rare in Cic., who commonly writes postea quam; v. postea); constr. usually with histor. pres., or
Latin: indicans statum post aliquam rem
Latin: ''indicans statum post aliquam rem

examples.original: Postquam id animum advertit, copias suas Caesar in proximum collem subducit equitatumque qui sustineret hostium impetum misit.
examples.translation: As soon as he remarked this, Caesar withdrew his troops to the nearest hill, and sent the horse to check the enemy’s charge.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed postquam subrepentibus vitiis in tyrannidem regna conversa sunt, opus esse legibus coepit, quas et ipsas inter initia tulere sapientes.
examples.translation: But when once vice stole in and kingdoms were transformed into tyrannies, a need arose for laws;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil ex eo tempore praetermissum est ad maiestatem eius augendam ac multo magis, postquam Agrippa abdicato atque seposito certum erat, uni spem successionis incumbere.
examples.translation: From this time on nothing was left undone which could add to his prestige, especially after the disowning and banishment of Agrippa made it clear that the hope of the succession lay in him alone.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the forms of gods, for gods
Latin: Facies et structura rei

examples.original: Muri autem omnes Gallici hac fere forma sunt.
examples.translation: All Gallic walls are, as a rule, of the following pattern.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: A! nimia est iuveni propriae fiducia formae, Expectat siquis, dum prior illa roget.
examples.translation: Ah, too confident in his own charms is a lover, if he wait until she ask him first.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iam valida admodum numero manus erat nec quicquam ad iusti exercitus formam praeter ducem deerat.
examples.translation: They were soon a very numerous body, and lacked no essential element of an army except a general.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the state or condition of a freeman, a being free, freedom, liberty, freedom from restraint or obligation, free will, etc.
Latin: Status quo liber es
Latin: L~: myth. Dea libertatis

examples.original: Haec libertas eius est, haec evagatio;
examples.translation: There it has its liberty, there it can roam abroada;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Causa tibi libertatis fui, ero et argumentum;
examples.translation: I have been the cause of your freedom, and I shall also be its proof;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo perducta res erat, ut aut libertas Scipioni aut Scipio libertati faceret iniuriam.
examples.translation: Matters had gone so far that either liberty must work harm to Scipio, or Scipio to liberty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: food for man and beast, victuals, fare, nutriment, fodder
Latin: Omne id, quo homines et animalia vēscuntur, ēsca, pābulum

examples.original: Non potest medicus per epistulas cibi aut balinei tempus eligere;
examples.translation: The physician cannot prescribe by letter the proper time for eating or bathing;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Singulis ibi militibus Vitellius paratos cibos ut gladiatoriam saginam dividebat;
examples.translation: There Vitellius was distributing cooked rations to each soldier, as if he were fattening gladiators;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Non est quod post cibum studeas, non est quod plenis oculis ac tumentibus imperes;
examples.translation: There is no reason why you should study immediately after eating;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a leader
Latin: Qui ducit
Latin: Qui ducit. dux itineris dux praefectusque classis

examples.original: Nunc flere potestas, Dum pendet fortuna ducum;
examples.translation: Do not delay your grief, nor keep it for the crowning sorrows.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Sedulius, dux et princeps Lemovicum, occiditur;
examples.translation: Sedulius, commander and chief of the Lemovices, was killed;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Is terror obstructas mentis consiliis ducis aperuit.
examples.translation: This alarming danger opened their obstinate ears to the plans of their general.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to go over or across, to cross over, pass over, pass by
Latin: (Intrans.) Ultra īre
Latin: Transgredi

examples.original: Transire in aliud non potest.
examples.translation: They cannot change into anything else.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis medicus aegros in transitu curat?
examples.translation: What physician can heal his patient on a flying visit?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hanc si nostri transirent, hostes exspectabant;
examples.translation: The enemy waited to see whether our men would cross it;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to throw, add, apply; to attach
Latin: Iacere (aliquid alicui rei); ponere (aliquid) prope (aliquid). trop. Adicere (animum, oculos, etc. alicui rei)
Latin: Iacere (aliquid alicui rei); ponere (aliquid) prope (aliquid)

examples.original: Adicio dolores continuos et graves;
examples.translation: I add afflictions which are unceasing and severe;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Multum enim adicit sibi virtus lacessita;
examples.translation: For manliness gains much strength by being challenged;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si quid adiecisset, fuisset simile praeterito.
examples.translation: Had another year been added, it would merely have been like the past.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a great number, multitude (class.; cf.: copia, vis, magnitudo).
Latin: Numerus magnus homines rerumve, collective
Latin: Grex magnus hominum

examples.original: Ad eam multitudinem urbs quoque amplificanda visa est.
examples.translation: Eighty thousand citizens are said to have been registered in that census;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Utrumne ingentis multitudinis causa, quae nondum erat?
examples.translation: Is it because of the great number of people?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Concitata multitudo erat certamenque instare videbatur.
examples.translation: The crowd was deeply moved and a conflict appeared to be imminent.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a city-gate, a gate.
Latin: Aditus urbis, vel alterius loci vallo fossave muniti, qua res importantur, ex exportantur
Latin: ianua

examples.original: Portis fores altioresque turres imposuit.
examples.translation: At the gateways he set doors and higher turrets.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sabinis proditae portae per virginem Tarpeiam.
examples.translation: To the Sabines the gates of Rome were betrayed by the maiden Tarpeia.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Vercingetorix iubet portas claudi, ne castra nudentur.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix ordered the gates to be shut, lest the camp should be deserted.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: beyond measure, excessive, too great, too much.

examples.original: Ne nimium in metu alieno spei ponerent;
examples.translation: Let them not trust too much to other men’s fears;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nimius honos inter secunda rebus adversis in solacium cessit.
examples.translation: These excessive honours in prosperity presently became a solace in misfortune.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quae enim res alia civiles furores peperit quam nimiae felicitates?
examples.translation: For what else produced those outbursts of domestic strife but excessive prosperity?
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to pursue something in the mind (cf. agito, II.), i. e.
Latin: Facultatibus intellectualibus uti
Latin: In animo habere

examples.original: De hoc loco aliquid cogitemus.
examples.translation: Let us reflect a moment on this topic.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cogitat semper, qualis vita, non quanta sit.
examples.translation: He always reflects concerning the quality, and not the quantity, of his life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum aspexeris, quot te antecedant, cogita, quot sequantur.
examples.translation: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a breathing or gentle blowing of air, a breath, breeze (syn.: aura, flatus).

examples.original: Quid enim est aliud animus quam quodam modo se habens spiritus?
examples.translation: For what else is the soul than air in a certain state?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita enim senectus honesta est, si se ipsa defendit, si ius suum retinet, si nemini emancipata est, si usque ad ultimum spiritum dominatur in suos.
examples.translation: For just as I approve of the young man in whom there is a touch of age, so I approve of the old man in whom there is some of the flavour of youth.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ut quid dicit similiter: Spiritus adiuvat infirmitatem nostram, si natura nostra sic creata est, ut spiritu ad opera iustitiae non indigeat adiuvari?
examples.translation: And why does he likewise say, ”The Spirit helpeth our infirmities,”f if our nature is created such that it does not need any help from the Spirit to do the works of righteousness?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: To reckon, calculate
Latin: Putare, opinari, censere

examples.original: Sic Numitori ad supplicium Remus deditur.
examples.translation: So Remus was given up to Numitor to be punished.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Homines optimi non intellegunt totam rationem everti si ita res se habeat.
examples.translation: These worthy people do not realize that, if this is true, it upsets the theory altogether.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque eleganter illis Catulus absoluto reo, ”quid vos,” inquit, ”praesidium a nobis petebatis?
examples.translation: Hence the witty remark of Catulus after the defendant had been acquitted: ”Why did you ask us for the guard?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: hard.

examples.original: Huius te amor contra durissima armabit.
examples.translation: The love of reason will arm you against the greatest hardships.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Durius tractandum est, ne animo male pareat.
examples.translation: The body should be treated more rigorously, that it may not be disobedient to the mind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare quaedam dura patiuntur? Ut alios pati doceant;
examples.translation: It is that they may teach others to endure them;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to bring, lay or put together (very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Latin: Plura coacervando facere, aedificare, instituere
Latin: cond|ō, -ere, condidī, conditum

examples.original: Census actus est, lustrum conditum.
examples.translation: The census was taken and the lustrum closed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et hi mortem timent, in quam se vivi condiderunt?
examples.translation: Do these men fear death, if they have buried themselves alive?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic omnem militarem disciplinam artemque bellandi condidit.
examples.translation: It was he who founded all military discipline and the art of warfare.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: nearest, next

examples.original: Sed quod proximum fuit non vidit.
examples.translation: But he failed to see what this involved.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Proximus a tectis ignis defenditur aegre;
examples.translation: A fire next door is ill repulsed;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nobis solvi perire est, proxima enim intuemur;
examples.translation: To our minds, this process means perishing, for we behold only that which is nearest;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: on the upper side
Latin: In superiore loco situm
Latin: In praeterito tempore

examples.original: Caesar Atrebas venit, quem supra demonstraveram a Caesare in Britanniam praemissum.
examples.translation: Commius the Atrebatian, who, as shown above, had been sent forward by Caesar into Britain.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cicero data facultate Gallum ab eodem Verticone, quem supra demonstravimus, repetit, qui litteras ad Caesarem deferat;
examples.translation: When a chance offered, Cicero again asked Vertico, whom we mentioned above, for a Gaul to deliver a despatch to Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Satis constat ne Ciceroni quidem obtrectatores defuisse, quibus inflatus et tumens, nec satis pressus sed supra modum exsultans et superfluens et parum Atticus videretur.
examples.translation: Cicero himself, as is well known, had his detractors: they thought him turgid and puffy, wanting in conciseness, inordinately exuberant and redundant—in short, not Attic enough.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to go away, depart.
Latin: Ire a loco; exire; Ire ab aliquo, periculo fugere, a persecutore celare
Latin: Dimittere de munere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n.; ĭvi or ii, ĭtum, īre

examples.original: Cum volet, accedes: cum te vitabit, abibis;
examples.translation: When she is willing, go to her; when she shuns you, depart;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Volscius damnatus Lanuvium in exsilium abiit.
examples.translation: Volscius was condemned and went into exile at Lanuvium.
examples.author: Livy
