examples.original: Ubi primum inluxit, abire sine certamine cupiunt;
examples.translation: As soon as it grew light they wished to retire without giving battle.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a limb, member of the body (class.).

examples.original: Non arma movendi Iam locus est pressis, stipataque membra teruntur;
examples.translation: The crowded soldiers have no longer space to ply their weapons;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quam multa ab iis conquisita et collecta sunt de omnium animantium genere, ortu, membris, aetatibus!
examples.translation: What stores of facts they observed and recorded about the classification, reproduction, morphology and life-history of animals of every kind!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Membraque vinxerunt tinctis ferrugine pannis, A male deserto quos rapuere rogo: Et, ne non fultum nuda tellure iaceret, Molle super silices inposuere caput.
examples.translation: They swathed his limbs in bands of dusky hue, snatched from a pyre abandoned as accursed; and lest it lie unpropped on the naked earth they set a flint-stone beneath his baby head.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a wave, billow, surge (syn. fluctus).
Latin: Moles procedens superficiei liquidi, ut maris; fluctus

examples.original: Per Styga detur iter, Stygias transnabimus undas;
examples.translation: Should a way be given me by Styx, o’er the Stygian waters we will swim;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cruor altus in unda Spumat, et obducti concreto sanguine fluctus.
examples.translation: Their blood foamed deep upon the wave, and a crust of gore covered the sea.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hinc montes natura vagis circumdedit undis, Qui Libyae te, Nile, negent;
examples.translation: From this point Nature has surrounded the wandering stream with mountains, which rob Libya of the Nile;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: After the division of the Roman people by Servius Tullius into six (or, the citizens who paid tribute alone being reckoned, into five) classes
Latin: Omnes populi qui statum definitum vel copiam pecuniae definitam habent
Latin: exercitus (vetus usus)

examples.original: In classem cadit omne nemus;
examples.translation: Cohorts are raised to their full strength with recruits;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Octo nimirum legiones unius classis accessionem fore.
examples.translation: No doubt eight legions are to go over to one poor fleet!
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Bormam et Gesoriacum pontibus iunxit classibusque firmavit.
examples.translation: He built bridges at Borma and Gesoriacum, and left fleets to protect them.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: shore, seashore, coast, strand; river bank; beach, landing place
Latin: Maris margo, vel regio inter mare et terram

examples.original: Cilicum per litora tutus Parva puppe fugit.
examples.translation: Now he flees unharmed along the coast of the pirates in his little vessel.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Coepi gubernatorem rogare, ut me in aliquo litore exponeret.
examples.translation: I began to ask the pilot to put me ashore somewhere;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cuius loci haec erat natura, atque ita montibus angustis mare continebatur, uti ex locis superioribus in litus telum adigi posset.
examples.translation: Such was the nature of the ground, so steep the heights which banked the sea, that a missile could be hurled from the higher levels on to the shore.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a being worthy, worth, worthiness, merit, desert (so, rarely, and perh. only in Cic.)
Latin: auctoritas, maiestas
Latin: (a "dignus") auctoritas, maiestas

examples.original: Confragosa in fastigium dignitatis via est;
examples.translation: It is a rough road that leads to the heights of greatness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnis est enim de virtutis dignitate contentio.
examples.translation: For the whole dispute turns on the true worth of virtue.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Senatoriam dignitatem recusantibus equestrem quoque ademit.
examples.translation: If any refused senatorial rank, he took from them that of knight also.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: sound, whole, healthy, physically or mentally (cf.: integer, incolumis, sospes, salvus).
Latin: Morbis vacans

examples.original: Pauca mutat, vel plura sane;
examples.translation: He makes a few modifications, or indeed a good many;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid tibi mentis erat, cum sic male sana lateres, Procri?
examples.translation: What were thy feelings, Procris, when thus frantic thou lurkedst there?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Illo sano ac valente oratio quoque robusta, fortis, virilis est;
examples.translation: When the soul is sound and strong, the style too is vigorous, energetic, manly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to overlay with gold, to gild: a metallorum quoque nominibus solent nasci verba, ut ab auro auro, auras

examples.original: Quis posuit secretam in auro dapem?
examples.translation: Who uses gold plate when he dines alone?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Minucius index bove aurata donatus est.
examples.translation: Lucius Minucius gave evidence against him and was presented with a gilded ox.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nulla ad aures nostras vox inpune perfertur;
examples.translation: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a staff (carried by persons of wealth, rank, high official station, etc.)

examples.original: Nihil mali accidisse Scipioni puto;
examples.translation: I believe that no ill has befallen Scipio;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Igitur in alium Scipionem conversa res publica finem belli reposcebat.
examples.translation: The State, therefore, turned to another Scipio and demanded that he should complete the war.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Eo perducta res erat, ut aut libertas Scipioni aut Scipio libertati faceret iniuriam.
examples.translation: Matters had gone so far that either liberty must work harm to Scipio, or Scipio to liberty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a train, i. e. a collected multitude in motion or moving forwards; of things of any kind, but esp. (so most freq. in prose) of men or animals. —
Latin: Res vel grex agitatus
Latin: Exercitus

examples.original: Consistit agmen; impedimenta intra legiones recipiuntur.
examples.translation: The column halted, and the baggage was drawn back inside the legions.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Postquam impulsos sensit Antonius, denso agmine obturbabat.
examples.translation: After Antonius saw that they were shaken, he assailed them in mass formation.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Non speciem agminis Gallorum per Tarpeiam rupem scandentis?
examples.translation: Could they not see the line of Gauls scaling the Tarpeian Rock?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: turned back or backwards, back, backwards (opp. prorsus): rursus retro, Non.

examples.original: Vide rursus retro. Dato hoc, dandum est illud.
examples.translation: Or again conversely: given the latter, you must grant the former.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In Hispaniam missi Gnaeus et Publius Scipiones paene totam Poenis eripuerant, sed insidiis Punicae fraudis oppressi rursum amiserant, magnis quidem illi proeliis cum Punicas opes cecidissent.
examples.translation: The two Scipios, Gnaeus and Publius, were sent into Spain and had wrested practically the whole of the country from the Carthaginians;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Licet hic rursus ea commemores quae optimis verbis ab Epicuro de laude amicitiae dicta sunt.
examples.translation: It is no good your once again repeating Epicurus’s admirable remarks in praise of friendship.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be away from, be absent.
Latin: Esse a loco; non esse in loco
Latin: distantiam habere ab aliquo loco

examples.original: Tormenta abesse a me velim;
examples.translation: I should prefer to be free from torture;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ab ipsa enim semper tantundem absumus.
examples.translation: For death itself is always the same distance from us;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et quae praeterierunt et quae futura sunt, absunt;
examples.translation: Past and future are both absent;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a fleeing, flight, a running away (cf.: effugium, exsilium).

examples.original: His rebus fugae similem profectionem effecit.
examples.translation: By this means he made his departure like a rout.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nostri, simul in arido constiterunt, suis omnibus consecutis in hostes impetum fecerunt atque eos in fugam dederunt;
examples.translation: The moment our men stood firm on dry land, they charged with all their comrades close behind, and put the enemy to rout;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Melius in Volscis imperatum est; fusi primo proelio hostes fugaque in urbem Antium, ut tum res erant, opulentissimam, acti.
examples.translation: The Volscian expedition was better directed: the enemy were routed in the first engagement and driven in flight to Antium, a very opulent city for those days.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: an even, flat place, a plain, field

examples.original: Erat ex oppido Alesia despectus in campum.
examples.translation: There was a bird’s-eye view from the town of Alesia over the plain.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Bellvm Sarmaticvm Sarmatae patentibus campis inequitant.
examples.translation: The Sarmatian War The Sarmatians range on horseback over wide-spreading plains.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sed tum acrius in castris quam in campo, nostro cum milite quam cum Numantino proeliandum fuit.
examples.translation: At first he had a harder struggle in the camp than in the field, and more with our own soldiers than with the Numantines;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: an expression of countenance, the countenance, visage, as to features and expression; hence, often to be translated by features, looks

examples.original: Inprobum risus, insanum vultus habitusque demonstrat.
examples.translation: The scamp is shown up by his laugh;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erras, si istorum tibi qui occurrunt vultibus credis;
examples.translation: You are wrong to trust the countenances of those you meet.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neque enim tantum arte et scientia, sed longe magis facultate et <usu> eloquentiam contineri, nec tu, puto, abnues et hi significare vultu videntur.”
examples.translation: To this view I am sure you will not demur, and our friends here, to judge by their looks, seem to indicate concurrence.”
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: come forth.
Latin: extrā venīre, exeundō accēdere
Latin: accidere, contingere

examples.original: Quod paulo minus utrumque evenit;
examples.translation: And both predictions were all but fulfilled;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quorum nihil sapienti viro potest evenire;
examples.translation: But none of these things can happen to the sage;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Fabioque ea provincia, Plautio Hernici evenere.
examples.translation: This campaign fell to Fabius, that against the Hernici to Plautius.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to press (class.).

examples.original: Tu illum premi putas malis?
examples.translation: Do you suppose that he is weighed down by evils?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haerentem dubiamque premens in templa sacerdos Inpulit.
examples.translation: When still she paused and hesitated, the priest thrust her by force into the temple.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non arma movendi Iam locus est pressis, stipataque membra teruntur;
examples.translation: The crowded soldiers have no longer space to ply their weapons;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: an attack, assault, onset

examples.original: Prae ardore impetuque tantae rei sensus non pervenit ad militem;
examples.translation: In the ardour and enthusiasm of the soldiers so important an event passed unnoticed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Te quoque instinctum esse et magno ad pulcherrima properare impetu video.
examples.translation: I see that you also have been aroused and are hastening with great zeal towards infinite beauty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At Germani celeriter ex consuetudine sua phalange facta impetus gladiorum exceperunt.
examples.translation: But the Germans, according to their custom, speedily formed mass, and received the sword-attack.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To take or draw out.

examples.original: Quid enim mutationis periculo exceptum?
examples.translation: For what is free from the risk of change?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quam multos fama non excepit, sed eruit!
examples.translation: And how many have been ruined, not rescued, by their reputation?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ibi benigne excepti divisique in hospitia.
examples.translation: There they were kindly received and were quartered about among the citizens.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to join or unite together, connect, attach, fasten, yoke, harness.
Latin: Cōnectō (aliquid cum aliqua re)

examples.original: Nolunt sine salebra esse iuncturam;
examples.translation: They would have jolts in all their transitions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iunxit parricidio matris amitae necem.
examples.translation: To matricide he added the murder of his aunt.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Samnites nobiscum foedere iuncti sunt;
examples.translation: The Samnites and we are united by a covenant;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to increase, to nourish (orig., to produce, bring forth that not already in existence; in which signification only the derivative auctor is now found).
Latin: Alicui rei naturale incrementum ac prosperitatem praebere et adquirere
Latin: Maius facere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; auxi, auctum, 2

examples.original: Eo successu studia populi aucta;
examples.translation: This success increased the enthusiasm of the people.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Aut augemus dolorem aut fingimus aut praecipimus.
examples.translation: We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita duo deinceps reges, alius alia via, ille bello, hic pace, civitatem auxerunt.
examples.translation: Thus two successive kings in different ways, one by war, the other by peace, promoted the nation’s welfare.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to make equal; hence
Latin: Fetum edere (proprie ad feminas pertinet). Gallina ovum parit
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Non pono utrique par pretium.
examples.translation: I do not set an equal value on benefits and injuries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Item equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt.
examples.translation: The horsemen of Ariovistus halted at an equal distance.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Duo autem, quibus nihil fieri melius potest, paria sunt.
examples.translation: And two goods, neither of which can possibly be better, are equal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To force asunder
Latin: In partes separare; agere separatim

examples.original: Hoc est non dividere sed frangere.
examples.translation: This is not dividing but hacking in pieces.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Totus inter stratum lectionemque divisus est.
examples.translation: The whole time has been divided between rest and reading.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vitiosum est enim in dividendo partem in genere numerare.
examples.translation: It is a fault in division to reckon a species as a genus.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: surely, certainly, to be sure, by all means, indeed, in fact.

examples.original: Quippe suspectior illis quam morbo pallentibus color est, languidi et evanidi albent, et in vivis caro morticina est.
examples.translation: Their complexions are more alarming than those of anaemic invalids; they are lackadaisical and flabby with dropsy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quippe confitenti consultantique supererant spes viresque: cum e contrario laeta omnia fingeret, falsis ingravescebat.
examples.translation: For if he had only acknowledged the truth and sought counsel, he had still some hope and resources left;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quippe L. Vitellio quamvis infami inerat industria, nec virtutibus, ut boni, sed quo modo pessimus quisque, vitiis valebat.
examples.translation: For all his infamous nature, Lucius Vitellius possessed industry, and drew strength not like good men from their virtues, but like the basest from his vices.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to take or bear off or away, to carry off, withdraw, remove (very freq. in prose and poetry; syn.: tollo, fero, rapio, eripio, diripio, adimo, averto).
Latin: Rem aut personam a loco, ubi ipsa est, ad alium ferre
Latin: Per vim abripere

examples.original: Multas enim civitates incendium vexavit, nullam abstulit.
examples.translation: For fire has damaged many a city, but has annihilated none.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Alia condicio est in iis, quae ablata in locum suum aliquid incommodi substituunt;
examples.translation: The situation is entirely different in the case of goods whose loss entails some hardship substituted in their place;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et fuere qui se statim dederent: plures abrupto ponte instanti hosti viam abstulerunt.
examples.translation: The larger part, however, broke down the bridge and so, by cutting off the road, blocked their foes’ advance.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: at length, at last
Latin: Post longum tempus, in fine; postrēmō

examples.original: Sed quae tandem ista ratio est?
examples.translation: But what is this method, pray?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed quid ages tandem si utilitas ab amicitia, ut fit saepe, defecerit?
examples.translation: But what, pray, will you do, if, as often happens, expediency parts company with friendship?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sero tandem dispensator Argivus et hoc et ceterum truncum in privatis eius hortis Aurelia via sepulturae dedit.
examples.translation: At last, however, his steward Argivus consigned it to the tomb with the rest of the body in Galba’s private gardens on the Aurelian Road.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: Seed.

examples.original: Id quibus ut fiat rebus cognoscere possis, principio meminisse decet quae diximus ante, semina multimodis in rebus mixta teneri.
examples.translation: That you may know how this comes about, in the first place you must remember what I said before,b that things contain many seeds mingled in various ways.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Quae cum gremio mollito ac subacto sparsum semen excepit, primum id occaecatum cohibet, ex quo occatio quae hoc efficit nominata est;
examples.translation: And yet what I enjoy is not the fruit alone, but I also enjoy the soil itself, its nature and its power.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to miss or mistake any thing; to do amiss, to transgress, to commit a fault, to offend
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Quot genera tibi in hac dabo, quibus peccetur?
examples.translation: In this department, what countless varieties of fault I can show you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Esto: non fuit in me poena ulla peccati: at fuit iudicii.
examples.translation: So far so good; it was for no misdoing that I suffered retribution.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cur ergo in hoc libro, cui respondi, Abel ita hic vixisse dicit, ut nihil omnino peccaverit?
examples.translation: Why then, in the book I have replied to, does he allege that Abel lived a life that was completely without sin?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to bring, carry, or convey to; to report, introduce
Latin: Ferre rem ad locum

examples.original: Grave est manus sibi afferre;
examples.translation: It is a hardship to lay hand upon oneself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Volscorum item exercitum duce Antiati populo consedisse ad Satricum allatum est.
examples.translation: It was also reported that a Volscian army, conducted by the Antiates, had encamped at Satricum.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Is epistulas complures attulerat, in his unam domo quae totum immutarat hominem.
examples.translation: Laetilius had brought several letters, including one from home that had at once changed Metellus completely.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: name of a Roman gens.

examples.original: Antonium quaestorem cum legione duodecima sibi coniungit.
examples.translation: Marcus Antonius, the quartermaster-general, with the Twelfth Legion he attached to his own force.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In hoc homine atque in eius modi causa quid facerent omnes Crassi et Antonii?
examples.translation: With such a client, and with such a case, what would any Crassus or Antonius do?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quis tibi vaesani veniam non donet amoris, Antoni, durum cum Caesaris hauserit ignis Pectus?
examples.translation: Who can refuse pardon to the infatuation of Antony, when even the stubborn heart of Caesar took fire?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a sickness, disease, disorder, distemper, ailment, illness, malady, of body or mind (class.).
Latin: Perturbatio sanitatis (corpore vel mente)

examples.original: Senectus enim insanabilis morbus est.
examples.translation: For old age is a disease which we cannot cure.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est bona valitudo mediocritas morbi.
examples.translation: No, for good health does not mean moderate illness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ostendes morbum posse superari vel certe sustineri.
examples.translation: You will be showing that a disease can be overcome, or at any rate endured.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: room, a space (very freq. and class.).
Latin: area

examples.original: De cuius spatio atque cultu suffecerit haec rettulisse.
examples.translation: Its size and splendour will be sufficiently indicated by the following details.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Cum autem venissemus in Academiae non sine causa nobilitata spatia, solitudo erat ea quam volueramus.
examples.translation: When we reached the walks of the Academy, which are so deservedly famous, we had them entirely to ourselves, as we had hoped.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dum haec ad Gergoviam geruntur, Aedui primis nuntiis ab Litavicco acceptis nullum sibi ad cognoscendum spatium relinquunt.
examples.translation: During these operations about Gergovia the Aedui received the first messages sent by Litaviccus.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to come in sight, to appear, become visible, make one's appearance (class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: Cui non faciliora apparuere in actu?
examples.translation: To what man did they not seem easier in the doing?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Bellum domi maius quam foris apparebat.
examples.translation: The war at home seemed more important than that abroad.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec ubicumque apparuit, omnia eiusdem mensurae ac pretii sunt.
examples.translation: For such critics think that whatever they themselves cannot do, is not done;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: place into, to plant
Latin: In aliquo loco statuere, ponere
Latin: condere, fundare, componere

examples.original: Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt.
examples.translation: All these are different one from another in language, institutions, and laws.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Verum quod institui dicere, miserias cognoscite sociorum.
examples.translation: But let us return to what I began to tell you of our allies’ unhappy position.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid loquar de nobis qui ad laudem et ad decus nati, suscepti, instituti sumus?
examples.translation: But I need not speak of ourselves, whose birth, breeding and education point us towards glory and towards honour;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: unfriendly, hostile, inimical.

examples.original: Venit ad me pro amico blandus inimicus.
examples.translation: An enemy comes to me full of compliments, in the guise of a friend.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O quam inimica nobis sunt vota nostrorum!
examples.translation: Alas, how hostile to us are the wishes of our own folk!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid sperem, si plus in me audeant inimici?
examples.translation: What can I expect, if my enemies grow bolder?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to begin to do something, to take in hand (syn. incoho; in class. prose, viz. in Cic., only in the tempp. press., while coepi is used in the tempp. perff.); constr
Latin: Incoho
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; cēpi, ceptum, 3

examples.original: Itaque cogenda est, ut incipiat;
examples.translation: The mind must, therefore, be forced to make a beginning;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed iam incipiamus epistulam conplicare.
examples.translation: But now I must begin to fold up my letter.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Plus incipit habere posse, qui plus habet.
examples.translation: He who possesses more begins to be able to possess still more.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a direction, line (rare but class.).
Latin: Linea, directio
Latin: Limes, finis

examples.original: Gaium Trebonium cum pari legionum numero ad eam regionem quae ad Aduatucos adiacet depopulandam mittit;
examples.translation: Gaius Trebonius with an equal number of legions to devastate the region which adjoins the Aduatuci;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In pace nullus est communis magistratus, sed principes regionum atque pagorum inter suos ius dicunt controversiasque minuunt.
examples.translation: Acts of brigandage committed outside the borders of each several state involve no disgrace;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ex his omnibus longe sunt humanissimi qui Cantium incolunt, quae regio est maritima omnis, neque multum a Gallica differunt consuetudine.
examples.translation: Of all the Britons the inhabitants of Kent, an entirely maritime district, are by far the most civilised, differing but little from the Gallic manner of life.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: unavoidable, inevitable, indispensable, needful, requisite, necessary: necessarium ait esse Opilius Aurelius, in quo non sit cessandum, aut sine quo vivi non possit
Latin: Qui fieri debet, non evitandus
Latin: Amicus

examples.original: Quod bonum est, utique necessarium est;
examples.translation: The good must in every case be necessary;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illa res discenti magis necessaria est, haec scienti.
examples.translation: For the one teaches, the other stirs the memory.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si probationes necessariae sunt, et decreta, quae veritatem argumentis colligunt.
examples.translation: If proofs are necessary, so are doctrines; for doctrines deduce the truth by reasoning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: aged, advanced in years; and
Latin: Qui est multorum annorum (et fere dicitur de provecta aetate animantium)
Latin: Vir aut femina grandis natu

examples.original: Quaeris, quid doceam? Etiam seni esse discendum.
examples.translation: That even an old man should keep learning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec inter seniores morti destinatos iactata solacia.
examples.translation: Such were the consolations which the old men appointed to die exchanged among themselves;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: At sunt morosi et anxii et iracundi et difficiles senes.
examples.translation: But, the critics say, old men are morose, troubled, fretful, and hard to please;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a woman, a female, whether married or not.
Latin: Homo feminea
Latin: → uxor

examples.original: Itaque in partem mulieres vocatae sunt.
examples.translation: In these circumstances the two women were notified to take their shares.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ut in pauca conferam, testamento facto mulier moritur.
examples.translation: Shortly afterwards she married Aulus Caecina.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et utique maritum habebat multarum mulierum virum et deorum alienorum falsorumque cultorem.
examples.translation: And yet her husband was a man with many wives and worshipped strange, false gods.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: sacred, holy
Latin: sacer

examples.original: At ubi coepi subscribere, sancta Melania contradixit.
examples.translation: But when I began to subscribe it, the saintly Melania opposed it.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Eodem anno M. Valerius consul de provocatione legem tulit diligentius sanctam.
examples.translation: In the same year Marcus Valerius the consul proposed a law of appeal with stricter sanctions.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In hac omnes sancti patres nostri et patriarchae et prophetae et apostoli placuerunt deo;
examples.translation: In this love all our holy fathers and patriarchs and prophets and apostles pleased God;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to turn or go different ways, to part
Latin: (Intransitivē) Separari, seiungi
Latin: movere aliquid in alium locum

examples.original: O quam diversus a patre!
examples.translation: But how great the difference between him and his father!
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quas enim ex diverso legiones?
examples.translation: What are these legions that are opposed to us?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Per quae desinunt, diversa sunt;
examples.translation: The methods of ending life are different;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To give one something as a present; to present, bestow; to grant, vouchsafe, confer (freq. and class.).
Latin: Aliquid, alicui gratis dare, liberaliter tribuere
Latin: Alicui aliquid muneri dare

examples.original: Hernicis ipsum agerque dono datus.
examples.translation: The town itself and its territory were given to the Hernici.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Minucius index bove aurata donatus est.
examples.translation: Lucius Minucius gave evidence against him and was presented with a gilded ox.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hectora donavit Priamo prece motus Achilles;
examples.translation: Entreaty moved Achilles to give Hector back to Priam;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Prov.
Latin: Mandere et sorbere (cibum)
Latin: Qui voraciter seu nimis edit

examples.original: Hic plus edit, ille minus;
examples.translation: A eats more and B eats less;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Edito imperio signum secutum est.
examples.translation: The signal followed close on the announcement.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ideo non est ante edendum quam illa imperat;
examples.translation: For that reason I must not eat until hunger bids me;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to learn, to learn to know, to become acquainted with, etc.
Latin: memoriae mandare, id est: scientiam accipere, rem ignotam, aliquo docente, percipere, vel etiam meditando assequi
Latin: personam aut rem cognoscere

examples.original: Quid enim quis discere, quid imitari velit?
examples.translation: For what can a man desire to learn or to imitate in them?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid faciendum sit, a faciente discendum est.
examples.translation: What ought to be done must be learned from one who does it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illa res discenti magis necessaria est, haec scienti.
examples.translation: For the one teaches, the other stirs the memory.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to vibrate from one side to the other
Latin: Non prorsus credere, fortasse falsum esse credere

examples.original: Non dubitas, an hoc sit bonum;
examples.translation: You do not doubt whether this is a good;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod senex Megalius defunctus sit, iam vos audisse quis dubitet?
examples.translation: You will have already heard, I am sure, of the death of the Senior Megaliusa;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: An, quod ad diem non venerunt, de eorum fide constantiaque dubitatis?
examples.translation: Or do you doubt their faithfulness, their resolution, because they are not arrived to the day?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: light.

examples.original: Quid fodis inmeritis, Phineu, sua lumina natis?
examples.translation: Why piercest thou, O Phineus, the eyes of thine innocent sons?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Scaenicos ludos et assidue et varii generis ac multifariam fecit, quondam et nocturnos accensis tota urbe luminibus.
examples.translation: He exhibited stage-plays continually, of various kinds and in many different places, sometimes even by night, lighting up the whole city.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Virtutis enim beataeque vitae, quae duo maxime expetenda sunt, serius lumen apparet, multo etiam serius, ut plane qualia sint intellegantur.
examples.translation: The radiance of virtue and of happiness, the two things most to be desired, dawns upon us later, and far later still comes a full understanding of their nature.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that is below, underneath, lower; opp. superus.

examples.original: Deiectus verbo qui potest esse quisquam, nisi in inferiorem locum de superiore motus?
examples.translation: And how can anyone be literally ”ejecteda” unless he has been removed from higher to lower ground?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Utque patrem Psamathes, condat te Phoebus in ima Tartara, quod natae fecerat ille suae.
examples.translation: And like Psamathe’s sire may Phoebus bury thee in lowest Tartarus, as he had done to his own daughter.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nullum erat genus hominum in castris intactum cupiditate pugnae, summi infimique aeque intenti erant;
examples.translation: There was no class of men in camp who were not affected by the lust of battle;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to send away from one's self, to dismiss (thus, anteclass., freq. in Plaut. and Ter.): quod nos dicimus dimittere, antiqui etiam dicebant amittere, Don. ad

examples.original: Simplicis illius verbi usus amissus est.
examples.translation: The plain word has become obsolete.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Habui enim illos tamquam amissurus, amisi tamquam habeam.
examples.translation: I have lost them as if I have them still.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Infantiam amisimus, deinde pueritiam, deinde adulescentiam.
examples.translation: We lose our childhood, then our boyhood, and then our youth.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a female.
Latin: mulier, vel alia sexus parturientis
Latin: animal sexu muliebri

examples.original: Non mutata feminarum natura, sed victa est;
examples.translation: This does not mean that woman’s physique has changed, but that it has been conquered;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Libidinis in feminas profusissimae, marum omnino expers.
examples.translation: He was immoderate in his passion for women, but wholly disinterested in male partners.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et, ne te capiat latebris sibi femina notis, Non uno est omnis convenienda loco;
examples.translation: And lest the lady catch you in some well-known retreat, meet not every mistress in one spot;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: altogether, wholly, entirely, utterly, at all (syn.: prorsus, penitus): Neoptolemus apud Ennium philosophari sibi ait necesse esse, sed paucis

examples.original: Expeditionem unam omnino suscepit eamque modicam.
examples.translation: He made but one campaign and that of little importance.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ex Antonia minore complures quidem liberos tulit, verum tres omnino reliquit: Germanicum, Livillam, Claudium.
examples.translation: Drusus had several children by the younger Antonia, but was survived by only three, Germanicus, Livilla, and Claudius.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Princeps neque opera ulla magnifica fecit—nam et quae sola susceperat, Augusti templum restitutionemque Pompeiani theatri, imperfecta post tot annos reliquit—neque spectacula omnino edidit;
examples.translation: While emperor he constructed no magnificent public works, for the only ones which he undertook, the temple of Augustus and the restoration of Pompey’s theatre, he left unfinished after so many years.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: eaten up, Arnob. 1, 3.—
Latin: Cadere ad aliquem vel in aliquo
Latin: Genuflecto. (saepe cum ad genua vel genibus)

examples.original: Nihil mali accidisse Scipioni puto;
examples.translation: I believe that no ill has befallen Scipio;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Si extra est, posteaquam acciderat, recessit.
examples.translation: If it is outside, it withdraws after having affected the object.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod ubi accidit, barbari vehementissimo cursu refugerunt.
examples.translation: When this occurred, the natives fled away at a most furious speed.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To bereave, deprive

examples.original: Privatae res vestrae quo statu sunt?
examples.translation: In what plight are your private interests?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Matri summam omnium rerum privatarum publicarumque permisit.
examples.translation: He left to his mother the management of all public and private business.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Tota cogitatio a privatis commodis quam longissime aversa sit.
examples.translation: You need not look about for the reward of a just deed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To hope (something desirable), to look for, trust, expect; to promise or flatter one's self (the predom. signif. of the word; syn.: confido, exspecto).
Latin: Optare et expectare ut aliquid bonum fiat

examples.original: Quid ut a vobis sperent?
examples.translation: What are they to expect of you?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec victoriam sperant nec reditum.
examples.translation: They have no hope of victory, no hope of returning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sapiam, spero, sed interim non sapio.
examples.translation: I hope some day to be wise, but meanwhile I am not wise.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To touch, handle, stroke, touch gently (rare)

examples.original: Aut augemus dolorem aut fingimus aut praecipimus.
examples.translation: We are in the habit of exaggerating, or imagining, or anticipating, sorrow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Habuit et pingendi fingendique non mediocre studium.
examples.translation: He likewise had no slight interest in painting and sculpture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quid cum fictas fabulas e quibus utilitas nulla elici potest cum voluptate legimus?
examples.translation: But what of our reading fiction, from which no utility can be extracted?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to promise solemnly or sacredly; to devote, dedicate, consecrate something to a deity (syn.: promitto, recipio, dico, dedico).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; vōvi, vōtum, 2

examples.original: Quidni tu ista vota saepe facias?
examples.translation: And of course you should offer those prayers frequently.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil autem video ex istis voto dignum.
examples.translation: But I do not see that any of them is worth praying for.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Votorum tuorum veterum licet dis gratiam facias, alia de integro suscipe;
examples.translation: As for your former prayers, you may dispense the gods from answering them; offer new prayers;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to this place, hither, =
Latin: Ad hoc locum; opp. hinc

examples.original: Accedebat huc quod in concilio Aeduorum Dumnorix dixerat sibi a Caesare regnum civitatis deferri;
examples.translation: Moreover, in the council of the Aedui Dumnorix had said that Caesar meant to offer him the kingship of the state;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Huc cum ab Ostia navigaret, vehementi circio bis paene demersus est, prope Liguriam iuxtaque Stoechadas insulas.
examples.translation: On the voyage thither from Ostia he was nearly cast away twice in furious north-westers, off Liguria and near the Stoechades islands.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Huc accedebant xviii onerariae naves, quae ex eo loco ab milibus passuum octo vento tenebantur quo minus in eundem portum venire possent: has equitibus distribuit.
examples.translation: To the total stated eighteen transports should be added, which were detained eight miles off by the wind, and prevented from entering the port of concentration; these he allotted to the cavalry.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: joyful, cheerful, glad, gay, joyous, rejoicing, pleased, delighted, full of joy.
Latin: Felix, beatus, fortunatus

examples.original: Sed tamen re quoque ipsa esse laetus volo.
examples.translation: But yet I wish to rejoice in the accomplished fact.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Caedem eius laetam fuisse Muciano accepimus.
examples.translation: According to report his death gave Mucianus pleasure.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Laeta enim principia magistratus eius nimis luxuriavere;
examples.translation: For the luxuriant beginnings of this magistracy took on too rank a growth;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to reach, arrive at (syn.: accedere, adventare, adire, appellere, adesse); constr.
Latin: Venīre ad locum

examples.original: Quem timorem Caesaris adventus sustulit.
examples.translation: This terror was removed by the arrival of Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ita extracta utraque res in consulum adventum est.
examples.translation: So both affairs dragged on till the arrival of the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Inumbrante vespera universum Flaviani exercitus robur advenit.
examples.translation: As evening fell, the great mass of the Flavian troops arrived in a body.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a thousand, thousands.
Latin: Decem centuriae; centum deniones; nongenti nonaginta novem et alius
Latin: Numerus indefinite magnus

examples.original: Nihil interest, centum per vesicam tuam an mille amphorae transeant;
examples.translation: You know the taste of wine and cordials.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eodem die castra promovit et milibus passuum sex a Caesaris castris sub monte consedit.
examples.translation: On the same day he advanced and pitched his camp under a hill-side six miles from Caesar’s.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar Locus erat castrorum editus et paulatim ab imo acclivis circiter passus mille.
examples.translation: The position of the camp was on high ground, with a gradual slope from the bottom of about a mile.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: Beyond this or that, besides

examples.original: Quid cum volumus nomina eorum qui quid gesserint nota nobis esse, parentes, patriam, multa praeterea minime necessaria?
examples.translation: What of our eagerness to learn the names of people who have done something notable, their parentage, birthplace, and many quite unimportant details beside?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quare triumphalia ornamenta et in brevi spatio duplex sacerdotium accepit, praeterea consulatum, quem gessit per duos novissimos anni menses.
examples.translation: For this he received the triumphal regalia, and shortly after two priesthoods, besides the consulship, which he held for the last two months of the year.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Perfecto enim et concluso neque virtutibus neque amicitiis usquam locum esse si ad voluptatem omnia referantur, nihil praeterea est magno opere dicendum.
examples.translation: For when it has been conclusively proved that if pleasure is the sole standard there is no room left either for virtue or friendship, there is no great need to say anything further.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a cock, dunghill-cock
Latin: Zool. Mas avis speciei qui taxonomice Gallus gallus vocatur
Latin: Gallorum vel qui ad Gallos pertinet

examples.original: Non speciem agminis Gallorum per Tarpeiam rupem scandentis?
examples.translation: Could they not see the line of Gauls scaling the Tarpeian Rock?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Coloniae deductae sunt in agro de Gallis capto Placentia et Cremona.
examples.translation: Colonies were established in the territory taken from the Gauls, at Placentia and Cremona.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Has ille in iaculo illigatas effert et Gallus inter Gallos sine ulla suspicione versatus ad Caesarem pervenit.
examples.translation: The man carried forth the despatch bound on a javelin, and moving, all unsuspected, as a Gaul among Gauls, he made his way to Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a slave, servant, serf, serving-man; a female slave, maid-servant.
Latin: Qui alicui servit
Latin: Qui liber non est atque aliis servire debet
entries.etymology: Origin debated; possibly borrowed from Etruscan.

examples.original: Egentes in locupletes, perditi in bonos, servi in dominos armabantur.
examples.translation: You say the senate was on my side. It was;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Qui cum non ambularet vias servorum dei, non bonam famam habere coeperat.
examples.translation: This alarmed me, but yet I did not lightly give it any credence;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ne illud quidem videtis, quam omnem invidiam maiores nostri dominis, omnem contumeliam servis detraxerint?
examples.translation: Do you not see even this,—how our ancestors removed from masters everything invidious, and from slaves everything insulting?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: by what means? how?

examples.original: Quare et pontifex in locum P. Scipionis substitutus et ad deducendas in Galliam colonias, in quis Narbo et Arelate erant, missus est.
examples.translation: For this he was made pontiff in place of Publius Scipio and sent to conduct colonies to Gaul, among them Narbo and Arelate.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quare triumphalia ornamenta et in brevi spatio duplex sacerdotium accepit, praeterea consulatum, quem gessit per duos novissimos anni menses.
examples.translation: For this he received the triumphal regalia, and shortly after two priesthoods, besides the consulship, which he held for the last two months of the year.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quare omnium in se odio incitato nihil contumeliarum defuit quin subiret. Statuae eius a vertice cirrus appositus est cum inscriptione Graeca;
examples.translation: When he had thus aroused the hatred of all, there was no form of insult to which he was not subjected.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: that can be known or is known, knowable, known.
Latin: quod vidi potest
Latin: quod multi noscunt

examples.original: Studia te tua clarum et nobilem efficient.
examples.translation: It is your own studies that will make you shine and will render you eminent.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non ita multo post Iuniam Claudillam M. Silani nobilissimi viri filiam duxit uxorem.
examples.translation: Not so very long afterward Gaius took as wife Junia Claudilla, daughter of Marcus Silanus, a man of noble rank.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Aspendum vetus oppidum et nobile in Pamphylia scitis esse, plenissimum signorum optimorum.
examples.translation: You are aware, gentlemen, that Aspendus is an old and famous town in Pamphylia, full of fine statuary.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: praise, commendation, glory, fame, renown, esteem (cf.: gloria, praeconium, elogium).

examples.original: O illam mirabilem laudem et singularem!
examples.translation: What wonderful and rare distinction!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nolo nolo laudes, nolo dicas: ”o magnum virum!
examples.translation: He has learned to despise all things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Magna scilicet laus est, si homo mansuetus homini est.
examples.translation: It is indeed worthy of great praise, when man treats man with kindness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to rejoice, be glad or joyful respecting any thing, to take pleasure in, be pleased with, delight in

examples.original: Nec his dolendum nec illis gaudendum;
examples.translation: We must neither grieve over the one, nor rejoice over the other.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non tantum delectatus, sed gavisus sum.
examples.translation: I was not merely pleased; I rejoiced.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Fortia Maeonio gaudent pede bella referri;
examples.translation: Valiant wars rejoice to be sung in Maeonian metre;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: in the distance, at a distance, a great way off
Latin: Quasi promotē, quasi porro ab oculis
Latin: quod longe distat

examples.original: Natus est Cn. Pompeio Magno M. Licinio Crasso primum coss. Iduum Octobrium die in pago qui Andes dicitur et abest a Mantua non procul.
examples.translation: He was born in the first consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius the Great and Marcus Licinius Crassus, on the Ides of October, in a district called Andes, not far distant from Mantua.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Quaedam vero procul arceantur ut iam oblitterata et olentia: nullum sit verbum velut rubigine infectum, nulli sensus tarda et inerti structura in morem annalium componantur;
examples.translation: There should be never a word of the rusty, mouldy tinge, never a sentence put together in the lame and listless style of the chroniclers.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: His rebus permotus Quintus Titurius, cum procul Ambiorigem suos cohortantem conspexisset, interpretem suum Gnaeum Pompeium ad eum mittit rogatum ut sibi militibusque parcat.
examples.translation: Alarmed by these events, Quintus Titurius, who had remarked Ambiorix at a distance encouraging his men, sent his interpreter, Gnaeus Pompeius, to him to ask him to spare himself and his troops.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to bring forth, produce, make, create, beget (very freq. in every period and species of composition).
Latin: Ex novo facere

examples.original: Ii tres collegas sibi creaverunt.
examples.translation: These appointed three others to be their colleagues.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Libri VII Periocha ob virtutem creatus est.
examples.translation: Summary of Book VII consul, at the age of twenty-three.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: M’. Valerium dictatorem Volesi filium creant.
examples.translation: An edict which the dictator soon promulgated strengthened their confidence.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: that has been or has been done before
Latin: Qui antehac exstitit; non modernus; praecedens; originalis

examples.original: Quam copiose ac varie vexavit antiquos!
examples.translation: With what readiness and versatility did he make war upon the ancients!
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Dicebant antiqui ”si iusso,” id est iussero.
examples.translation: The ancients used to say iusso, instead of iussero, in conditional clauses.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Id erat liber aliquis antiquus pulcher aut rarior.
examples.translation: This was some old book, either beautiful or rare.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to do harm, inflict injury, do hurt to (cf.: obsum, obficio, laedo).—Constr.
Latin: Facere noxam aut iniuriam. (cum dativo)

examples.original: Ne morti quidem hoc apud nos noceat;
examples.translation: Then let not this sort of thing damage death, either, in our estimation;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Proprium autem est nocentium trepidare.
examples.translation: But it is the property of guilt to be in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nulli non ad nocendum satis virium est.
examples.translation: For every one has strength enough to do you some harm.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to bring, join, combine into one whole; to join or put together, to connect, unite.
Latin: Sinere, ut duo simul iugantur, adeoque simul mittere, iungere
Latin: Morali ratione est sinere, ut actio contra legem fiat, adeoque facere, patrare, sed in malam partem

examples.original: Vitelliis Aquiliisque fratribus primo commissa res est.
examples.translation: The brothers Vitellii and Aquilii were the first to be entrusted with the project.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nondum me committo frigidae verae, adhuc rigorem eius infringo.
examples.translation: I do not yet trust myself to a bath which is absolutely cold;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nocti se potius ac solitudini quam ulli aut urbi aut hospiti committebat.
examples.translation: And so in no town was she allowed to halt;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: sharp, pointed, piercing, and the like.
Latin: Species arboris generis Acer
Latin: Lignum eius arboris

examples.original: Si ille acer est et ferox, concitari gradum?
examples.translation: That a keen and confident soul quickens the step?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Germani acrius usque ad munitiones secuntur.
examples.translation: The Germans pursued most vigorously right up to the fortifications.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non ultra paucos dies quamquam acribus initiis coeptum mendacium valuit.
examples.translation: A deception, which had a lively success at first, prevailed for only a few days.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: of or belonging to a deity
Latin: Divus, e dis ortus vel ad deos pertinens
Latin: Divinandi et praesentiendi vim habens, numine plenus

examples.original: Quid enim possumus hoc agere divinius?”
examples.translation: What sublimer occupation could we find?”
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nullum porro inter divina discrimen est;
examples.translation: And furthermore, there is no distinction between things divine;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare si ad melius cogitandum quies aliqua data est, utere divino beneficio.
examples.translation: So, if you do obtain some quietness for deeper reflection, avail yourself of what is a heavenly boon.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a tune, song; poem, verse; an oracular response, a prophecy; a form of incantation (cf.: cano, cantus, and canto).

Latin: cantus, vel quidquid certis modis ac numeris recitatur, pronunciatur, effertur. Carmen enim est antiquissima Latinorum vox, qua quodcumque a poetis oestro incitatis expromebatur, sive illud maxima, sive minima mole constaret, significabatur
Latin: cantus

examples.original: Ei mihi, non multum carmen honoris habet.
examples.translation: Alas, a poem is not much honoured.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid sibi vult ista carminis effeminati turpitudo?
examples.translation: What does he mean by making terms with panic fear?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eiusmodi vocibus referta sunt carmina, refertae historiae.
examples.translation: A single tree is not remarkable if the whole forest rises to the same height.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a business, employment, occupation, affair (cf. munus).

examples.original: Detraxi tibi non pusillum negotii;
examples.translation: You see, I have relieved you of no slight bother;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aiunt homines plus in alieno negotio videre.
examples.translation: They say that men see farther in the affairs of others than in their own.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: A plebe consensu consulibus negotium mandatur;
examples.translation: The plebs unanimously referred the matter to the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to derive enjoyment from a thing, to enjoy, delight in

examples.original: Quo facto tulit pietatis fructum.
examples.translation: By such conduct he reaped the fruits of his devotion;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Nemo autem sollicito bono fruitur;
examples.translation: No man, however, enjoys a blessing that brings anxiety;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In commune rerum natura fruebantur;
examples.translation: They enjoyed all nature in partnership.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to beget, bear, bring forth, produce; in
Latin: Parere, generare

examples.original: Mantua me genuit, Calabri rapuere, tenet nunc Parthenope;
examples.translation: Mantua gave me the light, Calabria slew me; now holds me Parthenope.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Corporum locus in hos primum, in ea quae faciunt et quae ex his gignuntur;
examples.translation: The topic concerning bodies deals, first, with these two grades: the creative and the createdb;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Primus ille et urbis et imperii conditor Romulus fuit, Marte genitus et Rhea Silvia.
examples.translation: The first founder both of the city and of the empire was Romulus, the son of Mars and Rhea Silvia.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to lurk, be or

examples.original: Sed non diu latent scelera.
examples.translation: But crimes do not long remain undetected.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Atque haec ratio late patet.
examples.translation: And this is a principle of wide application.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nocens habuit aliquando latendi fortunam, numquam fiduciam.
examples.translation: A wrongdoer sometimes has the luck to escape notice but never the assurance thereof.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a wall; esp. a city wall; mostly in
Latin: Lapideus ambitus circa urbem, munimenti causa
Latin: vallum

examples.original: Fata vetant, murique vicem Fortuna tuetur.
examples.translation: Fate is against them, and Fortune performs the office of a wall.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Muri autem omnes Gallici hac fere forma sunt.
examples.translation: All Gallic walls are, as a rule, of the following pattern.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Aequi se in oppida receperunt murisque se tenebant.
examples.translation: The Aequi retired to their towns and kept within their walls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: on the other side

examples.original: Drusus ulterius egit et vetuit transire Danuvium.
examples.translation: Drusus forced them still further and prevented them from recrossing the Danube.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Haec erit ultimum vitae instrumentum et, ut ita dicam, additamentum?
examples.translation: Is philosophy to be the last requisite in life,—a sort of supplement?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Numquid ultra quicquam ulli timendum est quam ut uratur, quam ut pereat?
examples.translation: Is there a worse fate that any man may fear than being burned or being killed?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: that is taken before other things (cf. princeps): excipuum quod excipitur, ut praecipuum, quod ante capitur, Paul. ex

examples.original: Quid est in virtute praecipuum?
examples.translation: Now what is the chief thing in virtue?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo proelio praecipua equitum gloria fuit;
examples.translation: In this battle the cavalry particularly distinguished themselves.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed tu praecipue curvis venare theatris: Haec loca sunt voto fertiliora tuo.
examples.translation: But specially do your hunting in the round theatres: more bountifully do these repay your vows.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to let go forward, to send or put forth, to let hang down, let grow, etc.

examples.original: Illius tibi noctem promitto nec differo;
examples.translation: That beauty whom you desire shall visit you.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex eodem tibi munere plura exempla promisi.
examples.translation: I have promised you, however, some more illustrations drawn from the same games.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil sibi quisquam de futuro debet promittere.
examples.translation: No one has any right to draw for himself upon the future.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A tree.
Latin: Alta planta lignea perennis

examples.original: Rapum autem arboris, antequam obruat, radit.
examples.translation: These are of necessity still soft;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est arbor solida nec fortis nisi in quam frequens ventus incursat;
examples.translation: No tree becomes rooted and sturdy unless many a wind assails it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Saepe suos casus nec mitia facta puellae Flesse sub arboribus Milaniona ferunt;
examples.translation: Often, they say, beneath the trees Milanion bewailed his lot and the maiden’s cruelty;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: To hold or keep back

examples.original: Quae res illum non patitur ad imum devolvi, retinet in summo.
examples.translation: That which prevents him from rolling to the bottom, keeps him at the summit.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam si illud argumentaberis, sapientem multo vino inebriari et retinere rectum tenorem, etiam si temulentus sit;
examples.translation: Do that which is easiest of all—namely, demonstrate that what men call pleasures are punishments as soon as they have exceeded due bounds.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod vobis venire in mentem profecto necesse est, nihil esse in civitate tam diligenter quam ius civile retinendum.
examples.translation: But in thinking that, though good lawyers, they deserve no attention, it is not the individuals that he is injuring: he is undermining law and justice.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a leaf (cf. frons).
Latin: Frons, pars plana plantae praesertim viridis, quae facit nutrimentum e luce
Latin: → charta, schedula

examples.original: Saetigerisque pares subus silvestria membra nuda dabant terrae nocturno tempore capti, circum se foliis ac frondibus involventes.
examples.translation: And when night overtook them, like bristly hogs they just cast their savage bodies naked upon the ground, rolling themselves in leaves and boughs.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Victoriae praemium quod petebatur, ut plebeius crearetur, nullum fuit; omnes patricii creati sunt, M. Fabius Vibulanus M. Folius L. Sergius Fidenas.
examples.translation: Though they hoped their victory would be rewarded by the choice of a plebeian, they were disappointed: all those who were elected were patricians, Marcus Fabius Vibulanus, Marcus Folius, Lucius Sergius Fidenas.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Firmly, steadily, steadfastly, unyieldingly (so only ante-class.)
Latin: Modō immediātō, sine morā; cōnfestim
Latin: Modō cōnstantī; cōnstanter

examples.original: Ac statim advenere litterae fusas apud Cremonam Vitelli copias, ipsum in urbe interemptum nuntiantes.
examples.translation: And immediately letters came with the news that Vitellius had been routed at Cremona and the emperor himself slain at Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ac ne tribuniciam quidem potestatem statim nec patris patriae appellationem nisi sero recepit. Nam consuetudinem scrutandi salutantes manente adhuc bello civili omiserat.
examples.translation: As for the custom of searching those who came to pay their morning calls, he gave that up before the civil war was over.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Idque non doctus modo et prudens auditor, sed etiam populus intellegit, ac statim ita laude prosequitur ut legitime studuisse, ut per omnes eloquentiae numeros isse, ut denique oratorem esse fateatur;
examples.translation: This fact is fully appreciated not only by the learned and scholarly portion of the audience, but also by the rank and file.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a living being
Latin: Ens vivens, quod animam habet, et quod movere potest
Latin: Bestia, animal quod non homo est

examples.original: Rationale enim animal est homo.
examples.translation: For man is a reasoning animal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Rursus animalia in quas species seco?
examples.translation: They are either perishable or imperishable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tenetur in priore animali, in aliud animal transire ei non licet;
examples.translation: The soul is kept within the first-named being, and cannot cross over into another;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: which is inserted into another (opp. cardo femina, into which another is inserted)

examples.original: Postquam pandi viam et mare prosperum accepit, de se per ambages interrogat caesis compluribus hostiis.
examples.translation: On learning that his path was open and the sea favourable, he slew many victims and then questioned indirectly about himself.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cuius loci haec erat natura, atque ita montibus angustis mare continebatur, uti ex locis superioribus in litus telum adigi posset.
examples.translation: Such was the nature of the ground, so steep the heights which banked the sea, that a missile could be hurled from the higher levels on to the shore.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Puteolis dedicatione pontis, quem excogitatum ab eo significavimus, cum multos e litore invitasset ad se, repente omnis praecipitavit, quosdam gubernacula apprehendentes contis remisque detrusit in mare.
examples.translation: At Puteoli, at the dedication of the bridge that he contrived, as has been said, after inviting a number to come to him from the shore, on a sudden he had them all thrown overboard;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: the mouth (syn. bucca): quam tibi ex ore orationem duriter dictis dedit, Enn. ap.
Latin: Pars sceleti cuiusquam animalis, ut, costa, os femoris, &c
Latin: Apertura per quem animal cibum recepit; etiam, bucca seu spatium in quo lingua et dentes sunt

examples.original: Nam rictus oraque monstri Quis timuit?
examples.translation: For who ever felt fear of the monster’s face and open mouth?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Et si esse vis felix, deos ora, ne quid tibi ex his, quae optantur, eveniat.
examples.translation: And, if you would be happy, entreat the gods that none of their fond desires for you may be brought to pass.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iulianus ad L. Vitellium perductus et verberibus foedatus in ore eius iugulatur.
examples.translation: Julianus was taken before Lucius Vitellius, flogged, and slain before his eyes.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: one who attests any thing (orally or in writing), a witness (cf. superstes)

examples.original: De hoc ego teste detraham?
examples.translation: Am I to disparage this witness?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Deos rerum omnium esse testes ait.
examples.translation: They maintain that the gods are witnesses of everything.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O te miserum, si contemnis hunc testem!
examples.translation: How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to take out of the midst, to take away, do away with, abolish; to destroy, slay, kill (syn.: interficio, perimo; class.).

examples.original: Ac statim advenere litterae fusas apud Cremonam Vitelli copias, ipsum in urbe interemptum nuntiantes.
examples.translation: And immediately letters came with the news that Vitellius had been routed at Cremona and the emperor himself slain at Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Suscepto igitur civili bello ac ducibus copiisque in Italiam praemissis interim Alexandriam transiit, ut claustra Aegypti optineret.
examples.translation: Therefore beginning a civil war and sending ahead generals with troops to Italy, he crossed meanwhile to Alexandria, to take possession of the key to Egypt.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Interim, dum de condicionibus inter se agunt longiorque consulto ab Ambiorige instituitur sermo, paulatim circumventus interficitur.
examples.translation: While they two were discussing terms together, and Ambiorix was purposely making a longer speech than necessary, Titurius was gradually surrounded and slain.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: color; pigment; shade/tinge

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Vel tu venandi studium cole: saepe recessit Turpiter a Phoebi victa sorore Venus.
examples.translation: Or cultivate the pleasures of the chase: ofttimes has Venus, vanquished by Phoebus’ sister, beaten a base retreat.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cum tot prodierint pretio leviore colores, Quis furor est census corpore ferre suos!
examples.translation: When so many cheaper colours walk abroad, what madness to carry whole incomes on one’s body! Lo!
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to choose rather, to prefer.
Latin: Magis velle, praeferre

examples.original: Ac tamen hic mallet non dolere.
examples.translation: Yet he would have preferred to have no pain at all.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In hoc bonis malisque conveniet.
examples.translation: Upon this point good and bad will agree.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Malo te legas quam epistulam meam.
examples.translation: I prefer that you should read your own words rather than my letter;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fire-place, hearth; others, with probability, compare
Latin: Templi genus minus, aedificium dis
Latin: Domus

examples.original: Aedes Mercuri dedicata est idibus Maiis.
examples.translation: The temple of Mercury was consecrated on the fifteenth of May.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Certamen consulibus inciderat uter dedicaret Mercuri aedem.
examples.translation: The senate referred the case to the people for decision.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eo anno aedis Martis Gallico bello vota dedicata est a T. Quinctio duumviro sacris faciendis.
examples.translation: In that year the temple of Mars vowed in the Gallic war was dedicated by Titus Quinctius, duumvir for sacrifices.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Latin
Latin: Qui ad Latium pertinet
Latin: Qui ad linguam Latinam pertinet, vel in ea scribitur diciturve

examples.original: Dic mihi Damoeta: ’cuium pecus’ anne Latinum?
examples.translation: Tell me, Damoetas, I pray, is ’cuium pecus’ really good Latin?
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Cato grammaticus, Latina Siren, Qui solus legit ac facit poetas.
examples.translation: Cato, teacher of letters, Siren Latin-born, He, and none other, poets reads and makes.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Eos per se ipsi Latini adsumptis Hernicis sine Romano aut duce aut auxilio castris exuerunt;
examples.translation: These the Latins, acting independently, with the assistance of the Hernici, but without either general or aid from Rome, despoiled of their camp.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: ugly, unsightly, unseemly, foul, filthy (class.; esp. freq. in a trop. sense; syn.: taeter, foedus, deformis, obscaenus, immundus).
Latin: Deformato aspectu
Latin: sensu morali malus

examples.original: Turpe est aliud loqui, aliud sentire;
examples.translation: It is ignoble to say one thing and mean another;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex honestiore causa coit turpis adfectus?
examples.translation: Can a cause which is more honourable produce a passion that is base?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid enim turpius philosophia captante clamores?
examples.translation: For what is baser than philosophy courting applause?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: friendship (very freq. in Cic., occurring more than 200 times).
Latin: Coniunctio affectionis inter homines, qui tum amici aut amicae nominantur

examples.original: Qui se spectat et propter hoc ad amicitiam venit, male cogitat.
examples.translation: He who regards himself only, and enters upon friendships for this reason, reckons wrongly.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed quid ages tandem si utilitas ab amicitia, ut fit saepe, defecerit?
examples.translation: But what, pray, will you do, if, as often happens, expediency parts company with friendship?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Licet hic rursus ea commemores quae optimis verbis ab Epicuro de laude amicitiae dicta sunt.
examples.translation: It is no good your once again repeating Epicurus’s admirable remarks in praise of friendship.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Stars united in a figure, a group of stars, a constellation
Latin: Figura ex stellis facta. Signum caeleste ex pluribus stellis compositum, ut sunt duodecim illa, quibus constat Zodiacus
Latin: stella, aster

examples.original: Ostendit terras Titan et sidera texit.
examples.translation: The sun revealed the earth and veiled the stars.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Bellum civile Marianum sive Sullanum tribus, ut sic dixerim, sideribus agitatum est.
examples.translation: The Marian or Sullan civil war was waged under three different constellations, if I may use the expression.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Evidentissimum id fuit, quod, quacumque equo invectus est, ibi haud secus quam pestifero sidere icti pavebant;
examples.translation: This was most clearly seen in that, wherever he rode, men cowered as though blasted by some baleful star;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: set forth

examples.original: Merces seditionis proposita confestim seditionem excitavit.
examples.translation: The reward held out to sedition soon brought sedition to a head.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Selecti ex conventu aut propositi ex negotiatoribus iudices nulli.
examples.translation: It was the staff that, as I say, supplied the judges;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Relinquantur istae voces illis artibus, quae propositum habent populo placere;
examples.translation: These outcries should be left for the arts which aim to please the crowd;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to achieve, execute, carry out, accomplish, perform, despatch, bring to an end or conclusion, finish, complete (class.; syn.: absolvo, conficio, exsequor).
Latin: facere aliquid completum, ad finem

examples.original: Animus et ratio in animo perfecta.
examples.translation: It is soul, and reason brought to perfection in the soul.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Per ista ad perfectum animi statum pervenitur.
examples.translation: It is by such methods that we arrive at a perfect condition of mind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam cum sola ratio perficiat hominem, sola ratio perfecta beatum facit;
examples.translation: It is this that is called virtue; this is what we mean by ”honourable”a;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to beat, strike, knock any thing or at any thing; to push, drive, hurl, impel, propel.

examples.original: Primo statim incursu pulsi hostes;
examples.translation: At the very first onset the enemy were routed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non cupiditas nos, non timor pellet.
examples.translation: Then neither desire nor fear shall rout us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Primo concursu pulsus se intra castra recepit.
examples.translation: At the first attack he was repulsed and withdrew into his camp.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a shade, shadow.
Latin: Imago obscura, quae corpore luci viam secante proicitur ad superficiem
Latin: creātūra mȳthologica, saepe sine corpore; lārva, spectrum

examples.original: Tota rerum natura umbra est aut inanis aut fallax.
examples.translation: The whole universe is then a vain or deceptive shadow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger
