examples.original: Numquam tibi, Magne, per umbras Perque meos manes genero non esse licebit;
examples.translation: In vain you sever with the sword the tie of kinship that binds you.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tristis felicibus umbris Voltus erat: vidi Decios, natumque patremque Lustrales bellis animas, flentemque Camillum Et Curios, Sullam de te, Fortuna, querentem.
examples.translation: For the blessed dead wore a sorrowful aspect: I saw the Decii, the father and son who devoted their lives to the gods in battle, and Camillus, and Curius;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: all together, all taken collectively, whole, entire, collective, general, universal (opp. singuli).
Latin: Ad unum reductus

examples.original: Subita aliqua et universa voce feriuntur aures meae.
examples.translation: My ears are smitten with sudden and general cheering.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inumbrante vespera universum Flaviani exercitus robur advenit.
examples.translation: As evening fell, the great mass of the Flavian troops arrived in a body.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Universis egi initio quantum potui: satis ornate agere nullo modo possum.
examples.translation: At the outset I thanked you collectively to the best of my ability;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: not yet
Latin: Adhuc non

examples.original: Sed haec etsi praeclare, nondum tamen perpolita;
examples.translation: But what he said on the subject, however excellent, nevertheless lacks the finishing touches;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De malis autem et bonis ab iis animalibus quae nondum depravata sint ait optime iudicari.
examples.translation: Creatures as yet uncorrupted are according to him the best judges of Good and Evil.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Allobrogibus sese vel persuasuros, quod nondum bono animo in populum Romanum viderentur, existimabant vel vi coacturos, ut per suos fines eos ire paterentur.
examples.translation: The last town of the Allobroges, the nearest to the borders of the Helvetii, is Geneva, from which a bridge stretches across to the Helvetii.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: how constituted, of what sort, kind, or nature, what kind of a (class.).
Latin: pronomen interrogativum substantivumv et cum talis respondens

examples.original: Pueritia ac iuventa, qualem monstravimus.
examples.translation: His boyhood and youth were such as we have already described.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Prius aliquid esse debet, deinde quale esse.
examples.translation: A thing must exist first, then may be of a certain kind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qualia autem haec fuerint, talis vita erit. In particulas suasisse totum ordinanti parum est.
examples.translation: It is not enough, when a man is arranging his existence as a whole, to give him advice about details.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to fall into or upon a thing, to fall, light upon (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Quidni ego malim non incidere bellum?
examples.translation: Of course I prefer that war should not occur;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Notum est totum carmen incisum in sepulcro.
examples.translation: But the entire epitaph is known because it is inscribed upon his tomb.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sane homini praeter opinionem improviso incidi.
examples.translation: My unexpected visit took him altogether by surprise.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a leafy branch, green bough, foliage.

examples.original: Impulsa frons prima et trepidatio subsidiis inlata;
examples.translation: Their front was first driven in and communicated its disorder to the supports;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec disputamus attractis superciliis, fronte rugosa?
examples.translation: Is this what we discuss with contracted brow and wrinkled forehead?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tunc veniunt risus, tum pauper cornua sumit, Tum dolor et curae rugaque frontis abit.
examples.translation: Then laughter comes, then even the poor find vigour, then sorrow and care and the wrinkles of the brow depart.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to sow, plant
Latin: Relinquere homines in periculo vel munus

examples.original: Semper enim ita assumit aliquid ut ea quae prima dederit non deserat.
examples.translation: For she continually superadds fresh faculties without abandoning her previous gifts.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed neque tu dominam velis maioribus usus Desere, nec cursus anteat illa tuos;
examples.translation: But neither do you, spreading too full sail, leave your mistress behind, nor let her outstrip your speed;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: In insuperabili loco stat animus, qui externa deseruit, et arce se sua vindicat;
examples.translation: The soul stands on unassailable ground, if it has abandoned external things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a current of air, a breeze, wind
Latin: Spiritus, principium vitale

examples.original: Egere, quod superest animae, Tyrrhene, per omnes Bellorum casus.
examples.translation: Tyrrhenus must spend what remains of life in every hazard of war.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Haec eadem ratio naturam animi atque animai corpoream docet esse;
examples.translation: This same reasoning teaches that the nature of mind and spirit is bodily;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: At tu, fretus armis animisque, concitatis equis invade mediam aciem;
examples.translation: But do you confide in arms and valour, and charge their centre at the gallop;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: roused to fierceness (while ferus signifies naturally fierce); raging, furious, fell, savage, ferocious, etc.

examples.original: Crescit insolenti superbia, crudelitas saevo, malignitas livido.
examples.translation: The haughty man increases his arrogance, the ruthless man his cruelty, the slanderer his spitefulness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Saeva quies pelagi, maestoque ignava profundo Stagna iacentis aquae;
examples.translation: A grim stillness broods over the dismal deep;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tum vero secundum tam saevum atque inhumanum dictum ”Auditis” inquit, ”Quirites, sicut servis malum minantem militibus?
examples.translation: On this particular occasion, after that savage and brutal threat, he cried, ”Do you hear him, Quirites, threatening his soldiers with punishment like slaves?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to break, break in pieces, dash to pieces, shiver, break in two (cf.: rumpo, diffringo).
Latin: In duas vel plures partes uno ictu disrumpere
Latin: In minutissimas partes redigere vel quomodocumque dividere

examples.original: Molaribus demum fracta saxis est.
examples.translation: It was finally destroyed by rocks equal in size to millstones.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc est non dividere sed frangere.
examples.translation: This is not dividing but hacking in pieces.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Volo luxuriam obiurgari, libidinem traduci, inpotentiam frangi.
examples.translation: I wish to see luxury rebuked, lust condemned, waywardness crushed out.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to feel awe of, to reverence, revere, respect; to fear, be afraid of any thing (good or bad); to fear or be afraid to do a thing, etc.
Latin: Timere, metuere

examples.original: Id enim tam supra nos est quam ipsa veritas.
examples.translation: For to do that is as far beyond our ken as truth itself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed cecidit Babylone sua Parthoque verendus.
examples.translation: He died, however, in Babylon he had conquered;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hic quoque suus est, de summoque bono dissentiens dici vere Peripateticus non potest.
examples.translation: He too stands by himself; differing about the Chief Good he cannot correctly be called a Peripatetic.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be on one's guard, either for one's self or (more rarely) for another; hence
Latin: Esse prudens adversum aliquam rem
Latin: Providere ne quid accidat

examples.original: Quae cum ita essent, sane benivolo animo me ut magno opere caverem praemonebat.
examples.translation: In view of all this my friend very kindly warned me to take every possible precaution.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ne parum locuples esset? at erat, et esset amplius si velles, populo cautum praedibus et praediis.
examples.translation: Even if the actual facts, the shamefulness of the wrong you were doing, left you unmoved;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam ob rem cave Catoni anteponas ne istum quidem ipsum, quem Apollo, ut ais, sapientissimum iudicavit;
examples.translation: Therefore, take care not to give the precedence over Cato even to that man, whom, as you say, Apollo adjudged the wisest of men;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to point out, indicate (class.).

examples.original: Ac nonnumquam horreis praeclusis populo famem indixit.
examples.translation: Sometimes too he would shut up the granaries and condemn the people to hunger.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Samnitibus bellum indictum est et adversus eos saepe prospere pugnatum est.
examples.translation: War was declared upon the Samnites and victories were often gained over them.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque non ego vobis ut indicem praedas vestras, sed vos id cogendi estis ut in medium proferatis.”
examples.translation: And so it is not I that must be forced to tell of your plunder, but you that must be compelled to give it up.”
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to cause to stand (cf.: colloco, pono).

examples.original: Ferro igitur eam arcere contumeliam statuunt.
examples.translation: They therefore determined to repel that insult with the sword.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed maturato opus est quidquid statuere placet;
examples.translation: That government is certainly by far the strongest to which its subjects yield obedience gladly.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque illi Syracusani statuam postea statuerunt;
examples.translation: The Syracusans, owing to this, later set up a statue in his honour;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: greatness, size, bulk, magnitude (class.).

examples.original: Nam magnitudo non habet modum certum;
examples.translation: For greatness is not absolute;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In edito stat admirabilis, celsus, magnitudinis verae.
examples.translation: He stands in a high place, worthy of admiration, lofty, and really great.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Testari vultis adtendere vos moverique magnitudine rerum?
examples.translation: You may do this at the proper time;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to call one to account, to make complaint against, to reproach, blame.
Latin: Ad causam provocare; culpare aliquem de aliquo

examples.original: Nemo eorum, qui illam accusant, expertus est.
examples.translation: But no one of those who malign death has made trial of it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Audebis ita accusare alterum ut quo minus tute condemnere recusare non possis?
examples.translation: If on the other hand you pass this charge over, what can be your value as a prosecutor?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cur igitur tu, qui pietate ad accusandum excitatus es, hunc Asellium esse inultum tam diu sinis?
examples.translation: Then why have you,a who were impelled to prosecute by loyalty to your father so long allowed this Asellius to go unpunished?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to make happy, to bless

examples.original: Ne forma quidem et vires beatum te facere possunt;
examples.translation: Neither can beauty or strength make you blessed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si quid est, quod vitam beatam potest facere, id bonum est suo iure.
examples.translation: If there is anything that can make life happy, it is good on its own merits;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Paupertas si malum est, mendicus esse beatus nemo potest quamvis sit sapiens.
examples.translation: If poverty is an evil, no beggar can be happy, be he as wise as you like.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to take or catch up, to take upon one.

examples.original: Numquam suscepti negotii eum pertaesum est;
examples.translation: He never wearied of an enterprise which he had once undertaken;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Expeditionem unam omnino suscepit eamque modicam.
examples.translation: He made but one campaign and that of little importance.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Votorum tuorum veterum licet dis gratiam facias, alia de integro suscipe;
examples.translation: As for your former prayers, you may dispense the gods from answering them; offer new prayers;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a contest, struggle, strife, whether friendly or hostile, physical or intellectual; most freq. of a pugilistic contest of any kind; but also of contention in war.

examples.original: Et ne is quidem finis certaminum fuit.
examples.translation: Even this did not end their disputes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et certamen honestum et disputatio splendida!
examples.translation: Here is an honourable quarrel, fought out in high debate!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Concitata multitudo erat certamenque instare videbatur.
examples.translation: The crowd was deeply moved and a conflict appeared to be imminent.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a root of a plant (cf. stirps).
Latin: Pars subterranea plantarum
Latin: Fons verbi, origo verbi

examples.original: Pugnatum est haud procul radicibus Vesuvii montis, qua via ad Veserim ferebat.
examples.translation: The engagement came off not far from the foot of Mount Vesuvius, where the road led to Veseris.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non vivunt contra naturam qui pomaria in summis turribus serunt? Quorum silvae in tectis domuum ac fastigiis nutant, inde ortis radicibus quo inprobe cacumina egissent?
examples.translation: Or raise waving forests upon the roofs and battlements of their houses—the roots starting at a point to which it would be outlandish for the tree-tops to reach?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec igitur natura tenetur corpore ab omni, ipsaque corporis est custos et causa salutis; nam communibus inter se radicibus haerent nec sine pernicie divelli posse videntur.
examples.translation: This natureb then is contained by the whole body, and is itself the body’s guardian and source of its existence;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: spouse, consort; husband or wife
Latin: Quisque pars matrimonii (uxor vel maritus)

examples.original: Prodierat: visa coniuge mutus erat.
examples.translation: His hands dropped, and from his hands the double tablet;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Si plura iuvant mea volnera, coniunx Est mihi, sunt nati;
examples.translation: If you desire to add to my afflictions, I have a wife, I have sons;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Qui Martem terra, Neptunum effugit in undis, Coniugis Atrides victima dira fuit.
examples.translation: Atreus, who escaped Mars on land and Neptune on the deep, was the dire victim of his wife.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the office or rank of a magister, a magisterial office, civil office, magistracy.
Latin: Status magistri
Latin: Munus magistrorum

examples.original: Abeuntes magistratu Cn. Genucius tribunus plebis arripuit.
examples.translation: As their term expired, Gnaeus Genucius, a plebeian tribune, haled them to trial.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Caesar Valetiacus proximo anno eundem magistratum gesserit.
examples.translation: Valetiacus had exercised the same office in the previous year.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Magistratus quae visa sunt occultant quaeque esse ex usu iudicaverunt multitudini produnt.
examples.translation: Magistrates conceal what they choose, and make known what they think proper for the public.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: an imitation, copy of a thing, an image, likeness

examples.original: Non facit nobilem atrium plenum fumosis imaginibus.
examples.translation: A hall full of smoke-begrimed busts does not make the nobleman.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Trierarchi magno tumultu Vitellii imagines invadunt;
examples.translation: The trierarchs with loud shouts attacked the statues of Vitellius;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Et quantum quaeque ab nobis res absit, imago efficit ut videamus et internoscere curat;
examples.translation: And the image enables us to see and takes care that we distinguish how far each thing is distant from us;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: demand, require, request, desire (syn.: posco, flagito, peto); constr. with aliquid, aliquid ab aliquo, aliquem aliquid, with

examples.original: Missis ad Vitellium litteris auxilium postulat.
examples.translation: He wrote to Vitellius asking for help.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ne sint in senectute vires : ne postulantur quidem vires a senectute.
examples.translation: But, grant that old age is devoid of strength; none is even expected of it.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Minime autem convenit, cum ipsi inter nos viles neglectique simus, postulare ut dis immortalibus cari simus et ab iis diligamur.
examples.translation: But how inconsistent it would be for us to expect the immortal gods to love and cherish us, when we ourselves despise and neglect one another!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to complain, lament, bewail (class.).
Latin: Lamentari aliquid, eiulare

examples.original: Potes queri, si here tantum.
examples.translation: You might complain if I said ”yesterday” merely.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iterum de Germano Tencteri querebantur.
examples.translation: Further complaints against the Germans were brought by the Tencteri.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Tamen de eo queruntur omnes, in quo uno nemo decipitur.
examples.translation: And yet all men complain about the one thing wherein none of them is deceived.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a tear.
Latin: Gutta aquae ab oculo fluens
Latin: Gutta aquae ab oculo fluens. Lacrimæ sunt arma feminarum. in hāc lacrimārum valle

examples.original: O quantum lacrimarum, quantum laborum exigit!
examples.translation: What tears and toil does money wring from us!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His lacrimis contentus eris sine crimine mortis;
examples.translation: Those tears will content thee, free from the reproach of death;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ex hoc quantum lacrimae, quantum sollicitudines occupant!
examples.translation: How much of this time is taken up with weeping, how much with worry!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a. [root Sanscr. pracch- prask-, to ask; Germ. fragen; v. posco].

examples.original: Assyriae paci finem, Fortuna, precamur;
examples.translation: We pray to Fortune that peace with Assyria may end;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ne parce, precor: da nomina rebus, Da loca;
examples.translation: Be not grudging, I pray: give events their names, their places;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Sed alii aversabantur preces aut verecundia aut metu;
examples.translation: But some turned away from the petitioner, through either embarrassment or fear;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To bring together, form, frame, construct (Lucretian)

examples.original: Et neglecta decet multas coma;
examples.translation: Even neglected hair is becoming to many;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nullo loco deest seditionis voluntarius comes;
examples.translation: At no point was there any lack of volunteers to join the rising;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huic decet inflatos laxe iacuisse capillos: Illa sit adstrictis impedienda comis;
examples.translation: This one it beseems to let her waving locks lie loose;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to send different ways, to send apart, i. e.

examples.original: His mandatis eum ab se dimittit.
examples.translation: With these instructions he dismissed him.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hac oratione habita concilium dimisit.
examples.translation: With this speech he dissolved the convention.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod repetam, si te dimisero, et redimam.
examples.translation: But, if I can once dispose of you, I shall reseek and rescue it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a Roman praenomen

examples.original: Curtius Nicia haesit Cn. Pompeio et C. Memmio;
examples.translation: Curtius Nicias was an adherent of Gnaeus Pompeius and Gaius Memmius;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Illi comparatis ingentibus copiis eandem illam, quae fatalis Gnaeo Pompeio fuit, harenam insederant.
examples.translation: Brutus and Cassius, having collected vast forces, had occupied the same ground as had been fatal to Gnaeus Pompeius.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Prima per Pyrenaeum iugum signa Romana Publius et Gnaeus Scipiones intulerunt proeliisque ingentibus Annonem et Hasdrubalem fratres Annibalis ceciderunt;
examples.translation: The two Scipios, Publius and Gnaeus, bore the first Roman standards over the Pyrenees, and defeated Hanno and Hasdrubal, the brothers of Hannibal, in important encounters.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: for indeed, for truly, for

examples.original: Namque Veiis castra quae amissa erant reciperata castellis praesidiisque firmantur; praeerant tribuni militum M.’ Aemilius et K. Fabius.
examples.translation: Thus, at Veii, they recovered the lost camp and strengthened it with fortresses and garrisons, led by the military tribunes Manius Aemilius and Caeso Fabius;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Namque Britannicum fratrem, quod se post adoptionem Ahenobarbum ex consuetudine salutasset, ut subditivum apud patrem arguere conatus est.
examples.translation: For merely because his brother Britannicus had, after his adoption, greeted him as usual as Ahenobarbus, he tried to convince his father that Britannicus was a changeling.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Namque horum posteri meliores illi quidem, mea sententia, quam reliquarum philosophi disciplinarum, sed ita degenerant ut ipsi ex se nati esse videantur.
examples.translation: Their successors are indeed in my opinion superior to the philosophers of any other school, but are so unworthy of their ancestry that one might imagine them to have been their own teachers.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to touch on all sides. to touch, take hold of, seize (very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Latin: Idem quod tangere sed plenius, sive valde et undique tangere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; tĭgi, tactum, 3

examples.original: Hoc contingere aliter non potest.
examples.translation: There is no other way to attain this end.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed quoto cuique habere se contigit?
examples.translation: But how few men are blessed with ownership of self!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quando ad hoc gaudium pervenire continget?
examples.translation: When will it be your lot to attain this joy?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: purchase (very freq. in all periods and kinds of composition).
Latin: Acquirere possessionem alicuius pretio

examples.original: Tanto te pignore, Caesar, Emimus;
examples.translation: By so dear a pledge have we bought you, Caesar;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Magno emisse illum non est quod mireris;
examples.translation: You need not wonder that he paid high prices for these slaves;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ab eis qui emerant capitum numerus ad eum relatus est milium quinquaginta trium.
examples.translation: The purchasers furnished a return to him of three-and-fifty thousand persons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: at some time or other, once; at any time, ever
Latin: Aliquo tempore
Latin: Nonnumquam

examples.original: Nam qui leviter dormit, et species secundum quietem capit et aliquando dormire se dormiens cogitat;
examples.translation: For he whose sleep is light pursues visions during slumber, and sometimes, though asleep, is conscious that he is asleep;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Idem decem fere annis summe dilectus a Paeto Thrasea est ita ut peregrinaretur quoque cum eo aliquando, cognatam eius Arriam uxorem habente.
examples.translation: He was also for nearly ten years so great a favourite of Paetus Thrasea that he sometimes even travelled abroad with him; and Paetus’s wife, Arria, was a relative of his.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Depopulata Gallia Cimbri magnaque illata calamitate finibus quidem nostris aliquando excesserunt atque alias terras petierunt; iura, leges, agros, libertatem nobis reliquerunt.
examples.translation: The Cimbri devastated Gaul, they brought great disaster upon us, yet they departed at length from our borders and sought other countries, leaving us our rights, laws, lands, liberty.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: property taken in war, booty, spoil, plunder, pillage (syn.: exuviae, spolium).

examples.original: Plus praedae ac sanguinis Caecina hausit.
examples.translation: Caecina gained even more booty and shed more blood.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Pauci hostium evasere ex insidiis; praeda omnis recepta est.
examples.translation: But few of them escaped the ambush, and the spoils were all recovered.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque non ego vobis ut indicem praedas vestras, sed vos id cogendi estis ut in medium proferatis.”
examples.translation: And so it is not I that must be forced to tell of your plunder, but you that must be compelled to give it up.”
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: be without, to want, be in want of

examples.original: Sed ne discriminibus quidem caruit.
examples.translation: But he was exposed also to actual dangers.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Bona autem omnia carere culpa decet;
examples.translation: All goods, however, ought properly to be free from blame;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pars vestrum tali munere magna caret.
examples.translation: A great part of you lack a gift so precious.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: To part asunder, divide, separate (rare but class.; cf.: linquo, relinquo, desero, desum, destituo, deficio).
Latin: Loco abeo

examples.original: Hac oratione habita discedit Ambiorix.
examples.translation: After delivering this address Ambiorix departed.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In diversum ecce sapientia et stultitia discedunt;
examples.translation: Lo, Wisdom and Folly are taking opposite sides.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Lucullum magnis rebus gestis ab eo bello discedere;
examples.translation: Lucius Lucullus, despite great achievements, is retiring from the campaign;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: silver, whose mineralogical description is found in
Latin: Elementum chemicum cuius numerus atomicus 47 est
Latin: Res argenteae

examples.original: Auro illos et argento et ebore adornavi, intus boni nihil est.
examples.translation: I have bedecked them with gold, and silver, and ivory, but within there is nothing good.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illi quidem non aurum nec argentum nec perlucidos lapides in ima terrarum faece quaerebant parcebantque adhuc etiam mutis animalibus;
examples.translation: They, at least, searched not in the lowest dregs of the earth for gold, nor yet for silver or transparent stones;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Patres bene coeptam rem perseveranter tueri; conferre ipsi primi, et quia nondum argentum signatum erat, aes grave plaustris quidam ad aerarium convehentes speciosam etiam conlationem faciebant.
examples.translation: They were themselves the first to contribute, and since there was as yet no silver coinage, some of them brought uncoined bronze in waggons to the treasury, and even made a display of their contributing.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to hold up, hold upright, uphold, to bear up, keep up, support, sustain (syn. fulcio).
Latin: sursum tenere
Latin: protegere

examples.original: Illi aegre ad noctem oppugnationem sustinent;
examples.translation: The others scarcely kept off the assault till nightfall;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ostendes morbum posse superari vel certe sustineri.
examples.translation: You will be showing that a disease can be overcome, or at any rate endured.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Me voces audire iuvat sua gaudia fassas, Quaeque morer meme sustineamque rogent.
examples.translation: I like to hear the words that confess rapture, that beg me hold back and stay awhile.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to look at attentively, to get sight of, to descry, perceive, observe (class. in prose and poetry).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; spexi, spectum, 3

examples.original: At bona conscientia prodire vult et conspici;
examples.translation: A good conscience, however, wishes to come forth and be seen of men;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc idem fit in reliquis civitatibus: in omnibus partibus incendia conspiciuntur;
examples.translation: The same was done in the other states, and in every direction fires were to be seen.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Rursus ad primum conspectum redditae lucis alacritas rediit incogitata et iniussa.
examples.translation: Then at the first glimpse of restored daylight my good spirits returned without forethought or command.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a seeking.

examples.original: Huic quaestioni suum diem dabimus;
examples.translation: The problem shall be treated at the proper time;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ecce altera quaestio, quomodo hominibus sit utendum.
examples.translation: Then comes the second problem,—how to deal with men.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad hunc tumultum accitus Postumius asperiora omnia fecit acerbis quaestionibus, crudelibus suppliciis.
examples.translation: Being summoned to deal with this disturbance, Postumius aggravated everything by his harsh inquisitions and savage punishments.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Reverence for God (the gods), the fear of God, connected with a careful pondering of divine things
Latin: Reverentia et pietas Deo; res divinae

examples.original: Adversae deinde res admonuerunt religionum.
examples.translation: Adversity then turned our thoughts upon religion.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Publiusne Clodius, qui ex pontificis maximi domo religionem eripuit, is in meam intulit?
examples.translation: Has Publius Clodius, who robbed the house of the supreme pontiff of its sanctity, conferred sanctity upon mine?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Movisse eos Camillus cum alia oratione tum ea quae ad religiones pertinebat maxime dicitur;
examples.translation: The speech of Camillus is said to have moved them, particularly where he touched upon religion;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to do something to one, i. e. to exert an influence on body or mind, so that it is brought into such or such a state (used by the poets rarely, by Hor. never).
Latin: Facere aliquid ad aliquem

examples.original: Ex honestiore causa coit turpis adfectus?
examples.translation: Can a cause which is more honourable produce a passion that is base?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In omnes personas hic exardescit affectus;
examples.translation: But indeed this emotion blazes out against all sorts of persons;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Contra evenit in his morbis, quibus adficiuntur animi;
examples.translation: The opposite holds true of diseases of the soul;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to take possession of, seize, occupy any thing (esp. a place; class.; cf.: expugno, obsideo).

examples.original: Ex hoc quantum lacrimae, quantum sollicitudines occupant!
examples.translation: How much of this time is taken up with weeping, how much with worry!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ti. Gracchus regnum occupare conatus est, vel regnavit is quidem paucos menses.
examples.translation: Tiberius Gracchus tried to obtain regal power—or rather, he actually did reign for a few months.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Prior ferrum occupavit Antonius, regina ad pedes Caesaris provoluta temptavit oculos ducis.
examples.translation: Antonius was the first to seize the sword of a suicide;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a blazing fire, a blaze, flame (cf. ignis).
Latin: vīsibilis pars ignis, quae flagrat
Latin: ignis

examples.original: Ipsae te fugient, quae carpunt omnia, flammae;
examples.translation: The very flames, which consume all things, shall shun thee;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Magna repente in ipsis operibus flamma exstitit.
examples.translation: A mighty flame suddenly shot forth in the midst of the works;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Natus ut Althaeae flammis absentibus arsit, Sic tuus ardescat stipitis igne rogus.
examples.translation: As absent flames consumed Althaea’s son, so may a firebrand kindle thy funeral pile.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a nodding with the head, a nod: numen quasi nutus dei ac potestas dicitur, Paul. ex

examples.original: Solis nosse deos et caeli numina vobis Aut solis nescire datum;
examples.translation: (To them alone is granted knowledge—or ignorance, it may be—of gods and celestial powers ;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Evolvam busto iam numen gentibus Isim Et tectum lino spargam per volgus Osirim, Suppositisque deis uram caput.
examples.translation: And the land I shall punish too; I shall leave their fields with none to till them;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Una per aetherios exit vox illa recessus Verbaque ad invitum perfert cogentia numen, Quod non cura poli caelique volubilis umquam Avocat.
examples.translation: Their voice alone speeds through the remote parts of heaven, and conveys the words that bind the reluctant deity, whom no care for the sky and revolving firmament ever distracts from listening.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: plqpf. sync. ignosset
Latin: Veniam dare, non punire quem iudices puniendum

examples.original: Non ignovit, mihi crede, non.
examples.translation: No, believe me, she has not forgiven you;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Malo ignoscas otio meo quam invideas.
examples.translation: I prefer you to pardon rather than envy my retirement.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Solacia fati Carthago Mariusque tulit, pariterque iacentes Ignovere deis.
examples.translation: Carthage and Marius both drew consolation for their destiny ;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to commit to one's charge, to enjoin, commission, order, command (syn.: praecipio, edico); constr. alicui aliquid, with

examples.original: His mandatis eum ab se dimittit.
examples.translation: With these instructions he dismissed him.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Habes aditum mansurae in saecula famae.
examples.translation: Here is your opportunity for undying fame.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ergo Fulvio Nobiliori mandata ultio est.
examples.translation: And so the task of vengeance was committed to Fulvius Nobilior.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: any broad and deep-flowing, rapid water; a stream, torrent, river
Latin: Flumen; aqua currens

examples.original: Quid turpius ”amne silvisque ripa comantibus?” Vide ut ”alveum lintribus arent versoque vado remittant hortos.” Quid?
examples.translation: What is more unbecoming than the words:c ”A stream and a bank covered with long-tressed woods”?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Latino Alba ortus, Alba Atys, Atye Capys, Capye Capetus, Capeto Tiberinus, qui in traiectu Albulae amnis submersus celebre ad posteros nomen flumini dedit.
examples.translation: This last king was drowned in crossing the River Albula, and gave the stream the name which has been current with later generations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mox clade conversa, cum ex mora obsidii regem fames et ex fame pestilentia urgueret, recedentem Lucullus adsequitur adeoque cecidit, ut Granicus et Aesepus amnes cruenti redderentur.
examples.translation: Lucullus followed him and dealt him so heavy a blow that the rivers Granicus and Aesepus ran with blood.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: the tongue.
Latin: Viscus quod in solo oris situm est in plerisque chordatis, et quod nexum est cum osse hyoideum
Latin: Potestas locutionis; locutio
entries.etymology: From an older form dingua, from PIE *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s; English 'tongue' is a cognate.

examples.original: Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt.
examples.translation: All these are different one from another in language, institutions, and laws.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hinc enim potius cavendae sunt linguae inimicorum, de quibus tamquam iaculis ad interficiendos infirmos maior ille utitur inimicus.
examples.translation: In this connexion we ought rather to safeguard ourselves against the tongues of our enemies, which our greater enemy employs like darts to slay the weak.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Heraclitus init quorum dux proelia primus, clarus ob obscuram linguam magis inter inanis quamde gravis inter Graios qui vera requirunt.
examples.translation: Of these Heraclitusc opens the fray as first champion, one illustrious for his dark speech rather amongst the frivolous part of the Greeks than amongst the serious who seek the truth.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: a commander-in-chief, general, =
Latin: Qui imperat
Latin: Titulus dignitatis ei qui imperium regnat

examples.original: Tum imperatori exercituique honos suus redditus;
examples.translation: The general and his army then received their meed of honour;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sermo erga patrem imperatoremque reverens, de se moderatus;
examples.translation: He answered with the reverence due to a father and an emperor;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Thrasymennus lacus, tertium fulmen Annibalis, imperatore Flaminio.
examples.translation: Hannibal’s third thunderbolt was launched at Lake Trasimene, where Flaminius commanded the Romans.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a maid, maiden, virgin (cf. puella).
Latin: vir vel mulier quae necdum coierit, vel animal quod nondum coivit
Latin: Ad virginem pertinens. (Dicitur de femina et etiam de viro, coniugii et Veneris expertibus)

examples.original: O quam te memorem, virgo?
examples.translation: O maiden, words are weak!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hunc tam inmaturum amorem virginis ultus est ferro.
examples.translation: The maiden’s girlish affection he punished with the sword.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Virginem ego hanc sum ducturus nuptamque pudicam habiturus.
examples.translation: This maiden I am going to wed;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: manner, custom, way, usage, practice, fashion, wont, as determined not by the laws, but by men's will and pleasure, humor, self-will, caprice (class.; cf.: consuetudo, usus).
Latin: Boni aut mali agendi modi, qui non a legibus, sed a libera hominum etiam singulorum voluntate quum processerint, habitu atque usu firmati sunt
Latin: Institutum consuetudine usuque firmatum, sive bonum, sive malum sit; id quod solitum est alicui facere

examples.original: In mores fortuna ius non habet.
examples.translation: Fortune has no jurisdiction over character.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vivere noluit, qui mori non vult.
examples.translation: He who does not wish to die cannot have wished to live.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Exploratores, ut mos est, longius curabant.
examples.translation: His scouts, as usual, watched the country still further from camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a Punic surname. The most celebrated of the name is Hannibal

examples.original: Cum duobus ducibus de imperio in Italia est decertatum, Pyrrho et Hannibale;
examples.translation: Against two leaders we had bitter struggles for the empire of Italy—Pyrrhus and Hannibal;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hoc responso Karthaginienses cognito, Hannibalem domum et Magonem revocarunt.
examples.translation: Upon receiving that reply the Carthaginians recalled Hannibal and Mago to Carthage.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

examples.original: Hannibal, dux Poenorum, victa classe cui praefuerat, a militibus suis in crucem sublatus est.
examples.translation: Hannibal, a Carthaginian general, on the defeat of the fleet which he commanded, was crucified by his own soldiers.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Of or pertaining to citizens, civil, civic (class. in prose and poetry, and very freq.): sanguine civili rem conflant, by the blood of citizens, *
Latin: Qui ad civem pertinet

examples.original: Cum duce Sullano gerimus civilia bella.
examples.translation: My anxiety is for you;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quae enim res alia civiles furores peperit quam nimiae felicitates?
examples.translation: For what else produced those outbursts of domestic strife but excessive prosperity?
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Iam is gravis annis non militaribus solum sed civilibus quoque abscesserat muneribus;
examples.translation: This man, bowed down with years, had already withdrawn not only from military but even from civic duties;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to drink (ante-class. and post-Aug.; syn. bibo), Caecil. ap.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, or pōtum, 1

examples.original: Potes queri, si here tantum.
examples.translation: You might complain if I said ”yesterday” merely.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Liber Quintus Quis potis est dignum pollenti pectore carmen condere pro rerum maiestate hisque repertis?
examples.translation: Who is able with mighty mind to build a song worthy of the majesty of nature and these discoveries?
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Da mihi hoc, iam tibi maximam partem defensionis praecideris; non enim poteris aratores tibi iratos esse atque inimicos dicere.
examples.translation: Allow me this and instantly you have cut away the main prop of your defence, being then unable to allege that the farmers are angry and hostile.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to place

examples.original: Portis fores altioresque turres imposuit.
examples.translation: At the gateways he set doors and higher turrets.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Falluntur quibus luxuria specie liberalitatis imponit: perdere iste sciet, donare nesciet.
examples.translation: They are deceived who are imposed upon by extravagance under the garb of generosity.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Rebus adversus Poenos a pluribus ducibus prospere gestis, summam victoriae C. Lutatius cos. victa ad Aegates insulas classe Poenorum imposuit.
examples.translation: After a number of generals had gained successes against the Carthaginians, Gaius Lutatius crowned the victory by defeating the Carthaginian fleet off the Aegatian Islands.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to choose, select

examples.original: Citius fieri quam optas, potest.
examples.translation: It may be sooner than thy prayer requests.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid huic optes nisi deos faciles?
examples.translation: What does he mean by such womanish and indecent verse?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aut dives opto vivere aut pauper mori.
examples.translation: If riches bless me, I should love to live;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: sleep: hostes vino domiti somnoque sepulti, Enn. ap.

examples.original: Non proelia fessos Ulla vocant, certos non rumpunt classica somnos.
examples.translation: No battles call them from where they rest; no trumpet-call breaks their sound slumbers.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tristes praesagia curas Exagitant, trepida quatitur formidine somnus, Thessaliam nox omnis habet;
examples.translation: For her sorrow is intensified by forebodings, and her sleep broken by anxious fears.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Clamor subito ortus non consulis modo vigiles, exercitum deinde omnem, sed dictatorem quoque ex somno excivit.
examples.translation: The shout which suddenly broke out aroused not only the consul’s sentries and after them his entire army, but the dictator as well.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the heart (very freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Latin: Musculus corporis hominum et animalium, qui palpitando sanguinem in toto corpore impellit
Latin: Sedes animae et sensuum

examples.original: En cor Zenodoti, en iecur Cratetis.
examples.translation: Lo! Crates’ heart, mind of Zenodotus.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Quid enim aliud furibundo corde concepit, cum diceret matri: ”Transferam me in partem Donati et bibam sanguinem tuum”?
examples.translation: What other purpose was in his raving heart when he said to his mother, ”I will go over to the Donatist party and will drink your blood”?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Quod posteaquam vidi me facere debere, ut eo modo error ipse nefarius de cordibus eorum perfectius auferretur, legi atque respondi.
examples.translation: After I saw that it was my duty to do so in order the more thoroughly to drive that wicked error from their hearts, I read it and composed an answer.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: defensive/town walls (pl.), bulwarks; fortifications; fortified town

examples.original: Sed nec populo aut moenibus patriae pepercit.
examples.translation: But he showed no greater mercy to the people or the walls of his capital.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Brundisium veni, vel potius ad moenia accessi.
examples.translation: I came to Brundisium, or rather approached the walls;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sabini Crustuminos campos citato agmine transgressi cum caedes et incendia circum Anienem flumen fecissent, a porta prope Collina moenibusque pulsi ingentes tamen praedas hominum pecorumque egere.
examples.translation: When almost at the Colline Gate and the City walls they were beaten back, yet they carried off immense spoils of men and cattle.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: rough stone; a detached fragment of rock; a rock (in gen.; whereas rupes is a steep rock, crag, cliff).
Latin: Lapis, petra, silex
Latin: Saepissime dicitur de rupe, caute, scopulo

examples.original: Molaribus demum fracta saxis est.
examples.translation: It was finally destroyed by rocks equal in size to millstones.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Utve soror Pelopis, saxo dureris oborto, Ut laesus lingua Battus ab ipse sua.
examples.translation: Or like Pelops’ sister mayst thou harden with a growth of stone, or like Battus harmed by his own tongue.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vlixes ad Ithacae suae saxa sic properat, quemadmodum Agamemnon ad Mycenarum nobiles muros.
examples.translation: Ulysses hastens back to the rocks of his Ithaca as eagerly as Agamemnon speeds to the kingly walls of Mycenae.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a weight.

examples.original: Ad hoc me natura grave corporis mei pondus adstrinxit.
examples.translation: Behold this clogging burden of a body, to which nature has fettered me!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed tum umido die et soluto gelu neque conti neque gladii, quos praelongos utraque manu regunt, usui, lapsantibus equis et catafractarum pondere.
examples.translation: No people is so cowardly when it comes to fighting on foot, but when they attack the foe on horseback, hardly any line can resist them.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: At tu nec voces (quid enim fallacius illis?) Crede, nec aeternos pondus habere deos.
examples.translation: But do not you believe that words (what more deceiving than they?) or the eternal gods have weight.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the back of men or beasts (syn. dor sum).

examples.original: Et iam ne tergo quidem abstinebatur;
examples.translation: And now they ceased even to respect a man’s person;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Commisso proelio diutius nostrorum militum impetum hostes ferre non potuerunt ac terga verterunt.
examples.translation: When battle was joined the enemy, unable to endure for long the attack of our troops, turned and fled.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nec illi tulere impetum, sed ab effusa fuga flumen obiectum ab tergo arcebat.
examples.translation: They, too, failed to withstand his attack, but their rout was stopped by the river in their rear.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to lead or bring away, to lead, fetch, bring or draw down (for syn. cf.: duco, comitor, prosequor, persequor, stipo, sequor, consequor—freq. and class.).
Latin: Ducere de aliquo

examples.original: Deinde succubui et eo perductus sum, ut ipse destillarem ad summam maciem deductus.
examples.translation: For when I was still young, I could put up with hardships and show a bold front to illness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His condicionibus composita pace exercitum ab Ianiculo deduxit Porsinna et agro Romano excessit.
examples.translation: On these terms peace was made, and Porsinna led his army down from Janiculum and evacuated the Roman territory.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Re impetrata contendunt ut ipsis summa imperi tradatur, et re in controversiam deducta totius Galliae concilium Bibracte indicitur.
examples.translation: The matter was disputed, and a convention of all Gaul was summoned at Bibracte.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to make a noise, to sound, resound: aes sonit, the trumpet sounds, Enn. ap.

examples.original: Et mea nescio quid carmina tale sonant.
examples.translation: My poems too sound somewhat in that strain.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Phoebus adest: sonuere lyrae, sonuere pharetrae;
examples.translation: Phoebus is here: his lyres and quivers have resounded;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tu quoque, cui veneris sensum natura negavit, Dulcia mendaci gaudia finge sono.
examples.translation: You to whom nature has denied the sensation of love, counterfeit the sweet bliss with lying sounds.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to remember, recollect, to think of, be mindful of a thing; not to have forgotten a person or thing, to bear in mind (syn.: reminiscor, recordor); constr. with

examples.original: Aliud autem est meminisse, aliud scire.
examples.translation: But it is one thing to remember, another to know.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Valde enim bonae memoriae est, si meminit!
examples.translation: He must have a particularly good memory if he can remember that!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Primum in nostrane est potestate quid meminerimus?
examples.translation: To begin with, have we the power to choose what we shall remember?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to bear or bring away a thing from a place; to bear, carry, bring down.
Latin: Vehere vel portare res deorsum, secundo flumine

examples.original: Haec a compluribus ad Caesarem deferebantur.
examples.translation: These plots were reported to Caesar by several persons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Postquam datas sensit, rem ad consules detulit.
examples.translation: When he saw that the letters had been given, he laid the matter before the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Arpineius et Iunius, quae audierunt, ad legatos deferunt.
examples.translation: Arpineius and Junius reported what they heard to the lieutenant-generals.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to look to or upon a person or thing, to behold, look at
Latin: Videre; ad aliquid specere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; others except Halm; spexi, spectum, 3

examples.original: Profert se, laudari et aspici credit.
examples.translation: This spirit thrusts itself forward, confident of commendation and esteem.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum aspexeris, quot te antecedant, cogita, quot sequantur.
examples.translation: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aspicit Hesiones scopulos silvaque latentes Anchisae thalamos;
examples.translation: He sees Hesione’s rock and the secret marriage-chamber of Anchises in the wood;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: at the time of day when; form donicum, Liv. And., Cato and Plaut. ap.
Latin: dum, quamdiu, quoad

examples.original: Pax erit haec nobis, donec mihi vita manebit, Cum pecore infirmo quae solet esse lupis.
examples.translation: That peace shall we enjoy, while life remains to me, which wolves are wont to keep with the defenceless flock.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Perseverandum est et adsiduo studio robur addendum, donec bona mens sit quod bona voluntas est.
examples.translation: You must persevere, must develop new strength by continuous study, until that which is only a good inclination becomes a good settled purpose.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potitii ab Euandro edocti antistites sacri eius per multas aetates fuerunt, donec tradito servis publicis sollemni familiae ministerio genus omne Potitiorum interiit.
examples.translation: The Potitii, instructed by Evander, were priests of this cult for many generations, until, having delegated to public slaves the solemn function of their family, the entire stock of the Potitii died out.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to play.
Latin: Se delectationis causa exercere
Latin: aliquid per ludum facere

examples.original: Hic, cum quo ludis, timet;
examples.translation: This friend, in whose company you are jesting, is in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quo die repulsus est, lusit, qua nocte periturus fuit, legit.
examples.translation: The day whereon he failed of election, he spent in play;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ludite, si sapitis, solas impune puellas: Hac minus est una fraude tuenda fides.
examples.translation: If you are wise, cheat women only, and avoid trouble; keep faith save for this one deceitfulness.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: without beginning or end, eternal
Latin: Qui in omnibus aevis exstitit; et sine principio et sine fine

examples.original: An cuiusquam tibi temporalis salus carior esse debuerat quam huius aeterna?
examples.translation: Or ought anyone’s temporal welfare to have been more precious to you than his eternal welfare?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: At tu nec voces (quid enim fallacius illis?) Crede, nec aeternos pondus habere deos.
examples.translation: But do not you believe that words (what more deceiving than they?) or the eternal gods have weight.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: De divinis humanisque discendum est, de praeteritis de futuris, de caducis de aeternis, de tempore.
examples.translation: One must learn about things divine and human, the past and the future, the ephemeral and the eternal;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fruit-bearing, fruitful, fertile, productive.

examples.original: Sed felix, qui ad meliora hunc inpetum dedit!
examples.translation: He will place himself beyond the jurisdiction of chance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec tua quam Pyrrhi felicius ossa quiescant, Sparsa per Ambracias quae iacuere vias.
examples.translation: Nor may thy bones rest more blissful than those of Pyrrhus, which lay scattered through Ambracian ways.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Obvia progrediar felixque per oppida dicar Collaque et hoc oculos illius ore premam.
examples.translation: I shall go forth to meet him, and through the cities I shall be called fortunate;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: with God's help

examples.original: Collatio igitur ista te nihil iuvat;
examples.translation: So your comparison does not help you;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ex illius imperio paratae sint iuvandis manus.
examples.translation: Through her orders, let our hands be ready for all that needs to be helped.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ac primo Valerius Festus legatus studia provincialium cum fide iuvit;
examples.translation: At first the commander, Valerius Festus, loyally supported the wishes of the provincials.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: dear, precious, valued, esteemed
Latin: De materiali seu mercatorio rerum pretio — carus est qui nimio pretio emitur, cui vilis opponitur
Latin: De morali alicujus personae aut rei pretio vel existimatione — carus dicitur et est qui magni fit vel ducitur, adeoque amatus, dilectus

examples.original: Non est quod mireris, Lucili carissime.
examples.translation: You need not be surprised, my beloved Lucilius.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ea enim parte sibi carus est homo, qua homo est.
examples.translation: For man is dear to himself in respect of that wherein he is a man.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam diligi et carum esse iucundum est propterea quia tutiorem vitam et voluptatum pleniorem efficit.
examples.translation: For esteem and affection are gratifying, because they render life safer and fuller of pleasure.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to wander, to wander or stray about, to wander up and down, to rove
Latin: Libere ultroque et nullo sibi proposito itineris fine vagari
Latin: Incertus viae ignarusque huc illuc ferri
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Ac fieri potest ut errem;
examples.translation: I may possibly be mistaken;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non ire istuc, sed errare est.
examples.translation: What you suggest is not travelling; it is mere tramping.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Victoriam illi proelio error dedit.
examples.translation: A mistake decided the victory in this battle.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: nearly, almost
Latin: Proximē, sed non omnīnō; fermē
Latin: prope minime; vix

examples.original: Huc cum ab Ostia navigaret, vehementi circio bis paene demersus est, prope Liguriam iuxtaque Stoechadas insulas.
examples.translation: On the voyage thither from Ostia he was nearly cast away twice in furious north-westers, off Liguria and near the Stoechades islands.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec minore livore ac malignitate quam superbia saevitiaque paene adversus omnis aevi hominum genus grassatus est.
examples.translation: He assailed mankind of almost every epoch with no less envy and malice than insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Et subinde matre etiam relegata paene inops atque egens apud amitam Lepidam nutritus est sub duobus paedagogis saltatore atque tonsore.
examples.translation: Then his mother was banished too, and he was brought up at the house of his aunt Lepida almost in actual want, under two tutors, a dancer and a barber.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: nothing; no; trifle/thing not worth mentioning

examples.original: Tum porro si nil esset quod inane vacaret, omne foret solidum;
examples.translation: Then further, if there were nothing void and empty, the universe would be solid;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Nil melius aeterna lex fecit, quam quod unum introitum nobis ad vitam dedit, exitus multos.
examples.translation: The best thing which eternal law ever ordained was that it allowed to us one entrance into life, but many exits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Detegit inbelles animas nil fortiter ausa Seditio tantumque fugam meditata iuventus Ac ducis invicti rebus lassata secundis.
examples.translation: That you have no stomach for fighting is revealed; for your mutiny ends in words;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To make a thing completely ready, to make, prepare, bring about, complete, accomplish, execute, etc. (except in Quint., freq. in all periods and species of composition).
Latin: Facere aliquid ad finem

examples.original: Ea qui conficeret, C. Trebonium legatum relinquit.
examples.translation: He left Gaius Trebonius, lieutenant-general, to carry out these orders.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Scio Caesarem singulorum annorum singulos commentarios confecisse;
examples.translation: I am aware that Caesar has compiled a separate Commentary for each year;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed neque iam ’duplicis’ nec iam ’sors altera partus,’ Gloria confectae nunc quoque matris, ubi es?
examples.translation: No more a ’twofold birth,’ no more ’one-half its fortune,’ yet still the glory of thy aged mother, where art thou?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: heavy, unwieldy, immovable (rare): brutum antiqui gravem dicebant, Paul. ex

examples.original: Cato illa honestissime usus est, turpissime Brutus.
examples.translation: Cato experienced death most honourably, Brutus most basely.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Mittit primo Brutum adulescentem cum cohortibus Caesar, post cum aliis Gaium Fabium legatum;
examples.translation: Caesar first sent young Brutus with some cohorts, and then Gaius Fabius, lieutenant-general, with others;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ut Antonius rediit in Italiam, nemo non magno in periculo Atticum putarat propter intimam familiaritatem Ciceronis et Bruti.
examples.translation: Antony returned to Italy, and there was no one but thought that Atticus was in extreme danger because of his intimacy with Cicero and Brutus.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

definitions: English: To follow, follow up, press upon, go after, attend, accompany, pursue any person or thing (class. in prose and poetry); constr. with

examples.original: Subinde itaque, Lucili, quam multa sis consecutus recordare.
examples.translation: Therefore continually remind yourself, Lucilius, how many ambitions you have attained.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ea scientia et verborum vis et natura orationis et consequentium repugnantiumve ratio potest perspici;
examples.translation: This sciencea explains to us the meaning of terms, the nature of predication, and the law of consistency and contradiction;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nostri, simul in arido constiterunt, suis omnibus consecutis in hostes impetum fecerunt atque eos in fugam dederunt;
examples.translation: The moment our men stood firm on dry land, they charged with all their comrades close behind, and put the enemy to rout;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: easily movable, pliant, flexible, supple; soft, tender, delicate, gentle, mild, pleasant (class.; syn.: tener, facilis, flexibilis, lentus).

examples.original: Numquam virtutis molle documentum est.
examples.translation: No proof of virtue is ever mild.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Molli consurgit Amyclas, Quem dabat alga, toro.
examples.translation: Amyclas rose up from the soft bed that seaweed gave him.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Chelidon, unus ex Cleopatrae mollibus, patrimonium grande possedit.
examples.translation: Chelidon, one of Cleopatra’s eunuchs, possessed great wealth;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to assign, impart, allot, bestow, give, etc. (syn.: do, dono, largior).
Latin: Donare, largiri

examples.original: Hos ignava iocos tribuit natura puellis;
examples.translation: These are the games that indolent nature has given to women;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Neque hoc illi quisquam tribuebat superbiae;
examples.translation: And no one regarded this as arrogance on his part;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Timoleon

examples.original: Si uni omnia tribuenda sint, dignissimum esse Pompeium, sed ad unum tamen omnia deferri non oportere.
examples.translation: That if one man is to be put in supreme command, the right man is Pompeius;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a written communication
Latin: Nuntium scriptum, litterae

examples.original: Sed iam debeo epistulam includere.
examples.translation: But now I ought to close my letter.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In eundem modum et Mucianus composuit epistulas;
examples.translation: Mucianus also wrote to him to the same effect;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nomen Attici perire Ciceronis epistulae non sinunt.
examples.translation: Cicero’s letters keep the name of Atticus from perishing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hold in front, i. e.
Latin: Curare ut aliquis aut aliquid procul restet
Latin: impedīre

examples.original: Conantes dicere prohibuit et in catenas coniecit.
examples.translation: To spy?” When they tried to speak he prevented them and flung them into chains.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: At Caesar dispositis in vallo custodibus recipi prohibebat.
examples.translation: But Caesar posted sentries on the rampart and prevented their admission.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid enim me prohiberet Epicureum esse, si probarem quae ille diceret?
examples.translation: What should prevent me from being an Epicurean, if I accepted the doctrines of Epicurus?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Useful, serviceable, beneficial, profitable, advantageous, etc. (cf. commodus).
Latin: Quo uti possumus, qui usui est; prōficuus, accommodātus
Latin: Commodus, lucrōsus

examples.original: Illa enim utilia vitaliaque sunt;
examples.translation: For the one condition is useful and life-giving;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dividi enim illam, non concidi, utile est.
examples.translation: For it is useful that philosophy should be divided, but not chopped into bits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ait utilem futuram et descriptionem cuiusque virtutis;
examples.translation: He remarks that it will also be useful to illustrate each particular virtue;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: sorrowful, mournful, dejected, melancholy, disconsolate, trist (syn.: maestus, severus, austerus, luctuosus).

examples.original: Sunt quaedam tristis voltus bona.
examples.translation: There are certain goods whose features are forbidding.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc est, quod tristes docemus et pallidi?
examples.translation: Is this the matter which we teach with sour and pale faces?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Imperioso quoque Manlio cognomen inditum; Postumius nulla tristi nota est insignitus.
examples.translation: Besides, Manlius was given the surname Imperiosus—”the Despotic”—while Postumius received no such grim distinction.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: hatred, grudge, illwill, animosity, enmity, aversion

examples.original: Odisse plebem plus quam paterno odio: quid?
examples.translation: He hated the plebs with a hatred that surpassed his father’s: What?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Odi concubitus, qui non utrumque resolvunt;
examples.translation: I hate embraces which leave not each outworn;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Eorum querella inveterata non modo familiaritates exstingui solere, sed odia etiam gigni sempiterna.
examples.translation: By their ceaseless recriminations not only are social intimacies usually destroyed, but also everlasting enmities are produced.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to drive out or forth, to thrust out, to take or turn out.

examples.original: Decessit aetatis exactae sub Tiberio.
examples.translation: He died at an advanced age under Tiberius.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Illud, ut non doleas, vix audebo exigere;
examples.translation: That you should not mourn at all I shall hardly dare to insist;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O quantum lacrimarum, quantum laborum exigit!
examples.translation: What tears and toil does money wring from us!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fear, dread, apprehension, anxiety; constr. with

examples.original: Numerare eos noli, qui tibi metum faciunt.
examples.translation: Do not count the number of those who inspire fear in you.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quantum ad successus accesserit, accedet ad metus.
examples.translation: But all that is added to your successes will be added to your fears.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His ac talibus inter spem metumque iactatum spes vicit.
examples.translation: These considerations and others like them made him waver between hope and fear;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: otherwise, differently; in any other way
Latin: Alio modo, alia ratione
Latin: Alio modo

examples.original: Nobis aliter videtur; recte secusne, postea;
examples.translation: We think otherwise—whether rightly or wrongly, I will consider later;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Corpus quoque, etiam si magnas habet vires, non aliter quam furiosi aut phrenetici validum est.
examples.translation: This, then, is the sort of health you should primarily cultivate;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quibusdam etiam constantissimis in conspectu populi sudor erumpit, non aliter quam fatigatis et aestuantibus solet, quibusdam tremunt genua dicturis, quorundam dentes colliduntur, lingua titubat, labra concurrunt.
examples.translation: The steadiest speaker, when before the public, often breaks into a perspiration, as if he had wearied or over-heated himself; some tremble in the knees when they rise to speak;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be between, lie between (class.; syn. interjaceo).
Latin: Inter aliqua esse
Latin: Medius esse, praesens adesse

examples.original: Et quid interest quis dixerit?
examples.translation: But what difference does it make who spoke the words?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Accelerat Caesar, ut proelio intersit.
examples.translation: Caesar hurried on to take part in the action.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non interfuit occidentium quid diceret.
examples.translation: His murderers cared nothing for what he said.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to be angry, to be in a rage (syn.: succenseo, indignor); constr.

examples.original: Quis enim phrenetico medicus irascitur?
examples.translation: What physician gets angry with a lunatic?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ut nunc res se habet, irati sunt, oderunt, negant missuros;
examples.translation: Just now they are angry and resentful, and declare that they will send none;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Da mihi hoc, iam tibi maximam partem defensionis praecideris; non enim poteris aratores tibi iratos esse atque inimicos dicere.
examples.translation: Allow me this and instantly you have cut away the main prop of your defence, being then unable to allege that the farmers are angry and hostile.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: care, solicitude, carefulness, thought, concern.

examples.original: Curam quoque solito exactiorem praestitit.
examples.translation: He also observed more scrupulous care than usual.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Mihi legiones peditumque pugna curae erunt;
examples.translation: I will see to the legions and the battle of the infantry;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nulla recantatas deponent pectora curas, Nec fugiet vivo sulpure victus amor.
examples.translation: No hearts will lay aside their passion by enchantment, nor love flee vanquished by strong sulphur.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a going in, en trance.
Latin: exordium, prima res

examples.original: Sursum illum vocant initia sua.
examples.translation: The soul is summoned upward by its very origin.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Similis exitus belli initiis fuit.
examples.translation: The course of the war resembled its beginning;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Initium atrocis in Caecinam sententiae a L. Vitellio factum;
examples.translation: Lucius Vitellius took the lead in proposing severe measures directed against Caecina;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to consider a person or thing as unimportant or of small value, to value little, esteem lightly, contemn, despise, disdain, defy, not to fear, etc.

examples.original: Ad contemptum nos doloris armavimus;
examples.translation: We have armed ourselves to scorn pain;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O te miserum, si contemnis hunc testem!
examples.translation: How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Contemptus corporis sui certa libertas est.
examples.translation: To despise our bodies is sure freedom.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: proper measure; hence

examples.original: At mores commodi. Quis contumacior?
examples.translation: Is it said that he is good-natured?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ab neutra parte satis commode instructi fuerunt;
examples.translation: On neither side had the forces been very advantageously marshalled;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Colloquuntur. Dies ex utriusque commodo sumitur.
examples.translation: A conference was held and a day chosen to suit both parties.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a sister: Th. Salve, mea soror.
Latin: Femina quae eosdem parentes quos aliquis habet
entries.etymology: From PIE *swésōr 'sister'; English 'sister' is a cognate.

examples.original: Et tibi dant Stygiae ius in sua fila sorores.
examples.translation: Yet even to it the Stygian sisters gave power over their spinning.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Utve soror Pelopis, saxo dureris oborto, Ut laesus lingua Battus ab ipse sua.
examples.translation: Or like Pelops’ sister mayst thou harden with a growth of stone, or like Battus harmed by his own tongue.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vel tu venandi studium cole: saepe recessit Turpiter a Phoebi victa sorore Venus.
examples.translation: Or cultivate the pleasures of the chase: ofttimes has Venus, vanquished by Phoebus’ sister, beaten a base retreat.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: or if; or

examples.original: Ceterum utraque caedes sinistre accepta, et inviso semel principi seu bene seu male facta parem invidiam adferebant.
examples.translation: But both executions were unfavourably received, and now that the emperor was once hated, his good and evil deeds alike brought him unpopularity.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Praemissus tamen in castra Piso, ut iuvenis magno nomine, recenti favore et infensus Tito Vinio, seu quia erat seu quia irati ita volebant;
examples.translation: Yet Piso was sent first to the camp, for he was young, had a great name, and enjoyed fresh popularity; he was also an enemy of Titus Vinius;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Accedebat huc Caecinae ambitio vetus, torpor recens, nimia fortunae indulgentia soluti in luxum, seu perfidiam meditanti infringere exercitus virtutem inter artes erat.
examples.translation: Another factor in the situation was furnished by Caecina’s old ambition and his newly acquired sloth, for an excess of Fortune’s favours had made him give way to luxury;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: even, level, flat

examples.original: Quae vobis alio loco planius explicabuntur: nunc hoc attendite.
examples.translation: The story of all this shall be told in clearer detail later on;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De qua re quid sentiam, satis, ut arbitror, in epistula quam ad fratrem meum scripsi, planissime aperui.
examples.translation: In the lettera I wrote to my brother I have, I think, revealed with sufficient clearness my opinion on this point.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Istiusmodi autem res dicere ornate velle puerile est, plane autem et perspicue expedire posse docti et intellegentis viri.”
examples.translation: A man of sense and education will be content to be able to express his meaning plainly and clearly.”
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to shut.

examples.original: Aera non potuit Minos, alia omnia clausit;
examples.translation: The air Minos could not close, though he had closed all else;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vercingetorix iubet portas claudi, ne castra nudentur.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix ordered the gates to be shut, lest the camp should be deserted.
