examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: I nunc, claude fores, custos odiose puellae, Et centum duris postibus obde seras!
examples.translation: Go now, hateful guardian, bar the lady’s door, and add a hundred bolts to the sturdy posts.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a wood, forest, woodland (syn.: saltus, nemus, lucus).
Latin: Aggregatio arborum

examples.original: Aspicit Hesiones scopulos silvaque latentes Anchisae thalamos;
examples.translation: He sees Hesione’s rock and the secret marriage-chamber of Anchises in the wood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non hos palus in bello latrociniisque natos, non silvae morantur.
examples.translation: No marsh, no woods check these children of war and brigandage.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non est admirationi una arbor, ubi in eandem altitudinem tota silva surrexit.
examples.translation: There is unevenness, you know, when some objects rise conspicuous above others.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to confess

examples.original: Metiri sua regna decet viresque fateri.
examples.translation: We must take the measure of our kingdom and confess our weakness.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Fateris et alia secundum naturam quidem esse, sed bona non esse.
examples.translation: You admit, too, that there are other things according to nature, which, however, are not good.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Me voces audire iuvat sua gaudia fassas, Quaeque morer meme sustineamque rogent.
examples.translation: I like to hear the words that confess rapture, that beg me hold back and stay awhile.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to fall upon or attack again or anew, to strike again (syn. repercutio).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3

examples.original: Quod repetam, si te dimisero, et redimam.
examples.translation: But, if I can once dispose of you, I shall reseek and rescue it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Stellarum iste discursus quicquid praeterit repetit;
examples.translation: The wandering stars retrace their former courses;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eum impetum non tulerunt Etrusci versisque signis fuga effusa castra repetunt.
examples.translation: Their onset was too much for the Etruscans, who faced about and fled headlong towards their camp.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to announce, declare, report, relate, narrate, make known, inform, give intelligence of, etc. (cf.: narro, indico, trado, scribo, dico, certiorem facio, etc.).
Latin: Dicere nuntium alicui

examples.original: Eo nuntio erecti patres, erecta plebes.
examples.translation: These tidings cheered the Fathers and encouraged the plebs.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Re nuntiata ad suos, quae imperarentur facere dixerunt.
examples.translation: They reported this to their tribesmen, and agreed to perform his commands.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod ubi consuli nuntiatum est, ”Di in proelio sunt” inquit;
examples.translation: The consul, on being told of this, exclaimed, ”The gods are present in the battle;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To give

examples.original: Extremam eius vocem, ut cuique odium aut admiratio fuit, varie prodidere.
examples.translation: His last words have been variously reported according to the hatred or admiration of individuals;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Magistratus quae visa sunt occultant quaeque esse ex usu iudicaverunt multitudini produnt.
examples.translation: Magistrates conceal what they choose, and make known what they think proper for the public.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Alia sententia, asperior in speciem, vim minorem aliquanto habuit, quae patricios coire ad prodendum interregem iubebat.
examples.translation: For by passing any measure whatsoever they declared those who presided over the senate to be magistrates;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to touch (syn. tracto).
Latin: Tactūs sensu deprehendere
Latin: Tactûs sensu deprehendere

examples.original: Nubila tanguntur velis et terra carina.
examples.translation: The sails reach the clouds, the keel rests on the bottom.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Si non tangent illum parva, ne maiora quidem;
examples.translation: If small things do not move him, neither will the greater ones;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil enim accidere sine tactu potest; quod tangit, corpus est.
examples.translation: For nothing can affect another object without touching it, and that which touches is corporeal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: In tmesi
Latin: (Trans.) in diversa ferre, dissipare
Latin: dissimilem diversumque esse, discrepare

examples.original: Illius tibi noctem promitto nec differo;
examples.translation: That beauty whom you desire shall visit you.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Germani multum ab hac consuetudine differunt.
examples.translation: The Germans differ much from this manner of living.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Vidi ego, quod fuerat primo sanabile, vulnus Dilatum longae damna tulisse morae.
examples.translation: I have seen a wound, that at first was healable, by tarrying suffer the penalty of long delay.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to rage, rave (in sickness or when in a passion), to be out of one's mind

examples.original: Non privatim solum, sed publice furimus.
examples.translation: We are mad, not only individually, but nationally.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis furor, o cives, quae tanta licentia ferri?
examples.translation: What madness was this, my countrymen, what fierce orgy of slaughter?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Adice nunc scordalum et furem deprensum et illum, cui vox sua in balineo placet.
examples.translation: Then, perhaps, a professional a comes along, shouting out the score; that is the finishing touch.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to let go through, suffer to pass through.

examples.original: Cura ripae Hordeonio Flacco permissa;
examples.translation: The duty of guarding the Rhine he assigned to Hordeonius Flaccus.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quid si illi etiam nunc permiseris crescere?
examples.translation: What if, even now, you allow that position to grow greater?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ipsis permittimus, unde velint sumere exemplaria.
examples.translation: We allow the purchasers themselves to get their samples from anywhere they please.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to snatch, tear, or pull out; to snatch away, take away (freq. and class.; cf.: capio, prehendo, sumo, demo, adimo, rapio, furor).

examples.original: Quid est aliud, quod tibi eripi doleas?
examples.translation: What else is there which you would regret to have taken from you?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Alimenta tibi leonum et vulturum eripio.”
examples.translation: I am merely depriving you of food which sustains lions and vultures.”
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Mihi quidem Scipio, quamquam est subito ereptus, vivit tamen semperque vivet ;
examples.translation: For me, indeed, though he was suddenly snatched away, Scipio still lives and will always live;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to undertake, endeavor, attempt, try, venture, presume, etc.
Latin: pergere ut aliquid efficeretur

examples.original: Tempus est etiam maiora conari.
examples.translation: The time has come to attempt even greater things.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Conantes dicere prohibuit et in catenas coniecit.
examples.translation: To spy?” When they tried to speak he prevented them and flung them into chains.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ad honestatem enim illum omnem conatum suum referebat, non ad voluptatem.
examples.translation: For honour and not pleasure was the aim of that great enterprise.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: sweet (very freq.; cf.: suavis, venustus, jucundus, gratus, acceptus, amoenus, etc.).

examples.original: Nec facile est animo dulcem sonum excutere;
examples.translation: It is not easy to rid the memory of a catching tune;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Serpens, sitis, ardor harenae Dulcia virtuti;
examples.translation: Serpents, thirst, burning sand—all are welcomed by the brave;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Si autem pax humana tam dulcis est pro temporali salute mortalium, quanto est dulcior pax divina pro aeterna salute angelorum!
examples.translation: So let it be your necessity and not your choice that slays the enemy who is fighting against you.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to throw or put before or towards, to throw to, to hold before or out, to offer, present, expose; constr. usu. aliquid (aliquem) alicui, or simply aliquid

examples.original: Interim ut piaculum obicitur centurio Crispinus.
examples.translation: In the meantime the centurion Crispinus was offered as a scapegoat.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quod ubi animadvertit Camillus, ignem in obiectam saepem coici iussit;
examples.translation: On perceiving this, Camillus ordered his men to throw fire on the barrier.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Scrutabitur scholas nostras et obiciet philosophis congiaria, amicas, gulam.
examples.translation: He will forestall every word which I am about to utter.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to gather or collect together into a whole or to a point, to assemble, draw or bring together, collect (class. and very freq.)
Latin: res primum quaerere et deinde in unum punctum collocare

examples.original: Sed quid ego aedilicias repulsas colligo?
examples.translation: But why this catalogue of failures to obtain this office?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nec diu exempla, quibus confirmeris, colligenda sunt;
examples.translation: And you need not spend a long time in gathering illustrations which will strengthen you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si probationes necessariae sunt, et decreta, quae veritatem argumentis colligunt.
examples.translation: If proofs are necessary, so are doctrines; for doctrines deduce the truth by reasoning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: place
Latin: Simul ponere
Latin: musicam creare

examples.original: In eundem modum et Mucianus composuit epistulas;
examples.translation: Mucianus also wrote to him to the same effect;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nam et haec ab habitu animi compositi validique proficiscitur.
examples.translation: For proof also originates from a well-ordered and firm mental attitude.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si ille sanus est, si compositus, gravis, temperans, ingenium quoque siccum ac sobrium est;
examples.translation: If his soul be wholesome, well-ordered, serious, and restrained, his ability also is sound and sober.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a horn.
Latin: Durum, proiectum et saepe acutum membrum, ex capite animalium, ut ruminantium
Latin: Acies militaris

examples.original: In acie Quinctius dextrum cornu, Agrippa sinistrum tenuit;
examples.translation: In the battle-line Quinctius held the right wing, Agrippa the left;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tunc veniunt risus, tum pauper cornua sumit, Tum dolor et curae rugaque frontis abit.
examples.translation: Then laughter comes, then even the poor find vigour, then sorrow and care and the wrinkles of the brow depart.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cornus tibi cura sinistri, Lentule, cum prima, quae tum fuit optima bello, Et quarta legione datur.
examples.translation: Lentulus had charge of the left wing with two legions—the first, which was then the most fit for war, and the fourth;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to set forth, expose (class.; most freq. in the trop. signif.; cf.: expedio, explano, explico).
Latin: Extra ponere
Latin: Coram ponere

examples.original: Coepi gubernatorem rogare, ut me in aliquo litore exponeret.
examples.translation: I began to ask the pilot to put me ashore somewhere;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil habent quo tegantur, ad ictum totis corporibus expositi numquam frustra manum mittunt.
examples.translation: They are exposed to blows at all points, and no one ever strikes in vain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nunc mihi temporis eius quod mihi ad dicendum datur, quoniam in animo est causam omnem exponere, habenda ratio est diligenter.
examples.translation: But I must now take careful account of the time allowed me for my speech, since I intend to set forth the case in full.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to accompany, attend, follow

examples.original: Comites illi tui delecti manus erant tuae;
examples.translation: The members of your select retinue were your hands;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quanta in altero diritas, in altero comitas!
examples.translation: What a disagreeable nature one of them has, and what an affable disposition has the other!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illic est individuus ille comitatus virtutum;
examples.translation: There is the whole inseparable company of virtues;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: furnish, provide with necessaries; to equip, to get ready, prepare (class.; syn. exorno, concinno).

examples.original: Universis egi initio quantum potui: satis ornate agere nullo modo possum.
examples.translation: At the outset I thanked you collectively to the best of my ability;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illi statim myoparonem egregium de sua classe ornatum atque armatum dederunt;
examples.translation: They promptly supplied him from their fleet with an excellent cruiser, fully furnished and equipped;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Deinde ea quae requirebant orationem ornatam et gravem, quam magnifice sunt dicta ab illis, quam splendide!
examples.translation: Then, in themes demanding ornate and dignified treatment, how imposing, how brilliant is their diction!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: solid, thick, dense, fat, gross, etc. (freq. and class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: In hoc homine atque in eius modi causa quid facerent omnes Crassi et Antonii?
examples.translation: With such a client, and with such a case, what would any Crassus or Antonius do?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iamque hebes et crasso non asper sanguine mucro Perdidit ensis opus, frangit sine volnere membra.
examples.translation: All the host and all the weapons make him their sole object; no hand missed its aim, no lance failed of its mark;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tribuni consulari potestate erant Ap. Claudius Crassus Sp. Nautius Rutulus L. Sergius Fidenas Sex. Iulius Iulus.
examples.translation: The tribunes with consular authority were Appius Claudius Crassus, Spurius Nautius Rutulus, Lucius Sergius Fidenas, and Sextus Julius lulus.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to carry, bring

examples.original: Infert pavidos fuga in mediam caedem;
examples.translation: In their panic they fled into the middle of the carnage.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Avaritia paupertatem intulit et multa concupiscendo omnia amisit.
examples.translation: It was avarice that introduced poverty and, by craving much, lost all.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et postquam multa iam dies erat neque movebatur quicquam ab hoste, iubet signa inferri consul;
examples.translation: So, when the day was now far spent and the enemy made no move, the consul ordered an advance.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: stuff, matter, materials of which any thing is composed; so the wood of a tree, vine, etc., timber for building (opp. lignum, wood for fuel)
Latin: Res, ex qua et in qua sunt omnia

examples.original: Hoc causa est, illud materia.
examples.translation: The former is its material, the latter its cause.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non praebiturum se illi eo die materiam;
examples.translation: He would furnish him no excuse for it that day;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ex quo fit: haec materia est.
examples.translation: The agent is God; the source, matter;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a master, chief, head, superior, director, president, leader, commander, conductor, etc.
Latin: Praefectus, praeses
Latin: Doctor; vir qui docet

examples.original: Magister equitum et ipse novat pugnam equestrem.
examples.translation: The master of the horse on his part invented a new kind of cavalry-fighting.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ipse deinde C. Servilium Ahalam magistrum equitum dicit.
examples.translation: He then himself named Gaius Servilius Ahala his master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Dictator L. Furius Camillus dictus, addito magistro equitum P. Cornelio Scipione, reddidit patribus possessionem pristinam consulatus.
examples.translation: Lucius Furius Camillus was appointed to that office, and Publius Cornelius Scipio was made his master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the Calends, the first day of the month: primi dies nominati Kalendae, ab eo quod his diebus calantur ejus mensis nonae a pontificibus, quintanae an septimanae sint futurae
Latin: Primus dies mensis in calendario Romano

examples.original: Pridie kalendas Novembris Rosius Regulus iniit eiuravitque.
examples.translation: On the thirty-first of October Rosius Regulus entered and gave up his office.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Kal. Dec. M. Aemilio Lepido iterum L. Munatio Planco conss. per bellum Philippense.
examples.translation: In fact it is so recorded both in the calendar and in the public gazette.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Omnes exclusi sunt non minus aperte quam pupillus. Diem praestituit operi faciundo Kalendas Decembres, locat circiter Idus Septembres;
examples.translation: The day Verres fixed for the undertaking to be completed was the 1st of December, and he let the contract about the 13th of September;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Spain
Latin: Natio Hispanorum, in Iberia
Latin: Una ex duabus partibus Hispaniae a flumine Ibero divisae

examples.original: Ii erant T. Vinius legatus eius in Hispania, cupiditatis immensae;
examples.translation: They were Titus Vinius, one of his generals in Spain, a man of unbounded covetousness;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hic finis Augusto bellicorum certaminum fuit, idem rebellandi finis Hispaniae.
examples.translation: This was the end of Augustus’ campaigns as well as of the rebellion in Spain.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Scriptae in Britanniam ad quartadecimanos, in Hispaniam ad primanos epistulae, quod utraque legio pro Othone, adversa Vitellio fuerat;
examples.translation: They addressed communications to the Fourteenth legion in Britain and to the First in Spain, for both these legions had been for Otho and opposed to Vitellius;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: subject to death, liable to die, mortal (class.).
Latin: Qui olim aut mox morietur, cuius vita non sempiterna est

examples.original: Quod nullius mortalium cogitatio recipit.
examples.translation: But no human being, on serious consideration, admits this idea.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atque hoc quidem omnes mortales et intellegunt et re probant.
examples.translation: And indeed this is a statement which all men not only understand but also approve.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mortalia minuuntur, cadunt, deteruntur, crescunt, exhauriuntur, inplentur.
examples.translation: Mortal things decay, fall, are worn out, grow up, are exhausted, and replenished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hold forth, reach out, proffer, offer (class., esp. in the trop. signif.; syn.: ministro, suppedito, suggero).

examples.original: Non praebiturum se illi eo die materiam;
examples.translation: He would furnish him no excuse for it that day;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Pestilentia eo anno aliarum rerum otium praebuit.
examples.translation: An epidemic that year afforded a respite from other troubles.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Gaudete, cohortes: Obvia praebentur fatorum munere bella.
examples.translation: By favour of destiny war is offered you in the course of your march.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to cover, veil.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; psi, ptum, 3

examples.original: Sol me invitabat, fames ad monebat, nubes minabantur;
examples.translation: The sunlight called to me, hunger warned, and clouds were lowering;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Virginem ego hanc sum ducturus nuptamque pudicam habiturus.
examples.translation: This maiden I am going to wed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nubit genero socrus, nullis auspicibus, nullis auctoribus, funestis ominibus omnium. VI.
examples.translation: She is reluctant that her fair fame should any longer be damaged by dim and doubtful suspicion;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to drink
Latin: Liquidum haurire, ut exempli causa sitem exstinguere
Latin: Homo qui consuete in perpotatione indulget

examples.original: Hic plus bibit, ille minus;
examples.translation: Or A drinks more and B drinks less;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Occidit Eurytion stulte data vina bibendo;
examples.translation: Eurytion fell by stupidly drinking the liquor set before him;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Post prandium aut cenam bibere vulgare est;
examples.translation: To them, a glass after lunch or one after dinner is bourgeois;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to weep
Latin: lacrimas effundere
Latin: deflere

examples.original: Satius est amicum reparare quam flere.
examples.translation: It is better to replace your friend than to weep for him.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Clamabat, flebatque simul, sed utrumque decebat;
examples.translation: She clamoured and wept together, but both became her;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quaeris, unde sint lamentationes, unde inmodici fletus?
examples.translation: Do you wish to know the reason for lamentations and excessive weeping?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Profit derived from booty, booty

examples.original: Cuius rei praemium sit in civitate, eam maximis semper auctibus crescere;
examples.translation: That tendency which a state rewarded always attained the greatest growth;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tum cuidam ex equitibus Gallis magnis praemiis persuadet uti ad Ciceronem epistolam deferat.
examples.translation: Then he persuaded one of the Gallic troopers with great rewards to deliver a letter to Cicero.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod petiit tulit ille, tibi ut sua facta placerent, Magnaque laudatus praemia mortis habet.
examples.translation: What he sought—that his deeds should please thee—that he won; in thy praise he wins great recompense for death.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: A loud call, a shout
Latin: magna eruptiō vocis vel vocum
Latin: acclāmātiō vel applausus

examples.original: Ad haec visa auditaque clamor ingens oritur.
examples.translation: The sight of these things and the man’s recital produced a mighty uproar.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid enim turpius philosophia captante clamores?
examples.translation: For what is baser than philosophy courting applause?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Audio circa horam sextam noctis clamorem concitatum;
examples.translation: I ask what the matter is, and they say he is exercising his voice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: uncertain, unsettled, doubtful, untrustworthy, not fast, not firm (class.): amicus certus in re incerta cernitur, Enn. ap.

examples.original: In Samnium incertis itum auspiciis est;
examples.translation: The expedition into Samnium was attended with ambiguous auspices;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Incertum est, quo loco te mors expectet;
examples.translation: You do not know where death awaits you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nondum enim incerta transgressus est, etiamnunc versatur in lubrico.
examples.translation: For such a man has not yet traversed the doubtful ground;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: though, although, albeit.
Latin: Etiamsi

examples.original: Hoc etsi multis modis reprendi potest, tamen accipio quod dant;
examples.translation: It is possible to take exception to this on several grounds;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De quibus etsi a Chrysippo maxime est elaboratum, tamen a Zenone minus multo quam ab antiquis;
examples.translation: Logic, no doubt, was very fully worked out by Chrysippus, but much less was done in it by Zeno than by the older schools;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod quidem mihi si quando dictum est (est autem dictum non parum saepe), etsi satis clemens sum in disputando, tamen interdum soleo subirasci.
examples.translation: I am a reasonably good-tempered disputant, but for my own part when I hear this assertion (and I have encountered it fairly often), I am sometimes inclined to be a little irritated.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: prove, put to the test.

examples.original: Experiri et exercere me volui.
examples.translation: I merely wished to test myself and to give myself practice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Experti in vicem sumus ego ac fortuna.
examples.translation: Do not reckon up the short duration of my rule;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nemo eorum, qui illam accusant, expertus est.
examples.translation: But no one of those who malign death has made trial of it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: majestic, august, venerable, worthy of honor
Latin: Venerābilis, sanctus
Latin: reverēns, verēcundus

examples.original: Statue sex et quinquaginta annos, quibus mox divus Augustus rem publicam rexit;
examples.translation: Count the fifty-six years in which the sainted Augustus thereafter held the helm of state;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Perit denique et is, qui honorem in colonia sua eodem die decerni sibi passus est, quo decreti et Augusto olim erant.
examples.translation: Finally, a man was put to death merely for allowing an honour to be voted him in his native town on the same day that honours had previously been voted to Augustus.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Fannium Caepionem, qui cum Varrone Murena in Augustum conspiraverat, reum maiestatis apud iudices fecit et condemnavit.
examples.translation: Fannius Caepio, who had conspired with Varro Murena against Augustus, he arraigned for high treason and secured his condemnation.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: A being accustomed, custom, habit, use, usage.

examples.original: Atque haec ad nostram consuetudinem sunt levia et potius contemnenda;
examples.translation: Now these last, according to our views, are trivial, or rather, contemptible;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

examples.original: At Germani celeriter ex consuetudine sua phalange facta impetus gladiorum exceperunt.
examples.translation: But the Germans, according to their custom, speedily formed mass, and received the sword-attack.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ut enim consuetudo loquitur, id solum dicitur honestum quod est popular fama gloriosum.
examples.translation: In common parlance ’moral’ (honourable)a means merely that which ranks high in popular esteem.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to turn, wind, twist, or whirl about often or violently (freq. and class.; syn.: verto, contorqueo).

examples.original: Patrum interim animos certamen regni ac cupido versabat.
examples.translation: The senators meanwhile were engaged in a struggle for the coveted kingship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nondum enim incerta transgressus est, etiamnunc versatur in lubrico.
examples.translation: For such a man has not yet traversed the doubtful ground;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Picentibus gratiae actae et magna pars curae patribus ab Etruria in Samnites versa est.
examples.translation: The Picentes were thanked, and the senate’s anxiety was diverted, in great measure, from Etruria to the Samnites.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: hard, difficult, troublesome (very freq. and class.).
Latin: Molestus factu

examples.original: Rem videlicet difficilem et obscuram!
examples.translation: As though it were a difficult or recondite notion!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed difficilius est provincias obtinere quam facere;
examples.translation: But it is more difficult to retain than to create provinces;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Intellego quam scopuloso difficilique in loco verser.
examples.translation: I am aware that I am here treading on dangerous and difficult ground.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to rest, repose, keep quiet.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ēvi, ētum, 3

examples.original: Ne tribunal quidem satis quietum erat;
examples.translation: Not even the tribunal itself was quiet;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum haec agerentur, iam consul via Labicana ad fanum Quietis erat.
examples.translation: Meanwhile the consul had already reached the shrine of Quies on the Labican road.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Multi in utroque exercitu sicut modesti quietique ita mali et strenui.
examples.translation: There were many in both armies obedient and law-abiding, as well as many unprincipled and energetic.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: African
Latin: poet. Africanus
Latin: subst.masc. Ventus inter Austrum et Zephyrum

examples.original: Pro consule Vitellium Siliani in Africa habuerant;
examples.translation: This detachment had served under Vitellius when he was proconsul in Africa;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Atilius Regulus cos. victis navali proelio Poenis in Africam traiecit.
examples.translation: Atilius Regulus the consul, having beaten the Carthaginians in a naval battle, crossed into Africa.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vides posse homines laborem pati: per medias Africae solitudines pedes duxit exercitum.
examples.translation: You see that man can endure toil: Cato, on foot, led an army through African deserts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: honey.
Latin: Quod ab apibus e nectare fit

examples.original: Quibus apte convenit illud vulgi proverbium: quia vespae favos quidem facere cum possint, non tamen in his mella, sed potius venena thesaurizent.
examples.translation: To the which the common proverb fittingly applieth: that wasps, though they may indeed build cells, yet do they not store up honey but rather poison therein.
examples.author: Bede

examples.original: Semper enim boni assiduique domini referta cella vinaria, olearia, etiam penaria est, villaque tota locuples est, abundat porco haedo agno gallina, lacte caseo melle.
examples.translation: For the provident and industrious proprietor always has his store-room and cellars well filled with oil and wine and provisions;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to show by signs; to show, point out, express, publish, make known, indicate; to intimate, notify, signify, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: monstro, declaro, indico).

examples.original: Haec vox significat voluntariam relationem;
examples.translation: The phrase implies a voluntary return;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quorum timor cum fremitu et concursu significaretur, milites nostri pristini diei perfidia incitati in castra irruperunt.
examples.translation: When their alarm was betrayed by the uproar and bustle, our troops, stung by the treachery of the day before, burst into the camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Neque enim tantum arte et scientia, sed longe magis facultate et <usu> eloquentiam contineri, nec tu, puto, abnues et hi significare vultu videntur.”
examples.translation: To this view I am sure you will not demur, and our friends here, to judge by their looks, seem to indicate concurrence.”
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: again, a second time, once more, anew.
Latin: tempus alium vel secundum; dēnuō

examples.original: Iterum ego tamquam Epicureus loquor?
examples.translation: Am I speaking again in the guise of an Epicureana?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Denique sententias nostras sic temperavimus, ut salvo episcopatu non tamen omnino inpunita relinquerentur, quae non deberent vel eidem ipsi deinceps iterumque facienda vel ceteris imitanda proponi.
examples.translation: In short, I so tempered my judgement with mercy that he was not deprived of office, although his faults were yet not left altogether unpunished;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Kal. Dec. M. Aemilio Lepido iterum L. Munatio Planco conss. per bellum Philippense.
examples.translation: In fact it is so recorded both in the calendar and in the public gazette.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to remind, put in mind of, bring to one's recollection; to admonish, advise, warn, instruct, teach (syn.: hortor, suadeo, doceo): bene mones; tute ipse cunctas, Enn. ap.
Latin: In alicuius animum ponere

examples.original: Sol me invitabat, fames ad monebat, nubes minabantur;
examples.translation: The sunlight called to me, hunger warned, and clouds were lowering;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In utrumque enim monendi ac firmandi sumus, et ne nimis amemus vitam et ne nimis oderimus.
examples.translation: For we need to be warned and strengthened in both directions,—not to love or to hate life overmuch;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is Valentem comiter exceptum, ne Galliam Narbonensem temere ingrederetur, monendo terruit;
examples.translation: He received Valens kindly, and persuaded him by his advice not to risk entering Narbonese Gaul.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a cognomen of several celebrated Romans in the gens Porcia, Valeria, Vettia al.

examples.original: Habet singulos: Catonem, Ciceronem, Lucretium.
examples.translation: The term comprises individuals also: Cato, Cicero, Lucretius.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil interest, utrum Pharsalica acie Cato vincatur an vincat?
examples.translation: Or whether Cato is conquered or conqueror in the battle-line of Pharsalia?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad meliores transi: cum Catonibus vive, cum Laelio, cum Tuberone.
examples.translation: Change therefore to better associations: live with the Catos, with Laelius, with Tubero.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a female child, a girl, maiden, lass.
Latin: Femina in tenera aetate
Latin: Proles femina
entries.etymology: Diminutive of puer 'boy' via the older form puellus.

examples.original: Hos ignava iocos tribuit natura puellis;
examples.translation: These are the games that indolent nature has given to women;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: At vestrae matres teneras peperere puellas.
examples.translation: But your mothers have borne delicate girls.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Illic et iuvenes votis oblivia poscunt, Et siqua est duro capta puella viro.
examples.translation: There youths seek oblivion for their vows, and maidens under the spell of a heartless lover.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: The means by which an assertion or assumption may be made clear, proved, an argument, evidence, proof

examples.original: Causa tibi libertatis fui, ero et argumentum;
examples.translation: I have been the cause of your freedom, and I shall also be its proof;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si probationes necessariae sunt, et decreta, quae veritatem argumentis colligunt.
examples.translation: If proofs are necessary, so are doctrines; for doctrines deduce the truth by reasoning.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pulveris exigui sparget non longa vetustas Congeriem, bustumque cadet, mortisque peribunt Argumenta tuae.
examples.translation: For a short space of time will scatter the little heap of dust; the grave will fall in;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to take fire, to kindle; hence

examples.original: Sine funeris ullo Ardet honore rogus;
examples.translation: The pyre burns on with no funeral honours;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Natus ut Althaeae flammis absentibus arsit, Sic tuus ardescat stipitis igne rogus.
examples.translation: As absent flames consumed Althaea’s son, so may a firebrand kindle thy funeral pile.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ardeam Rutuli habebant, gens ut in ea regione atque in ea aetate divitiis praepollens.
examples.translation: Ardea belonged to the Rutuli, who were a nation of commanding wealth, for that place and period.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: A place enclosed around, a court, enclosure, yard

examples.original: Septimam decimam cohortem e colonia Ostiensi in urbem acciri Otho iusserat;
examples.translation: Otho had given orders that the Seventeenth cohort be brought from the colony of Ostia to Rome.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Mittit primo Brutum adulescentem cum cohortibus Caesar, post cum aliis Gaium Fabium legatum;
examples.translation: Caesar first sent young Brutus with some cohorts, and then Gaius Fabius, lieutenant-general, with others;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quinque cohortes, quas minime firmas ad dimicandum esse existimabat, castris praesidio relinquit;
examples.translation: He left as garrison for the camp the five cohorts which he regarded as least steady for action;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: on the contrary, no indeed, by no means, or yes indeed, by all means
Latin: Ex contrario

examples.original: Immo enimvero ego sum, inquam, Orestes!
examples.translation: No, no,’tis I, I say, I am Orestes.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Immo contra nolo tibi umquam deesse laetitiam.
examples.translation: I do not wish you ever to be deprived of gladness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neque enim oratorius iste, immo hercle ne virilis quidem cultus est, quo plerique temporum nostrorum actores ita utuntur ut lascivia verborum et levitate sententiarum et licentia compositionis histrionales modos exprimant.
examples.translation: There is a fashion much in vogue with quite a number of counsel nowadays that ill befits an orator, and is indeed scarce worthy even of a man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: In a direct interrogation (no corresp. term in English).
Latin: Adverbium vel particula, quae in interrogatione recta et obliqua usurpatur

examples.original: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest quam forum?
examples.translation: Yet you can live quietly even there, if necessary.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid? Epicurei num desistunt de iisdem, de quibus et ab Epicuro scriptum est et ab antiquis, ad arbitrium suum scribere?
examples.translation: Nor do the Epicureans cease from writing as the spirit moves them on the same questions on which Epicurus and the ancients wrote.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Haec non erant eius qui innumerabiles mundos infinitasque regiones, quarum nulla esset ora, nulla extremitas, ’mente peragravisset.’ Num quid tale Democritus?
examples.translation: Such a provision ill became one whose ’intellect had roamed’b over unnumbered worlds and realms of infinite space, without shores or circumference. Did Democritus do anything of the kind?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: A speaker
Latin: Qui loquitur

examples.original: Cornelii Taciti Dialogus De Oratoribus 1.
examples.translation: Cornelius Tacitus A Dialogue on Oratory 1.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nam si causae ipsae pro se loqui possent, nemo adhiberet oratorem.
examples.translation: For if a case could speak for itself no one would employ a pleader.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam quemadmodum aliquis et poeta est et orator, et tamen unus, sic virtutes istae animalia sunt, sed multa non sunt.
examples.translation: For just as an individual may be both poet and orator in one, even so these virtues are living things, but they are not many.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a fight fist to fist
Latin: ( ) Dimicatio, inter vel homines vel exercitus
Latin: Acies exercitus

examples.original: Genus hoc est ex essedis pugnae.
examples.translation: Their manner of fighting from chariots is as follows.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Mihi autem de vocabulo pugna non est;
examples.translation: Now I am not going to fight about a word;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Post pugnam ad Regillum lacum non alia illis annis pugna clarior fuit.
examples.translation: From the time of the fight at Lake Regillus no other battle of those days was more famous.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: wild, untamed.
Latin: Agrestis, silvester, non domitus (dicitur de animalibus)

examples.original: Hominis an equi an ferae?
examples.translation: Is it that of man, or horse, or wild beast?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ordinem vitae hunc fere tenuit.
examples.translation: This was in general his manner of life.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et quidem quam sententiam feram, adtende.
examples.translation: Now listen carefully to the opinion which I shall offer;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: seven: septem menses sunt, quom, etc.
Latin: Sex et alius

examples.original: Primum stipendium meruit annorum decem septemque.
examples.translation: He served his first campaign at the age of seventeen.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Cato

examples.original: Titus Vinius quinquaginta septem annos variis moribus egit.
examples.translation: Titus Vinius lived fifty-seven years; his character varied at different times.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hunc vitae finem habuit septimo et tricensimo aetatis anno.
examples.translation: So he ended his life in the thirty-seventh year of his age.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: lying or being over against, opposite.

examples.original: Sapienti aliud auxilium est huic contrarium;
examples.translation: The wise man’s succour is of another sort, the opposite of this;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atqui pugnantibus et contrariis studiis consiliisque semper utens nihil quieti videre, nihil tranquilli potest.
examples.translation: But one who is perpetually swayed by conflicting and incompatible counsels and desires can know no peace or calm.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quippe confitenti consultantique supererant spes viresque: cum e contrario laeta omnia fingeret, falsis ingravescebat.
examples.translation: For if he had only acknowledged the truth and sought counsel, he had still some hope and resources left;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to let go back, send back, despatch back, drive back, cause to return (class. and very freq.; cf. reddo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; mīsi, missum, 3

examples.original: Captivi sine pretio remissi sunt.
examples.translation: The prisoners were released without a price.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Pluma tenebatur, quam remisit et fugit.
examples.translation: You grasped him only by a feather;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil remissum ab ulla parte curae aut laboris;
examples.translation: There was no relaxation anywhere of vigilance or effort;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a desire, wish, longing, in a good and (more freq.) in a bad sense.

examples.original: Non cupiditas nos, non timor pellet.
examples.translation: Then neither desire nor fear shall rout us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Habet pecuniae cupiditatem, sed modicam.
examples.translation: He has a craving for money, although in a moderate degree.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cupiditates non Epicuri divisione finiebat sed sua satietate.
examples.translation: Epicurus’s classification of the desires meant nothing to him;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: An island, isle, whether formed by the sea, a lake, or a river
Latin: Portio terrae, minor quam continens, aqua cincta
Latin: aedificium ubi multae diaetae seu domicilia sunt

examples.original: Expeditio in Cyprvm III, 9Aderat fatum insularum.
examples.translation: The Expedition to Cyprus 9. The fate of the islands was sealed;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quid, quod iacet insula ponto, Caesar eget ratibus?
examples.translation: Besides, Lesbos is an island, and Caesar has no fleet.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Huc cum ab Ostia navigaret, vehementi circio bis paene demersus est, prope Liguriam iuxtaque Stoechadas insulas.
examples.translation: On the voyage thither from Ostia he was nearly cast away twice in furious north-westers, off Liguria and near the Stoechades islands.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: The deep

examples.original: Tertius de Pharnace currus et Ponto.
examples.translation: A third procession celebrated the victory over Pharnaces of Pontus;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Et fuere qui se statim dederent: plures abrupto ponte instanti hosti viam abstulerunt.
examples.translation: The larger part, however, broke down the bridge and so, by cutting off the road, blocked their foes’ advance.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hos, Caesar, populos si nunc non usserit ignis, Uret cum terris, uret cum gurgite ponti.
examples.translation: If fire does not consume this host now, it will consume them hereafter, together with the earth and the waters of the sea;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a blow, stroke, stab, thrust, bite, sting (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Non certum ad hos ictus destinavi locum;
examples.translation: For these mortal strokes I have set no definite spot;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sp. Cassius deinde et Proculus Verginius consules facti. Cum Hernicis foedus ictum;
examples.translation: A treaty was struck with the Hernici, and two-thirds of their land was taken from them.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Evidentissimum id fuit, quod, quacumque equo invectus est, ibi haud secus quam pestifero sidere icti pavebant;
examples.translation: This was most clearly seen in that, wherever he rode, men cowered as though blasted by some baleful star;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to turn back, turn about; to come back, return (syn.: redeo, revenio).

examples.original: Ad me ipsum iam revertar.
examples.translation: Let me now return to myself.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ita re infecta in oppidum reverterunt.
examples.translation: So without success they returned to the town.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Huic mandat ut exploratis omnibus rebus ad se quam primum revertatur.
examples.translation: His orders were to spy out everything and to return to him at once.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to ask for urgently; to beg, demand, request, desire (syn.: flagito, postulo, peto).

examples.original: Et superos quid prodest poscere finem?
examples.translation: This frenzy will last for many years;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nil belli iure poposcit, Quaeque dari voluit, voluit sibi posse negari.
examples.translation: He acquired enormous wealth; but he paid into the treasury more than he kept back.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Illic et iuvenes votis oblivia poscunt, Et siqua est duro capta puella viro.
examples.translation: There youths seek oblivion for their vows, and maidens under the spell of a heartless lover.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to call by name, to name, to give a name to (esp. after, for a person or thing; cf.: appello, voco, dico).
Latin: Nomen imponere, suo nomen appellare

examples.original: Nomina ex ambitione aut ex iniuria nata.
examples.translation: They are mere titles, born of ambition or of wrong.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nominat quoque tribunos, Cn. Siccium, L. Numitorium, M. Duillium, Sp. Icilium, L. Maecilium.
examples.translation: He also gives the names of the tribunes: Gnaeus Siccius, Lucius Numitorius, Marcus Duillius, Spurius Icilius, Lucius Maecilius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed et illum quem nominavi et ceteros sophistas, ut e Platone intellegi potest, lusos videmus a Socrate.
examples.translation: But we read how Socrates made fun of the aforesaid Gorgias, and the rest of the Sophists also, as we can learn from Plato.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to make or set free, to free, liberate (syn. vindico).

examples.original: Ea libera coniectura est, sed, ut ego arbitror, vana;
examples.translation: Here is freedom for conjecture, but in my opinion it is idle;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ac mea quidem his tribus omnibus iudiciis, ut dixi antea, liberata est.
examples.translation: Mine, at all events, has been exonerated by pronouncements of all these three, as I have already shown.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Eo alter consul Aemilius cum exercitu ad liberandos obsidione socios venit.
examples.translation: Thither the other consul, Aemilius, came with an army, to relieve the blockade of the allies.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: distinguished by a mark; remarkable, noted, eminent, distinguished, prominent, extraordinary (class.)

examples.original: Insignis hic annus est nuntio Tarquini mortis.
examples.translation: This year was marked by the announcement of Tarquinius’s death.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Omnia iura, omnia insignia primi consules tenuere;
examples.translation: All the rights of the kings and all their insignia were possessed by the earliest consuls;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quod insigne mansit et in posteris eius, ac magna pars rutila barba fuerunt.
examples.translation: This sign was perpetuated in his descendants, a great part of whom had red beards.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: ornament, grace, embellishment, splendor, glory, honor, dignity (class. and freq.; a favorite word with Cicero, in oratorical lang.).

examples.original: Cum omnia feceris, a mutis animalibus decore vinceris.
examples.translation: After all your efforts, dumb animals surpass you in comeliness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Certare socii civesque, utri reciperatae arcis suum decus facerent;
examples.translation: The leader of each party urged on his followers.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Est et in incessu pars non temnenda decoris: Allicit ignotos ille fugatque viros.
examples.translation: In walk too there is no mean part of charm; it attracts or repels unknown admirers.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: fit, suitable
Latin: idoneus
Latin: Quid maximē deceat

examples.original: Ad utrosque casus aptus est: bonorum rector est, malorum victor.
examples.translation: He is ready for either outcome: if it brings goods, he controls them;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aptissimum tamen videtur mihi, quo Cicero usus est: cavillationes vocat.
examples.translation: But the word which Cicero used seems to me most suitable: he calls them cavillationes.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae est enim aut utilior aut ad bene vivendum aptior partitio quam illa qua est usus Epicurus?
examples.translation: Nothing could be more useful or more conducive to well-being than Epicurus’s doctrine as to the different classes of the desires.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: opinion, supposition, conjecture, imagination, fancy, belief (class.).

examples.original: Eadem opinio Veientes in urbe concitavit.
examples.translation: The same belief roused up the Veientes in the town.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non potest ergo quisquam beatus esse, qui huic se opinioni credidit.
examples.translation: No man therefore can be happy if he yields himself up to such foolish fancies.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Caesar consilio eius probato, etsi opinione trium legionum deiectus ad duas redierat, tamen unum communis salutis auxilium in celeritate ponebat.
examples.translation: Caesar approved his conclusion, although he was thereby disappointed in his expectation of obtaining three legions, and reduced to two;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: that for or by which any thing is bought or sold (class.).

examples.original: Non pono utrique par pretium.
examples.translation: I do not set an equal value on benefits and injuries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Captivi sine pretio remissi sunt.
examples.translation: The prisoners were released without a price.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid enim est tam necessarium quam pretia rebus inponere?
examples.translation: For what is so indispensable as giving to everything its proper value?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hold toward or to, to turn, bring
Latin: Habēre ad aliquem
Latin: Addere, adducere

examples.original: Nunc animum nobis adhibe veram ad rationem.
examples.translation: Now, I beg, apply your mind to true reasoning.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Discubuerat Vitellius Ticini adhibito ad epulas Verginio.
examples.translation: The emperor was dining at Ticinum, and Verginius was his guest.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nam si causae ipsae pro se loqui possent, nemo adhiberet oratorem.
examples.translation: For if a case could speak for itself no one would employ a pleader.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: beautiful, beauteous, fair, handsome, in shape and appearance (syn.: speciosus, venustus, formosus).
Latin: Sēnsibus placens; pulchritūdinem possidens; fōrmōsus
Latin: Quālitātēs honōrābilēs habens; honōrābilis, nōbilis
entries.etymology: Etymology uncertain.

examples.original: Id erat liber aliquis antiquus pulcher aut rarior.
examples.translation: This was some old book, either beautiful or rare.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Anceps et pulchra contentio exituque ipso mirabilis.
examples.translation: It was a well-contested and noble struggle and remarkable in the manner of its end.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Te quoque instinctum esse et magno ad pulcherrima properare impetu video.
examples.translation: I see that you also have been aroused and are hastening with great zeal towards infinite beauty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a bent surface (raised or depressed), a curve, fold, a hollow, etc.

examples.original: Iamque sinu laxo nudum sine corpore volnus.
examples.translation: The limbs are soaked with corrupted blood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Haruspices secreto ac sine testibus consuli vetuit.
examples.translation: He forbade anyone to consult soothsayers secretly and without witnesses.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quid sit, quod invenerim quaeris; sinum laxa, merum lucrum est.
examples.translation: If you wish to know what it is that I have found, open your pocket;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: verb and part. proper), entis (
Latin: Qui adhuc adolescit, seu nondum adolescevit
Latin: Homo aetate inter puerem et iuvenem, i.e., inter annum 15. vel 17. et 30

examples.original: Da mihi adulescentem incorruptum et ingenio vegetum;
examples.translation: But give me an unspoiled and sturdy-minded young man;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inviti summae spei adulescentes Eporedorix et Viridomarus Vercingetorigi parent.
examples.translation: Unwillingly, for they were young and very ambitious, Eporedorix and Viridomarus obeyed Vercingetorix.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hic et bella gerebat ut adulescens, cum plane grandis esset, et Hannibalem iuveniliter exsultantem patientia sua molliebat;
examples.translation: Though quite old he waged war like a young man, and by his patient endurance checked the boyish impetuosity of Hannibal.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to look out for a thing (syn.: prospecto, opperior, maneo, moror, praestolor).

examples.original: Hanc si nostri transirent, hostes exspectabant;
examples.translation: The enemy waited to see whether our men would cross it;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Consumetur, inquies. Scilicet exspectemus legitimum illud quinquennium;
examples.translation: It will be so spent, you will answer.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Interrogando exspectandoque responsum nuntius fessus, ut re imperfecta, redit Gabios;
examples.translation: He reported what he had said himself and what he had seen.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a stronghold, castle, citadel, fortress
Latin: Magnum castellum super oppidum iacens

examples.original: Sp. Tarpeius Romanae praeerat arci.
examples.translation: Spurius Tarpeius commanded the Roman citadel.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid mundi gladios a sanguine Caesaris arces?
examples.translation: Why do you keep away the swords of all mankind from Caesar’s throat?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Certare socii civesque, utri reciperatae arcis suum decus facerent;
examples.translation: The leader of each party urged on his followers.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: springing vegetation, grass, green stalks or blades, green crops, herbage, an herb
Latin: Planta sine stirpe lignea; praesertim, gramen

examples.original: Terra salutares herbas, eademque nocentes Nutrit, et urticae proxima saepe rosa est;
examples.translation: The same earth fosters healing herbs and noxious, and oft is the nettle nearest to the rose;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Femina canitiem Germanis inficit herbis, Et melior vero quaeritur arte color: Femina procedit densissima crinibus emptis, Proque suis alios efficit aere suos.
examples.translation: A woman stains her whitening locks with German juices, and by skill seeks a hue better than the real;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hoc tam segne solum raras tamen exerit herbas, Quas Nasamon, gens dura, legit, qui proxima ponto Nudus rura tenet;
examples.translation: Yet this barren soil here and there sends forth grass which is gathered by the Nasamonians, a rude and naked race who dwell close by the sea;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: Pleon. (freq. in Plaut.)
Latin: Hoc die

examples.original: Acriore hodie disciplina victi quam victores agunt.
examples.translation: The former are fired to brave action by rage, hatred, and eager desire for revenge;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Haec pro virtute tua fideque, qua una hoc bello res publica stetit, dicenda tibi sunt hodie;
examples.translation: In the name of your courage and your loyalty, which alone have preserved the republic in this war, you must now answer these questions;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Audire te arbitror, Scipio, hospes tuus avitus Masinissa quae faciat hodie nonaginta natus annos : cum ingressus iter pedibus sit, in equum omnino non ascendere;
examples.translation: I think, Scipio, that the news reaches you of the daily activities of your grandfather’s friend and host Masinissa, now ninety years old;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the covering for the body, clothes, clothing, attire, vesture

examples.original: Quo tibi, Pasiphaë, pretiosas sumere vestes?
examples.translation: Pasiphaë, to wear thy purple gowns?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid signorum, quid vestium quidve tabularum raptum incensumque atque proiectum est!
examples.translation: What a vast quantity of statues, garments and pictures was carried off, burnt, and thrown away!
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a league, treaty, compact (cf.: sponsio, pactio).
Latin: coniunctio hominum finem communem spectantium

examples.original: Pater patratus ad ius iurandum patrandum, id est sanciendum fit foedus;
examples.translation: The pater patratus is appointed to pronounce the oath, that is, to solemnize the pact;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hernici et Latini iussi milites dare ex foedere, duaeque partes sociorum in exercitu, tertia civium fuit.
examples.translation: The Hernici and the Latins were bidden to furnish soldiers, as by treaty bound; two-thirds of the army were allies, one-third citizens.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haecine foedera Tullus, Romanus rex, cum Albanis, patribus vestris, Latini, haec L. Tarquinius vobiscum postea fecit?
examples.translation: Are these the covenants, Latins, that Tullus, the Roman king, made with your Alban forefathers, that Lucius Tarquinius afterwards made with you?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: untouched, unhurt, unchanged.

examples.original: In integrum restituit quidquid erraverat;
examples.translation: He had wiped out all his previous mistakes;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ego quidem omnia integra illibataque habeo.
examples.translation: But I have still my all, untouched and undiminished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ibi integrae vires sistunt invehentem se iam Samnitem;
examples.translation: Their fresh strength halted the Samnites, who were now pressing forward;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: before one's self, forward, farther on, onward.
Latin: continuate et sine ullius rei interpositione

examples.original: Numquam epistulam tuam accipio, ut non protinus una simus.
examples.translation: I never receive a letter from you without being in your company forthwith.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Gratulatus sum protinus mihi et dixi: ”Non a summis labris ista venerunt, habent hae voces fundamentum.
examples.translation: I immediately congratulated myself and said: ”These words did not come from the edge of the lips; these utterances have a solid foundation.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex hac fuga protinus, quae undique convenerant, auxilia discesserunt, neque post id tempus umquam summis nobiscum copiis hostes contenderunt.
examples.translation: After this rout the succours which had assembled from all quarters took their departure; and never afterwards did the enemy engage us at their full strength.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: envy, grudge, jealousy

examples.original: Licet sapere sine pompa, sine invidia.
examples.translation: A man may be wise without parade and without arousing enmity.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non amicam habes, non puerum, qui amicae moveat invidiam;
examples.translation: You have no mistress, no favourite slave to make your mistress envious;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dictator de Volscis triumphavit, invidiaeque magis triumphus quam gloriae fuit;
examples.translation: The dictator triumphed over the Volsci, but gained more ill-will thereby than glory;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bear across; to carry or bring over; to convey over, transport, transfer (syn.: traduco, traicio).
Latin: Ex uno in alium locum ferre

examples.original: Nullum laborem recusant manus, quae ad arma ab aratro transferuntur;
examples.translation: The hand which turns from the plough to the sword never objects to toil;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Restant Stoici, qui, cum a Peripateticis et Academicis omnia transtulissent, nominibus aliis easdem res secuti sunt.
examples.translation: There remain the Stoics, who took over their whole system from the Peripatetics and the Academics, adopting the same ideas under other names.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid enim aliud furibundo corde concepit, cum diceret matri: ”Transferam me in partem Donati et bibam sanguinem tuum”?
examples.translation: What other purpose was in his raving heart when he said to his mother, ”I will go over to the Donatist party and will drink your blood”?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: fear, dread, apprehension, alarm, anxiety

examples.original: Non cupiditas nos, non timor pellet.
examples.translation: Then neither desire nor fear shall rout us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quem timorem Caesaris adventus sustulit.
examples.translation: This terror was removed by the arrival of Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Admiscenda tamen venus est secura timori, Ne tanti noctes non putet esse tuas.
examples.translation: Yet with fear must be mingled secure enjoyment, lest he think your nights are not worth while.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: An hour.
Latin: Spatium temporis, quorum duodecim sunt diu, et duodecim noctu; sexaginta minutae

examples.original: Omnis dies, omnis hora te mutat;
examples.translation: But in other men you more readily see what time plunders;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Audio circa horam sextam noctis clamorem concitatum;
examples.translation: I ask what the matter is, and they say he is exercising his voice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Orationibus instate horis et temporibus constitutis.
examples.translation: Be instant in prayerb at the appointed hours and seasons.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to press against, press together; to press down (class.; syn. obruo).

examples.original: Luce prima inermos plerosque oppressere.
examples.translation: At daybreak they cut down many of them quite unarmed.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Haec cum agere instituisset, oppressa morbo est.
examples.translation: No sooner had the quest started, than she fell ill;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iam comitia consularia instabant; quae res eum necdum compositis maturisve satis consiliis oppressit.
examples.translation: The consular election was now at hand, and found him with his plans not yet fully ripened.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the earth, opp. to the other planets or to the sea, the globe (a word belonging almost entirely to poetry).
Latin: Orbis terrarum; planeta noster
Latin: Regiō

examples.original: Nec tellus eadem parit omnia;
examples.translation: The same earth bears not everything;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Si saecula prima Victoris timuere minas, nunc excipe saltem Ossa tui Magni, si nondum subruta fluctu Invisa tellure sedent.
examples.translation: Who will fear to trouble the tomb, and dread to remove the dead so worthy of worship?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to tell, relate, narrate, report, recount, set forth (syn.: memoro, nuntio, trado).

examples.original: Utque coturnatum periisse Lycophrona narrant, Haereat in fibris fixa sagitta tuis.
examples.translation: And as they say buskined Lycophron perished, so in thy flesh may the barb stick fast.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Pedonem Albinovanum narrantem audieramus, erat autem fabulator elegantissimus, habitasse se supra domum S. Papini.
examples.translation: I heard Pedo Albinovanus, that most attractive story-teller, speaking of his residence above the town-house of Sextus Papinius.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed Asconius Pedianus adfirmat, ipsam postea maiorem natu narrare solitam, invitatum quidem a Vario ad communionem sui, verum pertinacissime recusasse.
examples.translation: But Asconius Pedianus declares that she herself used to say afterwards, when she was getting old, that Virgil was invited by Varius to associate with her, but obstinately refused.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: service, pains, exertion, work
Latin: Actio qua fit opus
Latin: labor, opus

examples.original: Videor mihi in re confessa perdere operam;
examples.translation: It looks as if I were wasting time over something that is an acknowledged fact;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Idea erat Vergilii facies, futuri operis exemplar.
examples.translation: The ”idea” was Vergil’s outward appearance, and this was the pattern of the intended work.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erras enim, si tibi illam putas tantum terrestres operas promittere;
examples.translation: You are indeed mistaken if you think that philosophy offers you nothing but worldly assistance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: whirl round, to wheel about, to cause to turn, to turn back, reverse
Latin: Efficere aliquid vertere
Latin: Aliquis textus alia lingua reddere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; ti, sum, 3

examples.original: Ad eos igitur converte te, quaeso.
examples.translation: Do you then join them, I beg of you.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Igitur in alium Scipionem conversa res publica finem belli reposcebat.
examples.translation: The State, therefore, turned to another Scipio and demanded that he should complete the war.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Faciunt hoc idem omnes eius equites paucosque nostros convertunt atque insequuntur.
examples.translation: All his horsemen did likewise, turning and pursuing our small party.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a potion, juice, drug (cf. virus).
Latin: Res sanitate nocens vel etiam mortifera

examples.original: Age vero, per quem venenum datum?
examples.translation: But come, by whom was the poison given?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Eodemque veneno C. Oppianicum fratrem necavit.
examples.translation: And he used poison, too, to murder his brother,G. Oppianicus.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et ad hanc mortem repentinam vocesque morientis omnia praeterea, quae solent esse indicia et vestigia veneni, in illius mortuae corpore fuerunt.
examples.translation: Besides the suddenness of her death and her dying utterance, all the usual indications and traces of poison were afterwards found on her body.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: As a suppliant.

examples.original: Sic Numitori ad supplicium Remus deditur.
examples.translation: So Remus was given up to Numitor to be punished.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: De supplicio agentibus, Caesar parcendum dignitati, Cato animadvertendum pro scelere censebant.
examples.translation: Cato thought that they ought to be punished in accordance with their crime.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ad hunc tumultum accitus Postumius asperiora omnia fecit acerbis quaestionibus, crudelibus suppliciis.
examples.translation: Being summoned to deal with this disturbance, Postumius aggravated everything by his harsh inquisitions and savage punishments.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: cattle, as a collective, a herd (opp.: pecus, pecudis, a single head of cattle).

examples.original: Alterum illud, voluptas, bonum pecoris est.
examples.translation: The second, pleasure, is simply the good of cattle.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dic mihi Damoeta: ’cuium pecus’ anne Latinum?
examples.translation: Tell me, Damoetas, I pray, is ’cuium pecus’ really good Latin?
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Pax erit haec nobis, donec mihi vita manebit, Cum pecore infirmo quae solet esse lupis.
examples.translation: That peace shall we enjoy, while life remains to me, which wolves are wont to keep with the defenceless flock.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to stand open, lie open, be open.

examples.original: Atque haec ratio late patet.
examples.translation: And this is a principle of wide application.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ego illam, si pateris, adiungam.
examples.translation: But, with your permission, I shall add it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ut fortiter amissorum desideria pateremur praecepimus nobis;
examples.translation: We have taught ourselves to endure bravely the loss of those we love;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to put in motion; hence, to move, stir, shake
entries.grammaticalClass: cīvi, cĭtum, 2; cīre, prevailing in the compounds accio, excio
principalParts: cīre, prevailing in the compounds accio, excio

examples.original: Ab ultimis deinde subsidiis cietur miles;
examples.translation: After that the last reserves were called upon;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid enim opus est longis in senatu sententiis, cum optimi cito consentiant?
examples.translation: What is the use of long arguments in the senate, when good citizens agree so quickly?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quicquid facies, cito redi a corpore ad animum. Illum noctibus ac diebus exerce;
examples.translation: The mind must be exercised both day and night, for it is nourished by moderate labour;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to allure, entice, attract, seduce, inveigle, decoy

examples.original: Ego tamen illic aliquid et doceo.
examples.translation: You ask, do you, what I can teach?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illic est individuus ille comitatus virtutum;
examples.translation: There is the whole inseparable company of virtues;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Crates, ut aiunt, huius ipsius Stilbonis auditor, cuius mentionem priore epistula feci, cum vidisset adulescentulum secreto ambulantem, interrogavit, quid illic solus faceret?
examples.translation: Crates, they say, the disciple of the very Stilbo whom I mentioned in a former letter, noticed a young man walking by himself, and asked him what he was doing all alone.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to feel pain, suffer pain, be in pain, to ache
Latin: Dolore afficere, dolorem afferre
Latin: dolore affici
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ŭi, ĭtum; 2

examples.original: In utroque finis dolendi est.
examples.translation: In either case there is an end of pain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ac tamen hic mallet non dolere.
examples.translation: Yet he would have preferred to have no pain at all.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nec his dolendum nec illis gaudendum;
examples.translation: We must neither grieve over the one, nor rejoice over the other.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Gaul
Latin: Natio Gallorum, nunc praesertim quae hodie Francia vocatur

examples.original: Edidit et peregre spectacula, in Sicilia Syracusis asticos ludos et in Gallia Luguduni miscellos;
examples.translation: He also gave shows in foreign lands, a city festival at Syracuse in Sicily, and mixed games at Lugdunum in Gaul;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Contionante Vitellio postulantur ad supplicium Asiaticus et Flavus et Rufinus duces Galliarum, quod pro Vindice bellassent.
examples.translation: When Vitellius was addressing his troops, the soldiers demanded the punishment of Asiaticus, Flavius, and Rufinus, Gallic chiefs who had fought for Vindex.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quare et pontifex in locum P. Scipionis substitutus et ad deducendas in Galliam colonias, in quis Narbo et Arelate erant, missus est.
examples.translation: For this he was made pontiff in place of Publius Scipio and sent to conduct colonies to Gaul, among them Narbo and Arelate.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a wicker basket or hamper, for various purposes; a fruit-hamper, wool-basket, winestrainer, etc. (cf. colum).

examples.original: Qualis ratio est, tales et actiones sunt;
examples.translation: As reason is, so also are actions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cogitat semper, qualis vita, non quanta sit.
examples.translation: He always reflects concerning the quality, and not the quantity, of his life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qualis sermo meus esset, si una sederemus aut ambularemus, inlaboratus et facilis, tales esse epistulas meas volo, quae nihil habent accersitum nec fictum.
examples.translation: I prefer that my letters should be just what my conversationb would be if you and I were sitting in one another’s company or taking walks together,—spontaneous and easy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A hundred
Latin: Nonaginta novem (undecentum) et alius, decies dena. Numerus C
Latin: Nonaginta novem (undecentum) et alius; decem decem vices

examples.original: Ita omnis insula est in circuitu viciens centum milium passuum.
examples.translation: Thus the whole island is two thousand miles in circumference.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nihil interest, centum per vesicam tuam an mille amphorae transeant;
examples.translation: You know the taste of wine and cordials.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam quae Cenabi oriente sole gesta essent, ante primam confectam vigiliam in finibus Arvernorum audita sunt, quod spatium est milium passuum circiter centum lx.
examples.translation: For the deeds done at Cenabum at sunrise were heard of before the end of the first watch in the borders of the Arverni, a distance of about one hundred and sixty miles.
