definitions: English: that acts according to duty, dutiful; esp. that performs what is due to the gods and religion in general, to parrents, kindred, teachers, country
Latin: Fidus in amicis, promissis, regibus; stabilis, fidelis
Latin: Fidus in dis

examples.original: Exeat aula, Qui volt esse pius.
examples.translation: If a man would be righteous, let him depart from a court.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Aut pia te caeso dicatur adultera, sicut Qua cecidit Leucon vindice, dicta pia est.
examples.translation: Or may an adulteress be called righteous for slaying thee, as she was called righteous by whose vengeance Leucon fell.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Dolet heu semperque dolebit, Quod scelerum, Caesar, prodest tibi summa tuorum, Cum genero pugnasse pio.
examples.translation: Grievous alas! is it, and ever will be, that Caesar profited by his worst crime—his fighting against a kinsman who had scruples.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to plough, to till.
Latin: Terram aratro scindere seminandi causa
Latin: tractare agrum i. e. conserere, arare, stercorare et similia tamquam species complecti

examples.original: Iam stat, ut ipse vides, funeris ara tui.
examples.translation: The procession is ready for thee;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Eo ille index confugit in araque consedit.
examples.translation: To this that informer fled and seated himself upon the altar.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Visite turicremas vaccae Memphitidos aras, Visite conspicuis terna theatra locis;
examples.translation: Visit the incense-burning altars of the Memphian heifer; visit three theatres in conspicuous seats.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: dutiful conduct towards the gods, one's parents, relatives, benefactors, country, etc., sense of duty.

examples.original: Quo facto tulit pietatis fructum.
examples.translation: By such conduct he reaped the fruits of his devotion;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Non ira saltem, iuvenes, pietate remota Stabitis?
examples.translation: If duty be disregarded, will not rage at least make you stand your ground, ye soldiers?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ab hoc discede iudicio; non pietas constabit, non fides.
examples.translation: Dissent from this judgment, and duty and loyalty will not abide.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a doing, performing, acting, action
Latin: executio
Latin: declamatio

examples.original: Sed laudare dignos honesta actio est;
examples.translation: But to praise worthy men is an honourable action;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qualis ratio est, tales et actiones sunt;
examples.translation: As reason is, so also are actions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vita autem honesta actionibus variis constat;
examples.translation: For example, I desire a life of honour.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: unavoidableness, inevitableness, necessity, compulsion, force, exigency.

examples.original: Modus enim omnium prout necessitas erat;
examples.translation: For the limit everywhere corresponded to the need;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed tabellas, si quae ibi nostrae sunt, propter huius modi necessitates mittas peto.
examples.translation: If you have any tablets of mine beside you, please send them back for such emergencies as this.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Sed forte iterum quaeris a me, quo modo ista facias tantis mundi huius necessitatibus implicatus.
examples.translation: But perhaps you ask me again how you are to accomplish this, involved as you are in the great distresses of this world.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: triumph; triumphal procession

examples.original: His ita decretis usque ad triumphum Plauti silentium de Privernatibus fuit;
examples.translation: These decrees having been promulgated, no more was said about the Privernates, until Plautius had triumphed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Dictator de Volscis triumphavit, invidiaeque magis triumphus quam gloriae fuit;
examples.translation: The dictator triumphed over the Volsci, but gained more ill-will thereby than glory;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nunc neque te longi remeantem pompa triumphi Excipit, aut sacras poscunt Capitolia laurus;
examples.translation: As it is, no long triumphal procession awaits your return, nor does the Capitol demand your consecrated laurels;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: spissa instead of aspra

examples.original: Quid fuit asperius Nonacrina Atalanta?
examples.translation: What could be more stern than Nonacrian Atalanta?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quae putas me passum, dum per aspera erepo, dum viam quaero, dum facio?
examples.translation: What do you think my feelings were, scrambling over the rocks, searching out the path, or making one for myself?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iamque hebes et crasso non asper sanguine mucro Perdidit ensis opus, frangit sine volnere membra.
examples.translation: All the host and all the weapons make him their sole object; no hand missed its aim, no lance failed of its mark;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To be over and above, either as a remainder or as a superfluity (class. and very freq.; cf. supero, B. 3.).
Latin: Supra aliquid esse
Latin: Reliquus esse

examples.original: Non multum mihi ad balneum superest.
examples.translation: I have very little energy left for bathing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Perstare militem, superesse studia populi;
examples.translation: In desperation at least you must gird yourself to bold action.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Tu licet et Thamyram superes et Amoebea cantu, Non erit ignotae gratia magna lyrae.
examples.translation: Though in song you may surpass Thamyras and Amoebeus, in an unknown lyre there is no great delight.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a meeting, assembly that is called together by a magistrate or priest

examples.original: Eo decurrunt tribuni contionemque secum trahunt.
examples.translation: The tribunes hastened to the place, drawing the people after them.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In contionem Appius escendit: sequuntur Horatius Valeriusque.
examples.translation: Appius mounted the platform; Horatius and Valerius followed him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In contione autem si loqueretur, si Hannibal ad portas venisset murumque iaculo traiecisset, negaret esse in malis capi, venire, interfici, patriam amittere?
examples.translation: Hannibal is at the gates and has flung a javelin over the city walls; could he say that captivity, enslavement, death, loss of country are no evils?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: crime, fault, blame, failure, defect

examples.original: Bona autem omnia carere culpa decet;
examples.translation: All goods, however, ought properly to be free from blame;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnia scelera etiam ante effectum operis, quantum culpae satis est, perfecta sunt.
examples.translation: All crimes, so far as guilt is concerned, are completed even before the accomplishment of the deed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ipse postremo Spurinna, non tam culpam exprobrans quam rationem ostendens, relictis exploratoribus ceteros Placentiam reduxit minus turbidos et imperia accipientis.
examples.translation: In the end Caecina himself, not so much reproving their faults as showing the reasons for his action, left some scouts and led the rest back to Placentia.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to bring to remembrance, remind of, to mention, recount, relate, speak about or of, say, tell (class.).

examples.original: O quam te memorem, virgo?
examples.translation: O maiden, words are weak!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cuius, uti memoror, rei simulacrum et imago ante oculos semper nobis versatur et instat.
examples.translation: Of this fact there is, I recall, an image and similitude always moving and present before our eyes.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Cum duci tum propter ducem patribus quoque placatior exercitus rediit, sibi parentem alteri exercitui dominum datum ab senatu memorans.
examples.translation: They declared that to them the senate had given a parent, to the other army a tyrant.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to throw, cast, hurl.
Latin: saepe iacere

examples.original: Hic teneat nostras ancora iacta rates.
examples.translation: Here let the anchor be thrown, and hold my bark secure.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Optimum itaque est non iactare otium suum.
examples.translation: It is therefore best not to vaunt one’s retirement.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec aliaque ab tribunis nequiquam iactata;
examples.translation: These and other objections were made by the tribunes to no purpose;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to hurt by striking, wound, injure, damage (syn.: saucio, vulnero).

examples.original: Non quicquid nos offendit, et laedit.
examples.translation: That which annoys us does not necessarily injure us;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid, nisi secretae laeserunt Phyllida silvae?
examples.translation: What, save the secret woods, were Phyllis’ bane?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ut semel Aetola Venus est a cuspide laesa, Mandat amatori bella gerenda suo.
examples.translation: No sooner was Venus hurt by the Aetolian spear than she bids her lover wage her wars.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: usefulness, utility, serviceableness, service, expediency, benefit, profit, advantage

examples.original: Sed quid ages tandem si utilitas ab amicitia, ut fit saepe, defecerit?
examples.translation: But what, pray, will you do, if, as often happens, expediency parts company with friendship?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Usus est familia, si utilitate iudicandum est, optima; si forma, vix mediocri.
examples.translation: He had slaves that were excellent in point of efficiency, although in personal appearance hardly mediocre;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Nec potest quisquam beate degere, qui se tantum intuetur, qui omnia ad utilitates suas convertit;
examples.translation: And no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To stand back, remain standing anywhere (cf. resideo); to stand still, halt, stop, stay; to stay behind, remain

examples.original: Patricii vi contra vim resistunt.
examples.translation: The patricians resisted force with force.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eadem ratione, qua pridie, ab nostris resistitur.
examples.translation: And exactly the same was done on the other days following.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quibus fortiter resistentibus vineas turresque egit.
examples.translation: When they offered a brave resistance he brought up mantlets and towers.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To destroy, ruin, waste, bring to naught

examples.original: Multum est non corrumpi divitiarum contubernio;
examples.translation: It means much not to be spoiled by intimacy with riches;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam id quoque ad corrumpendum iudicium pertinet.
examples.translation: That too is an act of judicial corruption.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Oppianicus autem orare hominem coepit, ut sibi rationem ostenderet iudicii corrumpendi.
examples.translation: And Oppianicus began to implore the fellow to show him some means of bribing the court.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to stretch out or forth, extend.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; di, tum and sum, 3

examples.original: Rigida re quid amplius intendi potest?
examples.translation: What can be made more tense than a thing which is already rigid?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Instructi intentique signum profectionis exposcunt.
examples.translation: They were drawn up in line and eager for action;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cum per totum diem stetissent intenti ad certamen, nocti cessere.
examples.translation: And they, on their side, were full of hope, as they ate their evening meal;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Neutr., to sit, stay, remain, abide anywhere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ēdi, essum, 2

examples.original: Iuppiter optimus maximus, Iuno regina et Minerva, alii di deaeque obsidentur;
examples.translation: Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Queen Juno, and Minerva, and the other gods and goddesses, are beleaguered;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Venit eodem cum suis copiis postero die Gaius Fabius partemque oppidi sumit ad obsidendum.
examples.translation: Next day Gaius Fabius joined him there with his own force and took a part of the town to blockade.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Q. Publilio, qui eos obsederat, primo et imperium prolatum est et pro cos. triumphus decretus.
examples.translation: Quintus Publilius, who had besieged them, was the first to have his authority extended and to be granted a triumph as proconsul.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a finger.
Latin: Membrum manus, quo aliquid ostendimus et indicamus. Quod est in extremis manibus, post palmas
Latin: Membrum pedis (pedum digiti)

examples.original: Non exsurgit in plantas nec summis ambulat digitis eorum more, qui mendacio staturam adiuvant longioresque quam sunt, videri volunt;
examples.translation: He does not stretch himself or walk on tiptoe like those who seek to improve their height by deceit, wishing to seem taller than they really are;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cetera saepe tamen potuere admissa negari, Et crimen nox est infitiata suum: Nostra notat fusco digitos iniuria suco Cortice contactas inficiente manus.
examples.translation: Yet other crimes when committed can often be denied, and night disavows her guilty deed: injury done to me marks the fingers with dark juice, and my bark stains the hands that touch it.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: set up again, i. e. either to replace in its former position, or (more freq.) to restore to its former condition, to rebuild, revive, etc.
Latin: Rursus statuere, rursus collocare
Latin: In pristino loco aut statu reponere

examples.original: In integrum restituit quidquid erraverat;
examples.translation: He had wiped out all his previous mistakes;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Epicrates quidem continuo restitutus est.
examples.translation: Epicrates was re-instated promptly.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Manlius quoque ad restituendam aciem se ipse coram offert.
examples.translation: Manlius also showed himself among them, helping to restore the line;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: once, a single time: ter sub armis malim vitam cernere, Quam semel modo parere, Enn. ap.
Latin: Una vice

examples.original: Nam ille alter fortasse tamquam phoenix semel anno quingentesimo nascitur.
examples.translation: And it is not surprising, either, that greatness develops only at long intervals;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ceterum utraque caedes sinistre accepta, et inviso semel principi seu bene seu male facta parem invidiam adferebant.
examples.translation: But both executions were unfavourably received, and now that the emperor was once hated, his good and evil deeds alike brought him unpopularity.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: T. Quinctius semel acie victor, binis castris hostium, novem oppidis vi captis, Praeneste in deditionem accepto Romam revertit triumphansque signum Praeneste devectum Iovis Imperatoris in Capitolium tulit.
examples.translation: He returned to Rome bringing with him from Praeneste the image of Jupiter Imperator. This he bore in triumph to the Capitol, where he dedicated it, between the shrine of Jupiter and that of Minerva.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to mourn, lament, bewail, deplore (syn. ploro).

examples.original: Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lugerent.
examples.translation: The relatives of the victims were forbidden to mourn for them.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Scilicet immunis si luctus una fuisset Livia, Fortunae regna minora forent.
examples.translation: Forsooth, if Livia alone had been immune from grief, then Fortune’s realm had suffered!
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quam quidem nunc multitudinem videtis, iudices, in squalore et luctu supplicem vobis.
examples.translation: You see them thronging this court to-day, gentlemen of the jury;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a final long; Key, Gr. § 802, regards these suffixes as corrupted from the
Latin: Ante quoddam tempus; ad tempus prius

examples.original: Docet longe alia ratione esse bellum gerendum atque antea gestum sit.
examples.translation: He pointed out that the campaign must be conducted in far different fashion from hitherto.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Huius opera Commi, ut antea demonstravimus, fideli atque utili superioribus annis erat usus in Britannia Caesar;
examples.translation: This Commius, as we have before mentioned, had rendered faithful and efficient service to Caesar in previous years in the expedition to Britain.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Institutum etiam ab iisdem consulibus ut senatus consulta in aedem Cereris ad aediles plebis deferrentur, quae antea arbitrio consulum supprimebantur vitiabanturque.
examples.translation: Up to that time they were wont to be suppressed or falsified, at the pleasure of the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to unfold, uncoil, unroll, unfurl, spread out, loosen

examples.original: Haec igitur nobis explicanda sunt;
examples.translation: This, then, is the theory that we have to expound;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Pro vitae varietate et pro actionibus explicantur;
examples.translation: They unfold themselves according as life varies and as actions differ;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potest quidem ille etiam relictus sibi explicare partes suas;
examples.translation: The latter, it is true, can by himself develop his own parts;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to turn, turn about or away; to twist, bend, wind (class.; syn. converto).

examples.original: Torquet ingratus se et macerat;
examples.translation: The ungrateful man tortures and torments himself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Torqueor, sed fortiter; bene est.
examples.translation: If I am tortured, but bear it bravely, all is well;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Penelopen absens sollers torquebat Ulixes;
examples.translation: In the absence of crafty Ulysses was Penelope racked;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to laugh (cf. cachinnor).
Latin: (Intransitivē) beatitatem exprimere ā mōto faciēī ōrisque
Latin: personam, aut rem aliquam, deridere

examples.original: O quantus risus inter ista tollendus est!
examples.translation: O what laughter should such things draw!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si niger aut ingens aut non erit ordine natus Dens tibi, ridendo maxima damna feres.
examples.translation: If you have a tooth that is black or too large or growing out of place, laughing will cost you dear.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Illa sonat raucum quiddam atque inamabile ridet, Ut rudit a scabra turpis asella mola.
examples.translation: That one’s laugh has a strident and unlovely harshness, as when a mean she-ass brays by the rough millstone.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a board, plank.

examples.original: Adest ad tabulam, licetur Aebutius;
examples.translation: Aebutius attends at the sale.a He does the bidding.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iam quae iste signa, quas tabulas pictas ex Achaia sustulerit, non dicam hoc loco;
examples.translation: What statues and pictures he carried off from Achaia I will not state here;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In iure nihil est eiusmodi, recuperatores, non tabulae falsae, non testis improbus;
examples.translation: In a question of law, gentlemen, there is nothing like that—no forged document, no dishonest witness;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To throw or bring together, to unite, = cogo, colligo.
Latin: putare quia indicia sunt

examples.original: Conantes dicere prohibuit et in catenas coniecit.
examples.translation: To spy?” When they tried to speak he prevented them and flung them into chains.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ea libera coniectura est, sed, ut ego arbitror, vana;
examples.translation: Here is freedom for conjecture, but in my opinion it is idle;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huc ut venit, ab ephoris in vincla publica est coniectus;
examples.translation: On his arrival he was imprisoned by the ephors;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: sick, unwell, diseased, suffering.
Latin: Morbo laborans

examples.original: Quis medicus aegros in transitu curat?
examples.translation: What physician can heal his patient on a flying visit?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aegre sedata ab Quinctio plebs, multo aegrius consul alter a patribus.
examples.translation: At length the council of the plebs was adjourned, and the consuls convened the senate.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nihil aeque, Lucili, virorum optime, aegrum reficit atque adiuvat quam amicorum adfectus;
examples.translation: Nothing, my excellent Lucilius, refreshes and aids a sick man so much as the affection of his friends;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: sometimes, occasionally, now and then, = nonnumquam

examples.original: Neque spectaculis semper ipse praesedit, sed interdum aut magistratibus aut amicis praesidendi munus iniunxit.
examples.translation: He did not always preside at the games in person, but sometimes assigned the honour to the magistrates or to friends.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Quod quidem mihi si quando dictum est (est autem dictum non parum saepe), etsi satis clemens sum in disputando, tamen interdum soleo subirasci.
examples.translation: I am a reasonably good-tempered disputant, but for my own part when I hear this assertion (and I have encountered it fairly often), I am sometimes inclined to be a little irritated.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In cognoscendo autem ac decernendo mira varietate animi fuit, modo circumspectus et sagax, interdum inconsultus ac praeceps, nonnumquam frivolus amentique similis.
examples.translation: But in hearing and deciding cases he showed strange inconsistency of temper, for he was now careful and shrewd, sometimes hasty and inconsiderate, occasionally silly and like a crazy man.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: who, as father of Romulus, was the primogenitor of the Roman people, the god of war, of husbandry, of shepherds and seers
Latin: Deus Romanus belli; bellum ipsum
Latin: Planeta quartus a Sole, inter Terram et Iovem; classice, stella Martis

examples.original: Post hunc Apollinem et Martem et Iovem et Minervam.
examples.translation: After him they set Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Numitoris filia a Marte compressa nati Romulus et Remus.
examples.translation: Romulus and Remus born to Mars by the daughter of Numitor.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mars pater, insano Veneris turbatus amore, De duce terribili factus amator erat.
examples.translation: Father Mars, plagued by frenzied love of Venus, from a terrible captain became a lover.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: ashes
Latin: Quod restat de ligno vel animalium corporibus combustis

examples.original: Ille fuit miserae Magni cinis.
examples.translation: Her example was followed by all loving hearts;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Fortuna recursus Si det in Hesperiam, non hac in sede quiescent Tam sacri cineres, sed te Cornelia, Magne, Accipiet nostraque manu transfundet in urnam.
examples.translation: If Fortune grant us a return to Italy, not here will these sacred ashes rest; but Cornelia will recover you, Magnus, and will transfer them from my hand to an urn.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Coronopus oblonga herba est cum fissuris. seritur interim, quoniam radix coeliacis praeclare facit in cinere tosta.
examples.translation: The coronopus is an elongated plant, with fissures in the leaves. It is sometimes cultivated, as the root, roasted in hot ashes, is found to be an excellent remedy for cœliac complaints.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: to build in or into; to build,, erect, construct (class.).
Latin: In aliquo loco struere
Latin: Aedificare, construere

examples.original: Ad quaecumque nos cogebat, instruxit.
examples.translation: For whatever she forced upon us, she equipped us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Instruenda est enim vita exemplis inlustribus.
examples.translation: For life should be provided with conspicuous illustrations.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ab neutra parte satis commode instructi fuerunt;
examples.translation: On neither side had the forces been very advantageously marshalled;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: inward joy

examples.original: Quando ad hoc gaudium pervenire continget?
examples.translation: When will it be your lot to attain this joy?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie.
examples.translation: The evil joys of the mind,c his words are eloquent, but not strictly appropriate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sapiens ille plenus est gaudio, hilaris et placidus, inconcussus;
examples.translation: The wise man is joyful, happy and calm, unshaken;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: too much, overmuch, excessively, beyond measure.

examples.original: In utrumque enim monendi ac firmandi sumus, et ne nimis amemus vitam et ne nimis oderimus.
examples.translation: For we need to be warned and strengthened in both directions,—not to love or to hate life overmuch;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atque hoc ut vere dicitur, parva esse ad beate vivendum momenta ista corporis commodorum, sic nimis violentum est nulla esse dicere;
examples.translation: Yet true though it is that these bodily advantages are of but slight importance for happiness, to say that they are of no importance is too sweeping;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nimis pauca et exigua de quibusdam minutis quaestiunculis edidit. Reliquit autem non mediocrem ”Silvam Observationum Sermonis Antiqui.”
examples.translation: He published a few slight works on divers minute points, and also left a good sized ”Grove of Observations on our Early Language.”
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to cover, cover over (syn.: tego, condo, celo, abdo).

examples.original: Verum ex ista reperietis hereditate ita istum praedatum ut perpauca occulte fecerit;
examples.translation: But you will in fact find little concealment about the way in which he plundered that estate;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Utque Milo, sub quo cruciata est Pisa tyranno, Vivus in occultas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: And like Milo, under whose tyranny Pisa groaned, mayst thou be hurled alive into hidden waters.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: T. Quinctium Poenum legatum occupare montes iubet occultumque id iugum capere quod ab tergo hostibus foret.
examples.translation: His lieutenant Titus Quinctius Poenus he commanded to secure the mountains and secretly to occupy the ridge which lay to the enemy’s rear.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Neutr., to labor, take pains, exert one's self, strive.
Latin: ŏpĕram dāre, tractāre
Latin: opus facere, contendere, patī
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Succurrit inimicus illi Vorenus et laboranti subvenit.
examples.translation: His enemy, Vorenus, ran up to him and helped him in his distress.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Equidem primum ut honore dignus essem, maxime semper laboravi;
examples.translation: For my own part, I have always first endeavoured to deserve honour;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nullum laborem recusant manus, quae ad arma ab aratro transferuntur;
examples.translation: The hand which turns from the plough to the sword never objects to toil;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: mistrust, distrust, suspicion.

examples.original: Quamquam ne id quidem suspicionem coitionis habuerit.
examples.translation: Yet even this circumstance should not involve them in any suspicion of collusion;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iacis adulteria, quae nemo non modo nomine, sed ne suspicione quidem possit agnoscere.
examples.translation: You hint darkly at acts of immorality, charges which cannot even be suspected, far less substantiated, against him.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Plerumque improborum facta primo suspicio insequitur, dein sermo atque fama, tum accusator, tum iudex;
examples.translation: The usual consequences of crime are, first suspicion, next gossip and rumour, then comes the accuser, then the judge;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to draw or take off, draw away, draw or take down; to pull down; to take away, remove, withdraw (class. and very freq.).
Latin: Deorsum trahere
Latin: sumere aliquid de aliquo

examples.original: De prandio nihil detrahi potuit;
examples.translation: Nothing could have been subtracted from our luncheon;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Detraxi tibi non pusillum negotii;
examples.translation: You see, I have relieved you of no slight bother;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil est enim, mihi crede, Laterensis, de te detractum: detractum dico?
examples.translation: Believe me, Laterensis, you have suffered no detraction. Detraction?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: corn, grain

examples.original: Frumentum omne ad se referri iubet;
examples.translation: He ordered all the corn to be brought in to his headquarters;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Is, quod in his locis inopia frumenti erat, praefectos tribunosque militum complures in finitimas civitates frumenti causa dimisit;
examples.translation: As there was a lack of corn in those parts, he despatched several commandants and tribunes into the neighbouring states to seek it.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: summit, surface (postAug. and very rare)

examples.original: Matri summam omnium rerum privatarum publicarumque permisit.
examples.translation: He left to his mother the management of all public and private business.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hoc Epicurus in voluptate ponit, quod summum bonum esse vult summumque malum dolorem;
examples.translation: This Epicurus finds in pleasure; pleasure he holds to be the Chief Good, pain the Chief Evil.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Caesar Avarici complures dies commoratus summamque ibi copiam frumenti et reliqui commeatus nactus exercitum ex labore atque inopia refecit.
examples.translation: Caesar halted at Avaricum for several days, and by the immense quantity of corn and all other supplies which he found there recuperated the army after toil and want.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: He who entertains a stranger, a host (one who entertains gratuitously, as a friend: caupo, one who entertains for pay)
Latin: Homo qui suum domo vīsitātōrem recipit
Latin: Acceptor hospitālitātis; homo qui domo recipitur; vīsitātōr

examples.original: Hospitem violare fas non putant;
examples.translation: They do not think it right to outrage a guest;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum his esse hospitium Ambiorigi sciebat;
examples.translation: He knew that Ambiorix had a formal friendship with them;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ibi benigne excepti divisique in hospitia.
examples.translation: There they were kindly received and were quartered about among the citizens.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to shun, seek to escape, avoid, evade (class.; syn.: fugio, effugio).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Non enim vitat, sed fugit.
examples.translation: For it does not avoid danger, but runs away.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Siquis amas, nec vis, facito contagia vites;
examples.translation: If you love, nor wish to love, see that you shun contagion;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: His enim rebus detractis negat se reperire in asotorum vita quod reprendat.
examples.translation: Eliminate those passions, he says, and he cannot find anything to blame in a life of profligacy.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to fasten, make fast
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; nxi, nctum, and pēgi or pĕpĭgi, pactum; 3
principalParts: nxi, nctum, and pēgi or pĕpĭgi, pactum

examples.original: Si bene promittent, totidem promittite verbis: Si dederint, et vos gaudia pacta date.
examples.translation: If they make fair promises, promise in as many words; if they give, give also your bargained joys.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Lex vetusta est, priscis litteris verbisque scripta, ut qui praetor maximus sit idibus Septembribus clavum pangat;
examples.translation: There is an ancient law, recorded in archaic words and letters, that the chief magistrate shall on the thirteenth of September drive a nail;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Omnino canorum illud in voce splendescit etiam nescio quo pacto in senectute, quod equidem adhuc non amisi, et videtis annos.
examples.translation: In old age, no doubt, the voice actually gains (I know not how) that magnificent resonance which even I have not lost, and you see my years;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be a servant or slave, to serve, be in service (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Nam vita, si moriendi virtus abest, servitus est.
examples.translation: For life, if courage to die be lacking, is slavery.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Egentes in locupletes, perditi in bonos, servi in dominos armabantur.
examples.translation: You say the senate was on my side. It was;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ne illud quidem videtis, quam omnem invidiam maiores nostri dominis, omnem contumeliam servis detraxerint?
examples.translation: Do you not see even this,—how our ancestors removed from masters everything invidious, and from slaves everything insulting?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hang or hold fast, to hang, stick, cleave, cling, adhere, be fixed, sit fast, remain close to any thing or in any manner

examples.original: Venit ad extremum; haeret in salebra;
examples.translation: But when it comes to its conclusion, it finds itself in trouble;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Trepidant enim, cum fecerunt, haerent;
examples.translation: For they tremble after the deed, and they are embarrassed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Curtius Nicia haesit Cn. Pompeio et C. Memmio;
examples.translation: Curtius Nicias was an adherent of Gnaeus Pompeius and Gaius Memmius;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to sell, vend.
Latin: Dare possessionem alicuius ob pretium

examples.original: Non dest prolato ieiunus venditor auro.
examples.translation: By now mounds and hills are hidden;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Reliqua vendita, quibus domini non exstitere.
examples.translation: That the consul had earned a triumph all agreed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eam propter inopiam aerarii consules vendiderunt.
examples.translation: These the consuls sold, owing to the impoverished condition of the treasury.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a step, pace (cf.: gressus, passus, incessus).
Latin: Gressus
Latin: scalarum pars, qua sursum deorsumve gradimur

examples.original: Unus autem dies gradus vitae est.
examples.translation: And one day, mind you, is a stage on life’s journey.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si ille acer est et ferox, concitari gradum?
examples.translation: That a keen and confident soul quickens the step?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ne procurri quidem ab acie velim, sed obnixos vos stabili gradu impetum hostium excipere.
examples.translation: I would have none run out from the line, but all stand firmly planted and receive the onset of our enemies.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: how often, how many times, as often as (class.)

examples.original: Quotiens enim felicitatis et causa et initium fuit, quod calamitas vocabatur?
examples.translation: For how often has so-called affliction been the source and the beginning of happiness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quotiens in mentem venerit, quantum tibi in servum liceat, veniat in mentem tantundem in te domino tuo licere.
examples.translation: And as often as you reflect how much power you have over a slave, remember that your master has just as much power over you.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et ideo ad rerum actus excitandi ac tractatione bonarum artium occupandi sumus, quotiens nos male habet inertia sui inpatiens.
examples.translation: We must therefore rouse ourselves to action and busy ourselves with interests that are good, as often as we are in the grasp of an uncontrollable sluggishness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: in what manner, how (cf.: quomodo, quī).

examples.original: Quisquis enim sentit quemadmodum sit affectus, eum necesse est aut in voluptate esse aut in dolore.
examples.translation: A man who is conscious of his condition at all must necessarily feel either pleasure or pain.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quaeque de virtutibus dicta sunt, quemadmodum eae semper voluptatibus inhaererent, eadem de amicitia dicenda sunt.
examples.translation: All that has been said about the essential connexion of the virtues with pleasure must be repeated about friendship.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et quemadmodum temeritas et libido et ignavia semper animum excruciant et semper sollicitant turbulentaeque sunt, sic improbitas si cuius in mente consedit, hoc ipso quod adest turbulenta est;
examples.translation: And just as Rashness, Licence and Cowardice ever torment the mind, ever awaken trouble and discord, so Unrighteousness, when firmly rooted in the heart, causes restlessness by the mere fact of its presence;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a form, shape, figure (syn.: forma, species; tropus).

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed quoniam totidem mores totidemque figurae, Non sunt iudiciis omnia danda meis.
examples.translation: What cannot offend your feelings, perhaps will be a reproach to another’s judgment.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Persecutus est Aristoteles animantium omnium ortus, victus, figuras, Theophrastus autem stirpium naturas omniumque fere rerum quae e terra gignerentur causas atque rationes;
examples.translation: Aristotle gave a complete account of the birth, nutrition and structure of all living creatures, Theophrastus of the natural history of plants and the causes and constitution of vegetable organisms in general;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to look askance at, to look maliciously or spitefully at, to cast an evil eye upon (only anteclass.).—With

examples.original: Non sunt di fastidiosi, non invidi;
examples.translation: The gods are not disdainful or envious;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Malo ignoscas otio meo quam invideas.
examples.translation: I prefer you to pardon rather than envy my retirement.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ille in se stupet, ille caligat, invidet caecis.
examples.translation: Such a man is internally dazed; his vision is darkened;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a stake

examples.original: Eum locum vallo fossaque munivit.
examples.translation: He fortified the place with rampart and trench.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Fabius Vibulanus corona primum vallum defendit;
examples.translation: Fabius Vibulanus first manned the rampart with a cordon of defenders;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ut prope perventum, comites in valle relinquit, Ipsa nemus tacito clam pede fortis init.
examples.translation: When she drew nigh, she left her comrades in the vale, and herself secretly with silent step bravely entered the wood.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of a shining, dazzling white, white, clear, bright
Latin: Haud niger; albus cum nitore
English: not.—So only in the combinations
Latin: Ut ne
Latin: Si non, nisi

examples.original: Ni statim recipiantur, noctem in armis agendam.
examples.translation: The soldier’s glory is in his camp: that is his native city, that his penates.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Lateque cladem intulisset ni duo milites praeclarum facinus ausi, arreptis e strage scutis ignorati, vincla ac libramenta tormentorum abscidissent.
examples.translation: They were at once run through and thus their names were lost; but there is no doubt about their deed.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Moti homines sunt in eo iudicio maxime P. Horatio patre proclamante se filiam iure caesam iudicare: ni ita esset, patrio iure in filium animadversurum fuisse.
examples.translation: What influenced men most of all in that trial was the assertion of Publius Horatius, the father, that his daughter had been justly slain;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: extreme age, senility

examples.original: Nulli non senectus sua est;
examples.translation: There is nothing that does not have its old age;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Apex est autem senectutis auctoritas.
examples.translation: But the crowning glory of old age is influence.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Plato ipse ad senectutem se diligentia protulit.
examples.translation: Plato himself, by taking pains, advanced to old age.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a deed

examples.original: Cuius totius facinoris nulla magis quam avaritia causa est.
examples.translation: And of all this evil-doing nothing is more cause than greed.
examples.author: Bede

examples.original: Quid umquam Habitus in se admisit, ut hoc tantum ab eo facinus non abhorrere videatur?
examples.translation: What crime has Habitus ever had upon his conscience that you should imagine such a deed to be otherwise than abhorrent from him?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Duobus facinoribus, altero flagitiosissimo, altero egregio, tantundem apud posteros meruit bonae famae quantum malae.
examples.translation: By two bold deeds, the one most outrageous, the other glorious, he gained with posterity as much fame as evil reputation.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: By Hercules!; assuredly, indeed

examples.original: Neque enim oratorius iste, immo hercle ne virilis quidem cultus est, quo plerique temporum nostrorum actores ita utuntur ut lascivia verborum et levitate sententiarum et licentia compositionis histrionales modos exprimant.
examples.translation: There is a fashion much in vogue with quite a number of counsel nowadays that ill befits an orator, and is indeed scarce worthy even of a man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a footstep, step; footprint, foot-track, track.

examples.original: Vestigia viri alieni, Collatine, in lecto sunt tuo;
examples.translation: The print of a strange man, Collatinus, is in your bed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Asuvius cum Avillio Romam est profectus: hos vestigiis Oppianicus consecutus est.
examples.translation: Asuvius and Avillius started for Rome together; Oppianicus followed closely in their footsteps.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Equestribus proeliis saepe ex equis desiliunt ac pedibus proeliantur, equosque eodem remanere vestigio adsuefecerunt, ad quos se celeriter, cum usus est, recipiunt;
examples.translation: In cavalry combats they often leap from their horses and fight on foot, having trained their horses to remain in the same spot, and retiring rapidly upon them at need;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to stand in or upon a thing (class.).

examples.original: Instant Volumnius et Scipio et perculsos sternunt.
examples.translation: Hard after them came Volumnius and Scipio, and made havoc of the disordered Samnites.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Orationibus instate horis et temporibus constitutis.
examples.translation: Be instant in prayerb at the appointed hours and seasons.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Concitata multitudo erat certamenque instare videbatur.
examples.translation: The crowd was deeply moved and a conflict appeared to be imminent.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to stretch, stretch out vigorously, to draw tight, strain.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; di, tum, 3

examples.original: Illud nobis et illis commune est: sapientem se ipso esse contentum.
examples.translation: But we and they alike hold this idea,—that the wise man is self-sufficient.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Naturales divitias dixit parabiles esse quod parvo esset natura contenta.
examples.translation: He said that natural wealth is easily won, because nature is satisfied with little.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In ea civitate duo de principatu inter se contendebant, Indutiomarus et Cingetorix;
examples.translation: Two men in the state were striving together for the chieftaincy, Indutiomarus and Cingetorix.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: great fear, affright, dread, alarm

examples.original: Nullum terrorem externum, nullum periculum esse;
examples.translation: There was no fear of foreign foes, no danger;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Is terror obstructas mentis consiliis ducis aperuit.
examples.translation: This alarming danger opened their obstinate ears to the plans of their general.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Et foris, cum tot terrores a finitimis ostentati essent, et domi otium fuit.
examples.translation: Things were quiet both abroad and at home, despite the numerous alarms which neighbouring states had caused.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a funeral procession, funeral rites, burial, funeral, usually with reference to the burning of the body; cf.: funus est jam ardens cadaver; quod dum portatur, exsequias dicimus
Latin: Caerimonia ad honorem hominis mortui, saepissime humationem includens

examples.original: Sine funeris ullo Ardet honore rogus;
examples.translation: The pyre burns on with no funeral honours;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Mihi funere nullo Est opus, o superi;
examples.translation: I ask no burial of the gods: let them leave my mutilated corpse amid the waves;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Collegae funus quanto tum potuit apparatu fecit;
examples.translation: His colleague’s funeral he celebrated with all the pomp then possible;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a sword
Latin: Ensis; species armorum offensivorum, qui laminam longam et plerumque acies et mucrone acuto habet
Latin: Caedes, mors

examples.original: Scuto vobis magis quam gladio opus est.
examples.translation: A shield is what you need more than a sword.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec bonum nec malum vagina gladium facit.
examples.translation: The scabbard does not make the sword good or bad.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid mundi gladios a sanguine Caesaris arces?
examples.translation: Why do you keep away the swords of all mankind from Caesar’s throat?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the most celebrated Roman poet of the ante-class. period, the father of Roman epic poetry, born at Rudiae

examples.original: Ait enim Ennius neminem potuisse Scipioni neque civem neque hostem reddere operae pretium.
examples.translation: For Ennius must mean that neither friend nor foe could pay Scipio a reward worthy of his efforts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: twice, at two times, on two occasions, in two ways, =
Latin: Duabus vicibus; semel et iterum

examples.original: Nam si bis dicere est commodum, certe utriusque commune est;
examples.translation: Ah, you say, but I am doing away with the object of the second hearing.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Huc cum ab Ostia navigaret, vehementi circio bis paene demersus est, prope Liguriam iuxtaque Stoechadas insulas.
examples.translation: On the voyage thither from Ostia he was nearly cast away twice in furious north-westers, off Liguria and near the Stoechades islands.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Curius Dentatus cos. Samnitibus caesis et Sabinis, qui rebellaverant, victis et in deditionem acceptis bis in eodem magistratu triumphavit.
examples.translation: Curius Dentatus the consul having slaughtered the Samnites and conquered the Sabines, who had revolted, and received their submission, triumphed twice in the same year of office.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the place for the assembling of the Romans voting by the curiœ situated near the Forum, and separated from it by the ancient Rostra, but sometimes considered as a part of the

examples.original: Nec variatum comitiis est, quin cum Manlio Naevio censor Marcius crearetur.
examples.translation: There was no dissenting opinion shown at the assembly, and Marcius was elected, along with Manlius Naevius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iam comitia consularia instabant; quae res eum necdum compositis maturisve satis consiliis oppressit.
examples.translation: The consular election was now at hand, and found him with his plans not yet fully ripened.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fabius nihil aliud precatus populum Romanum quam ut, priusquam intro vocarentur ad suffragium tribus, Ap. Claudi praetoris allatas ex Etruria litteras audirent, comitio abiit.
examples.translation: Fabius only prayed the Roman people to listen, before the tribes were called to vote, to a dispatch of Appius Claudius the praetor that had been brought in from Etruria.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: against one's will, unwilling, reluctant (syn. coactus; class.).

examples.original: Non est autem gloriosum, quod ab invito et tergiversante fit;
examples.translation: But nothing glorious can result from unwillingness and cowardice;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid enim relinques, quod invitus relictum a te possis cogitare?
examples.translation: For what will you leave behind you that you can imagine yourself reluctant to leave?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vix etiam fueras paucas vitalis in horas, Obtulit invitae cum tibi Caesar opem;
examples.translation: Scarce hadst thou been like to live for even a few hours, when Caesar brought thee succour against thy will;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the goddess of Love, the goddess Venus
Latin: Dea Romana amoris; amor ipse
Latin: Secundus planeta ab Sole

examples.original: Et Venus in silvis iungebat corpora amantum;
examples.translation: And Venus joined the bodies of lovers in the woods;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Brundisium veni, vel potius ad moenia accessi.
examples.translation: I came to Brundisium, or rather approached the walls;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ut Cremonam venere, novum immensumque opus occurrit.
examples.translation: When they reached Cremona they found a new task of enormous difficulty before them.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a daughter
Latin: Progenies feminina hominis

examples.original: Verginius viderit de filia ubi venerit quid agat;
examples.translation: Let Verginius decide what to do about his daughter, when he comes;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Reliquit filium Orbilium, et ipsum grammaticum professorem.
examples.translation: He left a son Orbilius, who was also a teacher of grammar.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Uxori ac filiae superstes fuit atque utramque adhuc privatus amisit.
examples.translation: He outlived his wife and daughter; in fact lost them both before he became emperor.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: empty, void (opp. plenus; freq. and class.).

examples.original: Tota rerum natura umbra est aut inanis aut fallax.
examples.translation: The whole universe is then a vain or deceptive shadow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tum porro si nil esset quod inane vacaret, omne foret solidum;
examples.translation: Then further, if there were nothing void and empty, the universe would be solid;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Ille enim habet suum finem, inania et ex libidine orta sine termino sunt.
examples.translation: For this has its bounds, but waywardness and the acts that spring from wilful lust are without boundaries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to imitate.

examples.original: Necesse est aut imiteris aut oderis.
examples.translation: You must either imitate or loathe the world.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid enim quis discere, quid imitari velit?
examples.translation: For what can a man desire to learn or to imitate in them?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Est tibi agendus amans, imitandaque vulnera verbis; Haec tibi quaeratur qualibet arte fides.
examples.translation: You must play the lover, and counterfeit heartache with words: her belief in that you must win by any device.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: philosophical: philosopha sententia, Pac. ap.
Latin: Sapientiae studens

examples.original: Quo magis hoc philosopho faciendum est;
examples.translation: All the more is the philosopher compelled to do likewise;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Oratio sollicita philosophum non decet;
examples.translation: A meticulous manner of writing does not suit the philosopher;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Oratio me istius philosophi non offendit;
examples.translation: With your master’s style I have no fault to find.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to fill up, fill full, to make full, fill (freq. and class.; cf. expleo, compleo).

examples.original: Ratio autem non impletur manifestis;
examples.translation: But reason is not satisfied by obvious facts;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Recepit, implevit. Et adhuc manus excelsa.
examples.translation: He received it back, he fulfilled his vow.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: De adventu autem ad vos nostro utrorumque desiderium deus impleat.
examples.translation: May God give fulfilment to the desire we both share, that I should visit you!
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to represent pictorially with the pencil or needle, to paint, embroider (cf.: depingo, delineo, adumbro).
Latin: Formam alicuius rei ductis lineis et inductis coloribus repraesentare
Latin: colores inducere; variis coloribus ornare

examples.original: Habuit et pingendi fingendique non mediocre studium.
examples.translation: He likewise had no slight interest in painting and sculpture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Iam quae iste signa, quas tabulas pictas ex Achaia sustulerit, non dicam hoc loco;
examples.translation: What statues and pictures he carried off from Achaia I will not state here;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quorum domus, cum honore et virtute florerent, signis et tabulis pictis erant vacuae;
examples.translation: These were men of high rank and eminent character,b but their houses were empty of statues and pictures;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: naked, bare, unclothed, uncovered, exposed.

examples.original: Non erat armatis aequum concurrere nudas;
examples.translation: It were not just that defenceless maids should fight with armed men;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iamque sinu laxo nudum sine corpore volnus.
examples.translation: The limbs are soaked with corrupted blood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tam inops autem ego eram ab amicis aut tam nuda res publica a magistratibus?
examples.translation: But was I so destitute of aid from friends, or was the republic so devoid of magistrates?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: firm (in opp. to frail, destructible), steadfast, stable, strong, powerful (freq. and class.; esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: constans, stabilis, solidus).

examples.original: Certe id firmissimum longe imperium est quo oboedientes gaudent.
examples.translation: You have at hand the means of waxing great and supremely glorious.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tamen longe maiora et firmiora de eo iudicia in morte ac post mortem exstiterunt.
examples.translation: Yet far greater and stronger tokens of regard were shown at the time of his death and immediately afterwards.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: At illud ex se ortum fidele firmumque est et crescit et ad extremum usque prosequitur;
examples.translation: But that joy which springs wholly from oneself is leal and sound; it increases and attends us to the last;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to bend
Latin: (Membra) torquere et detorquere
Latin: in re nautica flectere promontorium est navigando proram flectere ad promontorium superandum
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; xi, xum, 3

examples.original: Qui modo celabas monitu tua crimina nostro, Flecte iter, et monitu detege furta meo.
examples.translation: You who were but now concealing your fault by my advice, turn your path, and by my advice uncover your deceit.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Servilius, lenibus remediis aptior, concitatos animos flecti quam frangi putabat cum tutius tum facilius esse.
examples.translation: Servilius, more inclined to gentle measures, believed that it was safer, as well as easier, to assuage their fury than to quell it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et quoniam mentem sanari, corpus ut aegrum, cernimus et flecti medicina posse videmus, id quoque praesagit mortalem vivere mentem.
examples.translation: And since we see that the mind, like a sick body, can be healed and changed by medicine, this also foreshows that the mind has a mortal life.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: thin, fine, close, etc. (syn.: gracilis, exilis).

examples.original: Limes erat tenuis longa subnubilus umbra, Quo tulit illa suos ad mare saepe pedes.
examples.translation: There was a narrow way o’er-cast by the long shadows, by which she oft betook herself to the sea.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quam fuit imbecillus P. Africani filius, is qui te adoptavit, quam tenui aut nulla potius valetudine!
examples.translation: Note how weak, Scipio, was your adoptive father, the son of Publius Africanus! What feeble health he had, or rather no health at all!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quae porro tenuissima suspicio collata in Scamandrum est aut conferri potuit, ut is sua sponte necare voluisse Habitum putaretur?
examples.translation: Nay, what shadow of suspicion was, or could have been thrown on Scamander of having conceived a wish to murder Habitus without any instigation?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to go back, fall back, give ground, retire, withdraw, recede.

examples.original: Si extra est, posteaquam acciderat, recessit.
examples.translation: If it is outside, it withdraws after having affected the object.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed venio ad agricolas, ne a me ipso recedam.
examples.translation: But, lest I wander from my subject, I return to the farmers.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dum tibi tutum non est ad te recedere, circumspice singulos;
examples.translation: You ought to make yourself of a different stamp from the multitude.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or pertaining to healing, healing, curative, medical
Latin: Qui medetur, ad medicinam pertinens
Latin: Vir, qui in medicina versatur

examples.original: Quis medicus aegros in transitu curat?
examples.translation: What physician can heal his patient on a flying visit?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illa leget tempus (medici quoque tempora servant) Quo facilis dominae mens sit et apta capi.
examples.translation: She will choose a time (physicians also observe times) when her mistress is in an easy mood and apt for winning.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: In his sic illi opus est alieno consilio quomodo medico, quomodo gubernatori, quomodo advocato et litis ordinatori.
examples.translation: He needs outside advice on such matters, as does the physician, the pilot, the attorney, or the pleader of cases.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the moon.
Latin: Orbis caelestis qui circum orbem terrae revolvit; satelles terrae; planeta secundarius, cuius lux, quae hausta est a Sole, repercutitor terrae, et servit ut depellere tenebras noctis
Latin: Satelles similaris planetae alius

examples.original: Luna suis vicibus Tethyn terrenaque miscet;
examples.translation: The changes of the moon bring sea and land in contact.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Lunae quoque trinae, ut Cn. Domitio C. Fannio consulibus, apparuere.
examples.translation: Three moons have also been seen, as was the case in the consulship of Cn. Domitius and C. Fannius; they have generally been named nocturnal suns.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: pleasant, agreeable, delightful, pleasing

examples.original: Deinde quod acerbum fuit ferre, tulisse iucundum est;
examples.translation: And that which was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid si etiam iucunda memoria est praeteritorum malorum?
examples.translation: What if the memory of past evils be actually pleasant?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nihil est enim remuneratione benevolentiae, nihil vicissitudine studiorum officiorumque iucundius. Quid?
examples.translation: For nothing gives more pleasure than the return of goodwill and the interchange of zealous service.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: goes on foot.

examples.original: Mihi legiones peditumque pugna curae erunt;
examples.translation: I will see to the legions and the battle of the infantry;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Orcus vobis ducit pedes senatum gestu notarat.
examples.translation: Orcus guides your steps, he indicated the senate by a gesture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Pedites ab dextro cornu egregie pugnavere haud segniter resistentibus Volscis.
examples.translation: The infantry on the right fought brilliantly, and were vigorously resisted by the Volsci.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: flesh (animal or vegetable).

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ad hoc panis usu carnisque coctae et dulcedine vini mitigatos Marius in tempore adgressus est.
examples.translation: When they had been further demoralized by the use of bread and cooked meat and the delights of wine, Marius opportunely approached them.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quippe suspectior illis quam morbo pallentibus color est, languidi et evanidi albent, et in vivis caro morticina est.
examples.translation: Their complexions are more alarming than those of anaemic invalids; they are lackadaisical and flabby with dropsy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: leaning or supported on something, in a good or bad sense; relying or depending upon, trusting to; daring (class.; cf.: fultus, nixus).—Constr. with

examples.original: At tu, fretus armis animisque, concitatis equis invade mediam aciem;
examples.translation: But do you confide in arms and valour, and charge their centre at the gallop;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In contione, ut inter militares viros et factis potius quam dictis fretos, pauca verba habita.
examples.translation: In the assembly the speeches were short, as befitted soldiers and men who trusted more to deeds than to words.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Proxima inde nocte Volsci, discordia Romana freti, si qua nocturna transitio proditiove fieri posset, temptant castra.
examples.translation: But the sentries perceived them, the army was roused, and, the signal being given, rushed to arms.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the neck, of men and animals

examples.original: Ille caput labens et iam languentia colla Viso patre levat;
examples.translation: At sight of his father the son raised his sinking head and failing neck;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Obvia progrediar felixque per oppida dicar Collaque et hoc oculos illius ore premam.
examples.translation: I shall go forth to meet him, and through the cities I shall be called fortunate;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ipsa regit trepidum Pallas dextraque trementem Perseos aversi Cyllenida derigit harpen, Lata colubriferi rumpens confinia colli.
examples.translation: Pallas herself directed Perseus in his haste; her right hand guided the shaking scimitar of the Cyllenian which he held with his face averted;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to limit, bound, enclose within boundaries (class.).
Latin: mori
Latin: locorum fines vel terminos designare
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4

examples.original: In utroque finis dolendi est.
examples.translation: In either case there is an end of pain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Finisque ille tam effuse evagandi Etruscis fuit.
examples.translation: This was the last time the Etruscans roamed so far afield.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cupiditates non Epicuri divisione finiebat sed sua satietate.
examples.translation: Epicurus’s classification of the desires meant nothing to him;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to flow (cf.: mano, labor, etc.).

examples.original: Non enim excidunt, sed fluunt.
examples.translation: They do not drip forth occasionally;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illic et laxas vestes et fluxa virorum Velamenta vides.
examples.translation: There one sees loose garments and flowing robes worn even by men.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Dissiluit stringens uterum membrana, fluuntque Viscera;
examples.translation: The membrane that confines the belly snapped asunder, and the bowels gushed out.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to swear, to take an oath.
Latin: Sollemniter adfirmare
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Di impetrabunt, per quos iuravere;
examples.translation: The gods will persuade them, by whom they have sworn.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tectis ac parietibus iura dicturi estis?
examples.translation: Is it to roofs and walls you will render judgment?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Id primo quidam abnuentes iuraturos se obtruncati circa altaria sunt;
examples.translation: Some there were at first who refused to take this oath;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: change, interchange, alternation, alternate or reciprocal succession, vicissitude
Latin: Momentum proprium actionis (secundum regulas)
Latin: Pars spatii temporis

examples.original: Experti in vicem sumus ego ac fortuna.
examples.translation: Do not reckon up the short duration of my rule;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Luna suis vicibus Tethyn terrenaque miscet;
examples.translation: The changes of the moon bring sea and land in contact.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Is dato negotio suis ut corpus obtegerent, ipse in locum vicemque consulis provolat.
examples.translation: Charging his men to cover up the body, he threw himself into the consul’s place.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: thrust, strike, or dash against something (syn.: illido, impingo; class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; di, sum, 3

examples.original: Non quicquid nos offendit, et laedit.
examples.translation: That which annoys us does not necessarily injure us;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si quid in contraria parte in homine offendendum sit, habetis eum, ut nihil dicam amplius, qui se homines coegisse fateatur.
examples.translation: Should there be, on the opposite side, something in the man that causes offence, you have there one who, to say nothing more, admits that he collected his forces together.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum utraque divortium fecit, sed cum Paetina ex levibus offensis, cum Urgulanilla ob libidinum probra et homicidii suspicionem.
examples.translation: He divorced both these, Paetina for trivial offences, but Urgulanilla because of scandalous lewdness and the suspicion of murder.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to take wholly or completely, i. e.
Latin: Aliquid abscondere, tegere, ab aliorum oculis auferre; (et occurrit de loco seu spatio)
Latin: Aliquid a loco aliquo paullatim auferre, ut id in re aliqua impendatur; (et occurrit de materia, viribus, tempore etc.)

examples.original: His agendis dies est consumptus.
examples.translation: With these transactions the day was taken up.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Reliquum diei apparandis armis consumptum est.
examples.translation: The rest of the day they spent in making ready their arms.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Consumetur, inquies. Scilicet exspectemus legitimum illud quinquennium;
examples.translation: It will be so spent, you will answer.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: able, powerful
Latin: Qui potest
Latin: Fortis, validus

examples.original: Quis clarior in Graecia Themistocle, quis potentior?
examples.translation: Who was more eminent in Greece than Themistocles, who more powerful?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hi ferre agere plebem plebisque res, cum fortuna, quidquid cupitum foret, potentioris esset.
examples.translation: They bullied the plebs and plundered their possessions; for success attended the strong, no matter what they coveted.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hunc non ruricolae Panes nemorumque potentes Silvani Nymphaeque tenent, sed barbara ritu Sacra deum;
examples.translation: No rural Pan dwelt there, no Silvanus, ruler of the woods, no Nymphs;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the great mass, the multitude, the people, public (class.; cf.: plebs, turba).
Latin: Gentes mediae
Latin: multitudo, plebs

examples.original: Sese tamen et amore fraterno et existimatione vulgi commoveri.
examples.translation: For all that, I feel the force of brotherly love and public opinion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Vulgus tamen vacuum curis et sine falsi verique discrimine solitas adulationes edoctum clamore et vocibus adstrepebat;
examples.translation: Yet the populace, careless and unable to distinguish between truth and falsehood, shouted loud the usual flattery, as it had been taught to do;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Noscitabatur tamen in tanta deformitate, et ordines duxisse aiebant aliaque militiae decora vulgo miserantes eum iactabant;
examples.translation: He was recognized nevertheless, despite the hideousness of his appearance, and the word went round that he had commanded companies;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: darkness (stronger than obscuritas, and weaker than caligo; freq. and class.).
Latin: Obscuritas, caligo, absentia lucis
Latin: Obstarotasritas, caligo, absentia lucis

examples.original: Curio Dacia tenus venit, sed tenebras saltuum expavit.
examples.translation: Curio reached Dacia, but shrank from its gloomy forests.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Prospectu tenebris adempto multa utrimque vulnera accipiuntur.
examples.translation: As the darkness made it impossible to see far, many wounds were received on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ipse caput medio Titan cum ferret Olympo, Condidit ardentes atra caligine currus Involvitque orbem tenebris gentesque coegit Desperare diem;
examples.translation: The sun himself, while rearing his head in the zenith, hid his burning chariot in black darkness and veiled his sphere in gloom, forcing mankind to despair of daylight;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to lift or raise up, to raise, erect, elevate
Latin: me elevo

examples.original: Quisquis dixit ”vixi,” cotidie ad lucrum surgit.
examples.translation: When a man has said: ”have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Philosophiae acceptum fero, quod surrexi, quod convalui.
examples.translation: I place it to the credit of philosophy that I recovered and regained my strength.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est admirationi una arbor, ubi in eandem altitudinem tota silva surrexit.
examples.translation: There is unevenness, you know, when some objects rise conspicuous above others.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to lay legal claim to a thing, whether as one's own property or for its restoration to a free condition.

examples.original: Et utinam sic denique lues ista vindicetur!
examples.translation: And would that this pest might so at last be overcome!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atqui melius fuisset non queri quam vindicari.
examples.translation: Yet surely it were better to have no grievances than to need to seek redress.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: In insuperabili loco stat animus, qui externa deseruit, et arce se sua vindicat;
examples.translation: The soul stands on unassailable ground, if it has abandoned external things;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to lead forth, draw out, bring away (very freq. and class.).
Latin: Nutrire et nutriendo instituere, et usurpatur de pueris tum quod ad corpus, tum quod ad mentem attinet
Latin: Extra ducere, extrahere

examples.original: Ad hanc nos conemur educere.
examples.translation: Let us therefore strive to raise ourselves to this altitude.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tum abducto in secretum viro Tanaquil, ”Viden tu puerum hunc,” inquit, ”quem tam humili cultu educamus?
examples.translation: Then, taking her husband aside, Tanaquil said: ”Do you see this child whom we are bringing up in so humble a fashion?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huc atque illuc signa moveri ac modo in unum conferri modo educi videtis; opus quidem incipit nemo, cum iam circumdati vallo potuerimus esse.
examples.translation: You see their standards moving now this way, now that, first closing in together, then deploying, while no man falls to work, though we might ere this have been fenced in with a palisade.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a very hard kind of oak
Latin: Forma valde dura quercus, Quercus robur apud Linnaeum
Latin: Quisquam quercus

examples.original: Duae res plurimum roboris animo dant, fides veri et fiducia;
examples.translation: There are two strong supports to the soul—trusta in the truth and confidence;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inumbrante vespera universum Flaviani exercitus robur advenit.
examples.translation: As evening fell, the great mass of the Flavian troops arrived in a body.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Neque enim de more carinas Extendunt puppesque levant, sed firma gerendis Molibus insolito contexunt robora ductu.
examples.translation: They built no long hulls, no high sterns, as the custom is, but joined stout planks together on unwonted lines to carry heavy structures.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: Greece
Latin: Natio Graecorum, in Europa inter meridiem et ortum solis, vocatur Respublica Hellenica (Ελληνική Δημοκρατία)

examples.original: Quis clarior in Graecia Themistocle, quis potentior?
examples.translation: Who was more eminent in Greece than Themistocles, who more powerful?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Id si feceris, et Spartam et ceteram Graeciam sub tuam potestatem se adiuvante te redacturum pollicetur.
examples.translation: If you do so, he guarantees that with your help he will bring Sparta and all Greece under your sway.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Itaque missis Archelao Neoptolemoque praefectis, excepta Rhodo, quae pro nobis firmius stetit, ceterae Cyclades, Delos, Euboea et ipsum Graeciae decus Athenae tenebantur.
