examples.translation: He, therefore, sent his generals, Archelaus and Neoptolemus, and (except Rhodes, which supported us more loyally than ever) all the Cyclades, Delos, Euboea and Athens itself, the glory of Greece, were occupied.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: an uproar, bustle, violent commotion, disturbance, tumult (freq. and class.; cf.: turba, perturbatio).

examples.original: Remedium tumultus fuit alius tumultus.
examples.translation: The remedy for this disturbance was a second riot.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Trierarchi magno tumultu Vitellii imagines invadunt;
examples.translation: The trierarchs with loud shouts attacked the statues of Vitellius;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sex Liburnicae inter primum tumultum evasere, in quis praefectus classis Apollinaris;
examples.translation: Six Liburnian galleys escaped at the first alarm with Apollinaris the prefect of the fleet on board;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: agitu; cf.: quaero quaerito.
Latin: Frequent. ab agere; ante se pellere, impellere, efficere, fluctuare

examples.original: Tum de persequendo hoste agitari coeptum.
examples.translation: They then began to consider the feasibility of a pursuit.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tribuni plebem agitare suo veneno, agraria lege;
examples.translation: The tribunes roused the plebs to madness with their usual poison, a land-law.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec sua sponte agitata insuper tribuni plebis 11, 12accendunt.
examples.translation: This smouldering discontent was fanned into a blaze by the plebeian tribunes.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: undying, immortal (class.).

examples.original: Idem immortali memoria percepta retinebat beneficia;
examples.translation: He had besides an unfailing memory for kindnesses received;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Itaque de illo quaerendum est, an possit immortalis esse.
examples.translation: We therefore come to this question,—whether the soul can be immortal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O di immortales, incredibilem avaritiam singularemque audaciam!
examples.translation: God help us, what incredible greed, what matchless impudence!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that which separates or divides two things from each other (for syn. cf.: differentia, discrepantia, diversitas, distantia); hence
Latin: crisis, situatio periculosa seu dubia

examples.original: Sed ne discriminibus quidem caruit.
examples.translation: But he was exposed also to actual dangers.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nullum porro inter divina discrimen est;
examples.translation: And furthermore, there is no distinction between things divine;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo denique discriminum ventum est, ut foedus et pax cum hoste—si modo hostis Pompei filius—tamen feriretur.
examples.translation: At last the danger became so great that a treaty of peace was concluded with the enemy—if a son of Pompeius can be called an enemy.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: daring, in a good, but oftener in a bad sense, bold, courageous, spirited; audacious, rash, presumptuous, foolhardy (syn.: fortis, temerarius).

examples.original: Non est itaque, quod audax iudices promissum, cuius tibi, si parum fidei habeo, sponsorem dabo.
examples.translation: It is not for you, therefore, to call reckless this boast of minea;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec non et ratibus temptatur regia, qua se Protulit in medios audaci margine fluctus Luxuriosa domus.
examples.translation: They assailed the palace also by means of ships, at the point where the splendid pile projected with bold frontage right over the water.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Verum hoc adhuc percommode cadit, quod cum incredibili eius audacia singularis stultitia coniuncta est.
examples.translation: But it has very fortunately come about, hitherto, that his incredible audacity has been accompanied by unparalleled folly.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To boil away, boil down, diminish by boiling.
Latin: deminuere coquendo
English: slow, not swift, sluggish, tardy (freq. and class.; syn.: lentus, languidus).
Latin: Qui sine celeritate movetur

examples.original: Scriptitavit et raro et tarde.
examples.translation: He wrote rarely and slowly.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Tanti enim illam putas, ut tardius cenes?
examples.translation: Do you think enough of your country to be late to dinner?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et tardum est et varium, quod usus docet;
examples.translation: The teachings of experience are slow and irregular;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: an ambush, ambuscade (class.).

examples.original: Tempanius metu insidiarum suos ad lucem tenuit.
examples.translation: Tempanius feared an ambush and kept his soldiers close till daylight.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque dispositis insidiis saepius equites eius adgressus secunda proelia faciebat.
examples.translation: So he set ambuscades about, attacked the other’s horsemen frequently, and won his actions.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar ad colloquium Caesar adduceret: vereri se, ne per insidias ab eo circumveniretur: uterque cum equitatu veniret: alia ratione sese non esse venturum.
examples.translation: Caesar did not wish the parley to be broken off upon an excuse thus interposed; at the same time he could not venture to entrust his personal safety to Gallic horse.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: free from care, careless, unconcerned, untroubled, fearless, quiet, easy, composed.

examples.original: Sed securus de illo sum;
examples.translation: I am, however, comfortable in my mind regarding him;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Honestum omne securum est, tranquillum est;
examples.translation: The honourable is wholly free from anxiety and is calm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Admiscenda tamen venus est secura timori, Ne tanti noctes non putet esse tuas.
examples.translation: Yet with fear must be mingled secure enjoyment, lest he think your nights are not worth while.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: sour wine, wine-vinegar, or simply vinegar
English: to hasten, quicken, accelerate; to prepare, make, or do with haste
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Quod evenit in labyrintho properantibus;
examples.translation: This is what happens when you hurry through a maze;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed nimium properas: vivam modo, plura dolebis;
examples.translation: But you haste overmuch: if I but live, you will grieve the more;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Saepe ”mane!” dixit, cum iam properaret Achilles;
examples.translation: Often cried she, ”Stay,” when already Achilles was hasting from her;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to come forth, grow, to arise, spring, be born, become visible, appear
Latin: Maior fieri

examples.original: Haec bona non crescunt, si plena sunt.
examples.translation: These goods, if they are complete, do not increase;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Crescere posse inperfectae rei signum est.
examples.translation: The ability to increase is proof that a thing is still imperfect.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec hoc novum est, quaedam crescendo mutari.
examples.translation: It is no new idea that certain objects change as they grow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: instruction, teaching; learning, discipline

examples.original: Liberalis disciplinas omnis fere puer attigit.
examples.translation: When a boy he took up almost all the liberal arts;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Acriore hodie disciplina victi quam victores agunt.
examples.translation: The former are fired to brave action by rage, hatred, and eager desire for revenge;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hic omnem militarem disciplinam artemque bellandi condidit.
examples.translation: It was he who founded all military discipline and the art of warfare.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to put into the power of, to subject to any one

examples.original: Ut potiare, roga: tantum cupit illa rogari;
examples.translation: That you may gain her, ask: she only wishes to be asked;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Qua ut poteretur, virum eius Atticum Vestinum consulem in honore ipso trucidavit.
examples.translation: To possess the latter he slew her husband Atticus Vestinus while he held the office of consul.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Neque ita multo post Nicanor Piraeo est potitus, sine quo Athenae omnino esse non possunt.
examples.translation: Not long afterwards Nicanor got possession of the Piraeus, without which Athens cannot exist at all;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Phocion

definitions: English: to direct the mind or attention to a thing, to attend to, give heed to, to take heed, consider, regard, observe.
Latin: Mentem in rem aliquam intendere, animum ad aliquid attendere
Latin: Oculis animoque advertere

examples.original: Quod ubi animadvertit Camillus, ignem in obiectam saepem coici iussit;
examples.translation: On perceiving this, Camillus ordered his men to throw fire on the barrier.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum exsectio illa fundi in armario animadverteretur, quaerebant homines quonam modo fieri potuisset.
examples.translation: The theft was discovered next day, and the entire suspicion fell on the two slaves who were not forthcoming.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod quum ita sit, resque eiusmodi sit ut in primis a magistratibus animadvertenda esse videatur, iterum quaero, sitne eius rei aliqua actio an nulla.
examples.translation: This being so, and the case appearing preeminently one for cognizance by the magistrates, I ask again: ”Is there any legal process in my case or is there none?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: On the inside, within

examples.original: Auro illos et argento et ebore adornavi, intus boni nihil est.
examples.translation: I have bedecked them with gold, and silver, and ivory, but within there is nothing good.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil autem ad rem pertinet, utrum foris habeat exemplar, ad quod referat oculos, an intus, quod ibi ipse concepit et posuit.
examples.translation: Now it makes no difference whether he has his pattern outside himself, that he may direct his glance to it, or within himself, conceived and placed there by himself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Est quoque uti possit magnus congestus harenae fluctibus adversis oppilare ostia contra, cum mare permotum ventis ruit intus harenam;
examples.translation: It is possible also that a great collection of sand blocks up the mouth against the stream, when the sea, stirred by the winds, rolls the sand inwards;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: to be able, I (thou, he, etc.)
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n.; īvi and ii, ĭtum

examples.original: Nec accipere iniuriam queunt nec facere;
examples.translation: They cannot receive or inflict injury;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum haec agerentur, iam consul via Labicana ad fanum Quietis erat.
examples.translation: Meanwhile the consul had already reached the shrine of Quies on the Labican road.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In quo quae vestra defensio futura sit coniectura assequi non queo.
examples.translation: And here I cannot guess what your line of defence is to be.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to sigh, groan.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ŭi, ĭtum, 3

examples.original: Utque ferox Phalaris, lingua prius ense resecta More bovis Paphio clausus in aere gemas.
examples.translation: And like fierce Phalaris, thy tongue first severed with the sword, mayst thou bellow like an ox imprisoned in Paphian bronze.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non sunt illi eiulatus et gemitus Philoctetae tam miseri, quamquam sunt acerbi, quam illa exsultatio Athamantis et quam senium matricidarum.
examples.translation: The shrieks and groans of Philoctetes, heart-rending though they be, do not speak such wretchedness as the exulting cries of Athamasb or the remorse of long-lived matricides.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vocibus his correpta viri vix aegra levavit Membra solo tales gemitu rumpente querellas: ”O utinam in thalamos invisi Caesaris issem Infelix coniunx et nulli laeta marito!
examples.translation: Thus rebuked by her husband, slowly she raised her ailing limbs from the ground, and her wailing broke out into complaints like these: ”Would that I had been wedded to hated Caesar;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: likeness, resemblance, similitude (class.).

examples.original: Id ex similitudine floris lilium appellabant.
examples.translation: Eight rows of this kind were dug, three feet apart.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Iam hoc fere scitis omnes, quantam vim habeat ad coniungendas amicitias studiorum ac naturae similitudo.
examples.translation: Their lives were lived on the assumption that no source of profit was dishonourable;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quoniam hac similitudine usus sum, perseverabo: animus noster modo rex est, modo tyrannus.
examples.translation: To persist in my use of this simile—our soul is at one time a king, at another a tyrant.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to make or be ashamed, to feel shame; to be influenced or restrained by shame or by respect for a person or thing.—In the verb. finit. extremely rare

examples.original: Pudet dicere: honesta colimus, quantum vacat.
examples.translation: I am ashamed to say it;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo autem magis te deterreo ab isto morbo, quod non potest tibi ista res contingere aliter quam si te pudere desierit;
examples.translation: However, I have this further reason for frightening you away from the latter malady, namely, that you could only be successful in practising this style by losing your sense of modesty;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: De Verulis et Bovillis pudet, sed triumphavimus.
examples.translation: Over Verulae and Bovillae, I am ashamed to say it—but we triumphed.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to feel together: multa (corpora, i. e. substances) Quae neque conecti potuere neque intus Vitalis motus consentire atque imitari

examples.original: In hac mihi de re publica consensus ;
examples.translation: In it I found agreement on public questions;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illi enim consentire debet, quicquid agimus;
examples.translation: For whatever we do ought to be in harmony with this;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Consensu omnium dilectus decernitur habeturque.
examples.translation: By general consent a levy was proclaimed and held.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: imperat. persece for perseque, Poët. ap.
Latin: Sequi ut aliquid capere

examples.original: Tum de persequendo hoste agitari coeptum.
examples.translation: They then began to consider the feasibility of a pursuit.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Dicis tibi in animo esse alio tempore persequi.
examples.translation: You assert that you intend to do so on some other occasion.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hunc Epaminondas recuperavit, bello persequens Alexandrum.
examples.translation: He was rescued by Epaminondas, who made war upon Alexander.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pelopidas

definitions: English: To put under or among.
Latin: (Intransitivē) posse aliquid facere, satis posse aut esse
Latin: fundamentum ponere, subter facere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; fēci, fectum, 3

examples.original: De cuius spatio atque cultu suffecerit haec rettulisse.
examples.translation: Its size and splendour will be sufficiently indicated by the following details.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Unus mihi sufficit Pharius puer, ut scis, amabilis, sed mutabitur.
examples.translation: One is enough for me,—the slave Pharius, a pleasant fellow, as you know;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Scodram, caput gentis, delesse suffecit; statim secuta deditio est.
examples.translation: It sufficed to destroy Scodra, their capital, and their submission immediately followed.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: Vocat.

examples.original: Ab altero consule res gesta egregie est;
examples.translation: The other consul campaigned with great success.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Color egregius, integra valetudo, summa gratia;
examples.translation: He had excellent health and a sound constitution.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iam primum, ut ordiar ab ducibus comparandis, haud equidem abnuo egregium ducem fuisse Alexandrum;
examples.translation: First of all—to begin by comparing commanders—I do not deny that Alexander was a remarkable general;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: near, neighboring (class.).
Latin: Vicinus

examples.original: Interdictum ne capite damnatos propinqui lugerent.
examples.translation: The relatives of the victims were forbidden to mourn for them.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Antigonus autem Eumenem mortuum propinquis eius sepeliendum tradidit.
examples.translation: Antiochus, however, sent the body of Eumenes to his relatives for burial.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: P. Vetilius, propinquus Aebutii, se Aebutio cum armatis servis venisse advocatum.
examples.translation: Publius Vetilius, his neighbour, says that he came on the summons of Aebutius with some armed slaves.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to bear or carry through to a certain place or end.

examples.original: Vicere tamen tribuni ut legem perferrent;
examples.translation: Yet the tribunes prevailed and carried their law;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nulla ad aures nostras vox inpune perfertur;
examples.translation: There is no word which reaches our ears without doing us harm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eae res in Galliam Transalpinam celeriter perferuntur.
examples.translation: These events were speedily reported to Transalpine Gaul.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: it pleases, is pleasing, is agreeable: mihi, I am disposed, I like, I please, I will.— Constr. with

examples.original: Secum habet ingenium, qui, cum libet, ”accipe” dicit;
examples.translation: I give place: my devices will not please so much as he.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Mandubii, qui eos oppido receperant, cum liberis atque uxoribus exire coguntur.
examples.translation: The Mandubii, whose town had received them, were compelled to leave it with wives and children.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Probatos itaque semper lege, et si quando ad alios deverti libuerit, ad priores redi.
examples.translation: So you should always read standard authors; and when you crave a change, fall back upon those whom you read before.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: so as to meet, meeting, to meet (class.).

examples.original: Neutra parte hostis obvius fuit;
examples.translation: In neither region did they find the enemy.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Gaudete, cohortes: Obvia praebentur fatorum munere bella.
examples.translation: By favour of destiny war is offered you in the course of your march.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Vercingetorix, ubi de Caesaris adventu cognovit, oppugnatione destitit atque obviam Caesari proficiscitur.
examples.translation: As soon as he heard of Caesar’s approach Vercingetorix abandoned the siege and started to meet him.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to be noiseless, still, or silent, to keep silence; act., not to speak of, to keep silent respecting a thing (class.; stronger than tacere).

examples.original: Magno malo ulla voce interpellatum silentium luitur.
examples.translation: There is a grievous penalty for the slightest breach of silence.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At postquam leges bello siluere coactae, Pellimur e patriis laribus patimurque volentes Exilium;
examples.translation: But now law has been silenced by the constraint of war, and we have been driven from our country.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: At tibi nos, quando non proderit ista silere A quibus omne aevi senium sua fama repellit, Digna damus, iuvenis, meritae praeconia vitae.
examples.translation: But to suppress those deeds which are insured by their own glory against all decay of time will not avail;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: scanty in measure or number, small, little, petty, short, poor, mean.

examples.original: Exiguum est, quod deinde canam;
examples.translation: My next point is a small one;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Summa adiectio quare plurimum facit vel exigua?
examples.translation: And why does the last addition, although very slight, make a great deal of difference?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illic exiguo paulum distantia vallo Castra locant.
examples.translation: There the two camps with low ramparts were pitched not far apart.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: some time ago, once upon a time, once, formerly, in time past, whilom, erst (freq. and class.; syn. quondam): versibu' quos olim Fauni vatesque canebant, Enn. ap.
Latin: Illō tempore
Latin: longus abhinc, aliquo tempore in praeteritō

examples.original: Perit denique et is, qui honorem in colonia sua eodem die decerni sibi passus est, quo decreti et Augusto olim erant.
examples.translation: Finally, a man was put to death merely for allowing an honour to be voted him in his native town on the same day that honours had previously been voted to Augustus.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec durare valuit quin de condicionibus continuo tractaret, etiam de Paetinae, quam olim exegerat, deque Lolliae Paulinae, quae C. Caesari nupta fuerat.
examples.translation: Yet he could not refrain from at once planning another match, even with Paetina, whom he had formerly discarded, and with Lollia Paulina, who had been the wife of Gaius Caesar.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Inritaverant turbidum ingenium Helvetii, Gallica gens olim armis virisque, mox memoria nominis clara, de caede Galbae ignari et Vitellii imperium abnuentes.
examples.translation: His restless spirit had been provoked by the Helvetii, a Gallic people once famous for their deeds in arms and for their heroes, later only for the memory of their name.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to lead, bring, or conduct into a place; to lead or bring in (class.); constr. with in and
Latin: In aliquem locum ducere, introducere
Latin: obtegere, obducere, induere

examples.original: Ita induxisse in animum, hostibus potius quam regibus portas patefacere;
examples.translation: They had resolved to throw open their gates to enemies sooner than to kings;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sic enim ab Epicuro sapiens semper beatus inducitur: finitas habet cupiditates;
examples.translation: For Epicurus thus presents his Wise Man who is always happy: his desires are kept within bounds;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Fabianum, cum in senatum testis esset inductus, erubuisse memini, et hic illum mire pudor decuit.
examples.translation: Fabianus also, I remember, reddened when he appeared as a witness before the senate; and his embarrassment became him to a remarkable degree.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to urge one strongly to do a thing, to incite, instigate, encourage, cheer, exhort (freq. and class.; cf.: moneo, admoneo, suadeo).
Latin: Appellare ut alius aliquid faciat

examples.original: Tum alii alios hortari ut repeterent pugnam;
examples.translation: They then began to encourage each other to resume the fight;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sabinus suos hortatus cupientibus signum dat.
examples.translation: Sabinus exhorted his troops, and gave the signal which they longed for.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Iam omnibus locis ceditur nequiquam Sempronio consule obiurgante atque hortante.
examples.translation: There was no virtue either in his authority or in his dignity;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to move back, draw back; to take away, set aside, withdraw, remove (freq. and class.; syn.: amolior, repono, segrego).
Latin: ( ) Ab alicubi (aliquid) movere
Latin: (antiq.) Ab alicubi (aliquid) movere

examples.original: Non ira saltem, iuvenes, pietate remota Stabitis?
examples.translation: If duty be disregarded, will not rage at least make you stand your ground, ye soldiers?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ab amicitia Q. Pompei meo nomine se removerat, ut scitis, Scipio;
examples.translation: Scipio, as you both know, had severed his friendship with Quintus Pompeius on my account;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque declamationes istas de medio removeamus: ”Non est animus in sua potestate ebrietate devinctus.
examples.translation: So let us abolish all such harangues as this: ”No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: former, previous
Latin: Primus duorum; maturior

examples.original: Prior aliquanto Volumnius castra cepit;
examples.translation: Volumnius succeeded somewhat sooner in capturing the camp.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ceterum et prioribus civium bellis par scelus inciderat.
examples.translation: And yet a similar crime had happened in civil war before.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Tenetur in priore animali, in aliud animal transire ei non licet;
examples.translation: The soul is kept within the first-named being, and cannot cross over into another;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: come forth (class.).

examples.original: Reliqui se in castra recipiunt unde erant egressi.
examples.translation: The remainder retired to the camp from which they had marched out.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Tum pudore victus miles segniter arma capit, segniter e castris egreditur longo agmine nec continenti;
examples.translation: Then the soldiers began, for very shame, to arm, and slowly emerged from the stockade;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Adventus eius compressit Etruscos adeo ut nemo extra munimenta egredi auderet timorque ipsorum obsidioni similis esset.
examples.translation: His arrival so damped the ardour of the Etruscans that none ventured outside their fortifications, and their own fear was like a besieging host.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: of or belonging to a soldier, to war, or to military service, proper to or usual with soldiers, military, warlike, martial (class.)
Latin: Qui ad militem vel bellum pertinet
Latin: Homo militaris

examples.original: Atqui vivere, Lucili, militare est.
examples.translation: And yet life, Lucilius, is really a battle.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic omnem militarem disciplinam artemque bellandi condidit.
examples.translation: It was he who founded all military discipline and the art of warfare.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Multum cum in omnibus rebus tum in re militari potest fortuna.
examples.translation: In everything, and especially in warfare, great is the power of fortune.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To hold forth, offer, promise any thing

examples.original: Pollicitis dives quilibet esse potest.
examples.translation: In promises anyone can be rich.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Navium magnam copiam ad transportandum exercitum pollicebantur.
examples.translation: They promised a large supply of boats for the transport of his army.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Id si feceris, et Spartam et ceteram Graeciam sub tuam potestatem se adiuvante te redacturum pollicetur.
examples.translation: If you do so, he guarantees that with your help he will bring Sparta and all Greece under your sway.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: to write together, i. e.

examples.original: Gesta conscripta sunt, nostrae etiam subscriptiones tenentur.
examples.translation: The minutes were written down; further, our signatures are on record.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ad haec cum inflammarentur animi, ut ad quosque ventum erat, numerus iuniorum conscribebatur.
examples.translation: These words aroused indignation, and a number of young men were enlisted wherever the envoys went.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nihil ad Caudium, patres conscripti, humanis consiliis gestum est: di immortales et vestris et hostium imperatoribus mentem ademerunt.
examples.translation: There was nothing done at Caudium, Conscript Fathers, by man’s wisdom: the immortal gods deprived of understanding both your commanders and the enemy’s.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: especially, chiefly, principally, particularly

examples.original: Cuius tu tribus venditorem, et corruptorem, et sequestrem Plancium fuisse clamitas, eam tribum profecto, severissimorum praesertim hominum et gravissimorum, edere debuisti.
examples.translation: It was what we expected, and what would have been in keeping with your high principles.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to jut forth, project.

examples.original: Sol me invitabat, fames ad monebat, nubes minabantur;
examples.translation: The sunlight called to me, hunger warned, and clouds were lowering;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec raptis aut spes de se melior aut indignatio est minor.
examples.translation: The stolen maidens were no more hopeful of their plight, nor less indignant.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ac primo quidem omnibus illis iudicibus, qui Oppianicum condemnarant, minabatur.
examples.translation: Now you had cause to know the fellow’s insolence;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to cause to eat, to feed, pasture.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; pāvi, pastum, 3

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Facile est pascere paucos ventres et bene institutos et nihil aliud desiderantes quam inpleri.
examples.translation: It is easy to fill a few stomachs, when they are well trained and crave nothing else but to be filled.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vaesanus in ortus Cambyses longi populos pervenit ad aevi, Defectusque epulis et pastus caede suorum Ignoto te, Nile, redit.
examples.translation: The madman Cambyses penetrated the East as far as the land of the long-lived people; food ran short, and he had to feed on his own men;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: near, neighboring, in the neighborhood or vicinity.

examples.original: Etruria erat vicina, proximi Etruscorum Veientes.
examples.translation: Etruria was close by, and the nearest of the Etruscans were the Veientes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fertilior seges est alienis semper in agris, Vicinumque pecus grandius uber habet.
examples.translation: In fields not ours the crops are ever more bounteous, and the neighbouring herd has richer udders.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Caesar, ut inmensae conlecto robore vires Audendi maiora fidem fecere, per omnem Spargitur Italiam vicinaque moenia conplet.
examples.translation: When Caesar’s might was gathered together and his huge forces encouraged him to larger enterprise, he spread all over Italy and occupied the nearest towns.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a. [1. in-gradior]

examples.original: Is Valentem comiter exceptum, ne Galliam Narbonensem temere ingrederetur, monendo terruit;
examples.translation: He received Valens kindly, and persuaded him by his advice not to risk entering Narbonese Gaul.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Alteri consuli Aemilio ingresso Sabellum agrum non castra Samnitium, non legiones usquam oppositae.
examples.translation: The other consul, Aemilius, having entered the Sabellian territory, nowhere encountered a Samnite camp or levies.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec Pompei ab Italia quam senatus ab urbe fuga turpior: quam paene vacuam, metu Caesar ingressus consulem se ipse fecit.
examples.translation: Caesar on his entrance into Rome found it almost deserted owing to the fear which he inspired, and made himself consul.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: lightning that strikes or sets on fire, a thunderbolt (opp. fulgur, lightning).

examples.original: Thrasymennus lacus, tertium fulmen Annibalis, imperatore Flaminio.
examples.translation: Hannibal’s third thunderbolt was launched at Lake Trasimene, where Flaminius commanded the Romans.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Perfidus ille quidem, qui talia pignora servat, Sed tamen Aetnaei fulminis instar habent.
examples.translation: Perfidious indeed is he who keeps such pledges, but they hold what is like a thunderbolt of Aetna.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Dumque illi effusam longis anfractibus urbem Circumeunt, Arruns dispersos fulminis ignes Colligit et terrae maesto cum murmure condit Datque locis numen;
examples.translation: While the long procession winds its way round the wide city, Arruns collects the scattered fires of the thunderbolt and hides them in the earth with doleful muttering.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to show, point out, to indicate, intimate, inform, advise, teach, instruct, tell any thing
Latin: Significare, facere ut alius videat aliquid

examples.original: Monstras mihi, qui sint modi flebiles;
examples.translation: You are showing me what the doleful keysb are;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pueritia ac iuventa, qualem monstravimus.
examples.translation: His boyhood and youth were such as we have already described.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quomodo hoc fiat, sapientia sola monstrabit.
examples.translation: And wisdom alone can show you how this may be done.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: unequal.

examples.original: Securitatis magna portio est nihil inique facere.
examples.translation: The most important contribution to peace of mind is never to do wrong.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Consul, ubi ad iniquum locum ventum est, sistit aciem.
examples.translation: The consul ordered a halt when his army reached rising ground.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: A, quotiens vaccam vultu spectavit iniquo, Et dixit ”domino cur placet ista meo?
examples.translation: Ah, how oft did she look askance upon a cow, and say, ”Why does she find favour with my lord?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a being eloquent, eloquence

examples.original: Docuit autem et rhetoricam, ita ut quotidie praecepta eloquentiae traderet, declamaret vero nonnisi nundinis.
examples.translation: He taught rhetoric too, giving daily instruction in speaking, but declaiming only once a week.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Fuit etiam disertus ut nemo ei Thebanus par esset eloquentia, neque minus concinnus in brevitate respondendi quam in perpetua oratione ornatus.
examples.translation: Epaminondas was also so good a speaker that no Theban equalled him in eloquence, and he was not less clever in brief answers than brilliant in a set speech.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

examples.original: Neque enim tantum arte et scientia, sed longe magis facultate et <usu> eloquentiam contineri, nec tu, puto, abnues et hi significare vultu videntur.”
examples.translation: To this view I am sure you will not demur, and our friends here, to judge by their looks, seem to indicate concurrence.”
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: mown, *
Latin: Excīdere, excīdendo elaborare
Latin: In partes dividere

examples.original: (quo quidem concesso, nihil opus est secundo;
examples.translation: (and if this be granted there is no need of the minor;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hos secuti M. Genucius et C. Curtius consules.
examples.translation: It was a year of quarrels both at home and abroad.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nimius honos inter secunda rebus adversis in solacium cessit.
examples.translation: These excessive honours in prosperity presently became a solace in misfortune.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: both
Latin: Hic et ille (ūnā simul)
Latin: → uterque

examples.original: Duos tamen cum eo pudor tenuit, Sp. Larcium ac T. Herminium, ambos claros genere factisque.
examples.translation: Yet were there two who were prevented by shame from leaving him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Consules ambo profecti sint ad arcem Carventanam, an alter ad comitia habenda substiterit, incertum diversi auctores faciunt;
examples.translation: The levy was then begun and preparation made for war, with the consent of all the orders.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huic rursus circumvento fert subsidium Pullo, atque ambo incolumes compluribus interfectis summa cum laude sese intra munitiones recipiunt.
examples.translation: He was surrounded in his turn, but Pullo brought assistance; and both, unhurt, though they had slain several men, retired with the utmost glory within the entrenchments.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: joining, connecting with something, or hanging together, in space or time, uninterrupted, continuous.

examples.original: Adicio dolores continuos et graves;
examples.translation: I add afflictions which are unceasing and severe;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dimisimus catechumenos continuoque scriptum subscripsit.
examples.translation: We dismissed the catechumensa and straightway he subscribed the statement.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Omnis oratio aut continua est aut inter respondentem et interrogantem discissa.
examples.translation: Now all speech is either continuous, or split up between questioner and answerer.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Cornelius, a Roman gens; a male member of that gens
Latin: Praenomen masculum
Latin: Qui ad Cornelium pertinet

examples.original: Cornelii Taciti Dialogus De Oratoribus 1.
examples.translation: Cornelius Tacitus A Dialogue on Oratory 1.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Dictatorem T. Quinctium Poenum eo anno fuisse satis constat et magistrum equitum Ser. Cornelium Maluginensem.
examples.translation: It is well established that Titus Quinctius Poenus was dictator that year and that Servius Cornelius Maluginensis was master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Dictator L. Furius Camillus dictus, addito magistro equitum P. Cornelio Scipione, reddidit patribus possessionem pristinam consulatus.
examples.translation: Lucius Furius Camillus was appointed to that office, and Publius Cornelius Scipio was made his master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: then/next/afterward; thereon/henceforth/from there/then; in next position/place

examples.original: Plerumque improborum facta primo suspicio insequitur, dein sermo atque fama, tum accusator, tum iudex;
examples.translation: The usual consequences of crime are, first suspicion, next gossip and rumour, then comes the accuser, then the judge;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vocato dein senatu cum ex auctoritate patrum iustitio indicto profectus ad tutandos fines esset Q. Servilio praefecto urbis relicto, hostem in agris non invenit.
examples.translation: After that he set out to defend the frontier, leaving Quintus Servilius as prefect of the City, but did not meet with the enemy in the field.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: fitted; hence

examples.original: Nam et in arte musica quod bonum est, facit musicum.
examples.translation: For example, that which is good in the art of music makes the musician.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aut velut Eurylochi, qui sceptrum cepit ab illo, Sint artus avidis anguibus esca tui.
examples.translation: Or like Eurylochus, who took the sceptre from him, may thy limbs be food for greedy snakes.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fraudem profecto in re esse, et A. Sempronium comitiis plus artis adhibuisse quam fidei.
examples.translation: It was by his wrong-doing, they complained, that their relations had been defeated for office.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: The chief magistrate of other cities of Italy

examples.original: Mamilius Tusculi tum dictator erat.
examples.translation: Lucius Mamilius was then dictator at Tusculum.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque se dictatorem L. Quinctium dicturum;
examples.translation: He would therefore name Lucius Quinctius dictator;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Magister equitum dictatori additus Q. Servilius.
examples.translation: Quintus Servilius was assigned to the dictator as master of the horse.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to be of opinion, to suppose, imagine, conjecture, deem, believe, think, judge (freq. and class.; syn.: arbitror, reor, censeo, sentio, credo); constr. with

examples.original: Non, opinor, tam impudens esses.
examples.translation: I do not believe you would have the effrontery.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam avunculus maior Augustus quid de eo in utramque partem opinatus sit, quo certius cognoscatur, capita ex ipsius epistulis posui.
examples.translation: Finally to make it clearer what opinions, favourable and otherwise, his great uncle Augustus had of him, I have appended extracts from his own letters: IV.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Cum de mea dignitate in templo Iovis optimi maximi senatus frequentissimus, uno isto dissentiente, decrevisset, subito illo ipso die carissimam annonam nec opinata vilitas consecuta est.
examples.translation: And yet, with his whole mind bent on slaughter, he had proclaimed my name to his partisans, and openly hinted it to the ignorant mob.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Of or belonging to servants

examples.original: Facete M. Piso familiaris noster et alia multa et hoc loco Stoicos irridebat.
examples.translation: Our friend Marcus Piso was often witty, but never more so than when he ridiculed the Stoics on this score.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mnesarchum, Panaetium, multos alios, in primisque familiarem nostrum Posidonium.
examples.translation: Mnesarchus, Panaetius, and many others, not least our friend Posidonius.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ista tua pulcra Libertas deos penates et familiares meos lares expulit, ut se ipsa tamquam in captivis sedibus collocaret?
examples.translation: Did your darling Liberty drive out my household gods and the spirits of my family, that she might establish herself in what was virtually a captive’s dwelling?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to look back or behind, to look about, look; to see behind one; to look back upon, to look at, look to or for any thing (very freq. and class.).

examples.original: Nam voluptas non est digna, ad quam respiciat.
examples.translation: For pleasure does not deserve that virtue should even glance at it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et movet ipse suas, et nati respicit alas Daedalus, et cursus sustinet usque suos.
examples.translation: Daedalus, while he plies his own, looks back at his son’s wings, and ever keeps on his own course.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Respice Phylaciden et quae comes isse marito Fertur et ante annos occubuisse suos.
examples.translation: Consider Phylacides and her who is said to have accompanied her spouse, and to have died before her time.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a flowing, waving.

examples.original: Cruor altus in unda Spumat, et obducti concreto sanguine fluctus.
examples.translation: Their blood foamed deep upon the wave, and a crust of gore covered the sea.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Si saecula prima Victoris timuere minas, nunc excipe saltem Ossa tui Magni, si nondum subruta fluctu Invisa tellure sedent.
examples.translation: Who will fear to trouble the tomb, and dread to remove the dead so worthy of worship?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Est quoque uti possit magnus congestus harenae fluctibus adversis oppilare ostia contra, cum mare permotum ventis ruit intus harenam;
examples.translation: It is possible also that a great collection of sand blocks up the mouth against the stream, when the sea, stirred by the winds, rolls the sand inwards;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: To take hold of, hold

examples.original: Non obtinebis, ut desinat, si incipere permiseris.
examples.translation: If you allow it to begin, you cannot make sure of its ceasing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed difficilius est provincias obtinere quam facere;
examples.translation: But it is more difficult to retain than to create provinces;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quod si nihil aliud esset actum nisi ut hanc causam obtineremus, lege recitata perorassem.
examples.translation: But had our only concern been to get a verdict, I should have read the statute aloud and then sat down.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a priest; a priestess
Latin: Minister divinus

examples.original: In ea provincia legatus fuit C. Sacerdos: qua virtute, qua constantia vir!
examples.translation: You know the uprightness and strength of character of Gaius Sacerdos;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Huic eidem Sopatro idem inimici ad C. Verrem, cum is Sacerdoti successisset, eiusdem rei nomen detulerunt.
examples.translation: When Verres succeeded Sacerdos, this same Sopater was prosecuted before him by these same enemies again on the same charge.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nisi enim id faceret, cur Plato Aegyptum peragravit ut a sacerdotibus barbaris numeros et caelestia acciperet?
examples.translation: Were it not so, why did Plato travel through Egypt to learn arithmetic and astronomy from barbarian priests?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to the farther side, beyond, on the other side.

examples.original: Qui se ultro morti offerant facilius reperiuntur quam qui dolorem patienter ferant.
examples.translation: It is easier to find men to fling themselves recklessly on death than men to endure pain patiently.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed ubi fortuna contra fuit, non laxare ordines, non recipere turbatos, non obviam ire ultroque adgredi hostem tantum per spatium cursu et pugnando fessum.
examples.translation: But when fortune opposed them, they did not open out their lines, receive the fugitives, or advance and take the initiative in attacking their opponents, who were exhausted with their long advance and with fighting.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Equites Romani obtulere operam pecuniasque, etiam libertinis idem munus ultro flagitantibus.
examples.translation: This pretended devotion, which was in reality prompted by fear, resulted in enthusiasm for the emperor;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to take off, take away, to withdraw, subtract, remove (class. and very freq.; for syn. cf.: adimo, eripio, furor, rapio, prehendo, capio, sumo, excipio).

examples.original: Quae ista dementia est malum suum antecedere?
examples.translation: What madness it is to anticipate one’s troubles!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid ex his metum demit, cupiditatem eximit, libidinem frenat? .
examples.translation: The question is: do such men teach virtue, or not?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At ille post non multo sua sponte ad exercitum rediit et ibi non callida, sed dementi ratione cogitata patefecit;
examples.translation: But not long afterwards Pausanias returned to the army on his own account, and there he revealed his designs in a manner that was rather insane than adroit.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: a leek, scallion; of two kinds, capitatum and sectile, the latter our chives

examples.original: Nullum porro inter divina discrimen est;
examples.translation: And furthermore, there is no distinction between things divine;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tum porro si nil esset quod inane vacaret, omne foret solidum;
examples.translation: Then further, if there were nothing void and empty, the universe would be solid;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Quidquid porro animo cernimus, id omne oritur a sensibus; qui si omnes veri erunt, ut Epicuri ratio docet, tum denique poterit aliquid cognosci et percipi.
examples.translation: Further, every mental presentation has its origin in sensation: so that no certain knowledge will be possible, unless all sensations are true, as the theory of Epicurus teaches that they are.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that with which any thing is bound, a band, bond, rope, cord, fetter

examples.original: Verginius arripi iubet hominem et in vincula duci.
examples.translation: Verginius gave orders to seize the fellow and throw him into prison.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Victum eo die ob impotentem iniuriam unius ingens vinculum fidei;
examples.translation: The consuls were forced by the sudden tumult to convene the senate;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Lateque cladem intulisset ni duo milites praeclarum facinus ausi, arreptis e strage scutis ignorati, vincla ac libramenta tormentorum abscidissent.
examples.translation: They were at once run through and thus their names were lost; but there is no doubt about their deed.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: make, form, configuration, figure, shape.

examples.original: Idea erat Vergilii facies, futuri operis exemplar.
examples.translation: The ”idea” was Vergil’s outward appearance, and this was the pattern of the intended work.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cura dabit faciem; facies neglecta peribit, Idaliae similis sit licet illa deae.
examples.translation: Care will give good looks: looks neglected go to waste though they resemble the Idalian goddess.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Corpore et statura fuit grandi, aquilo colore, facie rusticana, valetudine varia;
examples.translation: He was tall and of full habit, with a dark complexion and a rustic appearance.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: the winter, winter time, rainy season (cf.: bruma, solstitium).
Latin: Unum ex duobus temporibus anni, qui ab 22. Septembris usque ad 22. Martii durat; opp. aestas
Latin: Unum ex quattuor temporibus anni, tres menses frigidissimi quorum tempus proprium varie dicitur inter nationes; saepissime, tempus inter bruma et aequinoctium vernale

examples.original: Saepe enim in hiemem revolvitur.
examples.translation: For it often slides back into winter weather.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Possem venire, si hiems non esset;
examples.translation: I might have come, had it not been winter;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Aberat tunc Caesar Ravennae dilectum agens, et hieme creverant Alpes: sic interclusum putabant iter.
examples.translation: Caesar was absent at the time holding a levy at Ravenna, and the Alps had been swollen by winter snows;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to kindle any thing above, so that it may burn downwards
Latin: Ignire; ardere facere
Latin: Illuminare

examples.original: Nos quoque et extinguimur et accendimur;
examples.translation: We mortals also are lighted and extinguished;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atrox ingenium accenderat eo facto magis quam conterruerat;
examples.translation: The man’s fierce nature was rather aroused by this than terrified;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec sua sponte agitata insuper tribuni plebis 11, 12accendunt.
examples.translation: This smouldering discontent was fanned into a blaze by the plebeian tribunes.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to put apart, to sunder, sever

examples.original: Quis posuit secretam in auro dapem?
examples.translation: Who uses gold plate when he dines alone?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid, nisi secretae laeserunt Phyllida silvae?
examples.translation: What, save the secret woods, were Phyllis’ bane?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Haruspices secreto ac sine testibus consuli vetuit.
examples.translation: He forbade anyone to consult soothsayers secretly and without witnesses.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a cheating, deceit, imposition, fraud
Latin: Quidquid ad fallendum fit aut dicitur, praecipue vero quum aliud promittitur, aliud praestatur

examples.original: Sic fraus proditorum irrita fuit.
examples.translation: Thus the deceit of the traitors proved fruitless.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Fraude Sex. Tarquini Gabi direpti.
examples.translation: Gabii sacked, in consequence of the fraud of Sextus Tarquinius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fraudem profecto in re esse, et A. Sempronium comitiis plus artis adhibuisse quam fidei.
examples.translation: It was by his wrong-doing, they complained, that their relations had been defeated for office.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: gerund.: EXDEICENDUM, S. C. de Bacchan.; imperat.

examples.original: Nepesinis inde edictum ut arma ponant, parcique iussum inermi: Etrusci pariter armati atque inermes caesi.
examples.translation: The Etruscans were put to death, whether armed or not. Of the Nepesini, too, those who were responsible for the surrender were executed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tu ipse ex Siciliensi edicto hoc sustulisti; voluisti, ex improviso si quae res nata esset, ex urbano edicto decernere.
examples.translation: You yourself removed the clause from your Sicilian edict, merely expressing your intention to apply the principles of your city edict to meet any unforeseen contingencies.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sub hanc pessimi exempli victoriam dilectus edicitur, paventibusque tribunis sine intercessione ulla consules rem peragunt.
examples.translation: But this time the commons were fairly roused to anger, more by the silence of the tribunes than by the consuls’ power.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a bull, bullock
Latin: Bos mas
Latin: signum zodiacum

examples.original: Taurus paucissimorum iugerum pascuo impletur;
examples.translation: The bull is filled when he feeds over a few acres;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hac delatus in Ciliciam, egressus inde, dies noctesque iter faciens Taurum transit eoque quo studuerat venit.
examples.translation: Sailing to Cilicia and disembarking there, Datames marched day and night, crossed the Taurus, and arrived at his destination.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

definitions: English: to not heed, not trouble one's self about, not attend to, to slight, neglect, be regardless of, indifferent to; constr. with

examples.original: Et neglecta decet multas coma;
examples.translation: Even neglected hair is becoming to many;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fabianus non erat neglegens in oratione, sed securus.
examples.translation: Fabianus’s style was not careless, it was assured.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Anxur in Volscis brevi receptum est neglectis die festo custodiis urbis.
examples.translation: Anxur of the Volsci was speedily recaptured, a holiday having relaxed the vigilance of their guard.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: absent; away
Latin: Qui separatus est a loco
Latin: Mortuus

examples.original: Penelopen absens sollers torquebat Ulixes;
examples.translation: In the absence of crafty Ulysses was Penelope racked;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Utrique, absente Caesare coniuratione facta, invasere legatos.
examples.translation: Caesar ordered that the forests should be burnt.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Natus ut Althaeae flammis absentibus arsit, Sic tuus ardescat stipitis igne rogus.
examples.translation: As absent flames consumed Althaea’s son, so may a firebrand kindle thy funeral pile.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: unworthy, undeserving (class.).

examples.original: Id primo acerbum indignumque Veientibus est visum;
examples.translation: At first the Veientes bitterly resented this;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Neque tamen quicquam fecit quod fide sua esset indignum.
examples.translation: Yet he did nothing to stain his honour;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: Caesaris illud opus, voti pars altera vestri, Occidit: indignas, Livia, solve comas.
examples.translation: That achievement of Caesar, the one half of your hopes, has perished: undo, Livia, thy undeserving locks.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Of gold, golden
Latin: Ex auro factus
Latin: qui est coloris aurei

examples.original: Non faciunt meliorem equum aurei freni.
examples.translation: A golden bit does not make a better horse.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Coronam auream Iovi donum in Capitolium mittunt.
examples.translation: They sent a golden crown as a gift to the Capitoline Jupiter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: His vaginae argenteae, baltea argentea: auratae vaginae, aurea baltea illis erant, et equorum inaurata tapeta.
examples.translation: The latter had silver sheaths and silver baldrics: the former gilded sheaths and golden baldrics, and their horses had gold-embroidered saddle-cloths.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a garland, chaplet, wreath.

examples.original: Fabius Vibulanus corona primum vallum defendit;
examples.translation: Fabius Vibulanus first manned the rampart with a cordon of defenders;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Coronam auream Iovi donum in Capitolium mittunt.
examples.translation: They sent a golden crown as a gift to the Capitoline Jupiter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huc inclinavit Antonius cingique vallum corona iussit.
examples.translation: Antonius inclined to meet his troops’ desires and ordered the investment of the enemy’s camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: in what manner
Latin: quomodo (adverbium interrogativum)''

examples.original: Quomodo hoc fiat, sapientia sola monstrabit.
examples.translation: And wisdom alone can show you how this may be done.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam aut Callipho aut Diodorus quomodo poterunt tibi istud concedere, qui ad honestatem aliud adiungunt, quod ex eodem genere non sit?
examples.translation: Or how will Callipho or Diodorus be able to grant your premise, who combine with Moral Worth another factor belonging to an entirely different category?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quomodo solitudinis odium est et adpetitio societatis, quomodo hominem homini natura conciliat, sic inest huic quoque rei stimulus, qui nos amicitiarum adpetentes faciat.
examples.translation: As we hate solitude and crave society, as nature draws men to each other, so in this matter also there is an attraction which makes us desirous of friendship.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to put something in violent motion, to move; both of removing from a place and backwards and forwards in a place; to shake, stir (freq. in every period and species of composition).
Latin: Idem quod movere, vel potius simul aut valde moveo
Latin: animum afficere et perturbare, incitare, agitare

examples.original: Ad rem commoveantur, non ad verba conposita;
examples.translation: But let them be roused to the matter, and not to the style;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sese tamen et amore fraterno et existimatione vulgi commoveri.
examples.translation: For all that, I feel the force of brotherly love and public opinion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et ais, si una littera commota sit, fore tota ut labet disciplina.
examples.translation: And you aver that if a single letter be altered, the whole system will totter.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to press or squeeze out, to force out (class.).

examples.original: Ruborem sibi exprimere non possunt;
examples.translation: They cannot, however, muster a blush;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae causa in speculo imagines exprimat, sciet sapiens;
examples.translation: The wise man will know what causes the reflection in a mirror;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic infantibus quoque animalibusque principalis partis suae sensus est non satis dilucidus nec expressus.
examples.translation: Thus even children and animals have a consciousness of their primary element, but it is not very clearly outlined or portrayed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a spade.

examples.original: Quid tamen hoc prodest, media si luce palamque Verberor et tutae non licet esse nuci?
examples.translation: Yet what does this avail, if openly in broad day I am beaten, and if a nut tree may not be safe?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Qui sunt homines a Q. Metello fratre tuo consule in senatu palam nominati, a quibus ille se lapidibus appetitum, etiam percussum esse dixit?
examples.translation: Who are the men whom the consul Quintus Metellus, your cousin, publicly named in the senate as having stoned, and even stabbed him?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ea posteaquam numerata est, contentus hac iniquitate non fuit; palam de sella ac tribunali pronuntiat si quis absentem sthenium rei capitalis reum facere vellet, sese eius nomen recepturum;
examples.translation: From his chair of office on the tribunal he announced publicly that if anyone should think fit to prosecute Sthenius in absence on a capital charge, permission to prosecute would be granted;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Foreseeing, foreknowing (very rare); constr. with an objective clause, or

examples.original: Hoc prudentem virum non decet;
examples.translation: This quality does not befit a man of sense;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Veneranda enim sunt iustitia, pietas, fides, fortitudo, prudentia;
examples.translation: For reverence is due to justice, duty, loyalty, bravery, and prudence;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Turpissimum autem est in homine prudente remedium maeroris lassitudo maerendi.
examples.translation: I should prefer you to abandon grief, rather than have grief abandon you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: haughty, proud, arrogant, insolent, discourteous, uncivil, rude, supercilious, domineering (cf.: arrogans, insolens, fastidiosus, vanus, elatus): reges odisse superbos, Poët. ap.
Latin: Superbia exhibens; arrogans, insolens

examples.original: Tarquinius Superbus occiso Tullio regnum invasit.
examples.translation: Tarquinius Superbus slew Tullius and seized the kingship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quis autem est qui Tarquinium Superbum, qui Sp. Cassium, Sp. Maelium non oderit?
examples.translation: On the other hand, is there anyone who does not hate Tarquin the Proud, Spurius Cassius, or Spurius Maelius?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Postremo Superbi illius inportuna dominatio non nihil, immo vel plurimum profuit.
examples.translation: Finally, the outrageous tyranny of Tarquinius Superbus was of some, nay, of great service;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: A mask, esp. that used by players, which covered the whole head, and was varied according to the different characters to be represented (syn. larva)

examples.original: In omnes personas hic exardescit affectus;
examples.translation: But indeed this emotion blazes out against all sorts of persons;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vide utrum in ipsum Caecilianum, de cuius persona praeiudicare conabantur ecclesiae, aliquid mali probare potuerint.
examples.translation: Notice whether they have succeeded in proving any evil against Caecilian himself, from whose person they attempted to compromise the Church;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Nec excusatur offensa necessitudine officii aut fide advocationis aut fortuitae et subitae dictionis impetu: meditatus videris \[aut\] elegisse personam notabilem et cum auctoritate dicturam.
examples.translation: And the offence you give cannot be held excused by the obligation to render a friendly service, or by loyalty to a client, or by the excitement of an unpremeditated utterance, made off-hand;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to make firm, establish, strengthen, confirm (class., esp. in prose).

examples.original: Nec diu exempla, quibus confirmeris, colligenda sunt;
examples.translation: And you need not spend a long time in gathering illustrations which will strengthen you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ea fama et confirmata et aucta est, ut primum urbem introiit.
examples.translation: This reputation was confirmed and even augmented immediately on his arrival in the city.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Polyperchontem misit, qui ab eo peterent ut sua decreta confirmaret.
examples.translation: Phocion sent envoys to Polyperchon, to beg him to confirm their decrees.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Phocion

definitions: English: dark, darksome, dusky, shady, obscure (class.).
Latin: Luce carens, sine luce
Latin: Abditus

examples.original: Rem videlicet difficilem et obscuram!
examples.translation: As though it were a difficult or recondite notion!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non erat obscurum quid homo improbus ac nefarius cogitaret;
examples.translation: The rascal’s immoral plan was not obscure;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mulciber obscuros lectum circaque superque Disponit laqueos: lumina fallit opus.
examples.translation: Mulciber disposes hidden snares around and above the couch; the device baffles the eye.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English:  redupl. concucurrit

examples.original: Cum hoc concurrit ipse Eumenes.
examples.translation: With the latter Eumenes fought hand to hand.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Et plebis concursus ingens fuit;
examples.translation: The plebeians too were gathered in great numbers;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non erat armatis aequum concurrere nudas;
examples.translation: It were not just that defenceless maids should fight with armed men;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to divide or proportion duly, mingle in due proportion; to combine or compound properly; to qualify, temper, etc. (class.; cf.: modifico, misceo).

examples.original: Vix temperavere animis quin extemplo impetum facerent;
examples.translation: They could hardly curb an impulse to assail them on the instant;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec magis post proelium quam in proelio caedibus temperatum est;
examples.translation: After the battle, as well as during its progress, no quarter was given.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Age vero, ceteris in rebus qua ille sit temperantia, considerate.
examples.translation: And further, consider the moderation which he displays in other ways as well.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the bank of a stream

examples.original: Cura ripae Hordeonio Flacco permissa;
examples.translation: The duty of guarding the Rhine he assigned to Hordeonius Flaccus.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Misso igitur Lentulo ultra ulteriorem perpulit ripam;
examples.translation: He, therefore, sent Lentulus and pushed them beyond the further bank of the river;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Erat inter Labienum atque hostem difficili transitu flumen ripisque praeruptis.
examples.translation: Between Labienus and the enemy was a steep-banked river, difficult to cross.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: grown or become great, great
Latin: Magnus caelum versus
Latin: De mare vel foramine vel cavo magnus deorsum

examples.original: Portis fores altioresque turres imposuit.
examples.translation: At the gateways he set doors and higher turrets.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Colle tumet modico lenique excrevit in altum Pingue solum tumulo;
examples.translation: The fertile land rises in a hill of moderate height and ascends with easy slope;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Sed hoc, quod liquet, firmandum et altius cotidiana meditatione figendum est;
examples.translation: This idea, however, clear though it is, must be strengthened and implanted more deeply by daily reflection;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Turned toward one or lying before one's eyes; hence

examples.original: Numerate saltem quot ipsi sitis, quot adversarios habeatis.
examples.translation: At least count up your numbers and the number of your adversaries.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quod si animo strenuo fecissent, futurum ut adversarii non possent resistere, cum et intra vallum et foris caederentur.
examples.translation: If they would act vigorously, the enemy would be unable to resist, since they would be assailed inside and outside of their intrenchments.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: Et tamen vehementer cum adversario dimicans saepe ab eo vulnera accipio, cum delectationem oblatae laudis mihi auferre non possum.
examples.translation: Yet, strenuously as I struggle with the adversary, I often receive wounds from him, since I cannot rid myself of delight in the praise that is offered me.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a family name in the gens Claudia, whose most famous member was the emperor C. Claudius Nero

examples.original: Et Nero quoque vos destituit, non vos Neronem.
examples.translation: It was Nero, too, who deserted you, not you Nero.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nero I. Ex gente Domitia duae familiae claruerunt, Calvinorum et Ahenobarborum.
examples.translation: Nero Nero I. Of the Domitian family two branches have acquired distinction, the Calvini and the Ahenobarbi.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec multo post diem obiit, utroque liberorum superstite, Tiberio Drusoque Neronibus.
examples.translation: Not long afterward he died, survived by both his sons, Tiberius Nero and Drusus Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: medicine
Latin: Ars medici
Latin: Officina medici

examples.original: Temporis ars medicina fere est: data tempore prosunt, Et data non apto tempore vina nocent.
examples.translation: The art of being timely is almost a medicine: wine timely given helps, untimely, harms.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Et quoniam mentem sanari, corpus ut aegrum, cernimus et flecti medicina posse videmus, id quoque praesagit mortalem vivere mentem.
examples.translation: And since we see that the mind, like a sick body, can be healed and changed by medicine, this also foreshows that the mind has a mortal life.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Quomodo ista perplexa sunt, sic ex istis non singulares morbi nascuntur, sed inexplicabiles, diversi, multiformes, adversus quos et medicina armare se coepit multis generibus, multis observationibus.
examples.translation: And as the food itself is complicated, so the resulting diseases are complex, unaccountable, manifold, variegated; medicine has begun to campaign against them in many ways and by many rules of treatment.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to lessen, diminish, lower, reduce, weaken, abate, restrict (very freq. and class.)
Latin: Minorem reddere frangendo
Latin: Minorem reddere aliquid detrahendo
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; ŭi, ūtum, 3

examples.original: Et adversus mortem tu tam minuta iacularis?
examples.translation: Are you, then, hurling petty weapons like yours even against death?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Graviora vectigalia aut abolevit aut minuit.
examples.translation: The more oppressive sources of revenue he either abolished or moderated.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Mortalia minuuntur, cadunt, deteruntur, crescunt, exhauriuntur, inplentur.
examples.translation: Mortal things decay, fall, are worn out, grow up, are exhausted, and replenished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to move gently along a smooth surface, to fall, slide; to slide, slip, or glide down, to fall down, to sink as the beginning of a fall; constr.
Latin: Actio laborandi
Latin: Quod laborando efficitur

examples.original: Quare enim qui labi coepit, alicubi subsistat?
examples.translation: For how, if one has begun to slip, can one stop at any particular place?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quantum aquarum per gradus cum fragore labentium!
examples.translation: And what masses of water that fall crashing from level to level!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Epicurus autem, in quibus sequitur Democritum, non fere labitur.
examples.translation: Epicurus for his part, where he follows Democritus, does not generally blunder.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the neck, including the back of the neck
Latin: Posterior colli pars ab occipitio ad dorsum, in qua sunt vertebrae et nervi caput sustinentes et moventes
Latin: de inanimis, quae partem aliquam cervicibus similem praeferunt

examples.original: Stulta est enim, mi Lucili, et minime conveniens litterato viro occupatio exercendi lacertos et dilatandi cervicem ac latera firmandi;
examples.translation: It is indeed foolish, my dear Lucilius, and very unsuitable for a cultivated man, to work hard over developing the muscles and broadening the shoulders and strengthening the lungs.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Statura fuit eminenti, colore expallido, corpore enormi, gracilitate maxima cervicis et crurum, oculis et temporibus concavis, fronte lata et torva, capillo raro at circa verticem nullo, hirsutus cetera.
examples.translation: His eyes and temples were hollow, his forehead broad and grim, his hair thin and entirely gone on the top of his head, though his body was hairy.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Fessa iacet cervix, fumant sudoribus artus, Oraque proiecta squalent arentia lingua, Pectora rauca gemunt, quae creber anhelitus urguet, Et defecta gravis longe trahit ilia pulsus, Siccaque sanguineis durescit spuma lupatis.
examples.translation: The weary neck sinks down, the limbs reek with sweat, the tongue protrudes and the mouth is rough and dry; the lungs, driven by quick pants, give a hoarse murmur;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to be in or upon.
Latin: In aliqua re esse aut versari

examples.original: Quippe L. Vitellio quamvis infami inerat industria, nec virtutibus, ut boni, sed quo modo pessimus quisque, vitiis valebat.
examples.translation: For all his infamous nature, Lucius Vitellius possessed industry, and drew strength not like good men from their virtues, but like the basest from his vices.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Haec est, inquam, societas, in qua omnia insunt, quae putant homines expetenda—honestas gloria tranquillitas animi atque iucunditas;
examples.translation: In such a partnership, I say, abide all things that men deem worthy of pursuit—honour and fame and delightful tranquillity of mind;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ego enim sic existimo, in summo imperatore quattuor has res inesse oportere, scientiam rei militaris, virtutem, auctoritatem, felicitatem.
examples.translation: For I consider that a perfect general must possess four attributes—knowledge of warfare, ability, prestige, and luck.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to take or lay hold of, to take to one's self, to take in, take, receive, etc. (class. in prose and poetry).
Latin: ad pauca verba summatim reducere

examples.original: Tota illi aetas aut in armis est exacta civilibus aut in toga concipiente iam civile bellum.
examples.translation: His whole life was passed either in civil warfare, or under a political regime which was soon to breed civil war.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam et creditur illi et, cum creditum est, magnos animus spiritus concipit ac fiducia impletur.
examples.translation: For men believe it, and when belief is established, the soul receives great inspiration and is filled with confidence.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illi statim ante aciem inmolato equo concepere votum, ut caesorum extis ducum et litarent et vescerentur.
examples.translation: I can well believe that the gods heard their boast, for they would not even endure the sound of our trumpets.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to entwine around a person or thing (cf. amplector; class. in prose and poetry).
