examples.original: Quid ergo illa laudata et omnibus praeferenda artibus rebusque philosophia praestabit?
examples.translation: The favour of ignoble men can be won only by ignoble means.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: hunger (syn.: inedia, jejunium, esuries, esuritio).

examples.original: Toleranda est enim ad hoc properantibus vel fames.
examples.translation: For when hastening after wisdom, we must endure even hunger.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ac nonnumquam horreis praeclusis populo famem indixit.
examples.translation: Sometimes too he would shut up the granaries and condemn the people to hunger.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Iam hoc non ignoratis, iudices, ut etiam bestiae fame monitae plerumque ad eum locum, ubi pastae sunt aliquando, revertantur.
examples.translation: Now you are not unaware, gentlemen, that even brute beasts, when prompted by hunger, generally return to the place where they have at some time previously found food.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To thrust through, pierce through, transfix

examples.original: Quis feret Andromaches peragentem Thaida partes?
examples.translation: Who could endure Thais playing Andromache’s part?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Peragit concilium Caesar equitesque imperat civitatibus.
examples.translation: Caesar closed the convention, and made requisition of cavalry upon the states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et uno proelio peractum erat bellum; iam enim urbem ipsam terrebat obsidio;
examples.translation: The war was thus finished by a single battle, and a siege already threatened the city itself;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: Egypt, sometimes reckoned by the ancients as belonging to Asia
Latin: Natio in Africa septentrionali cuius caput Cairus

examples.original: Nisi enim id faceret, cur Plato Aegyptum peragravit ut a sacerdotibus barbaris numeros et caelestia acciperet?
examples.translation: Were it not so, why did Plato travel through Egypt to learn arithmetic and astronomy from barbarian priests?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Is in maestitiam compositus et fidem suorum quondam militum invocans, ut eum in Syria aut Aegypto sisterent orabat.
examples.translation: The pretender, assuming a look of sorrow and calling on the soldiers, once his own, for protection, begged them to land him in Syria or Egypt.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Suscepto igitur civili bello ac ducibus copiisque in Italiam praemissis interim Alexandriam transiit, ut claustra Aegypti optineret.
examples.translation: Therefore beginning a civil war and sending ahead generals with troops to Italy, he crossed meanwhile to Alexandria, to take possession of the key to Egypt.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: sand

examples.original: Haec fiunt, dum vacat harena.
examples.translation: This sort of thing goes on while the arena is empty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Serpens, sitis, ardor harenae Dulcia virtuti;
examples.translation: Serpents, thirst, burning sand—all are welcomed by the brave;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cnosis in ignotis amens errabat harenis, Qua brevis aequoreis Dia feritur aquis.
examples.translation: The Cretan maid wandered distractedly on the unknown sand, where little Dia is lashed by the sea waves.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to push, drive, or strike against a thing; to strike, reach.

examples.original: Impulsa frons prima et trepidatio subsidiis inlata;
examples.translation: Their front was first driven in and communicated its disorder to the supports;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Postquam impulsos sensit Antonius, denso agmine obturbabat.
examples.translation: After Antonius saw that they were shaken, he assailed them in mass formation.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Illud in his rebus mirari mitte, quod aestus non valet e lapide hoc alias impellere item res.
examples.translation: In this connexion, you must not allow yourself to feel surprise that the current from this stone has not the power to propel other things also.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: to be empty, void, or vacant; to be void of, or without; not to contain (class.; cf.: careo, egeo).

examples.original: Non vaco ad istas ineptias;
examples.translation: I have no time for such nonsense;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nulla aetas vacavit a culpa.
examples.translation: No era in history has ever been free from blame.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec fiunt, dum vacat harena.
examples.translation: This sort of thing goes on while the arena is empty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: how many, as many, as: quot sunt?

examples.original: In quam angusto quodam quot gradus posuit!
examples.translation: How many steps for how short a climb!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quot oppida in Syria, quot in Macedonia devorata sunt?
examples.translation: How many towns in Syria, how many in Macedonia, have been swallowed up!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum aspexeris, quot te antecedant, cogita, quot sequantur.
examples.translation: When you see many ahead of you, think how many are behind!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hold back, hold fast, take hold of, seize, catch.

examples.original: Quis enim facile invenitur, qui velit reprehendi?
examples.translation: For who is easily found that is willing to endure reproof?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Sed alterum honestius dixerim vitium, alterum tutius: sic utrosque reprehendas, et eos qui semper inquieti sunt, et eos qui semper quiescunt.
examples.translation: In like manner you should rebuke these two kinds of men,—both those who always lack repose, and those who are always in repose.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Moleste enim fortasse tulerat se in eis orationibus reprehensum, quas de re publica habuisset, in quibus forsitan magis requiratur constantia.
examples.translation: For he may have been annoyed at being brought to book over speeches of public import in which consistency, perhaps, is more to be expected.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to look at, upon, or towards (syn.: adspicio, contemplor, specto).

examples.original: Aliter certe Claranum nostrum coepi intueri;
examples.translation: At any rate, I have begun to regard Claranus in a different light;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nobis solvi perire est, proxima enim intuemur;
examples.translation: To our minds, this process means perishing, for we behold only that which is nearest;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec potest quisquam beate degere, qui se tantum intuetur, qui omnia ad utilitates suas convertit;
examples.translation: And no one can live happily who has regard to himself alone and transforms everything into a question of his own utility;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to place here and there, to set in different places, to distribute regularly, to dispose, arrange (cf. dispenso, II.—freq. and class.).

examples.original: At Caesar dispositis in vallo custodibus recipi prohibebat.
examples.translation: But Caesar posted sentries on the rampart and prevented their admission.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quam stultum est aetatem disponere ne crastini quidem dominum!
examples.translation: O what madness it is to plot out far-reaching hopes!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is armata iuventute dispositisque praesidiis tuta omnia ac tranquilla fecit.
examples.translation: Arming the young men and disposing his defences, he made everything secure and tranquil.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to press, push, force, drive, impel, urge.

examples.original: Etiam atque etiam insto atque urgeo, insector, posco, atque adeo flagito crimen;
examples.translation: I demand that you shall produce your charges; nay, I importune you for them.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ita caesa ab tergo legio atque in medio, cum hostis undique urgeret, circumventa.
examples.translation: Thus the legion was attacked in the rear and found itself surrounded, with the enemy assailing it from every quarter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hic tibi versandus tenor est, cum libera dantur Otia, furtivum nec timor urget opus.
examples.translation: This is the tenor you must keep, when dallying is free, and no fear urges on the secret work.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to strip, to deprive of covering, rob of clothing.

examples.original: Spolia opima Feretrio Iovi lata.
examples.translation: Spolia opima dedicated to Jupiter Feretrius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tu, Caesar, quamvis spoliatus milite multo, Agnoscis superos;
examples.translation: Caesar, though robbed of many soldiers, recognised the hand of heaven.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Princeps Horatius ibat trigemina spolia prae se gerens;
examples.translation: In the van of the Romans came Horatius, displaying his triple spoils.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: poor, i. e. not wealthy, of small means, that has only enough for his moderate expenses (cf.: indigus, egenus, inops).—
Latin: Paucam pecuniam possidens

examples.original: Aut dives opto vivere aut pauper mori.
examples.translation: If riches bless me, I should love to live;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec omnia in dites a pauperibus inclinata onera. Deinde est honos additus;
examples.translation: All these burdens were shifted from the shoulders of the poor to those of the rich.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Si vis scire, quam nihil in illa mali sit, compara inter se pauperum et divitum vultus;
examples.translation: If you would know how little evil there is in poverty, compare the faces of the poor with those of the rich;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to watch, protect, keep, defend, guard (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Is armatos circa se in custodiam sui habuit.
examples.translation: He kept armed men about him to protect him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ingenti periculo transeundum per hostium custodias erat.
examples.translation: It was necessary at enormous risk to pass the enemy’s outposts.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mentior, nisi et quae alunt illum et quae valitudinem eius vel custodiunt vel restituunt, corpora sunt;
examples.translation: I am sadly astray if the elements which support man and preserve or restore his health, are not bodily;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to draw or bring several objects together, to collect, assemble (freq. and class.).
Latin: Trahendo simul adstringere, in angustum redigere
Latin: Plures personas vel res colligere, congregare

examples.original: Itaque copias contraxit, bellum adversus Antigonum comparavit.
examples.translation: Accordingly, he mustered his forces and prepared to make war upon Antigonus.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Tu tantum numero pugna, praeceptaque in unum Contrahe: de multis grandis acervus erit.
examples.translation: But since there are so many fashions and so many postures, trust not wholly to my counsels.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Dicimus et illa bona esse, quae a virtute profecta contractaque sunt, id est opera eius omnia;
examples.translation: This, moreover, is man’s only good, the only means by which he is made happy.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fearful, awful (for syn. cf.: saevus, atrox, ferox, crudelis, trux, furens, furiosus, immitis).

examples.original: At enim contagia belli Dira fugant.
examples.translation: They shall suffer for seeking peace;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec cruor emicuit solitus, sed volnere largo Diffusum rutilo dirum pro sanguine virus.
examples.translation: No red blood spouted forth from the gaping wound, but a slimy liquid, strange and dreadful, came out instead.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Deinde ”Catalepton” et ”Priapea” et ”Epigrammata” et ”Diras,” item ”Cirim” et ”Culicem,” cum esset annorum XVI.
examples.translation: Then he wrote the ”Catalepton,” ”Priapea,” ”Epigrams” and the ”Dirae,” as well as the ”Ciris” and the ”Culex,” when he was sixteen years old.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: to burn (class.).

examples.original: Tertium est genus eorum, qui uri appellantur.
examples.translation: A third species consists of the ure-oxen so-called.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Numquid ultra quicquam ulli timendum est quam ut uratur, quam ut pereat?
examples.translation: Is there a worse fate that any man may fear than being burned or being killed?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aspicis, ut prensos urant iuga prima iuvencos, Et nova velocem cingula laedat equum?
examples.translation: Do you see how the first yoke chafes the captured bullocks, how the new saddle hurts the flying steed?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: locat. Carthagini, like Tiburi, ruri, domi, etc.

examples.original: Multum fuit Carthaginem vincere, sed amplius mortem.
examples.translation: He therefore pierced his body with a sword;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Solacia fati Carthago Mariusque tulit, pariterque iacentes Ignovere deis.
examples.translation: Carthage and Marius both drew consolation for their destiny ;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Carthaginis.” Haec fuit illius viri non sine praesagio quodam fati inminentis prima confessio.
examples.translation: Carthage.” This was his first confession, fraught with foreknowledge of approaching failure.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to have royal power, to be king, to rule, reign
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Tullus magna gloria belli regnavit annos duos et triginta.
examples.translation: Tullus was greatly renowned in war and reigned thirty-two years.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Silvius deinde regnat, Ascanii filius, casu quodam in silvis natus.
examples.translation: Next Silvius reigned, son of Ascanius, born, as it chanced, in the forest.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ceterum id quoque ad gloriam accessit quod cum illo simul iusta ac legitima regna occiderunt.
examples.translation: But there was this to enhance his renown, that just and lawful kingship perished with him.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a star, a constellation

examples.original: Iam rarior aer Et par Phoebus aquis densas in vellera nubes Sparserat, et noctes ventura luce rubebant, Servatoque loco rerum discessit ab astris Umor, et ima petit, quidquid pendebat aquarum.
examples.translation: By this time the sky had cleared; the sun, a match for the waters, had broken up the thick clouds into fleeces;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: without reverence or respect for God, one's parents, or one's country; irreverent, ungodly, undutiful, unpatriotic; abandoned, wicked, impious

examples.original: Quis non impios recte iudicaret?
examples.translation: Who would not have been right in judging them inhuman?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Impia si nostros legisset Scylla libellos, Haesisset capiti purpura, Nise, tuo.
examples.translation: Had impious Scylla read my verse, the purple had stayed on thy head, O Nisus.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Verum haec ex comoedia quibus impiorum luxus et sacrilega superstitio convinceretur, proferre forsitan non debemus.
examples.translation: And yet perhaps I should not put forward these scenes from comedy to confute the wantonness and the sacrilegious superstition of the ungodly.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to forget; constr. with

examples.original: Quae autem natura suae primae institutionis oblita est?
examples.translation: What species ever forgot its own original constitution?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nec vero quemquam senem audivi oblitum, quo loco thesaurum obruisset.
examples.translation: I certainly never heard of any old man forgetting where he had hidden his money!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: An obliviscimur quanto opere in audiendo in legendoque moveamur cum pie, cum amice, cum magno animo aliquid factum cognoscimus?
examples.translation: Do we forget the strong emotion that we feel when we hear or read of some deed of piety, of friendship or of magnanimity?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a. [prob. from root men-, whence mens, memini, q. v. Original meaning, to invent; hence]
Latin: Veritatem (consilio) non dicere

examples.original: Verum in eo ipso homines impudentissime mentiuntur.
examples.translation: But actually the whole story is a bare-faced lie.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: O quando ille veniet dies, quo nemo in honorem tuum mentiatur!
examples.translation: O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie.
examples.translation: The evil joys of the mind,c his words are eloquent, but not strictly appropriate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Unpleasant, disagreeable (class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: Torquet ingratus se et macerat;
examples.translation: The ungrateful man tortures and torments himself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His rebus Eumenes permotus, satius duxit, si ita tulisset fortuna, perire bene meritis referentem gratiam quam ingratum vivere.
examples.translation: Deeply moved by these communications, Eumenes thought it better, if such were Fortune’s will, to lose his life in requiting kindnesses than save it by ingratitude.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Ingratus est, qui beneficium reddit sine usura.
examples.translation: A man is an ingrate if he repays a favour without interest.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to make sound, to heal, cure, restore to health (freq. and class.; syn.: curo, medeor, medico).
Latin: Morbo liberare, sanum facere

examples.original: Id tamen se celeriter maioribus commodis sanaturum.
examples.translation: However, he would speedily remedy it by greater advantages.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid tibi mentis erat, cum sic male sana lateres, Procri?
examples.translation: What were thy feelings, Procris, when thus frantic thou lurkedst there?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Illo sano ac valente oratio quoque robusta, fortis, virilis est;
examples.translation: When the soul is sound and strong, the style too is vigorous, energetic, manly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fruits of the earth (that may be enjoyed), produce of the fields, pulse, legumes (whereas fructus denotes chiefly tree-fruit, and frumentum halm-fruit, grain), sometimes also, in

examples.original: Sed qui ad voluptatem omnia referens vivit ut Gallonius, loquitur ut Frugi ille Piso, non audio, nec eum quod sentiat dicere existimo.
examples.translation: But I will not listen to one who makes pleasure the sole standard, when while living like Gallonius he talks like Piso the Thrifty; I refuse to believe in his sincerity.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Servus non incallidus et, ut res ipsa declaravit, frugi atque integer, sermonem Fabricii non est aspernatus: rem ad dominum detulit: Cleophantus autem cum Habito est collocutus.
examples.translation: The slave, who was no fool, but, as the event proved, honest and upright, did not reject Fabricius’s overtures, but reported the matter to his master, and Cleophantus talked it over with Habitus.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to cast or reckon up, to calculate a sum by going over its items; to estimate, compute
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: De qua paulo latius disputem.
examples.translation: Of which matter let me discuss more fully.
examples.author: Bede

examples.original: Haec disputamus attractis superciliis, fronte rugosa?
examples.translation: Is this what we discuss with contracted brow and wrinkled forehead?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Libenter haec coram cum Q. Catulo et Q. Hortensio, summis et clarissimis viris, disputarem;
examples.translation: I would gladly discuss the matter personally with eminent and distinguished men like Quintus Catulus and Quintus Hortensius;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: get into, to enter upon.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; vāsi, vāsum; 3

examples.original: Tarquinius Superbus occiso Tullio regnum invasit.
examples.translation: Tarquinius Superbus slew Tullius and seized the kingship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Trierarchi magno tumultu Vitellii imagines invadunt;
examples.translation: The trierarchs with loud shouts attacked the statues of Vitellius;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Utrique, absente Caesare coniuratione facta, invasere legatos.
examples.translation: Caesar ordered that the forests should be burnt.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to ride.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Omnis noster equitatus, omnis nobilitas interiit;
examples.translation: All our horsemen, all our chivalry is perished;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Item equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt.
examples.translation: The horsemen of Ariovistus halted at an equal distance.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Subito Labienus duabus portis omnem equitatum emittit;
examples.translation: Suddenly from two gates Labienus launched forth all his cavalry;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: troublesome, irksome, grievous, annoying

examples.original: Non est tamen molestus creditor;
examples.translation: And yet it is not a troublesome creditor;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cupiebam dissimulare me id moleste ferre;
examples.translation: I did my best to pretend that I felt no uneasiness myself;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Incitat et ficti tristis custodia servi, Et nimium duri cura molesta viri.
examples.translation: The surly guardianship of a pretended slave excites him, and the irksome vigilance of a husband too severe.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to throw across.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; jēci, jectum, 3

examples.original: Atilius Regulus cos. victis navali proelio Poenis in Africam traiecit.
examples.translation: Atilius Regulus the consul, having beaten the Carthaginians in a naval battle, crossed into Africa.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Latino Alba ortus, Alba Atys, Atye Capys, Capye Capetus, Capeto Tiberinus, qui in traiectu Albulae amnis submersus celebre ad posteros nomen flumini dedit.
examples.translation: This last king was drowned in crossing the River Albula, and gave the stream the name which has been current with later generations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In contione autem si loqueretur, si Hannibal ad portas venisset murumque iaculo traiecisset, negaret esse in malis capi, venire, interfici, patriam amittere?
examples.translation: Hannibal is at the gates and has flung a javelin over the city walls; could he say that captivity, enslavement, death, loss of country are no evils?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To be a witness, speak as witness, to bear witness, give evidence, depose, testify, attest any thing.

examples.original: Deos rerum omnium esse testes ait.
examples.translation: They maintain that the gods are witnesses of everything.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O te miserum, si contemnis hunc testem!
examples.translation: How wretched you are if you despise such a witness!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Testari vultis adtendere vos moverique magnitudine rerum?
examples.translation: You may do this at the proper time;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To hate (class.; cf.: detestor, abominor, aversor, abhorreo); constr. with

examples.original: Necesse est aut imiteris aut oderis.
examples.translation: You must either imitate or loathe the world.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: O superi, liceat terras odisse nocentes.
examples.translation: Ye gods, give us the power to curse the country that is guilty.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Odimus et maestas: Tecmessam diligat Aiax;
examples.translation: Melancholy women too I hate; let Ajax love Tecmessa;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a sword, brand.

examples.original: Cuius non militis ensem Agnoscam?
examples.translation: I shall know again the sword of every fighter;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec derat robur in enses Ire duci iuguloque pati vel pectore letum;
examples.translation: He lacked not the courage to confront the swords and offer throat or breast to the fatal blow;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Utque ferox Phalaris, lingua prius ense resecta More bovis Paphio clausus in aere gemas.
examples.translation: And like fierce Phalaris, thy tongue first severed with the sword, mayst thou bellow like an ox imprisoned in Paphian bronze.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: pleasant, agreeable, charming, fine, elegant, neat (esp. freq. in Plaut. and Ter.; in Cic. very rare).

examples.original: Kal. Dec. M. Aemilio Lepido iterum L. Munatio Planco conss. per bellum Philippense.
examples.translation: In fact it is so recorded both in the calendar and in the public gazette.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et subinde matre etiam relegata paene inops atque egens apud amitam Lepidam nutritus est sub duobus paedagogis saltatore atque tonsore.
examples.translation: Then his mother was banished too, and he was brought up at the house of his aunt Lepida almost in actual want, under two tutors, a dancer and a barber.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Haec scelera in Antonii Lepidique tabulis: Caesar percussoribus patris contentus fuit, ideo ne, si inulta fuisset, etiam iusta eius caedes haberetur.
examples.translation: Caesar contented himself with proscribing his father’s murderers, for fear lest his death might be considered to have been deserved if it had remained unavenged.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: longing eagerly for something (either lawful or unlawful), desirous, eager, earnest, greedy (diff. from avarus, q. v.).
Latin: Aliquid magnopere cupiens, cupidus

examples.original: Tam bibit hunc avide, quam bibit ante merum.
examples.translation: He drinks it as greedily as he drank undiluted wine before.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Stagna avidi texere soli laxaeque paludes Depositum, Fortuna, tuum;
examples.translation: Engulfing quicksands and spongy marshes hid the secret that Fortune had placed there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Me, quia nec noceo nec obuncis vindicor hamis, Missa petunt avida saxa proterva manu.
examples.translation: But I, because I harm not, nor am protected by hooked nails, am pelted by wanton stones flung by greedy hands.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: riches, wealth

examples.original: Quis sit divitiarum modus, quaeris?
examples.translation: Do you ask what is the proper limit to wealth?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qui eget divitiis, timet pro illis.
examples.translation: He who craves riches feels fear on their account.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hanc praecedentem causam divitiae habent;
examples.translation: It is this antecedent cause which inheres in riches;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: outward, external (class.).

examples.original: Iam illa externa parce tu quidem;
examples.translation: As for external goods, you were, it is true, cautious;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nullum terrorem externum, nullum periculum esse;
examples.translation: There was no fear of foreign foes, no danger;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Paci externae confestim continuatur discordia domi.
examples.translation: The foreign peace was immediately succeeded by quarrels at home.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to make empty or vacant, to leave untenanted or uninhabited, to desert.

examples.original: Non opus est vasto vulnere dividere praecordia;
examples.translation: If you would pierce your heart, a gaping wound is not necessary;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et ibi, quia hostis moenibus se tenebat, vastati agri sunt.
examples.translation: There, too, the enemy kept within his walls, and the Romans laid waste his fields.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ipse ad vastandos depopulandosque fines Ambiorigis proficiscitur;
examples.translation: He himself moved off to devastate and plunder the country of Ambiorix;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to raise up, elevate; only

examples.original: Recepit, implevit. Et adhuc manus excelsa.
examples.translation: He received it back, he fulfilled his vow.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Res enim gerebatur et excelso loco et in conspectu exercitus nostri, magnusque utrimque clamor oriebatur.
examples.translation: For the action went on at a considerable height and in sight of our army, and great shouting arose on both sides.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Iuno regina transvecta a Veiis nuper in Aventino quam insigni ob excellens matronarum studium celebrique dedicata est die!
examples.translation: Queen Juno was lately conveyed from Veii and enshrined on the Aventine, and how notable was that day, for the zeal of the matrons and the throng!
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: That has been ploughed, but not yet sown, ploughed, arable

examples.original: Nulli subigebant arva coloni, Ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum Fas erat;
examples.translation: No ploughman tilled the soil, nor was it right To portion off or bound one’s property.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec Libycos, pars tam flavos gerit altera crines, Ut nullis Caesar Rheni se dicat in arvis Tam rutilas vidisse comas;
examples.translation: Some had the hair of Africa, and others were so fair-headed that Caesar said he had never seen hair so red in the Rhine country;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Feta tibi occurrat patrio popularis in arvo, Sitque Phalaeceae causa leaena necis. Quique Lycurgiden letavit, et arbore natum, Idmonaque audacem, te quoque rumpat aper.
examples.translation: And may the boar that slew Lycurgus’ son, and him that was born of a tree, and courageous Idmon, tear thee too asunder.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: cold, coldness, coolness (for syn. cf.: algor, gelu, rigor, glacies, pruina).
English: a grandson, son's or daughter's son: primo gradu sunt supra pater, mater; infra filius, filia. Secundo gradu sunt supra avus, avia
Latin: Liberi filius
Latin: Fratris filius

examples.original: Cato excerptum e libro cornelii nepotis de latinis historicis 1.
examples.translation: Cato XXIV. Cato An Extract From The Book Of Cornelius Nepos On Latin Historians 1.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Cato

examples.original: Cum M. Valerio, Mani filio, Volesi nepote quaestor erat T. Quinctius Capitolinus, qui ter consul fuerat.
examples.translation: Marcus Valerius, son of Manius, and grandson of Volesus, shared the magistracy with Titus Quinctius Capitolinus, who had thrice been consul.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quare ab Augusto quoque nepotibus eius praeceptor electus, transiit in Palatium cum tota schola, verum ut ne quem amplius posthac discipulum reciperet;
examples.translation: He was therefore chosen by Augustus as the tutor of his grandsons and he moved to the Palace with his whole school, but with the understanding that he should admit no more pupils.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: even if, although, albeit.
Latin: Etiam si; particula concessiva condicionalis

examples.original: Verum ita est, uti dicis. Te deiectum debeo intelligere, etiamsi tactus non fueris.
examples.translation: But you are right—I am bound to consider you ejected even though you were not touched, am I not?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid autem est amare, e quo nomen ductum amicitiae est, nisi velle bonis aliquem affici quam maximis etiamsi ad se ex iis nihil redundet ?
examples.translation: What is the meaning of ’to love’—from which our word for friendship is derived—except to wish some one to receive the greatest possible benefits even though one gleans no advantage therefrom oneself?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Huic hereditas HS quingentorum milium venerat a muliere quadam propinqua, atque ita propinqua ut ea etiamsi intestata esset mortua Epicratem Bidinorum legibus heredem esse oporteret.
examples.translation: This man inherited £5000 from a female relative; so near a relative that, even had she died intestate, Epicrates would by the laws of Bidis have been her heir.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to make clean or

examples.original: Qua nos, si apud inimicos non possumus, saltem apud vos ratione purgamus?
examples.translation: If we cannot clear ourselves before our enemies, how at least shall we do so before you?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Si doceo non ab Habito, vinco ab Oppianico: si ostendo ab Oppianico, purgo Habitum.
examples.translation: If I demonstrate that it was used by Oppianicus, I clear Habitus.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mentis valitudinem et ipse senserat ac subinde de secessu deque purgando cerebro cogitavit.
examples.translation: He himself realised his mental infirmity, and thought at times of going into retirement and clearing his brain.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: flying, winged (class.; syn.: ales, volatilis).

examples.original: Ipse deum volucrem detinuisse paro.
examples.translation: I am planning to hold fast the winged god.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nihil est autem tam volucre, quam maledictum;
examples.translation: The inventions against my client have been multitudinous as their inventors;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam et signis insedit examen et adsuetae cadaverum pabulo volucres castra quasi iam sua circumvolabant, et in aciem prodeuntibus obvius Aethiops nimis aperte ferale signum fuit.
examples.translation: A swarm of bees settled on the standards; the birds which usually feed upon corpses flew round the camp, as though it were already their prey;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: The name of several Syrian kings, among whom Antiochus Magnus was most distinguished, on account of his war with the Romans

examples.original: Illi, desperatis rebus, cum solvissent naves ac vela ventis dedissent, Hannibal ad Antiochum pervenit.
examples.translation: Hannibal reached Antiochus; as to the death of Mago there are two accounts;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

definitions: English: an occasion, opportunity, fit time, convenient season, favorable moment for doing any thing

examples.original: Impetum illi dabit, occasiones actionum honestarum commonstrabit.
examples.translation: He can quicken his impulses, and point out to him opportunities for honourable action.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inest hoc tempore haud obscurum odium atque id insitum penitus et inustum animis hominum amplissimorum: dissident principes: captatur occasio.
examples.translation: At the present time hatred does more than merely rankle; it is engrained and inured in the souls of our proudest;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quorum adventu cum sibi Correus oblatam occasionem rei gerendae existimaret, primum cum paucis se ostendit atque in proximas turmas impetum fecit.
examples.translation: Their arrival led Correus to suppose that a chance of despatching the business was offered him;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To go into, to enter a place (class.).

examples.original: Eo anno—nec traditur causa—interregnum initum.
examples.translation: In this year—for no cause assigned—there befell an interregnum.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Aemilius et Opiter Verginius consulatum ineunt;
examples.translation: Lucius Aemilius and Opiter Verginius entered upon the consulship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Securitatis magna portio est nihil inique facere.
examples.translation: The most important contribution to peace of mind is never to do wrong.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a threshold; the head-piece or foot-piece of a doorway, the lintel or the sill (limen superum et inferum).

examples.original: Quid est turpius quam in ipso limine securitatis esse sollicitum?
examples.translation: But what is baser than to fret at the very threshold of peace?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: court, one of the thirty parts into which Romulus divided the Roman people, ten for each of the three tribes; each curia contained ten gentes, Varr. ap. Dion. Hal. 2, 83

examples.original: Ex curia in contionem itur.
examples.translation: Leaving the senate-house, they repaired to an assembly;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Venit in curiam tamen expeditionem Parthicam meditans.
examples.translation: Yet he came into the senate-house thinking of his campaign against Parthia.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Non est, mi Lucili, quod amicum tantum in foro et in curia quaeras;
examples.translation: You need not, my dear Lucilius, hunt for friends only in the forum or in the Senate-house;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: morally rude or unfeeling, with exclusive reference to conduct towards persons or things, hard, unmerciful, hard-hearted, cruel, severe, fierce

examples.original: Quid fieri crudelius vel miserius potest?
examples.translation: What could be more cruel or more wretched?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis acerbior, quis insidiosior, quis crudelior umquam fuit?
examples.translation: No one was ever more harsh and treacherous and brutal.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Haec cogitatio nihil sordidum animo subsidere sinit, nihil humile, nihil crudele.
examples.translation: Such thoughts permit nothing mean to settle in the soul, nothing low, nothing cruel.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: tender-heartedness, pity, compassion, mercy.
Latin: Motio miseria alicuius cum cupiditate eius iuvandi coniuncta

examples.original: Quicquid ante pugnatum est, misericordia fuit.
examples.translation: The previous combats were the essence of compassion;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non solum ergo non debetis minus facere opera misericordiae, sed etiam debetis amplius quam soletis.
examples.translation: So far then from having any right to curtail your works of mercy, you ought to increase them beyond your usual measure.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ideoque his litteris obtestor fidem tuam, quam habes in Christo, per ipsius domini Christi misericordiam, ut hoc nec facias nec fieri omnino permittas.
examples.translation: For that reason I implore you by the faith you have in Christ, by the mercy of Christ the Lord Himself, neither to do this nor to let it be done at all.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: the open space within the mound or breastwork of a camp, the space between two palisades.

examples.original: Sed hos tolerabiles intervalla faciunt.
examples.translation: The suffering, however, is rendered endurable by interruptions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Item equites Ariovisti pari intervallo constiterunt.
examples.translation: The horsemen of Ariovistus halted at an equal distance.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Brevis enim profecto res est, si uno tenore peragitur nec ipsi per intermissiones has intervallaque lentiorem spem nostram facimus.
examples.translation: For surely it is a thing soon done, if we carry it through without stopping, and do not ourselves drag out our hopes with these interruptions and delays.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to seek again; to look after, to seek or search for; to seek to know
Latin: Rursus aut saepius quaerere
Latin: Poscere, petere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; sīvi or sii, sītum, 3

examples.original: Sed quid attinet de rebus tam apertis plura requirere?
examples.translation: But what is the point of inquiring further into matters so obvious?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam cur tam variae res possent esse requiro, ex uno si sunt igni puroque creatae.
examples.translation: For I want to know why things could be so various, if they are made of fire pure and simple;
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Deinde ea quae requirebant orationem ornatam et gravem, quam magnifice sunt dicta ab illis, quam splendide!
examples.translation: Then, in themes demanding ornate and dignified treatment, how imposing, how brilliant is their diction!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to have frequently, to be wont to have (anteclass. and very rare): epicrocum, Varr. ap.
Latin: Frequenter habere
Latin: Incolere, commorari

examples.original: Hac oratione habita concilium dimisit.
examples.translation: With this speech he dissolved the convention.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In hoc obnoxio domicilio animus liber habitat.
examples.translation: In this dwelling, which is exposed to peril, my soul lives free.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si doceo non ab Habito, vinco ab Oppianico: si ostendo ab Oppianico, purgo Habitum.
examples.translation: If I demonstrate that it was used by Oppianicus, I clear Habitus.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a country-house, country-seat, farm

examples.original: De ipsa villa nihil tibi possum certi scribere.
examples.translation: I could not describe the villa accurately;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Numquam aliter hanc villam Vatia vivo praeteribam, quam ut dicerem: ”Vatia hic situs est.”
examples.translation: So I never drove past his country-place during Vatia’s lifetime without saying to myself: ”Here lies Vatia!”
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec villarum atque vicorum vastatione contenti Nolam atque Nuceriam, Thurios atque Metapontum terribili strage populantur.
examples.translation: Not content with the plundering of country houses and villages, they laid waste Nola, Nuceria, Thurii and Metapontum with terrible destruction.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to spread out, spread abroad; to stretch out, extend.

examples.original: Quid horum ad virtutem viam sternit?
examples.translation: But which of these paves the way to virtue?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Totus inter stratum lectionemque divisus est.
examples.translation: The whole time has been divided between rest and reading.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Instant Volumnius et Scipio et perculsos sternunt.
examples.translation: Hard after them came Volumnius and Scipio, and made havoc of the disordered Samnites.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: favorable, fortunate, prosperous

examples.original: Isdem diebus a Martio Macro haud procul Cremona prospere pugnatum;
examples.translation: During these same days, Martius Macer had had a successful engagement not far from Cremona;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ne mutas quidem bestias minus alere ac fovere si quid ex progenie sua parum prosperum sit;
examples.translation: Why even the dumb brutes, if one of their young is unfortunate, do none the less cherish it and foster it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Aliquid tamen adversus absentem ducem ausa Fortuna est circa Illyricum et Africam, quasi de industria prospera eius adversis radiaret;
examples.translation: Fortune, however, ventured some opposition to the absent leader, namely, in Illyricum and Africa, as though on purpose to make his successes more glorious in contrast with failure elsewhere.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a star
Latin: Unum ex innumerabilibus corporibus luminis quae in caelis videntur; corpus caeleste praeter lunas, cometas, nebulasque
Latin: sidus

examples.original: Stellarum iste discursus quicquid praeterit repetit;
examples.translation: The wandering stars retrace their former courses;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita enim parvae et exiguae sunt istae accessiones bonorum ut, quemadmodum stellae in radiis solis, sic istae in virtutum splendore ne cernantur quidem.
examples.translation: For those supplementary goods are so small and slight that in the full radiance of the virtues they are as invisible as the stars in sunlight.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Fieri videntur et discursus stellarum numquam temere, ut non ex ea parte truces venti cooriantur.
examples.translation: Stars are seen to move about in various directions, but never without some cause, nor without violent winds proceeding from the same quarter.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: to stand on end, stand erect, to bristle.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ui, ēre

definitions: English: to bear, carry, convey, on the shoulders, by wagon, by horse, by ship, etc.
Latin: trahere, transportare
Latin: mediopass ĭtĕr făcĕre
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; xi, ctum, 3

examples.original: Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus concedi corpora sepulturae cremarique permisit.
examples.translation: He was then carried through the heaps of dead bodies, while the forum still reeked with blood, first to the Capitol and then to the Palatine;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to strike, smite, beat, knock

examples.original: Magnis telis magna portenta feriuntur.
examples.translation: It takes great weapons to strike down great monsters.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cnosis in ignotis amens errabat harenis, Qua brevis aequoreis Dia feritur aquis.
examples.translation: The Cretan maid wandered distractedly on the unknown sand, where little Dia is lashed by the sea waves.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sed modo dilectam scelus est odisse puellam: Exitus ingeniis convenit iste feris.
examples.translation: But to hate a woman once loved is a crime: that is an end fitting to savage minds.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to cook, to prepare by cooking, to bake, boil, roast, parch, steep, melt, heat (very freq. and class.).

examples.original: Nihil praeter arma et quod cocti ad manum fuit cibi ferre militi licuit;
examples.translation: The soldiers were allowed to take nothing but their arms and such bread as happened to be at hand;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad hoc panis usu carnisque coctae et dulcedine vini mitigatos Marius in tempore adgressus est.
examples.translation: When they had been further demoralized by the use of bread and cooked meat and the delights of wine, Marius opportunely approached them.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Itaque per speciem adversus Samnites belli parandi crebra concilia indicentes omnibus consultationibus inter se principes occulte Romanum coquebant bellum.
examples.translation: Accordingly their leaders, under colour of forwarding the war against the Samnites, appointed numerous councils, and in all their deliberations secretly concocted war with Rome.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: wearied, tired, fatigued; worn out, weak, feeble, infirm (class.; esp. freq. in poets; syn.: fatigatus, defessus, lassus, languidus).
Latin: Conditionem seu statum eius significat, qui aliquid diu perpetiendo viribus deficit (proprie usurpatur de hominibus et brutis animantibus)

examples.original: Erat illi et fessa aetate parens;
examples.translation: He had also his mother, who was bowed with years;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hoc opus exegi: fessae date serta carinae;
examples.translation: I have finished my task; hang garlands on the weary vessel;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non proelia fessos Ulla vocant, certos non rumpunt classica somnos.
examples.translation: No battles call them from where they rest; no trumpet-call breaks their sound slumbers.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: mild, mellow, mature, ripe; of the soil, mellow, light, kindly, fruitful; of a river, calm, gentle, placid (class.; syn.: lenis, placidus, comis).

examples.original: Saepe suos casus nec mitia facta puellae Flesse sub arboribus Milaniona ferunt;
examples.translation: Often, they say, beneath the trees Milanion bewailed his lot and the maiden’s cruelty;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a rushing or tumbling down; a falling down, fall (syn.: casus, lapsus).

examples.original: Bellvm Macedonicvm Secvndvm II, 12Dum aliae aliaeque gentes Syriaci belli secuntur ruinam, Macedonia rursus se erexit.
examples.translation: The Second Macedonian War 12. While nation after nation was involved in the disaster of the Syrian war, Macedonia again raised her head.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Vix proelia Caesar Senserat, elatus specula quae prodidit ignis: Invenit inpulsos presso iam pulvere muros, Frigidaque, ut veteris, deprendit signa ruinae.
examples.translation: Caesar had hardly been aware of the fighting; the news of it was conveyed to him by a fire-signal from a lofty tower.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Multi, Pharsalica castra Cum peterent nondum fama prodente ruina, Occursu stupuere ducis vertigine rerum Attoniti, cladisque suae vix ipse fidelis Auctor erat.
examples.translation: Many who were on their way to the camp at Pharsalia, before rumour had published his defeat abroad, were startled to meet their leader and astounded by the sudden change of fortune;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: A whirl, eddy, whirlpool

examples.original: Ora ferox Siculae laxavit Mulciber Aetnae Nec tulit in caelum flammas, sed vertice prono Ignis in Hesperium cecidit latus.
examples.translation: In Sicily fierce Mulciber opened wide the mouths of Etna; nor did he lift its flames skyward, but the lire bowed its crest and fell on the Italian shore.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Statura fuit eminenti, colore expallido, corpore enormi, gracilitate maxima cervicis et crurum, oculis et temporibus concavis, fronte lata et torva, capillo raro at circa verticem nullo, hirsutus cetera.
examples.translation: His eyes and temples were hollow, his forehead broad and grim, his hair thin and entirely gone on the top of his head, though his body was hairy.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Quare omnium in se odio incitato nihil contumeliarum defuit quin subiret. Statuae eius a vertice cirrus appositus est cum inscriptione Graeca;
examples.translation: When he had thus aroused the hatred of all, there was no form of insult to which he was not subjected.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a foreteller, seer, soothsayer, prophet.

examples.original: Ecce, suum vatem Liber vocat;
examples.translation: Lo! Liber summons his bard;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non enim Cicero ea solum quae vivo se acciderunt futura praedixit, sed etiam quae nunc usu veniunt cecinit ut vates.
examples.translation: For he not only predicted the events that actually happened during his lifetime, but, like a seer, foretold those which are now being experienced.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Quod nisi dux operis vatem frustratur Apollo, Aemulus est nostri maxima causa mali: At tu rivalem noli tibi fingere quemquam, Inque suo solam crede iacere toro.
examples.translation: Yet, unless Apollo, prince of the craft, deceives the bard, a rival is the chief cause of our malady: but picture no rival to yourself, and think she lies on her couch alone.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: height or depth
Latin: Status altus

examples.original: Fluminis erat altitudo pedum circiter trium.
examples.translation: The depth of the river was about three feet.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non est admirationi una arbor, ubi in eandem altitudinem tota silva surrexit.
examples.translation: There is unevenness, you know, when some objects rise conspicuous above others.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to accomplish, effect, bring to pass; to get, obtain, procure, esp. by exertion, request, entreaty (class.; cf.: obtineo, adipiscor, consequor).

examples.original: Di impetrabunt, per quos iuravere;
examples.translation: The gods will persuade them, by whom they have sworn.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Qua re impetrata arma tradere iussi faciunt.
examples.translation: Their request was granted, and they proceeded to deliver up their arms as ordered.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Impetrant ut ne iurent; dat his possessionem.
examples.translation: Their request to be exempted from taking the oath was granted;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to send down; to drop; to let, sink, or bring down; to cause to hang or fall down; to lower, put down, let fall (freq. and class.).

examples.original: In eam demissus es vitam, quae numquam tibi terminum miseriarum ac servitutis ipsa factura sit.
examples.translation: You have been thrust into an existence which will never of itself put an end to your wretchedness and your slavery.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Animadvertit Caesar unos ex omnibus Sequanos nihil earum rerum facere quas ceteri facerent, sed tristes capite demisso terram intueri.
examples.translation: He noticed, however, that of all the company the Sequani alone did not act like the rest, but with head downcast stared sullenly upon the ground.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quaere hoc ex Clodio, scriptore legum tuarum: iube adesse: latitat omnino, sed si requiri iusseris, invenient hominem apud sororem tuam occultantem se capite demisso.
examples.translation: He is skulking away out of sight; but do but order search to be made for him, and the fellow will be discovered secreting himself shamefacedly at your sister’s house.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: without resources, helpless, weak (class.).

examples.original: Tam inops autem ego eram ab amicis aut tam nuda res publica a magistratibus?
examples.translation: But was I so destitute of aid from friends, or was the republic so devoid of magistrates?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Is, quod in his locis inopia frumenti erat, praefectos tribunosque militum complures in finitimas civitates frumenti causa dimisit;
examples.translation: As there was a lack of corn in those parts, he despatched several commandants and tribunes into the neighbouring states to seek it.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Is diu sordidus, repente dives mutationem fortunae male tegebat, accensis egestate longa cupidinibus im moderatus et inopi iuventa senex prodigus.
examples.translation: His desires had been increased by long poverty, so that he now put no restraint upon himself, and after a youth of poverty became a prodigal old man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a seat (freq. and class.).
Latin: Res supellecticaria in qua sedendum est; sella

examples.original: Consules in sedem processere suam, missique lictores ad sumendum supplicium.
examples.translation: The consuls advanced to their tribunal and dispatched the lictors to execute the sentence.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea res utique Troianis spem adfirmat tandem stabili certaque sede finiendi erroris.
examples.translation: The commanders then made a treaty, and the armies saluted each other.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vestalibus nempe una illa sedes est, ex qua eas nihil unquam praeterquam urbs capta movit;
examples.translation: The Vestals surely have but that one dwelling-place, from which nothing ever caused them to remove but the capture of the City;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bring over by talking, to convince of the truth of any thing, to persuade (cf. convinco).

examples.original: Facile hac oratione Nerviis persuadet.
examples.translation: With this speech he easily persuaded the Nervii.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Persuadebo deinde tibi, ne umquam boni viri miserearis;
examples.translation: I shall induce you, in fine, never to commiserate a good man.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc cum persuasi mihi et perbibi, quid ista praecepta proficiunt, quae eruditum docent?
examples.translation: To one who knows, it is superfluous to give precepts;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to make dry
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Odi quae praebet, quia sit praebere necesse, Siccaque de lana cogitat ipsa sua.
examples.translation: I hate her who gives because she must, and who, herself unmoved, is thinking of her wool.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fessa iacet cervix, fumant sudoribus artus, Oraque proiecta squalent arentia lingua, Pectora rauca gemunt, quae creber anhelitus urguet, Et defecta gravis longe trahit ilia pulsus, Siccaque sanguineis durescit spuma lupatis.
examples.translation: The weary neck sinks down, the limbs reek with sweat, the tongue protrudes and the mouth is rough and dry; the lungs, driven by quick pants, give a hoarse murmur;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: place against
Latin: Contra ponere, ex adverso statuere
Latin: Verbis obicere

examples.original: Partem unam in agro Veiente Etruriae opposuit, alteram ante urbem castra locare iussit;
examples.translation: One division he stationed in the Veientine district to confront Etruria; a second he ordered to encamp before the City.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Alteri consuli Aemilio ingresso Sabellum agrum non castra Samnitium, non legiones usquam oppositae.
examples.translation: The other consul, Aemilius, having entered the Sabellian territory, nowhere encountered a Samnite camp or levies.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Praefecerat hunc Perdiccas ei parti Asiae quae inter Taurum montem iacet atque Hellespontum, et illum unum opposuerat Europaeis adversariis;
examples.translation: Perdiccas had made him governor of the part of Asia lying between the Taurus mountains and the Hellespont and had left him to face his European opponents alone;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: Meanwhile, in the meantime

examples.original: Praetor interea, Piso, tanta de re tacebit?
examples.translation: Will the praetor, Piso, have nothing to say meanwhile about so important a matter?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Caesar Interea, dum haec geruntur, hostium copiae ex Arvernis equitesque qui toti Galliae erant imperati conveniunt.
examples.translation: In the meanwhile the enemy’s contingent from the Arverni and the horsemen requisitioned from the whole of Gaul were assembling.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar Legati haec se ad suos relaturos dixerunt et re deliberata post diem tertium ad Caesarem reversuros: interea ne propius se castra moveret, petierunt.
examples.translation: The envoys said that they would report this to their people and, after deliberation upon the matter, return to Caesar in three days: they asked him not to move his camp nearer in the meanwhile.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to touch, come in contact with; constr. with the
Latin: atting|ō, -ĕre, attinxī, attinctum

examples.original: Liberalis disciplinas omnis fere puer attigit.
examples.translation: When a boy he took up almost all the liberal arts;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Partito exercitu Titum Labienum cum legionibus tribus ad Oceanum versus in eas partes quae Menapios attingunt proficisci iubet;
examples.translation: Having divided the army, he ordered Titus Labienus to proceed with three legions towards the districts which touch the Menapii;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Qui ad illam pervenit, attigit non longissimum finem, sed maximum.
examples.translation: He who has attained wisdom has reached, not the furthermost, but the most important, goal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: nine
Latin: Octo et alius

examples.original: Hora nona illo ipso die tu es adoptatus.
examples.translation: At the ninth hour on that same day your adoption took place.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Scripta Nonas Novembris, indictione tertia.
examples.translation: Written on the 5th day of November, in the third indiction.
examples.author: Bede

examples.original: Vixit annis viginti novem, imperavit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.
examples.translation: He lived twenty-nine years and ruled three years, ten months and eight days.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: A possession in land, a landed estate, a farm

examples.original: Suessa et Pontia coloniae deductae sunt.
examples.translation: Colonies were planted at Suessa and Pontia.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iam non exercitus modo armatos sed colonias etiam in suos finis mitti;
examples.translation: They would presently be sending out, not merely armed expeditions across their borders, but colonies too;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Septimam decimam cohortem e colonia Ostiensi in urbem acciri Otho iusserat;
examples.translation: Otho had given orders that the Seventeenth cohort be brought from the colony of Ostia to Rome.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a narration
Latin: Narratio, historia

examples.original: Ut quamque adtigeris, fabula turpis erit?
examples.translation: As you touch upon each, shall there be a tale of shame?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Convocat turbam, quisquis otio suo aliquam fabulam inposuit.
examples.translation: To advertise one’s retirement is to collect a crowd.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid cum fictas fabulas e quibus utilitas nulla elici potest cum voluptate legimus?
examples.translation: But what of our reading fiction, from which no utility can be extracted?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a surname in the gens Cornelia. So, esp.

examples.original: Librum autem, quem Sulla novissimum ”De Rebus Suis” imperfectum reliquerat, ipse supplevit.
examples.translation: He himself completed the last book of Sulla’s ”Autobiography,” which the dictator left unwritten.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Tristis felicibus umbris Voltus erat: vidi Decios, natumque patremque Lustrales bellis animas, flentemque Camillum Et Curios, Sullam de te, Fortuna, querentem.
examples.translation: For the blessed dead wore a sorrowful aspect: I saw the Decii, the father and son who devoted their lives to the gods in battle, and Camillus, and Curius;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Bellvm Civile Svb Lepido III, 23Marco Lepido Quinto Catulo consulibus civile bellum paene citius oppressum est quam inciperet: sed quantulacumque fax illius motus ab ipso Sullae rogo exarsit.
examples.translation: The Civil War under Lepidus 23. In the consulship of Marcus Lepidus and Quintus Catulus, a civil war which arose was suppressed almost as soon as it began.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to sit down (esp. of a multitude), take a seat, be seated, to settle (freq. in all periods and species of composition); constr. with in and

examples.original: Eo ille index confugit in araque consedit.
examples.translation: To this that informer fled and seated himself upon the altar.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Ibi ad Caiatiam omnes considunt et Appius Volumniusque castra coniungunt.
examples.translation: Appius and Volumnius also combined their forces.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cui ratiocinationi utrum nihil valide inimicum sit, peto mecum consideres.
examples.translation: For the present I find it stimulating;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a month.
Latin: Spatium triginta circiter diebus, in quo luna ab una ad eandem vicem revertit, seu una ex duodecim partibus anni

examples.original: Consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit.
examples.translation: He commonly appointed consuls for a period of six months.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et vidi non tantum mense Februario positas, sed etiam Martio exacto;
examples.translation: I have seen such plantings made not only in February, but at the very end of March;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vixit annis viginti novem, imperavit triennio et decem mensibus diebusque octo.
examples.translation: He lived twenty-nine years and ruled three years, ten months and eight days.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: Fruitfulness, fertility (post-Aug. and rare)

examples.original: Hoc felicitatem suam fine designat.
examples.translation: Such are the bounds which he sets to his own happiness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Una felicitas est bene vitae facere.
examples.translation: The only way to be happy is to do yourself well.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae enim res alia civiles furores peperit quam nimiae felicitates?
examples.translation: For what else produced those outbursts of domestic strife but excessive prosperity?
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: fasten, drive or thrust in, attach, affix (class.; cf.: pango, configo, defigo).
Latin: Firmare aliquid alicui rei

examples.original: Non vagatur, quod fixum atque fundatum est.
examples.translation: But that which is settled and solid does not wander from its place.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed hoc, quod liquet, firmandum et altius cotidiana meditatione figendum est;
examples.translation: This idea, however, clear though it is, must be strengthened and implanted more deeply by daily reflection;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Fixus et in duris carparis viscera saxis, Ut cui Pyrrha sui filia fratris erat.
examples.translation: And chained on the hard rocks mayst thou have thine entrails torn, as he whose brother’s daughter Pyrrha was.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: left, on the left side

examples.original: Manlius dextro, Decius laevo cornu praeerat.
examples.translation: Manlius commanded the right wing, Decius the left.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sp. Furius M. Horatius dextrorsus in maritimam oram atque Antium, Q. Servilius et L. Geganius laeva ad montes et Ecetram pergunt.
examples.translation: Spurius Furius and Marcus Horatius marched to the right, towards Antium and the coast; Quintus Servilius and Lucius Geganius to the left, in the direction of Ecetra and the mountains.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: (In laevum cecidere latus veloxque Metaurus Crustumiumque rapax et iuncto Sapis Isauro Senaque et Hadriacas qui verberat Aufidus undas;
examples.translation: (Eastward flow the swift Metaurus and rushing Crustumium, the Sapis together with the Isaurus, the Sena, the Aufidus which buffets the waves of the Adriatic;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to fall out or down, to fall from (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense).

examples.original: Non enim excidunt, sed fluunt.
examples.translation: They do not drip forth occasionally;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quodque suae passa est paelex invita sororis, Excidat ante pedes lingua resecta tuos.
examples.translation: And, what the unwilling rival of her own sister suffered, may thy tongue cut out fall before thy feet.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Uxores habuit Mummiam Achaicam, neptem Catuli proneptemque L. Mummi, qui Corinthum excidit;
examples.translation: He married Mummia Achaica, the granddaughter of Catulus and great-granddaughter of Lucius Mummius who destroyed Corinth;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: soft, smooth, mild, gentle, easy, calm.
Latin: Lĕvis, mītis, minime acer
Latin: Lēvis et tactu nullam asperitatem habens

examples.original: Omnia enim vitia in aperto leniora sunt;
examples.translation: For all unconcealed vices are less serious;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Colle tumet modico lenique excrevit in altum Pingue solum tumulo;
examples.translation: The fertile land rises in a hill of moderate height and ascends with easy slope;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ut fuerit torva violentior illa Medusa, Fiet amatori lenis et aequa suo.
examples.translation: Though she be more violent than grim Medusa, she will be mild and gentle to her lover.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to place, put, lay, set, dispose, arrange.
Latin: In loco ponere
Latin: constituere

examples.original: Quid ergo hoc loco intellegit honestum?
examples.translation: What therefore does he understand by ’moral’ in this passage?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illic exiguo paulum distantia vallo Castra locant.
examples.translation: There the two camps with low ramparts were pitched not far apart.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Postquam ad diem praestitutum venerunt socii, consul extra portam Capenam castra locat.
examples.translation: When the allies had reported on the appointed day, the consul encamped outside the Porta Capena.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the hair of the head, the hair (while crinis is any hair).

examples.original: Huic decet inflatos laxe iacuisse capillos: Illa sit adstrictis impedienda comis;
examples.translation: This one it beseems to let her waving locks lie loose;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Et tibi iam venient cani, formose, capilli, Iam venient rugae, quae tibi corpus arent.
examples.translation: And to thee, O handsome youth, will soon come hoary hairs, soon will come wrinkles to make furrows in your body.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Statura fuit eminenti, colore expallido, corpore enormi, gracilitate maxima cervicis et crurum, oculis et temporibus concavis, fronte lata et torva, capillo raro at circa verticem nullo, hirsutus cetera.
examples.translation: His eyes and temples were hollow, his forehead broad and grim, his hair thin and entirely gone on the top of his head, though his body was hairy.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: Punic, Carthaginian

examples.original: Quam gaudebat Bello suo Punico Naevius, quam Truculento Plautus, quam Pseudolo!
examples.translation: How Naevius used to revel in his Punic War! and Plautus in his Savage and Cheat!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Libri XVII Periocha Cn. Cornelius consul a classe Punica circumventus et per fraudem, veluti in conloquium evocatus, captus est.
examples.translation: Summaries Summary of Book XVII The consul Gnaeus Cornelius was surrounded by a Carthaginian fleet and was made prisoner by fraud, having been lured out as to a colloquy.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In Hispaniam missi Gnaeus et Publius Scipiones paene totam Poenis eripuerant, sed insidiis Punicae fraudis oppressi rursum amiserant, magnis quidem illi proeliis cum Punicas opes cecidissent.
examples.translation: The two Scipios, Gnaeus and Publius, were sent into Spain and had wrested practically the whole of the country from the Carthaginians;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: no. II. B.), to catch, ensnare, entrap, beguile, elude, deceive, cheat (for syn.
Latin: Sumere
Latin: defraudare, fallere

examples.original: Ut iam decipiant, quid perditis?
examples.translation: Though they at last deceive you, what do you lose?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tamen de eo queruntur omnes, in quo uno nemo decipitur.
examples.translation: And yet all men complain about the one thing wherein none of them is deceived.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic ista sine noxa decipiunt, quomodo praestigiatorum acetabula et calculi, in quibus me fallacia ipsa delectat.
examples.translation: Such quibbles are just as harmlessly deceptive as the juggler’s cup and dice, in which it is the very trickery that pleases me.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: full
Latin: Natus ex isdem parentibus, vel solum ab eodem patre
Latin: Verus

examples.original: Iterum de Germano Tencteri querebantur.
examples.translation: Further complaints against the Germans were brought by the Tencteri.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Germani multum ab hac consuetudine differunt.
examples.translation: The Germans differ much from this manner of living.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Magnam manum Germanorum conductam Rhenum transisse;
examples.translation: A great company of Germans had been hired, and had crossed the Rhine;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: greatly/very/intensely; vigorously/strongly/powerfully/energetically; loudly

examples.original: Valde enim bonae memoriae est, si meminit!
examples.translation: He must have a particularly good memory if he can remember that!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et si quis deus mihi largiatur ut ex hac aetate repuerascam et in cunis vagiam, valde recusem, nec vero velim quasi decurso spatio ad carceres a calce revocari.
examples.translation: And when I shall have set out to join them, assuredly no one will easily draw me back, or boil me up again, as if I were a Pelias.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hic si quaerat aliquis quid me tandem in tuis tarn valde litteris delectaverit, utrum eloquium, respondebo: ”Non”; et ille forsitan respondebit: ”Ergo laudes tuae”;
examples.translation: At this point, if anyone were to ask what after all it was in your letter that pleased me so very much, if it was its eloquence, I shall say ”No”;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: harsh to the taste, of every object which has an astringent effect upon the tongue
Latin: Sapore acre; amarus; praesertim de sapore fructuum immaturorum

examples.original: Id primo acerbum indignumque Veientibus est visum;
examples.translation: At first the Veientes bitterly resented this;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quis acerbior, quis insidiosior, quis crudelior umquam fuit?
examples.translation: No one was ever more harsh and treacherous and brutal.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Idem tibi de bonis dico: hoc bonum inter meras voluptates est, hoc inter tristia et acerba.
examples.translation: The same thing holds true, I assure you, concerning goods; you will find one amid circumstances of pure pleasure, another amid sorrow and bitterness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a guard, watch, preserver, keeper, overseer, protector, defender, attendant, etc., protectress, etc., in a friendly or hostile sense (freq. and class.).

examples.original: At Caesar dispositis in vallo custodibus recipi prohibebat.
examples.translation: But Caesar posted sentries on the rampart and prevented their admission.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: I nunc, claude fores, custos odiose puellae, Et centum duris postibus obde seras!
examples.translation: Go now, hateful guardian, bar the lady’s door, and add a hundred bolts to the sturdy posts.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Di immortales suorum templorum custodem ac praesidem sceleratissime pulsum quum viderent, ex suis templis in eius aedes immigrare nolebant.
examples.translation: The immortal gods, when they saw the guardian and champion of their temples outrageously expelled, refused to remove themselves from those temples into his house.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to choose out, to select (for syn. cf.: lego, coopto, designo, eligo, seligo).

examples.original: Temporibus certis maturam rusticus uvam Deligit, et nudo sub pede musta fluunt;
examples.translation: At fixed seasons the countryman picks the ripened grapes, and the vintage flows beneath his naked foot;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hostiae, ut quisque vovit, sed mares deliguntur: certissima fides haedorum fibris.
examples.translation: The greatest confidence is put in the entrails of kids.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: His rebus cognitis exploratores centurionesque praemittit, qui locum idoneum castris deligant.
examples.translation: Upon this information Caesar sent forward scouts and centurions to choose a fit place for the camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: oh that! I wish that! if only! would to heaven! would that! etc.
Latin: significans “volo quiddam (esse)”

examples.original: Et utinam sic denique lues ista vindicetur!
examples.translation: And would that this pest might so at last be overcome!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Utinam quidem dicerent alium alio beatiorem!
examples.translation: I only wish that they did allow degrees of happiness!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vocibus his correpta viri vix aegra levavit Membra solo tales gemitu rumpente querellas: ”O utinam in thalamos invisi Caesaris issem Infelix coniunx et nulli laeta marito!
examples.translation: Thus rebuked by her husband, slowly she raised her ailing limbs from the ground, and her wailing broke out into complaints like these: ”Would that I had been wedded to hated Caesar;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: forth, to spring up (esp. suddenly, unexpectedly), to rise (class.).
