examples.original: Erat et nova exorta causa motus.
examples.translation: There had also arisen a new cause for disquiet.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iamque dies primos belli visura tumultus Exoritur;
examples.translation: So the day dawned that was to witness the first turmoil of the war;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Eodem anno novum bellum cum Volsiniensibus exortum;
examples.translation: In this year also a new war broke out, namely with the people of Volsinii.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: might, force, power.

examples.original: Armeniosne movet, Romana potentia cuius Sit ducis?
examples.translation: Do the Armenians care which among rivals has power at Rome?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Movet cerebrum non uno genere; alios in aliud irritat, hos in potentiam, illos in luxuriam.
examples.translation: It stirs the brain in more ways than one, goading men on to various aims,—some to power, and others to high living.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic igitur Caesare dignitatem conparare, Crasso augere, Pompeio retinere cupientibus, omnibusque pariter potentiae cupidis de invadenda re publica facile convenit.
examples.translation: Caesar, therefore, being desirous of winning, Crassus of increasing, and Pompeius of retaining his position, and all alike being eager for power, readily came to an agreement to seize the government.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a play.
Latin: Exercitatio quaevis animi vel corporis recreandi causa suscepta

examples.original: Hic, cum quo ludis, timet;
examples.translation: This friend, in whose company you are jesting, is in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hos ludos spectavit e proscaeni fastigio.
examples.translation: These plays he viewed from the top of the proscenium.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nuper in ludo bestiariorum unus e Germanis, cum ad matutina spectacula pararetur, secessit ad exonerandum corpus;
examples.translation: For example, there was lately in a training-school for wild-beast gladiators a German, who was making ready for the morning exhibition;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to know a person or thing well, as having known it before, to recognize: agnoscere always denotes a subjective knowledge or recognition

examples.original: Cuius non militis ensem Agnoscam?
examples.translation: I shall know again the sword of every fighter;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Agnosco Lucilium meum;
examples.translation: On Siren Songs Now I recognize my Lucilius!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tu, Caesar, quamvis spoliatus milite multo, Agnoscis superos;
examples.translation: Caesar, though robbed of many soldiers, recognised the hand of heaven.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the principal meal of the Romans in the early period, taken about midday, dinner, supper
Latin: caput cibi Romanorum, quod ederunt inter horam decimam quintam decimamque sextam

examples.original: In cena fit, quod fieri debebat in ventre.
examples.translation: The dinner table does work which the stomach ought to do.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Post prandium aut cenam bibere vulgare est;
examples.translation: To them, a glass after lunch or one after dinner is bourgeois;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to throw, cast, fling, hurl.
Latin: Mittere vel agere per vim; conicere

examples.original: Hic teneat nostras ancora iacta rates.
examples.translation: Here let the anchor be thrown, and hold my bark secure.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Loquor de operae et de temporis iactura.
examples.translation: I talk of the loss of time and labour;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sic mihi iuravit, sic me iurata fefellit, Ante suas quotiens passa iacere fores!
examples.translation: Thus did she swear to me, and swearing played me false;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the belly

examples.original: In cena fit, quod fieri debebat in ventre.
examples.translation: The dinner table does work which the stomach ought to do.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Di boni, quantum hominum unus venter exercet!
examples.translation: How many men are kept busy to humour a single belly!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Facile est pascere paucos ventres et bene institutos et nihil aliud desiderantes quam inpleri.
examples.translation: It is easy to fill a few stomachs, when they are well trained and crave nothing else but to be filled.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to heal, cure, be good for or against a disease (syn.: medico, sano, curo); constr. with
Latin: Sanare
English: earliest beginning, commencement, source, descent, lineage, birth, origin (class.; syn. ortus).
Latin: Ortus, principium

examples.original: Ipse Pompeius in originem fontemque belli Ciliciam;
examples.translation: Pompeius himself proceeded against Cilicia, the origin and source of the war;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Si cui virtus animusque in corpore praesens, hic deos aequat, illo tendit originis suae memor.
examples.translation: He in whose body virtue dwells, and spirit E’er present,a is equal to the gods;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Omnes, si ad originem primam revocantur, a dis sunt.
examples.translation: All men, if traced back to their original source, spring from the gods.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to decide something by a contest (cf. cerno, II. C. b.); hence, to fight, struggle, contend, combat, implying great exertion, and usually a measuring of strength

examples.original: Certatum eo quoque anno cum tribunis est.
examples.translation: This year also there was a conflict with the tribunes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Contemptus corporis sui certa libertas est.
examples.translation: To despise our bodies is sure freedom.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Certare socii civesque, utri reciperatae arcis suum decus facerent;
examples.translation: The leader of each party urged on his followers.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the goddess Juno, daughter of Saturn, sister and wife of Jupiter, and the guardian deity of women; as the foundress of marriage, she is also called pronuba Juno
Latin: Dea Romana feminae, regina deorum, uxor Iovis erat
Latin: Asteroides qui 3 Iuno vocatur

examples.original: Iuppiter optimus maximus, Iuno regina et Minerva, alii di deaeque obsidentur;
examples.translation: Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Queen Juno, and Minerva, and the other gods and goddesses, are beleaguered;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iuno regina transvecta a Veiis nuper in Aventino quam insigni ob excellens matronarum studium celebrique dedicata est die!
examples.translation: Queen Juno was lately conveyed from Veii and enshrined on the Aventine, and how notable was that day, for the zeal of the matrons and the throng!
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to shake out or
Latin: Quatere aliquid ex aliqua re

examples.original: Excutit redeuntem natura sicut intrantem.
examples.translation: You may take away no more than you brought in;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec facile est animo dulcem sonum excutere;
examples.translation: It is not easy to rid the memory of a catching tune;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec cogitationem meam excutiunt, ne interrumpunt quidem.
examples.translation: But this does not upset my thoughts or even break their continuity.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: nothing

examples.original: Post eius mortem nihilo minus Helvetii id, quod constituerant, facere conantur, ut e finibus suis exeant.
examples.translation: After his death the Helvetii essayed none the less to accomplish their determination to march forth from their borders.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum Vercingetorix nihilo magis in aequum locum descenderet, levi facto equestri proelio atque secundo in castra exercitum reduxit.
examples.translation: When Vercingetorix, notwithstanding, refused to come down to level ground, a cavalry skirmish ensued, favourable to the Romans, after which Caesar led the army back to camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ceterum nihilo minus foeda dedita urbe quam si capta foret Aurunci passi: principes securi percussi, sub corona venierunt coloni alii;
examples.translation: Their chief men were beheaded, and the rest of the colonists were sold as slaves. The town was razed;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to go away, depart, withdraw. (For syn. cf.: linquo, relinquo, desero, destituo, deficio, discedo, excedo. Often opp. to accedo, maneo; freq. and class.)—Constr.

examples.original: Decessit aetatis exactae sub Tiberio.
examples.translation: He died at an advanced age under Tiberius.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: In Samnio quoque, quia decesserat inde Fabius, novi motus exorti.
examples.translation: In Samnium, too, the departure of Fabius was the cause of fresh disturbances.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Egerat cum Vario, priusquam Italia decederet, ut siquid sibi accidisset, ”Aeneida” combureret; at is ita facturum se pernegarat;
examples.translation: He had arranged with Varius, before leaving Italy, that if anything befell him his friend should burn the ”Aeneid”;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: go forth
Latin: pro ire

examples.original: Obvia progrediar felixque per oppida dicar Collaque et hoc oculos illius ore premam.
examples.translation: I shall go forth to meet him, and through the cities I shall be called fortunate;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Illi equitatu atque essedis ad flumen progressi ex loco superiore nostros prohibere et proelium committere coeperunt.
examples.translation: They advanced their cavalry and chariots from the higher ground to a river, and sought to check our troops and to engage.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et si hanc, de qua loquor, oculi petulantiam in aliqua vestrum adverteritis, statim admonete, ne coepta progrediantur, sed e proximo corrigantur.
examples.translation: And if in anyone of your number you perceive this frowardness of eye of which I am speaking, at once admonish her, so that what has begun may go no farther, but.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to go round or about a thing (syn. circumeo)
Latin: circumeō
Latin: pro honores quaerere, suffragium populi captare

examples.original: Est qui totam pueritiam ambitu suo adstringit.
examples.translation: The third confines all of childhood in its circumference.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quapropter neminem dubitare existimo quin illa damnatio ambitus nulla ex parte cum causa Cluenti vestroque iudicio coniuncta esse possit.
examples.translation: Wherefore I hold it indisputable that this conviction for corrupt practice can in no way be connected with the case of Cluentius, and the jurisdiction of your court.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Legati quoque (nam senatus electionem Galbae permiserat) foeda inconstantia nominati, excusati, substituti, ambitu remanendi aut eundi, ut quemque metus vel spes impulerat.
examples.translation: With disgraceful lack of firmness he named men, excused them, made substitutions, as they pleaded with him to stay or go, according to their fears or hopes.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to throw, cast, or

examples.original: Quod factum omnibus maximum timorem iniecit;
examples.translation: That act filled all men with extreme fear;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Dion

examples.original: Hic tum iniectus est hominibus scrupulus et quaedam dubitatio quidnam esset actum.
examples.translation: This made people feel uneasy and somewhat doubtful as to what had happened.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Si altera mors cum tormento, altera simplex et facilis est, quidni huic inicienda sit manus?
examples.translation: If one death is accompanied by torture, and the other is simple and easy, why not snatch the latter?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: infin. pass. parag.

examples.original: Sic Numitori ad supplicium Remus deditur.
examples.translation: So Remus was given up to Numitor to be punished.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque se suaque omnia Caesari dediderunt.
examples.translation: Accordingly they surrendered themselves and all they had to Caesar.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Consulatum in senos plerumque menses dedit.
examples.translation: He commonly appointed consuls for a period of six months.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to mark, to designate with a mark (syn.: signo, designo).
Latin: Signum apponere

examples.original: Nos ex illa prima nota non sumus;
examples.translation: We ourselves are not of that first class, either;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tu quoque, cui rugis uterum Lucina notavit, Ut celer aversis utere Parthus equis.
examples.translation: And you whose belly Lucina has marked with wrinkles, like the swift Parthian, use a backward-turned steed.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hominis enim scelere et furore notato similis a re publica labes in posterum demovebatur.
examples.translation: No policy could have been more just, more dignified, more wise, or more beneficial to the republic.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the Capitol, the temple of Jupiter, at Rome, built on the summit of Mons Saturnius or Tarpeius

examples.original: Nondum dedicata erat in Capitolio Iovis aedes.
examples.translation: The temple of Jupiter on the Capitol had not yet been dedicated.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Coronam auream Iovi donum in Capitolium mittunt.
examples.translation: They sent a golden crown as a gift to the Capitoline Jupiter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Aspice quae nunc sunt Capitolia, quaeque fuerunt: Alterius dices illa fuisse Iovis.
examples.translation: See what the Capitol is now, and what it was: you would say they belonged to different Jupiters.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Julian; of the Roman gens Julia
Latin: Qui ad gentem Iuliam pertinet
Latin: Qui ad mensem septimum calendarii Gregoriani pertinet

examples.original: Capitur praefectus alae Iulius Flavianus;
examples.translation: Julius Flavianus, prefect of a squadron, was captured;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Iulium Burdonem Germanicae classis praefectum astu subtraxit.
examples.translation: Julius Burdo, commander of the German fleet, he saved by a clever ruse.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Stationem in castris agebat Iulius Martialis tribunus.
examples.translation: Julius Martialis the tribune was the officer of the day in the camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to drive, crowd, or thrust back; to reject, repulse, repel, etc., = reicere (freq. and class.; syn.: reicio, repono, removeo).

examples.original: Non galea, non scuto repellitur ferrum.
examples.translation: What is the need of defensive armour, or of skill?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed quid ego aedilicias repulsas colligo?
examples.translation: But why this catalogue of failures to obtain this office?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Repulsos deinde insecuti victores ingentem ediderunt caedem.
examples.translation: Then, as they retreated, the victors pursued them with great slaughter;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a. [2. salio], to dance (in the widest signif. of the word, including pantomime and gesticulation; mostly with a contemptuous accessory signif.).

examples.original: Numerate saltem quot ipsi sitis, quot adversarios habeatis.
examples.translation: At least count up your numbers and the number of your adversaries.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quodque vix auditu fas esse debeat, laudis et gloriae et ingenii loco plerique iactant cantari saltarique commentarios suos;
examples.translation: They make it their aim, by wantonness of language, by shallow-pated conceits, and by irregular arrangement, to produce the rhythms of stage-dancing;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quin, ut censuram patris, ut tres consulatus, ut tot egregiae domus honores deceret, desperatione saltem in audaciam accingeretur.
examples.translation: No. You must prove yourself worthy of your father’s censorship, of the three consulships, and all the honours belonging to your famous house.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: of or pertaining to Attica or Athens, Attic, Athenian

examples.original: Nomen Attici perire Ciceronis epistulae non sinunt.
examples.translation: Cicero’s letters keep the name of Atticus from perishing.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qua ut poteretur, virum eius Atticum Vestinum consulem in honore ipso trucidavit.
examples.translation: To possess the latter he slew her husband Atticus Vestinus while he held the office of consul.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Sic Atticus in summo timore non solum sibi, sed etiam ei quem carissimum habebat praesidio fuit.
examples.translation: Thus it was that Atticus in a time of extreme anxiety saved not only himself but also his dearest friend.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

definitions: English: having no light, devoid of light.
Latin: Non potens videndi
Latin: Luce egens, obscurus

examples.original: Quis furor, o caeci, scelerum?
examples.translation: What guilty madness, what blindness is this!
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ille in se stupet, ille caligat, invidet caecis.
examples.translation: Such a man is internally dazed; his vision is darkened;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad Appi Claudi senectutem accedebat etiam ut caecus esset;
examples.translation: To the old age of Appius Claudius was also added blindness;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: name of a Roman gens

examples.original: Per secessionem plebis Sp. Cassius et Postumus Cominius consulatum inierunt.
examples.translation: During the secession of the plebs Spurius Cassius and Postumus Cominius entered upon their consulship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quis autem est qui Tarquinium Superbum, qui Sp. Cassium, Sp. Maelium non oderit?
examples.translation: On the other hand, is there anyone who does not hate Tarquin the Proud, Spurius Cassius, or Spurius Maelius?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Primum adeo anceps fuit, ut—par utrimque discrimen—capta sint hinc Caesaris castra, inde Cassi. Sed quanto efficacior est fortuna, quam virtus!
examples.translation: At first the issue was so doubtful that, danger threatening both sides alike, the camp of Caesar was captured on the one hand and that of Cassius on the other.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: the belly, the paunch, the bowels.
English: a., to follow, to follow after or upon a person or thing (class.).

examples.original: Repulsos deinde insecuti victores ingentem ediderunt caedem.
examples.translation: Then, as they retreated, the victors pursued them with great slaughter;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Faciunt hoc idem omnes eius equites paucosque nostros convertunt atque insequuntur.
examples.translation: All his horsemen did likewise, turning and pursuing our small party.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Plerumque improborum facta primo suspicio insequitur, dein sermo atque fama, tum accusator, tum iudex;
examples.translation: The usual consequences of crime are, first suspicion, next gossip and rumour, then comes the accuser, then the judge;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a round, swelling, or bulging place, an elevation, protuberance, prominence; hence

examples.original: Molli consurgit Amyclas, Quem dabat alga, toro.
examples.translation: Amyclas rose up from the soft bed that seaweed gave him.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Fecit et in capta Lyrneside magnus Achilles, Cum premeret mollem lassus ab hoste torum.
examples.translation: Thus did the great Achilles with the Lyrnesian captive, when weary from the foe he burdened the soft couch.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Pars ”Hymenaee” canunt, pars clamant ”Euhion, euhoe!” Sic coeunt sacro nupta deusque toro.
examples.translation: Some chant ”Hail, Hymenaeus!” some shout ”Euhoe, Euhion !” So do the bride and the god meet on the sacred couch.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: strong, stout, able, powerful, robust, vigorous

examples.original: Nam et haec ab habitu animi compositi validique proficiscitur.
examples.translation: For proof also originates from a well-ordered and firm mental attitude.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At te Corfini validis circumdata muris Tecta tenent, pugnax Domiti;
examples.translation: But Domitius, eager for battle, lay behind strong walls in the city of Corfinium;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cui ratiocinationi utrum nihil valide inimicum sit, peto mecum consideres.
examples.translation: For the present I find it stimulating;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: the upper bone of the arm

examples.original: Hoc vos praecipue, niveae, decet: hoc ubi vidi, Oscula ferre umero, qua patet usque, libet.
examples.translation: This becomes you especially, you who have snowy skins; when I see this, fain would I kiss that shoulder, wherever it is exposed.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to wind or twine round a person or thing

examples.original: Abscidis frustra ferro tua pignora: bellum Te faciet civile meum.” Sic fata refugit Umbra per amplexus trepidi dilapsa mariti.
examples.translation: The civil war shall make you mine.” Thus speaking, the ghost fled away, dissolving in the arms of her eager husband.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non maesti pectora Magni Sustinet amplexu dulci, non colla tenere, Extremusque perit tam longi fructus amoris, Praecipitantque suos luctus, neuterque recedens Sustinuit dixisse ”vale”;
examples.translation: She cannot bear to clasp in her dear arms the breast or head of her sorrowing husband, and the last chance of enjoying their long and faithful love was thrown away.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nocte sub extrema pulso torpore quietis, Dum fovet amplexu gravidum Cornelia curis Pectus et aversi petit oscula grata mariti, Umentes mirata genas percussaque caeco Volnere non audet flentem deprendere Magnum.
examples.translation: Night was ending and the drowsiness of sleep was banished, when Cornelia clasped in her arms the care-laden breast of her husband and sought the dear lips of him who turned from her;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to dig out the earth needed for it

examples.original: Eum locum vallo fossaque munivit.
examples.translation: He fortified the place with rampart and trench.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid fodis inmeritis, Phineu, sua lumina natis?
examples.translation: Why piercest thou, O Phineus, the eyes of thine innocent sons?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Postero die prima luce Volsci fossis repletis vallum invadunt.
examples.translation: He waited a moment, to test the temper of the soldiers.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a burning, fire, conflagration.
Latin: Ignis dilatatio et augmentum, inflammatio
Latin: ignis, flamma

examples.original: Multas enim civitates incendium vexavit, nullam abstulit.
examples.translation: For fire has damaged many a city, but has annihilated none.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Deliberatur de Avarico in communi concilio, incendi placeret an defendi.
examples.translation: They deliberated in a general convention whether Avaricum should be burnt or defended.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hoc idem fit in reliquis civitatibus: in omnibus partibus incendia conspiciuntur;
examples.translation: The same was done in the other states, and in every direction fires were to be seen.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: full of sadness, sad, sorrowful, afflicted, dejected, melancholy (class.).
Latin: Aeger animi, tristis

examples.original: Odimus et maestas: Tecmessam diligat Aiax;
examples.translation: Melancholy women too I hate; let Ajax love Tecmessa;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Lucretiam sedentem maestam in cubiculo inveniunt.
examples.translation: Lucretia they found sitting sadly in her chamber.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Saeva quies pelagi, maestoque ignava profundo Stagna iacentis aquae;
examples.translation: A grim stillness broods over the dismal deep;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: of or belonging to winter, wintry, winter-.
Latin: Qui ad hiemem pertinet, hieme accidens

examples.original: Caesar in Belgis omnium legionum hiberna constituit.
examples.translation: Then Caesar established the winter quarters of all the legions in Belgic territory.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Tempus erat, quo Libra pares examinat horas, Non uno plus aequa die, noctique rependit Lux minor hibernae verni solacia damni.
examples.translation: It was the season when Libra balances the hours of day and night in equal scales, and stays level for one day only;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Urebant montana nives camposque iacentes Non duraturae conspecto sole pruinae, Atque omnis propior mergenti sidera caelo Aruerat tellus hiberno dura sereno.
examples.translation: The mountains were nipped by snow, and the low-lying plains by hoar frost that would vanish at first sight of the sun;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a hired servant, hireling, mercenary, satellite, bodyguard, etc. (only ante-class.): haec effatus ibi, latrones dicta facessunt, Enn. ap.
Latin: Qui rapit, raptor
English: military service, warfare, war.

examples.original: Haec eo anno domi militiaeque gesta.
examples.translation: Such were the events of this year at home and in the field.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nobis quoque militandum est, et quidem genere militiae, quo numquam quies, numquam otium datur.
examples.translation: We too have a war to wage, a type of warfare in which there is allowed no rest or furlough.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Faliscus, procul ab domo militiam aegre patiens satisque fidens sibi, poscere pugnam: Veienti Fidenatique plus spei in trahendo bello esse.
examples.translation: The Faliscans, chafing under service performed away from home and fairly self-confident, demanded battle: the Veientes and Fidenates anticipated greater success from a prolongation of the war.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: indecl., something contrary to divine law, sinful, unlawful, execrable, abominable, criminal; an impious or wicked deed, a sin, a crime (cf.: scelus, flagitium, peccatum).
Latin: Facinus contra leges religionis, iniuria, scelus
Latin: Aliquis, qui facinus contra religionem committit, homo scelestus

examples.original: Non equidem video quid magis nefas sit.
examples.translation: For my part I do not see what could be more abominable.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non uni cuncta dabantur, Sed fecit sibi quisque nefas;
examples.translation: The deeds done were not all done for the sake of one man;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Iamque irae patuere deum, manifestaque belli Signa dedit mundus, legesque et foedera rerum Praescia monstrifero vertit natura tumultu Indixitque nefas.
examples.translation: And now heaven’s wrath was revealed; the universe gave clear signs of battle;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to take to one's self from a person or thing, to take away, take any thing from, to deprive of (syn.: demere, eximere, auterre, eripere).
Latin: Capere ad se ipse ab aliquo

examples.original: Volscis devictis Veliternus ager ademptus;
examples.translation: The Volsci, having been conquered, were deprived of the Veliternian land;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Lucis vobis huius partem, si liceat, adimant;
examples.translation: They would take from you, were it possible, a part of this daylight.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Senatoriam dignitatem recusantibus equestrem quoque ademit.
examples.translation: If any refused senatorial rank, he took from them that of knight also.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: narrow, strait, esp. of local relations, close, contracted, small, not spacious

examples.original: In quam angusto quodam quot gradus posuit!
examples.translation: How many steps for how short a climb!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Angustissimum habet dies gyrum, sed et hic ab initio ad exitum venit, ab ortu ad occasum.
examples.translation: The smallest circle of all is the day; but even a day has its beginning and its ending, its sunrise and its sunset.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cuius loci haec erat natura, atque ita montibus angustis mare continebatur, uti ex locis superioribus in litus telum adigi posset.
examples.translation: Such was the nature of the ground, so steep the heights which banked the sea, that a missile could be hurled from the higher levels on to the shore.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to lead or bring forth, to lead forward or
Latin: Coram, ante, extra ducere
Latin: In longum ducere, longum facere

examples.original: Est quaedam dulcedo sermonis, quae inrepit et eblanditur et non aliter quam ebrietas aut amor secreta producit.
examples.translation: For there is a sort of charm about conversation, something very subtle and coaxing, which, like intoxication or love, draws secrets from us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hanc post rem gestam non ita multis diebus M. Minucium Rufum, magistrum equitum pari ac dictatorem imperio, dolo productum in proelium, fugavit.
examples.translation: Not so many days after this exploit, when Marcus Minucius Rufus, master of horse, had been given the same powers as the dictator, he craftily lured him into fighting, and utterly defeated the Roman.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

examples.original: Nam si est artius, ut ita dicam, holocleros, quid est quod dubitemus, quin per eosdem articulos et gradus producendus sit, per quos frater eius productus sit?
examples.translation: For if he be sound and so to say complete, what reason have we for doubting that he ought to be advanced through the same grades and steps through which his brother has been advanced?
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to cover, overlay, or smear with wax

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec piger ignis erat per stuppea vincula perque Manantes cera tabulas, et tempore eodem Transtraque nautarum summique arsere ceruchi.
examples.translation: He ordered brands steeped in resin to be hurled at the sails of the crowded ships;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Parcite ne castris: vallo tendetis in illo, Unde acies peritura venit.” Vix cuncta locuto Caesare quemque suum munus trahit, armaque raptim Sumpta Ceresque viris.
examples.translation: Be not careful of your camp; you will find quarters behind the rampart from which the doomed army is coming.” Almost before Caesar had ceased to speak, each went to his appointed task;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: foolish, simple, silly, fatuous, etc. (cf.: insulsus, ineptus, insipiens, brutus).
Latin: non callidus; stupidus, nullius consilii
Latin: Irrationalis, incongruus; delirus, absurdus, ridiculus

examples.original: Occidit Eurytion stulte data vina bibendo;
examples.translation: Eurytion fell by stupidly drinking the liquor set before him;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid sapiens faciet, stultus cum munere gaudet?
examples.translation: What will the wise man do, when the fool delights in a bribe?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quam stultum est aetatem disponere ne crastini quidem dominum!
examples.translation: O what madness it is to plot out far-reaching hopes!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: trust, confidence, reliance, assurance (class.).

examples.original: Quae bona sunt fiduciam faciunt, divitiae audaciam.
examples.translation: Those things which are goods produce confidence, but riches produce shamelessness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Duae res plurimum roboris animo dant, fides veri et fiducia;
examples.translation: There are two strong supports to the soul—trusta in the truth and confidence;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At ille, qui philosophiam in remedium suum exercuit, ingens fit animo, plenus fiduciae, inexsuperabilis et maior adeunti.
examples.translation: He, however, who has practised philosophy to effect his own cure, becomes high-souled, full of confidence, invincible, and greater as you draw near him.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: irreg. acc. mercem

examples.original: Aut merces hodie bellorum aut poena parata.
examples.translation: To-day either the reward or the penalty of war is before us.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Scire ruunt, quanta fuerint mercede nocentes.
examples.translation: They are wild to know what the wages of their wickedness amount to.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Habet praeterea in se non mediocre ista res gaudium et mercedem;
examples.translation: This is also a source of no mean joy and profit;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a branch, bough, twig (cf.: surculus, termes).

examples.original: Quam nodosi sunt et retorridi rami, quam tristes et squalidi trunci!
examples.translation: Their branches are so gnarled and shrivelled; the boles are so rough and unkempt!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At lapis, in ramo sedit quicumque bifurco, Haeret, et ut capta victor in arce manet.
examples.translation: But any stone that has wedged in a forked bough is fixed, and abides like a conqueror in a captured citadel.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the name of a Roman gens.

examples.original: Adtende omnia ista, senex Valeri;
examples.translation: Consider all these points, Senior Valerius;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: M’. Valerium dictatorem Volesi filium creant.
examples.translation: An edict which the dictator soon promulgated strengthened their confidence.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: In contionem Appius escendit: sequuntur Horatius Valeriusque.
examples.translation: Appius mounted the platform; Horatius and Valerius followed him.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To long for, seek after, aspire to, desire, covet, wish a thing (freq. and class.; syn.: appeto, affecto, cupio, concupisco, aveo, gestio, volo, opto, desidero, requiro).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; īvi or ĭi, ītum, 3

examples.original: Denique ceterae res, quae expetuntur, opportunae sunt singulae rebus fere singulis—divitiae, ut utare;
examples.translation: In short, all other objects of desire are each, for the most part, adapted to a single end—riches, for spending;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Haec est, inquam, societas, in qua omnia insunt, quae putant homines expetenda—honestas gloria tranquillitas animi atque iucunditas;
examples.translation: In such a partnership, I say, abide all things that men deem worthy of pursuit—honour and fame and delightful tranquillity of mind;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illud autem perabsurdum, bonum esse aliquid quod non expetendum sit, aut expetendum quod non placens, aut si id, non etiam diligendum;
examples.translation: But it would be paradoxical to maintain that there is something good which is not desirable; or desirable that is not pleasing;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to cover, cover up, wrap up, wrap, envelop, veil, etc. (class.; syn.: contego, induo).

examples.original: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
examples.translation: No awnings then hung o’er a marble theatre, nor was the platform ruddy with crocus-spray;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Prima dux fugae regina cum aurea puppe veloque purpureo in altum dedit Mo X secutus Antonius, sed instare vestigiis Caesar.
examples.translation: The queen led the retreat, putting out into the open sea in her golden vessel with purple sails. Antonius soon followed her, but Caesar was hard upon his tracks.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sed propera, ne vela cadant auraeque residant: Ut fragilis glacies, interit ira mora.
examples.translation: But be speedy, lest the sails sink and the breezes fail: like brittle ice, so perishes anger by delaying.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a Roman surname
Latin: Colore pellis sabeli; colore obscurissimo, ater splendens
Latin: homo niger

examples.original: Si niger aut ingens aut non erit ordine natus Dens tibi, ridendo maxima damna feres.
examples.translation: If you have a tooth that is black or too large or growing out of place, laughing will cost you dear.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Insertum manibus chalybem nigramque per artus Stillantis tabi saniem virusque coactum Sustulit, et nervo morsus retinente pependit.
examples.translation: She purloins the nails that pierced the hands, the clotted filth, and the black humour of corruption that oozes over all the limbs;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Niger inficit horror Terga maris, longo per multa volumina tractu Aestuat unda minax, flatusque incerta futuri Turbida testantur conceptos aequora ventos.
examples.translation: A shudder of darkness blackened the ridges of the sea; the angry deep boiled with a long swell, wave following wave;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the summer season, as one half of the year, from March twenty-second to September twenty-second
Latin: Una ex duobus temporibus anni, qui ab 22. Martii usque ad 22. Septembris durat; opp. hiems
Latin: Una ex quattuor temporibus anni, tres menses calidissimi quorum tempus proprium varie dicitur inter nationes; saepissime, tempus inter solstitium aestivum et aequinoctium autumnale

examples.original: Quid tractum in aestatem aliam bellum?
examples.translation: What profit shall we find in prolonging the war into another summer?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nilum non extulit aestas, Maeander derexit aquas, Rhodanumque morantem Praecipitavit Arar.
examples.translation: The Nile fails to rise in summer; the Maeander straightens its course;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: His nuntiis litterisque commotus Caesar duas legiones in citeriore Gallia novas conscripsit et inita aestate in interiorem Galliam qui deduceret Quintum Pedium legatum misit.
examples.translation: These reports and despatches prompted Caesar to enrol two new legions in Hither Gaul, and at the beginning of summer he sent Quintus Pedius, lieutenant-general, to lead them into Inner Gaul.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: of or belonging to a father, fatherly, paternal

examples.original: Odisse plebem plus quam paterno odio: quid?
examples.translation: He hated the plebs with a hatred that surpassed his father’s: What?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Numquam ante tam invisus plebi reus ad iudicium vocatus populi est, plenus suarum, plenus paternarum irarum.
examples.translation: The patricians, for their part, had not lightly put forth such exertions in behalf of any man.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nil ipsa paterni Iuris inire peto: culpa tantoque pudore Solve domum, remove funesta satellitis arma Et regem regnare iube.
examples.translation: I beg you only to free our house from such guilt and shame; destroy the dangerous strength of the favourite, and bid the king be a king indeed.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to stand before or against any thing.
Latin: esse contra aliquid; adverso stare
Latin: obst|ō, -āre, -itī, -ātūrus

examples.original: Ea ne impedirent tribuni dictatoris obstitit metus.
examples.translation: The awe in which the tribunes held the dictator prevented them from interfering with the trial.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed quid praecipue nostris conatibus obstet Eloquar, exemplo quemque docente suo.
examples.translation: But what particularly hinders our endeavours I will relate, though each may learn from his own case.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Obstitit Antonius datisque defensoribus ad Vespasianum dimisit.
examples.translation: Antonius interposed, gave him a guard, and sent him to Vespasian.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: supin. hauritu

examples.original: Plus praedae ac sanguinis Caecina hausit.
examples.translation: Caecina gained even more booty and shed more blood.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Catulus se ignis haustu ludibrio hostium exemit.
examples.translation: Catulus saved himself from the insults of his enemies by swallowing fire.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quae si cui levior videtur, illa quidem certe, quae summa sunt, ex quo fonte hauriam sentio.
examples.translation: Yet insignificant though these powers may seem to be, I fully realize from what source I draw all that is highest in them.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a lion.
Latin: Grandis feles, speciei Panthera leo
Latin: Pellis leonis

examples.original: Alimenta tibi leonum et vulturum eripio.”
examples.translation: I am merely depriving you of food which sustains lions and vultures.”
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit: Aut ubi muneribus nati sua munera mater Addidit, externo marmore dives opus.
examples.translation: Only walk leisurely beneath the Pompeian shade, when the sun draws nigh to Hercules’ shaggy lion, or where the mother has added her own gifts to her son’s, a work rich with marble coating.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or pertaining to a consul, consular (very freq.): aetas, the age required by law for the consular office, viz. the 43d year

examples.original: P. Volumnius consularis vidit cadentem.
examples.translation: Publius Volumnius, a former consul, saw him fall.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tiberius patruus petenti honores consularia ornamenta detulit;
examples.translation: His paternal uncle Tiberius gave him the consular regalia, when he asked for office;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Valerius Catullus, consulari familia iuvenis, stupratum a se ac latera sibi contubernio eius defessa etiam vociferatus est.
examples.translation: Valerius Catullus, a young man of a consular family, bragged that he had penetrated the emperor and worn himself out in intercourse with him.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: the age of youth (from the twentieth to the fortieth year), youth (rare, except in transf. meaning; cf. juventas).

examples.original: Iuventute armata immissa vastatur agri quod inter urbem ac Fidenas est.
examples.translation: Arming the young men, they sent them to ravage the land between the City and Fidenae.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hunc eximium florem iuventutis eo etiam quod ut duplex acciperent stipendium decreverant, spei animorumque implevere;
examples.translation: This choice flower of their manhood they inspired with additional hope and courage by a decree which allowed them double pay.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Detegit inbelles animas nil fortiter ausa Seditio tantumque fugam meditata iuventus Ac ducis invicti rebus lassata secundis.
examples.translation: That you have no stomach for fighting is revealed; for your mutiny ends in words;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: milk.
Latin: Potus albus, qui ab mammalibus femineis variis producitur

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Semper enim boni assiduique domini referta cella vinaria, olearia, etiam penaria est, villaque tota locuples est, abundat porco haedo agno gallina, lacte caseo melle.
examples.translation: For the provident and industrious proprietor always has his store-room and cellars well filled with oil and wine and provisions;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a likeness, image, form, representation, semblance (class.; syn.: imago, effigies, signum).

examples.original: Herculis magnum simulacrum in Capitolio positum dedicatumque.
examples.translation: The great statue of Hercules was set up and dedicated on the Capitol.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Illius exemplo violes simulacra Minervae, Aulidis a portu qui leve vertit iter.
examples.translation: Mayst thou violate Minerva’s image after example of him who pursued a nimble path from Aulis’ haven.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cuius, uti memoror, rei simulacrum et imago ante oculos semper nobis versatur et instat.
examples.translation: Of this fact there is, I recall, an image and similitude always moving and present before our eyes.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: soft fleshy body parts (usu. pl.), internal organs; entrails, flesh; offspring

examples.original: Infandum domini per viscera ferrum Exegit famulus;
examples.translation: The conqueror had once for all issued his orders which included every crime.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Illa purulenta et quae tantum non ex ipso igne in os transferuntur, iudicas sine noxa in ipsis visceribus extingui?
examples.translation: Do you judge that the corrupted dishes which a man swallows almost burning from the kitchen fire, are quenched in the digestive system without doing harm?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tunc laqueis captare feras et fallere visco Inventum et magnos canibus circumdare saltus. Omnia enim ista sagacitas hominum, non sapientia invenit.
examples.translation: Of setting traps for game, and liming twigs For birds, and girdling mighty woods with dogs.a It was man’s ingenuity, not his wisdom, that discovered all these devices.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to go round in a circle, to surround, encompass, environ, gird, wreathe, crown, etc. (class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: Huc inclinavit Antonius cingique vallum corona iussit.
examples.translation: Antonius inclined to meet his troops’ desires and ordered the investment of the enemy’s camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ab hac spe repulsi Nervii vallo pedum ix et fossa pedum xv hiberna cingunt.
examples.translation: Foiled of this hope, the Nervii encompassed the station with a rampart nine feet high and a trench fifteen feet wide.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Prima luce ad moenia omnibus copiis admotis corona cinxit urbem subsidiaque firma, ne qua eruptio fieret, portis opposuit.
examples.translation: With the dawn he led up all his forces under the walls and invested the city, posting strong supports to prevent any sally from the gates.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: somewhat, some

examples.original: Prior aliquanto Volumnius castra cepit;
examples.translation: Volumnius succeeded somewhat sooner in capturing the camp.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Praedae ex adsiduis populationibus, quod omnia in locum tutum congesta erant, fuit aliquantum.
examples.translation: There was a considerable accumulation of spoils from this constant raiding, because everything had been heaped up there for safety.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Resiluit aliquantum, ita tamen ut liberale adhuc spatium sit, si quis cum ipso, ut ita dicam, die surgat.
examples.translation: It has shrunk considerably, but yet will still allow a goodly space of time if one rises, so to speak, with the day itself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: restless, agitated, anxious, solicitous, disturbed, alarmed, in a state of trepidation, etc.

examples.original: Ab Suessula nuntii trepidi Capuam, inde equites citati ad Valerium consulem opem oratum veniunt.
examples.translation: From Suessula the alarming news was carried to Capua, whence gallopers were dispatched to Valerius the consul, to implore assistance.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tristes praesagia curas Exagitant, trepida quatitur formidine somnus, Thessaliam nox omnis habet;
examples.translation: For her sorrow is intensified by forebodings, and her sleep broken by anxious fears.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Et Fabius cum equitatu impetum dederat et consul eruptionem e castris in trepidos iam hostes fecerat;
examples.translation: Fabius had delivered a charge with his cavalry; the consul had made a sally from the camp against the enemy, who were already wavering;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the country (opp. to the city), lands, fields; a country-seat, farm, estate, etc.
Latin: Regio, quae ad agriculturam adhibetur, saepe urbi opponitur
Latin: Praedium

examples.original: Est tibi rure bono generosae fertilis uvae Vinea?
examples.translation: You have a fruitful estate and a vineyard abundant in fine grapes?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Infelix est Fabricius, quod rus suum, quantum a re publica vacavit, fodit?
examples.translation: Is Fabricius unfortunate because, whenever he has leisure from affairs of state, he tills his fields?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc tam segne solum raras tamen exerit herbas, Quas Nasamon, gens dura, legit, qui proxima ponto Nudus rura tenet;
examples.translation: Yet this barren soil here and there sends forth grass which is gathered by the Nasamonians, a rude and naked race who dwell close by the sea;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a bull
Latin: taurus aut vacca, animal mammiferum specie Bos taurus

examples.original: Minucius index bove aurata donatus est.
examples.translation: Lucius Minucius gave evidence against him and was presented with a gilded ox.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Utque ferox Phalaris, lingua prius ense resecta More bovis Paphio clausus in aere gemas.
examples.translation: And like fierce Phalaris, thy tongue first severed with the sword, mayst thou bellow like an ox imprisoned in Paphian bronze.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to steal, purloin, pilfer (syn.: latrocinor, clepo, rapio).

examples.original: Quis furor, o cives, quae tanta licentia ferri?
examples.translation: What madness was this, my countrymen, what fierce orgy of slaughter?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quae enim res alia civiles furores peperit quam nimiae felicitates?
examples.translation: For what else produced those outbursts of domestic strife but excessive prosperity?
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Adice nunc scordalum et furem deprensum et illum, cui vox sua in balineo placet.
examples.translation: Then, perhaps, a professional a comes along, shouting out the score; that is the finishing touch.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: It is seemly, comely, becoming; it beseems, behooves, is fitting, suitable, proper

examples.original: Hoc prudentem virum non decet;
examples.translation: This quality does not befit a man of sense;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex quo fit ut laudandus is sit qui mortem oppetat pro re publica, quod deceat cariorem nobis esse patriam quam nosmet ipsos.
examples.translation: This explains why praise is owed to one who dies for the commonwealth, because it becomes us to love our country more than ourselves.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Bona autem omnia carere culpa decet;
examples.translation: All goods, however, ought properly to be free from blame;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: full-grown

examples.original: Planities erat magna et in ea tumulus terrenus satis grandis.
examples.translation: There was a large plain, and in it a mound of earth of considerable size.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Chelidon, unus ex Cleopatrae mollibus, patrimonium grande possedit.
examples.translation: Chelidon, one of Cleopatra’s eunuchs, possessed great wealth;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Corpore et statura fuit grandi, aquilo colore, facie rusticana, valetudine varia;
examples.translation: He was tall and of full habit, with a dark complexion and a rustic appearance.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: to flee away; or, with reference to the result, to escape
Latin: vitare
Latin: ab hostibus persecutus currere et nondum capi posse

examples.original: Non avis utiliter viscatis effugit alis;
examples.translation: The bird cannot make good its escape when once its wings are limed;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Bene autem mori est effugere male vivendi periculum.
examples.translation: And dying well means escape from the danger of living ill.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Statim exercitus in fugam, nec duces fortiores quam ut effugerent.
examples.translation: The army immediately turned to flight, nor were the generals too brave to flee;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: natural, i. e.

examples.original: Nulla enim sapientia naturalia corporis vitia ponuntur.
examples.translation: For by no wisdom can natural weaknesses of the body be removed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad amicitiam fert illum nulla utilitas sua, sed naturalis inritatio.
examples.translation: Natural promptings, and not his own selfish needs, draw him into friendships.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Naturales divitias dixit parabiles esse quod parvo esset natura contenta.
examples.translation: He said that natural wealth is easily won, because nature is satisfied with little.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: greatness, grandeur, dignity, majesty.
Latin: Status maior magnitudinis; dignitas

examples.original: Liber Quintus Quis potis est dignum pollenti pectore carmen condere pro rerum maiestate hisque repertis?
examples.translation: Who is able with mighty mind to build a song worthy of the majesty of nature and these discoveries?
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Cum his cenare non sustinet et maiestatis suae deminutionem putat ad eandem mensam cum servo suo accedere.
examples.translation: With slaves like these the master cannot bear to dine; he would think it beneath his dignity to associate with his slave at the same table!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vicit disciplina militaris, vicit imperii maiestas, quae in discrimine fuerunt an ulla post hanc diem essent.
examples.translation: The discipline of war, the majesty of government, have got the victory, despite the danger that this day would see the end of them.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: immediately, straightway, forthwith, quickly, without delay

examples.original: Missus extemplo Varus cum expedita manu paucos repugnantium interfecit;
examples.translation: Varus was despatched at once with a force in light marching order.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quod ad me attinet, extemplo hinc domum abire in animo est, ne cuius facti dictive contagione praesens violer.” Haec locutus abiit.
examples.translation: For my own part I intend to go home at once, lest being on the spot I might be implicated in some act or word and be compromised.” With this he departed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Recipit extemplo animum pedestris acies, postquam iuventutis proceres aequato genere pugnae secum partem periculi sustinentes vidit.
examples.translation: It restored at once the courage of the foot to see the young nobles on even terms with themselves and sharing in the danger.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a blow, stroke, wound, stripe (class.; syn.: ictus, verbera, vulnus).
Latin: regio, area, zona

examples.original: Qua sua Penteliden proles est ulta Lycurgum, Haec maneat teli te quoque plaga novi.
examples.translation: As his own offspring was revenged upon Lycurgus, the Pentelid, so may the stroke of a strange weapon await thee also.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid mihi tunc animi est, ubi sumit tela viator Atque oculis plagae destinat ante locum?
examples.translation: What spirit have I then, when the traveller takes his weapons, and his eye picks out the spot for his blow?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ab hoc aliquot plagis Eumenes vulneratur neque eo magis ex proelio excessit, sed acrius hostis institit.
examples.translation: From his opponent Eumenes suffered several wounds, but he did not on that account leave the field, but attacked the enemy with renewed vigour.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: son of Jupiter and Latona, twinbrother of Diana

examples.original: Post hunc Apollinem et Martem et Iovem et Minervam.
examples.translation: After him they set Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Iubet igitur nos Pythius Apollo noscere nosmet ipsos;
examples.translation: Accordingly the Pythian Apollo bids us ’learn to know ourselves’;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam ob rem cave Catoni anteponas ne istum quidem ipsum, quem Apollo, ut ais, sapientissimum iudicavit;
examples.translation: Therefore, take care not to give the precedence over Cato even to that man, whom, as you say, Apollo adjudged the wisest of men;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: philosophy.
Latin: Studium sapientiae rationisque

examples.original: Ad philosophiam ergo confugiendum est;
examples.translation: One must therefore take refuge in philosophy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est quod nos paupertas a philosophia revocet, ne egestas quidem.
examples.translation: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy,—no, nor even actual want.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Incredibilis philosophiae vis est ad omnem fortuitam vim retundendam.
examples.translation: The power of philosophy to blunt the blows of chance is beyond belief.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: an insurrectionary separation (political or military); dissension, civil discord, insurrection, mutiny, sedition

examples.original: Quo facto maturata est seditio.
examples.translation: This brought the revolt to a head.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iamque haud procul seditione res erat;
examples.translation: By this time the feeling was grown well-nigh seditious;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nullo loco deest seditionis voluntarius comes;
examples.translation: At no point was there any lack of volunteers to join the rising;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Macedonia
Latin: Regio in superiore parte Graeciae
Latin: Regnum Antiquum Macedonicum

examples.original: Quot oppida in Syria, quot in Macedonia devorata sunt?
examples.translation: How many towns in Syria, how many in Macedonia, have been swallowed up!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Horum illa nihil fecit nam et in Macedoniam profecta est et ibi crudelissime se gessit.
examples.translation: She adopted neither of these recommendations; for she proceeded to Macedonia and conducted herself there most cruelly.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Hic ego nunc de praetore Macedoniae nihil dicam amplius, nisi eum et civem optimum semper et mihi amicum fuisse, sed eadem timuisse quae ceteros.
examples.translation: I shall not allude here to the praetor of Macedonia, save to remark that he had always been an unimpeachable patriot, and on good terms with myself, but the universal fears were also his;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to look or

examples.original: Si veritas tota perspecta est;
examples.translation: How does a man reach this condition?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ea scientia et verborum vis et natura orationis et consequentium repugnantiumve ratio potest perspici;
examples.translation: This sciencea explains to us the meaning of terms, the nature of predication, and the law of consistency and contradiction;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sic enim mihi perspicere videor, ita natos esse nos, ut inter omnis esset societas quaedam, maior autem, ut quisque proxime accederet.
examples.translation: For it seems clear to me that we were so created that between us all there exists a certain tie which strengthens with our proximity to each other.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: thick, dense, i. e. consisting of parts crowded together. opp. to rarus

examples.original: Postquam impulsos sensit Antonius, denso agmine obturbabat.
examples.translation: After Antonius saw that they were shaken, he assailed them in mass formation.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Praecipiti cursu vaesanum Caesaris agmen In densos agitur cuneos, perque arma, per hostem Quaerit iter.
examples.translation: With headlong speed and fury Caesar’s men charged the close-packed columns, forcing a way through shields and through soldiers.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ibi modico praesidio relicto egressus omnibus copiis partem militum locis circa densa virgulta obscuris subsidere in insidiis iussit;
examples.translation: A part of his men he ordered to lie in ambush, on this side and on that, where thick underbrush afforded cover;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a notice, information, discovery, disclosure, charge (class.).

examples.original: Ea res est Helvetiis per indicium enuntiata.
examples.translation: The design was revealed to the Helvetii by informers.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Haec ergo et eiusmodi vitia, quae alicui inpressit imitatio, non sunt indicia luxuriae nec animi corrupti;
examples.translation: These and similar faults, which imitation stamps upon one’s style, are not necessarily indications of loose standards or of debased mind;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pugna indicio fuit quos gesserint animos; namque ita conflixerunt ut aliquamdiu in neutram partem inclinarent acies.
examples.translation: The engagement testified how resolute they were, for they so fought that for some time neither battle-line gave ground.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To bring together several objects into one whole, to unite, connect (class. in prose and poetry, not in Hor.).

examples.original: Enati sunt dentes; huic constitutioni conciliatur.
examples.translation: Then his teeth grow, and he is fitted to that condition also.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si, ut tu dicis, gratiae conciliandae causa, quadraginta istorum accessio milium quid valet?
examples.translation: If, as you maintain, it was to effect a reconciliation, what is the point of the odd forty thousand?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Accedebat huc quod in concilio Aeduorum Dumnorix dixerat sibi a Caesare regnum civitatis deferri;
examples.translation: Moreover, in the council of the Aedui Dumnorix had said that Caesar meant to offer him the kingship of the state;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to hang up, hang, suspend (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Execranda autem superstitio ligaturarum, in quibus etiam inaures virorum in summis ex una parte auriculis suspensae deputantur: non ad placendum hominibus sed ad serviendum daemonibus adhibentur.
examples.translation: It is an accursed superstition to wear amulets,a among which must be reckoned also the earringsb that men wear on the top part of the ear on one side;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to bear or carry along; to convey any thing heavy (class.; syn.: fero, gero, veho).
Latin: (Generatim) movendo res ex uno loco in alium

examples.original: Vercingetorix iubet portas claudi, ne castra nudentur.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix ordered the gates to be shut, lest the camp should be deserted.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hunc Aurora diem spectacula tanta ferentem Quam primum croceis roscida portet equis!
examples.translation: The day that brings so great a spectacle—let dewy Aurora speed it hither on her saffron car!
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Has spes cogitationesque secum portantes urbem ingressi sunt, domicilioque ibi comparato L. Tarquinium Priscum edidere nomen.
examples.translation: Having obtained a house, they gave out the name of Lucius Tarquinius Priscus.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: unlike, dissimilar, different (as the opp. of similis and consimilis, v. 3. dis, II.; cf.: dispar, impar, absimilis; very freq. and class.).—Constr. with the

examples.original: Ad duas dissimiles res duo diiuncta interdicta sunt.
examples.translation: To meet the two different cases, two separate injunctions have been framed.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dissimilis utrique causa erat, sed utrique magnifica.
examples.translation: In each case, the reason was different, but it was in each case a noble reason.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Virtutem enim illi non eripiet, sed opera eius inpediet.” Hoc recte diceretur, nisi dissimilis esset gubernatoris condicio et sapientis.
examples.translation: The wise man’s purpose in conducting his life is not to accomplish at all hazards what he tries, but to do all things rightly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: gone by, past

examples.original: Si quid adiecisset, fuisset simile praeterito.
examples.translation: Had another year been added, it would merely have been like the past.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid si etiam iucunda memoria est praeteritorum malorum?
examples.translation: What if the memory of past evils be actually pleasant?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: De divinis humanisque discendum est, de praeteritis de futuris, de caducis de aeternis, de tempore.
examples.translation: One must learn about things divine and human, the past and the future, the ephemeral and the eternal;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be before a thing; hence, to be set over, to preside or rule over, to have the charge or command of, to superintend (class.).
Latin: Praesidere, curare

examples.original: Domi autem creant decem praetores, qui exercitui praeessent, in iis Miltiadem;
examples.translation: But at home they appointed ten generals to command the army, including Miltiades;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Militiades

examples.original: His autem omnibus druidibus praeest unus, qui summam inter eos habet auctoritatem.
examples.translation: Of all these Druids one is chief, who has the highest authority among them.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Praeerat classi Claudius Apollinaris, neque fidei constans neque strenuus in perfidia;
examples.translation: The fleet was commanded by Claudius Apollinaris, who was neither strong in loyalty nor determined in treachery;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a., to hunt, chase (cf.: capto, aucupor).

examples.original: Ut Cremonam venere, novum immensumque opus occurrit.
examples.translation: When they reached Cremona they found a new task of enormous difficulty before them.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cernit tabe iecur madidum, venasque minaces Hostili de parte videt.
examples.translation: He saw the liver flabby with corruption and with boding streaks in its hostile half.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Sed tu praecipue curvis venare theatris: Haec loca sunt voto fertiliora tuo.
examples.translation: But specially do your hunting in the round theatres: more bountifully do these repay your vows.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: before, sooner than; until
Latin: priusquam
Latin: (indicans statum prae alia re, quae post quam indicatur.), priusquam

examples.original: Rapum autem arboris, antequam obruat, radit.
examples.translation: These are of necessity still soft;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hic primo Carpinatius, antequam in istius familiaritatem tantam pervenisset, aliquotiens ad socios litteras de istius iniuriis miserat.
examples.translation: In the early days, before establishing this close connexion with Verres, Carpinatius had several times written to the company complaining of wrongs done by Verres;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ceterum antequam consules in Etruriam pervenirent, Senones Galli multitudine ingenti ad Clusium venerunt legionem Romanam castraque oppugnaturi.
examples.translation: But before the consuls could reach Etruria, the Senonian Gauls were come with a great multitude to Clusium, to besiege the Roman legion in camp there.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: an undulating, boiling, waving, tossing; a waving, heaving, billowy motion.
Latin: Calor, ardor, fervor
Latin: Undae fluctusque maris

examples.original: Cui enim dubium potest esse, quin si aestus malum est, et aestuare malum sit?
examples.translation: For who can doubt that, if heat is an evil, it is also an evil to be hot?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pastor fatigatus aestu cum sub arbore condormisset et serpens ad eum proreperet, e palude culex provolavit atque inter duo tempora aculeum fixit pastori.
examples.translation: When a shepherd, exhausted by the heat, had fallen asleep under a tree, and a snake was creeping upon him, a gnat flew from a marsh and stung the shepherd between his two temples;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Ne illud quidem, quod existimas facturum eum, faciet, ut ambitiosis rebus inplicitus semper aestus earum ferat.
examples.translation: Neither will he, as you imagine, become so involved in ambitious schemes that he will have continually to endure their ebb and flow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to treat with violence (corporeally, and, more freq., mentally), to injure, dishonor, outrage, violate (cf.: laedo, polluo, contamino).

examples.original: Hospitem violare fas non putant;
examples.translation: They do not think it right to outrage a guest;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quaecumque est veneris subita violata rapina, Gaudet, et inprobitas muneris instar habet.
examples.translation: She whom a sudden assault has taken by storm is pleased, and counts the audacity as a compliment.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sit igitur, iudices, sanctum apud vos, humanissimos homines, hoc poëtae nomen, quod nulla umquam barbaria violavit.
examples.translation: The very rocks of the wilderness give back a sympathetic echo to the voice;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Consisting of earth, earthy, earthen (class.).

examples.original: Luna suis vicibus Tethyn terrenaque miscet;
examples.translation: The changes of the moon bring sea and land in contact.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Planities erat magna et in ea tumulus terrenus satis grandis.
examples.translation: There was a large plain, and in it a mound of earth of considerable size.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to cause to break or burst forth; to burst, sunder (rare; mostly ante-class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; rūpi, ruptum, 3

examples.original: Erat hominum conventus maximus, summum silentium, summa exspectatio quonam esset eius cupiditas eruptura;
examples.translation: There was a great crowd present—dead silence—breathless anxiety as to what line of attack his greed would adopt.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed ubi totis castris in fama proditio, recurrens in principia miles praescriptum Vespasiani nomen, proiectas Vitellii effigies aspexit, vastum primo silentium, mox cuncta simul erumpunt.
examples.translation: But when the news of the treason spread through the whole camp, the soldiers ran to headquarters, where they saw Vespasian’s name put up on the standards and the statues of Vitellius overthrown;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quibusdam etiam constantissimis in conspectu populi sudor erumpit, non aliter quam fatigatis et aestuantibus solet, quibusdam tremunt genua dicturis, quorundam dentes colliduntur, lingua titubat, labra concurrunt.
examples.translation: The steadiest speaker, when before the public, often breaks into a perspiration, as if he had wearied or over-heated himself; some tremble in the knees when they rise to speak;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to drive out or away, thrust out or away, to eject, expel (class.).

examples.original: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
examples.translation: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quis enim iam meminisset eum bene de re publica meritum, nisi et ab improbis expulsus esset et per bonos restitutus?
examples.translation: For who at this time would remember the services he conferred upon the state, had he not been banished by traitors and restored by the efforts of patriots?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: At milites legionis septimae, testudine facta et aggere ad munitiones adiecto, locum ceperunt eosque ex silvis expulerunt paucis vulneribus acceptis.
examples.translation: The enemy came out of the woods to fight in small groups, and sought to prevent our troops from entering the fortifications.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: of or belonging to the city or town
Latin: Qui ad urbem (Romam) pertinet

examples.original: Is labor urbano militi insolitus contundit animos.
examples.translation: The work involved was strange to the town troops and broke their spirit.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Reliquum anni quietum ab urbanis motibus et ab externis mansit.
examples.translation: The remainder of the year passed without disturbances in either domestic or foreign relations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Igitur tamquam omnis res publica in Vespasiani sinum cecidisset, primores senatus et plerique equestris ordinis omnisque miles urbanus et vigiles domum Flavii Sabini complevere.
examples.translation: Therefore, as if the entire state had fallen into Vespasian’s arms, the leading senators, a majority of the equestrian order, and all the city guards and watchmen crowded the house of Flavius Sabinus.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: Athena
Latin: Dea Graeca quae Minervae respondet

examples.original: Ateius Philologus libertinus Athenis est natus.
examples.translation: Lucius Ateius Philologus was a freedman, born at Athens.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Neque ita multo post Nicanor Piraeo est potitus, sine quo Athenae omnino esse non possunt.
examples.translation: Not long afterwards Nicanor got possession of the Piraeus, without which Athens cannot exist at all;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Phocion

examples.original: Huius cum sententiam plurimi essent secuti, Miltiades, non dubitans tam multis consciis ad regis aures consilia sua perventura, Chersonesum reliquit ac rursus Athenas demigravit.
examples.translation: When the opinion of Histiaeus met with general approval, Miltiades, feeling sure that with so many witnesses his proposal would come to the king’s ears, left the Chersonesus and returned to Athens.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Militiades

definitions: English: pliant, flexible, tough, tenacious, sticky, viscous (syn.: flexilis, tardus, serus).
Latin: Qui tempus certum non magnopere movetur
Latin: Viscōsus, tenāx

examples.original: Consistam lentisque oculis laetusque videbo Strata per obscenas corpora nuda vias.
examples.translation: I will stop, and leisurely with glad eyes gaze on naked bodies strewn on the unsightly roads.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis.
examples.translation: Read Cicero: his style has unity; it moves with a modulated pace, and is gentle without being degenerate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Brevis enim profecto res est, si uno tenore peragitur nec ipsi per intermissiones has intervallaque lentiorem spem nostram facimus.
examples.translation: For surely it is a thing soon done, if we carry it through without stopping, and do not ourselves drag out our hopes with these interruptions and delays.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the great sea that encompasses the land, the ocean

examples.original: Inde cum Venetis etiam navale bellum, sed maior cum Oceano quam cum ipsis navibus rixa.
examples.translation: Next came a naval war with the Veneti; but it was a struggle rather against the ocean than against the enemy’s fleet.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Partito exercitu Titum Labienum cum legionibus tribus ad Oceanum versus in eas partes quae Menapios attingunt proficisci iubet;
examples.translation: Having divided the army, he ordered Titus Labienus to proceed with three legions towards the districts which touch the Menapii;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar in patriam victor invehitur, primum de Gallia triumphum trahens: hic erat Rhenus et Rhodanus et ex auro captivus Oceanus.
examples.translation: Caesar returned home victorious and celebrated a triumph first over Gaul, in which figured the Rhine and the Rhone and the captive Ocean represented in gold.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a standing, a standing still.
