examples.original: Hi iaculo pisces, illi capiuntur ab hamis: Hos cava contento retia fune trahunt.
examples.translation: These fish are caught with spears, those with hooks; these ones are dragged with taut ropes in bulging nets.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iamque ubi pulvereae fuerint confusa farinae, Protinus in cumeris omnia cerne cavis.
examples.translation: And now when it is mixed with the dusty grain, sift it all straightway in hollow sieves.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quam ob rem cave Catoni anteponas ne istum quidem ipsum, quem Apollo, ut ais, sapientissimum iudicavit;
examples.translation: Therefore, take care not to give the precedence over Cato even to that man, whom, as you say, Apollo adjudged the wisest of men;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to weary, tire, fatigue; to vex, harass (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; but defatigare is freq. in Cic. and Caes.).

examples.original: Alit lectio ingenium et studio fatigatum, non sine studio tamen, reficit.
examples.translation: We ought not to confine ourselves either to writing or to reading;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pastor fatigatus aestu cum sub arbore condormisset et serpens ad eum proreperet, e palude culex provolavit atque inter duo tempora aculeum fixit pastori.
examples.translation: When a shepherd, exhausted by the heat, had fallen asleep under a tree, and a snake was creeping upon him, a gnat flew from a marsh and stung the shepherd between his two temples;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Quibusdam etiam constantissimis in conspectu populi sudor erumpit, non aliter quam fatigatis et aestuantibus solet, quibusdam tremunt genua dicturis, quorundam dentes colliduntur, lingua titubat, labra concurrunt.
examples.translation: The steadiest speaker, when before the public, often breaks into a perspiration, as if he had wearied or over-heated himself; some tremble in the knees when they rise to speak;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a sacrifice

examples.original: Etenim quod sacrificium tam vetustum est quam hoc, quod a regibus aequale huius urbis accepimus?
examples.translation: And indeed what sacrifice is so ancient as that which we received from our kings, and which is coeval with our city?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Is quibusdam piacularibus sacrificiis factis, quae deinde genti Horatiae tradita sunt, transmisso per viam tigillo capite adoperto velut sub iugum misit iuvenem.
examples.translation: And so, that the flagrant murder might yet be cleansed away, by some kind of expiatory rite, the father was commanded to make atonement for his son at the public cost.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: good, proper, serviceable, excellent

examples.original: De quibis tris video sententias ferri, quarum nullam probo : unam, ut eodem modo erga amicum affecti simus quo erga nosmet ipsos;
examples.translation: On this point I observe that three views are usually advanced, none of which I approve : first, ”That we should have the same feeling for our friends that we have for ourselves”;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ratio ista quam defendis, praecepta quae didicisti, quae probas, funditus evertunt amicitiam, quamvis eam Epicurus, ut facit, in caelum efferat laudibus.
examples.translation: The system you uphold, the principles you have studied and accept, undermine the very foundations of friendship, however much Epicurus may, as he does, praise friendship up to the skies.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illud nullo modo probo, quod ait Metrodorus: esse aliquam cognatam tristitiae voluptatem, hanc esse captandam in eiusmodi tempore. Ipsa Metrodori verba subscripsi.
examples.translation: And in no wise do I approve of the remark of Metrodorus—that there is a certain pleasure akin to sadness, and that one should give chase thereto at such times as these.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: make ready beforehand, to prepare, equip, make preparations for, etc. (class.; cf.: paro, apparo).

examples.original: Ante ad mortem quam ad vitam praeparandi sumus.
examples.translation: We must make ready for death before we make ready for life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non enim ex praeparato locutus est, sed subito deprehensus.
examples.translation: For he spoke not from forethought, but was suddenly caught off his guard.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et ille quidem ad praeparatum a Manlio in Etruria exercitum proficiscitur signa inlaturus urbi.
examples.translation: He set out for the army which Manlius had already prepared in Etruria, intending to march upon the city.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: A roll of writing, a roll, book, volume

examples.original: Quis de exceptione et formula perpetietur ilea immensa volumina quae pro M. Tullio aut Aulo Caecina legimus?
examples.translation: Would anyone endure the interminable arguments about pleas and procedure which we get in the speeches delivered in defence of M. Tullius or Aulus Caecina?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Illud autem vide, ne ista lectio auctorum multorum et omnis generis voluminum habeat aliquid vagum et instabile.
examples.translation: Be careful, however, lest this reading of many authors and books of every sort may tend to make you discursive and unsteady.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Niger inficit horror Terga maris, longo per multa volumina tractu Aestuat unda minax, flatusque incerta futuri Turbida testantur conceptos aequora ventos.
examples.translation: A shudder of darkness blackened the ridges of the sea; the angry deep boiled with a long swell, wave following wave;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a delay.
Latin: Cunctatio, dilatio, tarditas
Latin: intervallum et spatium temporis

examples.original: Alioqui quid in mora est?
examples.translation: At any rate, what is there to hinder?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vidi ego, quod fuerat primo sanabile, vulnus Dilatum longae damna tulisse morae.
examples.translation: I have seen a wound, that at first was healable, by tarrying suffer the penalty of long delay.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cum ad id moris eius insueta expavisset minor Fabia, risui sorori fuit miranti ignorare id sororem;
examples.translation: At this the younger Fabia, being unused to the custom, went white, which made the elder laugh with surprise at her sister’s ignorance.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: futur. dormibo
Latin: Quietem capere
Latin: indormire alci rei

examples.original: Tu quoque dum coleris, nos te dormire putemus; Aptius a summa conspiciere manu.
examples.translation: So while you are at your toilet let us think that you are asleep;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quod nisi quieris, Menelae, hac dextra occides, diurnum accipit, in centunculo dormit.
examples.translation: Peace, Menelaus, or this hand shall slay thee!a receives a daily pittance and sleeps on rags.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam qui leviter dormit, et species secundum quietem capit et aliquando dormire se dormiens cogitat;
examples.translation: For he whose sleep is light pursues visions during slumber, and sometimes, though asleep, is conscious that he is asleep;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to cover, cover over any thing (class.; syn.: tego, velo, induo).
Latin: Tegere, ponere tectum

examples.original: Idea erat Vergilii facies, futuri operis exemplar.
examples.translation: The ”idea” was Vergil’s outward appearance, and this was the pattern of the intended work.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Atqui haec patefactio quasi rerum opertarum, cum quid quidque sit aperitur, definitio est;
examples.translation: Now this process of disclosing latent meanings, of revealing what a particular thing is, is the process of definition;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque Pometinae manubiae, quae perducendo ad culmen operi destinatae erant, vix in fundamenta suppeditavere.
examples.translation: Hence the Pometian spoils, which had been destined to carry the building up to the roof, barely sufficed for the foundations.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to gnaw (class.).

examples.original: Syllaba autem caseum non rodit;
examples.translation: Now a syllable does not eat cheese.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Terra salutares herbas, eademque nocentes Nutrit, et urticae proxima saepe rosa est;
examples.translation: The same earth fosters healing herbs and noxious, and oft is the nettle nearest to the rose;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a stake

examples.original: Anxur fuit, quae nunc Tarracinae sunt, urbs prona in paludes.
examples.translation: Anxur, the Tarracinae of our day, was a city which sloped down towards the marshes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non hos palus in bello latrociniisque natos, non silvae morantur.
examples.translation: No marsh, no woods check these children of war and brigandage.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Labienus primo vineas agere, cratibus atque aggere paludem explere atque iter munire conabatur.
examples.translation: Labienus at first tried to move up mantlets, fill in the marsh with hurdles and earth, and build a roadway.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: walk; esp. to go hastily or rapidly, to rush (syn. incedo).
Latin: Vadō traicere
Latin: Ambulare incipere, ire

examples.original: Non ego per praeceps et acuta cacumina vadam, Nec iuvenum quisquam me duce captus erit.
examples.translation: I am not the man to go by precipitous paths and rocky heights; no youth under my leadership will be captured.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid turpius ”amne silvisque ripa comantibus?” Vide ut ”alveum lintribus arent versoque vado remittant hortos.” Quid?
examples.translation: What is more unbecoming than the words:c ”A stream and a bank covered with long-tressed woods”?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ibi vadis repertis partem suarum copiarum traducere conati sunt, eo consilio ut, si possent, castellum, cui praeerat Quintus Titurius legatus, expugnarent pontemque interscinderent;
examples.translation: There they found fords, and endeavoured to throw part of their forces across, intending if they could to storm the fort commanded by the lieutenant-general, Quintus Titurius, and break down the bridge;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to delay, hesitate, Enn. ap.

examples.original: Legio classica nihil cunctata praetorianis adiungitur;
examples.translation: The legion of marines without hesitation joined the praetorians.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Nec diutius Galba cunctatus speciosiora suadentibus accessit.
examples.translation: Galba did not delay any longer, but favoured those who offered the more specious advice.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cunctati aliquamdiu sunt, dum alius alium, ut proelium incipiant, circumspectant.
examples.translation: They hesitated for a moment, each looking to his neighbour to begin the fight.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: A vessel made of logs fastened together, a raft: rates vocantur tigna colligata, quae per aquam aguntur; quo vocabulo interdum etiam naves significantur, Paul. ex

examples.original: Hic teneat nostras ancora iacta rates.
examples.translation: Here let the anchor be thrown, and hold my bark secure.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quis ratibus tantis fugientia crederet ire Agmina?
examples.translation: But they were scattered round the coasts;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Eam rem consules rati, ut erat, perniciosam ad patres deferunt, sed delatam consulere ordine non licuit;
examples.translation: This seemed to the consuls, as indeed it was, a mischievous practice.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to prepare or make ready for something (esp. with effort, care, expense), to put in order

examples.original: Reliquum diei apparandis armis consumptum est.
examples.translation: The rest of the day they spent in making ready their arms.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Collegae funus quanto tum potuit apparatu fecit;
examples.translation: His colleague’s funeral he celebrated with all the pomp then possible;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quid sibi autem illi scribae, quid lictores, quid ceteri, quos apparere huic quaestioni video, volunt?
examples.translation: What, indeed, is the meaning of those clerks, of the lictors, of the other officers whom I see in attendance at this court?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: enough, adequately; sufficiently; well enough, quite

examples.original: Ad manum est, quod sat est.
examples.translation: That which is enough is ready to our hands.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Idem est autem omni saeculo, quod sat est.
examples.translation: But in every age, what is enough remains the same.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the name of a Roman gens; e. g.

examples.original: Q. Sulpicium legatum praeficit castris;
examples.translation: The lieutenant Quintus Sulpicius he put in charge of the camp;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sulpicio Samnites, Apuli Aemilio sorte evenerunt.
examples.translation: The lots assigned the Samnites to Sulpicius, the Apulians to Aemilius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: P. Sulpicius per mediam hostium aciem cum equitatu perrupit.
examples.translation: Publius Sulpicius broke through the enemy’s centre with his cavalry.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bend, turn, incline; to verge
English: to weigh out
Latin: pecuniam dare pro aliqua re

examples.original: Sed redeo ad mortem impendentem.
examples.translation: But I return to the question of impending death.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ab eodem collegaque eius M. Valerio Maximo viae per agros publica impensa factae.
examples.translation: He and his colleague, Marcus Valerius Maximus, built roads through the countryside at the public costs.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to pour in, upon, or into (syn. invergere).
English: tearing away, seizing.
English: to make again, make anew, put in condition again; to remake, restore, renew, rebuild, repair, refit, recruit, etc. (freq. and class.; syn.: renovo, restauro, redintegro).
Latin: reconstituo, facere aliquid de novo

examples.original: Ita tribuni plebis magna ex parte iidem refecti.
examples.translation: So, for the most part, the same tribunes were returned to office.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Locatur opus id quod ex mea pecunia reficiatur; ego me refecturum dico;
examples.translation: Here is a contract to be made for doing a repair for which I shall have to pay;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Alit lectio ingenium et studio fatigatum, non sine studio tamen, reficit.
examples.translation: We ought not to confine ourselves either to writing or to reading;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: impious, execrable, abominable, nefarious

examples.original: Non erat obscurum quid homo improbus ac nefarius cogitaret;
examples.translation: The rascal’s immoral plan was not obscure;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Multa enim et in deos et in homines impie nefarieque commisit, quorum scelerum poenis agitatur et a mente consilioque deducitur.
examples.translation: The thought of retribution for his evil deeds, for his sins against heaven and his crimes against man, is distracting his mind and expelling good sense and sanity.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hunc tamen hominem tam audacem, tam nefarium, tam nocentem numquam accusasset Habitus, iudices, si id praetermittere suo salvo capite potuisset.
examples.translation: And yet, for all his effrontery, his wickedness, and his guilt, Habitus would never have undertaken to accuse him, gentlemen, had any other course been consistent with his own safety.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to strive after a thing
Latin: Ad aliquid accedere conor
Latin: Vehementer petere ac
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; Ritschl; ii, ītum, 3

examples.original: Simul atque natum animal est, gaudet voluptate et eam appetit ut bonum, aspernatur dolorem ut malum.
examples.translation: As soon as an animal is born, it delights in pleasure and seeks it as a good, but shuns pain as an evil.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Restat ergo ut iste pecuniae turpissimus appetitus ex obliquo in clericos et maxime in episcopum dirigatur.
examples.translation: It remains, then, that your charge of a most sordid lust for money is indirectly levelled at the clergy, and especially at the bishop.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Qui sunt homines a Q. Metello fratre tuo consule in senatu palam nominati, a quibus ille se lapidibus appetitum, etiam percussum esse dixit?
examples.translation: Who are the men whom the consul Quintus Metellus, your cousin, publicly named in the senate as having stoned, and even stabbed him?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: heirship, inheritance.

examples.original: Maior ista hereditas a me ad posteros transeat.
examples.translation: This inheritance shall pass from me to my descendants larger than before.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Verum ex ista reperietis hereditate ita istum praedatum ut perpauca occulte fecerit;
examples.translation: But you will in fact find little concealment about the way in which he plundered that estate;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Malleolo quaestore Cn. Dolabellae occiso, duas sibi hereditates venisse arbitratus est;
examples.translation: When Gaius Malleolus, Dolabella’s quaestor, was killed, Verres reckoned that two inheritances had come to him;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to bind, tie, fasten; to join, bind, or fasten together, connect.

examples.original: Ita undique regi dolus nectitur.
examples.translation: Thus on every hand the toils were woven about the king.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Conseruere manus et multo bracchia nexu;
examples.translation: They locked hands and arms in manifold embrace;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Verba mihi captiosa conponis et interrogatiunculas nectis?
examples.translation: Do you propose to construct catchwords for me, or to string together petty syllogisms?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A taking possession of, seizing, occupying, taking

examples.original: Impetrant ut ne iurent; dat his possessionem.
examples.translation: Their request to be exempted from taking the oath was granted;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ergo, quia possessor est, non moves possessione; si possessor non esset, non dares?
examples.translation: Is not the point to be settled which of the two ought to be in possession?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hoc si ita statuetis, non modo non erit cur depugnare quisquam posthac possessionis caussa velit, sed ne illud quidem, cur repugnare.
examples.translation: If you so decide, you will remove all future motive for resorting to battle over possession; nay more, there will be no motive even for accepting battle.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a beast
Latin: Animal ferum et periculosum

examples.original: Primus in Numidiam Calpurnius Bestia consul inmittitur;
examples.translation: The consul Calpurnius Bestia was the first general to be sent against Numidia;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ne mutas quidem bestias minus alere ac fovere si quid ex progenie sua parum prosperum sit;
examples.translation: Why even the dumb brutes, if one of their young is unfortunate, do none the less cherish it and foster it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iam hoc non ignoratis, iudices, ut etiam bestiae fame monitae plerumque ad eum locum, ubi pastae sunt aliquando, revertantur.
examples.translation: Now you are not unaware, gentlemen, that even brute beasts, when prompted by hunger, generally return to the place where they have at some time previously found food.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a watcher

examples.original: Accurrunt tamen ad tempus tutores;
examples.translation: They hastened to the spot, nevertheless, at the day fixed;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Parumper subsidiarios tutatus est locus;
examples.translation: For a little while the reserves were protected by their position.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Dixit iuratus P. Titius, tutor pupilli Iunii;
examples.translation: It has been told on oath by Publius Titius, guardian of young Iunius.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a guider, leader, director, ruler, master (cf.: moderator, gubernator).

examples.original: Navigio ista obsunt, non rectori eius, qua rector est.
examples.translation: These mishaps obstruct the voyage but not the steersman qua steersman.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Armenios victo rege Tigrane in hoc unum servitutis genus Pompeius adsueverat, ut rectores a nobis acciperent.
examples.translation: Pompeius, after defeating Tigranes, had accustomed the Armenians to a state of bondage which merely obliged them to accept rulers appointed by Rome.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ad utrosque casus aptus est: bonorum rector est, malorum victor.
examples.translation: He is ready for either outcome: if it brings goods, he controls them;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: perhaps, peradventure.

examples.original: Et ne illud quidem, quod quosdam forsitan moveat, refert, consul an dictator an praetor spoponderit.
examples.translation: Nor does it matter, either, as some are perhaps inclined to think, whether consul or dictator or praetor have given the guarantee.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed querellae, ne tum quidem gratae futurae cum forsitan necessariae erunt, ab initio certe tantae ordiendae rei absint;
examples.translation: But complaints are sure to be disagreeable, even when they shall perhaps be necessary; let the beginning, at all events, of so great an enterprise have none.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et forsitan, quem ille obrutum ignem reliquerit, ita ut totiens novum ex improviso incendium daret, eum se exstincturum.
examples.translation: And perhaps that fire which Fabius had left covered up, but so that it was continually breaking out into new flames, might be by him extinguished.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: violently; deeply; severely

examples.original: Potest quisquam vir in rebus magnis cum invidia versatus satis graviter in inimici contumeliis sine sua laude respondere?
examples.translation: Is there any man, whose weighty activities have gained him enemies, who can reply with adequate impressiveness to the insults of an opponent without glorifying himself?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Mox non ipsum modo, sed Bocchum quoque Mauretaniae regem, iure sanguinis Numidas vindicantem, apud oppidum Cirtam graviter cecidit.
examples.translation: Presently he defeated not only Jugurtha himself but also Bocchus, king of Mauretania, who from ties of kinship was supporting the Numidians, near the city of Cirta.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Certe, cum commotus ira se a vestibulo templi citato gradu proriperet, lapsus per gradus capite graviter offenso impactus imo ita est saxo ut sopiretur.
examples.translation: At all events, as he hurried, beside himself with rage, from the entrance of the temple, he slipped on the stairs, and struck his head so hard on the lowest stone that he lost consciousness.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to purify by means of a propitiatory offering (syn.: procuro, expio).

examples.original: Cum alter ex censoribus C. Iulius decessisset, in locum eius M. Cornelius suffectus est. Nec id postea factum est, quoniam eo lustro a Gallis Roma capta est.
examples.translation: On the death of one of the censors, Gaius Julius, Marcus Cornelius was chosen to fill out his term, but this was never afterwards done because in that five-year period Rome was taken.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: strongly; bravely; boldly
Latin: Magnis viribus

examples.original: Illud opto ”fortiter,” quod est virtus.
examples.translation: I therefore desire that ”brave” endurance; and this is virtue.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Spartacus ipse in primo agmine fortissime dimicans quasi imperator occisus est.
examples.translation: Spartacus himself fell, as became a general, fighting most bravely in the front rank.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam et hi, dum se putant vincere, fortius sequi, et Pompeiani, dum fugere credunt suos, fugere coeperunt.
examples.translation: His men, thinking that they were winning the day, followed more boldly, while the Pompeians, thinking that their own side was in flight, began to flee.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a garden, a pleasure - garden, fruit - garden, kitchen - garden, vineyard (syn.: pomarium, viretum, viridarium).
Latin: Locus maceria aut saepe clausus, in quo olera cibi causa coluntur
Latin: locus in quo arbores, poma, flores et viriditas voluptatis causa coluntur

examples.original: In hortos, in quibus devertebatur Saturninus, pergunt.
examples.translation: They hurried to the gardens where Saturninus had his quarters;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ipse potes riguis plantam deponere in hortis, Ipse potes rivos ducere lenis aquae.
examples.translation: You yourself can plant a shoot in a well-watered garden, you yourself can guide the runnels of gentle water.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sero tandem dispensator Argivus et hoc et ceterum truncum in privatis eius hortis Aurelia via sepulturae dedit.
examples.translation: At last, however, his steward Argivus consigned it to the tomb with the rest of the body in Galba’s private gardens on the Aurelian Road.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a begetter, parent, father
English: to be wondered at, wonderful, marvellous, extraordinary, admirable, strange, singular (class.)

examples.original: O illam mirabilem laudem et singularem!
examples.translation: What wonderful and rare distinction!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Anceps et pulchra contentio exituque ipso mirabilis.
examples.translation: It was a well-contested and noble struggle and remarkable in the manner of its end.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Itaque horum adventu decem milia armatorum completa sunt, quae manus mirabili flagrabat pugnandi cupiditate.
examples.translation: They sent a thousand soldiers, whose arrival raised the number of combatants to ten thousand.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Militiades

definitions: English: a notice sent to a higher tribunal or judge

examples.original: In hac omnes sancti patres nostri et patriarchae et prophetae et apostoli placuerunt deo;
examples.translation: In this love all our holy fathers and patriarchs and prophets and apostles pleased God;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a covering, garment.
Latin: Exterior vestis communis omnium Romanorum

examples.original: Non splendeat toga, ne sordeat quidem.
examples.translation: Do not wear too fine, nor yet too frowzy, a toga.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tota illi aetas aut in armis est exacta civilibus aut in toga concipiente iam civile bellum.
examples.translation: His whole life was passed either in civil warfare, or under a political regime which was soon to breed civil war.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ipse ego privatae cupidus me reddere vitae Plebeiaque toga modicum conponere civem, Omnia dum vobis liceant, nihil esse recuso.
examples.translation: My own desire is to return to private life, to wear the people’s dress, and to play the part of an ordinary citizen;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: swiftness, quickness, speed, celerity

examples.original: Atque haec qua celeritate gesta sint, quamquam videtis, tamen a me in dicendo praetereunda non sunt.
examples.translation: The rapidity with which this feat was accomplished you all know, but I cannot omit to mention it in my speech.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Fabianus, vir egregius et vita et scientia et, quod post ista est, eloquentia quoque, disputabat expedite magis quam concitate, ut posses dicere facilitatem esse illam, non celeritatem.
examples.translation: Fabianus, a man noteworthy because of his life, his knowledge, and, less important than either of these, his eloquence also, used to discuss a subject with dispatch rather than with haste;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eadem autem celeritate adverso colle ad nostra castra atque eos qui in opere occupati erant contenderunt.
examples.translation: Then with the same speed they hastened up-hill against our camp and the troops engaged in entrenching it.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: Germanic, German
Latin: Qui ad Germanos vel Germaniam pertinet
Latin: subst. Agnomen Romanum

examples.original: Iulium Burdonem Germanicae classis praefectum astu subtraxit.
examples.translation: Julius Burdo, commander of the German fleet, he saved by a clever ruse.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ex Antonia minore complures quidem liberos tulit, verum tres omnino reliquit: Germanicum, Livillam, Claudium.
examples.translation: Drusus had several children by the younger Antonia, but was survived by only three, Germanicus, Livilla, and Claudius.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Gaio et Lucio intra triennium defunctis adoptatur ab Augusto simul cum fratre eorum M. Agrippa, coactus prius ipse Germanicum fratris sui filium adoptare.
examples.translation: When Gaius and Lucius died within three years, he was adopted by Augustus along with their brother Marcus Agrippa, being himself first compelled to adopt his nephew Germanicus.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: good-will, inclination, partiality, esp. of a party

examples.original: Malis artibus popularis favor quaeritur.
examples.translation: It takes trickery to win popular approval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Maiore adeo et favore et auctoritate adeptus est quam gessit imperium, quanquam multa documenta egregii principis daret;
examples.translation: Thus his popularity and prestige were greater when he won, than while he ruled the empire, though he gave many proofs of being an excellent prince;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Tum pectore curas Expulit armorum pacique intentus agebat, Quoque modo vanos populi conciret amores, Gnarus et irarum causas et summa favoris Annona momenta trahi.
examples.translation: At once he banished thoughts of battle from his mind, and passed his time over problems of peace and the means of winning the fickle favour of the populace;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: A husbandman, tiller of the soil (opp. pastor), Cato, R. R. prooem. § 2

examples.original: Hic Opiterginis moles onerata colonis Constitit;
examples.translation: Here the hulk halted, weighed down with men of Opitergium;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nux OVID, Nux Ovid Sed, puto, magna mea est operoso cura colono!
examples.translation: But the toilsome husbandman, I ween, takes great thought for me!
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nulli subigebant arva coloni, Ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum Fas erat;
examples.translation: No ploughman tilled the soil, nor was it right To portion off or bound one’s property.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a precious stone, esp. one already cut, a jewel

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quique bibunt tenera dulces ab harundine sucos, Et qui tinguentes croceo medicamine crinem Fluxa coloratis astringunt carbasa gemmis, Quique suas struxere pyras vivique calentes Conscendere rogos.
examples.translation: Up rose the men who drink sweet juices from soft reeds; and those who colour their hair with saffron dye and loop up their robes of cotton with brighthued gems;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the young of animals, a whelp

examples.original: Catulus se ignis haustu ludibrio hostium exemit.
examples.translation: Catulus saved himself from the insults of his enemies by swallowing fire.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Uxores habuit Mummiam Achaicam, neptem Catuli proneptemque L. Mummi, qui Corinthum excidit;
examples.translation: He married Mummia Achaica, the granddaughter of Catulus and great-granddaughter of Lucius Mummius who destroyed Corinth;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Libenter haec coram cum Q. Catulo et Q. Hortensio, summis et clarissimis viris, disputarem;
examples.translation: I would gladly discuss the matter personally with eminent and distinguished men like Quintus Catulus and Quintus Hortensius;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: init.; inf. praes. explerier

examples.original: Tam celer adsiduos explevit cursus honores;
examples.translation: So swiftly did thy career fill office after office;
examples.author: Claudian
examples.work: Panegyric On The Consulship Of Fl. Manlius Theodorus (A.D. 399)

examples.original: His rebus celeriter id quod Avarici deperierat expletur.
examples.translation: By this means the loss at Avaricum was speedily made up.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Si enim, ut mihi quidem videtur, non explet bona naturae voluptas, iure praetermissa est;
examples.translation: If, as I hold, pleasure adds nothing to the sum-total of nature’s goods, it has rightly been omitted.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: place

examples.original: Et numquid ad rem pertinet, sive interposita sit ad recedendum necessitatis excusatio sive non sit?
examples.translation: And does it really affect the point, whether the excuse of necessity for leaving the town was inserted or was not?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Petimus non singula busta Discretosque rogos: unum da gentibus ignem, Non interpositis urantur corpora flammis;
examples.translation: We ask not a pyre for each or a separate burning: provide a single fire for all;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ac vix uno interposito die confecit nuptias, non repertis qui sequerentur exemplum, excepto libertino quodam et altero primipilari, cuius nuptiarum officium et ipse cum Agrippina celebravit.
examples.translation: And he married her with hardly a single day’s delay; but none were found to follow his example save a freedman and a chief centurion, whose marriage ceremony he himself attended with Agrippina.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to put to death on the cross, to crucify (only in eccl. Lat.)

examples.original: Utque Milo, sub quo cruciata est Pisa tyranno, Vivus in occultas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: And like Milo, under whose tyranny Pisa groaned, mayst thou be hurled alive into hidden waters.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Eodem modo non erit dubium, quin maius bonum sit gaudium quam obnixus animus ad perpetiendos cruciatus vulnerum aut ignium.” Minime.
examples.translation: For things that result from hazard admit of wide distinctions, since they are rated according to their usefulness in the eyes of those who experience them;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam si modo tanta cura, tanta intentione, tanto labore agitis ne in aliquos cruciatus transitorios incidatis, quantum vos oportet esse sollicitos, ut sempiternas miserias fugiatis!
examples.translation: And if the death which ends the toil of this life inspires such fear, how greatly that death is to be feared which casts men into everlasting pain!
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: dark-colored
Latin: Color inter colorem nigrum et fuscum

examples.original: Corpore et statura fuit grandi, aquilo colore, facie rusticana, valetudine varia;
examples.translation: He was tall and of full habit, with a dark complexion and a rustic appearance.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Ut fugiunt aquilas, timidissima turba, columbae, Ut fugit invisos agna novella lupos: Sic illae timuere viros sine more ruentes;
examples.translation: As doves, most timorous of birds, flee from the eagles, as the weanling lamb from the hated wolf, so feared they the men rushing wildly on them;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Interea domitis Caesar remeabat Hiberis Victrices aquilas alium laturus in orbem, Cum prope fatorum tantos per prospera cursus Avertere dei.
examples.translation: Meanwhile Caesar was returning triumphant over conquered Spain to carry into a new world his victorious eagles, when the flowing tide of his successes was almost turned aside by Heaven.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that acts according to his own will and pleasure, is his own master; free, unrestricted, unrestrained, unimpeded, unshackled; independent, frank, open, bold
Latin: Qui suam voluntatem sequitur et non aliorum debet
Latin: Deus Italicus vini culturae, Baccho assimulatus
entries.etymology: From PIE *h₁leudʰ- 'grow, become free'; Greek ἐλεύθερος is related.

examples.original: Non potest honestum esse, quod non est liberum;
examples.translation: That which is not free cannot be honourable;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Id erat liber aliquis antiquus pulcher aut rarior.
examples.translation: This was some old book, either beautiful or rare.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Non adfligitur sapiens liberorum amissione, non amicorum.
examples.translation: The wise man is not distressed by the loss of children or of friends.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: neither the one nor the other, neither of two
Latin: Non uter; nec unus nec alter
Latin: nec masculinus nec femininus

examples.original: Neutra parte hostis obvius fuit;
examples.translation: In neither region did they find the enemy.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Supellex modica, non multa, ut in neutram partem conspici posset.
examples.translation: His furniture was modest, not abundant, so that it attracted attention in neither direction.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Septem milia passuum cum abessent a Cominio, revocati ab suis neutri proelio occurrerunt.
examples.translation: Recalled by their leaders when seven miles from Cominium, they had not been present at either engagement.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to tear asunder, tear in pieces (class.).

examples.original: Captum oppidum ac direptum est;
examples.translation: The town was captured and sacked;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fraude Sex. Tarquini Gabi direpti.
examples.translation: Gabii sacked, in consequence of the fraud of Sextus Tarquinius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Diripiantque tuos insanis unguibus artus Strymoniae matres, Orpheos esse ratae.
examples.translation: And may Strymonian mothers rend thy limbs with frenzied nails, deeming them those of Orpheus.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: wakefulness, sleeplessness, a lying awake

examples.original: Munus vigiliarum senatores, qui per aetatem ac valetudinem poterant, per se ipsi obibant;
examples.translation: The watchmen’s duty was performed by those of the senators themselves whose years and strength admitted of it;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ille ex castris prima vigilia egressus prope confecto sub lucem itinere post montem se occultavit militesque ex nocturno labore sese reficere iussit.
examples.translation: He left camp in the first watch, and having almost completed his march just before dawn, he concealed himself behind the height and ordered his soldiers to rest after their night’s work.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nam quae Cenabi oriente sole gesta essent, ante primam confectam vigiliam in finibus Arvernorum audita sunt, quod spatium est milium passuum circiter centum lx.
examples.translation: For the deeds done at Cenabum at sunrise were heard of before the end of the first watch in the borders of the Arverni, a distance of about one hundred and sixty miles.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: wooded, forested
Latin: Silvis tectus
Latin: Qui ad silvas pertinet; in silva vivens

examples.original: Saetigerisque pares subus silvestria membra nuda dabant terrae nocturno tempore capti, circum se foliis ac frondibus involventes.
examples.translation: And when night overtook them, like bristly hogs they just cast their savage bodies naked upon the ground, rolling themselves in leaves and boughs.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Ita duplici proditione et praesidium Samnitium insessis circa viam silvestribus locis necopinato oppressum est, et ab urbe plena hostium clamor sublatus;
examples.translation: Thus, in one crowded hour, the Samnites were slain and the Satricans captured, and all things brought under the power of the consul;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a fruit-tree of any kind
Latin: Arbor quae pōma fert
English: to be lord and master, to have dominion, bear rule domineer (freq. and class.; for syn. cf.: regno, impero, jubeo, praesum).
Latin: Dominus alicui esse

examples.original: Tu quoque, qui causam finiti reddis amoris, Deque tua domina multa querenda refers, Parce queri;
examples.translation: You too who relate the cause of ended love, and recount your many complaints against your mistress, cease to complain;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Ager iure possidetur, sapientia natura. Ille abalienari potest et alteri tradi, haec non discedit a domino.
examples.translation: The field can change hands and go into the ownership of another: but wisdom never departs from its owner.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita enim senectus honesta est, si se ipsa defendit, si ius suum retinet, si nemini emancipata est, si usque ad ultimum spiritum dominatur in suos.
examples.translation: For just as I approve of the young man in whom there is a touch of age, so I approve of the old man in whom there is some of the flavour of youth.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: quickly/fast/speedily, with speed; soon, before long; readily

examples.original: Citius fieri quam optas, potest.
examples.translation: It may be sooner than thy prayer requests.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid enim opus est longis in senatu sententiis, cum optimi cito consentiant?
examples.translation: What is the use of long arguments in the senate, when good citizens agree so quickly?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Citatur reus, \[agitur causa:\] paucis verbis accusat, ut de re iudicata, Cannutius: incipit longo et alte petito prooemio respondere maior Caepasius.
examples.translation: Well, Fabricius was summoned; Cannutius opened the prosecution with a short speech, for he held the case prejudged.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Of or belonging to the prœtor or prœtors, prœtorian

examples.original: In extructionibus praetoriorum atque villarum omni ratione posthabita nihil tam efficere concupiscebat quam quod posse effici negaretur.
examples.translation: He built villas and country houses with utter disregard of expense, caring for nothing so much as to do what men said was impossible.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Equidem e Cn. Aufidio, praetorio, erudito homine, oculis capto, saepe audiebam cum se lucis magis quam utilitatis desiderio moveri diceret.
examples.translation: I myself frequently heard the blind ex-praetor and scholar Gnaeus Aufidius declare that he felt the actual loss of light more than the inconvenience of blindness.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Peditum equitumque copiis Suetonius Paulinus, Marius Celsus, Annius Gallus rectores destinati, sed plurima fides Licinio Proculo praetorii praefecto.
examples.translation: As commanders of the foot and horse he named Suetonius Paulinus, Marius Celsus, Annius Gallus, but he trusted most in Licinius Proculus, prefect of the praetorian guard.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: Macedonian, one from Macedonia; Macedonia, the territory; men Macedonian armed

examples.original: Harum utraque Macedonum patrociniis utebatur;
examples.translation: Both these parties depended upon the patronage of the Macedonians;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Phocion

examples.original: Etsi ille domestico summo genere erat, tamen Macedones eum sibi aliquando anteponi indigne ferebant, neque tamen non patiebantur;
examples.translation: Although he was of the highest rank in his own country, yet the Macedonians were indignant that he was sometimes preferred to them;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Quippe Thracas in res suas traxerant, atque ita industriam Macedonum viribus Thracum, ferociam Thracum disciplina Macedonica temperavere.
examples.translation: They had induced the Thracians to support their efforts and had thus tempered the Macedonian persistence with Thracian energy, and Thracian savagery with Macedonian discipline.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: dearness, costliness, high price, etc. (opp. vilitas)

examples.original: No. 49 (Ep. CCXI) Sicut parata est severitas peccata quae invenerit, vindicare, ita non vult caritas quod vindicet, invenire.
examples.translation: No. 49 (Ep. CCXI)a (a.d. 423) Just as severity is ready to punish the sins it discovers, so love is anxious not to discover sins to punish.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ipse enim se quisque diligit, non ut aliquam a se ipse mercedem exigat caritatis suae, sed quod per se quisque sibi carus est;
examples.translation: For everyone loves himself, not with a view of acquiring some profit for himself from his self-love, but because he is dear to himself on his own account;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ad quod negotium mihi parvum tempus velut usque ad pascha impetrare volui per fratres a tua sincerissima et venerabili caritate et nunc per has preces volo.
examples.translation: It was for this task that I sought through my brethren to obtain from your dear Reverence a short space of time, say until Easter, and to that I now add this present supplication.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: in other respects, for the rest, otherwise; Gr.
entries.grammaticalClass: prep.; but if they are genuine

examples.original: Alioqui quid in mora est?
examples.translation: At any rate, what is there to hinder?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a nail of a person's finger or toe.

examples.original: Diripiantque tuos insanis unguibus artus Strymoniae matres, Orpheos esse ratae.
examples.translation: And may Strymonian mothers rend thy limbs with frenzied nails, deeming them those of Orpheus.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: indeed, certainly, without doubt, to be sure, assuredly (cf.: nimirum, scilicet).
Latin: quidem
Latin: scilicet

examples.original: Etiamnunc interrogo: nempe fortitudo optabilis est?
examples.translation: At this point I ask you: Is not bravery desirable?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec nempe sunt elementa, quibus hic mundus administratur, aqua, terra, spiritus.
examples.translation: These, namely, are the elements, by which the world’s work is carried on—water, earth, air.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vestalibus nempe una illa sedes est, ex qua eas nihil unquam praeterquam urbs capta movit;
examples.translation: The Vestals surely have but that one dwelling-place, from which nothing ever caused them to remove but the capture of the City;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a becoming acquainted with, learning to know, acquiring knowledge, knowledge as a consequence of perception or of the exercise of our mental powers, knowing, acquaintance

examples.original: Quid cognitio urbium aut locorum?
examples.translation: Or in surveying cities and spots of interest?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc illud est praecipue in cognitione rerum salubre ac frugiferum, omnis te exempli documenta in inlustri posita monumento intueri;
examples.translation: What chiefly makes the study of history wholesome and profitable is this, that you behold the lessons of every kind of experience set forth as on a conspicuous monument;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fama fuit quosdam ex Fidenatium iuventute participes eius populationis fuisse, cognitioque eius rei L. Sergio et Q. Servilio et Mam. Aemilio permissa.
examples.translation: It was rumoured that certain young men of Fidenae had shared in the pillaging. The investigation of this report was intrusted to Lucius Sergius, Quintus Servilius, and Mamercus Aemilius;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: meet, convenient, suitable, seasonable

examples.original: Atqui si nox opportuna est eruptioni, sicut est, haec profecto noctis aptissima hora est.
examples.translation: And yet, if night is favourable for our sally, as it is, this is surely the fittest hour of the night.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Denique ceterae res, quae expetuntur, opportunae sunt singulae rebus fere singulis—divitiae, ut utare;
examples.translation: In short, all other objects of desire are each, for the most part, adapted to a single end—riches, for spending;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Castra opportunis locis erant posita ibique castella viginti tria facta, quibus in castellis interdiu stationes ponebantur, ne qua subito eruptio fieret: haec eadem noctu excubitoribus ac firmis praesidiis tenebantur.
examples.translation: In these piquets would be posted by day to prevent any sudden sortie; by night the same stations were held by sentries and strong garrisons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: place

examples.original: Quis in meum locum iudicem subdidit?
examples.translation: Who substituted another name on the list of jurymen for my own?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum mora non tuta est, totis incumbere remis Utile, et admisso subdere calcar equo.
examples.translation: When delay is dangerous, it is best to press on with all oars, and to spur the galloping horse.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a turmoil, hubbub, uproar, disorder, tumult, commotion, disturbance, of a crowd of people (syn. tumultus): praetor ait: cujus dolo malo in turbā damnum quod factum esse dicetur
Latin: Motus et trepidatio plurium, perturbatio multitudinis
Latin: incondita multitudo hominum

examples.original: Is erat ex hac turba lucifugarum.
examples.translation: Papinius belonged to the tribe of those who shun the light.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Convocat turbam, quisquis otio suo aliquam fabulam inposuit.
examples.translation: To advertise one’s retirement is to collect a crowd.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nemo oculis suis lautus est, ne paucorum quidem aut familiarium, sed apparatum vitiorum suorum pro modo turbae spectantis expandit.
examples.translation: No one makes himself elegant only for his own beholding, or even for the admiration of a few friends or relatives.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: following thereafter, next following: deinceps qui deinde cepit, ut princeps qui primum cepit, Paul. ex

examples.original: Deinceps procedente tempore duodetriginta consulatus, dictaturas quinque, censuras septem, triumphos sex, duas ovationes adepta est.
examples.translation: Then as time went on it was honoured with twenty-eight consulships, five dictatorships, seven censorships, six triumphs, and two ovations.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Iamque pars egressa portis erat, deincepsque alii servabant ordinem in suum quisque locum descendentes, cum consul Romanus, priusquam totis viribus fulta constaret hostium acies, intulit signa;
examples.translation: A part had already passed out through the gates and the rest were following in good order, each man coming out into his proper place;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Licet haec ipsa et quae deinceps dicturus sum aures tuae, Materne, respuant, cui bono est si apud te Agamemnon aut Iason diserte loquitur?
examples.translation: Very likely you will not relish what I am saying, Maternus, or what I intend to state in the course of my argument;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to make clear, plain, evident (by disclosing, uncovering), to show, manifest, declare, etc.

examples.original: Quorum si neutrum est, opera danda est ut verbis utamur quam usitatissimis et quam maxime aptis, id est rem declarantibus.
examples.translation: If neither source of difference is present, we must be careful to employ the terms most generally accepted and those most suitable, that is, those that convey the fact clearly.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed cum tot signis eadem natura declaret quid velit anquirat desideret, tamen obsurdescimus nescio quo modo nec ea, quae ab ea monemur, audimus.
examples.translation: But though this same nature declares by so many utterances what she wishes, what she seeks, and what she ardently longs for, yet we somehow grow deaf and do not hearken to her voice.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum autem exprimere imaginem consuetudinis atque vitae velimus Epaminondae, nihil videmur debere praetermittere quod pertineat ad eam declarandam.
examples.translation: Since, then, I wish to portray the life and habits of Epaminondas, it seems to me that I ought to omit nothing which contributes to that end.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

definitions: English: a leader, commander, chief, general (class.; a favorite word of Vergil, used by him more than 20 times; cf.: dux, imperator, princeps, praetor, praefectus, etc.): exercitus, *
English: to look at attentively, to view, behold, survey (class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. freq. a. and n.; si, sum, 3

examples.original: Iamque dies primos belli visura tumultus Exoritur;
examples.translation: So the day dawned that was to witness the first turmoil of the war;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ad eam multitudinem urbs quoque amplificanda visa est.
examples.translation: Eighty thousand citizens are said to have been registered in that census;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ergo ubi visus eris nostra medicabilis arte, Fac monitis fugias otia prima meis.
examples.translation: When therefore I shall find you amenable to my skill, obey my counsels and first of all shun leisure.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or belonging to the holidays (in opp. to the working-days), solemn

examples.original: Licet enim sine luxuria agere festum diem.
examples.translation: For one may keep holiday without extravagance.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ac primo Valerius Festus legatus studia provincialium cum fide iuvit;
examples.translation: At first the commander, Valerius Festus, loyally supported the wishes of the provincials.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Anxur in Volscis brevi receptum est neglectis die festo custodiis urbis.
examples.translation: Anxur of the Volsci was speedily recaptured, a holiday having relaxed the vigilance of their guard.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Christian
Latin: Qui ad Christianismum pertinet
Latin: Qui Iesui Christo fidit

examples.original: Damna, quae inlata sunt, vel tolerantur a Christianis vel resarciuntur per Christianos.
examples.translation: The losses that were inflicted are either being borne by Christians or are being made good by Christians.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Animum virilem et Christianum nec debent, si accedunt, extollere nec debent frangere, si recedunt.
examples.translation: The manly Christian spirit ought neither to be elated by their accession nor depressed by their departure.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Nobis itaque cordi est neque Christianam amittere mansuetudinem neque perniciosum ceteris imitationis exemplum in illa civitate relinquere.
examples.translation: Therefore is it our dear desire neither to put away Christian meekness nor to leave your country as a baleful example for others to follow.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to take by assault, to storm, capture, reduce, subdue (freq. and class.; syn.: obsideo, oppugno, capio).

examples.original: Nihil est, quod non expugnet pertinax opera et intenta ac diligens cura;
examples.translation: There is nothing that will not surrender to persistent treatment, to concentrated and careful attention;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed Asprenati cuncta ex fide nuntiata, cuius cohortatione expugnata navis et interfectus quisquis ille erat.
examples.translation: But they faithfully reported everything to Asprenas, at whose bidding they captured the pretender’s ship and killed him, whoever he was.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ipsum erat oppidum Alesia in colle summo admodum edito loco, ut nisi obsidione expugnari non posse videretur;
examples.translation: The actual stronghold of Alesia was set atop of a hill, in a very lofty situation, apparently impregnable save by blockade.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to stretch out, spread outextend (class.).

examples.original: Per totam vitam opus eius extenditur.
examples.translation: His work goes on throughout his whole life.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Utique enim quo prudentior est, hoc magis se ad id, quod est optimum, extendet et id omni modo consequi cupiet.
examples.translation: For certainly, the more prudent he is, the more he will strive after the best, and he will desire to attain it by every possible means.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neque enim de more carinas Extendunt puppesque levant, sed firma gerendis Molibus insolito contexunt robora ductu.
examples.translation: They built no long hulls, no high sterns, as the custom is, but joined stout planks together on unwonted lines to carry heavy structures.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: or curri
Latin: Deorsum currere
Latin: deorsum currere

examples.original: Eo decurrunt tribuni contionemque secum trahunt.
examples.translation: The tribunes hastened to the place, drawing the people after them.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ardet et adsuetas Circe decurrit ad artes, Nec tamen est illis adtenuatus amor.
examples.translation: Circe aflame has recourse to her wonted arts, yet not by them is her passion calmed.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Caesar necessariis rebus imperatis ad cohortandos milites, quam in partem fors obtulit, decucurrit et ad legionem decumam devenit.
examples.translation: Caesar gave the necessary commands, and then ran down in a chance direction to harangue the troops, and came to the Tenth Legion.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to draw out or

examples.original: Eos per se ipsi Latini adsumptis Hernicis sine Romano aut duce aut auxilio castris exuerunt;
examples.translation: These the Latins, acting independently, with the assistance of the Hernici, but without either general or aid from Rome, despoiled of their camp.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tunc urbibus exutum regem et iam finium suorum regnique fugitivum per Mauros atque Gaetuliam sequebatur.
examples.translation: He then pursued the king, stripped of his cities and now a fugitive from his country and kingdom, through Mauretania and Gaetulia.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quid enim tandem passurum fuisse filium suum, si exercitum amisisset, si fusus, fugatus, castris exutus fuisset?
examples.translation: What, pray, would his son have suffered, if he had lost his army, if he had been discomfited, routed, and driven from his camp?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to project over or towards a thing, to bend or lean towards, to hang down over, overhang (syn. impendeo).

examples.original: Imminebant enim Seleucus, Lysimachus, Ptolemaeus, opibus iam valentes, cum quibus ei de summis rebus erat dimicandum.
examples.translation: For Antigonus was menaced by Seleucus, Lysimachus and Ptolemy, men already possessed of formidable power, with whom he must fight for the supremacy.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Regno est expulsus Ariobarzanes rex, socius populi Romani atque amicus; imminent duo reges toti Asiae non solum vobis inimicissimi, sed etiam vestris sociis atque amicis;
examples.translation: King Ariobarzanes, the ally and friend of Rome, has been driven from his kingdom: Asia is threatened by two kings who are the sworn enemies of your allies and friends as well as of yourselves;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hic diffisus suae atque omnium saluti inermis ex tabernaculo prodit: videt imminere hostes atque in summo esse rem discrimine: capit arma a proximis atque in porta consistit.
examples.translation: He saw that the enemy were threateningly close and that the issue was in the greatest danger; he took arms from the nearest men and stationed himself in the gate.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: on the day before (class.; opp. postridie).— Constr.

examples.original: Eadem ratione, qua pridie, ab nostris resistitur.
examples.translation: And exactly the same was done on the other days following.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Pridie kalendas Novembris Rosius Regulus iniit eiuravitque.
examples.translation: On the thirty-first of October Rosius Regulus entered and gave up his office.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: To leave, quit, forsake, depart from something

examples.original: Urbem populis victisque frequentem Gentibus et generis, coeat si turba, capacem Humani facilem venturo Caesare praedam Ignavae liquere manus.
examples.translation: Rome that was crowded with citizens and conquered peoples, Rome that could contain the human race assembled, was left by coward hands an easy prey to invading Caesar.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to ascend, mount up, climb; and in eccl. Lat. simply

examples.original: Atque idem quanto in odio postea suis ipsis fuit, per quos in altiorem locum ascenderat! neque iniuria.
examples.translation: But subsequently how he came to be hated even by his own followers on whose backs he had climbed to a higher place!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Audire te arbitror, Scipio, hospes tuus avitus Masinissa quae faciat hodie nonaginta natus annos : cum ingressus iter pedibus sit, in equum omnino non ascendere;
examples.translation: I think, Scipio, that the news reaches you of the daily activities of your grandfather’s friend and host Masinissa, now ninety years old;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a soothing, assuaging; a comfort, relief, consolation, solace

examples.original: Haec inter seniores morti destinatos iactata solacia.
examples.translation: Such were the consolations which the old men appointed to die exchanged among themselves;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nimius honos inter secunda rebus adversis in solacium cessit.
examples.translation: These excessive honours in prosperity presently became a solace in misfortune.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Fruetur Vitellius fratre, coniuge, liberis: mihi non ultione neque solaciis opus est.
examples.translation: Vitellius shall enjoy his brother, his wife, and his children; I require neither vengeance nor solace.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: wound; mental/emotional hurt; injury to one's interests

examples.original: Tractentur volnera nulla Sacra manu.
examples.translation: No other hand should meddle with the wounds of gods.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Iamque sinu laxo nudum sine corpore volnus.
examples.translation: The limbs are soaked with corrupted blood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec cruor emicuit solitus, sed volnere largo Diffusum rutilo dirum pro sanguine virus.
examples.translation: No red blood spouted forth from the gaping wound, but a slimy liquid, strange and dreadful, came out instead.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: deceitful, deceptive, fallacious

examples.original: Tota rerum natura umbra est aut inanis aut fallax.
examples.translation: The whole universe is then a vain or deceptive shadow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At tu nec voces (quid enim fallacius illis?) Crede, nec aeternos pondus habere deos.
examples.translation: But do not you believe that words (what more deceiving than they?) or the eternal gods have weight.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sic ista sine noxa decipiunt, quomodo praestigiatorum acetabula et calculi, in quibus me fallacia ipsa delectat.
examples.translation: Such quibbles are just as harmlessly deceptive as the juggler’s cup and dice, in which it is the very trickery that pleases me.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: eager, zealous, assiduous, anxious after any thing, fond or studious of any thing.
Latin: Magno studio aliquid faciens, industrius

examples.original: Haec quoque, quae praebet lectum studiosa locumque Crede mihi, mecum non semel illa fuit.
examples.translation: She too, who eagerly offers bed and room, not once only, believe me, has she been with me.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to roll, turn about, turn round, tumble any thing.
Latin: In orbem torquere, in gyrum agere
Latin: Rem agere illam circum seipsam movendo

examples.original: Experiri et exercere me volui.
examples.translation: I merely wished to test myself and to give myself practice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed ecce facimus quod voluisti;
examples.translation: But see, we shall do as you have desired;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Quid igitur voluit sibi qui illa mutaverit?
examples.translation: What then did he want by altering their old name?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to loosen asunder, to unloose, disunite

examples.original: Quid, si iis verbis scripta est ista proscriptio, ut se ipsa dissolvat?
examples.translation: But what if your proscription was made in such terms that it destroys itself?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod est gravius et cuius rei caussa maxime iudicia constituta sunt, id iam mala consuetudine dissolutum est.
examples.translation: And now the weightier function, the chief purpose for which our courts exist, is abrogated by this evil practice.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Atque etiam, cum hominis natura morte dissolvitur, ceterarum rerum perspicuum est quo quaeque discedat, abeunt enim illuc omnia, unde orta sunt;
examples.translation: And even when man is dissolved by death it is evident to the sight whither each bodily element departs;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to throw, cast, or fling back (freq. and class.; cf.: remitto, retorqueo).

examples.original: Reiecti a Chelidone capiunt consilium necessarium, ut suscipiant ipsi negotium.
examples.translation: Rejected by Chelidon, they could do nothing but resolve to undertake the obligationa themselves.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Caesar loquendi finem facit seque ad suos recepit suisque imperavit ne quod omnino telum in hostes reicerent.
examples.translation: Caesar made an end of speaking, and, withdrawing to his own men, commanded them not to discharge a single dart against the enemy in reply.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ita reieci iudices ut hoc constet, post hunc statum reipublicae quo nunc utimur simili splendore et dignitate consilium nullum fuisse.
examples.translation: As the result of my own challenging, it is agreed that never, since the present form of governmenta was established, has a court of such illustrious and acknowledged merit assembled.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to form an agger, or to heap up like an agger; hence, in gen., to heap up, pile up

examples.original: Quos primo Camillus vallo circumdare et aggere atque operibus oppugnare est adortus.
examples.translation: Camillus at first set about confining them with a palisade and mound, intending to lay siege to them;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Forte quodam loco male densatus agger pondere superstantium in fossam procubuit; atque ea, cum deos pandere viam fugae conclamassent, plures inermes quam armati evadunt.
examples.translation: By that opening—crying out that the gods were providing them a means of flight—they saved themselves, but more got away without their arms than with them.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Labienus primo vineas agere, cratibus atque aggere paludem explere atque iter munire conabatur.
examples.translation: Labienus at first tried to move up mantlets, fill in the marsh with hurdles and earth, and build a roadway.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: A computing, calculating, considering
Latin: sermō sententiārum oppōnēntum; dissēnsus; discussiō
Latin: actus disputandī

examples.original: Et certamen honestum et disputatio splendida!
examples.translation: Here is an honourable quarrel, fought out in high debate!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Res disputatione ad mediam noctem perducitur.
examples.translation: The matter continued in dispute till midnight.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: De ingenio eius in his disputationibus, non de moribus quaeritur.
examples.translation: In these discussions it is his intellect and not his character that is in question.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to spread among the multitude; to make general, common, or universal; to put forth to the world, publish (cf. publico).

examples.original: Post prandium aut cenam bibere vulgare est;
examples.translation: To them, a glass after lunch or one after dinner is bourgeois;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Noscitabatur tamen in tanta deformitate, et ordines duxisse aiebant aliaque militiae decora vulgo miserantes eum iactabant;
examples.translation: He was recognized nevertheless, despite the hideousness of his appearance, and the word went round that he had commanded companies;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vulgata dicentium gaudia et imperitorum quoque oculis exposita percenseo: illa secretiora et tantum ipsis orantibus nota maiora sunt.
examples.translation: It is the notorious delights of speech-making that I am enumerating—those that are full in view even of the uninitiated;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: thoroughly moved, agitated, disturbed.
Latin: penitus mōtus; commōtus
Latin: pavorem patiens; dolore turbātus; ānxius

examples.original: Nemo autem sollicito bono fruitur;
examples.translation: No man, however, enjoys a blessing that brings anxiety;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Oratio sollicita philosophum non decet;
examples.translation: A meticulous manner of writing does not suit the philosopher;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid est turpius quam in ipso limine securitatis esse sollicitum?
examples.translation: But what is baser than to fret at the very threshold of peace?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: an assembly of the (Greek) people.
Latin: Congregatio, praesertim Christiana
Latin: Aedes ubi Christiani congregant

examples.original: Quam rem inlicitissimam atque indignissimam clericis prohibere temptantibus, ecclesia lapidata est.
examples.translation: When the clergy attempted to stop this most illegal and insulting procedure, the church was stoned.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Vide utrum in ipsum Caecilianum, de cuius persona praeiudicare conabantur ecclesiae, aliquid mali probare potuerint.
examples.translation: Notice whether they have succeeded in proving any evil against Caecilian himself, from whose person they attempted to compromise the Church;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: In aliis enim civitatibus tantum agimus quod ad ecclesiam pertinet, quantum vel nos permittunt vel nobis inponunt earundem civitatium episcopi, fratres et consacerdotes nostri.
examples.translation: For in other towns we deal with matters concerning the Church only so far as the bishops of those towns, our brethren and fellow-priests, allow us or enjoin upon us.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a cave, cavern, grotto (almost entirely confined to the poets).

examples.original: Illo Lotophagos, illo Sirenas in antro Esse puta;
examples.translation: Think that in this cave there are Lotophagi, in that Sirens;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Foedus Lucanis provolvitur ursus ab antris, Quid nisi pondus iners stolidaeque ferocia mentis?
examples.translation: From his Lucanian den waddles forth the ugly Bear,—what save sluggish weight and stolid fierceness?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a pledge, gage, pawn, security, mortgage (of persons as well as things).

examples.original: Tanto te pignore, Caesar, Emimus;
examples.translation: By so dear a pledge have we bought you, Caesar;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Perfidus ille quidem, qui talia pignora servat, Sed tamen Aetnaei fulminis instar habent.
examples.translation: Perfidious indeed is he who keeps such pledges, but they hold what is like a thunderbolt of Aetna.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Invictus ergo Alexander cum invictis ducibus bella gessisset et eadem fortunae pignora in discrimen detulisset;
examples.translation: So then, an undefeated Alexander would have warred against undefeated generals, and would have brought the same pledges of Fortune to the crisis.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to tear to pieces, to mangle, rend, mutilate, lacerate (class., esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: lanio, discerpo).

examples.original: Aquileiam progressae, proturbatis qui de Othone nuntiabant laceratisque vexillis nomen Vitellii praeferentibus, rapta postremo pecunia et inter se divisa, hostiliter egerant.
examples.translation: Their conduct filled them with fear, and then fear brought the reflection that acts might win them credit with Vespasian for which they would have to apologize to Vitellius.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: fearfulness, fear

examples.original: Tristes praesagia curas Exagitant, trepida quatitur formidine somnus, Thessaliam nox omnis habet;
examples.translation: For her sorrow is intensified by forebodings, and her sleep broken by anxious fears.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Putatisne vos illis rebus frui posse, nisi eos, qui vobis fructui sunt, conservaritis, non solum, ut ante dixi, calamitate, sed etiam calamitatis formidine liberatos?
examples.translation: Do you imagine that you can enjoy these advantages unless you preserve those from whom you derive them and keep them free not only, as I said before, from disaster but from fear of disaster?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Pauci gladiatorum resistentes neque inulti cecidere: ceteri ad navis ruebant, ubi cuncta pari formidine implicabantur, permixtis paganis, quos nullo discrimine Vitelliani trucidabant.
examples.translation: The rest rushed to the ships; but there an equal panic caused utter confusion, for the Vitellians slew without distinction the townspeople who joined the soldiers in their flight.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: turned forward, bent or inclined, leaning or hanging forward, stooping, bending down (class.; opp. supinus; cf. cernuus).

examples.original: Anxur fuit, quae nunc Tarracinae sunt, urbs prona in paludes.
examples.translation: Anxur, the Tarracinae of our day, was a city which sloped down towards the marshes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed ambitionem scriptoris facile averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur;
examples.translation: So between the hostility of the one class and the servility of the other, posterity was disregarded.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ora ferox Siculae laxavit Mulciber Aetnae Nec tulit in caelum flammas, sed vertice prono Ignis in Hesperium cecidit latus.
examples.translation: In Sicily fierce Mulciber opened wide the mouths of Etna; nor did he lift its flames skyward, but the lire bowed its crest and fell on the Italian shore.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a dream

examples.original: Haud ita multo post T. Latinio, de plebe homini, somnium fuit;
examples.translation: Not long after, Titus Latinius, a plebeian, had a dream.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Terrebatur ad hoc evidentibus portentis somniorum et auspiciorum et ominum, cum veteribus tum novis.
examples.translation: In addition he was frightened by manifest portents from dreams, auspices and omens, both old and new.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Itaque ne si iucundissimis quidem nos somniis usuros putemus, Endymionis somnum nobis velimus dari, idque si accidat mortis instar putemus.
examples.translation: The prospect of the most delightful dreams would not reconcile us to falling asleep for ever: Endymion’s fate we should consider no better than death.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: The ruler of a small country

examples.original: Pridie kalendas Novembris Rosius Regulus iniit eiuravitque.
examples.translation: On the thirty-first of October Rosius Regulus entered and gave up his office.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Atilius Regulus cos. victis navali proelio Poenis in Africam traiecit.
examples.translation: Atilius Regulus the consul, having beaten the Carthaginians in a naval battle, crossed into Africa.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: immeasurable, boundless, endless, vast, immense (freq. and class.; syn.: infinitus, ingens, interminatus).

examples.original: Ut Cremonam venere, novum immensumque opus occurrit.
