examples.translation: When they reached Cremona they found a new task of enormous difficulty before them.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ii erant T. Vinius legatus eius in Hispania, cupiditatis immensae;
examples.translation: They were Titus Vinius, one of his generals in Spain, a man of unbounded covetousness;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Accessit ad immensum civium amorem notabilis etiam externorum favor.
examples.translation: To this unbounded love of his citizens was added marked devotion from foreigners.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a deadly, esp. an infectious or contagious disease, a plague, pest, pestilence; also, a noxious atmosphere, unhealthy weather

examples.original: Nam primum tacta designat membra saliva, Quae cohibet virus retinetque in volnere pestem;
examples.translation: The native begins by marking the part with the touch of his spittle;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Sine cupiditatibus vos genui, sine timoribus, sine superstitione, sine perfidia ceterisque pestibus;
examples.translation: I brought you into the world without desires or fears, free from superstition, treachery and the other curses.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illae pestes non minus graves sunt, famem dico et sitim et praecordiorum subpurationes et febrem viscera ipsa torrentem.
examples.translation: Those other troubles are of course not less serious; I mean hunger, thirst, ulcers of the stomach, and fever that parches our very bowels.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: long ago, long since, a long time ago; without a negative

examples.original: Ira militum in Tampium Flavianum incubuit, nullo criminis argumento, sed iam pridem invisus turbine quodam ad exitium poscebatur: propinquum Vitellii, proditorem Othonis, interceptorem donativi clamitabant.
examples.translation: The soldiers’ wrath fell on Tampius Flavianus, of whose guilt there was not the slightest proof; but the troops already hated him and now in a whirlwind of rage demanded his death.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to follow (in a friendly or hostile manner), to accompany, attend; to follow after, pursue (class.; cf.: comitor, stipo).

examples.original: At illud ex se ortum fidele firmumque est et crescit et ad extremum usque prosequitur;
examples.translation: But that joy which springs wholly from oneself is leal and sound; it increases and attends us to the last;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Datae e classe Misenensi duae triremes ad prosequendum, cum quibus Cythnum insulam tenuit: nec defuere qui trierarchos nomine Neronis accirent.
examples.translation: With these Calpurnius reached the island of Cythnus, where there were many who tried to win over the captains in Nero’s name.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Longius prosequi veritus, quod silvae paludesque intercedebant neque etiam parvulo detrimento illorum locum relinqui videbat, omnibus suis incolumibus copiis eodem die ad Ciceronem pervenit.
examples.translation: He feared to pursue very far, because there were woods and marshes in the way, and, as he saw, there was no chance now of doing even slight damage to the enemy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To inflict punishment upon, to punish (syn.: castigo, animadverto, plecto, multo).

examples.original: Noli ergo atrocius vindicare quod lenius invenisti. Inquirendi quam puniendi neces-sitas maior est;
examples.translation: Do not then punish with harsher sentence what you found out by gentler methods.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: pure, unmixed, unadulterated, esp. of wine not mixed with water: merum antiqui dicebant solum: at nunc merum purum appellamus, Paul. ex

examples.original: Tam bibit hunc avide, quam bibit ante merum.
examples.translation: He drinks it as greedily as he drank undiluted wine before.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Plenum epulis madidumque mero Venerique paratum Invenies;
examples.translation: You will find him sated with feasting, drunken with wine, and ripe for amorous dalliance;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Idem tibi de bonis dico: hoc bonum inter meras voluptates est, hoc inter tristia et acerba.
examples.translation: The same thing holds true, I assure you, concerning goods; you will find one amid circumstances of pure pleasure, another amid sorrow and bitterness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to ships, ship-, naval
Latin: Qui ad navem pertinet

examples.original: Atilius Regulus cos. victis navali proelio Poenis in Africam traiecit.
examples.translation: Atilius Regulus the consul, having beaten the Carthaginians in a naval battle, crossed into Africa.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Inde cum Venetis etiam navale bellum, sed maior cum Oceano quam cum ipsis navibus rixa.
examples.translation: Next came a naval war with the Veneti; but it was a struggle rather against the ocean than against the enemy’s fleet.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sic uno tempore et de navali pugna Sabinus et de Sabina victoria Caesar certior factus est, civitatesque omnes se statim Titurio dediderunt.
examples.translation: So it chanced that in the same hour Sabinus learnt of the naval battle, and Caesar of Sabinus’ victory; and all the states at once surrendered to Sabinus.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a knowing or being skilled in any thing, knowledge, science, skill, expertness, = cognitio, eruditio (freq. and class.).
Latin: actus sciendi, cognitio, intelligentia
Latin: tanta memoria praeteritorum futurorumque prudentia

examples.original: Saepe ab Aristotele, a Theophrasto mirabiliter est laudata per se ipsa rerum scientia;
examples.translation: Aristotle and Theophrastus often and admirably praised knowledge for its own sake;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Circa eadem fere Pyrrhonei versantur et Megarici et Eretrici et Academici, qui novam induxerunt scientiam, nihil scire.
examples.translation: The Pyrrhonean, Megarian, Eretrian, and Academic schools are all engaged in practically the same task; they have introduced a new knowledge, non-knowledge.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tantus est igitur innatus in nobis cognitionis amor et scientiae ut nemo dubitare possit quin ad eas res hominum natura nullo emolumento invitata rapiatur.
examples.translation: So great is our innate love of learning and of knowledge, that no one can doubt that man’s nature is strongly attracted to these things even without the lure of any profit.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: of or belonging to the sea, sea-, maritime (class.).

examples.original: Victor ergo apud Liparas mersa aut fugata hostium classe primum illum maritimum egit triumphum.
examples.translation: Thus victorious off the Liparae Islands, after sinking or routing the enemy’s fleet, they celebrated their first naval triumph.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sp. Furius M. Horatius dextrorsus in maritimam oram atque Antium, Q. Servilius et L. Geganius laeva ad montes et Ecetram pergunt.
examples.translation: Spurius Furius and Marcus Horatius marched to the right, towards Antium and the coast; Quintus Servilius and Lucius Geganius to the left, in the direction of Ecetra and the mountains.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ex his omnibus longe sunt humanissimi qui Cantium incolunt, quae regio est maritima omnis, neque multum a Gallica differunt consuetudine.
examples.translation: Of all the Britons the inhabitants of Kent, an entirely maritime district, are by far the most civilised, differing but little from the Gallic manner of life.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: loftiness, haughtiness, pride, arrogance

examples.original: Neque hoc illi quisquam tribuebat superbiae;
examples.translation: And no one regarded this as arrogance on his part;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Timoleon

examples.original: Simili superbia violentiaque ceteros tractavit ordines.
examples.translation: He treated the other orders with like insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Nec nominis homines tum pertaesum esse, quippe quo Iovem appellari fas sit, quo Romulum, conditorem urbis, deincepsque reges, quod sacris etiam ut sollemne retentum sit: superbiam violentiamque tum perosos regis.
examples.translation: Nor was it the name, said he, which had then disgusted men, since by this name Jupiter was duly called; and Romulus, the founder of the City: and the successive kings;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to fall off, fall down (class.).

examples.original: Si non potest, ut dicitis, sapiens ex beato in miserum decidere, non potest in non beatum.
examples.translation: Then if, as you say, the wise man cannot fall from happiness to wretchedness, he cannot fall into non-happiness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aspiciam regum liventia colla catenis Duraque per saevas vincula nexa manus Et tandem trepidos vultus inque illa ferocum Invitis lacrimas decidere ora genis.
examples.translation: I shall see the necks of kings livid with chains, and ruthless fetters entwining cruel hands, and faces cowed at last, and the tears falling down unwilling, haughty cheeks.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: son of Jupiter and a Theban woman

examples.original: In nemus et saltus thalamo regina relicto Fertur, ut Aonio concita Baccha deo.
examples.translation: Leaving her bower the queen hies her to the woods and glens, like a Bacchanal sped by the Aonian god.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the muscular part of the arm, from the shoulder to the elbow, the upper arm.

examples.original: Iam non excussis torquentur tela lacertis, Nec longinqua cadunt iaculato volnera ferro, Miscenturque manus.
examples.translation: No longer were weapons hurled from vigorous arms, no longer were the wounds of the hurtling steel inflicted at a distance;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Stulta est enim, mi Lucili, et minime conveniens litterato viro occupatio exercendi lacertos et dilatandi cervicem ac latera firmandi;
examples.translation: It is indeed foolish, my dear Lucilius, and very unsuitable for a cultivated man, to work hard over developing the muscles and broadening the shoulders and strengthening the lungs.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to free from faults, to correct, improve, amend

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Intellego, Lucili, non emendari me tantum sed transfigurari.
examples.translation: On Sharing Knowledge I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Edidit autem auctore Augusto Varius, sed summatim emendata, ut qui versus etiam inperfectos sicut erant reliquerit;
examples.translation: However, Varius published the ”Aeneid” at Augustus’ request, making only a few slight corrections, and even leaving the incomplete lines just as they were.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Nam quod dixisti: ”Cavendum est, ne cum rem dubiam emendari volumus, maiora vulnera faciamus,” tantundem valebit, si eis dimidium concedatur.
examples.translation: For your remark that we must beware, while endeavouring to settle a doubtful matter, of causing more serious wounds, will have as much force if they be granted a half.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a door (class.; cf.: porta, janua, fores, valvae).

examples.original: Conversus ad ianuam ”Quis est iste?” inquam, ”iste decrepitus et merito ad ostium admotus?
examples.translation: You have done well to place him at the entrance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Huc cum ab Ostia navigaret, vehementi circio bis paene demersus est, prope Liguriam iuxtaque Stoechadas insulas.
examples.translation: On the voyage thither from Ostia he was nearly cast away twice in furious north-westers, off Liguria and near the Stoechades islands.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Et ille quidem ad rei famam veneno fata praecepit. Ceterum Porcius Cato Cyprias opes Liburnis per Tiberinum ostium invexit.
examples.translation: Ptolemy, on hearing the news of this, anticipated fate by taking poison, and Porcius Cato brought the wealth of Cyprus in Liburnian galleys to the mouth of the Tiber.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a drinking-vessel

examples.original: Morsu virus habent, et fatum dente minantur, Pocula morte carent.” Dixit dubiumque venenum Hausit;
examples.translation: There is no death in the cup.” He spoke and drank down the dreaded poison;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to make straight, set right, bring into order.

examples.original: Ingenii vis praeceptis alitur et crescit novasque persuasiones adicit innatis et depravata corrigit.
examples.translation: The strength of the wit is nourished and kept growing by precepts;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Persius Lives of Illustrious Men ut quasi finitus esset. Leviter correxit Cornutus et Caesio Basso petenti, ut ipse ederet, tradidit edendum.
examples.translation: Cornutus made some slight corrections, and on the request of Caesius Bassus that he might publish it, turned it over to him for that purpose.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Atque utinam, cum magna et dura quatiuntur, parva et flexibilia corrigantur. De domo illa quid dicam, nisi benignissimae tuae curae gratias agam?
examples.translation: And would that, when the tall and sturdy things are shaken, the lowly and yielding may receive correction!
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: That pertains to or is made of copper, bronze, etc.

examples.original: Eam propter inopiam aerarii consules vendiderunt.
examples.translation: These the consuls sold, owing to the impoverished condition of the treasury.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Patres bene coeptam rem perseveranter tueri; conferre ipsi primi, et quia nondum argentum signatum erat, aes grave plaustris quidam ad aerarium convehentes speciosam etiam conlationem faciebant.
examples.translation: They were themselves the first to contribute, and since there was as yet no silver coinage, some of them brought uncoined bronze in waggons to the treasury, and even made a display of their contributing.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: very lately

examples.original: Nobis solvi perire est, proxima enim intuemur;
examples.translation: To our minds, this process means perishing, for we behold only that which is nearest;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Caesar Valetiacus proximo anno eundem magistratum gesserit.
examples.translation: Valetiacus had exercised the same office in the previous year.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quorum adventu cum sibi Correus oblatam occasionem rei gerendae existimaret, primum cum paucis se ostendit atque in proximas turmas impetum fecit.
examples.translation: Their arrival led Correus to suppose that a chance of despatching the business was offered him;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a small pick-axe, hatchet

examples.original: Verbum tamen facere non audebant, ne forte ea res ad Dolabellam ipsum pertineret.
examples.translation: However, they dared not say a word, fearing that Dolabella himself might be concerned in the outrage.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Malleolo quaestore Cn. Dolabellae occiso, duas sibi hereditates venisse arbitratus est;
examples.translation: When Gaius Malleolus, Dolabella’s quaestor, was killed, Verres reckoned that two inheritances had come to him;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iam iam, Dolabella, neque me tui neque tuorum liberum, quos tu miseros in egestate atque in solitudine reliquisti, misereri potest.
examples.translation: After this, Dolabella, I can feel no pity for you; nor, after this, for the unhappy children you have left behind you in poverty and loneliness.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: dangerous, hazardous, perilous (class.)
Latin: Qui periculum in se continet, cum periculo coniunctus

examples.original: Magnum crimen et, nisi falsum esset, periculosissimum.
examples.translation: A serious charge, and were it not untrue, very threatening to our friendship.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Eum autem, cum modo regressus sum, periculosissime scandalizatum comperi de absentia mea;
examples.translation: When I returned recently, I found them offended to a very dangerous degree at my absence.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Caesar His rebus comparatis, represso iam Lucterio et remoto, quod intrare intra praesidia periculosum putabat, in Helvios proficiscitur.
examples.translation: By these measures of security Lucterius was checked and set back, for he deemed it dangerous to penetrate the line of garrisons;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: small, thin, slender, lank, meagre, poor, feeble

examples.original: Exilium Metellus fortiter tulit, Rutilius etiam libenter;
examples.translation: Exile was endured by Metellus with courage, by Rutilius even with gladness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Erit enim instructus ad mortem contemnendam, ad exilium, ad ipsum etiam dolorem.
examples.translation: For he will have been schooled to make light of death, of exile, even of pain itself.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Numquid accidere tibi, si damnaris, potest durius quam ut mittaris in exilium, ut ducaris in carcerem?
examples.translation: If you lose this case, can anything more severe happen to you than being sent into exile or led to prison?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a raging abyss, whirlpool, gulf (syn.: vorago, barathrum).

examples.original: Hos, Caesar, populos si nunc non usserit ignis, Uret cum terris, uret cum gurgite ponti.
examples.translation: If fire does not consume this host now, it will consume them hereafter, together with the earth and the waters of the sea;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: His igitur rebus retractis terra repente, maxuma qua nunc se ponti plaga caerula tendit, succidit et salso suffudit gurgite fossas.
examples.translation: Therefore when these bodies were withdrawn, suddenly the earth sank down where now the blue expanse of the sea extends so wide, and drowned its hollows with the salt flood.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Hispana tibi Germanaque Tethys paruit et nostro diducta Britannia mundo, diversoque tuas coluerunt gurgite voces lentus Arar Rhodanusque ferox et dives Hiberus.
examples.translation: The seas of Spain, the German ocean obeyed thee and Britain, so far removed from our continent. Rivers of all lands observed thy statutes, slow-flowing Saône, swift Rhone, and Ebro rich in gold.
examples.author: Claudian
examples.work: Panegyric On The Consulship Of Fl. Manlius Theodorus (A.D. 399)

definitions: English: The keel of a ship

examples.original: Nubila tanguntur velis et terra carina.
examples.translation: The sails reach the clouds, the keel rests on the bottom.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hoc opus exegi: fessae date serta carinae;
examples.translation: I have finished my task; hang garlands on the weary vessel;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Neque enim de more carinas Extendunt puppesque levant, sed firma gerendis Molibus insolito contexunt robora ductu.
examples.translation: They built no long hulls, no high sterns, as the custom is, but joined stout planks together on unwonted lines to carry heavy structures.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to draw tight, to bind or tie tight; to draw, bind, or press together, etc. (syn. ligo).

examples.original: Dissiluit stringens uterum membrana, fluuntque Viscera;
examples.translation: The membrane that confines the belly snapped asunder, and the bowels gushed out.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ergo vos prius in me strinxeritis ferrum quam in vos ego;
examples.translation: You shall therefore sooner draw sword on me than I on you.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Hurtful, harmful, injurious, noxious

examples.original: Et ista quamdiu furtim et a singulis fiunt, minus noxia minusque monstruosa sunt;
examples.translation: And as long as such crimes are committed by stealth and by individuals, they are less harmful and less portentous;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to thunder at; hence, to stun, stupefy

examples.original: Multi, Pharsalica castra Cum peterent nondum fama prodente ruina, Occursu stupuere ducis vertigine rerum Attoniti, cladisque suae vix ipse fidelis Auctor erat.
examples.translation: Many who were on their way to the camp at Pharsalia, before rumour had published his defeat abroad, were startled to meet their leader and astounded by the sudden change of fortune;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to call out, call forth; to bring out, draw forth (class. —syn. invito, cito, etc.).

examples.original: An tu ad suum finem hanc evocas, in quantum potest plurimum crescere?
examples.translation: Are you willing to develop this to its farthest limits—to its greatest degree of increase?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illum saepe minis Caesar precibusque morantem Evocat: ”O mundo tantorum causa laborum, Quid superos et fata tenes?
examples.translation: Again and again Caesar urged him to haste with threats and entreaties: ”On you lies the blame for the sore troubles that afflict mankind;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Libri XVII Periocha Cn. Cornelius consul a classe Punica circumventus et per fraudem, veluti in conloquium evocatus, captus est.
examples.translation: Summaries Summary of Book XVII The consul Gnaeus Cornelius was surrounded by a Carthaginian fleet and was made prisoner by fraud, having been lured out as to a colloquy.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to lift or raise up, raise, elevate, lift on high (in the poets and postAug. prose writers very frequent, but not in Cic.; syn.: tollo, erigo).

examples.original: Thessaliam, qua parte diem brumalibus horis Attollit Titan, rupes Ossaea coercet;
examples.translation: Thessaly is bounded by the peak of Ossa in the quarter where the sun rises in winter;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quem postquam propius famulae videre fideles, Non ultra gemitus tacitos incessere fatum Permisere sibi, frustraque attollere terra Semianimem conantur eram;
examples.translation: When her faithful handmaids saw him close at hand, they dared not rail at destiny except with stifled groans, and tried in vain to lift their fainting mistress from the ground;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to enclose something on all sides or wholly, to hold together, to surround, encompass

examples.original: Thessaliam, qua parte diem brumalibus horis Attollit Titan, rupes Ossaea coercet;
examples.translation: Thessaly is bounded by the peak of Ossa in the quarter where the sun rises in winter;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Per octo annos varie et inaequabiliter provinciam rexit, primo acer et vehemens et in coercendis quidem delictis vel immodicus.
examples.translation: For eight years he governed the province in a variable and inconsistent manner. At first he was vigorous and energetic and even over severe in punishing offences;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: To reconcile; constr. alicui, aliquem (class. and freq.)

examples.original: Haecine tandem tibi placent, vir gravissime?
examples.translation: Do you, a man of sober judgement, really approve of this?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: In praesentia omnia praeter bellum omitti placere;
examples.translation: For the present he thought they should pay no attention to anything but the war.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quis enim placere populo potest, cui placet virtus?
examples.translation: For who that is pleased by virtue can please the crowd?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to hurry with alarm, to bustle about anxiously, be in a state of confusion, agitation, or trepidation (class., but not in Cic.)
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Trepidant enim, cum fecerunt, haerent;
examples.translation: For they tremble after the deed, and they are embarrassed;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Proprium autem est nocentium trepidare.
examples.translation: But it is the property of guilt to be in fear.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tristes praesagia curas Exagitant, trepida quatitur formidine somnus, Thessaliam nox omnis habet;
examples.translation: For her sorrow is intensified by forebodings, and her sleep broken by anxious fears.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to consider as unworthy or improper, to be angry or displeased at, to be indignant (syn. stomachor).

examples.original: Caesaris illud opus, voti pars altera vestri, Occidit: indignas, Livia, solve comas.
examples.translation: That achievement of Caesar, the one half of your hopes, has perished: undo, Livia, thy undeserving locks.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Si autem ille qui corripit, reddere vult malum pro malo ei qui corripienti indignatur, non fuit dignus qui corriperet, sed dignus plane, qui etiam ipse corripi deberet.
examples.translation: If the reprover, however, choose to render evil for evil to the man who takes offence at being reproved, he was not fit to reprove another, but clearly fit to be reproved himself.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a device, artifice; hence, evil intent, wrongdoing with a view to the consequences (opp. culpa, negligence; cf. also: fallacia, fraus, astutia, calliditas).—In the older, and esp

examples.original: Ita undique regi dolus nectitur.
examples.translation: Thus on every hand the toils were woven about the king.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iuravit autem uterque se sine dolo indutias conservaturum.
examples.translation: The two parties took oath that they would loyally observe the armistice.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Agesilaus

examples.original: Nec non subrepta paratis A famulo Ganymede dolis pervenit ad hostes Caesaris Arsinoe;
examples.translation: Moreover, Arsinoe was carried off secretly by a trick of Ganymede, her chamberlain, and conveyed to Caesar’s enemies.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To allow or permit to go by, to let pass (class.; syn.: omitto, neglego).

examples.original: Quid enim est a Chrysippo praetermissum in Stoicis?
examples.translation: Take Stoicism: what aspect of it has Chrysippus left untouched?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Si enim, ut mihi quidem videtur, non explet bona naturae voluptas, iure praetermissa est;
examples.translation: If, as I hold, pleasure adds nothing to the sum-total of nature’s goods, it has rightly been omitted.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Eorum enim omnium, multa praetermittentium dum eligant aliquid quod sequantur, quasi curta sententia;
examples.translation: They pick and choose, pass over a great deal and fasten on a single aspect;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that which grows forth; esp. of human beings, offspring, progeny, child, descendant; and collect., descendants, race, progeny, posterity

examples.original: Qua sua Penteliden proles est ulta Lycurgum, Haec maneat teli te quoque plaga novi.
examples.translation: As his own offspring was revenged upon Lycurgus, the Pentelid, so may the stroke of a strange weapon await thee also.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Et quidem unum esse deum summum sine initio, sine prole naturae ceu patrem magnum atque magnificum quis tam demens, tam mente captus neget esse certissimum?
examples.translation: And indeed, who is so foolish, so mentally astray, as to deny the very certain truth that there is one supreme god, without beginning, without natural offspring, like a great and splendid father?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Iamque dies medius tenues contraxerat umbras, Inque pari spatio vesper et ortus erant: Ecce, redit Cephalus silvis, Cyllenia proles, Oraque fontana fervida pulsat aqua.
examples.translation: And now midday had drawn short the unsubstantial shadows, and evening and morning were equally removed: lo! Cephalus, son of Cyllene, returns from the woods, and scatters spring water on his glowing cheeks.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a being alone or solitary, loneliness, solitariness, solitude (of a person or place); a lonely place, desert, wilderness

examples.original: Vastae tum in his locis solitudines erant.
examples.translation: In those days this was a wild and uninhabited region.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nocti se potius ac solitudini quam ulli aut urbi aut hospiti committebat.
examples.translation: And so in no town was she allowed to halt;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum autem venissemus in Academiae non sine causa nobilitata spatia, solitudo erat ea quam volueramus.
examples.translation: When we reached the walks of the Academy, which are so deservedly famous, we had them entirely to ourselves, as we had hoped.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a votingtablet, a ballot (syn. tabella), and in gen., a vote, voice, suffrage (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Summoveri Laetorius iubet, praeterquam qui suffragium ineant.
examples.translation: Laetorius ordered the removal of all but those who were voting.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sublata sunt studia, exstinctae suffragationes, nullae contentiones, nulla libertas populi in mandandis magistratibus, nulla exspectatio suffragiorum: nihil, ut plerumque evenit, praeter opinionem accidet: nulla erit posthac varietas comitiorum.
examples.translation: But if, on the other hand, it commonly happens that we are surprised at the election of some and the non-election of others;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sane liceat; ut quidem iudicetis et feratis de meliore suffragium, quidni non permittam?
examples.translation: I shall of course allow you to pass judgment and cast a vote as to the better course.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: unsound in mind.
Latin: non serenum vel rectum animum habens; dēmēns
Latin: Irrationalis, incongruus; delirus, absurdus, ridiculus

examples.original: Inprobum risus, insanum vultus habitusque demonstrat.
examples.translation: The scamp is shown up by his laugh;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Diripiantque tuos insanis unguibus artus Strymoniae matres, Orpheos esse ratae.
examples.translation: And may Strymonian mothers rend thy limbs with frenzied nails, deeming them those of Orpheus.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Mars pater, insano Veneris turbatus amore, De duce terribili factus amator erat.
examples.translation: Father Mars, plagued by frenzied love of Venus, from a terrible captain became a lover.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: an elephant.—Form
Latin: zool. Aliquis animalium mammiferorum sub Elephantidis familia. Hodie maxima animalia terrestria sunt
Latin: Ebur elephantinum

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quinam illi fuerunt viri quos ab elephantis primo proelio obtritos accepimus?
examples.translation: The wounds of all of them were upon their chests;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Libri XIII Periocha Valerius Laevinus cos. parum prospere adversus Pyrrhum pugnavit, elephantorum maxime inusitata facie territis militibus.
examples.translation: Summary of Book XIII The consul Valerius Laevinus fought a losing engagement with Pyrrhus, the soldiers being greatly terrified by the strange sight of the elephants.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to be boiling hot, to boil, ferment, glow (class.; most freq. in poets.; syn.: calere, aestuare, ebullire, ardescere, ignescere; ardere, flagrare, tepere).

examples.original: Mancino deinde consule terra marique fervebat obsidio.
examples.translation: The harbours were blocked up;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to puke, spew, throw up, vomit (a common method among the Romans of renewing the appetite).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ŭi, ĭtum, 3

examples.original: Aut ut Trinacrius salias super ora gigantis, Plurima qua flammas Sicanis Aetna vomit.
examples.translation: Or like the Trinacrian mayst thou leap into the giant’s mouth, where in full might Sicanian Aetna vomits flames.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a muse, one of the goddesses of poetry, music, and the other liberal arts. The ancients reckoned nine of them, viz.: Clio, the muse of history; Melpomene, of tragedy
English: a watching, watch, guard, care, protection (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Is armatos circa se in custodiam sui habuit.
examples.translation: He kept armed men about him to protect him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ingenti periculo transeundum per hostium custodias erat.
examples.translation: It was necessary at enormous risk to pass the enemy’s outposts.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Anxur in Volscis brevi receptum est neglectis die festo custodiis urbis.
examples.translation: Anxur of the Volsci was speedily recaptured, a holiday having relaxed the vigilance of their guard.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a cheek; plur., the cheeks (cf.: bucca, mala).

examples.original: Iamque volaturus parvo dedit oscula nato, Nec patriae lacrimas continuere genae.
examples.translation: There was a hill smaller than a mountain, but rising above the level plains;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Aspiciam regum liventia colla catenis Duraque per saevas vincula nexa manus Et tandem trepidos vultus inque illa ferocum Invitis lacrimas decidere ora genis.
examples.translation: I shall see the necks of kings livid with chains, and ruthless fetters entwining cruel hands, and faces cowed at last, and the tears falling down unwilling, haughty cheeks.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nocte sub extrema pulso torpore quietis, Dum fovet amplexu gravidum Cornelia curis Pectus et aversi petit oscula grata mariti, Umentes mirata genas percussaque caeco Volnere non audet flentem deprendere Magnum.
examples.translation: Night was ending and the drowsiness of sleep was banished, when Cornelia clasped in her arms the care-laden breast of her husband and sought the dear lips of him who turned from her;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a prophetic sign, token

examples.original: Habita, ut erat, res prodigii loco est;
examples.translation: This heifer was regarded as a prodigy, as indeed it was;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ipse enim aversissimus ab istis prodigiis sum;
examples.translation: I particularly disapprove of these freaks;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo anno prodigia multa fuerunt, quorum averruncandorum causa supplicationes in biduum senatus decrevit;
examples.translation: In that year were many portents, to avert which the senate decreed supplications for two days.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: made free, set free, only as subst., one made free, a freedman, an emancipated person

examples.original: Sevius Nicanor Marci libertus negabit;
examples.translation: Sevius Nicanor, the freedman of Marcus, may deny this;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Nec dubitavit postero die Claudius ordinem rei gestae perferre ad senatum ac liberto gratias agere, quod pro salute sua etiam dormiens excubaret.
examples.translation: And Claudius did not hesitate to recount the whole affair to the senate next day and to thank the freedman for watching over his emperor’s safety even in his sleep.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Aurelius Opillus, Epicurei cuiusdam libertus, philosophiam primo, deinde rhetoricam, novissime grammaticam docuit.
examples.translation: Aurelius Opilius, freedman of an Epicurean, first taught philosophy, afterwards rhetoric, and finally grammar.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: in a middle state between too much and too little, middling, moderate, tolerable, ordinary; sometimes also, not remarkable, indifferent, mediocre.
Latin: Medium tenens
Latin: Neque bonus neque malus

examples.original: Habuit et pingendi fingendique non mediocre studium.
examples.translation: He likewise had no slight interest in painting and sculpture.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Usus est familia, si utilitate iudicandum est, optima; si forma, vix mediocri.
examples.translation: He had slaves that were excellent in point of efficiency, although in personal appearance hardly mediocre;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Disciplinis tamen liberalibus ab aetate prima non mediocrem operam dedit ac saepe experimenta cuiusque etiam publicavit.
examples.translation: Yet he gave no slight attention to liberal studies from his earliest youth, and even published frequent specimens of his attainments in each line.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: on the under side, below, underneath.

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Transeunt Rhenum navibus ratibusque triginta milibus passuum infra eum locum, ubi pons erat perfectus praesidiumque ab Caesare relictum: primos Eburonum fines adeunt;
examples.translation: On boats and rafts they crossed the Rhine thirty miles below the spot where the bridge had been built and a garrison left by Caesar;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: pass. signif, nactus

examples.original: Hodiernum hoc est, quod apud Epicurum nanctus sum;
examples.translation: The thought for to-day is one which I discovered in Epicurusa;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed potest in penetralibus suis ostendi, si modo non institorem, sed antistitem nancta est.
examples.translation: But she can still be viewed in her sanctuary, if her exhibitor is a priest and not a pedlar.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Caesar Avarici complures dies commoratus summamque ibi copiam frumenti et reliqui commeatus nactus exercitum ex labore atque inopia refecit.
examples.translation: Caesar halted at Avaricum for several days, and by the immense quantity of corn and all other supplies which he found there recuperated the army after toil and want.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: an under-garment of the Romans worn by both sexes, a tunic.
Latin: Vestis interior, corpori adhaerens, cui toga superinduitur

examples.original: Nec puto, nec sensi tunicam laniasse;
examples.translation: I do not think nor did I notice that I tore her vest;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: To copy off, transcribe any thing from an original
Latin: Ex exemplo alicuius rei scribere; de aliquo scribere

examples.original: Ista, quam tu describis, negotiatio est, non amicitia, quae ad commodum accedit, quae quid consecutura sit spectat.
examples.translation: The friendship which you portray is a bargain and not a friendship;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Denique ut breviter includam quod sentio, et istos satagios ac sibi molestos describam tibi, tam intemperantes in ipsis miseriis quam sunt ante illas.
examples.translation: In fine, to express my thoughts in brief compass and portray to you those busybodies and self-tormentors—they are as uncontrolled in the midst of their troubles as they are before them.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: rich in lands, substantial, opulent (syn.: dives, abundans, copiosus).

examples.original: Huius, Lyco, oratione locuples, rebus ipsis ieiunior.
examples.translation: His successor Lyco has a copious style, but his matter is somewhat barren.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Egentes in locupletes, perditi in bonos, servi in dominos armabantur.
examples.translation: You say the senate was on my side. It was;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ad hunc Epicurus illam nobilem sententiam scripsit, qua hortatur, ut Pythoclea locupletem non publica nec ancipiti via faciat.
examples.translation: It was to him that Epicurus addressed the well-known saying,c urging him to make Pythocles rich, but not rich in the vulgar and equivocal way.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: name of two Roman gentes, one patrician and one plebeian

examples.original: Publiusne Clodius, qui ex pontificis maximi domo religionem eripuit, is in meam intulit?
examples.translation: Has Publius Clodius, who robbed the house of the supreme pontiff of its sanctity, conferred sanctity upon mine?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quaere hoc ex Clodio, scriptore legum tuarum: iube adesse: latitat omnino, sed si requiri iusseris, invenient hominem apud sororem tuam occultantem se capite demisso.
examples.translation: He is skulking away out of sight; but do but order search to be made for him, and the fellow will be discovered secreting himself shamefacedly at your sister’s house.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a demi-god

examples.original: Potes queri, si here tantum.
examples.translation: You might complain if I said ”yesterday” merely.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Paruit imperio dominae Tirynthius heros: I nunc et dubita ferre, quod ille tulit.
examples.translation: The Tirynthian hero obeyed a mistress’ command: go, shrink from enduring what he endured!
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Aut ut Abantiades, aut ut Cycneïus heros, Clausus in aequoreas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: Or like Abantiades or the Cycnean hero mayst thou be hurled, imprisoned, into the sea’s waters.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the quality of being aequus (syn.: aequalitas, jus, justitia, fas).

examples.original: Prima autem pars est aequitatis aequalitas.
examples.translation: The chief part of equity, however, is equality.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non ita se invidiam pertimuisse ut nihil in aequitate et misericordia civium suorum spei habeat.
examples.translation: He did not so fear men’s malice as to have no hope in the justice and pity of his fellow citizens.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et in unica concordia inter ipsos, qui consensus privatis interdum inutilis est, summa adversus alios aequitas erat.
examples.translation: And while they maintained an unparalleled harmony amongst themselves—a unanimity sometimes prejudicial to the governed,—they treated others with the utmost fairness.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the form and manner of religious observances; a religious usage or ceremony

examples.original: Suspiciendi tamen sunt et ritu deorum colendi.
examples.translation: They deserve respect, however, and should be worshipped with a divine ritual.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hos scelerum ritus, haec dirae crimina gentis Effera damnarat nimiae pietatis Erictho Inque novos ritus pollutam duxerat artem.
examples.translation: These criminal rites and malpractices of an accursed race fierce Erictho had scouted as not wicked enough, and had turned her loathsome skill to rites before unknown.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hunc non ruricolae Panes nemorumque potentes Silvani Nymphaeque tenent, sed barbara ritu Sacra deum;
examples.translation: No rural Pan dwelt there, no Silvanus, ruler of the woods, no Nymphs;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to busy one's self with or be engaged in something; to perform, execute
Latin: officium vel munerem habere, explere
Latin: fung|or, -ī, functus

examples.original: Scholam eius claros quoque viros frequentasse aiunt, in iis M. Ciceronem, etiam cum praetura fungeretur.
examples.translation: They say also that distinguished men attended his school, including Cicero even while he was praetor.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Nam et amici cultus et parentis ei qui officio fungitur in eo ipso prodest quod ita fungi officio in recte factis est, quae sunt orta a virtutibus.
examples.translation: For example, dutiful conduct towards friends and parents benefits the doer from the very fact that such performance of duty is a right action, and right actions take their rise from virtues.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Atque in sensibus est sua cuiusque virtus, ut ne quid impediat quo minus suo sensus quisque munere fungatur in iis rebus celeriter expediteque percipiendis quae subiectae sunt sensibus.
examples.translation: The senses also possess their several virtues or excellences, consisting in the unimpeded performance of their several functions of swiftly and readily perceiving sensible objects.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Furnished abundantly with a thing, well supplied, having abundance, rich, copious, plentiful, abounding (in wealth, means of living, etc.) (very freq. and class., esp. in prose).

examples.original: Quam copiose ac varie vexavit antiquos!
examples.translation: With what readiness and versatility did he make war upon the ancients!
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Erat et cupidus voluptatum et eius generis intellegens et copiosus;
examples.translation: His appetite for pleasures was only equalled by his taste and ingenuity in devising them.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Homo, qui semper hospitalissimus amicissimusque nostrorum hominum existimatus esset, noluit videri ipsum illum Rubrium invitus domum suam recepisse: magnifice et ornate, ut erat in primis inter suos copiosus, convivium comparat;
examples.translation: He had always been considered most hospitable and cordial towards our people, and he did not wish to give the impression that he was receiving even a man like Rubrius into his house unwillingly.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: dip into any thing; hence

examples.original: Ita re infecta in oppidum reverterunt.
examples.translation: So without success they returned to the town.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non enim inquinati sumus, sed infecti.
examples.translation: We are not merely defiled; we are dyed by them.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Itaque eam infectam rem M. Fulvius Paetus T. Manlius Torquatus novi consules acceperunt.
examples.translation: The enterprise was therefore still unfinished when Marcus Fulvius Paetus and Titus Manlius Torquatus, the new consuls, took it over.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: sometimes

examples.original: Ac nonnumquam horreis praeclusis populo famem indixit.
examples.translation: Sometimes too he would shut up the granaries and condemn the people to hunger.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: In cognoscendo autem ac decernendo mira varietate animi fuit, modo circumspectus et sagax, interdum inconsultus ac praeceps, nonnumquam frivolus amentique similis.
examples.translation: But in hearing and deciding cases he showed strange inconsistency of temper, for he was now careful and shrewd, sometimes hasty and inconsiderate, occasionally silly and like a crazy man.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to put away, remove: and abdere se, to go away, betake one's self to some place
Latin: Deponere, removere
Latin: Celare, occultare, recondere

examples.original: Quis enim toto mari locus per hos annos aut tam firmum habuit praesidium, ut tutus esset, aut tam fuit abditus, ut lateret?
examples.translation: For what position on the whole seaboard during those years was either so strongly defended as to be secure or so well hidden as to escape notice?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Gregarius miles futuri socors et ignobilitate tutior perstabat: vagi per vias, in domibus abditi pacem ne tum quidem orabant, cum bellum posuissent.
examples.translation: They wandered through the streets or concealed themselves in houses, but did not beg for peace even when they had given up fighting.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: Lucilius, a Roman gens; especially the satirist Gaius Lucilius

examples.original: Subinde itaque, Lucili, quam multa sis consecutus recordare.
examples.translation: Therefore continually remind yourself, Lucilius, how many ambitions you have attained.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Intellego, Lucili, non emendari me tantum sed transfigurari.
examples.translation: On Sharing Knowledge I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Bassum Aufidium, virum optimum, vidi quassum, aetati obluctantem.
examples.translation: On Conquering the Conqueror I have beheld Aufidius Bassus, that noble man, shattered in health and wrestling with his years.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to untie, unfasten, unbind; to loose, loosen, release, open (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; cf.: relaxo, resero, recludo, libero).
Latin: Dilabi facere
Latin: A vinculis liberare

examples.original: Odi concubitus, qui non utrumque resolvunt;
examples.translation: I hate embraces which leave not each outworn;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Diu infructuosam et asperam militiam toleraverant ingenio loci caelique et severitate disciplinae, quam in pace inexorabilem discordiae civium resolvunt, paratis utrimque corruptoribus et perfidia impunita.
examples.translation: The soldiers had long endured a profitless service which was severe because of the character of the district and of the climate, and also because discipline was strict.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: useless, needless, unnecessary, superfluous, redundant

examples.original: Alia enim fortasse exercentur in supervacuum.
examples.translation: For our training in other things is perhaps superfluous.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Necessaria iudicat, quorum magna pars supervacua est.
examples.translation: At present it holds things to be essential of which the greater part is superfluous.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec sunt, per quae probatur hanc philosophiae partem supervacuam non esse.
examples.translation: Such facts as these prove that this department of philosophy is not superfluous.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: To avenge one's self on, take vengeance on, or punish for wrong done (very freq. and class.; cf.: vindico, punio, persequor).

examples.original: Hunc tam inmaturum amorem virginis ultus est ferro.
examples.translation: The maiden’s girlish affection he punished with the sword.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nec illis aut honorare eam caedem ius hominum aut ulcisci ratio belli permittebat.
examples.translation: The common dictates of humanity did not permit them to honour such a murder or military policy to punish it.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Qua sua Penteliden proles est ulta Lycurgum, Haec maneat teli te quoque plaga novi.
examples.translation: As his own offspring was revenged upon Lycurgus, the Pentelid, so may the stroke of a strange weapon await thee also.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to draw out, to empty by drawing, to exhaust (class., esp. in the transf. and trop. senses).

examples.original: Id exhauriri aliis potius patimur, ut nobis faecem reservemus?
examples.translation: Let this phrase cleave to your soul;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Mortalia minuuntur, cadunt, deteruntur, crescunt, exhauriuntur, inplentur.
examples.translation: Mortal things decay, fall, are worn out, grow up, are exhausted, and replenished.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quemadmodum clepsydram non extremum stillicidium exhaurit, sed quicquid ante defluxit, sic ultima hora, qua esse desinimus, non sola mortem facit, sed sola consummat;
examples.translation: It is not the last drop that empties the water-clock, but all that which previously has flowed out; similarly, the final hour when we cease to exist does not of itself bring death;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a building of any kind, an edifice, structure, even though not suitable for a dwelling (while aedes designates only a structure for habitation).—Hence
Latin: Quod aedificatum est, ut domus vel ecclesia

examples.original: Ceterum ad Nequinum oppidum cum segni obsidione tempus tereretur, duo ex oppidanis, quorum erant aedificia iuncta muro, specu facto ad stationes Romanas itinere occulto perveniunt;
examples.translation: Meantime, at the town of Nequinum, while the siege dragged slowly on, two of the townsmen, whose dwellings abutted on the wall, dug a tunnel and made their way in secret to the Roman outposts.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bend from the straight path; to turn aside or away (freq. and class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

definitions: English: a projecting point of rock; a rock, cliff, crag, esp. a rock, shelf, ledge in the sea.

examples.original: Aspicit Hesiones scopulos silvaque latentes Anchisae thalamos;
examples.translation: He sees Hesione’s rock and the secret marriage-chamber of Anchises in the wood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hinc, Abaton quam nostra vocat veneranda vetustas, †Terra potens† primos sentit percussa tumultus, Et scopuli, placuit fluvii quos dicere venas, Quod manifesta novi primum dant signa tumoris.
examples.translation: Here too are the rocks which are commonly called the springs of the river, because they give the first clear indication when the water begins to rise.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Electum tandem traiecto gutture corpus Ducit, et inserto laqueis feralibus unco Per scopulos miserum trahitur, per saxa, cadaver Victurum, montisque cavi, quem tristis Erictho Damnarat sacris, alta sub rupe locatur.
examples.translation: The hapless body was dragged over rocks and stones, to live a second time, and was laid beneath a high rock of the hollow mountain which cruel Erictho had condemned to witness her rites.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: an axletree, about which a round body, e.g. a wheel, turns
Latin: Fusus seu acus per quem rota revolvit, vel cum rota revolvit
Latin: Axis mundi

examples.original: Hoc fuit Andromache, cum vir religatus ad axem Terruit admissos sanguinolentus equos;
examples.translation: Such a sight was Andromache, when her husband bound all bloody to the axle frightened the galloping steeds;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Medio cum Phoebus in axe est Aut caelum nox atra tenet, pavet ipse sacerdos Accessus dominumque timet deprendere luci.
examples.translation: For, when the sun is in mid-heaven or dark night fills the sky, the priest himself dreads their approach and fears to surprise the lord of the grove.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a siege, investment, blockade of a place (class.): obsidionem potias dicendum esse, quam obsidium, adjuvat nos testimonio suo Ennius in Telamone, Paul. ex

examples.original: Nec obsidio sed bellum ex aequo erat;
examples.translation: It was not a siege, but war upon even terms;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad famam obsidionis dilectus haberi coeptus erat;
examples.translation: On the rumour of a blockade they had begun to hold a levy;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eo alter consul Aemilius cum exercitu ad liberandos obsidione socios venit.
examples.translation: Thither the other consul, Aemilius, came with an army, to relieve the blockade of the allies.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a lie, untruth, falsehood.

examples.original: Magnum crimen et impudens mendacium.
examples.translation: It is a monstrous charge, and a shameless lie!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Tu quoque, cui veneris sensum natura negavit, Dulcia mendaci gaudia finge sono.
examples.translation: You to whom nature has denied the sensation of love, counterfeit the sweet bliss with lying sounds.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sed adeo, mi Lucili, philosophia sacrum quiddam est et venerabile, ut etiam, si quid illi simile est, mendacio placeat.
examples.translation: But, my dear Lucilius, philosophy is a thing of holiness, something to be worshipped, so much so that the very counterfeit pleases.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: scarcely, with difficulty, painfully, hardly; reluctantly, uncomfortably
Latin: Difficulter
Latin: Vix

examples.original: Aegre eo die sustentatum est.
examples.translation: The defence was with difficulty maintained on that day.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Aegre sedata ab Quinctio plebs, multo aegrius consul alter a patribus.
examples.translation: At length the council of the plebs was adjourned, and the consuls convened the senate.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Debet enim, misere si forte aegreque futurumst, ipse quoque esse in eo tum tempore, cui male possit accidere.
examples.translation: For,c if by chance anyone is to have misery and pain in the future, he must himself also exist then in that time to be miserable.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: a Roman goddess, identified with the Grecian Pallas Athene, the daughter of Zeus, and the goddess of wisdom, of sense and reflection, of the arts and sciences, of poetry, and of
Latin: Dea Romana sapientiae, belli, artium et scientiae, poëticae, et lanificii

examples.original: Post hunc Apollinem et Martem et Iovem et Minervam.
examples.translation: After him they set Apollo, Mars, Jupiter, and Minerva.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Iuppiter optimus maximus, Iuno regina et Minerva, alii di deaeque obsidentur;
examples.translation: Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Queen Juno, and Minerva, and the other gods and goddesses, are beleaguered;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Illius exemplo violes simulacra Minervae, Aulidis a portu qui leve vertit iter.
examples.translation: Mayst thou violate Minerva’s image after example of him who pursued a nimble path from Aulis’ haven.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: sudden, hasty, unlooked for, unexpected (freq. and class.)

examples.original: Diebus circiter xv, quibus in hiberna ventum est, initium repentini tumultus ac defectionis ortum est ab Ambiorige et Catuvolco;
examples.translation: In about a fortnight after the troops had moved into winter quarters, disorder and revolt suddenly began.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et ad hanc mortem repentinam vocesque morientis omnia praeterea, quae solent esse indicia et vestigia veneni, in illius mortuae corpore fuerunt.
examples.translation: Besides the suddenness of her death and her dying utterance, all the usual indications and traces of poison were afterwards found on her body.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam mihi non facit fidem tam multorum onerum, quae aliquando numeraveram, tam repentina depositio, quamvis te accepisse litteras meas non dubitem, quarum rescripta non habeo.
examples.translation: I can hardly believe I have so speedily discharged tasks I had once reckoned so numerous. Yet I am sure you must have had letters from me, to which I have received no answers.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: only, sole, single (class.).
Latin: Singularis, sui generis solus

examples.original: Laudis in hoc sexu non legum cura nec arma, Unica materia est coniunx miser.
examples.translation: To your sex neither peaceful government nor war is a field for glory: a husband’s sorrow alone can win it.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ita non omnibus obesis mannis et asturconibus et tolutariis praeferres unicum illum equum ab ipso Catone defrictum?
examples.translation: I see that there will be no end in dealing with such a theme unless I make an end myself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et in unica concordia inter ipsos, qui consensus privatis interdum inutilis est, summa adversus alios aequitas erat.
examples.translation: And while they maintained an unparalleled harmony amongst themselves—a unanimity sometimes prejudicial to the governed,—they treated others with the utmost fairness.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a cloud.
Latin: Vapor densatus in aere, et obumbrans

examples.original: Sol me invitabat, fames ad monebat, nubes minabantur;
examples.translation: The sunlight called to me, hunger warned, and clouds were lowering;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non tamen in caeca bellorum nube cadendum est, Aut cum permixtas acies sua tela tenebris Involvent.
examples.translation: Yet we are not compelled to fall on the blind haze of battle, or when their own missiles cover the confused armies with darkness.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non caeli nox illa fuit: latet obsitus aer Infernae pallore domus nimbisque gravatus Deprimitur, fluctusque in nubibus accipit imbrem.
examples.translation: The darkness was not the common darkness of night: the heavens were hidden and veiled with the dimness of the infernal regions, and weighed down by clouds;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to bend
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Hic locus ab hoste circiter passus sescentos, uti dictum est, aberat.
examples.translation: The spot, as has been said, was about six hundred paces away from the enemy.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quae putas me passum, dum per aspera erepo, dum viam quaero, dum facio?
examples.translation: What do you think my feelings were, scrambling over the rocks, searching out the path, or making one for myself?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eam rem aegre passi Romani M. Furium Camillum sextum tribunum militum creavere.
examples.translation: This incensed the Romans, and they elected Marcus Furius Camillus tribune of the soldiers, for the sixth time.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a taste, relish, flavor, savor

examples.original: Et hunc tu, non dico inter viros numeras, sed inter homines, cuius summum bonum saporibus et coloribus sonisque constat?
examples.translation: And do you rate, I will not say among heroes, but among men, the person whose Supreme Good is a matter of flavours and colours and sounds?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Reliqui arborum fructus vix specie figurave, non modo saporibus sucisque totiens permixtis atque insitis, enumerari queunt.
examples.translation: The other fruits found on trees can hardly be enumerated, from their diversity in shape and figure, without reference to their different flavours and juices, which have again been modified by repeated combinations and graftings.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: to look into; to look at, inspect; to consider, contemplate, examine (class.).

examples.original: Si quid est aliud in philosophia boni, hoc est, quod stemma non inspicit.
examples.translation: If there is any good in philosophy, it is this,—that it never looks into pedigrees.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quomodo enim scies, qui habendi sint, nisi quid homini sit optimum, inveneris, nisi naturam eius inspexeris?
examples.translation: For how are you to know what character is desirable, unless you have discovered what is best suited to man?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum Verginius maxime ex tribunis de lege ageret, duum mensum spatium consulibus datum est ad inspiciendam legem ut cum edocuissent populum quid fraudis occultae ferretur, sinerent deinde suffragium inire.
examples.translation: The consuls were allowed two months’ time to inspect the measure, that having explained to the people what hidden mischief was being proposed they might then permit them to vote.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To look down upon any thing (for syn. cf.: contemno, sperno, aspernor).

examples.original: Erat ex oppido Alesia despectus in campum.
examples.translation: There was a bird’s-eye view from the town of Alesia over the plain.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Sed vide, ne haec ipsa, quae despicis, huic suffragata sint.
examples.translation: And consider whether the very deficiencies which you despise in him did not help him.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Multa dicta sunt ab antiquis de contemnendis ac despiciendis rebus humanis;
examples.translation: The ancients enlarged on the duty of rising proudly superior to human fortunes;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: disgrace, dishonor, infamy, shame (for syn. cf.: offensio, contumelia, infamia, ignominia, turpitudo, obscoenitas, injuria—freq. and class.).

examples.original: Mille licet gladii mortis nova signa sequantur, Degener o populus, vix saecula longa decorum Sic meruisse viris, nedum breve dedecus aevi Et vitam dum Sulla redit.
examples.translation: Though a thousand swords obey this new signal of death, it scarce would befit brave men to buy centuries of life so dear, far less the short and shameful respite—till Sulla returns.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Mitto illam primam libidinis iniuriam, mitto nefarias generi nuptias, mitto cupiditate matris expulsam ex matrimonio filiam: quae nondum ad huiusce vitae periculum, sed ad commune familiae dedecus pertinebant.
examples.translation: I say nothing of the first outrage of her passion; nothing of her infamous marriage with her step-son, nothing of the mother’s lust that drove the daughter from her husband’s arms.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a toll

examples.original: Graviora vectigalia aut abolevit aut minuit.
examples.translation: The more oppressive sources of revenue he either abolished or moderated.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Namque ei Grynium dederat, in Phrygia castrum, ex quo quinquagena talenta vectigalis capiebat.
examples.translation: In fact Pharnabazus gave him Grynium, a stronghold of Phrygia, from which he received a yearly revenue of fifty talents.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Alcibiades

examples.original: Et tamen tantis vectigalibus ad liberalitatem utens, etiam sine hac Pyladea amicitia multorum te benevolentia praeclare tuebere et munies.
examples.translation: And in any case, with so large an income to give away, you can dispense with the romantic sort of friendship that we have in mind;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: standing on end, sticking out, rough, shaggy, bristly, prickly

examples.original: Discolor et vario furialis cultus amictu Induitur, voltusque aperitur crine remoto, Et coma vipereis substringitur horrida sertis.
examples.translation: She put on motley raiment, whose parti-coloured woof was fit for a fiend to wear; she threw back her hair and revealed her face;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a troop, squadron of horse.
Latin: Grex triginta equitum

examples.original: Pugna levis bellumque fugax turmaeque vagantes, Et melior cessisse loco quam pellere miles;
examples.translation: They have no battering-rams and no war-engines of any kind, and no strength to level ditches;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quorum adventu cum sibi Correus oblatam occasionem rei gerendae existimaret, primum cum paucis se ostendit atque in proximas turmas impetum fecit.
examples.translation: Their arrival led Correus to suppose that a chance of despatching the business was offered him;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Is victorem detractum ex equo magistrum equitum plenus maeroris atque irae trucidavit, nec multum afuit quin corpore etiam, quia inter hostilis ceciderat turmas, Samnites potirentur.
examples.translation: Indeed the Samnites almost got possession of the body, which had fallen in the midst of their troops. But the Romans at once dismounted, and the Samnites were forced to do the same;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to scatter on all sides, to scatter about, disperse

examples.original: Erat, ut supra demonstravimus, manus certa nulla, non oppidum, non praesidium, quod se armis defenderet, sed in omnes partes dispersa multitudo.
examples.translation: As above mentioned, there was nowhere any definite body of troops, any stronghold, any garrison to defend itself in arms; but the population was scattered in all directions.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Dumque illi effusam longis anfractibus urbem Circumeunt, Arruns dispersos fulminis ignes Colligit et terrae maesto cum murmure condit Datque locis numen;
examples.translation: While the long procession winds its way round the wide city, Arruns collects the scattered fires of the thunderbolt and hides them in the earth with doleful muttering.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tum incubuit hostium acies, integris ordinibus, robore et numero praestantior: Othoniani, quamquam dispersi, pauciores, fessi, proelium tamen acriter sumpsere.
examples.translation: The fact that in places the ground was encumbered by trees and vineyards gave the battle many aspects: the troops fought now hand to hand, again at a distance;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to be near as an aid, to attend upon, to assist, to serve (ministrum esse ad aliquam rem)
Latin: Ministrum esse ad aliquam rem
Latin: Disponere, dirigere, magisterare

examples.original: Haec nempe sunt elementa, quibus hic mundus administratur, aqua, terra, spiritus.
examples.translation: These, namely, are the elements, by which the world’s work is carried on—water, earth, air.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic census habitus est te praetore ut eo censu nullius civitatis res publica posset administrari;
examples.translation: The assessment made during your praetorship was made in a way that brought the financial administration in every city to a standstill.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: His rebus celeriter administratis ipse, cum primum per anni tempus potuit, ad exercitum contendit.
examples.translation: These requirements were rapidly executed, and so soon as the season allowed he himself hastened to join the army.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to stretch out, extend, to make wide or roomy, to expand.

examples.original: Iamque sinu laxo nudum sine corpore volnus.
examples.translation: The limbs are soaked with corrupted blood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quo plus recipit animus, hoc se magis laxat.
examples.translation: For the more the mind receives, the more does it expand.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illic et laxas vestes et fluxa virorum Velamenta vides.
examples.translation: There one sees loose garments and flowing robes worn even by men.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: Jurid. and publicists' t. t.

examples.original: Sed neque vos tulissetis nec nos spopondissemus;
examples.translation: But neither would you have voted one, nor should we have given it;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vergini patris sponsique Icili populare nomen celebrabatur.
examples.translation: Their acquaintance were led to support the girl out of regard for them;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Inplent enim me bona spe et iam non promittunt de te, sed spondent.
examples.translation: For they fill me with hope; they are now not mere assurances concerning you, but guarantees.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: The round brazen shield of Roman soldiers (diff. from scutum, which was oval, and made of wood covered with bull's hide; cf. Dict. of Antiq. p. 268 sq.), Enn. ap.

examples.original: Clipeus ardens ab occasu ad ortum scintillans transcucurrit solis occasu L. Valerio C. Mario consulibus.
examples.translation: A burning shield darted across at sunset, from west to east, throwing out sparks, in the consulship of L. Valerius and C. Marius.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: to come around something; hence (the coming being considered as accomplished; cf. advenio and adventus, II.).

examples.original: Ita circumventi Samnites, qua potest quisque, fugam per diversa petunt;
examples.translation: Being thus hemmed in, the Samnites fled, as each best might, in different directions;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ita caesa ab tergo legio atque in medio, cum hostis undique urgeret, circumventa.
examples.translation: Thus the legion was attacked in the rear and found itself surrounded, with the enemy assailing it from every quarter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Samnitium agmen cum per Paelignum agrum fugeret, circumventum a Paelignis est; ex milibus quinque ad mille caesi.
examples.translation: The Samnite army, as it fled through the Paelignian territory, was surrounded by the inhabitants, and of five thousand men about a thousand were slain.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: reddish, of all shades, acc. to
Latin: Color ruber, usurpatur de omnibus rubri coloris gradibus
Latin: Ruber, refertur ad colorem capillorum

examples.original: Redditus Cadio Rufo, Pedio Blaeso, Saevino P .
examples.translation: Cadius Rufus, Pedius Blaesus, and Saevinus P. . .
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Publium Sulpicium Rufum legatum cum eo praesidio, quod satis esse arbitrabatur, portum tenere iussit.
examples.translation: He commanded Publius Sulpicius Rufus, lieutenant-general, with a garrison he considered sufficient, to hold the port.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Creati T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Q. Servilius Fidenas quintum L. Iulius Iulus L. Aquilius Corvus L. Lucretius Tricipitinus Ser. Sulpicius Rufus.
examples.translation: Those chosen were Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus, Quintus Servilius Fidenas (for the fifth time), Lucius Julius lulus, Lucius Aquilius Corvus, Lucius Lucretius Tricipitinus, and Servius Sulpicius Rufus.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the wood of the citrus, q. v., citrus-wood
English: a famous pugilist, son of Tyndarus and Leda, and brother of Castor, in connection with whom, as the constellation of the Twins
English: to lay hold of something on all sides; to take or catch hold of, seize, grasp, apprehend; to comprehend, comprise (class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: Vercassivellaunus Arvernus vivus in fuga comprehenditur;
examples.translation: Vercassivellaunus the Arvernian was captured alive in the rout;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hae celeriter ignem comprehenderunt et venti magnitudine in omnem locum castrorum distulerunt.
examples.translation: These speedily caught fire, which the strength of the wind carried to every corner of the camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Comprehensae extemplo earum comites magnum numerum matronarum indicaverunt; ex quibus ad centum septuaginta damnatae.
examples.translation: Their attendants being instantly arrested informed against a large number of matrons, of whom one hundred and seventy were found guilty;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to throw into confusion or disorder

examples.original: Perturbatum enim id est, quod esse aliquando et non perturbatum potest;
examples.translation: For that is said to be ”disturbed” which can also at some other time be ”not disturbed”;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod ex multorum episcoporum desiderio peto, quos mecum de hac re fama incerta perturbat;
examples.translation: This I beg at the desire of many bishops who have, like me, been troubled by the indefinite rumour about this;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Huc ex ephoris quidam descenderunt. Pausanias ut audivit Argilium confugisse in aram, perturbatus venit eo.
examples.translation: When Pausanias heard that the Argilian had taken refuge at the altar, he went there in a state of great anxiety;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: the posteriors, fundament.
Latin: vetus femina
English: the knee.
Latin: curvatura, qua crus et femur committuntur
Latin: (Anat.) curvatura, qua crus et femur committuntur

examples.original: Nec minore livore ac malignitate quam superbia saevitiaque paene adversus omnis aevi hominum genus grassatus est.
examples.translation: He assailed mankind of almost every epoch with no less envy and malice than insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Latentem discurrens forte gregarius miles, animadversis pedibus, studio sciscitandi quisnam esset, adgnovit extractumque et prae metu ad genua sibi accidentem imperatorem salutavit.
examples.translation: As he cowered there, a common soldier, who was prowling about at random, saw his feet, and intending to ask who he was, pulled him out and recognized him;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ex hac stirpe Tiberius Caesar genus trahit, et quidem utrumque: paternum a Tiberio Nerone, maternum ab Appio Pulchro, qui ambo Appi Caeci filii fuerunt.
examples.translation: Such was the stock from which Tiberius Caesar derived his origin, and that too on both sides: on his father’s from Tiberius Nero;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a (military) giving up, a surrender, capitulation (freq. in the historians).—With

examples.original: Scodram, caput gentis, delesse suffecit; statim secuta deditio est.
examples.translation: It sufficed to destroy Scodra, their capital, and their submission immediately followed.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Fusa primo concursu acies; in fugam versa milia octo armatorum ab equitibus interclusa positis armis in deditionem venerunt.
examples.translation: Their line broke at the first assault, and in the rout eight thousand soldiers were cut off by the cavalry, and laying down their arms, surrendered.
