examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quod ad tribunos attinet, consulite utrum praesens deditio eorum fieri possit an in diem differatur;
examples.translation: As for the tribunes, you must determine whether their surrender can take place at once or had better be deferred;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: any body, any thing? in impassioned interrogation, i. q. num quis, quid (class.).

examples.original: Itaque cum abs te caput illud tam multis verbis mercennarioque prooemio esset ornatum, ecquis est inventus postea praetor, qui idem illud ediceret?
examples.translation: That is why, after all the verbiage and the profit-hunting preamble with which you adorned the clause, no subsequent praetor, you will find, has reproduced it in his edict.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: that has two heads, twoheaded

examples.original: Ita ancipiti proelio diu atque acriter pugnatum est.
examples.translation: Thus the engagement became twofold, and. the fight was fierce and long.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Anceps et pulchra contentio exituque ipso mirabilis.
examples.translation: It was a well-contested and noble struggle and remarkable in the manner of its end.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Animum format et fabricat, vitam disponit, actiones regit, agenda et omittenda demonstrat, sedet ad gubernaculum et per ancipitia fluctuantium derigit cursum.
examples.translation: It moulds and constructs the soul; it orders our life, guides our conduct, shows us what we should do and what we should leave undone;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to excite, provoke, challenge, exasperate, irritate (syn.: irrito, provoco).

examples.original: Multum enim adicit sibi virtus lacessita;
examples.translation: For manliness gains much strength by being challenged;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Principio omnibus ab rebus, quascumque videmus, perpetuo fluere ac mitti spargique necessest corpora quae feriant oculos visumque lacessant.
examples.translation: In the first place, from everything that we see there must of necessity continually flow and discharge and scatter bodies which strike our eyes and excite vision.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Qua pacta acceptaque cum parata cetera ad bellum essent sequique Etruscus iuberet, infitias eunt mercedem se belli Romanis inferendi pactos: quidquid acceperint accepisse ne agrum Etruscum vastarent armisque lacesserent cultores;
examples.translation: When this had been agreed upon and received, and the Etruscans, having completed the rest of their preparations for the war, bade their new allies follow them, the Gauls demurred.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to go before, precede (seems not to occur in Cic., Nep., Tac., or Sall.; once in Cæs.; syn.: antecedo, anteverto).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; cessi, cessum, 3

examples.original: Habet virtus quoque praecedentem causam;
examples.translation: The antecedent cause inheres in virtue also;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hanc praecedentem causam divitiae habent;
examples.translation: It is this antecedent cause which inheres in riches;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a staff

examples.original: Tela iugo vincta est, stamen secernit harundo, Inseritur medium radiis subtemen acutis, Quod lato paviunt insecti pectine dentes.
examples.translation: The web is bound to frame; asunder now The reed doth part the warp.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ita enim parvae et exiguae sunt istae accessiones bonorum ut, quemadmodum stellae in radiis solis, sic istae in virtutum splendore ne cernantur quidem.
examples.translation: For those supplementary goods are so small and slight that in the full radiance of the virtues they are as invisible as the stars in sunlight.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to go to, approach; to attempt, undertake
Latin: Adire

examples.original: Bovianum inde adgressus nec ita multo post Aufidenam vi cepit.
examples.translation: He then attacked and captured Bovianum, and not long afterwards Aufidena.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hic cum maximo studio compararet exercitum Aegyptumque proficisci pararet, subito a rege litterae sunt ei missae, ut Aspim aggrederetur, qui Cataoniam tenebat;
examples.translation: While Datames was busily engaged in organizing this army and preparing to embark for Egypt, suddenly a letter was sent to him by the king, ordering him to attack Aspis, the ruler of Cataonia;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: Itaque dispositis insidiis saepius equites eius adgressus secunda proelia faciebat.
examples.translation: So he set ambuscades about, attacked the other’s horsemen frequently, and won his actions.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a gutter
English: a prænomen of Etruscan origin

examples.original: At postquam leges bello siluere coactae, Pellimur e patriis laribus patimurque volentes Exilium;
examples.translation: But now law has been silenced by the constraint of war, and we have been driven from our country.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ista tua pulcra Libertas deos penates et familiares meos lares expulit, ut se ipsa tamquam in captivis sedibus collocaret?
examples.translation: Did your darling Liberty drive out my household gods and the spirits of my family, that she might establish herself in what was virtually a captive’s dwelling?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to shape, fashion, form (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense).
Latin: Formam alicui rei dare

examples.original: Muri autem omnes Gallici hac fere forma sunt.
examples.translation: All Gallic walls are, as a rule, of the following pattern.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quid lapideas moles in rotundum ac leve formatas, quibus porticus et capacia populorum tecta suscipimus?
examples.translation: Or the rounded and polished masses of stone by means of which we erect colonnades and buildings roomy enough for nations?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quod facit, corpus est. Bonum agitat animum et quodammodo format et continet, quae propria sunt corporis.
examples.translation: The good stimulates the mind and, in a way, moulds and embraces that which is essential to the body.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: The Rhine, the river which divided Gaul from Germany
Latin: Flumen Europaeum, qui Germaniam ab Francia, Belgia et Batavia dividit
Latin: Flumen in Italia, qui in Padum fluit

examples.original: Magnam manum Germanorum conductam Rhenum transisse;
examples.translation: A great company of Germans had been hired, and had crossed the Rhine;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Haec Libycos, pars tam flavos gerit altera crines, Ut nullis Caesar Rheni se dicat in arvis Tam rutilas vidisse comas;
examples.translation: Some had the hair of Africa, and others were so fair-headed that Caesar said he had never seen hair so red in the Rhine country;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cogunt equitum duo milia Sugambri, qui sunt proximi Rheno, a quibus receptos ex fuga Tencteros atque Vsipetes supra docuimus.
examples.translation: Two thousand horsemen were collected by the Sugambri, who live nearest the Rhine, and, as we set forth above, had received the Tencteri and the Usipetes after their flight.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to grind, bruise, pound, to crumble, separate into small pieces.

examples.original: Quod verum est, nondum sciebam, quid mihi deesset ad tale opus, quale me nunc torquet et conterit.
examples.translation: The truth is, I did not realize my lack of qualifications for the duties that now vex and harass me.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to take away; hence, to diminish by taking away. Of things, to consume, to annihilate; of persons, orig. to ruin, to corrupt; later, in a phys. sense, to kill
Latin: Aliquid ab aliquo loco, ac proinde auferre, amovere; (qua tamen significatione raro admodum occurrit)
Latin: Minuere, consumere, abolere sumendo vel auferendo aliquid ab aliquo loco

examples.original: Non de me nunc tecum loquor, qui multum ab homine tolerabili, nedum a perfecto absum, sed de illo, in quem fortuna ius perdidit.
examples.translation: Of course I am not speaking to you of myself at this point, because I am far from being a perfect person, or even a man of middling qualities;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: An admiring, admiration.—Absol.

examples.original: Extremam eius vocem, ut cuique odium aut admiratio fuit, varie prodidere.
examples.translation: His last words have been variously reported according to the hatred or admiration of individuals;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Non est admirationi una arbor, ubi in eandem altitudinem tota silva surrexit.
examples.translation: There is unevenness, you know, when some objects rise conspicuous above others.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed et conloquium fuit inter ipsos de legibus pacis, et steterunt diu mutua admiratione defixi.
examples.translation: But first a conference was held between them about terms of peace, and they stood for a while motionless in mutual admiration.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: countless, innumerable (class.)

examples.original: Haec non erant eius qui innumerabiles mundos infinitasque regiones, quarum nulla esset ora, nulla extremitas, ’mente peragravisset.’ Num quid tale Democritus?
examples.translation: Such a provision ill became one whose ’intellect had roamed’b over unnumbered worlds and realms of infinite space, without shores or circumference. Did Democritus do anything of the kind?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sic igitur Plancius nihilominus quaestor est factus, et tribunus plebis, et aedilis, quam si esset summo loco natus: sed haec, pari loco orti, sunt innumerabiles alii consecuti.
examples.translation: So in the same way Plancius has been elected quaestor, tribune of the plebs, and aedile, just as much as if his birth had been of the highest;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Videmus enim planeque cernimus in eo fieri multarum rerum visibilium et ad ceteros sensus corporis pertinentium innumerabiles imagines, quae nunc non interest quam ordinate vel turbide fiant;
examples.translation: For we see and clearly perceive that in it are found countless images of many objects that are discernible by the eye or by the other bodily senses;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: poverty, small means, moderate circumstances (opp. as well to egestas, inopia, penuria, as to abundantia and luxuria, v. Doed. Syn. 3, pp. 111 and 118; class.)

examples.original: Ex multis paupertatibus divitiae fiunt;
examples.translation: But riches result from numerous cases of poverty;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Dolor et paupertas deteriorem non faciunt;
examples.translation: But pain and poverty do not make a man worse;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cui cum paupertate bene convenit, dives est.
examples.translation: He who has made a fair compact with poverty is rich.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: shortly, briefly, in a nut shell; quickly; for/within a short distance/time

examples.original: Sentio, iudices, vos pro vestra humanitate his tantis sceleribus breviter a me demonstratis vehementer esse commotos.
examples.translation: What then do you suppose their feelings were who had not only to listen to such a story, but to pass judgement on it?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Scripsit enim et multis saepe verbis et breviter aperteque in eo libro quem modo nominavi, ’mortem nihil ad nos pertinere;
examples.translation: For he repeatedly argued at length, and also stated briefly and plainly in the book I have just mentioned, that ’death does not affect us at all;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Denique ut breviter includam quod sentio, et istos satagios ac sibi molestos describam tibi, tam intemperantes in ipsis miseriis quam sunt ante illas.
examples.translation: In fine, to express my thoughts in brief compass and portray to you those busybodies and self-tormentors—they are as uncontrolled in the midst of their troubles as they are before them.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to disjoin, sever

examples.original: A qua professione dissimilitudo nos separabit.
examples.translation: We part company with our promise if we are unlike other men.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nihil est illis, dum fiunt et a faece sua separantur, informius.
examples.translation: There is nothing uglier than these metals during the process of refinement and separation from the ore.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hos igitur omnis domesticos motus separatos ab externis iustisque bellis ex ordine persequemur.
examples.translation: We will, therefore, now describe in their order all these domestic disturbances as distinct from foreign wars properly so called.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a murmur, murmuring; a humming, roaring, growling, grumbling; a rushing, crashing, etc.

examples.original: Dumque illi effusam longis anfractibus urbem Circumeunt, Arruns dispersos fulminis ignes Colligit et terrae maesto cum murmure condit Datque locis numen;
examples.translation: While the long procession winds its way round the wide city, Arruns collects the scattered fires of the thunderbolt and hides them in the earth with doleful muttering.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to pour over

examples.original: Dignatur viles isto quoque sanguine dextras, Quo Fortuna parat victos perfundere patres, Poenaque civilis belli, vindicta senatus, Paene data est famulo.
examples.translation: Once again he aspires to shed blood by base-born hands—that blood with which Fortune intended to drench the defeated Senators;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Et hostes quidem, nihil aliud quam perfusis vano timore Romanis, citato agmine abeunt: Numicius Antium adversus Volscos, Verginius contra Aequos profectus.
examples.translation: As for the enemy, they did no more than cause the Romans a needless panic, and hastily retreated. Numicius marched to Antium against the Volsci, Verginius against the Aequi.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad quem etiam ipsas quas ego iam legeram, litteras tuas ipse portavit. Quae nos quanta laetitia perfuderint, quid homo nitatur loqui quod non potest eloqui?
examples.translation: As for the great joy with which your letter filled me, why should one attempt to utter feelings that defy utterance?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: more than one

examples.original: Ibidem saepius et per complures cantavit dies;
examples.translation: In the same city he sang frequently and for several successive days.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Huc Mithridates cum uno cui maxime habebat fidem ante aliquot dies venit compluribusque locis separatim gladios obruit eaque loca diligenter notat.
examples.translation: Mithridates went to the spot several days in advance, with a single companion in whom he had the greatest confidence; and in several different places, which he carefully marked, he buried swords.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: Book VIIGalba • Otho • Vitellus Galba I. Progenies Caesarum in Nerone defecit: quod futurum compluribus quidem signis, sed vel evidentissimis duobus apparuit.
examples.translation: Galba Book VIIGalba • Otho • Vitellus Galba I. The race of the Caesars ended with Nero. That this would be so was shown by many portents and especially by two very significant ones.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to cast forth, throw out; to dig, tear, or pluck out (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Quam multos fama non excepit, sed eruit!
examples.translation: And how many have been ruined, not rescued, by their reputation?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc ego, Lucili, facere soleo: ex omni notione, etiam si a philosophia longissime aversa est, eruere aliquid conor et utile efficere.
examples.translation: That is my habit, Lucilius: I try to extract and render useful some element from every field of thought, no matter how far removed it may be from philosophy.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cadaver eius clam in hortos Lamianos asportatum et tumultuario rogo semiambustum levi caespite obrutum est, postea per sorores ab exsilio reversas erutum et crematum sepultumque.
examples.translation: His body was conveyed secretly to the gardens of the Lamian family, where it was partly consumed on a hastily erected pyre and buried beneath a light covering of turf;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: lead together, to assemble, collect (class. in prose and poetry).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; xi, ctum, 3

examples.original: Magnam manum Germanorum conductam Rhenum transisse;
examples.translation: A great company of Germans had been hired, and had crossed the Rhine;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quod si vos aliquis casus conducet in unum, Mente memor tota quae damus arma, tene.
examples.translation: But if some chance brings you together, use all your memory and wit to wield the arms I give you.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: treat, feast, entertain (cf. illicio; class.).

examples.original: Sol me invitabat, fames ad monebat, nubes minabantur;
examples.translation: The sunlight called to me, hunger warned, and clouds were lowering;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non est autem gloriosum, quod ab invito et tergiversante fit;
examples.translation: But nothing glorious can result from unwillingness and cowardice;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Rubrius istius comites invitat: eos omnes Verres certiores facit quid opus esset.
examples.translation: Rubrius invited Verres’ staff, and Verres gave them instructions what to do.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to speak out, speak plainly, to utter; to pronounce, declare, state, express
Latin: Plane loqui, vel oratorie

examples.original: Sed quid praecipue nostris conatibus obstet Eloquar, exemplo quemque docente suo.
examples.translation: But what particularly hinders our endeavours I will relate, though each may learn from his own case.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fuit etiam disertus ut nemo ei Thebanus par esset eloquentia, neque minus concinnus in brevitate respondendi quam in perpetua oratione ornatus.
examples.translation: Epaminondas was also so good a speaker that no Theban equalled him in eloquence, and he was not less clever in brief answers than brilliant in a set speech.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

examples.original: Ad quem etiam ipsas quas ego iam legeram, litteras tuas ipse portavit. Quae nos quanta laetitia perfuderint, quid homo nitatur loqui quod non potest eloqui?
examples.translation: As for the great joy with which your letter filled me, why should one attempt to utter feelings that defy utterance?
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: excepted, exempt (rare but class. = exemptus, exceptus)

examples.original: Quid autem est in beata vita eximium?
examples.translation: Now, in the happy life, what is the distinctive quality?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quae bene et eximie quamvis disposta ferantur, longe sunt tamen a vera ratione repulsa.
examples.translation: But well and excellently as all this is set forth and told, yet it is far removed from true reasoning.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Non enim bellandi virtus solum in summo ac perfecto imperatore quaerenda est, sed multae sunt artes eximiae huius administrae comitesque virtutis.
examples.translation: For in a general of the highest and most perfect type we must not look for military genius alone. For there are many notable qualities which support and go with it.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: nourishment, nutriment; and concr., food, provisions, aliment

examples.original: Id praecipuum alimentum famae erat.
examples.translation: Nothing furnished rumour with more food.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Alimenta tibi leonum et vulturum eripio.”
examples.translation: I am merely depriving you of food which sustains lions and vultures.”
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quando autem aliqua non potest ieiunare, non tamen extra horam prandii aliquid alimentorum sumat, nisi cum aegrotat.
examples.translation: When, however, anyone is unable to fast, let her not take any nourishment outside of the hour of repast, unless when ill.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: that is contrary to right and justice, unjust, wrongful, unreasonable, excessive, oppressive

examples.original: Iniuria autem non potest fieri nisi iniuste;
examples.translation: But no injury can be done without injustice;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec ut iniustus in pace rex, ita dux belli pravus fuit;
examples.translation: But if the king was unjust in peace, yet he was not a bad general in war.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Irae atque iracundiae conscius sibi, utramque excusavit edicto distinxitque, pollicitus alteram quidem brevem et innoxiam, alteram non iniustam fore.
examples.translation: He was conscious of his tendency to wrath and resentment and excused both in an edict;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to be eager or zealous, to take pains about, be diligent in, anxious about, busy one's self with, strive after, to apply one's self to or pursue some course of action, etc

examples.original: Nemo Arpinas non Plancio studuit, nemo Soranus, nemo Casinas, nemo Aquinas.
examples.translation: There was no one at Arpinum, at Sora, at Casinum, at Aquinum, but was Plancius’ adherent.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Non est quod post cibum studeas, non est quod plenis oculis ac tumentibus imperes;
examples.translation: There is no reason why you should study immediately after eating;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hisce ego auxiliis studentibus atque incitatis uti me, Laterensis, potuisse confiteor;
examples.translation: Of these helpers, Laterensis, so zealous and so enthusiastic, I admit that I might have availed myself.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: accident

examples.original: Sed profusa cupidine et insigni temeritate legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens;
examples.translation: But the commanders of the legions, Alienus Caecina and Fabius Valens, were men of boundless greed and extraordinary recklessness.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Recte igitur, si omnibus in rebus temeritas ignoratioque vitiosa est, ars ea quae tollit haec virtus nominata est.
examples.translation: If therefore rashness and ignorance are in all matters fraught with mischief, the art which removes them is correctly entitled a virtue.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Beluarum hoc quidem extremum, illa autem superiora caduca et incerta, posita non tam in consiliis nostris quam in fortunae temeritate.
examples.translation: This last is the highest aim of brutes; the others are fleeting and unstable things and dependent less upon human foresight than upon the fickleness of fortune.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: swift, quick, fleet, rapid, speedy (class.; syn.: celer, pernix, praepes).
Latin: Qui tempus parvum longe movetur

examples.original: Non solebat mihi tam velox tempus videri;
examples.translation: In other years time did not seem to me to go so swiftly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Aspicis, ut prensos urant iuga prima iuvencos, Et nova velocem cingula laedat equum?
examples.translation: Do you see how the first yoke chafes the captured bullocks, how the new saddle hurts the flying steed?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: (In laevum cecidere latus veloxque Metaurus Crustumiumque rapax et iuncto Sapis Isauro Senaque et Hadriacas qui verberat Aufidus undas;
examples.translation: (Eastward flow the swift Metaurus and rushing Crustumium, the Sapis together with the Isaurus, the Sena, the Aufidus which buffets the waves of the Adriatic;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: bordering upon, adjoining, neighboring (class.; syn.: vicinus, confinis, conterminus, contiguus, continens).

examples.original: Scaptione hoc, contionali seni, adsignaturos putarent finitimos populos?
examples.translation: What grief it would cause the former, and what joy the latter!
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cuius adventu ab hostibus cognito magnae ex finitimis civitatibus copiae convenerunt.
examples.translation: When the enemy had news of his coming a large force assembled from the neighbouring states.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Mittuntur etiam ad eas civitates legati quae sunt citerioris Hispaniae finitimae Aquitaniae: inde auxilia ducesque arcessuntur.
examples.translation: They even sent deputies to those states of Nearer Spain which border on Aquitania, inviting succours and leaders from thence.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: purple-colored, purple; including very different shades of color, as
Latin: Colorem pupurae habens

examples.original: Est prope purpureos colles florentis Hymetti Fons sacer et viridi caespite mollis humus: Silva nemus non alta facit;
examples.translation: Near the purple hills of flowery Hymettus there is a sacred spring and ground soft with green turf: trees of no great height form a grove;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Prima dux fugae regina cum aurea puppe veloque purpureo in altum dedit Mo X secutus Antonius, sed instare vestigiis Caesar.
examples.translation: The queen led the retreat, putting out into the open sea in her golden vessel with purple sails. Antonius soon followed her, but Caesar was hard upon his tracks.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: seriousness, gravity, sternness, strictness, severity, in a good and bad sense

examples.original: Tribulibus enim iudicibus non modo severitatem illorum, si ista vera sunt, sed ne vultus quidem ferre possemus.
examples.translation: For were his jury to-day his tribesmen, we should find not merely their severity but even their gaze intolerable, supposing that your allegations were true.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: No. 49 (Ep. CCXI) Sicut parata est severitas peccata quae invenerit, vindicare, ita non vult caritas quod vindicet, invenire.
examples.translation: No. 49 (Ep. CCXI)a (a.d. 423) Just as severity is ready to punish the sins it discovers, so love is anxious not to discover sins to punish.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Diu infructuosam et asperam militiam toleraverant ingenio loci caelique et severitate disciplinae, quam in pace inexorabilem discordiae civium resolvunt, paratis utrimque corruptoribus et perfidia impunita.
examples.translation: The soldiers had long endured a profitless service which was severe because of the character of the district and of the climate, and also because discipline was strict.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to lead, bring, or conduct across; to lead, bring, or carry over any thing (syn. traicio).
Latin: De loco in locum ducere, per locum aliquem ducere
Latin: ab uno in alium sensum transferre, et ab una in aliam linguam transferre

examples.original: In Rusellanum agrum exercitus traductus;
examples.translation: The army was then led into the territory of Rusellae.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Volo luxuriam obiurgari, libidinem traduci, inpotentiam frangi.
examples.translation: I wish to see luxury rebuked, lust condemned, waywardness crushed out.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum ego quae mihi videbantur dicerem, traduxit me ad suam sententiam.
examples.translation: I gave him my own views, but he brought me over to his opinion;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to wander

examples.original: Non vagatur, quod fixum atque fundatum est.
examples.translation: But that which is settled and solid does not wander from its place.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Pugna levis bellumque fugax turmaeque vagantes, Et melior cessisse loco quam pellere miles;
examples.translation: They have no battering-rams and no war-engines of any kind, and no strength to level ditches;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: His rebus fiebat ut et minus late vagarentur et minus facile finitimis bellum inferre possent;
examples.translation: In such circumstances their range of movement was less extensive, and their chances of waging war on their neighbours were less easy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to hide something from one, to keep secret, to conceal; constr.

examples.original: Iter quo habeat omnis celat.
examples.translation: He concealed his proposed route from everyone.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Id Alcibiades diutius celari non potuit;
examples.translation: That design could not long be concealed from Alcibiades;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Alcibiades

examples.original: Tam celer adsiduos explevit cursus honores;
examples.translation: So swiftly did thy career fill office after office;
examples.author: Claudian
examples.work: Panegyric On The Consulship Of Fl. Manlius Theodorus (A.D. 399)

definitions: English: an apartment for reclining or (more freq.) for sleeping (cf. cubo), a resting- or sleepingchamber, a bedchamber.
Latin: Conclave, praesertim pro cubando

examples.original: Lucretiam sedentem maestam in cubiculo inveniunt.
examples.translation: Lucretia they found sitting sadly in her chamber.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: how long?
Latin: dum, quamdiu, donec
English: of small price or value, purchased at a low rate, cheap (opp. carus).

examples.original: Minime autem convenit, cum ipsi inter nos viles neglectique simus, postulare ut dis immortalibus cari simus et ab iis diligamur.
examples.translation: But how inconsistent it would be for us to expect the immortal gods to love and cherish us, when we ourselves despise and neglect one another!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Dignatur viles isto quoque sanguine dextras, Quo Fortuna parat victos perfundere patres, Poenaque civilis belli, vindicta senatus, Paene data est famulo.
examples.translation: Once again he aspires to shed blood by base-born hands—that blood with which Fortune intended to drench the defeated Senators;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: meeting, assembly; crowd, company

examples.original: Iam turba soluto Arma petit coetu;
examples.translation: Then the meeting dispersed, and all took up arms.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: O praeclarum diem cum in illud divinum animorum concilium coetumque proficiscar cumque ex hac turba et colluvione discedam!
examples.translation: O glorious day, when I shall set out to join the assembled hosts of souls divine and leave this world of strife and sin!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Unum hercule virum—id enim plus esse quam consulem—qualis Ap. Claudius fuerit, momento temporis discussurum illos coetus fuisse.
examples.translation: One single man—a more significant word than consul—of the type of Appius Claudius, would have dispersed those assemblages in a moment.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: ruddy (class.).

examples.original: Nec cerussa tibi nec nitri spuma rubentis Desit et Illyrica quae venit iris humo.
examples.translation: Nor let white lead nor foam of red nitre be lacking, nor the iris that comes from Illyrian soil.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iam rarior aer Et par Phoebus aquis densas in vellera nubes Sparserat, et noctes ventura luce rubebant, Servatoque loco rerum discessit ab astris Umor, et ima petit, quidquid pendebat aquarum.
examples.translation: By this time the sky had cleared; the sun, a match for the waters, had broken up the thick clouds into fleeces;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to beget, procreate, engender, produce, create; in
Latin: gignere, genere, procreare
Latin: producere

examples.original: Quot genera tibi in hac dabo, quibus peccetur?
examples.translation: In this department, what countless varieties of fault I can show you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Numquam tibi, Magne, per umbras Perque meos manes genero non esse licebit;
examples.translation: In vain you sever with the sword the tie of kinship that binds you.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Horum autem morborum mater superbia est et humanae laudis aviditas, quae etiam hypocrisin saepe generat.
examples.translation: These evils are the offspring of pride and eagerness for the praise of men, which often begets hypocrisy as well.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: thickness, density.
English: wool
Latin: Pellis ovium, e qua vestis fabricari potest
Latin: Materia e lana ovium

examples.original: Odi quae praebet, quia sit praebere necesse, Siccaque de lana cogitat ipsa sua.
examples.translation: I hate her who gives because she must, and who, herself unmoved, is thinking of her wool.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: healthy, salubrious; salutary, beneficial; in good condition (body)

examples.original: Ego non video, quomodo salubris esse aut utilis possit ulla mediocritas morbi.
examples.translation: I, however, do not understand how any half-way disease can be either wholesome or helpful.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed ut praecipua commemorem, Appius Caecus societatem cum rege Pyrrho ut parum salubrem iniri dissuasit.
examples.translation: But to mention only the principal instances, Appius the Blind advised against forming an alliance with king Pyrrhus as not at all expedient.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hoc illud est praecipue in cognitione rerum salubre ac frugiferum, omnis te exempli documenta in inlustri posita monumento intueri;
examples.translation: What chiefly makes the study of history wholesome and profitable is this, that you behold the lessons of every kind of experience set forth as on a conspicuous monument;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a jest, joke (class.)

examples.original: Hos ignava iocos tribuit natura puellis;
examples.translation: These are the games that indolent nature has given to women;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Proelia cum Parthis, cum culta pax sit amica, Et iocus, et causas quicquid amoris habet.
examples.translation: Battle with Parthians, but with a cultured mistress have peace and mirth and whatever is the cause of love.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: constant, continual; persistent in application

examples.original: Iudaeos impulsore Chresto assidue tumultuantis Roma expulit.
examples.translation: Since the Jews constantly made disturbances at the instigation of Chrestus, he expelled them from Rome.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Semper enim boni assiduique domini referta cella vinaria, olearia, etiam penaria est, villaque tota locuples est, abundat porco haedo agno gallina, lacte caseo melle.
examples.translation: For the provident and industrious proprietor always has his store-room and cellars well filled with oil and wine and provisions;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Lavacrum etiam corporum ususque balnearum non sit assiduus, sed eo, quo solet, intervallo temporis tribuatur, hoc est semel in mense. Cuius autem infirmitatis necessitas cogit lavandum corpus, non longius differatur;
examples.translation: If, however, the need arising from any illness demands the washing of the body, let it not be too long postponed, and let it be done without murmuring for medical reasons;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to make naked or bare; to strip, bare, lay bare, expose to view, uncover (syn.: exuo, detego, revelo).

examples.original: Non erat armatis aequum concurrere nudas;
examples.translation: It were not just that defenceless maids should fight with armed men;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vercingetorix iubet portas claudi, ne castra nudentur.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix ordered the gates to be shut, lest the camp should be deserted.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Tam inops autem ego eram ab amicis aut tam nuda res publica a magistratibus?
examples.translation: But was I so destitute of aid from friends, or was the republic so devoid of magistrates?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a being still or silent, noiselessness, stillness, silence

examples.original: Magno malo ulla voce interpellatum silentium luitur.
examples.translation: There is a grievous penalty for the slightest breach of silence.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tum dictator silentio facto ”Bene habet” inquit, ”Quirites.
examples.translation: Then said the dictator, when silence was obtained, ”It is well, Quirites.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: His ita decretis usque ad triumphum Plauti silentium de Privernatibus fuit;
examples.translation: These decrees having been promulgated, no more was said about the Privernates, until Plautius had triumphed.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: night.
Latin: De nocte

examples.original: Vercingetorix, priusquam munitiones ab Romanis perficiantur, consilium capit omnem ab se equitatum noctu dimittere.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix now made up his mind to send away all his horsemen by night, before the Romans could complete their entrenchments.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Cum esset in aedibus armarium, in quo sciret esse nummorum aliquantum et auri, noctu duos conservos dormientes occidit in piscinamque deiecit: ipse armarii fundum exsecuit, et HS . .
examples.translation: There was a safe in the house which he knew to contain a quantity of cash and of gold;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Castra opportunis locis erant posita ibique castella viginti tria facta, quibus in castellis interdiu stationes ponebantur, ne qua subito eruptio fieret: haec eadem noctu excubitoribus ac firmis praesidiis tenebantur.
examples.translation: In these piquets would be posted by day to prevent any sudden sortie; by night the same stations were held by sentries and strong garrisons.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to mark out, trace out (freq. in the Aug. per.); to describe, designate, define (for syn. cf.: nomino, appello; voco, dico; facio, coöpto, evoco, prodo, declaro, renuntio, seligo).

examples.original: Hoc felicitatem suam fine designat.
examples.translation: Such are the bounds which he sets to his own happiness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam primum tacta designat membra saliva, Quae cohibet virus retinetque in volnere pestem;
examples.translation: The native begins by marking the part with the touch of his spittle;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: watch, observe, examine, explore

examples.original: Quid tibi cum speculo, montana armenta petenti?
examples.translation: What dost thou with a mirror, seeking the herds upon the mountains?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vix proelia Caesar Senserat, elatus specula quae prodidit ignis: Invenit inpulsos presso iam pulvere muros, Frigidaque, ut veteris, deprendit signa ruinae.
examples.translation: Caesar had hardly been aware of the fighting; the news of it was conveyed to him by a fire-signal from a lofty tower.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quae causa in speculo imagines exprimat, sciet sapiens;
examples.translation: The wise man will know what causes the reflection in a mirror;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A Greek weight of a hundred Attic drachmas, a mina

examples.original: Illum saepe minis Caesar precibusque morantem Evocat: ”O mundo tantorum causa laborum, Quid superos et fata tenes?
examples.translation: Again and again Caesar urged him to haste with threats and entreaties: ”On you lies the blame for the sore troubles that afflict mankind;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Si saecula prima Victoris timuere minas, nunc excipe saltem Ossa tui Magni, si nondum subruta fluctu Invisa tellure sedent.
examples.translation: Who will fear to trouble the tomb, and dread to remove the dead so worthy of worship?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Venientem Volsci benigne excepere benigniusque in dies colebant, quo maior ira in suos eminebat crebraeque nunc querellae, nunc minae percipiebantur.
examples.translation: Condemned in his absence, he went into exile with the Volsci, uttering threats against his country, and even then breathing hostility.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: , to fail, be wanting.

examples.original: In illis excusatius est voluntate peccare quam casu, in hac maxima culpa est sponte delinquere.
examples.translation: In the case of the latter, it is more pardonable to err voluntarily rather than by accident;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Per octo annos varie et inaequabiliter provinciam rexit, primo acer et vehemens et in coercendis quidem delictis vel immodicus.
examples.translation: For eight years he governed the province in a variable and inconsistent manner. At first he was vigorous and energetic and even over severe in punishing offences;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Legatos quippe nostros, ob ea quae deliquerant iure agentes, ne gladio quidem, sed ut victimas securi percutiunt, praefectos navium igne comburunt;
examples.translation: To make their action still more insulting, it was a woman that gave the order.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to polish, educate, instruct, teach (freq. and class.; cf.: doceo, edoceo, praecipio, instituo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; īvi or ii, ītum, 4

examples.original: Hoc cum persuasi mihi et perbibi, quid ista praecepta proficiunt, quae eruditum docent?
examples.translation: To one who knows, it is superfluous to give precepts;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qui quod tibi parum videtur eruditus, ea causa est quod nullam eruditionem esse duxit nisi quae beatae vitae disciplinam iuvaret.
examples.translation: You are pleased to think him uneducated. The reason is that he refused to consider any education worth the name that did not help to school us in happiness.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Equidem e Cn. Aufidio, praetorio, erudito homine, oculis capto, saepe audiebam cum se lucis magis quam utilitatis desiderio moveri diceret.
examples.translation: I myself frequently heard the blind ex-praetor and scholar Gnaeus Aufidius declare that he felt the actual loss of light more than the inconvenience of blindness.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to drive out, drive away, remove, expel; to drive, thrust, or cast down (class. and very freq.).

examples.original: Aut beatum praestare debet, aut si ab hoc depulsa est, non prohibebit fieri miserum.
examples.translation: She either must preserve one in happiness, or, if driven from this position, she will not prevent us from becoming unhappy.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Post id proelium eundem Pausaniam cum classe communi Cyprum atque Hellespontum miserunt, ut ex iis regionibus barbarorum praesidia depelleret.
examples.translation: After that battle Pausanias again commanded the allied Greeks, being sent with a fleet to Cyprus and the Hellespont to dislodge the garrisons of the barbarians from those regions.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Ac primum illud attende, te iam ex illa ratione esse depulsum, quod negabas quemquam deiici posse, nisi inde ubi tum esset: iam posse concedis;
examples.translation: And observe first of all that you have been forced to abandon your principle that, as you maintained, no one can be driven out except from the place in which he was at the time.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: on that account, for that reason, therefore (freq. and class.; cf.: itaque, igitur, ergo; ideo, propterea; quare, quam ob rem, etc.).

examples.original: Si ex lege subsortitus non erat Iunius aut si in aliquam legem aliquando non iuraverat, idcirco illius damnatione aliquid de Cluentio iudicabatur?
examples.translation: If Junius was irregular in the filling up of vacancies, or if he had at any time omitted to take any official oath, did his conviction imply any sentence on Cluentius?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to go about, to walk

examples.original: Quid si velis deinde quemadmodum ambules discere?
examples.translation: What if you should next propose to take lessons in walking!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non enim minus secundum naturam est sedere quam stare aut ambulare.
examples.translation: For sitting is an act that is not less according to nature than standing or walking.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qui cum non ambularet vias servorum dei, non bonam famam habere coeperat.
examples.translation: This alarmed me, but yet I did not lightly give it any credence;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to cover with a garment, to dress, clothe, vest (syn.: induo, amicio).

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam verus ornatus maxime Christianorum et Christianarum non tantum nullus fucus mendax verum ne auri quidem vestisque pompa, sed mores boni sunt.
examples.translation: For not only is lying paint no real adornment of Christian men and women, nor yet is the ostentation of gold and finery; but a good character is.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: a marriage portion, dowry (for syn. cf.: donum, largitio, munus, donatio, etc.).
Latin: Id quod datur puellae, quae in matrimonium collocatur
Latin: ingenium
English: infin. pass. parag. defungier

examples.original: Quod senex Megalius defunctus sit, iam vos audisse quis dubitet?
examples.translation: You will have already heard, I am sure, of the death of the Senior Megaliusa;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Decimus Iunius Brutus munus gladiatorium in honorem defuncti patris primus edidit Colonia Aesernia deducta est.
examples.translation: Decimus Junius Brutus was the first to give a gladiatorial exhibition, in honour of his dead father. The colony of Aesernia was planted.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Gaio et Lucio intra triennium defunctis adoptatur ab Augusto simul cum fratre eorum M. Agrippa, coactus prius ipse Germanicum fratris sui filium adoptare.
examples.translation: When Gaius and Lucius died within three years, he was adopted by Augustus along with their brother Marcus Agrippa, being himself first compelled to adopt his nephew Germanicus.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: Of or belonging to the Gauls; v. 1. Galli, II. B.—
Latin: De Gallia, eius populo, lingua, vel sim

examples.original: Muri autem omnes Gallici hac fere forma sunt.
examples.translation: All Gallic walls are, as a rule, of the following pattern.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Eo anno aedis Martis Gallico bello vota dedicata est a T. Quinctio duumviro sacris faciendis.
examples.translation: In that year the temple of Mars vowed in the Gallic war was dedicated by Titus Quinctius, duumvir for sacrifices.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nam quod ad thesauros Gallicos attinet, rem suapte natura facilem difficilem interrogatio facit.
examples.translation: And touching the Gallic treasure—the thing itself is simple, but your questioning makes it difficult.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a beast used for drawing or carrying, draught-cattle, a beast of bur- den, esp. a horse, mule, or
Latin: Animal (velut bos), quod ad instrumenta (velut aratrum) trahenda usurpatur

examples.original: Quo factum est, quod omnibus mirabile est visum, ut aeque nitida iumenta ex castello educeret, cum complures menses in obsidione fuisset, ac si in campestribus ea locis habuisset.
examples.translation: The result was that, to the surprise of all, the animals were led out of the fortress after a siege of several months in as good condition as if he had kept them in pasture.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: a serpent, a snake (syn.: serpens, coluber, draco).
Latin: Serpens

examples.original: Aut velut Eurylochi, qui sceptrum cepit ab illo, Sint artus avidis anguibus esca tui.
examples.translation: Or like Eurylochus, who took the sceptre from him, may thy limbs be food for greedy snakes.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a cornfield.

examples.original: Fertilior seges est alienis semper in agris, Vicinumque pecus grandius uber habet.
examples.translation: In fields not ours the crops are ever more bounteous, and the neighbouring herd has richer udders.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Abstulimus terras, exclusimus aequore toto, Ad praematuras segetum ieiuna rapinas Agmina conpulimus, votumque effecimus hosti, Ut mallet sterni gladiis mortemque suorum Permiscere meis.
examples.translation: We have wrenched the land from the enemy, and expelled him utterly from the sea; we have forced his starving ranks to snatch the corn ere it was ripe;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: going about, hither and thither.

examples.original: Ut et levi momento nec ambigue est victus, ita brevitate ipsa loci facili-que receptu in tam propinqua castra haud aegre militem a multa caede est tutatus;
examples.translation: He was easily and decisively defeated; yet, because his camp was so near and so readily accessible, he was able without great difficulty to save his men from heavy losses;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Perinde legati provinciaeque cunctabantur, Hordeonius Flaccus suspectis iam Batavis anxius proprio bello, Vettius Bolanus numquam satis quieta Britannia, et uterque ambigui.
examples.translation: The governors and the provinces moved as slowly as he. Hordeonius Rufus already suspected the Batavians and was disturbed by the possibility of having a war of his own ;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: of or belonging to freedom, relating to the freeborn condition of a man.
Latin: Qui ad libertatem pertinet
Latin: Homini libero dignus

examples.original: Liberalis disciplinas omnis fere puer attigit.
examples.translation: When a boy he took up almost all the liberal arts;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Potest quidem etiam illud dici: sine liberalibus studiis veniri ad sapientiam posse;
examples.translation: We might even make the statement that it is possible to attain wisdom without the ”liberal studies”;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cessat omne studium et liberalia professi sine ulla frequentia desertis angulis praesident.
examples.translation: You need not wonder that diseases are beyond counting: count the cooks! All intellectual interests are in abeyance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A short time ago, a little while ago
English: to beat down, throw down; to overturn, upset (class.; syn.: percutio, deicio).

examples.original: Primo Aricinos res necopinata perculerat;
examples.translation: At first the Aricini were paralysed with surprise.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Instant Volumnius et Scipio et perculsos sternunt.
examples.translation: Hard after them came Volumnius and Scipio, and made havoc of the disordered Samnites.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Volscos consilii poenam non metuentes necopinata res perculit; armorum immemores obsides dant trecentos principum a Cora atque Pometia liberos.
examples.translation: They had no thought of resisting, and surrendered as hostages three hundred children of the nobility of Cora and Pometia, and so the legions were withdrawn without a conflict.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: it is easy to see, it is clear or evident, clearly, plainly, evidently, manifestly, etc. (class., but much less freq. than scilicet).

examples.original: Rem videlicet difficilem et obscuram!
examples.translation: As though it were a difficult or recondite notion!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Exemplis nunc uti videlicet mihi necesse est harum rerum omnium.
examples.translation: And now I suppose I must produce examples of all these points;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Videlicet, quia res ipsa non recipiebatur a nobis nec in usu erat, nomini quoque repugnatum est.
examples.translation: This is natural, inasmuch as the thing itself has not been admitted to general use by us; the name, too, has met with opposition.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to allay, settle, still, calm, assuage, appease, quiet, check
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Nullum telum in corpore eius sedet;
examples.translation: No missile can settle in her body;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Oportet me sedere: tunc demum sedeo.
examples.translation: Or suppose that I ought to seat myself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vesperascente die sitim haustu gelidae aquae sedavit.
examples.translation: As evening approached he slaked his thirst with a draught of cold water.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: two and a half; only in the phrases sestertius nummus and milia sestertia; v. I. A. and I. B. 1. infra.— Mostly as

examples.original: Cum Habonio tutore, quod erat vix HS quadraginta milium, transigunt HS ducentis milibus.
examples.translation: They agreed with the guardian Habonius to pay £2000 for an operation whose real cost was barely £400.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum esset in aedibus armarium, in quo sciret esse nummorum aliquantum et auri, noctu duos conservos dormientes occidit in piscinamque deiecit: ipse armarii fundum exsecuit, et HS . .
examples.translation: There was a safe in the house which he knew to contain a quantity of cash and of gold;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Huic hereditas HS quingentorum milium venerat a muliere quadam propinqua, atque ita propinqua ut ea etiamsi intestata esset mortua Epicratem Bidinorum legibus heredem esse oporteret.
examples.translation: This man inherited £5000 from a female relative; so near a relative that, even had she died intestate, Epicrates would by the laws of Bidis have been her heir.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To strike one upon another, to strike together (rare): utrum cavae manus concutiantur, an planae, Sen. Q. N. 2, 28, 1

examples.original: Nec sine causa concussus est;
examples.translation: And not without reason has he been shaken;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic pleno Padus ore tumens super aggere tutas Excurrit ripas et totos concutit agros;
examples.translation: Thus the river Po, swollen with brimming estuary, overflows its banks though defended by dykes, and oversets whole districts;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Concussa statim flagitio domus: pro marito studia civitatis, pro adultero libido reginae et saevitia.
examples.translation: Her house was at once shaken by this scandalous act. Her husband was favoured by the sentiments of all the citizens;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a maidservant, handmaid, female slave

examples.original: Sed prius ancillam captandae nosse puellae Cura sit: accessus molliet illa tuos.
examples.translation: But take care first to know the handmaid of the woman you would win;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a servant, attendant; a maid - servant, handmaid (class.).

examples.original: Quantosne tumores Mente gerit famulus!
examples.translation: What pride the menial cherishes in his heart!
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nec non subrepta paratis A famulo Ganymede dolis pervenit ad hostes Caesaris Arsinoe;
examples.translation: Moreover, Arsinoe was carried off secretly by a trick of Ganymede, her chamberlain, and conveyed to Caesar’s enemies.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quem postquam propius famulae videre fideles, Non ultra gemitus tacitos incessere fatum Permisere sibi, frustraque attollere terra Semianimem conantur eram;
examples.translation: When her faithful handmaids saw him close at hand, they dared not rail at destiny except with stifled groans, and tried in vain to lift their fainting mistress from the ground;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To fill with breath or
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Ut dicam: aut animantia sunt aut inanima.
examples.translation: By saying that it is either animate or inanimate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Itaque erit aliquid animantibus antiquius, corpus scilicet.
examples.translation: But there is still something superior to ”substance”;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quam multa ab iis conquisita et collecta sunt de omnium animantium genere, ortu, membris, aetatibus!
examples.translation: What stores of facts they observed and recorded about the classification, reproduction, morphology and life-history of animals of every kind!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to make a triumphal procession, to hold or celebrate a triumph, to triumph (cf. ovo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Dictator ex senatus consulto triumphavit.
examples.translation: The dictator triumphed by resolution of the senate.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: De Verulis et Bovillis pudet, sed triumphavimus.
examples.translation: Over Verulae and Bovillae, I am ashamed to say it—but we triumphed.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ab triumpho exercitum in agrum Vescinum, quia regio ea infesta ab Samnitibus erat, hibernatum duxit.
examples.translation: After triumphing, Papirius led his army into the country of the Vescini—a district infested by the Samnites—to pass the winter.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: in vain, to no purpose, fruitlessly
Latin: Sine successu, frustra
Latin: Sine ratione

examples.original: Iam omnibus locis ceditur nequiquam Sempronio consule obiurgante atque hortante.
examples.translation: There was no virtue either in his authority or in his dignity;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tum, ut bellum iuberent, latum ad populum est et nequiquam dissuadentibus tribunis plebis omnes tribus bellum iusserunt.
examples.translation: They then asked the people for a declaration of war, and notwithstanding the opposition of the plebeian tribunes, all the tribes voted for war.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: His orationibus incitata plebs denis milibus aeris gravis reos condemnat, nequiquam Sergio Martem communem belli fortunamque accusante, Verginio deprecante ne infelicior domi quam militiae esset.
examples.translation: It was in vain that Sergius blamed Fortune and the common chance of war, while Verginius begged that he might not be more unlucky at home than he had been in the campaign.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to produce melodious sounds (by the voice or an instrument), to sound
Latin: Sonos bene emittere, carmen proferre
Latin: Divisio administrativa exempli gratia Helvetiae, pagus
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Ibidem saepius et per complures cantavit dies;
examples.translation: In the same city he sang frequently and for several successive days.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quodque vix auditu fas esse debeat, laudis et gloriae et ingenii loco plerique iactant cantari saltarique commentarios suos;
examples.translation: They make it their aim, by wantonness of language, by shallow-pated conceits, and by irregular arrangement, to produce the rhythms of stage-dancing;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a taking care of something, administration, oversight, care, management, charge (rare but class.).

examples.original: Hoc idem transfero in magistratus, curationes, sacerdotia; quibus in rebus non solum hominum iura sed etiam deorum immortalium religiones omnes repudiavit.
examples.translation: The same thing may be said of magistracies, directorships, and priesthoods, in dealing with which he trampled down not only the rights of men but all the commandments of the powers above.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: elsewhere.
Latin: Alio loco

examples.original: Id modo non conveniebat, quod senatus consulesque nusquam alibi spem quam in armis ponebant, plebes omnia quam bellum malebat.
examples.translation: In this one point they were unable to agree, that the senate and the consuls saw no hope anywhere but in arms, while the plebs preferred anything to war.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: disgrace, dishonor, ignominy, esp. as the result of civil or military punishment

examples.original: Quis enim umquam tanta a quoquam contumelia, quis tanta ignominia affectus est?
examples.translation: For did ever one man inflict upon another such an insult, such a humiliation as this?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Si erunt plures, qui ob innocentem condemnandum pecuniam acceperint, tu non animadvertes in omnes, sed carpes, ut velis, et paucos ex multis ad ignominiam sortiere?
examples.translation: And do you propose to do the same when making up the list of the senate in your capacity as censor?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Haec moverunt Veientes, ac pro se quisque Romano saltem duce ignominias demendas belloque amissa repetenda minaciter fremunt. Tarquinienses nomen ac cognatio movet: pulchrum videbatur suos Romae regnare.
examples.translation: The Tarquinienses were influenced by his name and kinship: it seemed a fine thing to them that one of their blood should be king in Rome.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: secretly, privately; and in the predicate after sum and fore, hidden, secret, unknown

examples.original: Ne id quidem satis est, nisi docet ita se possedisse, ut nec vi nec clam nec precario possederit.
examples.translation: And even that is not sufficient unless he can show that his possession arose neither from force, fraud, or favour.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: A quibus placide oratio accepta est, iis litteras ab Tarquiniis reddunt et de accipiendis clam nocte in urbem regibus conloquuntur.
examples.translation: To those who gave them a friendly hearing they delivered letters from the Tarquinii, and plotted with them to admit the royal family secretly by night into the City.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cadaver eius clam in hortos Lamianos asportatum et tumultuario rogo semiambustum levi caespite obrutum est, postea per sorores ab exsilio reversas erutum et crematum sepultumque.
examples.translation: His body was conveyed secretly to the gardens of the Lamian family, where it was partly consumed on a hastily erected pyre and buried beneath a light covering of turf;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a. [sors].

examples.original: Si sortis, nullum crimen est in casu;
examples.translation: If you impute it to chance, then you have nothing to charge him with;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Valerius Horatiusque consules sortiti uter dedicaret.
examples.translation: Valerius and Horatius the consuls drew lots to determine which should do it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Homo, id quod erat facillimum, primo vetat sortiri, iubet extra sortem Theomnastum renuntiari.
examples.translation: The man first tried the simple plan of forbidding the lot, ordering Theomnastus to be returned as appointed without it.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to crook, bend, bow, curve

examples.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis.
examples.translation: Read Cicero: his style has unity; it moves with a modulated pace, and is gentle without being degenerate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to step across, step over, climb over
Latin: transire

examples.original: Nondum enim incerta transgressus est, etiamnunc versatur in lubrico.
examples.translation: For such a man has not yet traversed the doubtful ground;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Adcelerata interim Vespasiani coepta Illyrici exercitus studio transgressi in partis; tertia legio exemplum ceteris Moesiae legionibus praebuit;
examples.translation: Meantime Vespasian’s enterprise received a favourable impulse from the enthusiasm with which the army in Illyricum came over to his side.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hunc iuvenem Galba, quaestorem in Baetica impigre in partis suas transgressum, legioni praeposuit: mox compertum publicam pecuniam avertisse ut peculatorem flagitari iussit.
examples.translation: This youth Galba had put in command of a legion, for when he was quaestor in Baetica, he had not hesitated to join Galba’s party.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to make four-cornered, to square, make square
Latin: e re aliam rem facere quae quattuor angulos habet
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Erat attributus Antonio praefectus equitum C. Volusenus Quadratus qui cum eo hibernaret. Hunc Antonius ad persequendum equitatum hostium mittit.
examples.translation: Gaius Volusenus Quadratus had been attached as cavalry commander to Antonius, to winter with him, and Antonius despatched him to pursue the enemy’s horse.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Postquam in agrum Romanum ventum est, obviam hosti consules eunt: Valerius quadrato agmine peditem ducit; Brutus ad explorandum cum equitatu antecessit.
examples.translation: When they had come into Roman territory the consuls went out to meet the enemy: Valerius led the foot in defensive formation;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: sidelong, slanting, awry, oblique (freq. and class.; cf.: transversus, imus).

examples.original: Restat ergo ut iste pecuniae turpissimus appetitus ex obliquo in clericos et maxime in episcopum dirigatur.
examples.translation: It remains, then, that your charge of a most sordid lust for money is indirectly levelled at the clergy, and especially at the bishop.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ignota obscurae viderunt sidera noctes Ardentemque polum flammis caeloque volantes Obliquas per inane faces crinemque timendi Sideris et terris mutantem regna cometen.
examples.translation: The darkness of night saw stars before unknown, the sky blazing with fire, lights shooting athwart the void of heaven, and the hair of the baleful star—the comet which portends change to monarchs.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nam saevus in ipso Septimius sceleris maius scelus invenit actu, Ac retegit sacros scisso velamine voltus Semianimis Magni spirantiaque occupat ora Collaque in obliquo ponit languentia transtro.
examples.translation: The head was severed; for savage Septimius, in the very doing of his crime, devised a crime still worse.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a piece of standing water

examples.original: Stagna avidi texere soli laxaeque paludes Depositum, Fortuna, tuum;
examples.translation: Engulfing quicksands and spongy marshes hid the secret that Fortune had placed there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Saeva quies pelagi, maestoque ignava profundo Stagna iacentis aquae;
examples.translation: A grim stillness broods over the dismal deep;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to glory, boast, vaunt, to brag of any thing, pride one's self on any thing (class.); constr. with

examples.original: Gloriari otio iners ambitio est.
examples.translation: To boast of our retirement is but idle self-seeking.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo proelio praecipua equitum gloria fuit;
examples.translation: In this battle the cavalry particularly distinguished themselves.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quod sua victoria tam insolenter gloriarentur quodque tam diu se impune iniurias tulisse admirarentur, eodem pertinere.
examples.translation: Their insolent boast of their own victory, their surprise that their outrages had gone on so long with impunity, pointed the same way;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: pertaining to land, fields, or the country, country, rural, rustic, wild
Latin: Qui ad agros pertinet; rusticus

examples.original: Et primo in agrestes ingruerant servitiaque;
examples.translation: At first they attacked country people and slaves;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea conluvio mixtorum omnis generis animantium et odore insolito urbanos et agrestem confertum in arta tecta aestu ac vigiliis angebat, ministeriaque in vicem ac contagio ipsa volgabant morbos.
examples.translation: This conflux of all kinds of living things distressed the citizens with its strange smells, while the country-people, being packed into narrow quarters, suffered greatly from the heat and want of sleep;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to quench, extinguish (class.; esp. freq. in Cic. and in the trop. signif.).

examples.original: Eorum querella inveterata non modo familiaritates exstingui solere, sed odia etiam gigni sempiterna.
examples.translation: By their ceaseless recriminations not only are social intimacies usually destroyed, but also everlasting enmities are produced.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et forsitan, quem ille obrutum ignem reliquerit, ita ut totiens novum ex improviso incendium daret, eum se exstincturum.
examples.translation: And perhaps that fire which Fabius had left covered up, but so that it was continually breaking out into new flames, might be by him extinguished.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quae aut plane neglegenda est, si omnino exstinguit animum, aut etiam optanda, si aliquo eum deducit ubi sit futurus aeternus.
examples.translation: For clearly death is negligible, if it utterly annihilates the soul, or even desirable, if it conducts the soul to some place where it is to live for ever.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: inner

examples.original: Interiores plerique frumenta non serunt, sed lacte et carne vivunt pellibusque sunt vestiti.
examples.translation: Of the inlanders most do not sow corn, but live on milk and flesh and clothe themselves in skins.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Difficile est in Asia, Cilicia, Syria regnisque interiorum nationum ita versari nostrum imperatorem, ut nihil aliud nisi de hoste ac de laude cogitet.
examples.translation: It is difficult for a general of ours to be engaged in Asia, Cilicia, and Syria and the kingdoms of the interior without entertaining a thought save of the enemy and of glory.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: His nuntiis litterisque commotus Caesar duas legiones in citeriore Gallia novas conscripsit et inita aestate in interiorem Galliam qui deduceret Quintum Pedium legatum misit.
examples.translation: These reports and despatches prompted Caesar to enrol two new legions in Hither Gaul, and at the beginning of summer he sent Quintus Pedius, lieutenant-general, to lead them into Inner Gaul.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a queen.
Latin: Mulier regnum possidens, vel regis uxor
Latin: Pro regis filia

examples.original: Iuppiter optimus maximus, Iuno regina et Minerva, alii di deaeque obsidentur;
examples.translation: Jupiter Optimus Maximus, Queen Juno, and Minerva, and the other gods and goddesses, are beleaguered;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Concussa statim flagitio domus: pro marito studia civitatis, pro adultero libido reginae et saevitia.
examples.translation: Her house was at once shaken by this scandalous act. Her husband was favoured by the sentiments of all the citizens;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cum in praesidium Reginorum legio Campana cum praefecto Decio Vibellio missa esset, occisis Reginis Regium occupavit.
examples.translation: A Campanian legion, commanded by Decius Vibellius, being sent to protect the people of Regium, put the inhabitants to death and seized the city.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: at or in any place, anywhere (usu. in neg. clauses, while uspiam, corresp. to quispiam, is used also affirmatively).
Latin: Aliquo loco

examples.original: Tum Verginius ubi nihil usquam auxilii vidit, ”Quaeso” inquit, ”Appi, primum ignosce patrio dolori, si quo inclementius in te sum invectus;
examples.translation: Then Verginius, seeing no help anywhere, said, ”I ask you, Appius, first to pardon a father’s grief if I have somewhat harshly inveighed against you;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cerberus et Furiae iam vero et lucis egestas, Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus— qui neque sunt usquam nec possunt esse profecto.
examples.translation: Cerberusb also and the Furies and the with-holding of light, and Tartarus belching horrible fires from his throat—these neither exist anywhere nor in truth can exist.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Perfecto enim et concluso neque virtutibus neque amicitiis usquam locum esse si ad voluptatem omnia referantur, nihil praeterea est magno opere dicendum.
examples.translation: For when it has been conclusively proved that if pleasure is the sole standard there is no room left either for virtue or friendship, there is no great need to say anything further.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: gain, profit, advantage (syn.: quaestus, compendium; cf.: commodum, fructus).
Latin: Compendium, quaestus

examples.original: Quisquis dixit ”vixi,” cotidie ad lucrum surgit.
examples.translation: When a man has said: ”have lived!”, every morning he arises he receives a bonus.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic reus ille fere est de quo victoria lucro Esse potest;
examples.translation: So is he generally accused whose defeat means gain;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Minus avaritiae in Caecina, plus ambitionis: Valens ob lucra et quaestus infamis eoque alienae etiam culpae dissimulator.
examples.translation: Caecina was less avaricious, but more eager for popularity; Valens, notorious for his greed and sordid gains, was more inclined to overlook the crimes of others.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: To live with

examples.original: Haerebit tibi avaritia, quamdiu avaro sordidoque convixeris;
examples.translation: As long as this companion is avaricious and mean, greed will stick to you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eadem causa est, cur nos mancipiorum nostrorum urbanitas in dominos contumeliosa delectet, quorum audacia ita demum sibi in convivas ius facit, si coepit a domino;
examples.translation: For the same reason the waggery of slaves, insulting to their masters, amuses us, and their boldness at the expense of guests has licence only because they begin with their master himself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: uneasiness of mind

examples.original: Et accesserunt maioris sollicitudinis causae.
examples.translation: He had besides reasons for still greater anxiety;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ex hoc quantum lacrimae, quantum sollicitudines occupant!
examples.translation: How much of this time is taken up with weeping, how much with worry!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neque ullum fere totius hiemis tempus sine sollicitudine Caesaris intercessit, quin aliquem de consiliis ac motu Gallorum nuntium acciperet.
examples.translation: And scarcely a moment the whole winter through passed without anxiety for Caesar, without the receipt of some message concerning the projected rising of the Gauls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to make a noise; to rattle, rustle, rumble

examples.original: Senatus tumultuose vocatus tumultuosius consulitur, quaestionem postulantibus iis qui pulsati fuerant, decernente ferocissimo quoque non sententiis magis quam clamore et strepitu.
examples.translation: Those who had been roughly handled demanded an investigation, and all the more violent members urged the resolution, not only with speeches but with shouts and uproar.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to make or lay open, to open, throw open (freq. and class.; syn.: pando, recludo, aperio).

examples.original: Ita induxisse in animum, hostibus potius quam regibus portas patefacere;
examples.translation: They had resolved to throw open their gates to enemies sooner than to kings;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: At ille post non multo sua sponte ad exercitum rediit et ibi non callida, sed dementi ratione cogitata patefecit;
examples.translation: But not long afterwards Pausanias returned to the army on his own account, and there he revealed his designs in a manner that was rather insane than adroit.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

examples.original: Romanos terror per tota castra trepidos agit, et ad extrema ventum foret, ni legati rapto consulis corpore patefecissent una porta hostibus viam.
