examples.translation: We get some help from the service which mathematics renders;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: At si inutile ministeriis corpus est, quidni oporteat educere animum laborantem?
examples.translation: But if the body is useless for service, why should one not free the struggling soul?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potitii ab Euandro edocti antistites sacri eius per multas aetates fuerunt, donec tradito servis publicis sollemni familiae ministerio genus omne Potitiorum interiit.
examples.translation: The Potitii, instructed by Evander, were priests of this cult for many generations, until, having delegated to public slaves the solemn function of their family, the entire stock of the Potitii died out.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: an estate inherited from a father, a paternal estate, inheritance, patrimony (syn. hereditas).

examples.original: Chelidon, unus ex Cleopatrae mollibus, patrimonium grande possedit.
examples.translation: Chelidon, one of Cleopatra’s eunuchs, possessed great wealth;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: wedlock, marriage, matrimony.

examples.original: Post has Valeriam Messalinam, Barbati Messalae consobrini sui filiam, in matrimonium accepit.
examples.translation: Then he married Valeria Messalina, daughter of his cousin Messala Barbatus.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hi autem erant inimici Agathinus, homo nobilis, et Dorotheus, qui habebat in matrimonio Callidamam, Agathini eius filiam;
examples.translation: These enemies were a man of some note named Agathinus, and Dorotheus, who was married to Callidama the daughter of Agathinus;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Inde opes et rerum secundarum luxus: spreto Venutio (is fuit maritus) armigerum eius Vellocatum in matrimonium regnumque accepit.
examples.translation: She grew to despise her husband Venutius, and took as her consort his squire Vellocatus, whom she admitted to share the throne with her.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a defending, fortifying, protecting (class.).

examples.original: Huius munitionis duplex erat consilium.
examples.translation: The object of this fortification was twofold.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ex his Pullo, cum acerrime ad munitiones pugnaretur, ”Quid dubitas,” inquit, ”Vorene?
examples.translation: One of them, Pullo, when the fight was fiercest by the entrenchments, said: ”Why hesitate, Vorenus?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Eo circiter hominum numero sedecim milia expedita cum omni equitatu Ariovistus misit, quae copiae nostros perterrerent et munitione prohiberent.
examples.translation: Towards it Ariovistus sent some sixteen thousand light-armed troops with all the horse, as a force to frighten our men and to prevent their entrenching work.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: destruction, death, ruin, overthrow, disaster, calamity (syn.: exitium, labes).

examples.original: Ego vero ne immortalitatem quidem contra rem publicam accipiendam putarem, nedum emori cum pernicie rei publicae vellem.
examples.translation: But the truth is, that I could not look upon even immortality as desirable, if it was to be achieved at my country’s cost;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Haec igitur natura tenetur corpore ab omni, ipsaque corporis est custos et causa salutis; nam communibus inter se radicibus haerent nec sine pernicie divelli posse videntur.
examples.translation: This natureb then is contained by the whole body, and is itself the body’s guardian and source of its existence;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: of or belonging to a man, manly, virile (cf.: mas, masculus).
Latin: Qui ad viros pertinet

examples.original: Illo sano ac valente oratio quoque robusta, fortis, virilis est;
examples.translation: When the soul is sound and strong, the style too is vigorous, energetic, manly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Animum virilem et Christianum nec debent, si accedunt, extollere nec debent frangere, si recedunt.
examples.translation: The manly Christian spirit ought neither to be elated by their accession nor depressed by their departure.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Quippe et Theodotus magister auctorque totius belli, et ne virilia quidem portenta, Pothinus atque Ganymedes diversa per mare et terras fuga morte consumpti.
examples.translation: Theodotus, the director and instigator of the whole war, and Pothinus and Ganymedes, monsters who were not even men, met their deaths after fleeing in different directions over sea and land.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: To hold together, to hold, contain, confine, embrace, comprise

examples.original: Sed me ipse cohibeo, ne a te rhetorice potius quam veridice agere existimer.
examples.translation: But I refrain, in case you imagine that I am quarrelling about words rather than seeking truth.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Nam primum tacta designat membra saliva, Quae cohibet virus retinetque in volnere pestem;
examples.translation: The native begins by marking the part with the touch of his spittle;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cohibe itaque iam iniquum et inpacatum animum, ut in vera ecclesia Christi invenias salutare convivium.
examples.translation: So curb your hostile and rebellious spirit, that you may find the feast of salvation within the true Church of Christ.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: One who fends, wards, averts, or keeps off

examples.original: Obstitit Antonius datisque defensoribus ad Vespasianum dimisit.
examples.translation: Antonius interposed, gave him a guard, and sent him to Vespasian.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Itaque magnus ille defensor et amicus eius tibi suffragatur, me oppugnat;
examples.translation: That is why his great friend and defender is canvassing on your behalf and working against me.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ceterum ibi plus laboris ac periculi fuit: et defensa summa vi moenia sunt, et locus erat munimento naturaque tutus;
examples.translation: But there they encountered more difficulty and danger: the city was defended with the utmost energy, and fortification and nature had combined to make it safe;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a. [patior], to bear steadfastly, suffer with firmness or patience; to stand out, abide, endure (class.): animus aeger neque pati neque perpeti potis est, Enn. ap.

examples.original: Nulla virtus est, quae non sentiat se perpeti.
examples.translation: There is no virtue that fails to realize that it does endure.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quis de exceptione et formula perpetietur ilea immensa volumina quae pro M. Tullio aut Aulo Caecina legimus?
examples.translation: Would anyone endure the interminable arguments about pleas and procedure which we get in the speeches delivered in defence of M. Tullius or Aulus Caecina?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Eodem modo non erit dubium, quin maius bonum sit gaudium quam obnixus animus ad perpetiendos cruciatus vulnerum aut ignium.” Minime.
examples.translation: For things that result from hazard admit of wide distinctions, since they are rated according to their usefulness in the eyes of those who experience them;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a pole

examples.original: Consurgere in ipsis Ius tibi solstitiis, aliena crescere bruma Atque hiemes adferre tuas, solique vagari Concessum per utrosque polos.
examples.translation: He is privileged to rise at midsummer, to be flooded by a winter out of season, and to bring with him a rainy season of his own;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Una per aetherios exit vox illa recessus Verbaque ad invitum perfert cogentia numen, Quod non cura poli caelique volubilis umquam Avocat.
examples.translation: Their voice alone speeds through the remote parts of heaven, and conveys the words that bind the reluctant deity, whom no care for the sky and revolving firmament ever distracts from listening.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ignota obscurae viderunt sidera noctes Ardentemque polum flammis caeloque volantes Obliquas per inane faces crinemque timendi Sideris et terris mutantem regna cometen.
examples.translation: The darkness of night saw stars before unknown, the sky blazing with fire, lights shooting athwart the void of heaven, and the hair of the baleful star—the comet which portends change to monarchs.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: one who writes.

examples.original: Quid, si iis verbis scripta est ista proscriptio, ut se ipsa dissolvat?
examples.translation: But what if your proscription was made in such terms that it destroys itself?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam multos scriptores rerum suarum magnus ille Alexander secum habuisse dicitur!
examples.translation: We read that Alexander the Great carried in his train numbers of epic poets and historians.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed ambitionem scriptoris facile averseris, obtrectatio et livor pronis auribus accipiuntur;
examples.translation: So between the hostility of the one class and the servility of the other, posterity was disregarded.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to hide, conceal

examples.original: Utque Milo, sub quo cruciata est Pisa tyranno, Vivus in occultas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: And like Milo, under whose tyranny Pisa groaned, mayst thou be hurled alive into hidden waters.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Magistratus quae visa sunt occultant quaeque esse ex usu iudicaverunt multitudini produnt.
examples.translation: Magistrates conceal what they choose, and make known what they think proper for the public.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Atque ut a corpore ordiar, videsne ut si quae in membris prava aut debilitata aut imminuta sint occultent homines?
examples.translation: To start with the body, do you notice how men try to hide a deformed or infirm or maimed limb?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: An oblong shield, made of boards fastened together, and covered with leather, a buckler
Latin: genus armorum figura quadrata oblonga, quod laeva gestatur ad protegendum corpus, ex assibus confectum valvarum instar
Latin: auxilium, praesidium

examples.original: Non galea, non scuto repellitur ferrum.
examples.translation: What is the need of defensive armour, or of skill?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hinc illi cognomen novum et rei publicae salutare Cunctator; hinc illud ex populo, ut imperii scutum vocaretur.
examples.translation: Hence he received a new title, significant of the way in which he saved the State, namely, Cunctator (”the Delayer”);
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Lateque cladem intulisset ni duo milites praeclarum facinus ausi, arreptis e strage scutis ignorati, vincla ac libramenta tormentorum abscidissent.
examples.translation: They were at once run through and thus their names were lost; but there is no doubt about their deed.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to flee back; to run away, flee, escape.
Latin: rursum fugere
Latin: fugiendo devitare

examples.original: Quod ubi accidit, barbari vehementissimo cursu refugerunt.
examples.translation: When this occurred, the natives fled away at a most furious speed.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Abscidis frustra ferro tua pignora: bellum Te faciet civile meum.” Sic fata refugit Umbra per amplexus trepidi dilapsa mariti.
examples.translation: The civil war shall make you mine.” Thus speaking, the ghost fled away, dissolving in the arms of her eager husband.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quo praecepto ab eis diligentissime observato, cum quaepiam cohors ex orbe excesserat atque impetum fecerat, hostes velocissime refugiebant.
examples.translation: This instruction they most carefully observed. When any cohort left the square and made a charge the enemy would run back with great rapidity.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a swordsman, fighter in the public games
Latin: Qui cum gladio pugnat

examples.original: Decimus Iunius Brutus munus gladiatorium in honorem defuncti patris primus edidit Colonia Aesernia deducta est.
examples.translation: Decimus Junius Brutus was the first to give a gladiatorial exhibition, in honour of his dead father. The colony of Aesernia was planted.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quin et natalem Vitellii diem Caecina ac Valens editis tota urbe vicatim gladiatoribus celebravere, ingenti paratu et ante illum diem insolito.
examples.translation: Moreover, Caecina and Valens celebrated his birthday by giving gladiatorial shows in every precinct of the city on an enormous scale unheard of up to that time.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Pauci gladiatorum resistentes neque inulti cecidere: ceteri ad navis ruebant, ubi cuncta pari formidine implicabantur, permixtis paganis, quos nullo discrimine Vitelliani trucidabant.
examples.translation: The rest rushed to the ships; but there an equal panic caused utter confusion, for the Vitellians slew without distinction the townspeople who joined the soldiers in their flight.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a wheel.
English: place under or below

examples.original: Summitti te ac deprimi veto.
examples.translation: I forbid you to be cast down or depressed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Naturae est enim potioribus deteriora summittere.
examples.translation: For nature has the habit of subjecting the weaker to the stronger.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: adapt one thing to another
Latin: Commodo aliquem alicui; impono vel appendo
English: full of faults or defects, faulty, defective

examples.original: Quid ita? Ne vitiosum opus fieret?
examples.translation: Here let me ask this.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Recte igitur, si omnibus in rebus temeritas ignoratioque vitiosa est, ars ea quae tollit haec virtus nominata est.
examples.translation: If therefore rashness and ignorance are in all matters fraught with mischief, the art which removes them is correctly entitled a virtue.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vitiosum est enim in dividendo partem in genere numerare.
examples.translation: It is a fault in division to reckon a species as a genus.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: codd.; abl. lauru

examples.original: Nunc neque te longi remeantem pompa triumphi Excipit, aut sacras poscunt Capitolia laurus;
examples.translation: As it is, no long triumphal procession awaits your return, nor does the Capitol demand your consecrated laurels;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: Continuing a year, annual
Latin: Qui per annum durat
Latin: Qui ad annum pertinet

examples.original: In quibusdam annalibus pro T. Quinctio M. Popilium consulem invenio.
examples.translation: In certain annals I find Marcus Popilius given as consul instead of Titus Quinctius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Meriti aequitate curaque sunt, ut per omnium annalium monumenta celebres nominibus essent; fuere autem C. Duillius P. Decius Mus M. Papirius Q. Publilius et T. Aemilius.
examples.translation: These men by their impartiality and diligence fairly earned the distinction which attaches, in all the histories, to the names of Gaius Duillius, Publius Decius Mus, Marcus Papirius, Quintus Publilius, and Titus Aemilius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vopiscum Iulium pro Verginio in quibusdam annalibus consulem invenio.
examples.translation: Vopiscus Julius I find given as consul in certain annals, instead of Verginius.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to grow ripe, ripen, to come to maturity
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Quo facto maturata est seditio.
examples.translation: This brought the revolt to a head.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed maturato opus est quidquid statuere placet;
examples.translation: That government is certainly by far the strongest to which its subjects yield obedience gladly.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Maturo ceterisque remanere et in verba Vespasiani adigi volentibus fuit.
examples.translation: Maturus and the rest chose to remain and take the oath of fidelity to Vespasian.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: daily, everyday
Latin: Qui omni die accidit

examples.original: Nunc ad cotidianam stipem manum porrigis.
examples.translation: Now you are stretching forth your hand for the daily gift.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed hoc, quod liquet, firmandum et altius cotidiana meditatione figendum est;
examples.translation: This idea, however, clear though it is, must be strengthened and implanted more deeply by daily reflection;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam nec tu agitare et insequi poetas intermittis, et ego, cui desidiam advocationum obicis, cotidianum hoc patrocinium defendendae adversus te poeticae exerceo.
examples.translation: You on your part are never done assailing the poets with your invective, and I, whom you charge with neglect of professional duty, am daily retained to defend the art of poetry against you.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to fill, satisfy; to sate
English: Troy, the city of the Troad
Latin: Urbs Anatoliae quae ab Graecis deleta est

examples.original: Infelix gemino cecidit prope Pergamon igni, Et paene est alio Troia cremata rogo.
examples.translation: All but twice in the flames unhappy Pergamum perished Troy on a second pyre narrowly failed of her doom.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: the founder of the power of Carthage

examples.original: Quas ille, dii boni, Hasdrubalis copias fudit, quos Syphacis Numidici regis equitatus!
examples.translation: Ye gods, what forces of Hasdrubal, what cavalry of Syphax, king of Numidia, did Scipio put to flight!
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Deploratis novissime rebus triginta sex milia virorum se dediderunt, quo minus credas, duce Hasdrubale.
examples.translation: When the position finally became hopeless, 36,000 men led—though it is scarcely credible—by Hasdrubal surrendered themselves.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Tiberius Nero advenientem ex Hispania cum ingentibus copiis Hasdrubalem, prius quam Hannibali fratri coniungeretur, oppressit.
examples.translation: Tiberius Nero crushed Hasdrubal, on his arrival from Spain with a vast army, before he could unite with his brother Hannibal.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the name of a Roman gens. Its most celebrated members were Ti. and C. Sempronius Gracchus, after whom are named the leges Semproniae (v. infra, A.)

examples.original: Iam omnibus locis ceditur nequiquam Sempronio consule obiurgante atque hortante.
examples.translation: There was no virtue either in his authority or in his dignity;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fraudem profecto in re esse, et A. Sempronium comitiis plus artis adhibuisse quam fidei.
examples.translation: It was by his wrong-doing, they complained, that their relations had been defeated for office.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Pontifices creantur suasor legis P. Decius Mus P. Sempronius Sophus C. Marcius Rutulus M. Livius Denter;
examples.translation: To be pontiffs were chosen the advocate of the law, Publius Decius Mus, with Publius Sempronius Sophus, Gaius Marcius Rutulus, and Marcus Livius Denter;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: moist, humid, damp, dank

examples.original: Sed tum umido die et soluto gelu neque conti neque gladii, quos praelongos utraque manu regunt, usui, lapsantibus equis et catafractarum pondere.
examples.translation: No people is so cowardly when it comes to fighting on foot, but when they attack the foe on horseback, hardly any line can resist them.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: everlasting, ever-during, perpetual, continual, imperishable, eternal, sempiternal

examples.original: In qua quid est boni praeter summam voluptatem et eam sempiternam?
examples.translation: But what good has everlasting life to offer beside supreme and never-ending pleasure?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Eorum querella inveterata non modo familiaritates exstingui solere, sed odia etiam gigni sempiterna.
examples.translation: By their ceaseless recriminations not only are social intimacies usually destroyed, but also everlasting enmities are produced.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid denique illo die, quem P. Lentulus mihi fratrique meo liberisque nostris natalem constituit non modo ad nostram, verum etiam ad sempiterni memoriam temporis?
examples.translation: And that a request should be made to them to assemble with undiminished fervour on the day appointed for the resumption of public business?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Full of glory, glorious, famous, renowned

examples.original: Non est autem gloriosum, quod ab invito et tergiversante fit;
examples.translation: But nothing glorious can result from unwillingness and cowardice;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si enim sapiens aliquis miser esse possit, ne ego istam gloriosam memorabilemque virtutem non magno aestimandam putem.”
examples.translation: For if anyone who is wise could be miserable, why, I should not set much value on your vaunted and belauded virtue.”
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid ego gloriosius meis posteris potui relinquere quam hoc, senatum iudicasse, qui civis me non defendisset, eum rem publicam salvam noluisse?
examples.translation: What prouder boast could I have handed on to posterity than that the senate had pronounced that the citizen who had not helped me had shown his unwillingness to preserve the state?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To bound, to set bounds to; to limit, terminate, define (for syn. v. decerno—freq. in Cic.).

examples.original: Primum enim ipsa illa quae subtiliter disserenda erant polite apteque dixerunt, tum definientes, tum partientes, ut vestri etiam;
examples.translation: In the first place, even the topics that required close reasoning they handled in a neat and polished manner, employing now definition, now division;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: tempp. perff. the sync. forms prevail: consuesti, consuestis, consuerunt; consueram, etc.; consuero, etc.; consuerim, etc.; consuessem, etc.

examples.original: Ceterum postquam ibi neque stationes pro portis nec quemquam in vallo nec fremitum consuetum castrorum animadverterunt, insolito silentio moti metu insidiarum subsistunt.
examples.translation: But not perceiving any outposts before the gates or anybody on the rampart, and missing the usual noises of a camp, they were troubled by the unaccustomed silence, and apprehending an ambush, halted.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to smoke, steam, reek, fume.

examples.original: Dimidium fere spatium confecerat, cum ex fumo castrorum eius suspicio adlata est ad Eumenem hostem appropinquare.
examples.translation: He had covered nearly half the distance, when the smoke from his camp led Eumenes to suspect that the enemy were approaching.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: Excepi et pro patria solus exarsi, sic tamen, ut vos iisdem ignibus circumsaepti me primum ictum pro vobis et fumantem videretis.
examples.translation: I blazed alone for my country; but nevertheless those flames hedged you about on all sides, and I was but the first victim whom you saw smitten and smoking to save you.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Fessa iacet cervix, fumant sudoribus artus, Oraque proiecta squalent arentia lingua, Pectora rauca gemunt, quae creber anhelitus urguet, Et defecta gravis longe trahit ilia pulsus, Siccaque sanguineis durescit spuma lupatis.
examples.translation: The weary neck sinks down, the limbs reek with sweat, the tongue protrudes and the mouth is rough and dry; the lungs, driven by quick pants, give a hoarse murmur;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to clap, strike, beat any thing
Latin: acclamare
Latin: percutere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; si, sum, 3

examples.original: Ad profectum omnia tendunt, ad bonam mentem, non quaeritur plausus.
examples.translation: All his work makes for progress and for sanity, without any search for applause.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a step-mother, step-dame.

examples.original: Kal. Ian. in villa colli superposita prope Tarracinam sinistrorsus Fundos petentibus, adoptatusque a noverca sua Livia nomen et Ocellare cognomen assumpsit mutato praenomine;
examples.translation: Adopted by his stepmother Livia, he took her name and the surname Ocella, and also changed his forename;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the stalk or stem of a plant
Latin: stipula plantae
English: to cultivate (late Lat.): in his terris, quas incolunt (rusticani), Cod. Th. 13, 1, 3. —

examples.original: Tum ab incolis deserta civitas direpta primum, deinde tuba praecinente deleta est.
examples.translation: The city, deserted by its inhabitants, was first plundered and then destroyed at a signal given by trumpets.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sed privati ac separati agri apud eos nihil est, neque longius anno remanere uno in loco incolendi causa licet.
examples.translation: They have no private or separate holding of land, nor are they allowed to abide longer than a year in one place for their habitation.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ex his omnibus longe sunt humanissimi qui Cantium incolunt, quae regio est maritima omnis, neque multum a Gallica differunt consuetudine.
examples.translation: Of all the Britons the inhabitants of Kent, an entirely maritime district, are by far the most civilised, differing but little from the Gallic manner of life.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: A calm, tranquil state of the elements, calmness, mildness, tranquillity (like clemens in this signif. mostly post-Aug.)

examples.original: Petere non solum Bellovacos, sed etiam pro his Aeduos, ut sua clementia ac mansuetudine in eos utatur.
examples.translation: Not only the Bellovaci, but the Aedui also on their behalf, beseech you to show your wonted mercy and kindness towards them.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: To hold forth, tender, present; to deliver, give up, produce (class.; syn.: praebeo, porrigo, praesto, tribuo, ministro, do, dono, dedo, etc.).
Latin: Extra secretum habere
Latin: Ante iudicem sistere
English: to renew, restore (class., esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: instauro, redintegro).

examples.original: His consulibus cum Ardeatibus foedus renovatum est;
examples.translation: In their consulship the treaty with the Ardeates was renewed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non mihi falx nimias Saturnia deputat umbras, Duratam renovat non mihi fossor humum;
examples.translation: Saturn’s sickle prunes not my superfluous shade, no digger renews my hardened soil;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Gabiis receptis Tarquinius pacem cum Aequorum gente fecit, foedus cum Tuscis renovavit.
examples.translation: He next turned his attention to affairs in the city.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: of or belonging to a slave, slavish, servile (class.).

examples.original: Coluit ut patrem Servilium Nonianum.
examples.translation: Servilius Nonianus he revered as a father.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Tum dictator ”Macte virtute” inquit, ”C. Servili, esto liberata re publica.”
examples.translation: Whereat the dictator exclaimed, ”Well done, Gaius Servilius; you have delivered the commonwealth!”
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Bellvm Servile III, 19Etsi cum sociis—nefas—cum liberis tamen et ingenuis dimicatum est: quis aequo animo ferat in principe populo bella servorum?
examples.translation: The Servile War 19. Although we fought with allies—in itself an impious act—yet we fought with men who enjoyed liberty and were of free birth;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: sheen, brightness, brilliance, lustre

examples.original: Hunc tu vitae splendorem maculis adspergis istis?
examples.translation: And would you dim with your sullying insinuations the lustre of that untarnished life?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam doleo abesse ab huius iudicio L. Volusienum, summo splendore hominem ac virtute praeditum.
examples.translation: How much I regret, gentlemen, the absence from my client’s trial of the eminent and virtuous L. Volusienus!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ita enim parvae et exiguae sunt istae accessiones bonorum ut, quemadmodum stellae in radiis solis, sic istae in virtutum splendore ne cernantur quidem.
examples.translation: For those supplementary goods are so small and slight that in the full radiance of the virtues they are as invisible as the stars in sunlight.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: compliance, yieldingness, complaisance, indulgence (class.; syn.: indulgentia, obsequentia): prosequium a prosequendo, obsequium ab obsequendo dicuntur, Paul. ex

examples.original: Obsequio tranantur aquae: nec vincere possis Flumina, si contra, quam rapit unda, nates.
examples.translation: By compliance are waters swum; nor can you conquer rivers if you swim against the current’s flow.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Si cur iubeantur quaerere singulis liceat, pereunte obsequio etiam imperium intercidit. An et illic nocte intempesta rapientur arma?
examples.translation: For if individuals may inquire the reason for the orders given them, then discipline is at an end and authority also ceases.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Erectus Samnis Paelignusque et Marsi aemulatione quod Campania praevenisset, ut in novo obsequio, ad cuncta belli munia acres erant.
examples.translation: The Samnites, Paelignians, and Marsians were jealous because Campania had anticipated them, and eagerly undertook all services required by war with the enthusiasm that attaches to every new devotion.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to give bountifully, to lavish, bestow, dispense, distribute, impart (class.; cf.: dono, suppedito).

examples.original: Ex alieno igitur aliis largitos.
examples.translation: The senators had therefore been generous at other men’s expense;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum Octavio collega Cinna dissedit: utrique horum secunda fortuna regnum est largita, adversa mortem.
examples.translation: Cinna fell out with his colleague Octavius; upon each of these prosperity bestowed a tyrant’s power, adversity death.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et si quis deus mihi largiatur ut ex hac aetate repuerascam et in cunis vagiam, valde recusem, nec vero velim quasi decurso spatio ad carceres a calce revocari.
examples.translation: And when I shall have set out to join them, assuredly no one will easily draw me back, or boil me up again, as if I were a Pelias.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: immediately, speedily, without delay, forthwith (class. in prose and poetry)

examples.original: Paci externae confestim continuatur discordia domi.
examples.translation: The foreign peace was immediately succeeded by quarrels at home.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ut Hostius cecidit, confestim Romana inclinatur acies fusaque est ad veterem portam Palatii.
examples.translation: But when he fell, the Roman line gave way at once and fled towards the old gate of the Palatine.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mittuntur ad Caesarem confestim ab Cicerone litterae magnis propositis praemiis, si pertulissent: obsessis omnibus viis missi intercipiuntur.
examples.translation: Despatches were at once sent by Cicero to Caesar, with promise of great rewards if the bearers carried them safe;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: wild, rough, hard, harsh, savage, fierce, ferocious, grim, stern

examples.original: Ceterum in oculis exemplum erat Q. Fabius M. Valerio legato, qui castris praeerat, ne quam vim hostium magis quam trucem dictatoris iram timeret.
examples.translation: But with the example of Quintus Fabius before his eyes, Marcus Valerius, the lieutenant who commanded in the camp, could not fear any violence of the enemy more than the dread displeasure of the dictator.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fieri videntur et discursus stellarum numquam temere, ut non ex ea parte truces venti cooriantur.
examples.translation: Stars are seen to move about in various directions, but never without some cause, nor without violent winds proceeding from the same quarter.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: the extreme end, extremity, or point of a thing; the peak

examples.original: Non ego per praeceps et acuta cacumina vadam, Nec iuvenum quisquam me duce captus erit.
examples.translation: I am not the man to go by precipitous paths and rocky heights; no youth under my leadership will be captured.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non vivunt contra naturam qui pomaria in summis turribus serunt? Quorum silvae in tectis domuum ac fastigiis nutant, inde ortis radicibus quo inprobe cacumina egissent?
examples.translation: Or raise waving forests upon the roofs and battlements of their houses—the roots starting at a point to which it would be outlandish for the tree-tops to reach?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to shut up closely, to close up, enclose, confine.

examples.original: Perfecto enim et concluso neque virtutibus neque amicitiis usquam locum esse si ad voluptatem omnia referantur, nihil praeterea est magno opere dicendum.
examples.translation: For when it has been conclusively proved that if pleasure is the sole standard there is no room left either for virtue or friendship, there is no great need to say anything further.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: an (artistic) copy, imitation of an object (in concreto— for syn. cf.: imago, pictura, simulacrum, signum, statua, tabula).

examples.original: En vobis” inquit ”iuvenem” filium tenens, ”effigiem atque imaginem eius quem vos antea tribunum militum ex plebe primum fecistis.
examples.translation: Here,” he cried, laying hold of his son, ”here is a young man, the effigy and likeness of him you formerly chose for military tribune first of all plebeians.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed ubi totis castris in fama proditio, recurrens in principia miles praescriptum Vespasiani nomen, proiectas Vitellii effigies aspexit, vastum primo silentium, mox cuncta simul erumpunt.
examples.translation: But when the news of the treason spread through the whole camp, the soldiers ran to headquarters, where they saw Vespasian’s name put up on the standards and the statues of Vitellius overthrown;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a tail.

examples.original: Victoria deinde penes patres fuit.
examples.translation: The victory then rested with the senators.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non posse aequo iure agi ubi imperium penes illos, penes se auxilium tantum sit;
examples.translation: There could be no question of equal rights, where the other side commanded and they themselves could do nothing but protest.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ac ne inermes provinciae barbaris nationibus exponerentur, principes Sarmatarum Iazugum, penes quos civitatis regimen, in commilitium adsciti.
examples.translation: To avoid exposing the provinces in their unprotected condition to barbarous nations, the ruling chiefs of the Sarmatian Iazuges were called into service with the army.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to be struck with fear or
Latin: terrore et metu superari
Latin: tremere, timere (de aliqua re)

examples.original: Sic quisque pavendo Dat vires famae, nulloque auctore malorum, Quae finxere, timent.
examples.translation: Thus each by his fears adds strength to rumour, and all dread the unconfirmed dangers invented by themselves.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Evidentissimum id fuit, quod, quacumque equo invectus est, ibi haud secus quam pestifero sidere icti pavebant;
examples.translation: This was most clearly seen in that, wherever he rode, men cowered as though blasted by some baleful star;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Medio cum Phoebus in axe est Aut caelum nox atra tenet, pavet ipse sacerdos Accessus dominumque timet deprendere luci.
examples.translation: For, when the sun is in mid-heaven or dark night fills the sky, the priest himself dreads their approach and fears to surprise the lord of the grove.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: A fire-place, hearth (syn.: clibanus, furnus, fornax, caminus): Varro focos ait dictos, quod foveat ignes, nam ignis ipsa flamma est
English: unequalness.

examples.original: Ea posteaquam numerata est, contentus hac iniquitate non fuit; palam de sella ac tribunali pronuntiat si quis absentem sthenium rei capitalis reum facere vellet, sese eius nomen recepturum;
examples.translation: From his chair of office on the tribunal he announced publicly that if anyone should think fit to prosecute Sthenius in absence on a capital charge, permission to prosecute would be granted;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: above

examples.original: Haec sua sponte agitata insuper tribuni plebis 11, 12accendunt.
examples.translation: This smouldering discontent was fanned into a blaze by the plebeian tribunes.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a learner, scholar, pupil, disciple.
Latin: puer, qui dum scholam frequentat
Latin: homo, qui discit

examples.original: Hic non tam discipulos quam sectatores aliquot habuit.
examples.translation: He had a few followers, rather than pupils;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Apud Pythagoram discipulis quinque annis tacendum erat;
examples.translation: Pythagoras made his pupils keep silence for five years;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare ab Augusto quoque nepotibus eius praeceptor electus, transiit in Palatium cum tota schola, verum ut ne quem amplius posthac discipulum reciperet;
examples.translation: He was therefore chosen by Augustus as the tutor of his grandsons and he moved to the Palace with his whole school, but with the understanding that he should admit no more pupils.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: To run different ways, to run to and fro, run about (not freq. till after the Aug. per.; in Cic not at all): in muris armata civitas, *

examples.original: Stellarum iste discursus quicquid praeterit repetit;
examples.translation: The wandering stars retrace their former courses;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Latentem discurrens forte gregarius miles, animadversis pedibus, studio sciscitandi quisnam esset, adgnovit extractumque et prae metu ad genua sibi accidentem imperatorem salutavit.
examples.translation: As he cowered there, a common soldier, who was prowling about at random, saw his feet, and intending to ask who he was, pulled him out and recognized him;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Fieri videntur et discursus stellarum numquam temere, ut non ex ea parte truces venti cooriantur.
examples.translation: Stars are seen to move about in various directions, but never without some cause, nor without violent winds proceeding from the same quarter.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: , to be hopeless; to have no hope of, to despair of, to give up (freq. and class.).—Constr. most freq. with
Latin: spem perdere, abicere
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: At ei qui ab Alesia processerant maesti prope victoria desperata se in oppidum receperunt.
examples.translation: But the Gauls who had come forth from Alesia, almost despairing of victory, sadly withdrew again into the town.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et si sciret, quid esset vir bonus, nondum esse se crederet, fortasse etiam fieri posse desperaret.
examples.translation: And if he knew what it meant to be ”a good man,” he would not yet believe himself such;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illi, desperatis rebus, cum solvissent naves ac vela ventis dedissent, Hannibal ad Antiochum pervenit.
examples.translation: Hannibal reached Antiochus; as to the death of Mago there are two accounts;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Hannibal

definitions: English: enmity, hostility, usu. in

examples.original: Cavendum vero ne etiam in gravis inimicitias convertant se amicitiae ex quibus iurgia maledicta contumeliae gignuntur.
examples.translation: And you must indeed be on your guard lest friendships be changed into serious enmities, which are the source of disputes, abuse, and invective.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quin etiam si minus felices in deligendo fuissemus, ferendum id Scipio potius quam inimicitiarum tempus cogitandum putabat.
examples.translation: Indeed, Scipio thought that, even if we had been unfortunate in our choice, we should endure it rather than plan an opportunity for a breach.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Circiter annos octoginta, usque ad extremam aetatem ab adulescentia, rei publicae causa suscipere inimicitias non destitit.
examples.translation: For about eighty years, from youth to the end of his life, he never ceased to incur enmity through his devotion to his country.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Cato

definitions: English: to suckle, nourish, feed, foster, bring up, rear (syn. alere; not in Cic., but v. nutrix and nutrimentum).

examples.original: Non potest recipere rationem, non potest nutrire.
examples.translation: He cannot receive reason, nor can he nourish it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nutritur vento, vento restinguitur ignis: Lenis alit flammas, grandior aura necat.
examples.translation: By wind is a fire fostered, and by wind extinguished;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Terra salutares herbas, eademque nocentes Nutrit, et urticae proxima saepe rosa est;
examples.translation: The same earth fosters healing herbs and noxious, and oft is the nettle nearest to the rose;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: apart from State affairs, for one's self, as an individual, in private, privately, in a private capacity

examples.original: Non privatim solum, sed publice furimus.
examples.translation: We are mad, not only individually, but nationally.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Privatim quoque id sacrum celebratum est.
examples.translation: They also observed the rite in their homes.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Alter consul Fabius infestus privatim Papirio erat;
examples.translation: The other consul, Fabius, had a private grudge against Papirius;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the front court of a Grecian house
Latin: ārea mūrāta sine tēctō
Latin: ārea rēgia

examples.original: Exeat aula, Qui volt esse pius.
examples.translation: If a man would be righteous, let him depart from a court.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Pompeio vincite, Parthi, Vinci Roma volet.’” Regem parere iubenti Ardua non piguit, positisque insignibus aulae Egreditur famulo raptos indutus amictus.
examples.translation: If the Parthians conquer for Pompey’s sake, Rome will welcome her conqueror.’” Hard was the task enjoined, but the king did not refuse;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that which contains a multitude, numerous; hence
Latin: Qui a multis hominibus habitatur
Latin: Qui a multis hominibus notus est

examples.original: Iuno regina transvecta a Veiis nuper in Aventino quam insigni ob excellens matronarum studium celebrique dedicata est die!
examples.translation: Queen Juno was lately conveyed from Veii and enshrined on the Aventine, and how notable was that day, for the zeal of the matrons and the throng!
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Latino Alba ortus, Alba Atys, Atye Capys, Capye Capetus, Capeto Tiberinus, qui in traiectu Albulae amnis submersus celebre ad posteros nomen flumini dedit.
examples.translation: This last king was drowned in crossing the River Albula, and gave the stream the name which has been current with later generations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum Romani auxilii adventus tum Camilli nomen celeberrimum apud hostes sociosque et in praesentia rem inclinatam sustinuit et spatium ad opem ferendam dedit.
examples.translation: The arrival of succour from Rome, and particularly the great reputation which Camillus enjoyed with both friends and foes, checked for the moment the disastrous course of events and afforded time to render assistance.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: that by which one is entangled or impeded, a hinderance, impediment (freq. and class.; cf.: obstaculum, difficultas).

examples.original: Consistit agmen; impedimenta intra legiones recipiuntur.
examples.translation: The column halted, and the baggage was drawn back inside the legions.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quae ne impedimentis gravibus agmen oneraret, convocari milites Decius iubet. ”Hacine” inquit ”victoria sola aut hac praeda contenti estis futuri?
examples.translation: Lest these should encumber the marching army with heavy baggage, Decius called the soldiers together and thus addressed them: ”Will this single victory or these spoils content you?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Prima luce magnum numerum impedimentorum ex castris mulorumque produci deque his stramenta detrahi mulionesque cum cassidibus equitum specie ac simulatione collibus circumvehi iubet.
examples.translation: With them he put a few cavalry, to range more widely by way of demonstration, and ordered them all to make for the same general destination by a long circuit.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: unarmed, without weapons, defenceless.

examples.original: Nepesinis inde edictum ut arma ponant, parcique iussum inermi: Etrusci pariter armati atque inermes caesi.
examples.translation: The Etruscans were put to death, whether armed or not. Of the Nepesini, too, those who were responsible for the surrender were executed;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hic diffisus suae atque omnium saluti inermis ex tabernaculo prodit: videt imminere hostes atque in summo esse rem discrimine: capit arma a proximis atque in porta consistit.
examples.translation: He saw that the enemy were threateningly close and that the issue was in the greatest danger; he took arms from the nearest men and stationed himself in the gate.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Flavium Sabinum inermem neque fugam coeptantem circumsistunt, et Quintium Atticum consulem, umbra honoris et suamet vanitate monstratum, quod edicta in populum pro Vespasiano magnifica, probrosa adversus Vitellium iecerat.
examples.translation: Flavius Sabinus, who was unarmed and did not attempt to flee, the Vitellians surrounded; they likewise took Quintus Atticus, the consul.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: the age of youth, youth (mostly post-Aug. for the class. juventus).

examples.original: Pueritia ac iuventa, qualem monstravimus.
examples.translation: His boyhood and youth were such as we have already described.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Is diu sordidus, repente dives mutationem fortunae male tegebat, accensis egestate longa cupidinibus im moderatus et inopi iuventa senex prodigus.
examples.translation: His desires had been increased by long poverty, so that he now put no restraint upon himself, and after a youth of poverty became a prodigal old man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: an animal sacrificed, a victim, sacrifice (cf.: victima).

examples.original: Milites e loco superiore pilis missis facile hostium phalangem perfregerunt.
examples.translation: Then after a speech to encourage his troops he joined battle.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Hostiae, ut quisque vovit, sed mares deliguntur: certissima fides haedorum fibris.
examples.translation: The greatest confidence is put in the entrails of kids.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Postquam pandi viam et mare prosperum accepit, de se per ambages interrogat caesis compluribus hostiis.
examples.translation: On learning that his path was open and the sea favourable, he slew many victims and then questioned indirectly about himself.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to throw or cast down headlong, to precipitate (class.; syn.. deicio, deturbo, proruo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: In eam Curtius armatus sedens equo praecipitavit;
examples.translation: Into it leaped Curtius, fully armed and bestriding his horse;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Aut ut Abantiades, aut ut Cycneïus heros, Clausus in aequoreas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: Or like Abantiades or the Cycnean hero mayst thou be hurled, imprisoned, into the sea’s waters.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non maesti pectora Magni Sustinet amplexu dulci, non colla tenere, Extremusque perit tam longi fructus amoris, Praecipitantque suos luctus, neuterque recedens Sustinuit dixisse ”vale”;
examples.translation: She cannot bear to clasp in her dear arms the breast or head of her sorrowing husband, and the last chance of enjoying their long and faithful love was thrown away.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a pipe, tube, e. g. a water-pipe

examples.original: Et adhuc plebeias fistulas loquor;
examples.translation: I have so far been speaking of the ordinary bathing-establishments;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: trembling, quaking, fearful, terrified, alarmed, timid, timorous (perhaps not in Cic.).

examples.original: Infert pavidos fuga in mediam caedem;
examples.translation: In their panic they fled into the middle of the carnage.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Terruerant satis haec pavidam praesagia plebem;
examples.translation: These forebodings were enough to alarm and terrify the populace;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ad omne fortuitum bonum suspiciosi pavidique subsistite;
examples.translation: Halt before every good which Chance brings to you, in a spirit of doubt and fear;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: transparent, clear (syn. tralucidus).

examples.original: Sed quae perspicua sunt longa esse non debent;
examples.translation: But there is really no need to labour what is self-evident;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Atqui hoc perspicuum est, vitia alia aliis esse maiora;
examples.translation: Now, that some vices are worse than others is certain;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Istiusmodi autem res dicere ornate velle puerile est, plane autem et perspicue expedire posse docti et intellegentis viri.”
examples.translation: A man of sense and education will be content to be able to express his meaning plainly and clearly.”
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to begin a web, to lay the warp; hence, also, in gen., to begin, undertake a thing

examples.original: Iam primum, ut ordiar ab ducibus comparandis, haud equidem abnuo egregium ducem fuisse Alexandrum;
examples.translation: First of all—to begin by comparing commanders—I do not deny that Alexander was a remarkable general;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed querellae, ne tum quidem gratae futurae cum forsitan necessariae erunt, ab initio certe tantae ordiendae rei absint;
examples.translation: But complaints are sure to be disagreeable, even when they shall perhaps be necessary; let the beginning, at all events, of so great an enterprise have none.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Atque ut a corpore ordiar, videsne ut si quae in membris prava aut debilitata aut imminuta sint occultent homines?
examples.translation: To start with the body, do you notice how men try to hide a deformed or infirm or maimed limb?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: of ill report, ill spoken of, disreputable, notorious, infamous (class.)

examples.original: Quid enim interest, utrum deos neges an infames?”
examples.translation: For what difference is there between denying the gods and dishonouring them?”
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis.
examples.translation: Read Cicero: his style has unity; it moves with a modulated pace, and is gentle without being degenerate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Minus avaritiae in Caecina, plus ambitionis: Valens ob lucra et quaestus infamis eoque alienae etiam culpae dissimulator.
examples.translation: Caecina was less avaricious, but more eager for popularity; Valens, notorious for his greed and sordid gains, was more inclined to overlook the crimes of others.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: marble.
Latin: massa vel fragmentum metamorphōsis calcis (ecce imago)
Latin: pulverizāta calx huiusmodi

examples.original: Tu modo Pompeia lentus spatiare sub umbra, Cum sol Herculei terga leonis adit: Aut ubi muneribus nati sua munera mater Addidit, externo marmore dives opus.
examples.translation: Only walk leisurely beneath the Pompeian shade, when the sun draws nigh to Hercules’ shaggy lion, or where the mother has added her own gifts to her son’s, a work rich with marble coating.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: beyond, besides, except, save (class.)

examples.original: Summoveri Laetorius iubet, praeterquam qui suffragium ineant.
examples.translation: Laetorius ordered the removal of all but those who were voting.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Et illa quidem nocte nihil praeterquam vigilatum est in urbe.
examples.translation: That night nothing more was done than to keep a watch in the City.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Atque ego hanc sententiam probarem (tantum apud me dignitas potest), si nullam praeterquam vitae nostrae iacturam fieri viderem: sed in consilio capiendo omnem Galliam respiciamus, quam ad nostrum auxilium concitavimus.
examples.translation: And yet I might now have approved this view (so much weight with me has the authority of those who hold it) if I saw therein the loss of nothing but our life;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: for what, wherefore, why.

examples.original: Quapropter neminem dubitare existimo quin illa damnatio ambitus nulla ex parte cum causa Cluenti vestroque iudicio coniuncta esse possit.
examples.translation: Wherefore I hold it indisputable that this conviction for corrupt practice can in no way be connected with the case of Cluentius, and the jurisdiction of your court.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a native of Corduba (in Hispania Baetica), a celebrated rhetorician in the time of Augustus and Tiberius, whose writings (Controversiae and Suasoriae) are now extant only in

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Agnosco Lucilium meum;
examples.translation: On Siren Songs Now I recognize my Lucilius!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ferunt Senecam proxima nocte visum sibi per quietem C. Caesari praecipere, et fidem somnio Nero brevi fecit prodita immanitate naturae quibus primum potuit experimentis.
examples.translation: They say that on the following night Seneca dreamed that he was teaching Gaius Caesar, and Nero soon proved the dream prophetic by revealing the cruelty of his disposition at the earliest possible opportunity.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Intellego, Lucili, non emendari me tantum sed transfigurari.
examples.translation: On Sharing Knowledge I feel, my dear Lucilius, that I am being not only reformed, but transformed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a dead body of man or brute, a corpse, carcass (class.).

examples.original: Quam tamen mihi ex illis mulierculis dabis vix retractis a rogo, vix a cadavere revulsis, cui lacrimae in totum mensem duraverint?
examples.translation: In the case of men, no rules are laid down, because to mourn at all is not regarded as honourable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam et signis insedit examen et adsuetae cadaverum pabulo volucres castra quasi iam sua circumvolabant, et in aciem prodeuntibus obvius Aethiops nimis aperte ferale signum fuit.
examples.translation: A swarm of bees settled on the standards; the birds which usually feed upon corpses flew round the camp, as though it were already their prey;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Cadaver eius clam in hortos Lamianos asportatum et tumultuario rogo semiambustum levi caespite obrutum est, postea per sorores ab exsilio reversas erutum et crematum sepultumque.
examples.translation: His body was conveyed secretly to the gardens of the Lamian family, where it was partly consumed on a hastily erected pyre and buried beneath a light covering of turf;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a small member connecting various parts of the body, a joint, knot, knuckle.

examples.original: Nam si est artius, ut ita dicam, holocleros, quid est quod dubitemus, quin per eosdem articulos et gradus producendus sit, per quos frater eius productus sit?
examples.translation: For if he be sound and so to say complete, what reason have we for doubting that he ought to be advanced through the same grades and steps through which his brother has been advanced?
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a., to come between, come upon, to come in during, to intervene, interrupt (class.; syn. intercedo).
Latin: (Intrans.) inter aliqua venīre
Latin: in media re venire

examples.original: Ac primo eatenus interveniebat, ne quid perperam fieret.
examples.translation: His intervention too was at first limited to the prevention of abuses.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Si quando intervenerunt epistulae tuae, tecum esse mihi videor et sic adficior animo, tamquam tibi non rescribam, sed respondeam.
examples.translation: Whenever your letters arrive, I imagine that I am with you, and I have the feeling that I am about to speak my answer, instead of writing it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to spread by pouring, to pour out, pour forth (very freq. and class.).

examples.original: Nec cruor emicuit solitus, sed volnere largo Diffusum rutilo dirum pro sanguine virus.
examples.translation: No red blood spouted forth from the gaping wound, but a slimy liquid, strange and dreadful, came out instead.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a Roman family name in the gens Aurelia

examples.original: Cotta se ad armatum hostem iturum negat atque in eo perseverat.
examples.translation: Cotta refused to go to an armed enemy, and persisted in the refusal.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Eis militibus Quintum Titurium Sabinum et Lucium Aurunculeium Cottam legatos praeesse iussit.
examples.translation: He ordered Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta, lieutenant-generals, to command those detachments.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ibi Lucius Cotta pugnans interficitur cum maxima parte militum.
examples.translation: There Lucius Cotta was killed fighting, with the greatest part of the troops.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a way of thinking befitting a freeman; a noble, kind, or friendly disposition, noble spirit, kindness, affability.

examples.original: Auxit hoc officium alia quoque liberalitate;
examples.translation: He added to this service still another act of generosity;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Falluntur quibus luxuria specie liberalitatis imponit: perdere iste sciet, donare nesciet.
examples.translation: They are deceived who are imposed upon by extravagance under the garb of generosity.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Illud unum intellegi volumus, illius liberalitatem neque temporariam neque callidam fuisse.
examples.translation: This one thing I wish to make clear, that his generosity was neither time-serving nor calculated.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

definitions: English: A bride, a mistress

examples.original: Hunc non ruricolae Panes nemorumque potentes Silvani Nymphaeque tenent, sed barbara ritu Sacra deum;
examples.translation: No rural Pan dwelt there, no Silvanus, ruler of the woods, no Nymphs;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: swollen, swelling, rising high, protuberant, tumid (class.).

examples.original: Hinc aemulatio ducibus: Caecina ut foedum ac maculosum, ille ut tumidum ac vanum inridebant.
examples.translation: This caused rivalry between the generals. Caecina made sport of Valens as a shameful and disgraceful character;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: an œdile, a magistrate in Rome who had the superintendence of public buildings and works, such as temples, theatres, baths, aqueducts, sewers, highways
Latin: Genus apparitoris Romani

examples.original: Catonem tibi aedilem aut Fabium Maximum aut ex Corneliis aliquem manu sua temperasse?
examples.translation: Epistle LXXXVI. as aedile, or Fabius Maximus, or one of the Cornelii, has warmed the water with his own hands!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Eo anno plerisque dies dicta ab aedilibus, quia plus quam quod lege finitum erat agri possiderent;
examples.translation: In that year many men were prosecuted by the aediles on the charge of possessing more land than the law allowed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eodem anno Cn. Flavius Cn. filius scriba, patre libertino humili fortuna ortus, ceterum callidus vir et facundus, aedilis curulis fuit.
examples.translation: In the same year a government clerk, Gnaeus Flavius, the son of Gnaeus, was curule aedile.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a Roman family name in the gens Sempronia

examples.original: Ti. Gracchus regnum occupare conatus est, vel regnavit is quidem paucos menses.
examples.translation: Tiberius Gracchus tried to obtain regal power—or rather, he actually did reign for a few months.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the name of a Roman gens.

examples.original: Aemilius inde et C. Servilius consules facti.
examples.translation: Lucius Aemilius and Gaius Servilius were then chosen consuls.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Fama fuit quosdam ex Fidenatium iuventute participes eius populationis fuisse, cognitioque eius rei L. Sergio et Q. Servilio et Mam. Aemilio permissa.
examples.translation: It was rumoured that certain young men of Fidenae had shared in the pillaging. The investigation of this report was intrusted to Lucius Sergius, Quintus Servilius, and Mamercus Aemilius;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tandem invisi plebi consules magistratu abeunt, Servilius neutris, Appius patribus mire gratus.
examples.translation: Servilius had the goodwill of neither party, but Appius was in high esteem with the senators.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a throwing down, throwing to the ground, overthrowing; an overthrow; confusion, confused heap or mass

examples.original: Pedes restantes ac circumventos cecidit: ab equite fugientium strages est facta, inter quos et ipse imperator cecidit.
examples.translation: The foot-soldiers surrounded those who resisted and put them to the sword; the cavalry made havoc of the fugitives, amongst whom perished their general himself.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus concedi corpora sepulturae cremarique permisit.
examples.translation: He was then carried through the heaps of dead bodies, while the forum still reeked with blood, first to the Capitol and then to the Palatine;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Mors tamen eminuit clarorum in strage virorum Pugnacis Domiti, quem clades fata per omnes Ducebant: nusquam Magni fortuna sine illo Succubuit.
examples.translation: Yet one death was most noticeable in that carnage of famous men—the death of that stubborn warrior, Domitius. Fate led him from defeat to defeat;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: bloody, bleeding, trickling with blood, etc.
English: to move, prevail upon, persuade by entreaty; to gain or obtain by entreaty (class.): quem ego, ut mentiatur, inducere possum

examples.original: Proximus huic labor est placitam exorare puellam: Tertius, ut longo tempore duret amor.
examples.translation: The next task is, to win the girl that takes your fancy; the third, to make love long endure.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a town, particularly in Italy, which possessed the right of Roman citizenship (together with, in most cases, the right of voting), but was governed by its own laws
Latin: Oppidum iure suo utens et legibus, cuius incolae iure civium Romanorum gaudebant

examples.original: Exceptus est Caesaris adventus ab omnibus municipiis et coloniis incredibili honore atque amore.
examples.translation: The arrival of Caesar was welcomed by all the boroughs and colonies with honour and affection beyond all belief;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Summa est enim, iudices, hominis in communem municipii rem diligentia, in singulos municipes benignitas, in omnes homines iustitia et fides.
examples.translation: For nothing, gentlemen, can exceed my client’s devotion to the general good of his town, his kindness to its individual members, his uprightness and sincerity to all men.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Fulcinius fuit, recuperatores, e municipio Tarquiniensi, qui et domi suae cum primis honestus existimatus est, et Romae argentariam non ignobilem fecit.
examples.translation: There was one M. Fulcinius, gentlemen, a native of Tarquinii, who in his native place enjoyed an eminently honourable reputation and at Rome had a considerable business as a banker.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: That lasts a year or continues through a year, of a year's duration
Latin: Unum annum permanens
Latin: Quotannis accidens

examples.original: Veientes contra taedio annuae ambitionis, quae interdum discordiarum causa erat, regem creavere.
examples.translation: But the Veientes, weary of annual canvassing, which was sometimes the cause of brawls, chose a king.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: An si ad calculos eum res publica vocet, non merito dicat: ’annua aera habes, annuam operam ede;
examples.translation: Why, if the commonwealth should call him to a reckoning, would it not justly say, ’You have a year’s stipend, render a year’s service;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Liberi iam hinc populi Romani res pace belloque gestas, annuos magistratus, imperiaque legum potentiora quam hominum peragam.
examples.translation: This liberty was the more grateful as the last king had been so great a tyrant.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a boundary-line, boundary, bound, limit (syn.: finis, limes, meta).
Latin: Finis, limes
Latin: Lapis ad finem agri, qui agri finem designat

examples.original: Nullus enim terminus falso est.
examples.translation: The false has no limits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ille enim habet suum finem, inania et ex libidine orta sine termino sunt.
examples.translation: For this has its bounds, but waywardness and the acts that spring from wilful lust are without boundaries.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In eam demissus es vitam, quae numquam tibi terminum miseriarum ac servitutis ipsa factura sit.
examples.translation: You have been thrust into an existence which will never of itself put an end to your wretchedness and your slavery.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to tread something or upon something, to tread under foot.

examples.original: Quis calcare tuas metuat, salpuga, latebras?
examples.translation: Who would fear to tread on the lair of the salpuga?
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: lightly/gently/softly/quietly/mildly/slightly; groundlessly/thoughtlessly

examples.original: Nam qui leviter dormit, et species secundum quietem capit et aliquando dormire se dormiens cogitat;
examples.translation: For he whose sleep is light pursues visions during slumber, and sometimes, though asleep, is conscious that he is asleep;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Persius Lives of Illustrious Men ut quasi finitus esset. Leviter correxit Cornutus et Caesio Basso petenti, ut ipse ederet, tradidit edendum.
examples.translation: Cornutus made some slight corrections, and on the request of Caesius Bassus that he might publish it, turned it over to him for that purpose.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: to draw apart; to part, split, separate, sever, sunder, divide (class.).

examples.original: Hispana tibi Germanaque Tethys paruit et nostro diducta Britannia mundo, diversoque tuas coluerunt gurgite voces lentus Arar Rhodanusque ferox et dives Hiberus.
examples.translation: The seas of Spain, the German ocean obeyed thee and Britain, so far removed from our continent. Rivers of all lands observed thy statutes, slow-flowing Saône, swift Rhone, and Ebro rich in gold.
examples.author: Claudian
examples.work: Panegyric On The Consulship Of Fl. Manlius Theodorus (A.D. 399)

definitions: English: of long duration, lasting, long

examples.original: Minus insignis, quia non diuturna, mutatio fuit.
examples.translation: It was not so remarkable a change, because it did not last long.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec Alcibiadi laetitia non nimis fuit diuturna.
examples.translation: But this joy of Alcibiades was of none too long duration.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Alcibiades

definitions: English: an inquiry of the people as to whether they will decree this or that, a proposal to the people for passing a law or decree, a proposed law or decree, a bill

examples.original: Postquam rogationis dies aderat, ingenti stipatus agmine rostra conscendit, nec deerat obvia manu tota inde nobilitas;
examples.translation: When the day for bringing forward the bill was at hand, he ascended the rostra surrounded by a large following;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ergo si esset libera haec civitas, non tibi frequentes succlamassent, ’abi hinc cum tribunatibus ac rogationibus tuis!’ Quid?
examples.translation: If you will not propose what is profitable to the people to accept, shall there be none to do it?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Oratio Appi ad id modo valuit ut tempus rogationum iubendarum proferretur. Refecti decumum iidem tribuni, Sextius et Licinius, de decemviris sacrorum ex parte de plebe creandis legem pertulere.
examples.translation: Returned for the tenth time to office, the tribunes Sextius and Licinius obtained the enactment of a law requiring that half the board of ten who had charge of sacred rites should be plebeians.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Germany
Latin: Natio Germanorum, in Europa centrali

examples.original: Sed insidiatores ab Othone in Germaniam, a Vitellio in urbem missi.
examples.translation: Otho sent secret agents to Germany, and Vitellius sent his agents to Rome.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: At tibi ius veniae superest, Germania, nullum: Postmodo tu poenas, barbare, morte dabis.
examples.translation: But for thee, Germania, no right of pardon remains; thou shalt atone hereafter, barbarian, by thy death.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Caesar Quoniam ad hunc locum perventum est, non alienum esse videtur de Galliae Germaniaeque moribus et quo differant hae nationes inter sese proponere.
examples.translation: Since I have arrived at this point, it would seem to be not inappropriate to set forth the customs of Gaul and of Germany, and the difference between these nations.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: that is taught wisdom by experience and practice, shrewd, expert, experienced, adroit, skilful

examples.original: Illud unum intellegi volumus, illius liberalitatem neque temporariam neque callidam fuisse.
examples.translation: This one thing I wish to make clear, that his generosity was neither time-serving nor calculated.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Hic tamen tam callidus vir extremo tempore captus est Mithridatis, Ariobarzanis filii, dolo.
examples.translation: Yet this man, cunning as he was, finally fell victim to the craft of Mithridates, the son of Ario-barzanes;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: At ille post non multo sua sponte ad exercitum rediit et ibi non callida, sed dementi ratione cogitata patefecit;
examples.translation: But not long afterwards Pausanias returned to the army on his own account, and there he revealed his designs in a manner that was rather insane than adroit.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Pausanias

definitions: English: to come forth, appear (not in Cic.; syn. appareo).
English: defilement, dishonor, disgrace.

examples.original: Ecquo in oppido pedem posuit ubi non plura stuprorum flagitiorumque suorum quam adventus sui vestigia reliquerit? Sed ego omnia quae negari poterunt praetermittam;
examples.translation: Is there one town in which he set foot where the traces left by his arriving feet are not outnumbered by those of his adulteries and criminal assaults?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a cross-path, balk between fields.
Latin: Via ad finem fundi vel terrae
Latin: Finis imperii

examples.original: Per limitem viae sparguntur festinatione consectandi victores.
examples.translation: The victorious troops in their hasty pursuit were strung out along the sides of the road.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Limes erat tenuis longa subnubilus umbra, Quo tulit illa suos ad mare saepe pedes.
examples.translation: There was a narrow way o’er-cast by the long shadows, by which she oft betook herself to the sea.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nulli subigebant arva coloni, Ne signare quidem aut partiri limite campum Fas erat;
examples.translation: No ploughman tilled the soil, nor was it right To portion off or bound one’s property.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: quiet, calm, still, tranquil, opp. to motion or excitement (syn. serenus).

examples.original: Honestum omne securum est, tranquillum est;
examples.translation: The honourable is wholly free from anxiety and is calm;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Is armata iuventute dispositisque praesidiis tuta omnia ac tranquilla fecit.
examples.translation: Arming the young men and disposing his defences, he made everything secure and tranquil.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Atqui pugnantibus et contrariis studiis consiliisque semper utens nihil quieti videre, nihil tranquilli potest.
examples.translation: But one who is perpetually swayed by conflicting and incompatible counsels and desires can know no peace or calm.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: two hundred each, two hundred

examples.original: Nobis quadringentae amplius naves, ducentae minus hostium;
examples.translation: We had more than four hundred ships, the enemy less than two hundred;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Legionem Caesar, quam equis devexerat, passibus ducentis ab eo tumulo constituit.
examples.translation: Caesar stationed the legion which he had brought on horseback two hundred paces from the mound.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesa ibi milia hominum duo ferme atque octingenti, capta quattuor milia ducenti septuaginta.
examples.translation: There about two thousand eight hundred men were slain and four thousand two hundred and seventy made prisoners.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bring into a state of peace and quietness, to make peaceful, to quiet, pacify, subdue, soothe (class.; cf.: pacifico, placo).
Latin: Tranquillāre, pācātum reddere
Latin: Pacī restituere, quiētum reddere bellum et turbās sedando

examples.original: Bellvm Civile Caesaris et Pompei IIII, 2Iam toto orbe paene pacato maius erat imperium Romanum, quam ut ullis exteris viribus opprimi posset.
examples.translation: The Civil War between Caesar and Pompeius 2. Almost the whole world having been now subjugated, the Roman Empire was too strong to be overcome by any foreign power.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Gregarius miles futuri socors et ignobilitate tutior perstabat: vagi per vias, in domibus abditi pacem ne tum quidem orabant, cum bellum posuissent.
examples.translation: They wandered through the streets or concealed themselves in houses, but did not beg for peace even when they had given up fighting.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Iussi cum coniugibus ac liberis supplicatum ire pacemque exposcere deum, ad id quod sua quemque mala cogebant auctoritate publica evocati omnia delubra implent.
examples.translation: Thus summoned by the state’s authority to do what each was impelled to by his own distress, they crowded all the shrines.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: at leisure, unoccupied, disengaged, unemployed, idle (class.; cf. feriatus, immunis; opp. negotiosus).

examples.original: Ego vero non gravarer, si mihi ipse confiderem, nam et praeclara res est et sumus, ut dixit Fannius, otiosi.
examples.translation: I certainly should raise no objection if I felt confidence in myself, for the subject is a noble one, and we are, as Fannius said, free from public business.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Otiosum enim hominem seductum existimat vulgus et securum et se contentum, sibi viventem, quorum nihil ulli contingere nisi sapienti potest.
