examples.original: Sed tamen est artis tristissima ianua nostrae, Et labor est unus tempora prima pati.
examples.translation: Yet the gateway of my art is the severest trial, and your only labour will be to endure the first beginning.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Conversus ad ianuam ”Quis est iste?” inquam, ”iste decrepitus et merito ad ostium admotus?
examples.translation: You have done well to place him at the entrance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Si tibi per tutum planumque negabitur ire, Atque erit opposita ianua fulta sera, At tu per praeceps tecto delabere aperto: Det quoque furtivas alta fenestra vias.
examples.translation: If it is denied you to go by a safe and easy road, and if the door be held by a fastened bolt, yet slip down headlong through an opening in the roof;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a long, Carey, Lat. Pros. § 47: āriĕtis, Enn. ap.
Latin: Ovis mas
Latin: A~ (astronomia) Quoddam sidus. ( ♈)
English: to weave (class.; syn. neo).

examples.original: Ostendit terras Titan et sidera texit.
examples.translation: The sun revealed the earth and veiled the stars.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Stagna avidi texere soli laxaeque paludes Depositum, Fortuna, tuum;
examples.translation: Engulfing quicksands and spongy marshes hid the secret that Fortune had placed there;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a scar, cicatrice (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Vulnus in antiquum rediit male firma cicatrix, Successumque artes non habuere meae.
examples.translation: The scar ill-healed relapsed to the old wound, and my arts sustained defeat.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to frequent, make busy: omnes istae artes, quibus aut circitatur civitas aut strepit.

examples.original: Hic locus ab hoste circiter passus sescentos, uti dictum est, aberat.
examples.translation: The spot, as has been said, was about six hundred paces away from the enemy.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Tandem vulneribus defessi et pedem referre et, quod mons suberat circiter mille passuum, eo se recipere coeperunt.
examples.translation: At length, worn out with wounds, they began to retreat, retiring towards a height about a mile away. They gained the height;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Eo circiter hominum numero sedecim milia expedita cum omni equitatu Ariovistus misit, quae copiae nostros perterrerent et munitione prohiberent.
examples.translation: Towards it Ariovistus sent some sixteen thousand light-armed troops with all the horse, as a force to frighten our men and to prevent their entrenching work.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: hurt, harm, damage, injury, loss; opp. to lucrum (syn. jactura, detrimentum, incommodum, dispendium. Freq. and class.).

examples.original: Quod istic credulitatis tuae damnum est?
examples.translation: And what harm does it do to you to give such credence?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam famae quidem ac fidei damna maiora esse quam quae aestimari possent.
examples.translation: For reputation at least and trustworthiness were things the loss of which was beyond all reckoning.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tempus erat, quo Libra pares examinat horas, Non uno plus aequa die, noctique rependit Lux minor hibernae verni solacia damni.
examples.translation: It was the season when Libra balances the hours of day and night in equal scales, and stays level for one day only;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a wood, grove, or thicket of trees sacred to a deity.

examples.original: Luce prima inermos plerosque oppressere.
examples.translation: At daybreak they cut down many of them quite unarmed.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Lucis vobis huius partem, si liceat, adimant;
examples.translation: They would take from you, were it possible, a part of this daylight.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Erat in proximo lucus; hunc asylum facit, et statim mira vis hominum;
examples.translation: There was in the neighbourhood a grove, and this he made a place of refuge;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a. [gratus].

examples.original: Gratulatus sum protinus mihi et dixi: ”Non a summis labris ista venerunt, habent hae voces fundamentum.
examples.translation: I immediately congratulated myself and said: ”These words did not come from the edge of the lips; these utterances have a solid foundation.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: fixed or appointed by law, according to law, lawful, legal, legitimate.
Latin: Conveniens cum legibus

examples.original: Consumetur, inquies. Scilicet exspectemus legitimum illud quinquennium;
examples.translation: It will be so spent, you will answer.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ceterum id quoque ad gloriam accessit quod cum illo simul iusta ac legitima regna occiderunt.
examples.translation: But there was this to enhance his renown, that just and lawful kingship perished with him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quum de iure et legitimis hominum controversiis loquimur, et in his rebus vim nominamus, pertenuis vis intelligi debet.
examples.translation: When we are speaking of rights and disputes at law and in that connexion use the word ”force,” a very slight degree of force should be understood.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to take away entirely, to annihilate, extinguish, destroy; to cut off, hinder, prevent.

examples.original: Sed non vaesana Pothini Mens inbuta semel sacra iam caede vacabat A scelerum motu: Magno nihil ille perempto Iam putat esse nefas;
examples.translation: But the frenzied bosom of Pothinus, once stained with sacrilegious murder, was never again free from guilty excitement: after the slaughter of Magnus he no longer counts any deed a crime;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To write back or in return, to reply in writing (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Rescriptae ex eodem milite novae legiones ductusque ad Caudium exercitus.
examples.translation: The same soldiers were enrolled into new legions, and the army marched on Caudium.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Si quando intervenerunt epistulae tuae, tecum esse mihi videor et sic adficior animo, tamquam tibi non rescribam, sed respondeam.
examples.translation: Whenever your letters arrive, I imagine that I am with you, and I have the feeling that I am about to speak my answer, instead of writing it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam mihi non facit fidem tam multorum onerum, quae aliquando numeraveram, tam repentina depositio, quamvis te accepisse litteras meas non dubitem, quarum rescripta non habeo.
examples.translation: I can hardly believe I have so speedily discharged tasks I had once reckoned so numerous. Yet I am sure you must have had letters from me, to which I have received no answers.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to drive, bring, or take a person or thing to a place (syn.: appello, adduco, affero).—Constr. usu. with

examples.original: Maturo ceterisque remanere et in verba Vespasiani adigi volentibus fuit.
examples.translation: Maturus and the rest chose to remain and take the oath of fidelity to Vespasian.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hic ubi quaerentes socios iam Marte relicto Tuta fugae cernit, ”Quo vos pavor,” inquit ”adegit Inpius et cunctis ignotus Caesaris armis?
examples.translation: When he saw his comrades drop their arms and seek safety in flight, ”Whither,” he cried, ”has fear driven you—disloyal fear that no soldier of Caesar’s has ever felt?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Admovebatur altaribus magis ut victima quam ut sacri particeps adigebaturque iure iurando quae visa auditaque in eo loco essent, non enuntiaturum.
examples.translation: The man was brought up to the altar, more like a victim than a partaker in the rite, and was sworn not to divulge what he should there see or hear.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a. [epulum], to hold an entertainment, to feast, banquet.

examples.original: Discubuerat Vitellius Ticini adhibito ad epulas Verginio.
examples.translation: The emperor was dining at Ticinum, and Verginius was his guest.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Negat enim tenuissimo victu, id est contemptissimis escis et potionibus, minorem voluptatem percipi quam rebus exquisitissimis ad epulandum.
examples.translation: He tells us that the simplest fare, that is, the meanest sorts of food and drink, afford no less pleasure than a banquet of the rarest delicacies.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: full of confusion or disorder, wild, confused, disordered (class.; cf.: agitatus, tumultuosus).

examples.original: Sanguine Romano quam turbidus ibit Enipeus!
examples.translation: How dark the Enipeus will flow with Roman blood!
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Num quid tam turbidum fieri potest quam forum?
examples.translation: Yet you can live quietly even there, if necessary.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec illud nego, ad ea, quae videntur secundum naturam, magnos esse mutis animalibus impetus et concitatos, sed inordinatos ac turbidos.
examples.translation: I do not indeed deny that dumb animals have strong and swift impulses toward actions which seem according to nature, but such impulses are confused and disordered.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to diversify, variegate, change (class.).

examples.original: Nam quoniam variant animi, variabimus artes;
examples.translation: For since natures vary, I will vary my arts;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nec variatum comitiis est, quin cum Manlio Naevio censor Marcius crearetur.
examples.translation: There was no dissenting opinion shown at the assembly, and Marcius was elected, along with Manlius Naevius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Corpore et statura fuit grandi, aquilo colore, facie rusticana, valetudine varia;
examples.translation: He was tall and of full habit, with a dark complexion and a rustic appearance.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: The sexual organs

examples.original: Laudis in hoc sexu non legum cura nec arma, Unica materia est coniunx miser.
examples.translation: To your sex neither peaceful government nor war is a field for glory: a husband’s sorrow alone can win it.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to seize, take, or catch at eagerly, to snatch at, lay hold of

examples.original: Orare eum collegamque ut capesserent rem publicam;
examples.translation: They begged him and his colleague to undertake the guidance of the state;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tum ad equites dictator advolat obtestans ut fesso iam pedite descendant ex equis et pugnam capessant.
examples.translation: The dictator then dashed up to the knights and besought them, since the foot-soldiers were exhausted, to dismount and enter the fight.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a thorn.

examples.original: O flores non plane fructuum sed spinarum!
examples.translation: Flowers indeed, but promising thorns, certainly not fruit!
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Hos ego, qui canent, frutices violaria vidi: Hac mihi de spina grata corona data est.
examples.translation: These plants, now withering, I saw as violet-beds; from this thorn was a pleasing garland given me.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: having no part in, not sharing in, not privy to.

examples.original: Experti in vicem sumus ego ac fortuna.
examples.translation: Do not reckon up the short duration of my rule;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Libidinis in feminas profusissimae, marum omnino expers.
examples.translation: He was immoderate in his passion for women, but wholly disinterested in male partners.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Serpit enim nescio quo modo per omnium vitas amicitia nec ullam aetatis degendae rationem patitur esse expertem sui.
examples.translation: For it creeps imperceptibly, I know not how, into every life, and suffers no mode of existence to be devoid of its presence.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: from that place, thence.

examples.original: Tunc inter primores duorum populorum res geritur; quidquid hinc aut illinc communis Mars belli aufert, multiplex quam pro numero damnum est.
examples.translation: The struggle then lay between the best men of both nations, and whatever losses the chance of war inflicted on either side were serious out of all proportion to their number.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Numquam ullo loco tantum virium populi Romani, tantum dignitatis Fortuna respexit: trecenta amplius milia hinc vel illinc praeter auxilia, reges et senatum.
examples.translation: Never did Fortune see so much of the might and dignity of the Roman people collected in one place;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Non dicam illinc hoc signum ablatum esse et illud: hoc dico, nullum te Aspendi signum, Verres, reliquisse, omnia ex fanis, ex locis publicis, palam, spectantibus omnibus, plaustris evecta exportataque esse.
examples.translation: I shall not allege that from this town this or that particular statue was removed. My charge is that Verres did not leave one single statue behind;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: of or belonging to Janus.—Esp.
Latin: Qui ad Ianum pertinet
Latin: Qui ad mensis Ianuarius pertinet

examples.original: Kal. Ian. in villa colli superposita prope Tarracinam sinistrorsus Fundos petentibus, adoptatusque a noverca sua Livia nomen et Ocellare cognomen assumpsit mutato praenomine;
examples.translation: Adopted by his stepmother Livia, he took her name and the surname Ocella, and also changed his forename;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: moderateness, moderation; esp. in one's behavior, unassuming conduct, modesty (opp. immodestia, superbia, licentia; class.).

examples.original: Exanimati omnes tam atroci imperio nec aliter quam in se quisque destrictam cernentes securem, metu magis quam modestia quievere.
examples.translation: All were astounded at so shocking a command; every man looked upon the axe as lifted against himself, and they were hushed with fear more than with reverence.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed Pacensis per licentiam militum vinctus, Antonio Novello nulla auctoritas: Suedius Clemens ambitioso imperio regebat, ut adversus modestiam disciplinae corruptus, ita proeliorum avidus.
examples.translation: Antonius Novellus had no authority; and Suedius Clemens used his office to secure popularity, being as reckless toward maintaining discipline as he was eager to fight.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quo pacto plerosque modestia et pudore deterruit, in quibus Hortalum, Quinti Hortensi oratoris nepotem, qui permodica re familiari auctore Augusto quattuor liberos tulerat.
examples.translation: Therefore diffidence and a sense of shame kept many from applying, among them Hortalus, grandson of Quintus Hortensius the orator, who though of very limited means had begotten four children with the encouragement of Augustus.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to hold out, extend, present, produce, bestow, grant, give, afford; to attribute, ascribe, assign, etc.

examples.original: In his erat sanctus David, cui dominus tam magnum perhibuit testimonium; in his etiam plurimi illius temporis iusti;
examples.translation: Among such was the holy David, to whom the Lord gave so great a testimony, and among such were also many righteous men.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: The highest part of a chain of mountains, a mountain-ridge
English: long, extensive.

examples.original: Sed quid ego longinqua commemoro?
examples.translation: But why do I remind you of events in distant places?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Video enim et magnos et eosdem bene longinquos dolores;
examples.translation: For I see pains that are at once severe and considerably prolonged;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Feliciorem ergo tu Maecenatem putas, cui amoribus anxio et morosae uxoris cotidiana repudia deflenti somnus per symphoniarum cantum ex longinquo lene resonantium quaeritur?
examples.translation: Do you, then, think Maecenas a happier man, who, distressed by love and grieving over the daily repulses of his wayward wife, courted slumber by means of harmonious music, echoing faintly from a distance?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the first place, pre-eminence, preference (class.).
Latin: Status principis

examples.original: In principatu maturius semper ac de nocte vigilabat;
examples.translation: While emperor, he always rose very early, in fact before daylight;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Cingetorigi, quem ab initio permansisse in officio demonstravimus, principatus atque imperium est traditum.
examples.translation: The prerogative of chieftaincy was delivered to Cingetorix, who, as we have shown, had remained loyal from the beginning.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Deinde orta dissensio est inter eum et Heraclidem, qui, quod ei principatum non concedebat, factionem comparavit.
examples.translation: Next, dissension arose between him and Heraclides, who, unwilling to yield the first place to Dion, formed a party against him.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Dion

definitions: English: Dark-colored, blackish-gray, dusky, blackish
Latin: Color similis nigro colori

examples.original: Ex his Pullo, cum acerrime ad munitiones pugnaretur, ”Quid dubitas,” inquit, ”Vorene?
examples.translation: One of them, Pullo, when the fight was fiercest by the entrenchments, said: ”Why hesitate, Vorenus?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Erant in ea legione fortissimi viri, centuriones, qui primis ordinibus appropinquarent, Titus Pullo et Lucius Vorenus.
examples.translation: In that legion there were two most gallant centurions, now not far from the first class of their rank, Titus Pullo and Lucius Vorenus.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Huic rursus circumvento fert subsidium Pullo, atque ambo incolumes compluribus interfectis summa cum laude sese intra munitiones recipiunt.
examples.translation: He was surrounded in his turn, but Pullo brought assistance; and both, unhurt, though they had slain several men, retired with the utmost glory within the entrenchments.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to differ in sentiment, to dissent, disagree (freq. and class.).—Constr. usually

examples.original: Hic quoque suus est, de summoque bono dissentiens dici vere Peripateticus non potest.
examples.translation: He too stands by himself; differing about the Chief Good he cannot correctly be called a Peripatetic.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: In illo quoque dissentio a Posidonio, quod ferramenta fabrilia excogitata a sapientibus viris iudicat.
examples.translation: On another point also I differ from Posidonius, when he holds that mechanical tools were the invention of wise men.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Observa te itaque, numquid vestis tua domusque dissentiant, numquid in te liberalis sis, in tuos sordidus, numquid cenes frugaliter, aedifices luxuriose.
examples.translation: Observe yourself, then, and see whether your dress and your house are inconsistent, whether you treat yourself lavishly and your family meanly, whether you eat frugal dinners and yet build luxurious houses.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to give out tidings, a notice, etc.; hence, to affirm, declare, announce any thing (cf. de in denuncio and depromo).

examples.original: Aedes Mercuri dedicata est idibus Maiis.
examples.translation: The temple of Mercury was consecrated on the fifteenth of May.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Valerius Horatiusque consules sortiti uter dedicaret.
examples.translation: Valerius and Horatius the consuls drew lots to determine which should do it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Herculis magnum simulacrum in Capitolio positum dedicatumque.
examples.translation: The great statue of Hercules was set up and dedicated on the Capitol.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to demand any thing fiercely or violently, to entreat, solicit a thing; or, with a personal object, to press earnestly

examples.original: Etiam atque etiam insto atque urgeo, insector, posco, atque adeo flagito crimen;
examples.translation: I demand that you shall produce your charges; nay, I importune you for them.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Equites Romani obtulere operam pecuniasque, etiam libertinis idem munus ultro flagitantibus.
examples.translation: This pretended devotion, which was in reality prompted by fear, resulted in enthusiasm for the emperor;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hunc iuvenem Galba, quaestorem in Baetica impigre in partis suas transgressum, legioni praeposuit: mox compertum publicam pecuniam avertisse ut peculatorem flagitari iussit.
examples.translation: This youth Galba had put in command of a legion, for when he was quaestor in Baetica, he had not hesitated to join Galba’s party.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: countless, innumerable, numberless.

examples.original: Artibus innumeris mens oppugnatur amantum, Ut lapis aequoreis undique pulsus aquis.
examples.translation: By innumerable arts are lovers’ feelings assailed, as the rock is beaten by waves on every side.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to write in or upon any thing, to inscribe (class.).

examples.original: Fecit et novum genus togatarum inscripsitque trabeatas.
examples.translation: He likewise originated a new kind of togatae, to which he gave the name of trabeatae.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Ut quondam iuvenes, ita nunc, mea turba, puellae Inscribant spoliis ”Naso magister erat.”
examples.translation: As once the youths, so now let the women, my votaries, write upon their spoils, Naso was our master.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nam si ad naturam rerum respexeris, etiam Nestoris et Sattiae brevis est, quae inscribi monumento suo iussit annis se nonaginta novem vixisse.
examples.translation: Compared with the world of nature, even Nestor’s life was a short one, or Sattia’s,a the woman who bade carve on her tombstone that she had lived ninety and nine years.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the marrow of bones; the pith of plants (class.).
English: usefully/profitably/to advantage; interestedly; validly/effectively/practically

examples.original: Non avis utiliter viscatis effugit alis;
examples.translation: The bird cannot make good its escape when once its wings are limed;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to flee before or from, to flee

examples.original: Itaque illa nocte Syracusis profugit.
examples.translation: That night, accordingly, he fled from Syracuse.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Omnia experti Galli, quod res nulla successerat, postero die consilium ceperunt ex oppido profugere hortante et iubente Vercingetorige.
examples.translation: The Gauls had tried every expedient, and as nothing had succeeded they resolved next day to escape from the town, as Vercingetorix urged and ordered.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ob eam causam cum dictator de magistro equitum supplicium sumpturus videretur, Fabius Romam profugit, et cum parum causa proficeret, populi precibus donatus est.
examples.translation: For this reason it appeared that the dictator would punish the master of the horse; but Fabius fled to Rome, and though his cause was weak, was begged off by the people.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a dolt, simpleton, blockhead
English: a. [id.], to trade, traffic, deal in commodities
Latin: vendere atque emere

examples.original: Aut merces hodie bellorum aut poena parata.
examples.translation: To-day either the reward or the penalty of war is before us.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Postulo ut mihi respondeat qui sit is Verrucius, mercator an negotiator an arator an pecuarius, in Sicilia sit an iam decesserit.
examples.translation: I demanded therefore that Carpinatius should tell me who this Verrucius was, merchant or banker or arable or pastoral farmer, and whether he was still in Sicily or had gone away.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ab isto et praeco qui voluit istum ordinem pretio mercatus est, et pueri annorum senum septenumque denum senatorium nomen nundinati sunt;
examples.translation: Verres was bribed to sell the title to an auctioneer who wanted it; from Verres boys of sixteen and seventeen purchased the rank of senator.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to sit back, remain sitting anywhere (cf. resisto); to remain behind, to remain, rest, linger, tarry, abide, reside (syn. remaneo; class.).

examples.original: Quorum non in sententia solum, sed etiam in nutu residebat auctoritas.
examples.translation: These men had power, not only in their speech, but in their very nod.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to declare or set apart as sacred; to consecrate, dedicate, or

examples.original: Tractentur volnera nulla Sacra manu.
examples.translation: No other hand should meddle with the wounds of gods.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Nunc neque te longi remeantem pompa triumphi Excipit, aut sacras poscunt Capitolia laurus;
examples.translation: As it is, no long triumphal procession awaits your return, nor does the Capitol demand your consecrated laurels;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Pars ”Hymenaee” canunt, pars clamant ”Euhion, euhoe!” Sic coeunt sacro nupta deusque toro.
examples.translation: Some chant ”Hail, Hymenaeus!” some shout ”Euhoe, Euhion !” So do the bride and the god meet on the sacred couch.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: bitter (syn. acerbus).
Latin: Acerbus; sapore absinthii vel quininae

examples.original: Naso legendus erat tum, cum didicistis amare: Idem nunc vobis Naso legendus erit.
examples.translation: You should have read Naso then when you learnt to love: you should read the same Naso now.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Itaque minime amarus eis visus est, qui aliquid ex eius sermone speculae degustarant. Unus et alter dies intercesserat, cum res parum certa videbatur: sequester et confirmator pecuniae desiderabatur.
examples.translation: A day or two passed, and the scheme was looking far from safe: a need was felt of a depository and a security for the money.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quid autem est amare, e quo nomen ductum amicitiae est, nisi velle bonis aliquem affici quam maximis etiamsi ad se ex iis nihil redundet ?
examples.translation: What is the meaning of ’to love’—from which our word for friendship is derived—except to wish some one to receive the greatest possible benefits even though one gleans no advantage therefrom oneself?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: desire, wish, longing, eagerness, in a good and (more usu.) in a bad sense (very freq. in the poets and histt., esp. in Sall.; twice in Quint., but in Cic. only as personified).
Latin: Desideratio naturalis quae ab fruitione vel cogitiatione alicuius excitatur, et quae ad aliquem agere vel studere impellit ut continere vel habere

examples.original: Facile est auditorem concitare ad cupidinem recti;
examples.translation: It is easy to rouse a listener so that he will crave righteousness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Patrum interim animos certamen regni ac cupido versabat.
examples.translation: The senators meanwhile were engaged in a struggle for the coveted kingship.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed profusa cupidine et insigni temeritate legati legionum Alienus Caecina et Fabius Valens;
examples.translation: But the commanders of the legions, Alienus Caecina and Fabius Valens, were men of boundless greed and extraordinary recklessness.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to call or cry aloud, to call or
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Etiam si exclamaveritis, non aliter audiam, quam si ad tactum vitiorum vestrorum ingemescatis.
examples.translation: Do you wish to bear witness that you are attentive, that you are stirred by the grandeur of the subject?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: inactive, lazy, slothful, idle, sluggish, listless, without spirit, cowardly, dastardly (syn.: iners, socors; opp.: strenuus, alacer, fortis).

examples.original: Hos ignava iocos tribuit natura puellis;
examples.translation: These are the games that indolent nature has given to women;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Urbem populis victisque frequentem Gentibus et generis, coeat si turba, capacem Humani facilem venturo Caesare praedam Ignavae liquere manus.
examples.translation: Rome that was crowded with citizens and conquered peoples, Rome that could contain the human race assembled, was left by coward hands an easy prey to invading Caesar.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Certatim, ut quisque animo ignavus, procax ore, Annium Gallum et Suetonium Paulinum et Marium Celsum—nam eos quoque Otho praefecerat—variis criminibus incessebant.
examples.translation: This roused suspicion in the minds of Otho’s troops, who put a bad construction upon every act of their leaders.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: Sardinia
Latin: Insula italicae quae hodie est pars rei publicae italicae
Latin: Insula medii Mediterranei quae hodie est pars Rei Publicae Italicae

examples.original: Sunt qui tradant, ob infamiam quandam eum in Sardiniam secessisse ibique diem obisse.
examples.translation: Some write that because of some disgrace he retired to Sardinia and there died.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Cornelius consul in Sardinia et Corsica contra Sardos et Corsos et Hannonem, Poenorum ducem, feliciter pugnavit.
examples.translation: The consul Lucius Cornelius fought successfully in Sardinia and Corsica against the Sardinians and Corsicans and against Hanno, the Carthaginian general.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: A raised semicircular or square platform, on which the seats of magistrates were placed, a judgment-seat

examples.original: Ne tribunal quidem satis quietum erat;
examples.translation: Not even the tribunal itself was quiet;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea posteaquam numerata est, contentus hac iniquitate non fuit; palam de sella ac tribunali pronuntiat si quis absentem sthenium rei capitalis reum facere vellet, sese eius nomen recepturum;
examples.translation: From his chair of office on the tribunal he announced publicly that if anyone should think fit to prosecute Sthenius in absence on a capital charge, permission to prosecute would be granted;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Postulamus ut ii, qui maxime ignaviam increpant, adsint nobis habentibus dilectum. Acerrimi cuiusque arbitrio, quando ita placet, rem agemus.” Redeunt in tribunal;
examples.translation: The most severe amongst you, since such is your pleasure, shall guide our procedure.” They returned to the tribunal, and purposely commanded to cite by name one of those who were present.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Catiline, a Roman who was notorious for several times attempting insurrections against his country

examples.original: Quamvis parte coniurationis oppressa, tamen ab incepto Catilina non destitit;
examples.translation: Though part of the conspiracy was thus put down, Catiline did not abandon his designs;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Lentulus, destinatum familiae suae Sibyllinis versibus regnum sibi vaticinans, ad praestitutum a Catilina diem urbe tota viros, faces, tela disponit.
examples.translation: Lentulus, prophesying for himself the kingship which the Sibylline verses foretold should belong to his family, disposed throughout the city men, torches and arms ready for the day prearranged by Catiline.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a point, the pointed end of any thing (freq., esp. in the poets).
Latin: Acuta extremitas alicuius rei

examples.original: Ut semel Aetola Venus est a cuspide laesa, Mandat amatori bella gerenda suo.
examples.translation: No sooner was Venus hurt by the Aetolian spear than she bids her lover wage her wars.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a palace

examples.original: Ut Hostius cecidit, confestim Romana inclinatur acies fusaque est ad veterem portam Palatii.
examples.translation: But when he fell, the Roman line gave way at once and fled towards the old gate of the Palatine.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus concedi corpora sepulturae cremarique permisit.
examples.translation: He was then carried through the heaps of dead bodies, while the forum still reeked with blood, first to the Capitol and then to the Palatine;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quare ab Augusto quoque nepotibus eius praeceptor electus, transiit in Palatium cum tota schola, verum ut ne quem amplius posthac discipulum reciperet;
examples.translation: He was therefore chosen by Augustus as the tutor of his grandsons and he moved to the Palace with his whole school, but with the understanding that he should admit no more pupils.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to force apart, separate, divide, distribute (cf.: dispono, distribuo, divido, dispenso, ordino, compono).
English: wounded, hurt.

examples.original: Hunc quidem in secundam aciem Latini recepere: Aebutius cum saucio bracchio tenere telum non posset, pugna excessit.
examples.translation: Mamilius was received by the Latins within their second line: Aebutius, being unable to manage a weapon with his wounded arm, retired from the battle.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to move quickly to and fro, to have a vibrating or tremulous motion, to quiver, shake, tremble, e. g. of the pulse; to beat, palpitate; to spring forth, of fountains

examples.original: Aspicies oculos tremulo fulgore micantes, Ut sol a liquida saepe refulget aqua.
examples.translation: You will see her eyes shooting tremulous gleams, as the sun often glitters in clear water.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Est etiam calor ille animo, quem sumit, in ira cum fervescit et ex oculis micat acrius ardor;
examples.translation: The mind has also that heat, which it takes on when it boils in wrath and fire flashes more fiercely from the eyes;
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: depon.

examples.original: Memoriae Domiti patris honores maximos habuit.
examples.translation: He paid the highest honours to the memory of his father Domitius.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: O quando ille veniet dies, quo nemo in honorem tuum mentiatur!
examples.translation: O when will that time come, when no one shall tell lies to compliment you!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec illis aut honorare eam caedem ius hominum aut ulcisci ratio belli permittebat.
examples.translation: The common dictates of humanity did not permit them to honour such a murder or military policy to punish it.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a swearing together.

examples.original: Utrique, absente Caesare coniuratione facta, invasere legatos.
examples.translation: Caesar ordered that the forests should be burnt.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quamvis parte coniurationis oppressa, tamen ab incepto Catilina non destitit;
examples.translation: Though part of the conspiracy was thus put down, Catiline did not abandon his designs;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: Defection, desertion, rebellion, revolt.

examples.original: Secuti Marsorum defectionem Paeligni eandem fortunam habuerunt.
examples.translation: The Paeligni imitated the defection of the Marsi, and met with the same fate.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: De Praenestinorum quoque defectione eo anno primum fama exorta;
examples.translation: The Praenestines, too, were that year, for the first time, reported as disloyal;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Diebus circiter xv, quibus in hiberna ventum est, initium repentini tumultus ac defectionis ortum est ab Ambiorige et Catuvolco;
examples.translation: In about a fortnight after the troops had moved into winter quarters, disorder and revolt suddenly began.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a first principle, element (cf.: initium, principium, exordium, primordium); Gr.
Latin: Quisquam simplicissimarum essentialiumve partium vel principiorum in quo aliquid consistit, aut in quo constitutio vel vis fundamentalis alicuius sunt
Latin: chem. substantia simplex chemicae

examples.original: Haec nempe sunt elementa, quibus hic mundus administratur, aqua, terra, spiritus.
examples.translation: These, namely, are the elements, by which the world’s work is carried on—water, earth, air.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ipse de elementis locus, ut quidam putaiit, simplex est, ut quidam, in materiam et causam omnia moventem et elementa dividitur.
examples.translation: Now this very topic of the elements, as some writers hold, is integralc; as others hold, it is divided into matter, the cause which moves all things, and the elements.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hoc interest inter decreta philosophiae et praecepta, quod inter elementa et membra;
examples.translation: There is the same difference between philosophical doctrines and precepts as there is between elements and membersa;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a proof, test, trial, experiment (mostly post-Aug.; cf.: documentum periculum): nimirum hoc maximum est experimentum, cum constet aegritudinem vetustate tolli, etc., *

examples.original: Disciplinis tamen liberalibus ab aetate prima non mediocrem operam dedit ac saepe experimenta cuiusque etiam publicavit.
examples.translation: Yet he gave no slight attention to liberal studies from his earliest youth, and even published frequent specimens of his attainments in each line.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ferunt Senecam proxima nocte visum sibi per quietem C. Caesari praecipere, et fidem somnio Nero brevi fecit prodita immanitate naturae quibus primum potuit experimentis.
examples.translation: They say that on the following night Seneca dreamed that he was teaching Gaius Caesar, and Nero soon proved the dream prophetic by revealing the cruelty of his disposition at the earliest possible opportunity.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a defence, fortification, intrenchment, rampart, bulwark, protection (class. but not in Cic.).

examples.original: Bona eius solidis et inexsuperabilibus munimentis praecincta sunt.
examples.translation: His goods are girt about by strong and insurmountable defences.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Locus erat arduus atque in parte una praeceps, ubi nunc Narnia sita est, nec vi nec munimento capi poterat.
examples.translation: It was a steep place and on one side precipitous—the site is now occupied by Narnia—and could be captured neither by assault nor by siege operations.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Adventus eius compressit Etruscos adeo ut nemo extra munimenta egredi auderet timorque ipsorum obsidioni similis esset.
examples.translation: His arrival so damped the ardour of the Etruscans that none ventured outside their fortifications, and their own fear was like a besieging host.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to burn, consume by fire (freq. and class.; cf. comburo).

examples.original: Infelix gemino cecidit prope Pergamon igni, Et paene est alio Troia cremata rogo.
examples.translation: All but twice in the flames unhappy Pergamum perished Troy on a second pyre narrowly failed of her doom.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Falisci sponte se dediderunt, crematae suo igne Fidenae, direpti funditus deletique Veientes.
examples.translation: The Falisci surrendered voluntarily; Fidenae was consumed by its own flames;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Otho cruento adhuc foro per stragem iacentium in Capitolium atque inde in Palatium vectus concedi corpora sepulturae cremarique permisit.
examples.translation: He was then carried through the heaps of dead bodies, while the forum still reeked with blood, first to the Capitol and then to the Palatine;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to be or look pale.

examples.original: Vidi ego pallentes isto terrore puellas Servitium miseras tempus in omne pati.
examples.translation: I have seen women pale with terror on that account, suffering in their misery unending servitude.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quippe suspectior illis quam morbo pallentibus color est, languidi et evanidi albent, et in vivis caro morticina est.
examples.translation: Their complexions are more alarming than those of anaemic invalids; they are lackadaisical and flabby with dropsy;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: any hard stone, flintstone

examples.original: Lex de provocatione ad populum a Murena cos. tertio tunc lata est.
examples.translation: A law about appeals was then for the third time laid before the people by the consul Murena.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Q. Publilio, qui eos obsederat, primo et imperium prolatum est et pro cos. triumphus decretus.
examples.translation: Quintus Publilius, who had besieged them, was the first to have his authority extended and to be granted a triumph as proconsul.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Curius Dentatus cos. Samnitibus caesis et Sabinis, qui rebellaverant, victis et in deditionem acceptis bis in eodem magistratu triumphavit.
examples.translation: Curius Dentatus the consul having slaughtered the Samnites and conquered the Sabines, who had revolted, and received their submission, triumphed twice in the same year of office.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to stand out or forth, to project, to stand above.
Latin: pro ire
English: a thong, strap.
English: an angle, a corner.

examples.original: Cessat omne studium et liberalia professi sine ulla frequentia desertis angulis praesident.
examples.translation: You need not wonder that diseases are beyond counting: count the cooks! All intellectual interests are in abeyance;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nero in ultimum Italiae angulum summoverat Annibalem, Livius in diversissimam partem, id est in ipsas nascentis Italiae fauces signa converterat.
examples.translation: Nero had driven Hannibal into the uttermost corner of Italy, while Livius had advanced to the very opposite end of the country, the very entrance of the Italian frontier.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: fruitful, fertile (of plants and animals).—Constr. with

examples.original: Certior hic amor est: brevis et fecundior ille;
examples.translation: Such love is surer; the other is richer but brief;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: moisten, water, bedew any thing with a liquid
English: to bear, to carry
entries.grammaticalClass: v. freq. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Ita re bene gesta se recipiunt in castra.
examples.translation: So, their business well done, they retired to camp.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Res praeterea gestas adversus Vulscos et Fidenates et Faliscos continet.
examples.translation: It contains also campaigns waged against the Volsci and the Fidenates and the Faliscans.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed me nec sanguis nec tantum volnera nostri Adfecere senis, quantum gestata per urbem Ora ducis, quae transfixo sublimia pilo Vidimus;
examples.translation: But the blood and wounds of our aged sire moved me less than the carrying of his head through the city: I saw it borne aloft on a pike driven through it;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a calling to mind, a cursory speaking of, a making mention, mentioning, naming, mention

examples.original: Et mala mentis gaudia, diserte quidem dicit, sed parum proprie.
examples.translation: The evil joys of the mind,c his words are eloquent, but not strictly appropriate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ceterum hic ipse M. Cato, a cuius mentione haec disputatio processit, vereor ne supra nostrum exemplar sit.
examples.translation: But this self-same Marcus Cato, the mention of whom started this discussion,a I almost think surpasses even our exemplar.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et de Latino Hernicoque bello mentio facta in senatu maioris belli cura, quod Etruria in armis erat, dilata est.
examples.translation: The senate talked also of war with the Latins and the Hernici, but dread of a greater war—Etruria being up in arms—caused them to defer it.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to burn out, burn up, consume (class.; syn.: incendo, accendo, inflammo, cremo).
English: per tmesin
Latin: Ad hoc locum
Latin: Ad hoc tempus
English: in nowise, by no means, not at all (class.)

examples.original: Nequaquam hoc de te crediderim;
examples.translation: I should never believe it of you;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Recipiunt inde se ad stationem, et duo in medio armati spectaculi magis more quam lege belli destituuntur, nequaquam visu ac specie aestimantibus pares.
examples.translation: They then retired to their station, and the two armed men were left by themselves in the midst, like gladiators more than soldiers, and by no means evenly matched, to judge from outward show.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Q. vero Maximum fratrem, egregium virum omnino, sibi nequaquam parem, quod is anteibat aetate, tamquam superiorem colebat suosque omnis per se posse esse ampliores volebat.
examples.translation: For example, his brother Quintus Maximus, a distinguished man, no doubt, though by no means his equal, was treated by him as a superior, because he was older than himself.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the stage, boards, scene of a theatre

examples.original: Ambitio et luxuria et inpotentia scaenam desiderant;
examples.translation: Ambition, luxury, and waywardness need a stage to act upon;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A kind of prickly sea-fish: Cottus scorpio, Linn.
Latin: Quoddam animal invertebratum
Latin: Signum zodiaci inter Libram et Sagittarium
English: skilled, skilful, clever, dexterous, adroit, expert (class.; syn.; sagax, subtilis, expertus).

examples.original: Penelopen absens sollers torquebat Ulixes;
examples.translation: In the absence of crafty Ulysses was Penelope racked;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sollerti animo rem novam excogitat, qua deinde multi nostri atque externi imperatores, nostra quoque quidam aetate, usi sunt.
examples.translation: He began therefore to cast about and every way to consider how he might strike terror into the enemy by some stratagem.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ea ingenia consularia esse: callidos sollertesque, iuris atque eloquentiae consultos, qualis Ap. Claudius esset, urbi ac foro praesides habendos praetoresque ad reddenda iura creandos esse.
examples.translation: But shrewd and clever men, masters of the law and of eloquence, like Appius Claudius, should be had to preside over the City and the Forum, and should be elected praetors to administer justice.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a long and wide upper garment of the Roman ladies, held together by brooches, a robe, mantle

examples.original: Ipsa regit trepidum Pallas dextraque trementem Perseos aversi Cyllenida derigit harpen, Lata colubriferi rumpens confinia colli.
examples.translation: Pallas herself directed Perseus in his haste; her right hand guided the shaking scimitar of the Cyllenian which he held with his face averted;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to raise one's self, to rise (esp. of a multitude), to rise up together, stand up, arise (class. in prose and poetry).

examples.original: Molli consurgit Amyclas, Quem dabat alga, toro.
examples.translation: Amyclas rose up from the soft bed that seaweed gave him.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cum omne Latium atque Picenum, Etruria omnis atque Campania, postremo Italia contra matrem suam ac parentem urbem consurgeret;
examples.translation: All Latium and Picenum, all Etruria and Campania, and finally all Italy rose against their mother and parent city.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Consurgere in ipsis Ius tibi solstitiis, aliena crescere bruma Atque hiemes adferre tuas, solique vagari Concessum per utrosque polos.
examples.translation: He is privileged to rise at midsummer, to be flooded by a winter out of season, and to bring with him a rainy season of his own;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: till now, still, even now, even to this time, even at this time.
English: In good class. Lat., a jurid. and milit. t. t.

examples.original: Nec cuiquam ultra fides aut memoria prioris sacramenti, sed quod in seditionibus accidit, unde plures erant omnes fuere.
examples.translation: No man had any loyalty or thought for his former oath, but as happens in mutinies all joined the majority.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Sapiens adsectatorque sapientiae adhaeret quidem in corpore suo, sed optima sui parte abest et cogitationes suas ad sublimia intendit. Velut sacramento rogatus hoc, quod vivit, stipendium putat.
examples.translation: The wise man, the seeker after wisdom, is bound closely, indeed, to his body, but he is an absentee so far as his better self is concerned, and he concentrates his thoughts upon lofty things.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to swell, be swollen or tumid, to be puffed out or inflated

examples.original: Colle tumet modico lenique excrevit in altum Pingue solum tumulo;
examples.translation: The fertile land rises in a hill of moderate height and ascends with easy slope;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Non est quod post cibum studeas, non est quod plenis oculis ac tumentibus imperes;
examples.translation: There is no reason why you should study immediately after eating;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic pleno Padus ore tumens super aggere tutas Excurrit ripas et totos concutit agros;
examples.translation: Thus the river Po, swollen with brimming estuary, overflows its banks though defended by dykes, and oversets whole districts;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To fill again, refill; to fill up, replenish, complete, etc.

examples.original: Postero die prima luce Volsci fossis repletis vallum invadunt.
examples.translation: He waited a moment, to test the temper of the soldiers.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Equitum acies, qualis quae esse instructissima potest, invecta in dissipatos impeditosque hostes caede omnia replet.
examples.translation: The cavalry, drawn up in the most perfect order, charged their scattered and embarrassed enemies and cut them down on every hand.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to go apart or asunder, to separate, part; to go away, depart, = discedere (class.).

examples.original: Caecina e complexu Vitellii multo cum honore digressus partem equitum ad occupandam Cremonam praemisit.
examples.translation: Caecina, departing from the embraces of Vitellius with great honours, sent a part of his horse ahead to occupy Cremona.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Et erant in civitate Lingonum octo Batavorum cohortes, quartae decimae legionis auxilia, tum discordia temporum a legione digressae, prout inclinassent, grande momentum sociae aut adversae.
examples.translation: Moreover there were in the country of the Lingones eight cohorts of Batavians, auxiliaries belonging to the Fourteenth legion, who at that time, owing to the discord of the moment, had withdrawn from the legion;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Dum haec in partibus Vitellii geruntur, digressus Narnia Vespasiani exercitus festos Saturni dies Ocriculi per otium agitabat.
examples.translation: While these things were happening on the side of Vitellius, Vespasian’s forces left Narnia and quietly celebrated the Saturnalia at Ocriculum.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a temple, shrine, sanctuary (class., esp. freq. in poets and in elevated prose; usually in the plur.; for syn. cf.: templum, aedes, fanum, cella, sacellum, sacrarium).

examples.original: Dique latent templis neque iniqua ad funera vultus Praebent nec poscunt tura ferenda rogo: Obscuros delubra tenent;
examples.translation: The gods are hidden in their temples, nor show their faces at this unrighteous death, nor demand the incense needed by the pyre;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iussi cum coniugibus ac liberis supplicatum ire pacemque exposcere deum, ad id quod sua quemque mala cogebant auctoritate publica evocati omnia delubra implent.
examples.translation: Thus summoned by the state’s authority to do what each was impelled to by his own distress, they crowded all the shrines.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a foundation, ground-work

examples.original: Huius fundamentum quod sit quaeris?
examples.translation: Do you ask what is the foundation of a sound mind?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quaedam ingenia facilia, expedita, quaedam manu, quod aiunt, facienda sunt et in fundamentis suis occupata.
examples.translation: I should accordingly deem more fortunate the man who has never had any trouble with himself;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Itaque Pometinae manubiae, quae perducendo ad culmen operi destinatae erant, vix in fundamenta suppeditavere.
examples.translation: Hence the Pometian spoils, which had been destined to carry the building up to the roof, barely sufficed for the foundations.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: I

examples.original: Erras enim, si existimas nobiscum vitia nasci;
examples.translation: For you are mistaken if you suppose that our faults are inborn in us;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ex hac fuga protinus, quae undique convenerant, auxilia discesserunt, neque post id tempus umquam summis nobiscum copiis hostes contenderunt.
examples.translation: After this rout the succours which had assembled from all quarters took their departure; and never afterwards did the enemy engage us at their full strength.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Nationes aliquas occupavit Vitellius, imaginem quandam exercitus habet, senatus nobiscum est: sic fit ut hinc res publica, inde hostes rei publicae constiterint.
examples.translation: Vitellius has won over some peoples; he has a certain shadow of an army, but the senate is with us.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a father's brother, paternal uncle (opp. avunculus, a mother's brother, maternal uncle)
Latin: Patris frater
Latin: Qui ad patruum pertinet

examples.original: Nam Claudium patruum non nisi in ludibrium reservavit.
examples.translation: As for his uncle Claudius, he spared him merely as a laughingstock.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Tiberius patruus petenti honores consularia ornamenta detulit;
examples.translation: His paternal uncle Tiberius gave him the consular regalia, when he asked for office;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Is de honore regni cum Agesilao, patruo suo, contendit neque id quod petivit consecutus est;
examples.translation: He it was that disputed the title of king with his uncle Agesilaus, but he was unsuccessful;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Agesilaus

definitions: English: one who hears, in relation to his protector (patronus), a client

examples.original: Hunc Venus e templis, quae sunt confinia, ridet: Qui modo patronus, nunc cupit esse cliens.
examples.translation: Venus laughs at him from her neighbouring shrine: he who was of late an advocate would fain be a client now.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Imperant Aeduis atque eorum clientibus, Segusiavis, Ambivaretis, Aulercis Brannovicibus, Blannoviis, milia xxxv;
examples.translation: Of the Aedui and their dependents, Segusiavi, Ambivareti, Aulerci Brannovices, and Blannovii, they required five-and-thirty thousand;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Praecipiti in occasum die ob pavorem magistratuum senatorumque, qui dilapsi ex urbe aut per domos clientium semet occultabant, vocari senatus non potuit.
examples.translation: The day hurried to its close. It was impossible to summon the senate because the senators had stolen away from the city or were hiding in their clients’ houses.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to give a particular direction to; di-rigo, to arrange in distinct lines, set or move different ways; cf. describo and discribo. But the distinction is not observed in the MSS

examples.original: Restat ergo ut iste pecuniae turpissimus appetitus ex obliquo in clericos et maxime in episcopum dirigatur.
examples.translation: It remains, then, that your charge of a most sordid lust for money is indirectly levelled at the clergy, and especially at the bishop.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Sed quid ego haec interrogo, cum, si ego tacitus abissem, tamen tibi ad voluntatis interpretationem meae dirigenda tua sententia fuerit?
examples.translation: But why do I put these questions, since, had I gone off without a word, nevertheless your thoughts should have been directed to the interpretation of my will?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a dart, javelin

examples.original: Hi iaculo pisces, illi capiuntur ab hamis: Hos cava contento retia fune trahunt.
examples.translation: These fish are caught with spears, those with hooks; these ones are dragged with taut ropes in bulging nets.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hinc enim potius cavendae sunt linguae inimicorum, de quibus tamquam iaculis ad interficiendos infirmos maior ille utitur inimicus.
examples.translation: In this connexion we ought rather to safeguard ourselves against the tongues of our enemies, which our greater enemy employs like darts to slay the weak.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Ecce procul saevus sterilis se robore trunci Torsit et inmisit—iaculum vocat Africa—serpens Perque caput Pauli transactaque tempora fugit.
examples.translation: Behold! a fierce serpent, called by Africa iaculus, aimed and hurled itself at Paulus from a barren tree far off;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a Roman family name.

examples.original: Agrippa inde Tiberini filius, post Agrippam Romulus Silvius a patre accepto imperio regnat.
examples.translation: Then Agrippa, son of Tiberinus, reigned, and after Agrippa Romulus Silvius was king, having received the power from his father.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Agrippinam, Marco Agrippa genitam, neptem Caecili Attici equitis R., ad quem sunt Ciceronis epistulae, duxit uxorem;
examples.translation: Tiberius He married Agrippina, daughter of Marcus Agrippa, and granddaughter of Caecilius Atticus, a Roman knight, to whom Cicero’s letters are addressed;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Gaio et Lucio intra triennium defunctis adoptatur ab Augusto simul cum fratre eorum M. Agrippa, coactus prius ipse Germanicum fratris sui filium adoptare.
examples.translation: When Gaius and Lucius died within three years, he was adopted by Augustus along with their brother Marcus Agrippa, being himself first compelled to adopt his nephew Germanicus.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a sum of 1,000 sesterces

examples.original: Expugnatus autem a quadam, quasi amore suo deperiret, cum perductae pro concubitu sestertia quadringenta donasset, admonente dispensatore, quem ad modum summam rationibus vellet inferri: ”Vespasiano,” inquit, ”adamato.” XXIII.
examples.translation: Being asked by his steward how he would have the sum entered in his accounts, he replied: ”To a passion for Vespasian.” XXIII.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to hold off, keep back, detain.

examples.original: Ipse deum volucrem detinuisse paro.
examples.translation: I am planning to hold fast the winged god.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Et tua sic latos spargantur membra per agros, Tamquam quae patrias detinuere vias.
examples.translation: And may thy limbs be so scattered o’er the broad fields as those which stayed a father’s march.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Quid illa in exitu lenta, qualis Ciceronis est, devexa et molliter detinens nec aliter quam solet, ad morem suum pedemque respondens?
examples.translation: Or again of that softly-concluding style, Cicero-fashion,b with a gradual and gently poised descent, always the same and always with the customary arrangement of the rhythm!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or pertaining to summer, summer-like, summer (freq. and class.)
Latin: Aestatis seu qui ad aestatem pertinet; aestivalis

examples.original: Consul educto in aestiva milite, dum quietos Samnites habebat, exercitum purgare missionibus turbulentorum hominum instituit, aliis emerita dicendo stipendia esse, alios graves iam aetate aut viribus parum validos.
examples.translation: The consul having led out his troops to the summer encampment, and finding the Samnites quiet, resolved to purge the army of its troublemakers by discharging them.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to conduct, carry, convey, bear, bring, etc., a person or thing to a place; and
English: a constitution, disposition, nature

examples.original: Enati sunt dentes; huic constitutioni conciliatur.
examples.translation: Then his teeth grow, and he is fitted to that condition also.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic, quamvis alia atque alia cuique constitutio sit, conciliatio constitutionis suae eadem est.
examples.translation: For nature does not consign boyhood or youth, or old age, to me;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ostendat ex constitutione vulgi beatos in illo invidioso fastigio suo trementes et adtonitos longeque aliam de se opinionem habentes quam ab aliis habetur.
examples.translation: He should point out persons, happy in the popular estimation, who totter on their envied heights of power, who are dismayed and hold a far different opinion of themselves from what others hold of them.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a hiding-place, lurking-hole, covert, retreat

examples.original: Quis calcare tuas metuat, salpuga, latebras?
examples.translation: Who would fear to tread on the lair of the salpuga?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quae latebra est, in quam non intret metus mortis?
examples.translation: What hiding-place is there, where the fear of death does not enter?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Periere latebrae Tot scelerum, populo venia est erepta nocenti: Agnovere suos.
examples.translation: For at this moment our age can exercise a mighty influence upon the future.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to send or drive off or away, to remove (freq. and class.; cf.: repello, amolior).

examples.original: Summoveri Laetorius iubet, praeterquam qui suffragium ineant.
examples.translation: Laetorius ordered the removal of all but those who were voting.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nero in ultimum Italiae angulum summoverat Annibalem, Livius in diversissimam partem, id est in ipsas nascentis Italiae fauces signa converterat.
examples.translation: Nero had driven Hannibal into the uttermost corner of Italy, while Livius had advanced to the very opposite end of the country, the very entrance of the Italian frontier.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: an ointment, unguent, perfume

examples.original: Inde in omnem vitam unguento abstinemus, quoniam optimus odor in corpore est nullus.
examples.translation: That is why I have also throughout my life avoided perfumes;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: one of the three days in each month from which the other days were reckoned in the Roman calendar, the Ides; it fell upon the fifteenth day of March

examples.original: Aedes Mercuri dedicata est idibus Maiis.
examples.translation: The temple of Mercury was consecrated on the fifteenth of May.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Natus est Cn. Pompeio Magno M. Licinio Crasso primum coss. Iduum Octobrium die in pago qui Andes dicitur et abest a Mantua non procul.
examples.translation: He was born in the first consulship of Gnaeus Pompeius the Great and Marcus Licinius Crassus, on the Ides of October, in a district called Andes, not far distant from Mantua.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Omnes exclusi sunt non minus aperte quam pupillus. Diem praestituit operi faciundo Kalendas Decembres, locat circiter Idus Septembres;
examples.translation: The day Verres fixed for the undertaking to be completed was the 1st of December, and he let the contract about the 13th of September;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to be of unsound mind (syn.: furo, deliro, desipio).

examples.original: Diripiantque tuos insanis unguibus artus Strymoniae matres, Orpheos esse ratae.
examples.translation: And may Strymonian mothers rend thy limbs with frenzied nails, deeming them those of Orpheus.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: eagerly desirous of something, esp. of possessions, avaricious, covetous, greedy

examples.original: Haerebit tibi avaritia, quamdiu avaro sordidoque convixeris;
examples.translation: As long as this companion is avaricious and mean, greed will stick to you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cuius avari modum ignorant, etiam non avari usum. ”Tolle,” inquit, ”errores;
examples.translation: Then comes the reply: ”Do away with error, and your precepts become unnecessary.” That is wrong;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ergo et avarus erit, sed finite, et adulter, verum habebit modum, et luxuriosus eodem modo.
examples.translation: He will be a miser—within limits; an adulterer—in moderation;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to smell (class.; cf. odoro, fragro).

examples.original: Quaedam vero procul arceantur ut iam oblitterata et olentia: nullum sit verbum velut rubigine infectum, nulli sensus tarda et inerti structura in morem annalium componantur;
examples.translation: There should be never a word of the rusty, mouldy tinge, never a sentence put together in the lame and listless style of the chroniclers.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a division, separation.

examples.original: Cupiditates non Epicuri divisione finiebat sed sua satietate.
examples.translation: Epicurus’s classification of the desires meant nothing to him;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Bellvm Pervsinvm IIII, 5Alterum bellum concitavit agrorum divisio, quod Caesar veteranis patris pretium militiae persolvebat.
examples.translation: The War round Perusia 5. The distribution of lands to the soldiers was the cause of another war;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a mourning, sadness, grief, sorrow, lamentation, whether secret or open (class.)

examples.original: Turpissimum autem est in homine prudente remedium maeroris lassitudo maerendi.
examples.translation: I should prefer you to abandon grief, rather than have grief abandon you;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec minimam partem ex agris is maeror in urbem confluxit, languens quem contulit agricolarum copia conveniens ex omni morbida parte.
examples.translation: And in no small degree this affliction flowed from the country into the city, for the fainting crowd people of countrymen brought it, gathering from all quarters with disease.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: O acerbam mihi, iudices, memoriam temporis illius et loci, cum hic in me incidit, cum complexus est conspersitque lacrimis nec loqui prae maerore potuit!
examples.translation: How bitter to me, gentlemen, is the memory of that time and that place, when he fell upon my neck, embraced me, bedewed me with his tears, and was dumb for very grief!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Neptune, the god of the sea and of other waters, brother of Jupiter and husband of Amphitrite
Latin: Deus Romanus maris aquarumque; mare ipsum
Latin: Solis octavus planeta

examples.original: Qui Martem terra, Neptunum effugit in undis, Coniugis Atrides victima dira fuit.
examples.translation: Atreus, who escaped Mars on land and Neptune on the deep, was the dire victim of his wife.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cui tempus locumque aptum ut daret Romulus, aegritudinem animi dissimulans ludos ex industria parat Neptuno equestri sollemnis; Consualia vocat.
examples.translation: Expressly to afford a fitting time and place for this, Romulus, concealing his resentment, made ready solemn games in honour of the equestrian Neptune, which he called Consualia.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To bind or tie around, to bind or fasten to any thing (very rare)

examples.original: Non est iniquum fortes viros arma sumere et in castris pernoctare et pro vallo obligatis stare vulneribus, interim in urbe securos esse percisos et professos impudicitiam?
examples.translation: Is it not unjust that brave men should take up arms, and stay all night in camp, and stand with bandaged wounds before the rampart, while perverts and professional profligates rest secure within the city?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a royal staff, a sceptre.

examples.original: Aut velut Eurylochi, qui sceptrum cepit ab illo, Sint artus avidis anguibus esca tui.
examples.translation: Or like Eurylochus, who took the sceptre from him, may thy limbs be food for greedy snakes.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nam sibi quod numquam tactam Briseida iurat Per sceptrum, sceptrum non putat esse deos.
examples.translation: For that he swears by his sceptre that Briseis ne’er was touched, he deems not his sceptre to be heaven.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a knot (cf. nexus).
English: of or belonging to spring

examples.original: Tempus erat, quo Libra pares examinat horas, Non uno plus aequa die, noctique rependit Lux minor hibernae verni solacia damni.
examples.translation: It was the season when Libra balances the hours of day and night in equal scales, and stays level for one day only;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a proneness to anger, hastiness of temper, irascibility; violence of anger, wrath, rage, passion (class.)

examples.original: Impellit alios avaritia, alios iracundia et temeritas, quae maxime illi hominum generi est innata, ut levem auditionem habeant pro re comperta.
examples.translation: They left themselves no time to investigate: some were influenced by avarice, others by anger and the recklessness which is specially characteristic of their race, treating frivolous hearsay as assured fact.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Irae atque iracundiae conscius sibi, utramque excusavit edicto distinxitque, pollicitus alteram quidem brevem et innoxiam, alteram non iniustam fore.
examples.translation: He was conscious of his tendency to wrath and resentment and excused both in an edict;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: Julian, a Roman proper name.

examples.original: Iulianus ad L. Vitellium perductus et verberibus foedatus in ore eius iugulatur.
examples.translation: Julianus was taken before Lucius Vitellius, flogged, and slain before his eyes.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a small stream of water, a brook (cf.: fluvius, amnis).

examples.original: Ipse potes riguis plantam deponere in hortis, Ipse potes rivos ducere lenis aquae.
examples.translation: You yourself can plant a shoot in a well-watered garden, you yourself can guide the runnels of gentle water.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: folly, foolishness, simplicity, silliness, fatuity, etc.

examples.original: In diversum ecce sapientia et stultitia discedunt;
examples.translation: Lo, Wisdom and Folly are taking opposite sides.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Verum hoc adhuc percommode cadit, quod cum incredibili eius audacia singularis stultitia coniuncta est.
examples.translation: But it has very fortunately come about, hitherto, that his incredible audacity has been accompanied by unparalleled folly.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: reverencing or fearing God (the gods), pious, devout, religious
Latin: Qui deos veneratur
Latin: Quod ad religionem pertinet

examples.original: Tu meam domum religiosam facere potuisti?
examples.translation: Could you, Sir, attach inviolability to my house?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Tum de diebus religiosis agitari coeptum, diemque a. d.
examples.translation: Then they proceeded to deliberate about days of evil omen.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huic ego testi gratias agam, quod et in re misericordem se praebuerit et in testimonio religiosum.
examples.translation: I will ask this witness to accept my thanks for having shown himself merciful in his conduct and scrupulous in his evidence.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: away, to depart.
Latin: Cedere ab loco
Latin: abscedo ab [aliquo]: Desistere de aliquo; linquere aliquid

examples.original: Iam is gravis annis non militaribus solum sed civilibus quoque abscesserat muneribus;
examples.translation: This man, bowed down with years, had already withdrawn not only from military but even from civic duties;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed mane cognovimus, et in qua domo fuerit et quod post galli cantum cum illo abscesserit qui eum tenuerat.
examples.translation: I also sent to the place to which it was said he had been carried off.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: De fratre vero eius, in cuius vel maxime causa de monasterio etiam ipse Donatus abscessit, cum intellegas quid sentiam, nescio quid respondeam.
examples.translation: But since you understand what I feel, I am at a loss what to say about his brother, for whose sake most of all Donatus himself left his monastery.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: The name of several mountains, the most celebrated of which is one on the borders of Macedonia and Thessaly (now Lacha), of great height, and consequently regarded as the seat of

examples.original: Tolostobogi Olympum, Tectosagi Magabam insederant.
examples.translation: The Tolostobogi had occupied Olympus, the Tectosagi Magaba.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ipse caput medio Titan cum ferret Olympo, Condidit ardentes atra caligine currus Involvitque orbem tenebris gentesque coegit Desperare diem;
examples.translation: The sun himself, while rearing his head in the zenith, hid his burning chariot in black darkness and veiled his sphere in gloom, forcing mankind to despair of daylight;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: an image, statue
Latin: Simulacrum ex aere, aliove metallo factum

examples.original: Aes prima statuae causa est.
examples.translation: The ”second cause” is the artist;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid vero? modum statuarum haberi nullum placet?
examples.translation: And then again, can an unlimited number of statues be approved?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Itaque illi Syracusani statuam postea statuerunt;
examples.translation: The Syracusans, owing to this, later set up a statue in his honour;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: quick, speedy, hastening

examples.original: Sed nimium properas: vivam modo, plura dolebis;
examples.translation: But you haste overmuch: if I but live, you will grieve the more;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Sed propera, ne vela cadant auraeque residant: Ut fragilis glacies, interit ira mora.
examples.translation: But be speedy, lest the sails sink and the breezes fail: like brittle ice, so perishes anger by delaying.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to take apart; to part, separate, divide (class.; esp. freq. in the trop. sense—cf.: findo, scindo, divello, separo, sejungo, segrego, secerno).

examples.original: Iamque haud procul iusto proelio res erat, ni celeriter diremptum certamen per centuriones esset;
examples.translation: And now the mellay was likely to end in a regular battle, had not the centurions speedily parted the combatants.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum parum decorum inter collegas certamen mirabundi patres conspicerent, Q. Servilius ”Quando nec ordinis huius ulla” inquit, ”nec rei publicae est verecundia, patria maiestas altercationem istam dirimet.
examples.translation: While the astonished senators watched this unseemly rivalry amongst the colleagues, Quintus Servilius exclaimed, ”Since you have no respect for this order nor for the republic, a father’s authority shall end your quarrel.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to cast off a person or thing (ab se spernari; cf. sperno and spernor)

examples.original: Et primo fremitus fuit aspernantium imperium;
examples.translation: They had indeed murmured at first, and had flouted the order;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec aspernanda res visa neque incaute credenda.
examples.translation: It was not thought wise to spurn this offer, nor yet rashly to confide in it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Id vero haud secus quam praesentem mercedem regni aspernata plebes;
examples.translation: But this the people spurned, as a downright attempt to purchase regal power;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: generally, universally, everywhere; publicly, in/to the crowd/multitude/world

examples.original: Volgares opificum, quae manu constant et ad instruendam vitam occupatae sunt, in quibus nulla decoris, nulla honesti simulatio est.
examples.translation: The common sort belong to workmen and are mere hand-work; they are concerned with equipping life;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ea conluvio mixtorum omnis generis animantium et odore insolito urbanos et agrestem confertum in arta tecta aestu ac vigiliis angebat, ministeriaque in vicem ac contagio ipsa volgabant morbos.
