examples.translation: If Junius was irregular in the filling up of vacancies, or if he had at any time omitted to take any official oath, did his conviction imply any sentence on Cluentius?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a rubbing off. *

examples.original: Omnis iniuria deminutio eius est in quem incurrit, nec potest quisquam iniuriam accipere sine aliquo detrimento vel dignitatis vel corporis vel rerum extra nos positarum.
examples.translation: All injury is damaging to him who encounters it, and no man can receive injury without some loss either in respect to his position or his person or things external to us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Longius prosequi veritus, quod silvae paludesque intercedebant neque etiam parvulo detrimento illorum locum relinqui videbat, omnibus suis incolumibus copiis eodem die ad Ciceronem pervenit.
examples.translation: He feared to pursue very far, because there were woods and marshes in the way, and, as he saw, there was no chance now of doing even slight damage to the enemy;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Et ipse magnus abbas Benedictus, sicut de illo beatus papa Gregorius scribit, duodecim abbates suis discipulis, prout utile iudicavit, sine charitatis detrimento, immo pro augmento charitatis praefecit.
examples.translation: And the great abbot Benedict himself, as blessed Gregory telleth us of him, set 12 abbots over his disciples, as he judged expedient, neither did he thereby lessen brotherly love but rather enlarged it.
examples.author: Bede

definitions: English: to invoke with tears, call to one's assistance, call upon for aid; to invoke, beseech, entreat, implore (freq. and class.; cf. invoco).
English: four hundred each

examples.original: Nobis quadringentae amplius naves, ducentae minus hostium;
examples.translation: We had more than four hundred ships, the enemy less than two hundred;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Per eos cognitum est Interamnam proximis campis praesidio quadringentorum equitum teneri.
examples.translation: From them the Flavians learned that Interamna in the neighbouring plain was defended by four hundred horse.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Vectigal quoque eis Campanus populus iussus pendere in singulos quotannis—fuere autem mille et sexcenti—denarios a.u.c. 415nummos quadringenos quinquagenos.
examples.translation: Moreover, the 340Campanian people were commanded to pay them each a yearly stipend—there were sixteen hundred of them—amounting to four hundred and fifty denarii.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: indigence, extreme poverty, necessity, want

examples.original: Non est quod nos paupertas a philosophia revocet, ne egestas quidem.
examples.translation: There is no reason why poverty should call us away from philosophy,—no, nor even actual want.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam iam, Dolabella, neque me tui neque tuorum liberum, quos tu miseros in egestate atque in solitudine reliquisti, misereri potest.
examples.translation: After this, Dolabella, I can feel no pity for you; nor, after this, for the unhappy children you have left behind you in poverty and loneliness.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cerberus et Furiae iam vero et lucis egestas, Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus— qui neque sunt usquam nec possunt esse profecto.
examples.translation: Cerberusb also and the Furies and the with-holding of light, and Tartarus belching horrible fires from his throat—these neither exist anywhere nor in truth can exist.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: from without, from abroad.

examples.original: Ita dico: extrinsecus aliqua sunt incommoda, velut in corpore interdum robusto solidoque eruptiones quaedam pusularum et ulcuscula, nullum in alto malum est.
examples.translation: This is what I mean: there are external disadvantages, like pimples and boils that break out upon a body which is normally strong and sound; but there is no deep-seated malady.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to survey, behold, observe, consider, contemplate, etc.; freq. in

examples.original: Nunc autem vester, iudices, conspectus et consessus iste reficit et recreat mentem meam, cum intueor et contemplor unumquemque vestrum.
examples.translation: But at the present moment, gentlemen, the sight of you assembled here bids me take. fresh heart of grace;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a solemn feast for religious purposes, a sacrificial feast

examples.original: Quis posuit secretam in auro dapem?
examples.translation: Who uses gold plate when he dines alone?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: prove, test any thing, to make a trial of, put to the test
Latin: In periculum volens ire

examples.original: Alia est autem spes piorum, alius laboris fructus, alia periculorum merces. Nam in hoc mundo non timere, non dolere, non laborare, non periclitari inpossibile est;
examples.translation: So it is with all the things that are sought in the tribulation of this mortal life with more eagerness than reflection, but it is far different with the hope of the godly;
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: by snatching or hurrying away, i. e.

examples.original: Fabius omissis omnibus praedam ex castris raptim Antium convehit; ibi modico praesidio relicto citatum agmen Tusculum rapit.
examples.translation: Letting everything else go, Fabius quickly conveyed the plunder of the camp to Antium, and leaving there a moderate garrison, hastened by forced marches to Tusculum.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Parcite ne castris: vallo tendetis in illo, Unde acies peritura venit.” Vix cuncta locuto Caesare quemque suum munus trahit, armaque raptim Sumpta Ceresque viris.
examples.translation: Be not careful of your camp; you will find quarters behind the rampart from which the doomed army is coming.” Almost before Caesar had ceased to speak, each went to his appointed task;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ante tamen Pharias victor quam tangat harenas, Pompeio raptim tumulum fortuna paravit, Ne iaceat nullo vel ne meliore sepulchro: E latebris pavidus decurrit ad aequora Cordus.
examples.translation: In fear and haste Cordus came down from his hiding-place to the sea; as quaestor he had made the ill-starred voyage with Magnus from the Icarian shore of Cyprus, where Cinyras once reigned.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a teacher of oratory or rhetoric, a rhetorician

examples.original: Studuit Flaccus usque ad annum XII. aetatis suae Volaterris, inde Romae apud grammaticum Remmium Palaemonem et apud rhetorem Verginium Flavum.
examples.translation: Flaccus studied until the twelfth year of his age at Volaterrae, and then at Rome with the grammarian Remmius Palaemon and the rhetorician Verginius Flavus.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: a falsely assumed appearance, a false show, feigning, shamming, pretence, feint, insincerity, deceit, hypocrisy, simulation, etc. (class. and very freq.; cf. imitatio).

examples.original: Dux deerat abducto Verginio per simulationem amicitiae;
examples.translation: But they had no leader, for Verginius had been taken away under the cloak of friendship.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Volgares opificum, quae manu constant et ad instruendam vitam occupatae sunt, in quibus nulla decoris, nulla honesti simulatio est.
examples.translation: The common sort belong to workmen and are mere hand-work; they are concerned with equipping life;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Prima luce magnum numerum impedimentorum ex castris mulorumque produci deque his stramenta detrahi mulionesque cum cassidibus equitum specie ac simulatione collibus circumvehi iubet.
examples.translation: With them he put a few cavalry, to range more widely by way of demonstration, and ordered them all to make for the same general destination by a long circuit.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to wrestle.

examples.original: Habes, quod agas: bene luctare cum morbo.
examples.translation: You have something to do: wrestle bravely with disease.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a being forgotten, forgetfulness, oblivion (class.)

examples.original: Orbilius ubinam est, litterarum oblivio?
examples.translation: Where is Orbilius, pray, great learning’s tomb?
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Quid alia quae auspicato agimus omnia fere intra pomerium, cui oblivioni aut cui neglegentiae damus?
examples.translation: What about the other matters nearly all of which we transact, after taking auspices, within the pomerium?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Est autem situm in nobis ut et adversa quasi perpetua oblivione obruamus et secunda iucunde ac suaviter meminerimus.
examples.translation: We have the power both to obliterate our misfortunes in an almost perpetual forgetfulness and to summon up pleasant and agreeable memories of our successes.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: into, to enter (syn.: intro, ingredior); constr. with in or

examples.original: Non immerito inter spectacula ab eo edita et Tiridatis in urbem introitum rettulerim.
examples.translation: I may fairly include among his shows the entrance of Tiridates into the city.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Atque iste ad omnes introitus, qua adiri poterat non modo in eum fundum, de quo controversia erat, sed etiam in illum proximum de quo nihil ambigebatur, armatos homines opponit.
examples.translation: The defendant, then, stationed armed men at every possible way of approach not only to the estate under dispute but even to the adjoining one about which there was no contention.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nil melius aeterna lex fecit, quam quod unum introitum nobis ad vitam dedit, exitus multos.
examples.translation: The best thing which eternal law ever ordained was that it allowed to us one entrance into life, but many exits.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to place

examples.original: Quare omnium in se odio incitato nihil contumeliarum defuit quin subiret. Statuae eius a vertice cirrus appositus est cum inscriptione Graeca;
examples.translation: When he had thus aroused the hatred of all, there was no form of insult to which he was not subjected.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Verres calumniatorem apponebat, Verres adesse iubebat, Verres cognoscebat, Verres iudicabat, pecuniae maximae dabantur, qui dabant causas obtinebant.
examples.translation: Verres put up the false claimant, Verres summoned the defendants, Verres tried the case, Verres pronounced judgement;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: saffron: Crocus sativus, Linn.

examples.original: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
examples.translation: No awnings then hung o’er a marble theatre, nor was the platform ruddy with crocus-spray;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: unity, a unit; as a standard for different coins, weight, measure, etc.
Latin: Unitas
Latin: Nummus aereus
English: the wax cells of the hives

examples.original: Nec piger ignis erat per stuppea vincula perque Manantes cera tabulas, et tempore eodem Transtraque nautarum summique arsere ceruchi.
examples.translation: He ordered brands steeped in resin to be hurled at the sails of the crowded ships;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to kneel down or humble one's self, to pray or beg humbly, to beseech, implore, supplicate (class.; cf.: oro, adoro, precor).

examples.original: Appellavi populum tributim, submisi me et supplicavi;
examples.translation: I demeaned myself to becoming a suppliant.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam quidem nunc multitudinem videtis, iudices, in squalore et luctu supplicem vobis.
examples.translation: You see them thronging this court to-day, gentlemen of the jury;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ceterum exercitus honorarium ei tumulum excitavit, circa quem deinceps stato die quotannis miles decurreret Galliarumque civitates publice supplicarent.
examples.translation: It is the general belief that he was as eager for glory as he was democratic by nature;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: To furnish with a surname, to surname, denominate

examples.original: Censuerunt etiam quidam ut Pannonicus, alii ut Invictus, nonnulli ut Pius cognominaretur.
examples.translation: Some also recommended that he be given the surname of Pannonicus, others of Invictus, others of Pius.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Liberos ex tribus uxoribus tulit: ex Urgulanilla Drusum et Claudiam, ex Paetina Antoniam, ex Messalina Octaviam et quem primo Germanicum, mox Britannicum cognominavit.
examples.translation: He had children by three of his wives: by Urgulanilla, Drusus, and Claudia; by Paetina, Antonia;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a country extending from the Indus to China
Latin: Natio Indorum, cuius caput Dellium Novum
English: Mithridates the Great, king of Pontus, who waged war with the Romans, was at last conquered by Pompey, and stabbed himself

examples.original: Mithridates in Asia, cum eam provinciam totam occupasset, Mucia non sustulit;
examples.translation: When Mithridates overran Asia from end to end, he did not suppress the Scaevola Festival;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hic tamen tam callidus vir extremo tempore captus est Mithridatis, Ariobarzanis filii, dolo.
examples.translation: Yet this man, cunning as he was, finally fell victim to the craft of Mithridates, the son of Ario-barzanes;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Datames

examples.original: Huius adventus et Mithridatem insolita inflammatum victoria continuit et Tigranem magnis copiis minitantem Asiae retardavit.
examples.translation: His arrival restrained Mithridates, who was elated by the unusual experience of victory, and checked Tigranes, who was threatening Asia with great forces.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: nearer, nigher.

examples.original: Tiburtes Praenestinique, quorum ager propior erat, Pedum pervenere;
examples.translation: The Tiburtes and Praenestini, whose territories lay near by, reached Pedum;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Urebant montana nives camposque iacentes Non duraturae conspecto sole pruinae, Atque omnis propior mergenti sidera caelo Aruerat tellus hiberno dura sereno.
examples.translation: The mountains were nipped by snow, and the low-lying plains by hoar frost that would vanish at first sight of the sun;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: wherever, wheresoever.

examples.original: In uno iacetis, Non est vestrum ubicumque non estis.
examples.translation: No place is yours where you yourselves are not.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec ubicumque apparuit, omnia eiusdem mensurae ac pretii sunt.
examples.translation: For such critics think that whatever they themselves cannot do, is not done;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et ideo ei negari non potest, ubicumque illum esse cognoverit et iure poposcerit;
examples.translation: So he cannot be denied him, when he learns his whereabouts and claims him by law.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to take into use; to make use of; to use, employ, apply, practise, exercise, enjoy (class.; cf. utor).
Latin: Uti, adhibere
Latin: Potiri, vi in possessionem suam ducere

examples.original: Accepta itaque res saepiusque usurpando excitata.
examples.translation: And so the amusement was adopted, and frequent use kept it alive.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed ille, quod a nobis aut benigne aut remisse factum est, in praescriptionem vertere atque usurpare conatur;
examples.translation: But what we did, either from kindness or from carelessness, he is now trying to turn to account and employ as a legal objection.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to shrink back from a thing, to shudder at, abhor.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; ui, ēre, 2

examples.original: Namque eos vocabat, quorum mores a suis non abhorrerent.
examples.translation: For he invited those whose tastes did not differ from his own.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Quid umquam Habitus in se admisit, ut hoc tantum ab eo facinus non abhorrere videatur?
examples.translation: What crime has Habitus ever had upon his conscience that you should imagine such a deed to be otherwise than abhorrent from him?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to give a smell or fragrance to, to perfume a thing

examples.original: Nec non in meridiem verso agmine Libanum Syriae Damascumque transgressus per nemora illa odorata, per turis et balsami silvas Romana signa circumtulit.
examples.translation: Furthermore, turning his army southwards, he passed through the Lebanon in Syria and through Damascus, and bore the Roman standards through the famous scented groves and woods of frankincense and balm.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam et ante iam fama et nunc fratres, qui venerunt a vobis, Eustasius et Andreas bonum Christi odorem de vestra sancta conversatione ad nos adtulerunt.
examples.translation: For a good savour of Christ from your holy conduct had already reached me, first through rumour and now through the brethren, Eustasius and Andrew, who have come from you.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to set foot upon, to stand, tread, or press upon; constr. mostly with

examples.original: Ab hoc aliquot plagis Eumenes vulneratur neque eo magis ex proelio excessit, sed acrius hostis institit.
examples.translation: From his opponent Eumenes suffered several wounds, but he did not on that account leave the field, but attacked the enemy with renewed vigour.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

examples.original: At hostes etiam in extrema spe salutis tantam virtutem praestiterunt, ut, cum primi eorum cecidissent, proximi iacentibus insisterent atque ex eorum corporibus pugnarent;
examples.translation: The enemy, however, even when their hope of safety was at an end, displayed a prodigious courage. When their front ranks had fallen, the next stood on the prostrate forms and fought from them;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to swallow, swallow down, gulp down, devour (class.; esp. freq. in transf. signif.—for syn. cf.: edo, comedo, vescor, pascor, mando).

examples.original: Quot oppida in Syria, quot in Macedonia devorata sunt?
examples.translation: How many towns in Syria, how many in Macedonia, have been swallowed up!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: eternity.
English: she that has borne any one, or produced any thing, a mother
English: upon any thing; mostly with
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; sēdi, sessum, 2

examples.original: Ita duplici proditione et praesidium Samnitium insessis circa viam silvestribus locis necopinato oppressum est, et ab urbe plena hostium clamor sublatus;
examples.translation: Thus, in one crowded hour, the Samnites were slain and the Satricans captured, and all things brought under the power of the consul;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nam illa quoque inopia et exilitas minus intentum auditorem habet taedio interruptae tarditatis, facilius tamen insidit, quod exspectatur, quam quod praetervolat.
examples.translation: For that poverty-stricken and thin-spun style also makes the audience less attentive because they are weary of its stammering slowness;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nam ab Saticula profectus Cornelius consul exercitum incaute in saltum cava valle pervium circaque insessum ab hoste induxit nec prius quam recipi tuto signa non poterant imminentem capiti hostem vidit.
examples.translation: For the consul Cornelius, marching from Saticula, had unwarily led his army into a forest which was penetrated by a deep defile, and was there beset on either hand by the enemy;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: in like manner, so, just
English: An adducing of proof, an argumentation
English: Of or belonging to the public revenue, or to the farming of the revenue: muliercula, the wife of a farmer-general (with an odious secondary meaning)

examples.original: Itaque socii fecerunt vetere instituto publicanorum, non quo istum ullo honore dignum arbitrarentur, sed quod sua interesse putabant se memores gratosque existimari;
examples.translation: The company accordingly observed the traditional practice of revenue-contractors, not because they thought he deserved any marks of respect, but because they felt it would pay them not to seem forgetful or ungrateful;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: whose; of whom
English: to make or create anew, to remake, reproduce, restore, renew

examples.original: Et tunc quidem Caesar recreatus est ex volnere in tempus, sed * * *.
examples.translation: Caesar recovered from the wound for the time being but . .
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nunc autem vester, iudices, conspectus et consessus iste reficit et recreat mentem meam, cum intueor et contemplor unumquemque vestrum.
examples.translation: But at the present moment, gentlemen, the sight of you assembled here bids me take. fresh heart of grace;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hunc in illo timore et fuga Tigranes, rex Armenius, excepit diffidentemque rebus suis confirmavit et adflictum erexit perditumque recreavit.
examples.translation: Mithridates meanwhile, a panic-stricken fugitive, found a welcome with Tigranes, king of Armenia, who comforted his despair, raised his drooping spirits and restored his ruined fortunes.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: sixty
Latin: Sexies dena. Numerus LX

examples.original: Caesa aut capta eo die hostium milia ad sexaginta.
examples.translation: On that day the enemy lost sixty thousand slain or captured.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum haberet annos circiter sexaginta, usus est aetatis vacatione neque se quoquam movit ex urbe.
examples.translation: He took advantage of the exemption due his years and did not stir from the city.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

definitions: English: a note-book, sketch-book, memorandum
Latin: Liber memorandorum vel adumbrationum

examples.original: Scio Caesarem singulorum annorum singulos commentarios confecisse;
examples.translation: I am aware that Caesar has compiled a separate Commentary for each year;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Quodque vix auditu fas esse debeat, laudis et gloriae et ingenii loco plerique iactant cantari saltarique commentarios suos;
examples.translation: They make it their aim, by wantonness of language, by shallow-pated conceits, and by irregular arrangement, to produce the rhythms of stage-dancing;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: not foreseeing, not anticipating or expecting, without knowing, unaware, ignorant

examples.original: Quinque omnino fuerunt, qui illum vestrum innocentem Oppianicum sive imprudentia sive misericordia sive aliqua suspicione sive ambitione adducti absolverunt.
examples.translation: There were five persons in all who, whether from mistaken judgement, or pity, or a suspicion of foul play, or interested motives, voted your poor innocent Oppianicus not guilty.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hac si proficisceretur, intellegebat prius adversarios rescituros de suo adventu quam ipse tertiam partem confecisset itineris; sin per loca sola contenderet, sperabat se imprudentem hostem oppressurum.
examples.translation: If he marched by the latter road, he knew that his opponents would be informed of his coming before he had gone a third part of the way;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: to carry or conduct forwards, to carry or convey along, to conduct, convey, transport, etc., to a place; and freq.

examples.original: Hic cum aetate iam provectus esset, sine ullo morbo lumina oculorum amisit.
examples.translation: When he was already advanced in years, without suffering any disease he lost the sight of his eyes.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Timoleon

examples.original: Sic Scribonianum sub Claudio interfectum, sic percussorem eius Volaginium e gregario ad summa militiae provectum: facilius universos impelli quam singulos vitari.
examples.translation: Thus Scribonianus was killed under Claudius; thus his assassin Volaginius won advancement from the lowest to the highest rank.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: out of the right way; also, untrodden, unfrequented, solitary, lonely, etc.

examples.original: Quid? aviam tuam, Oppianice, Dinaeam, cui tu es heres, pater tuus non manifesto necavit?
examples.translation: Again, is it not patent, Oppianicus, that your father murdered your grandmother, Dinea, whose heir you are?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: At liquidas avium voces imitarier ore ante fuit multo quam levia carmina cantu concelebrare homines possent aurisque iuvare.
examples.translation: To imitate with the mouth the liquid notes of the birds came long before men could delight their ears by warbling smooth carols in song.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: a plough

examples.original: Nullum laborem recusant manus, quae ad arma ab aratro transferuntur;
examples.translation: The hand which turns from the plough to the sword never objects to toil;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Medium erat tempus forte sementis, cum patricium virum innixum aratro suo lictor in ipso opere deprehendit.
examples.translation: It happened to be the middle of the season of sowing, when the lictor found the patrician actually at work bending over his plough.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Sed hos praecipue Titus Quinctius domuit, ille dictator ab aratro, qui obsessa et paene iam capta Manili consulis castra egregia victoria recuperavit.
examples.translation: These were subdued chiefly by Titus Quinctius, the dictator who was summoned from the plough and by a famous victory rescued the camp of the consul Manilius, which was beleaguered and almost captured.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: of or from snow, snowy, snow-
Latin: Qui ad nivem pertinet, in nive consistens
Latin: Qui colorem nivis habet

examples.original: Hoc vos praecipue, niveae, decet: hoc ubi vidi, Oscula ferre umero, qua patet usque, libet.
examples.translation: This becomes you especially, you who have snowy skins; when I see this, fain would I kiss that shoulder, wherever it is exposed.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: A goad for driving cattle, slaves, etc. (class., esp. in the trop. sense).

examples.original: Fortunam adhuc tantum adversam tulisti: secundae res acrioribus stimulis animos explorant, quia miseriae tolerantur, felicitate corrumpimur.
examples.translation: Thus far you have known only adversity; prosperity tests the spirit with sharper goads, because we simply endure misfortune, but are corrupted by success.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quomodo solitudinis odium est et adpetitio societatis, quomodo hominem homini natura conciliat, sic inest huic quoque rei stimulus, qui nos amicitiarum adpetentes faciat.
examples.translation: As we hate solitude and crave society, as nature draws men to each other, so in this matter also there is an attraction which makes us desirous of friendship.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the name of several Roman women.

examples.original: Agrippinam, Marco Agrippa genitam, neptem Caecili Attici equitis R., ad quem sunt Ciceronis epistulae, duxit uxorem;
examples.translation: Tiberius He married Agrippina, daughter of Marcus Agrippa, and granddaughter of Caecilius Atticus, a Roman knight, to whom Cicero’s letters are addressed;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Prius igitur quam ultra progrederetur, praeventus est ab Agrippina, quam praeter haec conscientia quoque nec minus delatores multorum criminum arguebant.
examples.translation: But before he could go any farther, he was cut short by Agrippina, who was being accused besides of many other crimes both by her own conscience and by informers.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ac vix uno interposito die confecit nuptias, non repertis qui sequerentur exemplum, excepto libertino quodam et altero primipilari, cuius nuptiarum officium et ipse cum Agrippina celebravit.
examples.translation: And he married her with hardly a single day’s delay; but none were found to follow his example save a freedman and a chief centurion, whose marriage ceremony he himself attended with Agrippina.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to make thin, fine, or small, to thin, reduce, diminish (class.; syn.: attenuo, minuo; opp. augeo, amplifico).
English: a grain, seed, small kernel
English: Hence

examples.original: Hinc montes natura vagis circumdedit undis, Qui Libyae te, Nile, negent;
examples.translation: From this point Nature has surrounded the wandering stream with mountains, which rob Libya of the Nile;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tum Sadalam fortemque Cotyn fidumque per arma Deiotarum et gelidae dominum Rhascypolin orae Conlaudant, Libyamque iubent auctore senatu Sceptrifero parere Iubae.
examples.translation: Praise was given also to Sadalas and brave Cotys, to the faithful ally, Deiotarus, and to Rhascypolis, lord of a frozen land;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: His igitur depulsa locis eiectaque classis Syrtibus haud ultra Garamantidas attigit undas, Sed duce Pompeio Libyae melioris in oris Mansit.
examples.translation: Thus the ships, driven from their course and cast forth from the Syrtes, remained in this region, on the shore of the better part of Libya, with Pompeius as commander;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to hold up or upriqht, to uphold, support

examples.original: Aegre eo die sustentatum est.
examples.translation: The defence was with difficulty maintained on that day.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to make out of wood, stone, metal, etc., to frame, forge, construct, build.

examples.original: Animum format et fabricat, vitam disponit, actiones regit, agenda et omittenda demonstrat, sedet ad gubernaculum et per ancipitia fluctuantium derigit cursum.
examples.translation: It moulds and constructs the soul; it orders our life, guides our conduct, shows us what we should do and what we should leave undone;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Fabricavit et deceris Liburnicas gemmatis puppibus, versicoloribus velis, magna thermarum et porticuum et tricliniorum laxitate magnaque etiam vitium et pomiferarum arborum varietate;
examples.translation: He also built Liburnian galleys with ten banks of oars, with sterns set with gems, particoloured awnings, huge spacious baths, colonnades, and banquet-halls, and even a great variety of vines and fruit trees;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Classi quoque faces intulit, vacuo mari eludens, quia lectissimas Liburnicarum omnemque militem Mucianus Byzantium adegerat: quin et barbari contemptim vagabantur, fabricatis repente navibus.
examples.translation: He also set fire to the fleet and escaped by sea, which was unpatrolled since Mucianus had concentrated the best light galleys and all the marines at Byzantium.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: that stands firm; firm, steadfast, steady, stable (class.; esp. in the trop. sense; syn.: firmus, constans).

examples.original: Ea res utique Troianis spem adfirmat tandem stabili certaque sede finiendi erroris.
examples.translation: The commanders then made a treaty, and the armies saluted each other.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quae enim domus tam stabilis, quae tam firma civitas est, quae non odiis et discidiis funditus possit everti?
examples.translation: For what house is so strong, or what state so enduring that it cannot be utterly overthrown by animosities and division?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ne procurri quidem ab acie velim, sed obnixos vos stabili gradu impetum hostium excipere.
examples.translation: I would have none run out from the line, but all stand firmly planted and receive the onset of our enemies.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a cough
English: to make glittering or bright, to make white (eccl. Lat.)

examples.original: Ne candidatis quidem honores reisve tam innoxiis quam nocentibus absolutiones venditare cunctatus est.
examples.translation: He made no bones of selling offices to candidates and acquittals to men under prosecution, whether innocent or guilty.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: One who seizes beforehand, an anticipator (postclass.)
Latin: Qui praecipit, docet

examples.original: Aeacidae Chiron, ego sum praeceptor Amoris: Saevus uterque puer, natus uterque dea.
examples.translation: Chiron taught Aeacides, I am Love’s teacher: a fierce lad each, and each born of a goddess.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hanc itaque rationem dii sequuntur in bonis viris quam in discipulis suis praeceptores, qui plus laboris ab is exigunt, in quibus certior spes est.
examples.translation: And so, in the case of good men the gods follow the same rule that teachers follow with their pupils; they require most effort from those of whom they have the surest hopes.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quare ab Augusto quoque nepotibus eius praeceptor electus, transiit in Palatium cum tota schola, verum ut ne quem amplius posthac discipulum reciperet;
examples.translation: He was therefore chosen by Augustus as the tutor of his grandsons and he moved to the Palace with his whole school, but with the understanding that he should admit no more pupils.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to finish play, i. e. cease to sport or roll
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; si, sum, 3

examples.original: Classi quoque faces intulit, vacuo mari eludens, quia lectissimas Liburnicarum omnemque militem Mucianus Byzantium adegerat: quin et barbari contemptim vagabantur, fabricatis repente navibus.
examples.translation: He also set fire to the fleet and escaped by sea, which was unpatrolled since Mucianus had concentrated the best light galleys and all the marines at Byzantium.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Quid aliud infestis patribus nuper Eprius Marcellus quam eloquentiam suam opposuit, qui accinctus et minax disertam quidem sed inexercitatam et eius modi certaminum rudem Helvidii sapientiam elusit?
examples.translation: Ready for the fray and breathing defiance, he could parry the blows of the philosopher Helvidius, who for all his clever speaking was, as regards that sort of contest, an inexperienced novice.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Multa erumpentis seditionis indicia per conscios oppressa: quaedam apud Galbae auris praefectus Laco elusit, ignarus militarium animorum consiliique quamvis egregii, quod non ipse adferret, inimicus et adversus peritos pervicax.
examples.translation: There were many signs of the outbreak of the revolt, but these were repressed by the plotters. Some things reached Galba’s ears, but the prefect Laco made light of them;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: lively, brisk, quick, eager

examples.original: Animus esse debet alacer et fidens et super omnia erectus.
examples.translation: The very soul must be happy and confident, lifted above every circumstance.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to follow to the end, to pursue, follow.

examples.original: Exsequebatur inde quae sollemnis derivatio esset.
examples.translation: He then went on to explain the appointed method of draining it.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Iussa miles exsequitur; clamor hostes circumsonat;
examples.translation: The men did as they had been bidden.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Singillatim crudeliter facta eius exsequi longum est;
examples.translation: It is a long story to run through his acts of cruelty in detail;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: jutting out, projecting.

examples.original: Cernit tabe iecur madidum, venasque minaces Hostili de parte videt.
examples.translation: He saw the liver flabby with corruption and with boding streaks in its hostile half.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tu, qui flagrante minacem Scorpion incendis cauda chelasque peruris, Quid tantum, Gradive, paras?
examples.translation: But Mars—what dreadful purpose has he, when he kindles the Scorpion menacing with fiery tail and scorches its claws?
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Niger inficit horror Terga maris, longo per multa volumina tractu Aestuat unda minax, flatusque incerta futuri Turbida testantur conceptos aequora ventos.
examples.translation: A shudder of darkness blackened the ridges of the sea; the angry deep boiled with a long swell, wave following wave;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: keeping due measure, moderate; esp. in behavior, modest; as respects anger, calm, gentle, dispassionate; towards others, kind, forbearing, temperate, mild

examples.original: Disserebat populo Fabianus, sed audiebatur modeste.
examples.translation: Fabianus used to give popular talks, but his audience listened with self-control.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Multi in utroque exercitu sicut modesti quietique ita mali et strenui.
examples.translation: There were many in both armies obedient and law-abiding, as well as many unprincipled and energetic.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Satis ipsum nomen philosophiae, etiam si modeste tractetur, invidiosum est;
examples.translation: The mere name of philosophy, however quietly pursued, is an object of sufficient scorn;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: and/but not yet

examples.original: Iam comitia consularia instabant; quae res eum necdum compositis maturisve satis consiliis oppressit.
examples.translation: The consular election was now at hand, and found him with his plans not yet fully ripened.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: bad quality, badness (very rare)

examples.original: An ab hac eius infamia ac nequitia vestros animos in aliam partem fortitudinis commemoratione traducat?
examples.translation: Is he to divert your attention from his scandalous immorality by dwelling upon his bravery?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to break through.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; rūpi, ruptum, 3

examples.original: P. Sulpicius per mediam hostium aciem cum equitatu perrupit.
examples.translation: Publius Sulpicius broke through the enemy’s centre with his cavalry.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Non est quod existimes magnis tantum viris hoc robur fuisse, quo servitutis humanae claustra perrumperent;
examples.translation: You need not think that none but great men have had the strength to burst the bonds of human servitude;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a manager, overseer, superintendent, agent

examples.original: Ornamenta consularia etiam procuratoribus ducenariis indulsit.
examples.translation: He gave the consular regalia even to the second grade of stewards.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: to follow close after or immediately; to follow, succeed, ensue (class.).

examples.original: Itaque arma suos capere et se subsequi iubet.
examples.translation: He accordingly bade his men stand to arms and follow him.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vercingetorix minoribus Caesarem itineribus subsequitur et locum castris deligit paludibus silvisque munitum ab Avarico longe milia passuum xvi.
examples.translation: Vercingetorix followed after Caesar by shorter stages, and chose for his camp a place fenced by marshes and woods, about sixteen miles from Avaricum.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ob eam causam spatia omnis temporis non numero dierum sed noctium finiunt; dies natales et mensum et annorum initia sic observant ut noctem dies subsequatur.
examples.translation: For that reason they determine all periods of time by the number, not of days, but of nights, and in their observance of birthdays and the beginnings of months and years day follows night.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to inflict censure, to blame, censure, disparage, vituperate (class.; syn.: culpo, objurgo, damno).
English: to write before, in front, or previously, to prefix in writing (syn.: praefinio, praestituo).

examples.original: Sed ubi totis castris in fama proditio, recurrens in principia miles praescriptum Vespasiani nomen, proiectas Vitellii effigies aspexit, vastum primo silentium, mox cuncta simul erumpunt.
examples.translation: But when the news of the treason spread through the whole camp, the soldiers ran to headquarters, where they saw Vespasian’s name put up on the standards and the statues of Vitellius overthrown;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to fall back (class., and very freq., esp. in the trop. signif.; but not found in Virg. or Hor.).

examples.original: Caedes principum ostenditur: id, quod interitum optimatium sequi necesse est, adiungitur: ne in unius imperium res recidat, admonemur.
examples.translation: The murder of our highest is portended; and there is a further reference to what must inevitably follow the destruction of our nobility;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: dominion, sovereignty, authority, rule, sway, power.

examples.original: Ita Nequinum in dicionem populi Romani venit.
examples.translation: Thus Nequinum came under the sway of the Roman People.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Itaque M. Scaurus, qui Cn. Dolabellam accusavit, istum in sua potestate ac dicione tenuit.
examples.translation: And that, gentlemen, is why Marcus Scaurus, the prosecutor of Dolabella, kept Verres in his power and under his control.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Achaiam, Lyciam, Rhodum, Byzantium, Samum libertate adempta, item Trachiam Ciliciam et Commagenen dicionis regiae usque ad id tempus, in provinciarum formam redegit.
examples.translation: He made provinces of Achaia, Lycia, Rhodes, Byzantium and Samos, taking away their freedom, and likewise of Trachian Cilicia and Commagene, which up to that time had been ruled by kings.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: pertaining to the ether, ethereal.

examples.original: Una per aetherios exit vox illa recessus Verbaque ad invitum perfert cogentia numen, Quod non cura poli caelique volubilis umquam Avocat.
examples.translation: Their voice alone speeds through the remote parts of heaven, and conveys the words that bind the reluctant deity, whom no care for the sky and revolving firmament ever distracts from listening.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To this extent
English: Going round, encompassing

examples.original: Ne illud quidem, quod existimas facturum eum, faciet, ut ambitiosis rebus inplicitus semper aestus earum ferat.
examples.translation: Neither will he, as you imagine, become so involved in ambitious schemes that he will have continually to endure their ebb and flow.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Inrationalis pars animi duas habet partes, alteram animosam, ambitiosam, inpotentem, positam in adfectionibus, alteram humilem, languidam, voluptatibus deditam;
examples.translation: The irrational part of the soul is twofoldb: the one part is spirited, ambitious, uncontrolled; its seat is in the passions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed Pacensis per licentiam militum vinctus, Antonio Novello nulla auctoritas: Suedius Clemens ambitioso imperio regebat, ut adversus modestiam disciplinae corruptus, ita proeliorum avidus.
examples.translation: Antonius Novellus had no authority; and Suedius Clemens used his office to secure popularity, being as reckless toward maintaining discipline as he was eager to fight.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: growth, increase, augmentation (class.).
Latin: Factum vel effectum increscendi

examples.original: Quaedam post multa incrementa ultima demum vertit adiectio et novam illis aliamque quam in qua fuerunt, condicionem inprimit.
examples.translation: There are others, however, which, after many increments, are altered by the last addition; there is stamped upon them a new character, different from that of yore.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to a mountain, mountain-; full of mountains, mountainous (class.)

examples.original: Quid tibi cum speculo, montana armenta petenti?
examples.translation: What dost thou with a mirror, seeking the herds upon the mountains?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: In Britanniam inde et Hispanias nuntios famamque, in Galliam Iulium Calenum tribunum, in Germaniam Alpinium Montanum praefectum cohortis, quod hic Trevir, Calenus Aeduus, uterque Vitelliani fuerant, ostentui misere.
examples.translation: The Flavian leaders then despatched messengers to carry the news to Britain and to Spain; to Gaul they sent Julius Calenus, a tribune, and to Germany Apinius Montanus, a prefect of a cohort.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Urebant montana nives camposque iacentes Non duraturae conspecto sole pruinae, Atque omnis propior mergenti sidera caelo Aruerat tellus hiberno dura sereno.
examples.translation: The mountains were nipped by snow, and the low-lying plains by hoar frost that would vanish at first sight of the sun;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the month of April (as the month in which the earth opens and softens)
Latin: Qui ad mensem quartum calendarii Gregoriani pertinet
Latin: Mensis quartus calendarii Gregoriani
English: after this time, hereafter, henceforth, in future (class.)

examples.original: Hoc si ita statuetis, non modo non erit cur depugnare quisquam posthac possessionis caussa velit, sed ne illud quidem, cur repugnare.
examples.translation: If you so decide, you will remove all future motive for resorting to battle over possession; nay more, there will be no motive even for accepting battle.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quare ab Augusto quoque nepotibus eius praeceptor electus, transiit in Palatium cum tota schola, verum ut ne quem amplius posthac discipulum reciperet;
examples.translation: He was therefore chosen by Augustus as the tutor of his grandsons and he moved to the Palace with his whole school, but with the understanding that he should admit no more pupils.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Sublata sunt studia, exstinctae suffragationes, nullae contentiones, nulla libertas populi in mandandis magistratibus, nulla exspectatio suffragiorum: nihil, ut plerumque evenit, praeter opinionem accidet: nulla erit posthac varietas comitiorum.
examples.translation: But if, on the other hand, it commonly happens that we are surprised at the election of some and the non-election of others;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to set in tremulous motion, to move rapidly to and fro, to brandish, shake, agitate (class.; syn.: quatio, ventilo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

definitions: English: clearness, brightness

examples.original: Consentire in hoc plures insignes et spectabiles viri debent, ut claritas sit.
examples.translation: In order to constitute renown, the agreement of many distinguished and praiseworthy men is necessary.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Blaeso super claritatem natalium et elegantiam morum fidei obstinatio fuit. Integris quoque rebus a Caecina et primoribus partium iam Vitellium aspernantibus ambitus abnuere perseveravit.
examples.translation: Even while the position of Vitellius was still unshaken, he had been solicited by Caecina and the party leaders who already despised the emperor, but he persisted in rejecting their advances.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to take to one's self by wish, choice (optando); to choose, select.

examples.original: Hora nona illo ipso die tu es adoptatus.
examples.translation: At the ninth hour on that same day your adoption took place.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Adoptat annos viginti natus, etiam minor senatorem.
examples.translation: A man twenty years of age or even less adopts a senator.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quam fuit imbecillus P. Africani filius, is qui te adoptavit, quam tenui aut nulla potius valetudine!
examples.translation: Note how weak, Scipio, was your adoptive father, the son of Publius Africanus! What feeble health he had, or rather no health at all!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a sprout, shoot, twig, sprig, sucker, graft, scion, slip, cutting
Latin: Pedis imum
Latin: (class.) Pedis imum

examples.original: Ipse potes riguis plantam deponere in hortis, Ipse potes rivos ducere lenis aquae.
examples.translation: You yourself can plant a shoot in a well-watered garden, you yourself can guide the runnels of gentle water.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non exsurgit in plantas nec summis ambulat digitis eorum more, qui mendacio staturam adiuvant longioresque quam sunt, videri volunt;
examples.translation: He does not stretch himself or walk on tiptoe like those who seek to improve their height by deceit, wishing to seem taller than they really are;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to grow together; hence with the prevailing idea of uniting, and generally of soft or liquid substances which thicken; to harden, condense, curdle, stiffen, congeal, etc

examples.original: Cruor altus in unda Spumat, et obducti concreto sanguine fluctus.
examples.translation: Their blood foamed deep upon the wave, and a crust of gore covered the sea.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to set on fire, light up, kindle (syn. incendere).

examples.original: Ad haec cum inflammarentur animi, ut ad quosque ventum erat, numerus iuniorum conscribebatur.
examples.translation: These words aroused indignation, and a number of young men were enlisted wherever the envoys went.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huius adventus et Mithridatem insolita inflammatum victoria continuit et Tigranem magnis copiis minitantem Asiae retardavit.
examples.translation: His arrival restrained Mithridates, who was elated by the unusual experience of victory, and checked Tigranes, who was threatening Asia with great forces.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Res vero publica quamquam erat exterminata mecum, tamen obversabatur ante oculos exstinctoris sui et ab istius inflammato atque indomito furore iam tum se meque repetebat.
examples.translation: As for the republic, though it had shared my banishment, its phantom yet loomed before the eyes of its suppressor, and was even then demanding me (yes!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Military service for pay: apud regem in latrocinio fuisti, Plaut. ap.
Latin: Quaestus latronum

examples.original: Non hos palus in bello latrociniisque natos, non silvae morantur.
examples.translation: No marsh, no woods check these children of war and brigandage.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: In primis tuendae pacis a grassaturis ac latrociniis seditionumque licentia curam habuit.
examples.translation: He gave special attention to securing safety from highway banditry and lawless outbreaks.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the yearly produce, the annual income of natural products, in the widest sense

examples.original: Tum pectore curas Expulit armorum pacique intentus agebat, Quoque modo vanos populi conciret amores, Gnarus et irarum causas et summa favoris Annona momenta trahi.
examples.translation: At once he banished thoughts of battle from his mind, and passed his time over problems of peace and the means of winning the fickle favour of the populace;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Petebatur a me frumenti copia, annonae vilitas: possem aliquid in ea re necne ratio non habebatur: flagitabar bonorum expostulatione: improborum convitia sustinere non poteram.
examples.translation: I was asked to procure plentiful supplies of corn, and a decrease in its price; but whether I had any powers in the matter or not was never taken into account.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cum de mea dignitate in templo Iovis optimi maximi senatus frequentissimus, uno isto dissentiente, decrevisset, subito illo ipso die carissimam annonam nec opinata vilitas consecuta est.
examples.translation: And yet, with his whole mind bent on slaughter, he had proclaimed my name to his partisans, and openly hinted it to the ignorant mob.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a storming, assaulting, besieging; an attack, assault, siege (class.).

examples.original: Illi aegre ad noctem oppugnationem sustinent;
examples.translation: The others scarcely kept off the assault till nightfall;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Non segnior oppugnatio est quam pugna fuerat.
examples.translation: The assault was no less vigorous than the battle had been.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Vercingetorix, ubi de Caesaris adventu cognovit, oppugnatione destitit atque obviam Caesari proficiscitur.
examples.translation: As soon as he heard of Caesar’s approach Vercingetorix abandoned the siege and started to meet him.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: A pointing out, indicating, denoting, signifying; an expression, indication, mark, sign, token, = indicium, signum
English: to lame, cripple, maim; to debilitate, unnerve, disable, weaken (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Nos multa alligant, multa debilitant.
examples.translation: We human beings are fettered and weakened by many vices;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potius ergo illa dicantur, turpe esse, viri non esse debilitari dolore, frangi, succumbere.
examples.translation: If that be true, are you not guilty of a crime in advising him to end his life?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Atque ut a corpore ordiar, videsne ut si quae in membris prava aut debilitata aut imminuta sint occultent homines?
examples.translation: To start with the body, do you notice how men try to hide a deformed or infirm or maimed limb?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to distrust; to be diffident or distrustful, to despair (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Fit quoque longus amor, quem diffidentia nutrit: Hunc tu si quaeres ponere, pone metum.
examples.translation: That passion also lingers long that diffidence fosters; if you would be rid of this, be rid of fear.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Spes maior esset salutis, si praeter te nemo esset impurus: plures sunt: hoc et tu tibi confidis magis et nos prope iure diffidimus.
examples.translation: We should have better assurance of well-being if none save you were tainted: but there are others; and this fact, which increases your confidence, makes us, almost justly, less confident.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hunc in illo timore et fuga Tigranes, rex Armenius, excepit diffidentemque rebus suis confirmavit et adflictum erexit perditumque recreavit.
examples.translation: Mithridates meanwhile, a panic-stricken fugitive, found a welcome with Tigranes, king of Armenia, who comforted his despair, raised his drooping spirits and restored his ruined fortunes.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to turn around or about, to overturn, overthrow, throw down (class.).

examples.original: Numquam ille me opprimet consilio, numquam ullo artificio pervertet, numquam ingenio me suo labefactare atque infirmare conabitur.
examples.translation: He will never crush me with his cleverness; he will never lead me astray by any display of ingenuity;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed plerique perverse, ne dicam impudenter, habere talem amicum volunt, quales ipsi esse non possunt, quaeque ipsi non tribuunt amicis, haec ab eis desiderant.
examples.translation: But most men unreasonably, not to say shamelessly, want a friend to be such as they cannot be themselves and require from friends what they themselves do not bestow.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: come forth (class.; cf.: proficiscor, progredior).
Latin: Ire ex loco

examples.original: At bona conscientia prodire vult et conspici;
examples.translation: A good conscience, however, wishes to come forth and be seen of men;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sabinis proditae portae per virginem Tarpeiam.
examples.translation: To the Sabines the gates of Rome were betrayed by the maiden Tarpeia.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ad triginta milia caesa aut capta Samnitium proditum memoriae est.
examples.translation: Tradition avers that some thirty thousand Samnites were slain or captured.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to tear asunder, overthrow, demolish, destroy (class. —cf.: deleo, diluo, exstinguo, everto, demolior).
Latin: Rem alteram ab altera avellendo deicere
Latin: destruo

examples.original: Itaque hoste victo ruptorem foederis Mettum Fufetium religatum inter duos currus pernicibus equis distrahit, Albamque ipsam quamvis parentem, aemulam tamen diruit, cum prius omnes opes urbis ipsumque populum Romam transtulisset;
examples.translation: So after the defeat of the enemy Tullus bound Mettus Fufetius, the violator of the treaty, between two chariots, and tore him asunder with swift horses.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: sweetness.

examples.original: Nam ut aliarum nobis rerum innata dulcedo est, sic amicitiae.
examples.translation: For just as other things have for us an inherent attractiveness, so has friendship.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ad hoc panis usu carnisque coctae et dulcedine vini mitigatos Marius in tempore adgressus est.
examples.translation: When they had been further demoralized by the use of bread and cooked meat and the delights of wine, Marius opportunely approached them.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Est quaedam dulcedo sermonis, quae inrepit et eblanditur et non aliter quam ebrietas aut amor secreta producit.
examples.translation: For there is a sort of charm about conversation, something very subtle and coaxing, which, like intoxication or love, draws secrets from us.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A making, doing, preparing (very rare)

examples.original: Cum Caesar in Galliam venit, alterius factionis principes erant Aedui, alterius Sequani.
examples.translation: When Caesar arrived in Gaul the leaders of one party were the Aedui, of the other the Sequani.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Deinde orta dissensio est inter eum et Heraclidem, qui, quod ei principatum non concedebat, factionem comparavit.
examples.translation: Next, dissension arose between him and Heraclides, who, unwilling to yield the first place to Dion, formed a party against him.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Dion

examples.original: Nec tamen expers insidiarum usque quaque permansit, sed et a singulis et per factionem et denique civili bello infestatus est.
examples.translation: Yet he did not remain throughout without experience of treachery, but he was attacked by individuals, by a conspiracy, and finally by a civil war.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a noose, snare (class.; cf. tendicula).
Latin: Vinculum ita nexum, ut pondere magis claudatur
Latin: quidquid capere potest et constringere

examples.original: Mulciber obscuros lectum circaque superque Disponit laqueos: lumina fallit opus.
examples.translation: Mulciber disposes hidden snares around and above the couch; the device baffles the eye.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tunc laqueis captare feras et fallere visco Inventum et magnos canibus circumdare saltus. Omnia enim ista sagacitas hominum, non sapientia invenit.
examples.translation: Of setting traps for game, and liming twigs For birds, and girdling mighty woods with dogs.a It was man’s ingenuity, not his wisdom, that discovered all these devices.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Electum tandem traiecto gutture corpus Ducit, et inserto laqueis feralibus unco Per scopulos miserum trahitur, per saxa, cadaver Victurum, montisque cavi, quem tristis Erictho Damnarat sacris, alta sub rupe locatur.
examples.translation: The hapless body was dragged over rocks and stones, to live a second time, and was laid beneath a high rock of the hollow mountain which cruel Erictho had condemned to witness her rites.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: A dazzling, glossy whiteness, a clear lustre, clearness, radiance, brightness, brilliancy
English: to press down, weigh down, sink down, to depress (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Summitti te ac deprimi veto.
examples.translation: I forbid you to be cast down or depressed.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec tu intentionem vocis contempseris, quam veto te per gradus et certos modos extollere, deinde deprimere.
examples.translation: You need not scorn voice-culture; but I forbid you to practise raising and lowering your voice by scales and specific intonations.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non caeli nox illa fuit: latet obsitus aer Infernae pallore domus nimbisque gravatus Deprimitur, fluctusque in nubibus accipit imbrem.
examples.translation: The darkness was not the common darkness of night: the heavens were hidden and veiled with the dimness of the infernal regions, and weighed down by clouds;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that is above, on high, upper; celestial, supernal
English: to tie, bind, fasten, or join together, to connect, entwine, link together
English: need, want, trouble, toil, hardship, distress, tribulation, calamity, etc.
English: to lead or bring into a place, to conduct into or within (syn.: induco, immitto).

examples.original: Id fieri posse, si suas copias Aedui in fines Bellovacorum introduxerint et eorum agros populari coeperint.
examples.translation: This could be done if the Aedui led their own forces into the borders of the Bellovaci and began to lay waste their lands.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Legati introducti in senatum maxime in hanc sententiam locuti sunt.”"Populus nos Campanus legatos ad vos, patres conscripti, misit amicitiam in perpetuum, auxilium praesens a vobis petitum.
examples.translation: Their ambassadors, on being introduced into the senate, spoke substantially as follows: ”The Campanian people has sent us to you as ambassadors, Conscript Fathers, to solicit your lasting friendship and present help.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a meadow (class.).
English: One who at the close of his consulship in Rome became governor of a province, or military commander under a governor; a proconsul
English: stiff, hard, inflexible, rigid

examples.original: Rigida re quid amplius intendi potest?
examples.translation: What can be made more tense than a thing which is already rigid?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed rigidum ius est et inevitabile Mortis, Stant rata non ulla fila tenenda manu.
examples.translation: But fixed and inevitable is death’s law, unswerving are the threads, not to be checked by any hand.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the pivot and socket, upon which a door was made to swing at the lintel and the threshold, the hinge of a door or gate
English: To flow down.

examples.original: Quemadmodum clepsydram non extremum stillicidium exhaurit, sed quicquid ante defluxit, sic ultima hora, qua esse desinimus, non sola mortem facit, sed sola consummat;
examples.translation: It is not the last drop that empties the water-clock, but all that which previously has flowed out; similarly, the final hour when we cease to exist does not of itself bring death;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: That gives pleasure, i. e. alluring, charming, delightful; luxurious, voluptuous.

examples.original: Ubi vero inpotens, cupidus, delicatus est, transit in nomen detestabile ac dirum et fit tyrannus;
examples.translation: But an uncontrolled, passionate, and effeminate soul changes kingship into that most dread and detestable quality—tyranny;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: An tu existimas quemquam soluto vultu et, ut isti delicati locuntur, hilariculo mortem contemnere, paupertati domum aperire, voluptates tenere sub freno, meditari dolorum patientiam?
examples.translation: Can one, do you think, despise death with a care-free countenance, or with a ”blithe and gay” expression, as our young dandies are accustomed to say?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quomodo Maecenas vixerit notius est, quam ut narrari nunc debeat, quomodo ambulaverit, quam delicatus fuerit, quam cupierit videri, quam vitia sua latere noluerit.
examples.translation: We know how he walked, how effeminate he was, and how he desired to display himself; also, how unwilling he was that his vices should escape notice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: threefold, triple.

examples.original: Longe illi triplex murus totidemque arces, portus ille marmoreus et fons celebratus Arethusae;
examples.translation: Of no avail were its triple walls, its three citadels, its harbour of marble and the celebrated Fountain of Arethusa;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to feel pity, have compassion, to pity, compassionate, commiserate.

examples.original: Persuadebo deinde tibi, ne umquam boni viri miserearis;
examples.translation: I shall induce you, in fine, never to commiserate a good man.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Debet enim, misere si forte aegreque futurumst, ipse quoque esse in eo tum tempore, cui male possit accidere.
examples.translation: For,c if by chance anyone is to have misery and pain in the future, he must himself also exist then in that time to be miserable.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Iam iam, Dolabella, neque me tui neque tuorum liberum, quos tu miseros in egestate atque in solitudine reliquisti, misereri potest.
examples.translation: After this, Dolabella, I can feel no pity for you; nor, after this, for the unhappy children you have left behind you in poverty and loneliness.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a rower, oarsman

examples.original: Caesaris naves a binis remigum in senos nec amplius ordines creverant;
examples.translation: Caesar’s ships had from two to six banks of oars and no more;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Milites remigesque Miletum Myndo pedibus reverti iubet: ipse myoparonem pulcherrimum, de decem Milesiorum navibus electum, L. Magio et L. Fannio, qui Myndi habitabant, vendidit.
examples.translation: But I will ask you to listen to another story, which can neither by any means be suppressed nor be told as it deserves to be told.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: want, lack, scarcity.

examples.original: Eam propter inopiam aerarii consules vendiderunt.
examples.translation: These the consuls sold, owing to the impoverished condition of the treasury.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Is, quod in his locis inopia frumenti erat, praefectos tribunosque militum complures in finitimas civitates frumenti causa dimisit;
examples.translation: As there was a lack of corn in those parts, he despatched several commandants and tribunes into the neighbouring states to seek it.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Caesar Avarici complures dies commoratus summamque ibi copiam frumenti et reliqui commeatus nactus exercitum ex labore atque inopia refecit.
examples.translation: Caesar halted at Avaricum for several days, and by the immense quantity of corn and all other supplies which he found there recuperated the army after toil and want.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: The river Tiber, now Tevere

examples.original: Inter eum locum et Fidenas Veientium exercitus Tiberim transierat.
examples.translation: The Veientine army had crossed the Tiber between that place and Fidenae.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Idem tunc Faesulae quod Carrhae nuper, idem nemus Aricinum quod Hercynius saltus, Fregellae quod Gesoriacum, Tiberis quod Euphrates.
examples.translation: Faesulae meant the same to us then as Carrhae lately meant; the Arician Wood corresponded to the Hercynian Forest, Fregellae to Gesoriacum, the Tiber to the Euphrates.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Ager Tarquiniorum, qui inter urbem ac Tiberim fuit, consecratus Marti Martius deinde campus fuit.
examples.translation: The land of the Tarquinii, lying between the City and the Tiber, was consecrated to Mars and became the Campus Martius.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a hostage

examples.original: Cuius postulationem Antonius cum iudicaret ab iusto nasci timore, veniam petenti dedit, obsides accepit.
examples.translation: Judging that this demand proceeded from a legitimate fear, Antonius indulged his petition and accepted his hostages.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ille obsidibus acceptis hostium se habiturum numero confirmat, si aut Ambiorigem aut eius legatos finibus suis recepissent.
examples.translation: He accepted their hostages, and assured them that he would regard them as enemies if they received either Ambiorix or his deputies within their borders.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Volscos consilii poenam non metuentes necopinata res perculit; armorum immemores obsides dant trecentos principum a Cora atque Pometia liberos.
examples.translation: They had no thought of resisting, and surrendered as hostages three hundred children of the nobility of Cora and Pometia, and so the legions were withdrawn without a conflict.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to fear, dread any thing; to be afraid, terrified, frightened (class.; syn.: metuo, timeo, vereor, trepido, tremo, paveo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

definitions: English: sumptuous food or dishes (cf.: daps, commissatio, convivium, cena, etc.).

examples.original: Plenum epulis madidumque mero Venerique paratum Invenies;
examples.translation: You will find him sated with feasting, drunken with wine, and ripe for amorous dalliance;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: At vero praeclarum diem illis reposuisti Verria ut agerent, et ut ad eum diem quae sacris epulisque opus essent in complures annos locarentur.
examples.translation: What a day for which to make contracts, years in advance, for supplying the materials of its ceremonies and banquets!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Vaesanus in ortus Cambyses longi populos pervenit ad aevi, Defectusque epulis et pastus caede suorum Ignoto te, Nile, redit.
examples.translation: The madman Cambyses penetrated the East as far as the land of the long-lived people; food ran short, and he had to feed on his own men;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: fleeing away, fugitive; usually

examples.original: Tunc urbibus exutum regem et iam finium suorum regnique fugitivum per Mauros atque Gaetuliam sequebatur.
examples.translation: He then pursued the king, stripped of his cities and now a fugitive from his country and kingdom, through Mauretania and Gaetulia.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to shut out, shut off.

examples.original: Sed si veridico animo ista scribitis, quis vobis ad hanc veritatem interclusit viam?
examples.translation: But if what you wrote is a genuine expression of your mind, who has barred your way to this truth?
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Aberat tunc Caesar Ravennae dilectum agens, et hieme creverant Alpes: sic interclusum putabant iter.
examples.translation: Caesar was absent at the time holding a levy at Ravenna, and the Alps had been swollen by winter snows;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Fusa primo concursu acies; in fugam versa milia octo armatorum ab equitibus interclusa positis armis in deditionem venerunt.
examples.translation: Their line broke at the first assault, and in the rout eight thousand soldiers were cut off by the cavalry, and laying down their arms, surrendered.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a quality, property, nature, state, condition
English: that may be borne, bearable, supportable, endurable, passable, tolerable (class.)

examples.original: Sed hos tolerabiles intervalla faciunt.
examples.translation: The suffering, however, is rendered endurable by interruptions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Non de me nunc tecum loquor, qui multum ab homine tolerabili, nedum a perfecto absum, sed de illo, in quem fortuna ius perdidit.
examples.translation: Of course I am not speaking to you of myself at this point, because I am far from being a perfect person, or even a man of middling qualities;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sic invenies servum qui flagellis quam colaphis caedi malit et qui mortem ac verbera tolerabiliora credat quam contumeliosa verba.
examples.translation: And so you will find the slave who would rather be struck with the lash than the fist, who considers stripes and death more endurable than insulting words.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to seek or search for, to procure, bring together, collect (class.; esp. freq. in the histt.).

examples.original: Quam multa ab iis conquisita et collecta sunt de omnium animantium genere, ortu, membris, aetatibus!
examples.translation: What stores of facts they observed and recorded about the classification, reproduction, morphology and life-history of animals of every kind!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a standing-place, abode, habitation, dwelling.

examples.original: Ab eo ad stabula Larentiae uxori educandos datos. Sunt qui Larentiam vulgato corpore lupam inter pastores vocatam putent: inde locum fabulae ac miraculo datum.
examples.translation: Some think that Larentia, having been free with her favours, had got the name of ”she-wolf” among the shepherds, and that this gave rise to this marvellous story.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To draw violently hither and thither something that is firm or quiet (esp. a tree, house, and the like)

examples.original: Audisse te scribis Serapionem philosophum, cum istuc adplicuisset: ”Solet magno cursu verba convellere, quae non effundit una, sed premit et urguet.
examples.translation: You write me that you heard a lecture by the philosopher Serapio,a when he landed at your present place of residence.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to render sacred or inviolable by a religious act; to appoint as sacred or inviolable.

examples.original: At ubi coepi subscribere, sancta Melania contradixit.
examples.translation: But when I began to subscribe it, the saintly Melania opposed it.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Pater patratus ad ius iurandum patrandum, id est sanciendum fit foedus;
examples.translation: The pater patratus is appointed to pronounce the oath, that is, to solemnize the pact;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Eodem anno M. Valerius consul de provocatione legem tulit diligentius sanctam.
examples.translation: In the same year Marcus Valerius the consul proposed a law of appeal with stricter sanctions.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to make faulty, to injure, spoil

examples.original: Decessit autem vitio stomachi anno aetatis XXX.
examples.translation: He died of a stomach trouble in the thirtieth year of his age.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

examples.original: Atqui hoc perspicuum est, vitia alia aliis esse maiora;
examples.translation: Now, that some vices are worse than others is certain;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Institutum etiam ab iisdem consulibus ut senatus consulta in aedem Cereris ad aediles plebis deferrentur, quae antea arbitrio consulum supprimebantur vitiabanturque.
examples.translation: Up to that time they were wont to be suppressed or falsified, at the pleasure of the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: dumb, mute (class.; cf.: infans, elinguis).
Latin: Qui loqui non potest
Latin: Silens

examples.original: Nocte tota ieiuni mutique perstant.
examples.translation: All night long they must stand about, hungry and dumb.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Prodierat: visa coniuge mutus erat.
examples.translation: His hands dropped, and from his hands the double tablet;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cum omnia feceris, a mutis animalibus decore vinceris.
examples.translation: After all your efforts, dumb animals surpass you in comeliness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to handle, touch, feel a thing (class.; cf.: tango, tracto).
English: harmless, innoxious.

examples.original: Ne candidatis quidem honores reisve tam innoxiis quam nocentibus absolutiones venditare cunctatus est.
examples.translation: He made no bones of selling offices to candidates and acquittals to men under prosecution, whether innocent or guilty.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Qui se absolvere non rebantur ea lege ne innoxium quidem posse, cum condemnassent, tum alter ex iis ”P. Horati, tibi perduellionem iudico,” inquit;
examples.translation: They considered that they might not acquit, under that act, even one who was innocent, and having given a verdict of guilty, one of them pronounced the words, ”Publius Horatius, I adjudge you a traitor;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Irae atque iracundiae conscius sibi, utramque excusavit edicto distinxitque, pollicitus alteram quidem brevem et innoxiam, alteram non iniustam fore.
examples.translation: He was conscious of his tendency to wrath and resentment and excused both in an edict;
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a giving freely, a granting, bestowing, dispensing, distributing, imparting.

examples.original: Idem ille populus, postea quam maius imperium est nactus et largitione magistratuum corruptus est, trecentas statuas Demetrio Phalereo decrevit.
