examples.translation: But that same people, after it had gained greater power and was corrupted by the largess of the magistrates, voted three hundred statues to Demetrius of Phalerum.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Militiades

examples.original: Donativum militi neque Mucianus prima contione nisi modice ostenderat, ne Vespasianus quidem plus civili bello obtulit quam alii in pace, egregie firmus adversus militarem largitionem eoque exercitu meliore.
examples.translation: In his first speech Mucianus had held out hopes of only a moderate donative to the soldiers; even Vespasian did not offer more for civil war than others did in time of peace.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Eadem largitione civitatum quoque ac provinciarum animos adgressus Hispalensibus et Emeritensibus familiarum adiectiones, Lingonibus universis civitatem Romanam, provinciae Baeticae Maurorum civitates dono dedit;
examples.translation: With the same generosity Otho tried to win over the support of communities and provinces. To the colonies of Hispalis and Emerita he sent additional families.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: the Sabines, an ancient Italian people adjoining the Latins, a part of whom, as early as the time of Romulus, were united with the Romans as one people, under the name of Quirites

examples.original: Appius Claudius ex Sabinis Romam transfugit.
examples.translation: Appius Claudius came over from the Sabines to the Romans.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Super belli Sabini metum id quoque accesserat, quod triginta iam coniurasse populos concitante Octavio Mamilio satis constabat.
examples.translation: Besides the Sabine peril, it was generally known that the thirty Latin cities had already conspired, at the instigation of Octavius Mamilius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Alter consul Aemilius in Sabinis bellum gessit.
examples.translation: The other consul, Aemilius, conducted a campaign in the Sabine country.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to tear off or away, to pull or rend off (syn.: abripio, eximo).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; velli or vulsi, vulsum or volsum, 3
principalParts: velli or vulsi, vulsum or volsum, 3

examples.original: Et ais prioribus comitiis Aniensem a Plotio Pedio, Teretinam a Plancio tibi esse concessam: nunc ab utroque eas avulsas, ne in angustum venirent.
examples.translation: You allege, moreover, that at the former electionb Plotius agreed to surrender the tribe of Anio to Pedius, and Plancius the Teretine tribe to yourself;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the name of several cities of antiquity.—The most considerable were
Latin: Civitas praeclarissima Graeciae

examples.original: Damnat apud gentes sceleris non sponte peracti Oedipodionias infelix fabula Thebas: Parthorum dominus quotiens sic sanguine mixto Nascitur Arsacides!
examples.translation: Their own sisters lie on the couches of the kings, and, for all the sanctity of the relation, their own mothers.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Hic magno cum pondere auri Thebas venit et Micythum adulescentulum quinque talentis ad suam perduxit voluntatem, quem tum Epaminondas plurimum diligebat.
examples.translation: Diomedon came to Thebes with a great amount of gold, and with five talents won the support of a young man named Micythus, to whom Epaminondas was greatly attached at that time.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

examples.original: Et illi quidem consul pacem dedit regnumque concessit, mox, ne quid esset hostile, Thebas et Euboeam et grassantem sub Nabide tyranno suo Lacedaemona conpescuit.
examples.translation: To Philip, then, the consul granted peace and restored to him his kingdom, and afterwards, that no foe might remain, subdued Thebes and Euboea and Lacedaemon, which attempted resistance under its tyrant Nabis.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: twenty each, twenty distributively.

examples.original: Et quo sint mirabiliores quam Alexander aut quisquam rex, denos vicenosque dies quidam dictaturam, nemo plus quam annum consulatum gessit;
examples.translation: And what makes them more wonderful than Alexander or any king is this: some were dictators of ten or twenty days, and none held the consulship above a year;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a deep sleep.
English: to draw together, bind together, to bind, tie up (class. in prose and poetry).
English: a furnishing, providing, preparing; a preparation.

examples.original: Quid ego de M. Marcello loquar, qui Syracusas urbem ornatissimam cepit?
examples.translation: Need I quote the example of Marcus Marcellus, who captured Syracuse, that treasury of art?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: one who cuts or cuts off, a cutter (rare but class.).
Latin: Qui secat
Latin: Pars circuli
English: of fire, fiery, on fire, burning, burning-hot (cf.: fervidus, calidus).
Latin: Qui ignitus est; fervidus
English: to sit down, crouch down, squat; to set one's self down, settle down, sink down (class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; sēdi, sessum, 3

examples.original: Haec cogitatio nihil sordidum animo subsidere sinit, nihil humile, nihil crudele.
examples.translation: Such thoughts permit nothing mean to settle in the soul, nothing low, nothing cruel.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ibi modico praesidio relicto egressus omnibus copiis partem militum locis circa densa virgulta obscuris subsidere in insidiis iussit;
examples.translation: A part of his men he ordered to lie in ambush, on this side and on that, where thick underbrush afforded cover;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to fall, sink, slip down (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Si tibi per tutum planumque negabitur ire, Atque erit opposita ianua fulta sera, At tu per praeceps tecto delabere aperto: Det quoque furtivas alta fenestra vias.
examples.translation: If it is denied you to go by a safe and easy road, and if the door be held by a fastened bolt, yet slip down headlong through an opening in the roof;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: To knock, strike, or dash out, to tear out, to force out, squeeze out.
English: familiarity, intimacy, familiar intercourse, friendship, intimate acquaintance.

examples.original: Eorum querella inveterata non modo familiaritates exstingui solere, sed odia etiam gigni sempiterna.
examples.translation: By their ceaseless recriminations not only are social intimacies usually destroyed, but also everlasting enmities are produced.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ut Antonius rediit in Italiam, nemo non magno in periculo Atticum putarat propter intimam familiaritatem Ciceronis et Bruti.
examples.translation: Antony returned to Italy, and there was no one but thought that Atticus was in extreme danger because of his intimacy with Cicero and Brutus.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: Excerpt From The Book Of Latin Historians. Atticus

examples.original: Hic primo Carpinatius, antequam in istius familiaritatem tantam pervenisset, aliquotiens ad socios litteras de istius iniuriis miserat.
examples.translation: In the early days, before establishing this close connexion with Verres, Carpinatius had several times written to the company complaining of wrongs done by Verres;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: place, or set under (freq. and class.; cf.: submitto, subicio).

examples.original: Quattuor in nucibus, non amplius, alea tota est, Cum sibi suppositis additur una tribus.
examples.translation: In four nuts, and no more, is all his hazard, when one is added to the three beneath it.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Evolvam busto iam numen gentibus Isim Et tectum lino spargam per volgus Osirim, Suppositisque deis uram caput.
examples.translation: And the land I shall punish too; I shall leave their fields with none to till them;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the brain

examples.original: Mentis valitudinem et ipse senserat ac subinde de secessu deque purgando cerebro cogitavit.
examples.translation: He himself realised his mental infirmity, and thought at times of going into retirement and clearing his brain.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Movet cerebrum non uno genere; alios in aliud irritat, hos in potentiam, illos in luxuriam.
examples.translation: It stirs the brain in more ways than one, goading men on to various aims,—some to power, and others to high living.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to seek after, search for, inquire into any thing (cf. anquirere).
Latin: In aliqua re quaerere

examples.original: Quid inter sapientiam et sapere intersit, inquiris?
examples.translation: Do you ask what difference there is between wisdom and being wise?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Noli ergo atrocius vindicare quod lenius invenisti. Inquirendi quam puniendi neces-sitas maior est;
examples.translation: Do not then punish with harsher sentence what you found out by gentler methods.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to set right by word or deed, to correct, chastise, punish; to blame, reprove, chide, censure, find fault with
English: To assent to as good, to regard as good, to approve
Latin: Sentire aliquid bonum esse
Latin: Ostendere aliquid bonum esse

examples.original: Pontificibus bona causa visa est: approbaverunt.
examples.translation: The Pontifical College thought your reason a just one, and gave their sanction.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to stand at or near a person or thing, to stand by, stand (syn.: adsisto, adsum, faveo).
English: a dislocation (ante- and post-class.)

examples.original: Verum haec ex comoedia quibus impiorum luxus et sacrilega superstitio convinceretur, proferre forsitan non debemus.
examples.translation: And yet perhaps I should not put forward these scenes from comedy to confute the wantonness and the sacrilegious superstition of the ungodly.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Accedebat huc Caecinae ambitio vetus, torpor recens, nimia fortunae indulgentia soluti in luxum, seu perfidiam meditanti infringere exercitus virtutem inter artes erat.
examples.translation: Another factor in the situation was furnished by Caecina’s old ambition and his newly acquired sloth, for an excess of Fortune’s favours had made him give way to luxury;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Inde opes et rerum secundarum luxus: spreto Venutio (is fuit maritus) armigerum eius Vellocatum in matrimonium regnumque accepit.
examples.translation: She grew to despise her husband Venutius, and took as her consort his squire Vellocatus, whom she admitted to share the throne with her.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to make new, to renew

examples.original: Erat et nova exorta causa motus.
examples.translation: There had also arisen a new cause for disquiet.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Magister equitum et ipse novat pugnam equestrem.
examples.translation: The master of the horse on his part invented a new kind of cavalry-fighting.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ostendit enim novo modo, si quis quid de absente peteret, se auditurum.
examples.translation: He showed in a new way that he was ready to try any claims against an absent man.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to deprive or bereave of parents, children, or other dear persons; to make fatherless, motherless, childless, etc. (class.; syn.: privo, viduo).

examples.original: Non eadem belli totum fortuna per orbem Constitit, in partes aliquid sed Caesaris ausa est.
examples.translation: The fortune of war did not remain unchanged all the world over, but dared to strike one blow against Caesar’s side.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ipse caput medio Titan cum ferret Olympo, Condidit ardentes atra caligine currus Involvitque orbem tenebris gentesque coegit Desperare diem;
examples.translation: The sun himself, while rearing his head in the zenith, hid his burning chariot in black darkness and veiled his sphere in gloom, forcing mankind to despair of daylight;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quod ne intermitteretur opus neu sub terra continuus labor eosdem conficeret, in partes sex munitorum numerum divisit; senae horae in orbem operi attributae sunt;
examples.translation: That this work might not be interrupted nor the same men become exhausted by perpetually toiling under ground, he divided the workers into six parties and assigned them six-hour shifts in rotation;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: narrowness, straitness; a defile, strait (perhaps only in prose; syn.: fauces, angustum).
Latin: Locus angustus, in quo quis libere se movere et agere nequit
Latin: Partes terrae quae angustae sunt

examples.original: Hic ego in tantis angustiis quasi aura spirante recreatus nihil ei respondi, sed ad fratrem Alypium gradu concitatiore perrexi eique quid dixerit, dixi.
examples.translation: At such an impasse, this refreshed me like a breath of air, but I said nothing to him and went with hurried step to brother Alypius and told him what he had said.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: In what way soever, howsoever, however (class.).

examples.original: Horum alterum utcumque recipi potest.
examples.translation: But the former may be attained in any case.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Se tamen, utcumque sit, etiam nunc paenitere sua sponte Aequos quam pati hostilia malle.
examples.translation: If they did so, they could count on a safe refuge in the clemency they had already proved;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Aequiore animo utcumque ferrem, si plebei duces aut, si nobiles, mali saltem ducatum sceleri praebuissent. Tum vero—pro facinus—qui viri!
examples.translation: It would be possible to bear the calamity with greater equanimity, if plebeian leaders, or leaders who, if noble, were yet bad men, had taken the chief part in such wickedness.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to burn up, consume (class.).

examples.original: Egerat cum Vario, priusquam Italia decederet, ut siquid sibi accidisset, ”Aeneida” combureret; at is ita facturum se pernegarat;
examples.translation: He had arranged with Varius, before leaving Italy, that if anything befell him his friend should burn the ”Aeneid”;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

examples.original: Legatos quippe nostros, ob ea quae deliquerant iure agentes, ne gladio quidem, sed ut victimas securi percutiunt, praefectos navium igne comburunt;
examples.translation: To make their action still more insulting, it was a woman that gave the order.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam quaero abs te circumsessusne sis Lampsaci, coeperitne domum in qua deversabare illa multitudo incendere, voluerintne legatum populi Romani comburere vivum Lampsaceni? Negare non potes;
examples.translation: That you were besieged at Lampsacum, that the crowd there began to set fire to the house where you were staying, that the people of Lampsacum intended to burn a Roman governor alive?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To drive or turn in a circle, turn round
English: to stand in awe or fear of; to regard, respect

examples.original: Sermo erga patrem imperatoremque reverens, de se moderatus;
examples.translation: He answered with the reverence due to a father and an emperor;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Cum iam profeceris tantum, ut sit tibi etiam tui reverentia, licebit dimittas paedagogum;
examples.translation: And when you have progressed so far that you have also respect for yourself, you may send away your attendant;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: hardness.

examples.original: Vita omnis in venationibus atque in studiis rei militaris consistit: ab parvulis labori ac duritiae student.
examples.translation: Their whole life is composed of hunting expeditions and military pursuits; from early boyhood they are zealous for toil and hardship.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: the resemblance or agreement of several things; in gram., the analogy of language, analogy
Latin: Prōportiō, convenientia, similitūdō

examples.original: Quae sit haec analogia, dicam.
examples.translation: Now what this ”analogy” is, I shall explain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: it pleases, is pleasing, is agreeable: mihi, I am disposed, I like, I please, I will.— Constr. with
English: a striking against any thing; a tripping, stumbling (class.).

examples.original: Virtus enim tantum bonum est, ut istas accessiones minutas non sentiat, brevitatem aevi et dolorem et corporum varias offensiones.
examples.translation: For virtue is so great a good that it is not affected by such insignificant assaults upon it as shortness of life, pain, and the various bodily vexations.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Huius iudicii et laudis fructum et offensionis periculum vestrum, laborem sollicitudinemque nostram, scientiam quid agatur, memoriamque quid a quoque dictum sit, omnium puto esse oportere.
examples.translation: My calling of my witnesses at once will be no novelty; that has been done before, and by men who now hold leading positions in the country.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the quality of one benignus, an affable, kind bearing to others.

examples.original: Summa est enim, iudices, hominis in communem municipii rem diligentia, in singulos municipes benignitas, in omnes homines iustitia et fides.
examples.translation: For nothing, gentlemen, can exceed my client’s devotion to the general good of his town, his kindness to its individual members, his uprightness and sincerity to all men.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to associate
Latin: Donare ad aliquem, ad aliquam, ad aliquos

examples.original: Ne diutius teneam, pecunia attributa, numerata est;
examples.translation: To cut the story short: funds were allotted and paid over to the quaestor;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Titum Labienum duabus cum legionibus et equitatu in Sequanos proficisci iubet: huic Marcum Sempronium Rutilum attribuit.
examples.translation: He ordered Titus Labienus with two legions and cavalry to march off into the country of the Sequani, attaching Marcus Sempronius Rutilus to him.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Erat attributus Antonio praefectus equitum C. Volusenus Quadratus qui cum eo hibernaret. Hunc Antonius ad persequendum equitatum hostium mittit.
examples.translation: Gaius Volusenus Quadratus had been attached as cavalry commander to Antonius, to winter with him, and Antonius despatched him to pursue the enemy’s horse.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: A firm standing, steadiness, firmness, immutability, unchangeableness, constancy, perseverance

examples.original: Hanc dabit animi magnitudo, dabit constantia bene iudicati tenax.
examples.translation: This will be yours if you possess greatness of soul;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: An, quod ad diem non venerunt, de eorum fide constantiaque dubitatis?
examples.translation: Or do you doubt their faithfulness, their resolution, because they are not arrived to the day?
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Constantia non habet, quo procedat, non magis quam fiducia aut veritas aut fides.
examples.translation: Constancy cannot advance further, any more than fidelity, or truthfulness, or loyalty.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a dove, pigeon

examples.original: Ut fugiunt aquilas, timidissima turba, columbae, Ut fugit invisos agna novella lupos: Sic illae timuere viros sine more ruentes;
examples.translation: As doves, most timorous of birds, flee from the eagles, as the weanling lamb from the hated wolf, so feared they the men rushing wildly on them;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: beaver; pure Lat. fiber: Castor fiber, Linn.

examples.original: Hermionam Pylades quo Pallada Phoebus, amabat, Quodque tibi geminus, Tyndari, Castor, erat.
examples.translation: Pylades loved Hermione as Phoebus Pallas, and as twin Castor was to thee, O Tyndaris.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Cum arma in aedem Castoris comportabas, nihil aliud nisi uti ne quid per vim agi posset machinabare?
examples.translation: When you were storing weapons at the temple of Castor, you were merely contriving means to prevent violent proceedings;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sic, ubi detracta est a te tibi causa pericli, Quod superest, tutum, Pontice castor, habes.
examples.translation: So, when the cause of thy peril has been torn from thee, O Pontic beaver, thou keepest safe what is left.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: sidelong, askew, aslant, askance.
English: to be a soldier, to perform military service, to serve as a soldier (syn.: stipendium mereo; class.).

examples.original: Atqui vivere, Lucili, militare est.
examples.translation: And yet life, Lucilius, is really a battle.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Perstare militem, superesse studia populi;
examples.translation: In desperation at least you must gird yourself to bold action.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Hic omnem militarem disciplinam artemque bellandi condidit.
examples.translation: It was he who founded all military discipline and the art of warfare.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: Hospitality (class.)

examples.original: Cum his esse hospitium Ambiorigi sciebat;
examples.translation: He knew that Ambiorix had a formal friendship with them;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ibi benigne excepti divisique in hospitia.
examples.translation: There they were kindly received and were quartered about among the citizens.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nocti se potius ac solitudini quam ulli aut urbi aut hospiti committebat.
examples.translation: And so in no town was she allowed to halt;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to come continually nearer to a point

examples.original: Magna res est, Lucili, haec et diu discenda, cum adventat hora illa inevitabilis, aequo animo abire.
examples.translation: This is a great accomplishment, Lucilius, and one which needs long practice to learn,—to depart calmly when the inevitable hour arrives.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to fasten down or in; and with especial reference to the terminus, to drive, fix, or fasten into (class.). —

examples.original: Sed et conloquium fuit inter ipsos de legibus pacis, et steterunt diu mutua admiratione defixi.
examples.translation: But first a conference was held between them about terms of peace, and they stood for a while motionless in mutual admiration.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: the most celebrated of the Grecian orators
English: ivory.
Latin: Dens elephanti avulsus, qui candore et spissitudine materiae in operibus valde commendatur
Latin: Per synecdochen, dicitur de rebus ex ebore factis

examples.original: Auro illos et argento et ebore adornavi, intus boni nihil est.
examples.translation: I have bedecked them with gold, and silver, and ivory, but within there is nothing good.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to a woman, womanly
Latin: Ad feminam pertinens
Latin: Ad feminam pertinens. Femineus sexus Marte femineo cadere

examples.original: Omnia feminea sunt ista libidine mota;
examples.translation: All those crimes were prompted by women’s lust;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Epulis vaesana meroque Regia non ullis exceptos legibus audet Concubitus: tot femineis conplexibus unum Non lassat nox tota marem.
examples.translation: The king, maddened with feasting and wine, ventures on unions that no laws have ever specified;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Ipsa flagellabant gaudentis colla Medusae, Femineae cui more comae per terga solutae Surgunt adversa subrectae fronte colubrae, Vipereumque fluit depexo crine venenum.
examples.translation: It pleased Medusa, when snakes dangled close against her neck; in the way that women dress their hair, the vipers hang loose over her back but rear erect over her brow in front;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: imitation (class.; cf. aemulatio).

examples.original: Haec ergo et eiusmodi vitia, quae alicui inpressit imitatio, non sunt indicia luxuriae nec animi corrupti;
examples.translation: These and similar faults, which imitation stamps upon one’s style, are not necessarily indications of loose standards or of debased mind;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nobis itaque cordi est neque Christianam amittere mansuetudinem neque perniciosum ceteris imitationis exemplum in illa civitate relinquere.
examples.translation: Therefore is it our dear desire neither to put away Christian meekness nor to leave your country as a baleful example for others to follow.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: lean, meagre.

examples.original: Isdem diebus a Martio Macro haud procul Cremona prospere pugnatum;
examples.translation: During these same days, Martius Macer had had a successful engagement not far from Cremona;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Macer Licinius tertia etiam clade, quae ad Cremeram accepta est, abominandam eam curiam facit.
examples.translation: Licinius Macer makes this ward unlucky also for a third disaster—that of the Cremera.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nomina consulum horum Licinius Macer auctor est et in foedere Ardeatino et in linteis libris ad Monetae inventa.
examples.translation: Licinius Macer testifies that the names of these consuls were given both in the treaty with Ardea and in the Linen Rolls in the temple of Moneta.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the poppy.
Latin: Flos familiae Papaveraceae, praesertim generis Papaver
English: to show to be false; to disprove, rebut, confute, refute, repel
Latin: cuiusdam mendacium aperire
English: a rising again from the dead, resurrection
English: a punisher, avenger, revenger.

examples.original: Sulla quoque inmensis accessit cladibus ultor.
examples.translation: And then, to crown the infinite slaughter, came Sulla’s vengeance.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that can contain or hold much, wide

examples.original: Quid lapideas moles in rotundum ac leve formatas, quibus porticus et capacia populorum tecta suscipimus?
examples.translation: Or the rounded and polished masses of stone by means of which we erect colonnades and buildings roomy enough for nations?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Urbem populis victisque frequentem Gentibus et generis, coeat si turba, capacem Humani facilem venturo Caesare praedam Ignavae liquere manus.
examples.translation: Rome that was crowded with citizens and conquered peoples, Rome that could contain the human race assembled, was left by coward hands an easy prey to invading Caesar.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: unsuitable, impertinent, improper, tasteless, senseless, silly, pedantic, absurd, inept, without tact (class.)
English: To pull asunder, tear in pieces, to separate forcibly, divide (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Cum visum erit, distraham cum illo societatem.
examples.translation: When it seems proper, I shall sever my connexion with it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Itaque hoste victo ruptorem foederis Mettum Fufetium religatum inter duos currus pernicibus equis distrahit, Albamque ipsam quamvis parentem, aemulam tamen diruit, cum prius omnes opes urbis ipsumque populum Romam transtulisset;
examples.translation: So after the defeat of the enemy Tullus bound Mettus Fufetius, the violator of the treaty, between two chariots, and tore him asunder with swift horses.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: without shame, shameless, impudent

examples.original: Non, opinor, tam impudens esses.
examples.translation: I do not believe you would have the effrontery.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Defert ad istum rem Habonius: ut sibi videatur, satis grandem pecuniam et satis impudentem esse.
examples.translation: Habonius reported this to Verres, observing that in his opinion this was a fairly large and shameless sum.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Magnum crimen et impudens mendacium.
examples.translation: It is a monstrous charge, and a shameless lie!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: dirt, filth, uncleanness

examples.original: Alexandrini Cybiosacten eum vocare perseveraverunt, cognomine unius e regibus suis turpissimarum sordium.
examples.translation: The Alexandrians persisted in calling him Cybiosactes, the surname of one of their kings who was scandalously stingy.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Ulline Italiae alumni et Romana vere iuventus ad sanguinem et caedem depoposcerit ordinem, cuius splendore et gloria sordis et obscuritatem Vitellianarum partium praestringimus ?
examples.translation: Shall any child of Italy, any true Roman youth, demand the blood and murder of that order through whose splendid glory we outshine the meanness and base birth of the partisans of Vitellius?
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Atqui ista magis inquinant animos quam corpora, et in possessore eorum quam in artifice plus sordium est.
examples.translation: And yet the stuff they handle soils the soul more than the body, and there is more foulness in the owner than in the workman.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a solemn procession, a public procession of any kind (at public festivals, games, triumphs, marriages, funerals, etc.).

examples.original: Quid sibi vult ista pecuniae pompa?
examples.translation: What is the meaning of all this display of money?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Licet sapere sine pompa, sine invidia.
examples.translation: A man may be wise without parade and without arousing enmity.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nunc neque te longi remeantem pompa triumphi Excipit, aut sacras poscunt Capitolia laurus;
examples.translation: As it is, no long triumphal procession awaits your return, nor does the Capitol demand your consecrated laurels;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: slippery.

examples.original: Nondum enim incerta transgressus est, etiamnunc versatur in lubrico.
examples.translation: For such a man has not yet traversed the doubtful ground;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Virtus illa divina in lubricum desinit et superioribus eius partibus venerandis atque caelestibus animal iners ac marcidum adtexitur.
examples.translation: This divine virtue ends in foulness, and to the higher parts, which are worshipful and heavenly, there is fastened a sluggish and flabby animal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to twist out, wrench out, wrest away (class.).

examples.original: Quod si in hoc erro, qui animos hominum immortalis esse credam, libenter erro nec mihi hunc errorem, quo delector, dum vivo, extorqueri volo;
examples.translation: And if I err in my belief that the souls of men are immortal, I gladly err, nor do I wish this error which gives me pleasure to be wrested from me while I live.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illud quod proprie ad milites pertinet, quibus boni tribuni plebis tum stipendium extorquere voluerunt, nunc consultum repente volunt, quale est?
examples.translation: The rampart and the trench, each involving prodigious toil, they have carried all that distance;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: African

examples.original: Munera gladiatoria partim in amphitheatro Tauri partim in Saeptis aliquot edidit, quibus inseruit catervas Afrorum Campanorumque pugilum ex utraque regione electissimorum.
examples.translation: He gave several gladiatorial shows, some in the amphitheatre of Taurus and some in the Saepta, in which he introduced pairs of African and Campanian boxers, the pick of both regions.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a lesson, example (either for instruction or warning); a pattern, warning; a proof, instance

examples.original: Numquam virtutis molle documentum est.
examples.translation: No proof of virtue is ever mild.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Maiore adeo et favore et auctoritate adeptus est quam gessit imperium, quanquam multa documenta egregii principis daret;
examples.translation: Thus his popularity and prestige were greater when he won, than while he ruled the empire, though he gave many proofs of being an excellent prince;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Hoc illud est praecipue in cognitione rerum salubre ac frugiferum, omnis te exempli documenta in inlustri posita monumento intueri;
examples.translation: What chiefly makes the study of history wholesome and profitable is this, that you behold the lessons of every kind of experience set forth as on a conspicuous monument;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a hollow, a cavity.

examples.original: Quid turpius ”amne silvisque ripa comantibus?” Vide ut ”alveum lintribus arent versoque vado remittant hortos.” Quid?
examples.translation: What is more unbecoming than the words:c ”A stream and a bank covered with long-tressed woods”?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: on the day after, the following or next day (class.)

examples.original: Postridie eius diei Caesar praesidium utrisque castris, quod satis esse visum est, reliquit;
examples.translation: On the next day Caesar left what he deemed a sufficient garrison for each camp;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Postridie mane descendit; Agathinum ad sese vocat, iubet eum de litteris publicis in absentem Sthenium dicere.
examples.translation: The next morning he arrived early, sent for Agathinus, and bade him prosecute Sthenius for forgery in his absence.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: boyhood, childhood, youth (applied usually till the seventeenth year, but freq. later; v. puer, II.): qui enim citius adulescentiae senectus quam pueritiae adulescentia obrepit?

examples.original: Pueritia ac iuventa, qualem monstravimus.
examples.translation: His boyhood and youth were such as we have already described.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Est qui totam pueritiam ambitu suo adstringit.
examples.translation: The third confines all of childhood in its circumference.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Infantiam amisimus, deinde pueritiam, deinde adulescentiam.
examples.translation: We lose our childhood, then our boyhood, and then our youth.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Of or belonging to accounts (post-Aug.): LITTERAE, Inscr. (a. p. Chr. 193) Orell. 39.—Hence

examples.original: Rationale enim animal est homo.
examples.translation: For man is a reasoning animal.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Superest ut rationalem partem philosophiae dividam.
examples.translation: It remains for me to divide rational philosophy into its parts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quaedam enim, ut scis, moralibus rationalia inmixta sunt.
examples.translation: For, as you know, certain logical questions are mingled with ethical ones.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: according to religious ceremonies or observances; and pregn., with due religious observances or rites, according to religious usage
English: wicked, villanous, infamous, accursed, abominable; knavish, roguish; and

examples.original: Quae ubi Camillus audivit, ”Non ad similem” inquit ”tui nec populum nec imperatorem scelestus ipse cum scelesto munere venisti.
examples.translation: On hearing this Camillus answered: ”Neither the people nor the captain to whom you are come, you scoundrel, with your scoundrel’s gift, is like yourself.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the staff or rod with which a slave was touched in the ceremony of manumission, a liberating-rod, manumission - staff.

examples.original: Dignatur viles isto quoque sanguine dextras, Quo Fortuna parat victos perfundere patres, Poenaque civilis belli, vindicta senatus, Paene data est famulo.
examples.translation: Once again he aspires to shed blood by base-born hands—that blood with which Fortune intended to drench the defeated Senators;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: the place where the bodies of the dead were burned and buried; later also, in gen., for a tomb: bustum proprie dicitur locus, in quo mortuus est combustus et sepultus

examples.original: Viventes animas et adhuc sua membra regentes Infodit busto, fatis debentibus annos Mors invita subit;
examples.translation: At the first sound of her petition the gods grant every horror, dreading to hear a second spell.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Pulveris exigui sparget non longa vetustas Congeriem, bustumque cadet, mortisque peribunt Argumenta tuae.
examples.translation: For a short space of time will scatter the little heap of dust; the grave will fall in;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Petimus non singula busta Discretosque rogos: unum da gentibus ignem, Non interpositis urantur corpora flammis;
examples.translation: We ask not a pyre for each or a separate burning: provide a single fire for all;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To sew, stitch, or join together (very rare; mostly ante- and post-class.).

examples.original: Eo die quo consuerat intervallo hostes sequitur et milia passuum tria ab eorum castris castra ponit.
examples.translation: On that day he followed the enemy at the customary interval, and pitched his camp three miles from theirs.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Usque adeo magni refert studium atque voluntas, et quibus in rebus consuerint esse operati non homines solum, sed vero animalia cuncta.
examples.translation: Of so great import are devotion and inclination, and what those things are which not men only, but indeed all creatures, are in the habit of practising.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Tauromenitani, quorum est civitas foederata, homines quietissimi, qui maxime ab iniuriis nostrorum magistratuum remoti consuerant esse praesidio foederis, hi tamen istius evertere statuam non dubitaverunt;
examples.translation: The people of Tauromenium, a treaty state, are a most inoffensive body of persons, whom their treaty has regularly shielded from any contact with oppression on the part of our officials;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a leaf of the Egyptian papyrus, paper
English: to question strictly or particularly, to inquire earnestly: docte percontat, Aeneas quo pacto, etc., Naev. ap.
English: Another name for Ops, Cybele, Terra, the wife of Cœlus and mother of Saturn
Latin: Terra seu Ops, mater Saturni
Latin: Filia Saturni, dea Romana familiae ac ignis

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam verus ornatus maxime Christianorum et Christianarum non tantum nullus fucus mendax verum ne auri quidem vestisque pompa, sed mores boni sunt.
examples.translation: For not only is lying paint no real adornment of Christian men and women, nor yet is the ostentation of gold and finery; but a good character is.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Illa potest vigiles flammas extinguere Vestae, Et rapere e templis, Inachi, sacra tuis, Et dare mixta viro tritis aconita cicutis, Accepto venerem munere siqua negat.
examples.translation: That woman could extinguish Vesta’s watchful flame, and rob thy temple, Inachis, of its sanctities, and give aconite mixed with pounded hemlock to her lover, who receives a gift and then denies her favours.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: an old and celebrated commercial city of Ionia, with a temple to Diana, now ruins near the village of Ayasaluk
English: to flash, to lighten (syn.: fulguro, splendeo, luceo).

examples.original: Sed tonitrum fit uti post auribus accipiamus, fulgere quam cernant oculi, quia semper ad auris tardius adveniunt quam visum quae moveant res.
examples.translation: But the reason why we hear the thunder after the eyes see the lightning is that things always take longer to reach the ears than to produce vision.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Pari subinde periculo gloriaeque eventu bellum in Samnitibus erat, qui praeter cetoros belli apparatus, ut acies sua fulgeret novis armorum insignibus fecerunt.
examples.translation: The enemy, besides their other warlike preparations, had made their battle-line to glitter with new and splendid arms.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hic peradulescentulus ad amicitiam accessit Philippi, Amyntae filii, brevique tempore in intimam pervenit familiaritatem; fulgebat enim iam in adulescentulo indoles virtutis.
examples.translation: Eumenes, when very young, became the friend of Philip, son of Amyntas, and soon grew very intimate with the king, being conspicuous even in his youth for his high character.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Eumenes

definitions: English: name of a Roman gens.—So, M. Livius Andronicus, the first Roman tragic poet

examples.original: Pontifices creantur suasor legis P. Decius Mus P. Sempronius Sophus C. Marcius Rutulus M. Livius Denter;
examples.translation: To be pontiffs were chosen the advocate of the law, Publius Decius Mus, with Publius Sempronius Sophus, Gaius Marcius Rutulus, and Marcus Livius Denter;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nero in ultimum Italiae angulum summoverat Annibalem, Livius in diversissimam partem, id est in ipsas nascentis Italiae fauces signa converterat.
examples.translation: Nero had driven Hannibal into the uttermost corner of Italy, while Livius had advanced to the very opposite end of the country, the very entrance of the Italian frontier.
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: a talent, i. e.

examples.original: Hoc iudicio damnatur Timotheus lisque eius aestimatur centum talentis.
examples.translation: Timotheus was found guilty and his fine was fixed at one hundred talents.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Timotheus

examples.original: Namque ei Grynium dederat, in Phrygia castrum, ex quo quinquagena talenta vectigalis capiebat.
examples.translation: In fact Pharnabazus gave him Grynium, a stronghold of Phrygia, from which he received a yearly revenue of fifty talents.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Alcibiades

examples.original: Hic magno cum pondere auri Thebas venit et Micythum adulescentulum quinque talentis ad suam perduxit voluntatem, quem tum Epaminondas plurimum diligebat.
examples.translation: Diomedon came to Thebes with a great amount of gold, and with five talents won the support of a young man named Micythus, to whom Epaminondas was greatly attached at that time.
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Epaminondas

definitions: English: to drive away.
Latin: ago aliquid ab alicubi
Latin: abortum facio; syn. elido

examples.original: Temperantia voluptatibus imperat, alias odit atque abigit, alias dispensat et ad sanum modum redigit nec umquam ad illas propter ipsas venit.
examples.translation: Temperance controls our desires; some it hates and routs, others it regulates and restores to a healthy measure, nor does it ever approach our desires for their own sake.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: A Priverno Plautius alter consul pervastatis passim agris praedaque abacta in agrum Fundanum exercitum inducit. Ingredienti fines senatus Fundanorum occurrit;
examples.translation: From Privernum the other consul Plautius, after everywhere pillaging the fields and driving off the cattle, led his army into the domain of Fundi.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Son of Telamon, king of Salamis, and brother of Ajax

examples.original: Nam in provincias quoque grammatica penetraverat, ac nonnulli de notissimis doctoribus peregre docuerunt, maxime in Gallia Togata; inter quos Octavius Teucer et Sescenius Iaccus et Oppius Chares;
examples.translation: In fact, Grammar even made its way into the provinces, and some of the most famous teachers gave instruction abroad, especially in Gallia Togata, including Octavius Teucer, Sescenius Iaccus and Oppius Chares;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: a shrub, bush (cf. arbor).

examples.original: Hos ego, qui canent, frutices violaria vidi: Hac mihi de spina grata corona data est.
examples.translation: These plants, now withering, I saw as violet-beds; from this thorn was a pleasing garland given me.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a period or space of two years, two years: jam biennium est, cum, etc.

examples.original: Hos consules Piso Q. Fabio et P. Decio suggerit biennio exempto quo Claudium Volumniumque et Cornelium cum Marcio consules factos tradidimus.
examples.translation: Piso makes these men follow Quintus Fabius and Publius Decius, omitting the two years in which we have placed the consulship of Claudius and Volumnius and that of Cornelius and Marcius.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Liviam Orestillam C. Pisoni nubentem, cum ad officium et ipse venisset, ad se deduci imperavit intraque paucos dies repudiatam biennio post relegavit, quod repetisse usum prioris mariti tempore medio videbatur.
examples.translation: At the marriage of Livia Orestilla to Gaius Piso, he attended the ceremony himself, gave orders that the bride be taken to his own house, and within a few days divorced her;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: In the shade, shaded, shady (class.)
English: daily (class.; cf. in dies): ibatne ad Bacchidem?

examples.original: Quid enim aliud agis quam ut meliorem te ipse cottidie facias, ut aliquid ex erroribus ponas, ut intellegas tua vitia esse, quae putas rerum?
examples.translation: For what else are you busied with except improving yourself every day, laying aside some error, and coming to understand that the faults which you attribute to circumstances are in yourself?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A bounding, a boundary

examples.original: Atqui haec patefactio quasi rerum opertarum, cum quid quidque sit aperitur, definitio est;
examples.translation: Now this process of disclosing latent meanings, of revealing what a particular thing is, is the process of definition;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the month of expiation (because on the 15th of this month the great feast of expiation and purification, Februa, was held), February, until the time of the decemvirs the last
Latin: Qui ad secundum mensem calendarii Gregoriani, in quo Februa sunt, pertinet
Latin: Secundus mensis calendarii Gregoriani

examples.original: Et vidi non tantum mense Februario positas, sed etiam Martio exacto;
examples.translation: I have seen such plantings made not only in February, but at the very end of March;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: native mineral alkali, native soda, natron; found chiefly in Media, Egypt, Thrace, and Macedonia
Latin: Succus quidam concretus, salis genus, de quo multa Plin. 31. Hist. nat. 10. 46. (106)., ubi docet, colligi aput Medos…
Latin: Quod nos e parietibus et pavimentis colligimus, sal petrae quibusdam dictum

examples.original: Nec cerussa tibi nec nitri spuma rubentis Desit et Illyrica quae venit iris humo.
examples.translation: Nor let white lead nor foam of red nitre be lacking, nor the iris that comes from Illyrian soil.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: One who stands by or is present at any thing, a by-stander, witness (only in the foll. passages)

examples.original: Stante potest mundo Romaque superstite Magnus Esse miser.
examples.translation: The world may remain and Rome survive, though Magnus is doomed.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Uxori ac filiae superstes fuit atque utramque adhuc privatus amisit.
examples.translation: He outlived his wife and daughter; in fact lost them both before he became emperor.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Sic longius aevum Destruit ingentes animos et vita superstes Imperio.
examples.translation: Thus length of days and life surviving power humble the proudest heart.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to bind to, to fasten to, to attach
Latin: Alligare, affigere
English: piur. tantum

examples.original: Ast alias manicaeque ligant teretesque catenae, Seque tenent remis: tecto stetit aequore bellum.
examples.translation: The sea was no longer visible, and the battle became stationary.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Aspiciam regum liventia colla catenis Duraque per saevas vincula nexa manus Et tandem trepidos vultus inque illa ferocum Invitis lacrimas decidere ora genis.
examples.translation: I shall see the necks of kings livid with chains, and ruthless fetters entwining cruel hands, and faces cowed at last, and the tears falling down unwilling, haughty cheeks.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to exercise one's self in rhetorical delivery, to practise speaking, to declaim. For syn. cf.: dictito, concionor, pronuntio, palam dico, praedico, recito, declamito.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Docuit autem et rhetoricam, ita ut quotidie praecepta eloquentiae traderet, declamaret vero nonnisi nundinis.
examples.translation: He taught rhetoric too, giving daily instruction in speaking, but declaiming only once a week.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Sed neque declament medio sermone diserti, Nec sua non sanus scripta poeta legat!” Sic monuit Phoebus: Phoebo parete monenti;
examples.translation: But neither let the eloquent declaim in the midst of talk, nor the frenzied poet recite his verses.” So Phoebus counselled: obey ye Phoebus’ counsels;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: One who drives or moves something

examples.original: Neque enim oratorius iste, immo hercle ne virilis quidem cultus est, quo plerique temporum nostrorum actores ita utuntur ut lascivia verborum et levitate sententiarum et licentia compositionis histrionales modos exprimant.
examples.translation: There is a fashion much in vogue with quite a number of counsel nowadays that ill befits an orator, and is indeed scarce worthy even of a man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: skin, hide, leather.
English: to make prosperous or

examples.original: In mores fortuna ius non habet.
examples.translation: Fortune has no jurisdiction over character.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Etiam quae non est supervacua, nihil in se momenti habet in hoc, ut possit fortunatum beatumque praestare.
examples.translation: And even that which is not superfluous is of no significance in respect to its power of making one fortunate and blest.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Etenim cui non perspicuum est ad incertum revocari bona, fortunas, possessiones omnium, si ulla ex parte sententia huius interdicti deminuta aut infirmata sit?
examples.translation: Who indeed can fail to see that all men’s goods, fortunes and tenures are reduced to insecurity if this injunction be in any respect lessened in scope or weakened in power;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to furnish with a garland or crown, to crown, wreathe (class., esp. freq. in the poets).

examples.original: Fabius Vibulanus corona primum vallum defendit;
examples.translation: Fabius Vibulanus first manned the rampart with a cordon of defenders;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Huc inclinavit Antonius cingique vallum corona iussit.
examples.translation: Antonius inclined to meet his troops’ desires and ordered the investment of the enemy’s camp.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Ceterum nihilo minus foeda dedita urbe quam si capta foret Aurunci passi: principes securi percussi, sub corona venierunt coloni alii;
examples.translation: Their chief men were beheaded, and the rest of the colonists were sold as slaves. The town was razed;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to cleave, split

examples.original: At cum maturas fisso nova cortice rimas Nux agit, ad partes pertica saeva venit;
examples.translation: But when the new nut in due season shows chinks in its splitting rind thither comes the cruel rod;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Coronopus oblonga herba est cum fissuris. seritur interim, quoniam radix coeliacis praeclare facit in cinere tosta.
examples.translation: The coronopus is an elongated plant, with fissures in the leaves. It is sometimes cultivated, as the root, roasted in hot ashes, is found to be an excellent remedy for cœliac complaints.
examples.author: Pliny the Elder

definitions: English: The estimating a thing according to its extrinsic (money) value, valuation, appraisement

examples.original: Ita in aestimationem urbs agerque venit.
examples.translation: Thus the city and the land came into the estimate.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nam qui valetudinem aestimatione aliqua dignam iudicamus neque eam tamen in bonis ponimus, iidem censemus nullam esse tantam aestimationem ut ea virtuti anteponatur;
examples.translation: We deem health to be deserving of a certain value, but we do not reckon it a good; at the same time we rate no value so highly as to place it above virtue.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Piso M. Crasso et Scribonia genitus, nobilis utrimque, vultu habituque moris antiqui et aestimatione recta severus, deterius interpretantibus tristior habebatur: ea pars morum eius quo suspectior sollicitis adoptanti placebat.
examples.translation: Piso was the son of Marcus Crassus and Scribonia, thus being noble on both sides; his look and manner were those of a man of the ancient school, and he had justly been called stern;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: initial
Latin: Littera septima alphabeti Romani, ge dicitur

examples.original: Is ab inimicis suis apud G. Sacerdotem praetorem rei capitalis cum accusatus esset, facile eo iudicio est liberatus.
examples.translation: Prosecuted by his enemies for a criminal offence in the praetor-ship of Gaius Sacerdos, he had no trouble, on that occasion, in securing an acquittal.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: A putting together, compounding, connecting, arranging, composition, adjustment, etc.

examples.original: Lege Ciceronem: compositio eius una est, pedem curvat lenta et sine infamia mollis.
examples.translation: Read Cicero: his style has unity; it moves with a modulated pace, and is gentle without being degenerate.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Seneca Lvcilio svo salvtem Nimis anxium esse te circa verba et compositionem, mi Lucili, nolo;
examples.translation: On the Superficial Blessings I wish, my dear Lucilius, that you would not be too particular with regard to words and their arrangement;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Neque enim oratorius iste, immo hercle ne virilis quidem cultus est, quo plerique temporum nostrorum actores ita utuntur ut lascivia verborum et levitate sententiarum et licentia compositionis histrionales modos exprimant.
examples.translation: There is a fashion much in vogue with quite a number of counsel nowadays that ill befits an orator, and is indeed scarce worthy even of a man.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to approve wholly of something, to assent to, sanction, acknowledge (class and very freq., esp in prose)

examples.original: Quae cum ita sint, C. Manili, primum istam tuam et legem et voluntatem et sententiam laudo vehementissimeque comprobo;
examples.translation: Since this is so, Gaius Manilius, in the first place I applaud and most heartily commend this your law, your purpose and your proposal;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Grammarians Lives of Illustrious Men possit? Voluntas tamen eius mihi grata est.” Huius ”De Lucilio” libros etiam Santra comprobat.
examples.translation: Nevertheless I appreciate his desire.” Santra likewise commends his books ”On Lucilius.” XV.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Comprobat hominis consilium fortuna, et cum unum omnes peterent, in ipso fluminis vado deprehensus Indutiomarus interficitur, caputque eius refertur in castra: redeuntes equites quos possunt consectantur atque occidunt.
examples.translation: The event approved his plan, and as all the force were making for one man they caught Indutiomarus just in the ford of the river, slew him, and brought his head back to camp;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to go about or around

examples.original: Atque iste ad omnes introitus, qua adiri poterat non modo in eum fundum, de quo controversia erat, sed etiam in illum proximum de quo nihil ambigebatur, armatos homines opponit.
examples.translation: The defendant, then, stationed armed men at every possible way of approach not only to the estate under dispute but even to the adjoining one about which there was no contention.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Iam hoc ridiculum est: si de hereditate ambigetur, et tabulae testamenti obsignatae non minus multis signis quam e lege oportet ad me proferentur, secundum tabulas testamenti potissimum possessionem dabo.
examples.translation: That point you nowhere deal with; nor does your edict provide for anything else at all besides the case for which you got paid.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a helmet, commonly of metal
entries.grammaticalClass: ĭdis; ae, like chlamyda from chlamys; f.

examples.original: Quis autem est qui Tarquinium Superbum, qui Sp. Cassium, Sp. Maelium non oderit?
examples.translation: On the other hand, is there anyone who does not hate Tarquin the Proud, Spurius Cassius, or Spurius Maelius?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Primum adeo anceps fuit, ut—par utrimque discrimen—capta sint hinc Caesaris castra, inde Cassi. Sed quanto efficacior est fortuna, quam virtus!
examples.translation: At first the issue was so doubtful that, danger threatening both sides alike, the camp of Caesar was captured on the one hand and that of Cassius on the other.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Prima luce magnum numerum impedimentorum ex castris mulorumque produci deque his stramenta detrahi mulionesque cum cassidibus equitum specie ac simulatione collibus circumvehi iubet.
examples.translation: With them he put a few cavalry, to range more widely by way of demonstration, and ordered them all to make for the same general destination by a long circuit.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: The fore-court, hall, entrance-room, entry; that part of the Roman house into which one first came after passing the entrance (janua)

examples.original: Non facit nobilem atrium plenum fumosis imaginibus.
examples.translation: A hall full of smoke-begrimed busts does not make the nobleman.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Speluncae sunt duae magni operis, cuivis laxo atrio pares, manu factae, quarum altera solem non recipit, altera usque in occidentem tenet.
examples.translation: There are two grottoes, which cost a great deal of labour, as big as the most spacious hall, made by hand.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to weave before or in front, to fringe, edge, border.

examples.original: Scripserat in pueritia Flaccus etiam praetextam et hodoeporicon librum unum et paucos in socrum Thraseae versus, quae se ante virum occiderat.
examples.translation: In his boyhood Flaccus had written a praetexta, one book describing his travels, and a few verses on the mother-in-law of Thrasea, who had killed herself before her husband.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Persius

definitions: English: chance

examples.original: Deinde etiam tormentorum fortis patientia optabilis est.
examples.translation: And, lastly, because a brave endurance even under torture is desirable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Tu autem negas fortem esse quemquam posse qui dolorem malum putet.
examples.translation: You however say that no one can be brave who thinks pain an evil.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ego vero et in ipsa suffocatione non desii cogitationibus laetis ac fortibus adquiescere.
examples.translation: Yet in the midst of my difficult breathing I never ceased to rest secure in cheerful and brave thoughts.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a reed, cane
Latin: Culmus segetum
Latin: Planta aquatica
English: the back
English: bad quality, badness.

examples.original: Ex ea difficultate illae ’fallaciloquae,’ ut ait Attius, ’malitiae,’ natae sunt.
examples.translation: This is the difficulty that gave birth to those ’base conceits deceitful-tongued,’ as Attius has it.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Illud, mi Lucili, non est quod te inpediat, quo minus de nobis bene speres, quod malitia nos iam tenet, quod diu in possessione nostri est;
examples.translation: There is nothing, Lucilius, to hinder you from entertaining good hopes about us, just because we are even now in the grip of evil, or because we have long been possessed thereby.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: at no time, never; not in any circumstances

examples.original: Nunquam deos ipsos admovere nocentibus manus;
examples.translation: The gods themselves never laid hands upon the guilty;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nec se videre cur non lex quoque abrogetur, qua id liceat quod nunquam futurum sit;
examples.translation: They could see no reason, they said, why they should not even repeal a statute which authorized something that would never come;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Contra ipsis omnia opulenta et fida, Pannoniam Moesiam Dalmatiam Orientem cum integris exercitibus, Italiam et caput rerum urbem senatumque et populum, nunquam obscura nomina, etiam si aliquando obumbrentur;
examples.translation: On the other hand, our own resources are rich and certain: Pannonia, Moesia, Dalmatia and the East are with us; their armies are undiminished;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: an attack, a blow, thrust

examples.original: Ego Plancium, Laterensis, et ipsum gratiosum esse dico et habuisse in petitione multos cupidos sui gratiosos, quos tu si sodales vocas, officiosam amicitiam nomine inquinas criminoso.
examples.translation: I tell you, Laterensis, that not only is Plancius himself popular, but that the host of ardent supporters who backed his candidature were also popular.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a quiver for holding arrows

examples.original: Phoebus adest: sonuere lyrae, sonuere pharetrae;
examples.translation: Phoebus is here: his lyres and quivers have resounded;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the large shin-bone

examples.original: Non decoros corporis motus nec varios per tubam ac tibiam cantus, quibus exceptus spiritus aut in exitu aut in transitu formatur in vocem.
examples.translation: It is not the graceful poses of the body, or the varied notes produced by horn and flute, whereby the breath is received and, as it passes out or through, is transformed into voice.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A poisoning

examples.original: Ista veneficii vetus est via;
examples.translation: That is the old way of witchcraft;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Lex de veneficio tunc primum constituta est.
examples.translation: A law about poisoning was then for the first time enacted.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: forcible, violent, vehement, impetuous, boisterous (class.)

examples.original: Atque hoc ut vere dicitur, parva esse ad beate vivendum momenta ista corporis commodorum, sic nimis violentum est nulla esse dicere;
examples.translation: Yet true though it is that these bodily advantages are of but slight importance for happiness, to say that they are of no importance is too sweeping;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a looking-glass, mirror (usually made of polished metal)
Latin: Res levata lucem reflexans in qua imaginem videatur

examples.original: Quid tibi cum speculo, montana armenta petenti?
examples.translation: What dost thou with a mirror, seeking the herds upon the mountains?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Vix proelia Caesar Senserat, elatus specula quae prodidit ignis: Invenit inpulsos presso iam pulvere muros, Frigidaque, ut veteris, deprendit signa ruinae.
examples.translation: Caesar had hardly been aware of the fighting; the news of it was conveyed to him by a fire-signal from a lofty tower.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quae causa in speculo imagines exprimat, sciet sapiens;
examples.translation: The wise man will know what causes the reflection in a mirror;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: the north wind; Gr.

examples.original: Corpore et statura fuit grandi, aquilo colore, facie rusticana, valetudine varia;
examples.translation: He was tall and of full habit, with a dark complexion and a rustic appearance.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Poets. Virgil

definitions: English: who has drunk enough, had his fill, corresp. with satur.

examples.original: Prima enim illa interrogatio conplectitur eum, qui est ebrius, non eum, qui futurus est.
examples.translation: For the first syllogism refers to him who is actually drunk and not to him who is about to get drunk.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Potest et qui ebrius est, tunc primum esse nec habere hoc vitium, et qui ebriosus est, saepe extra ebrietatem esse.
examples.translation: He who is actually drunk may be in this state for the first time and may not have the habit, while the drunkard is often free from drunkenness.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: an inventing, invention (class.).
Latin: Actus inveniendi
Latin: Eventus inveniendi
English: redness of all shades

examples.original: Ruborem sibi exprimere non possunt;
examples.translation: They cannot, however, muster a blush;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a multitude of objects of the same kind, rising in a heap.
Latin: Res quae in cumulo collectae sunt
Latin: Multitudo

examples.original: Tu tantum numero pugna, praeceptaque in unum Contrahe: de multis grandis acervus erit.
examples.translation: But since there are so many fashions and so many postures, trust not wholly to my counsels.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to be strong, powerful, or potent, to be able, to prevail, avail (class.; cf.: valeo, possum): QVANTO MAGIS POTES POLLESQVE, an old formula in

examples.original: Liber Quintus Quis potis est dignum pollenti pectore carmen condere pro rerum maiestate hisque repertis?
examples.translation: Who is able with mighty mind to build a song worthy of the majesty of nature and these discoveries?
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: western
Latin: Occidentālis
Latin: Vespertīnus

examples.original: Ora ferox Siculae laxavit Mulciber Aetnae Nec tulit in caelum flammas, sed vertice prono Ignis in Hesperium cecidit latus.
examples.translation: In Sicily fierce Mulciber opened wide the mouths of Etna; nor did he lift its flames skyward, but the lire bowed its crest and fell on the Italian shore.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Fortuna recursus Si det in Hesperiam, non hac in sede quiescent Tam sacri cineres, sed te Cornelia, Magne, Accipiet nostraque manu transfundet in urnam.
examples.translation: If Fortune grant us a return to Italy, not here will these sacred ashes rest; but Cornelia will recover you, Magnus, and will transfer them from my hand to an urn.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: To reflect, consider maturely, to consult, take counsel, deliberate.

examples.original: Ea ita facta sunt ex senatus consulto.
examples.translation: By decree of the senate these things were done.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quippe confitenti consultantique supererant spes viresque: cum e contrario laeta omnia fingeret, falsis ingravescebat.
examples.translation: For if he had only acknowledged the truth and sought counsel, he had still some hope and resources left;
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Institutum etiam ab iisdem consulibus ut senatus consulta in aedem Cereris ad aediles plebis deferrentur, quae antea arbitrio consulum supprimebantur vitiabanturque.
examples.translation: Up to that time they were wont to be suppressed or falsified, at the pleasure of the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: Out at the doors, out of doors, abroad, without (opp. intus, domi, etc.)

examples.original: Nec minore saevitia foris et in exteros grassatus est.
examples.translation: Those outside his family he assailed with no less cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Eo anno non segnior discordia domi et bellum foris atrocius fuit.
examples.translation: The Aequi took up arms, and the Veientes even made a foray into Roman territory.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Nihil autem ad rem pertinet, utrum foris habeat exemplar, ad quod referat oculos, an intus, quod ibi ipse concepit et posuit.
examples.translation: Now it makes no difference whether he has his pattern outside himself, that he may direct his glance to it, or within himself, conceived and placed there by himself.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: from the very bottom, from the foundation (syn.: a fundamento, ab radicibus, radicitus, penitus; freq. and class.).

examples.original: Falisci sponte se dediderunt, crematae suo igne Fidenae, direpti funditus deletique Veientes.
examples.translation: The Falisci surrendered voluntarily; Fidenae was consumed by its own flames;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quae enim domus tam stabilis, quae tam firma civitas est, quae non odiis et discidiis funditus possit everti?
examples.translation: For what house is so strong, or what state so enduring that it cannot be utterly overthrown by animosities and division?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ratio ista quam defendis, praecepta quae didicisti, quae probas, funditus evertunt amicitiam, quamvis eam Epicurus, ut facit, in caelum efferat laudibus.
examples.translation: The system you uphold, the principles you have studied and accept, undermine the very foundations of friendship, however much Epicurus may, as he does, praise friendship up to the skies.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a rope, sheet, line, cord

examples.original: Hi iaculo pisces, illi capiuntur ab hamis: Hos cava contento retia fune trahunt.
examples.translation: These fish are caught with spears, those with hooks; these ones are dragged with taut ropes in bulging nets.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Compluribus navibus fractis reliquae cum essent funibus, ancoris reliquisque armamentis amissis ad navigandum inutiles, magna, id quod necesse erat accidere, totius exercitus perturbatio facta est.
examples.translation: This, as was inevitable, caused great dismay throughout the army. For there were no other ships to carry them back;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: uneven, unequal, dissimilar in number or quality (cf. dispar, dissimilis).
English: the skin or membrane that covers parts of the body (class.).

examples.original: Dissiluit stringens uterum membrana, fluuntque Viscera;
examples.translation: The membrane that confines the belly snapped asunder, and the bowels gushed out.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: that breaks his promise, faithless
Latin: Qui fidem violat, qui per fidem decipit
Latin: qui incertus est

examples.original: Perfidus ille quidem, qui talia pignora servat, Sed tamen Aetnaei fulminis instar habent.
examples.translation: Perfidious indeed is he who keeps such pledges, but they hold what is like a thunderbolt of Aetna.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Omnia pone feros (pones invitus) in ignes, Et dic ”ardoris sit rogus iste mei.” Thestias absentem succendit stipite natum: Tu timide flammae perfida verba dabis?
examples.translation: Consign them all, though unwillingly, to the fierce flames, and say, ”Let that be my passion’s funeral pyre.” Thestias burnt in the brand her absent son: will you be cowardly in burning treacherous words?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: first beginning; origin, commencement
English: To divide something with one, whether in giving or receiving.
Latin: res aliquas cum aliis communes facere
Latin: participem esse

examples.original: Non habeo, cum quo te communicatum velim.
examples.translation: I know of no one with whom I should be willing to have you shared.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Petunt a Vercingetorige Aedui ut ad se veniat rationesque belli gerendi communicet.
examples.translation: When their request was granted, they insisted that the supreme command should be assigned to them.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Ea legatione Papirius audita perinde ac motus dictis eorum cum collega se communicaturum respondit;
examples.translation: After listening to these envoys, Papirius as though moved by what they said, replied that he would consult his colleague.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to uncover, expose, lay bare (freq. in the Aug. per.).

examples.original: Si quid credis mihi, intimos adfectus meos tibi cum maxime detego;
examples.translation: Such affairs come by order, and not by accident.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Qui modo celabas monitu tua crimina nostro, Flecte iter, et monitu detege furta meo.
examples.translation: You who were but now concealing your fault by my advice, turn your path, and by my advice uncover your deceit.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Detegit inbelles animas nil fortiter ausa Seditio tantumque fugam meditata iuventus Ac ducis invicti rebus lassata secundis.
examples.translation: That you have no stomach for fighting is revealed; for your mutiny ends in words;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a calf.

examples.original: Quem taurum metuis, vitulum mulcere solebas: Sub qua nunc recubas arbore, virga fuit: Nascitur exiguus, sed opes adquirit eundo, Quaque venit, multas accipit amnis aquas.
examples.translation: The bull you fear, you were wont to stroke as a calf; the tree under which you lie was once a sapling: a river at birth is small, but acquires force by flowing;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Bestowing care or pains upon a thing, applying one's self assiduously, careful, diligent, thoughtful, devoted (class.; esp. freq. in Cic.).
English: unknowing, ignorant, unaware (syn.: inscius, ignarus).—With

examples.original: Inter sapientiam et sapere quid intersit nescio;
examples.translation: What the distinction is between wisdom and being wise I do not know;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed non in Caesare tantum Nomen erat nec fama ducis, sed nescia virtus Stare loco, solusque pudor non vincere bello;
examples.translation: But Caesar had more than a mere name and military reputation: his energy could never rest, and his one disgrace was to conquer without war. He was alert and headstrong;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cogeris voti nescius esse tui: Seu te forte iuvat sera et sapientior aetas, Hoc quoque, crede mihi, plenius agmen erit.
examples.translation: Or do you perchance prefer a later and staider age? still more numerous, believe me, will be their array.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or belonging to the best or noblest, aristocratic

examples.original: Caedes principum ostenditur: id, quod interitum optimatium sequi necesse est, adiungitur: ne in unius imperium res recidat, admonemur.
examples.translation: The murder of our highest is portended; and there is a further reference to what must inevitably follow the destruction of our nobility;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to-morrow
Latin: Die post hodiernum diem
Latin: posteā, in posterum
English: to fall asunder, go to pieces, melt away, dissolve (class.).

examples.original: Abscidis frustra ferro tua pignora: bellum Te faciet civile meum.” Sic fata refugit Umbra per amplexus trepidi dilapsa mariti.
examples.translation: The civil war shall make you mine.” Thus speaking, the ghost fled away, dissolving in the arms of her eager husband.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Inde pars per agros dilapsi, pars urbes petunt finitimas, sine ullo duce aut consensu suam quisque spem, sua consilia communibus deploratis sequentes.
examples.translation: They had neither leader nor concerted plan; each followed the promptings of his own hopes and his own counsels, in despair of the commonwealth.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Praecipiti in occasum die ob pavorem magistratuum senatorumque, qui dilapsi ex urbe aut per domos clientium semet occultabant, vocari senatus non potuit.
examples.translation: The day hurried to its close. It was impossible to summon the senate because the senators had stolen away from the city or were hiding in their clients’ houses.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a mockery, derision, wantonness.

examples.original: Catulus se ignis haustu ludibrio hostium exemit.
examples.translation: Catulus saved himself from the insults of his enemies by swallowing fire.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nam Claudium patruum non nisi in ludibrium reservavit.
examples.translation: As for his uncle Claudius, he spared him merely as a laughingstock.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a lute, lyre, a stringed instrument resembling the cithara, fabled to have been invented by Mercury and presented to Apollo

examples.original: Phoebus adest: sonuere lyrae, sonuere pharetrae;
examples.translation: Phoebus is here: his lyres and quivers have resounded;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tu licet et Thamyram superes et Amoebea cantu, Non erit ignotae gratia magna lyrae.
examples.translation: Though in song you may surpass Thamyras and Amoebeus, in an unknown lyre there is no great delight.
