examples.translation: Him, therefore, the consul Servilius, with the approval of the patricians, appointed dictator. An enrolment was proclaimed, and the courts were suspended.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to draw away from a place or person, to drag or pull away.
English: the sacred. the divine, that which has reference to the Deity (in class. prose)
Latin: sanctitudo
Latin: ostentio religionis

examples.original: B. Latinis victis montem Aventinum adsignavit, fines protulit, Hostiam coloniam deduxit, caerimonias a Numa institutas renovavit.
examples.translation: Summary of Book I B. Having beaten the Latins, he assigned them the Aventine Hill; planted a colony at Ostia;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to throw or cast between; to set, place, or put between; to join or

examples.original: Interiecto deinde haud magno spatio quod volneribus curandis supplendoque exercitui satis esset, cum ira maiore tum viribus etiam auctis Pometiae arma inlata.
examples.translation: When a short time had elapsed, long enough for healing wounds and recruiting the army, they returned, with heightened resentment and also with augmented forces, to the attack of Pometia.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a sitting long, remaining in a place.

examples.original: Nam nec tu agitare et insequi poetas intermittis, et ego, cui desidiam advocationum obicis, cotidianum hoc patrocinium defendendae adversus te poeticae exerceo.
examples.translation: You on your part are never done assailing the poets with your invective, and I, whom you charge with neglect of professional duty, am daily retained to defend the art of poetry against you.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: An agent between two parties, a broker

examples.original: His rebus permotus Quintus Titurius, cum procul Ambiorigem suos cohortantem conspexisset, interpretem suum Gnaeum Pompeium ad eum mittit rogatum ut sibi militibusque parcat.
examples.translation: Alarmed by these events, Quintus Titurius, who had remarked Ambiorix at a distance encouraging his men, sent his interpreter, Gnaeus Pompeius, to him to ask him to spare himself and his troops.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to spring vigorously, to leap or jump up (class.; esp. in the trop. signif.).

examples.original: Hic et bella gerebat ut adulescens, cum plane grandis esset, et Hannibalem iuveniliter exsultantem patientia sua molliebat;
examples.translation: Though quite old he waged war like a young man, and by his patient endurance checked the boyish impetuosity of Hannibal.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Satis constat ne Ciceroni quidem obtrectatores defuisse, quibus inflatus et tumens, nec satis pressus sed supra modum exsultans et superfluens et parum Atticus videretur.
examples.translation: Cicero himself, as is well known, had his detractors: they thought him turgid and puffy, wanting in conciseness, inordinately exuberant and redundant—in short, not Attic enough.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: a sort of grain, spelt, Gr.
English: to take away by violence, to drag away, to tear off or away (stronger than its synn. abduco, abigo, abstraho).

examples.original: Nunc desuper Alpis Nubiferae colles atque aeriam Pyrenen Abripimur.
examples.translation: Next I am spirited away over the cloud-capped Alps and soaring Pyrenees.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: unspeakable, unutterable, unheard of, unnatural, shocking, abominable (class.)

examples.original: Infandum domini per viscera ferrum Exegit famulus;
examples.translation: The conqueror had once for all issued his orders which included every crime.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: Guiltless, innocent; constr. with
English: in is frequently written
Latin: Littera tertia decima alphabeti Romani, en dicitur

examples.original: Larinas quaedam fuit Dinaea, socrus Oppianici, quae filios habuit M. et N. Aurios et Cn. Magium et filiam Magiam, nuptam Oppianico.
examples.translation: There was a lady of Larinum called Dinea, mother-in-law of Oppianicus, who had three sons, Marcus and Numerius Aurius and Gnaeus Magius, and a daughter Magia, married to Oppianicus.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to release or discharge completely; acc. to the signif. of the simple verb.

examples.original: Bellvm Pervsinvm IIII, 5Alterum bellum concitavit agrorum divisio, quod Caesar veteranis patris pretium militiae persolvebat.
examples.translation: The War round Perusia 5. The distribution of lands to the soldiers was the cause of another war;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: quench, extinguish (class.).

examples.original: Nutritur vento, vento restinguitur ignis: Lenis alit flammas, grandior aura necat.
examples.translation: By wind is a fire fostered, and by wind extinguished;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: situated near the city of Rome, suburban.

examples.original: Debeo hoc suburbano meo, quod mihi senectus mea, quocumque adverteram, apparuit.
examples.translation: I owe it to my country-place that my old age became apparent whithersoever I turned.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Haec et alia Scipio non neglegenter abiecerat, ut homo intellegens Verres auferre posset, sed Thermitanis restituerat: non quo ipse hortos aut suburbanum aut locum omnino ubi ea poneret nullum haberet;
examples.translation: These and other such objects Scipio had not thrown carelessly aside for a connoisseur like Verres to appropriate, but had returned them to their owners, the people of Thermae;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Rure suburbano poteris tibi dicere missa, Illa vel in Sacra sint licet empta via. Adferat aut uvas, aut quas Amaryllis amabat— At nunc castaneas non amat illa nuces.
examples.translation: You can say they were sent to you from your suburban property, though you bought them in the Sacred Way. Let him bring either grapes or the chestnuts ”that Amaryllis loved” but loves no more.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: shed, booth, stall, shop constructed of boards.
English: to chide, scold, blame, rebuke, reprove (freq. and class.; syn.: increpo, improbo, vitupero); constr. usually with

examples.original: Volo luxuriam obiurgari, libidinem traduci, inpotentiam frangi.
examples.translation: I wish to see luxury rebuked, lust condemned, waywardness crushed out.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Iam omnibus locis ceditur nequiquam Sempronio consule obiurgante atque hortante.
examples.translation: There was no virtue either in his authority or in his dignity;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to bring into the reckoning, enter into the account, to reckon, charge (not ante-Aug.; cf. deputo).

examples.original: Nec una cohors togata defendit nunc Galbam sed detinet: cum vos aspexerit, cum signum meum acceperit, hoc solum erit certamen, quis mihi plurimum imputet.
examples.translation: There is no time for delay in a plan which is not praiseworthy unless put into effect.” Then he ordered the armoury to be opened.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to decide, determine, judge a controversy, = dijudicare
English: To draw back, withdraw; to call back (class.).

examples.original: Quam tamen mihi ex illis mulierculis dabis vix retractis a rogo, vix a cadavere revulsis, cui lacrimae in totum mensem duraverint?
examples.translation: In the case of men, no rules are laid down, because to mourn at all is not regarded as honourable.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: His igitur rebus retractis terra repente, maxuma qua nunc se ponti plaga caerula tendit, succidit et salso suffudit gurgite fossas.
examples.translation: Therefore when these bodies were withdrawn, suddenly the earth sank down where now the blue expanse of the sea extends so wide, and drowned its hollows with the salt flood.
examples.author: Lucretius

definitions: English: to weigh out, weigh.
Latin: donare
Latin: (Transitivum) donare

examples.original: Profert alter, opinor duobus versiculis, expensum Niciae;
examples.translation: The one presents a note for payment, consisting of two lines, I believe.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Nunc ad sociorum tabulas accepti et expensi, quas removere honeste nullo modo potuerunt, et ad amicum tuum Carpinatium revertemur.
examples.translation: We will now go back to the company’s accounts of receipts and expenditure, which they had no respectable means of suppressing, and to your friend Carpinatius.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a measure, the half of a sextarius
English: down or woolly part of many plants, a catkin

examples.original: Alba tum erat Latio caput, Iuli opus;
examples.translation: Alba was at that time the chief city of Latium, having been built by lulus;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Tribuni consulari potestate erant Ap. Claudius Crassus Sp. Nautius Rutulus L. Sergius Fidenas Sex. Iulius Iulus.
examples.translation: The tribunes with consular authority were Appius Claudius Crassus, Spurius Nautius Rutulus, Lucius Sergius Fidenas, and Sextus Julius lulus.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Creati T. Quinctius Cincinnatus Q. Servilius Fidenas quintum L. Iulius Iulus L. Aquilius Corvus L. Lucretius Tricipitinus Ser. Sulpicius Rufus.
examples.translation: Those chosen were Titus Quinctius Cincinnatus, Quintus Servilius Fidenas (for the fifth time), Lucius Julius lulus, Lucius Aquilius Corvus, Lucius Lucretius Tricipitinus, and Servius Sulpicius Rufus.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a companion, an associate, comrade, partaker, sharer, partner, etc. (whether male or female; class. and freq.).

examples.original: Comites illi tui delecti manus erant tuae;
examples.translation: The members of your select retinue were your hands;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nullo loco deest seditionis voluntarius comes;
examples.translation: At no point was there any lack of volunteers to join the rising;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ad deteriora faciles sumus, quia nec dux potest nec comes deesse, et res ipsa etiam sine duce, sine comite procedit.
examples.translation: We degenerate easily, because we lack neither guides nor associates in our wickedness, and the wickedness goes on of itself, even without guides or associates.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: endeavor, exert one's self, take pains either successfully or perseveringly = eniti (class.; most freq. in Cic.).— Constr. with
Latin: Studiose et cum labore aliquid conficere
Latin: Multum laboris ponere, sedulam operam dare
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: De quibus etsi a Chrysippo maxime est elaboratum, tamen a Zenone minus multo quam ab antiquis;
examples.translation: Logic, no doubt, was very fully worked out by Chrysippus, but much less was done in it by Zeno than by the older schools;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a sickle, reaping-hook, a pruning-hook, scythe.
Latin: Ferramentum incurvum seu aduncum ad varios usus in re rustica
Latin: Instrumentum martiale, quo hastili oblongo, ferroque partim curvo et falcato, partim acuto rectoque

examples.original: Non mihi falx nimias Saturnia deputat umbras, Duratam renovat non mihi fossor humum;
examples.translation: Saturn’s sickle prunes not my superfluous shade, no digger renews my hardened soil;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: Not examined, untried

examples.original: Is mihi etiam Sthenium litteras publicas corrupisse causa incognita iudicavit, qui defendere non poterit se non in ipsius Sthenii nomine litteras publicas corrupisse?
examples.translation: Do I find that the man who without trial convicted Sthenius of altering an official record is a man who cannot deny that, dealing with this same Sthenius, he has altered an official record himself?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Neutr., to remove from one place to another, to depart, flit, migrate (class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Subinde paedagogum suum rogat ut migret.
examples.translation: She keeps asking her attendant to change her quarters;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Spernentibus Etruscis Lucumonem exsule advena ortum, ferre indignitatem non potuit oblitaque ingenitae erga patriam caritatis, dummodo virum honoratum videret, consilium migrandi ab Tarquiniis cepit.
examples.translation: She could not endure this indignity, and forgetting the love she owed her native land, if she could only see her husband honoured, she formed the project of emigrating from Tarquinii.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: loaded, laden, burdened, freighted, etc. (class.).
English: a means of aid; help
English: Of or belonging to an arrow

examples.original: Eo de media nocte Caesar, isdem ducibus usus qui nuntii ab Iccio venerant, Numidas et Cretas sagittarios et funditores Baleares subsidio oppidanis mittit;
examples.translation: Using again as guides the men who had come from Iccius to report, Caesar sent off to Bibrax in the middle of the night Numidian and Cretan archers and Balearic slingers, to reinforce the townsfolk.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to press into or upon, to stick, stamp, or dig into, to impress, imprint (class.).
English: to wage war again (said of the conquered), to make an insurrection, to revolt, rebel (mostly postAug.; not in Cic. or Cæs.; syn.: descisco).

examples.original: Uni Fidenatium populo rebellare placuit;
examples.translation: Only the people of Fidenae voted to renew the war;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Hic finis Augusto bellicorum certaminum fuit, idem rebellandi finis Hispaniae.
examples.translation: This was the end of Augustus’ campaigns as well as of the rebellion in Spain.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Curius Dentatus cos. Samnitibus caesis et Sabinis, qui rebellaverant, victis et in deditionem acceptis bis in eodem magistratu triumphavit.
examples.translation: Curius Dentatus the consul having slaughtered the Samnites and conquered the Sabines, who had revolted, and received their submission, triumphed twice in the same year of office.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: To keep asunder

examples.original: Est ille plus quam capit, et ingenti aviditate onerat distentum ventrem ac desuetum iam ventris officio, ut maiore opera omnia egerat quam ingessit;
examples.translation: The master eats more than he can hold, and with monstrous greed loads his belly until it is stretched and at length ceases to do the work of a belly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A spider
English: less, smaller inferior, etc.

examples.original: Nec minore saevitia foris et in exteros grassatus est.
examples.translation: Those outside his family he assailed with no less cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Nec raptis aut spes de se melior aut indignatio est minor.
examples.translation: The stolen maidens were no more hopeful of their plight, nor less indignant.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quis vetat a magnis ad res exempla minores Sumere, nec nomen pertimuisse ducis?
examples.translation: Who forbids me to use great things as examples for little, or to fear the name of leader?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or belonging to the people, proceeding from or designed for the people.

examples.original: Malis artibus popularis favor quaeritur.
examples.translation: It takes trickery to win popular approval;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Vergini patris sponsique Icili populare nomen celebrabatur.
examples.translation: Their acquaintance were led to support the girl out of regard for them;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Haec tutior visa sententia est quae popularem senatum faceret.
examples.translation: This policy seemed the safer, since it would make the senate popular.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a loathing, aversion for any thing, esp. for any sort of enjoyment (very freq. and class.; cf. taedium, nausea, etc.).

examples.original: Rerum naturam peragranti numquam in fastidium veritas veniet;
examples.translation: To one who roamsa through the universe, the truth can never pall;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed rursus etiam illae quae aliquid esse videbantur in saeculo, non habeant fastidio sorores suas quae ad illam sanctam societatem ex paupertate venerunt;
examples.translation: But again, let not those who in the world considered themselves something, hold in scorn their sisters who have come to that holy fellowship from povertyb;
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Fecit statim, ut fit, fastidium copia, adeoque pauci nomina dedere ut ad explendum numerum coloni Volsci adderentur;
examples.translation: There at once appeared the fastidiousness which usually attends abundance, and so few persons enrolled that Volscian colonists were added to fill out the number;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to light up, make light

examples.original: Atque idem ego hoc contendo, cum ad naturam eximiam et illustrem accesserit ratio quaedam conformatioque doctrinae, tum illud nescio quid praeclarum ac singulare solere exsistere.
examples.translation: Yet I do at the same time assert that when to a lofty and brilliant character is applied the moulding influence of abstract studies, the result is often inscrutably and unapproachably noble.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sola fuit ea fide benivolentiaque erga populum Romanum ut civitates eius insulae, quae semel in amicitiam nostram venissent, numquam postea deficerent, pleraeque autem et maxime illustres in amicitia perpetuo manerent.
examples.translation: No other nation has equalled her in loyal goodwill towards us: once the various states in the island had embraced our friendship, they never thereafter seceded from it;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to weigh or weigh out carefully
English: In space.
English: depart, decease, v. Doed. Syn. 3, p. 183 sq. (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Mihi quidem numquam persuaderi potuit animos dum in corporibus essent mortalibus vivere, cum excessissent ex eis emori;
examples.translation: I, for my part, could never be persuaded that souls, which lived while they were in human bodies, perished when they left those bodies;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ego vero ne immortalitatem quidem contra rem publicam accipiendam putarem, nedum emori cum pernicie rei publicae vellem.
examples.translation: But the truth is, that I could not look upon even immortality as desirable, if it was to be achieved at my country’s cost;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: eloquence, fluency
English: A limiting, limit, boundary
English: to strike upon or against (syn.: impingo, illido, infligo; class.; in Cic. only in the trop. signif.).

examples.original: Dictator tamen, ut qui magis animis quam viribus fretus ad certamen descenderet, omnia circumspicere atque agitare coepit ut arte aliqua terrorem hostibus incuteret.
examples.translation: Yet the dictator was entering a struggle in which he relied more on the spirit of his troops than on their strength.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: A going to one in order to accost or make a request of him (not found in earlier Lat.).

examples.original: Philologi appellationem assumpsisse videtur, quia sic ut Eratosthenes, qui primus hoc cognomen sibi vindicavit, multiplici variaque doctrina censebatur.
examples.translation: And that he was such is evident from his commentaries, though very few of them survive;
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Ac ne tribuniciam quidem potestatem statim nec patris patriae appellationem nisi sero recepit. Nam consuetudinem scrutandi salutantes manente adhuc bello civili omiserat.
examples.translation: As for the custom of searching those who came to pay their morning calls, he gave that up before the civil war was over.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Sed supervenientibus ab urbe nuntiis ut occisum Neronem cunctosque in verba sua iurasse cognovit, deposita legati suscepit Caesaris appellationem iterque ingressus est paludatus ac dependente a cervicibus pugione ante pectus;
examples.translation: But when some messengers came from the city, reporting that Nero was dead and that all the people had sworn allegiance to him, he laid aside the title of governor and assumed that of Caesar.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: sharpness, sourness, harshness, the harsh taste of fruits.

examples.original: At illa commota veteres quosdam ad se Augusti codicillos de acerbitate et intolerantia morum eius e sacrario protulit atque recitavit.
examples.translation: Then Livia, in a rage, drew from a secret place and read some old letters written to her by Augustus with regard to the austerity and stubbornness of Tiberius’ disposition.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: suck in, drink down, swallow (freq. and class.).
English: of or belonging to the right time, done or happening at the proper time, timely, seasonable
English: Foreign, strange, outlandish, barbarous, in opp. to Grecian or Roman

examples.original: Parthe, dabis poenas: Crassi gaudete sepulti, Signaque barbaricas non bene passa manu.
examples.translation: Parthian, thou shalt pay penalty; rejoice, ye buried Crassi, and ye standards that shamefully endured barbarian violence.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or pertaining to goats
Latin: Capri seu caprae; ad capros pertinens
English: sick.
Latin: Aeger esse; morbo laborare

examples.original: Quando autem aliqua non potest ieiunare, non tamen extra horam prandii aliquid alimentorum sumat, nisi cum aegrotat.
examples.translation: When, however, anyone is unable to fast, let her not take any nourishment outside of the hour of repast, unless when ill.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Et doleas oportet et sitias et esurias et senescas, si tibi longior contigerit inter homines mora, et aegrotes et perdas aliquid et pereas.
examples.translation: You must suffer pain, and thirst, and hunger, and old age too, if a longer stay among men shall be granted you; you must be sick, and you must suffer loss and death.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Cum vagus et exsul erraret atque undique exclusus Oppianicus in Falernum se ad L. Quinctium contulisset, ibi primum in morbum incidit ac satis vehementer diuque aegrotavit.
examples.translation: Wandering about, a vagabond and an exile, and finding all doors shut against him, Oppianicus betook himself to L. Quinctius in the Falernian district. It was there that he first fell sick;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: an orphan boy, an orphan; also, a ward

examples.original: Dixit iuratus P. Titius, tutor pupilli Iunii;
examples.translation: It has been told on oath by Publius Titius, guardian of young Iunius.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Is mortuus est; reliquit pupillum parvum filium.
examples.translation: He died, leaving a young son, not yet of age.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Omnes exclusi sunt non minus aperte quam pupillus. Diem praestituit operi faciundo Kalendas Decembres, locat circiter Idus Septembres;
examples.translation: The day Verres fixed for the undertaking to be completed was the 1st of December, and he let the contract about the 13th of September;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: untilled, uncultivated (class.).
English: to bind fast, tie up (class.; esp. freq. in trop. signif.).

examples.original: Itaque declamationes istas de medio removeamus: ”Non est animus in sua potestate ebrietate devinctus.
examples.translation: So let us abolish all such harangues as this: ”No man in the bonds of drunkenness has power over his soul.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Et consul alter Fabius proeliis primum parvis, postremo una insigni pugna, cum hostes totis adorti copiis essent, Hernicos devincit.
examples.translation: And the other consul Fabius defeated the Hernici—at first in little skirmishes, but ultimately in one remarkable battle, in which the enemy attacked with all their forces.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to pursue (ante- and postclass.)

examples.original: Etiam atque etiam insto atque urgeo, insector, posco, atque adeo flagito crimen;
examples.translation: I demand that you shall produce your charges; nay, I importune you for them.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: to make lonely or desolate; to lay waste, desolate (only a few times in the post-Aug. poets)

examples.original: Quomodo hoc fiat, sapientia sola monstrabit.
examples.translation: And wisdom alone can show you how this may be done.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ista enim, quae dici solent, falsa sunt: ”Non potui aliter.
examples.translation: The usual explanation which men offer is wrong: ”I was compelled to do it.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Secuti alium ducem sequimini nunc Camillum et quod ductu meo soletis vincite.
examples.translation: You have followed another leader: follow now Camillus, and, as your habit is when I am leading, conquer.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: common people, general citizens, commons/plebeians; lower class/ranks; mob/mass

examples.original: Eo nuntio erecti patres, erecta plebes.
examples.translation: These tidings cheered the Fathers and encouraged the plebs.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tribuni plebem agitare suo veneno, agraria lege;
examples.translation: The tribunes roused the plebs to madness with their usual poison, a land-law.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Mortuus consul Quinctilius, quattuor tribuni plebi.
examples.translation: Death took the consul Quinctilius, and four tribunes of the plebs.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to form, fashion, shape (rare but class.).

examples.original: Hi sunt magnitudine paulo infra elephantos, specie et colore et figura tauri.
examples.translation: In size these are somewhat smaller than elephants; in appearance, colour, and shape they are as bulls.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Persecutus est Aristoteles animantium omnium ortus, victus, figuras, Theophrastus autem stirpium naturas omniumque fere rerum quae e terra gignerentur causas atque rationes;
examples.translation: Aristotle gave a complete account of the birth, nutrition and structure of all living creatures, Theophrastus of the natural history of plants and the causes and constitution of vegetable organisms in general;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Ulteriora pudet docuisse: sed alma Dione ”Praecipue nostrum est, quod pudet” inquit ”opus.” Nota sibi sit quaeque: modos a corpore certos Sumite: non omnes una figura decet.
examples.translation: What remains I blush to tell; but kindly Dione says, ”What brings a blush is before all else my business.” Let each woman know herself;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to accuse, make an accusation

examples.original: Trachalum adversus criminantis Galeria uxor Vitellii protexit.
examples.translation: Trachalus was protected against his accusers by Galeria, the wife of Vitellius.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Qui modo celabas monitu tua crimina nostro, Flecte iter, et monitu detege furta meo.
examples.translation: You who were but now concealing your fault by my advice, turn your path, and by my advice uncover your deceit.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Hos scelerum ritus, haec dirae crimina gentis Effera damnarat nimiae pietatis Erictho Inque novos ritus pollutam duxerat artem.
examples.translation: These criminal rites and malpractices of an accursed race fierce Erictho had scouted as not wicked enough, and had turned her loathsome skill to rites before unknown.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to scrape, scratch, shave

examples.original: Rapum autem arboris, antequam obruat, radit.
examples.translation: These are of necessity still soft;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: this very instant, without delay, forthwith, immediately, directly
English: To bind to or about; to bind, tie, or fasten up (rare)

examples.original: Aureum in manu baculum, in latere acinaces, purpurea vestis ingentibus obstricta gemmis: diadema deerat, ut regina rex et ipse frueretur.
examples.translation: In his hand was a golden sceptre, at his side a scimitar; he wore a purple robe studded with huge gems;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: an agreeing, covenanting; an agreement, covenant, contract, bargain, pact (syn. pactum)

examples.original: In qua pactione summa fide mansit Agesilaus;
examples.translation: That promise Agesilaus kept with the utmost scrupulousness;
examples.author: Cornelius Nepos
examples.work: The Book On The Great Generals Of Foreign Nations. Agesilaus

examples.original: Alter consul, ut me et rem publicam non modo desereret, sed etiam hostibus rei publicae proderet, pactionibus se suorum praemiorum obligarat.
examples.translation: The other consul had engaged himself by bargaining for his rewards not only to desert me and the state, but also to betray us to the state’s enemies.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Cui quidem cum Ciliciam dedisses, mutasti pactionem et Ciliciam ad praetorem item extra ordinem transtulisti: Gabinio pretio amplificato Syriam nominatim dedisti.
examples.translation: It was to such an one that you first assigned Cilicia; then you altered your bargain, and transferred Cilicia, again by an extraordinary bestowal, upon a praetor;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: Persian
Latin: Persarum vel qui ad Persas pertinet
Latin: subst.f. persicus, etiam persica — Arbor Pruno genere qui fructum nomine persicum fert
English: A frog
Latin: Animal parvum amphibium
Latin: pars gentis Amphibiae
English: to be born again; to grow, rise, or spring up again (class.; cf. regeneror).

examples.original: Ut terrorem Italiae possessa Mevania ac velut renatum ex integro bellum intulerat, ita haud dubium erga Flavianas partis studium tam pavidus Vitellii discessus addidit.
examples.translation: While the occupation of Mevania had terrified Italy and had seemed to start a new war, it was also true that the timid retreat of Vitellius had increased the favourable feeling toward the Flavian party.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: made of roses
English: the time when the sun seems to stand still, either in Cancer or in Capricorn, the (summer or winter) solstice (so in gen. not till after the Aug. period)
Latin: tempus illud, quo sol stare videtur aliquantisper
Latin: tempus quo sol aliquantisper stare videtur et signum Cancri accidit in mense Iunio

examples.original: Consurgere in ipsis Ius tibi solstitiis, aliena crescere bruma Atque hiemes adferre tuas, solique vagari Concessum per utrosque polos.
examples.translation: He is privileged to rise at midsummer, to be flooded by a winter out of season, and to bring with him a rainy season of his own;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: holding fast, griping, tenacious.

examples.original: Sola ratio inmutabilis et iudicii tenax est.
examples.translation: It is reason alone that is unchangeable, that holds fast to its decisions.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hanc dabit animi magnitudo, dabit constantia bene iudicati tenax.
examples.translation: This will be yours if you possess greatness of soul;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: a sign and memorial of victory, a trophy; orig. a trunk of a tree, on which were fixed the arms, shields, helmets, etc., taken from the enemy
English: each one, every one
Latin: (pronomen indefinitum substantivum) omnis homo singularis, omne singulare
Latin: omnis homo singularis, omne singulare
English: an ancient town in Calabria, with a very convenient harbor, the chief naval station of the Romans in the Adriatic, and their regular point of departure for Greece, now Brindisi

examples.original: Brundisium veni, vel potius ad moenia accessi.
examples.translation: I came to Brundisium, or rather approached the walls;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Coloniae deductae sunt Fregenae, in agro Sallentino Brundisium.
examples.translation: Colonies were founded at Fregenae and in the Sallentine country at Brundisium.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Tum consilio repente mutato a Vibone Brundisium terra petere contendi;
examples.translation: Then, forced suddenly to change my plans, I started on the overland journey to Brundisium;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a comedy

examples.original: Verum haec ex comoedia quibus impiorum luxus et sacrilega superstitio convinceretur, proferre forsitan non debemus.
examples.translation: And yet perhaps I should not put forward these scenes from comedy to confute the wantonness and the sacrilegious superstition of the ungodly.
examples.author: Augustine

definitions: English: to nod, assent
Latin: Agere nutum ad aliquem
English: an edge, brink, border, margin (class., but not in Cic. or Cæs.)

examples.original: Nec non et ratibus temptatur regia, qua se Protulit in medios audaci margine fluctus Luxuriosa domus.
examples.translation: They assailed the palace also by means of ships, at the point where the splendid pile projected with bold frontage right over the water.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: bee; swarm regarded as a portent; Apis, sacred bull worshiped in Egypt
Latin: Animal parvum volatile notum, mellis artifex
English: to caress, coax, court

examples.original: Quis sapiens blandis non misceat oscula verbis?
examples.translation: Who that is wise would not mingle kisses with coaxing words?
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Tum neque subiectus, solito nec blandior esto: Haec animi multum signa nocentis habent: Sed lateri ne parce tuo: pax omnis in uno est;
examples.translation: Be not submissive then, nor more flattering than of wont; such signs point overmuch to guilt;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the observation and interpretation of omens, augury (v. augur and the pass. there cited).

examples.original: Ille rem expertus augurio, posse respondit.
examples.translation: He made trial by augury and replied that it was possible.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Quanta notitia antiquitatis, scientia iuris auguri!
examples.translation: What a knowledge of ancient history! What skill in augural law!
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quod primo ut augurium caelo missum laetus accepit tribunus, precatus deinde, si divus si diva esset qui sibi praepetem misisset, volens propitius adesset.
examples.translation: This the tribune first received with joy, as a heavensent augury, and then prayed that whosoever, be it god or goddess, had sent the auspicious bird might attend him with favour and protection.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to spend, expend, lay out, bestow upon a thing (postAug.)
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; di, sum, 3

examples.original: Sed iam finis faciendus est et aliquid, ut institui, pro hac epistula dependendum.
examples.translation: But I must stop, and pay my customary contribution, to balance this letter.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Sed supervenientibus ab urbe nuntiis ut occisum Neronem cunctosque in verba sua iurasse cognovit, deposita legati suscepit Caesaris appellationem iterque ingressus est paludatus ac dependente a cervicibus pugione ante pectus;
examples.translation: But when some messengers came from the city, reporting that Nero was dead and that all the people had sworn allegiance to him, he laid aside the title of governor and assumed that of Caesar.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the daughter of Saturn and Ops
Latin: Dea Romana frumentorum ac agriculturae

examples.original: Non pabula tellus Pascendis summittit equis, non proserit ullam Flava Ceres segetem;
examples.translation: The earth sends up no fodder to feed his horses; golden Ceres puts forth no corn there;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Parcite ne castris: vallo tendetis in illo, Unde acies peritura venit.” Vix cuncta locuto Caesare quemque suum munus trahit, armaque raptim Sumpta Ceresque viris.
examples.translation: Be not careful of your camp; you will find quarters behind the rampart from which the doomed army is coming.” Almost before Caesar had ceased to speak, each went to his appointed task;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Institutum etiam ab iisdem consulibus ut senatus consulta in aedem Cereris ad aediles plebis deferrentur, quae antea arbitrio consulum supprimebantur vitiabanturque.
examples.translation: Up to that time they were wont to be suppressed or falsified, at the pleasure of the consuls.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: wide, loose, open; spacious, roomy; opp. adstrictus (not freq. till after the Aug. per.).

examples.original: Iamque sinu laxo nudum sine corpore volnus.
examples.translation: The limbs are soaked with corrupted blood;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Illic et laxas vestes et fluxa virorum Velamenta vides.
examples.translation: There one sees loose garments and flowing robes worn even by men.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Quid sit, quod invenerim quaeris; sinum laxa, merum lucrum est.
examples.translation: If you wish to know what it is that I have found, open your pocket;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: Pertaining to the air, aërial
Latin: Qui ad aërem pertinet

examples.original: Nunc desuper Alpis Nubiferae colles atque aeriam Pyrenen Abripimur.
examples.translation: Next I am spirited away over the cloud-capped Alps and soaring Pyrenees.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to spring or leap at or upon a thing, to leap, bound, jump, spring.
entries.grammaticalClass: v. n. and a.; āvi, ātum, 1

definitions: English: hoarse.

examples.original: Illa sonat raucum quiddam atque inamabile ridet, Ut rudit a scabra turpis asella mola.
examples.translation: That one’s laugh has a strident and unlovely harshness, as when a mean she-ass brays by the rough millstone.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Fessa iacet cervix, fumant sudoribus artus, Oraque proiecta squalent arentia lingua, Pectora rauca gemunt, quae creber anhelitus urguet, Et defecta gravis longe trahit ilia pulsus, Siccaque sanguineis durescit spuma lupatis.
examples.translation: The weary neck sinks down, the limbs reek with sweat, the tongue protrudes and the mouth is rough and dry; the lungs, driven by quick pants, give a hoarse murmur;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: to be silent, keep silence
English: goblet, a drinking-vessel
English: of or pertaining to the comitia

examples.original: Herodotus cum Roma revertitur, diebus, ut ipse putabat, quindecim ante comitia, offendit eum mensem qui consequitur mensem comitialem, comitiis iam abhinc triginta diebus habitis.
examples.translation: Herodotus on his return from Rome, fifteen days, as he imagined, before the election, found himself in the month following the election month, and the election over for a month already.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: harsh, sour, tart
English: to tear or rend in pieces, to mangle, lacerate (class.; cf.: lacero, discerpo, dilanio).

examples.original: Nam timor unus erat, facies non una timoris: Pars laniat crines, pars sine mente sedet;
examples.translation: For their fear was one, but not one was the appearance of their fear: some tear their hair, some sit crazed;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: overthrow, demolition, subversion, ruin (especially of cities, buildings, etc.), destruction
English: Full of air, airy (cf. anima, I. and II. A.)

examples.original: Inrationalis pars animi duas habet partes, alteram animosam, ambitiosam, inpotentem, positam in adfectionibus, alteram humilem, languidam, voluptatibus deditam;
examples.translation: The irrational part of the soul is twofoldb: the one part is spirited, ambitious, uncontrolled; its seat is in the passions;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A fish of the herring kind
English: having a broad, turned-up nose, pug-nosed, snub-nosed
English: to demand, require, request earnestly (freq. and class.).

examples.original: Amor enim, ira, cupiditas pericula depoposcerunt.
examples.translation: It is love, for example, anger, lust, which have challenged dangers.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Ulline Italiae alumni et Romana vere iuventus ad sanguinem et caedem depoposcerit ordinem, cuius splendore et gloria sordis et obscuritatem Vitellianarum partium praestringimus ?
examples.translation: Shall any child of Italy, any true Roman youth, demand the blood and murder of that order through whose splendid glory we outshine the meanness and base birth of the partisans of Vitellius?
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: of or pertaining to the sea

examples.original: Cnosis in ignotis amens errabat harenis, Qua brevis aequoreis Dia feritur aquis.
examples.translation: The Cretan maid wandered distractedly on the unknown sand, where little Dia is lashed by the sea waves.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Aut ut Abantiades, aut ut Cycneïus heros, Clausus in aequoreas praecipiteris aquas.
examples.translation: Or like Abantiades or the Cycnean hero mayst thou be hurled, imprisoned, into the sea’s waters.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Nunc redit ad Syrtes et fluctus accipit ore, Aequoreusque placet, sed non et sufficit, umor.
examples.translation: Aulus searches for water deep down in the barren sand, and then returns to the Syrtes, and swallows the brine;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: fabulous, celebrated in fable
English: well-made, choice, elegant, fine.

examples.original: Facete M. Piso familiaris noster et alia multa et hoc loco Stoicos irridebat.
examples.translation: Our friend Marcus Piso was often witty, but never more so than when he ridiculed the Stoics on this score.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a manifestation of joy; a wishing joy, congratulation; a rejoicing
English: the country of the Jews, Judea, Palestine
Latin: Provincia romana in Asiae pars judaica
Latin: Provincia Romana Iudaica in Asia

examples.original: Cappadoces mea signa timent et dedita sacris Incerti Iudaea dei mollisque Sophene.
examples.translation: My standards overawe Cappadocia, and Judaea given over to the worship of an unknown god, and effeminate Sophene;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: very much, greatly, exceedingly, particularly, earnestly.
Latin: Valde, multum (adverbium ad sola verba vel participia firmanda)

examples.original: Magnopere se suadere populo, ne inutili pudore suam ipse causam damnaret.
examples.translation: He earnestly counselled the people not to condemn their own cause from an unreasonable motive of propriety.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Sed illud plane, quod tales deos quaedam dei unius magni membra esse dixisti, admoneo, quia dignaris, ut ab huius modi sacrilegis facetiis te magnopere abstineas.
examples.translation: But as to your statement that such gods are portions of one great god, I give you plain warning: please refrain altogether from such irreverent jocularity.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Caesar cum ab hoste non amplius passuum xii milibus abesset, ut erat constitutum, ad eum legati revertuntur; qui in itinere congressi magnopere ne longius progrederetur orabant.
examples.translation: When Caesar was no more than twelve miles away from the enemy, the deputies returned to him as agreed: they met him on the march, and besought him earnestly not to advance further.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: made or consisting of marble, marble-.

examples.original: Tunc neque marmoreo pendebant vela theatro, Nec fuerant liquido pulpita rubra croco;
examples.translation: No awnings then hung o’er a marble theatre, nor was the platform ruddy with crocus-spray;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Longe illi triplex murus totidemque arces, portus ille marmoreus et fons celebratus Arethusae;
examples.translation: Of no avail were its triple walls, its three citadels, its harbour of marble and the celebrated Fountain of Arethusa;
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Statuam habet Praeneste, in inferiore fori parte contra hemicyclium, in quo fastos a se ordinatos et marmoreo parieti incisos publicarat.
examples.translation: His statue stands at Praeneste in the upper part of the forum near the hemicycle, on which he exhibited the calendar which he had arranged and inscribed upon its marble walls.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

definitions: English: to call as a witness to any thing; to protest or assert by a person or thing (syn.: testor, obsecro, supplico; class.).

examples.original: Tum ad equites dictator advolat obtestans ut fesso iam pedite descendant ex equis et pugnam capessant.
examples.translation: The dictator then dashed up to the knights and besought them, since the foot-soldiers were exhausted, to dismount and enter the fight.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Ideoque his litteris obtestor fidem tuam, quam habes in Christo, per ipsius domini Christi misericordiam, ut hoc nec facias nec fieri omnino permittas.
examples.translation: For that reason I implore you by the faith you have in Christ, by the mercy of Christ the Lord Himself, neither to do this nor to let it be done at all.
examples.author: Augustine

examples.original: Haec monendo obtestandoque prope restitantes consules in contionem pertraxerunt. Ibi orationes longiores habitae in eandem ferme sententiam in quam inter paucos certatum verbis fuerat.
examples.translation: Thus admonishing and entreating them they dragged the all but resisting consuls to the place of assembly.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a covering, cover [cf. palla].
English: to stand firmly, continue standing.

examples.original: Nocte tota ieiuni mutique perstant.
examples.translation: All night long they must stand about, hungry and dumb.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Perstare militem, superesse studia populi;
examples.translation: In desperation at least you must gird yourself to bold action.
examples.author: Tacitus

examples.original: Et ille quidem in recusando perstabat: quid ergo attineret leges ferri, quibus per eosdem qui tulissent fraus fieret.
examples.translation: Fabius, for his part, stoutly persisted in his refusal. What, in that case, he demanded, was the good of making laws, when their very makers broke them?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: to deprive of feeling or sense; esp. by sleep
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a.; īvi or ĭi, ītum, 4

examples.original: Certe, cum commotus ira se a vestibulo templi citato gradu proriperet, lapsus per gradus capite graviter offenso impactus imo ita est saxo ut sopiretur.
examples.translation: At all events, as he hurried, beside himself with rage, from the entrance of the temple, he slipped on the stairs, and struck his head so hard on the lowest stone that he lost consciousness.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a tragedy.

examples.original: Sophocles ad summam senectutem tragoedias fecit;
examples.translation: Sophocles composed tragedies to extreme old age;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a band, esp. a fillet or chaplet worn round the head; and, in relig. lang., a head-band, a sacrificial or sacerdotal fillet

examples.original: Tu quoque, quid dubitas ferales sumere vittas?
examples.translation: Already thy funeral altar is set up, as thou dost see thyself.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: to differ in sound, to sound differently, discordantly, not to harmonize (for syn. cf.: differo, disto, intersum).
English: to run back or over, to pour over, stream over, overflow (freq. and class.; a favorite word of Cic., esp. in trop. senses; not in Cæs., Verg., or Hor.; cf.: refluo, recurro).

examples.original: Nec mirum, quod inconstans variusque ex discordi cibo morbus est et illa ex contrariis naturae partibus in eundem compulsa redundant.
examples.translation: And no wonder, that diseases which result from ill-assorted food are variable and manifold; there must be an overflow when so many unnatural combinations are jumbled together.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Quid autem est amare, e quo nomen ductum amicitiae est, nisi velle bonis aliquem affici quam maximis etiamsi ad se ex iis nihil redundet ?
examples.translation: What is the meaning of ’to love’—from which our word for friendship is derived—except to wish some one to receive the greatest possible benefits even though one gleans no advantage therefrom oneself?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: any harsh, shrill, hissing, grating, or creaking sound; a creaking, hissing, rattling, buzzing, whizzing, whistling, etc.
English: a well
Latin: Opus quo aqua salubri potu praebetur
English: a snail
English: A multitude issuing forth or flying out, a swarm. Primarily and class. of a swarm of bees

examples.original: Nam et signis insedit examen et adsuetae cadaverum pabulo volucres castra quasi iam sua circumvolabant, et in aciem prodeuntibus obvius Aethiops nimis aperte ferale signum fuit.
examples.translation: A swarm of bees settled on the standards; the birds which usually feed upon corpses flew round the camp, as though it were already their prey;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to break off, to break, bruise, crack.

examples.original: Nondum me committo frigidae verae, adhuc rigorem eius infringo.
examples.translation: I do not yet trust myself to a bath which is absolutely cold;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Accedebat huc Caecinae ambitio vetus, torpor recens, nimia fortunae indulgentia soluti in luxum, seu perfidiam meditanti infringere exercitus virtutem inter artes erat.
examples.translation: Another factor in the situation was furnished by Caecina’s old ambition and his newly acquired sloth, for an excess of Fortune’s favours had made him give way to luxury;
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: very little, very small
English: to punish one with any thing; used mostly of judicial punishment

examples.original: Multas enim civitates incendium vexavit, nullam abstulit.
examples.translation: For fire has damaged many a city, but has annihilated none.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec multo post diem obiit, utroque liberorum superstite, Tiberio Drusoque Neronibus.
examples.translation: Not long afterward he died, survived by both his sons, Tiberius Nero and Drusus Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Quam multa ab iis conquisita et collecta sunt de omnium animantium genere, ortu, membris, aetatibus!
examples.translation: What stores of facts they observed and recorded about the classification, reproduction, morphology and life-history of animals of every kind!
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the priesthood, the office or dignity of priests, the sacerdotal office

examples.original: Huic eidem Sopatro idem inimici ad C. Verrem, cum is Sacerdoti successisset, eiusdem rei nomen detulerunt.
examples.translation: When Verres succeeded Sacerdos, this same Sopater was prosecuted before him by these same enemies again on the same charge.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Quis dubitat quin in aeternum urbe condita, in immensum crescente nova imperia, sacerdotia, iura gentium hominumque instituantur?
examples.translation: Who can question that in a city founded for eternity and of incalculable growth, new powers, priesthoods, and rights of families and individuals, must be established?
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Quare triumphalia ornamenta et in brevi spatio duplex sacerdotium accepit, praeterea consulatum, quem gessit per duos novissimos anni menses.
examples.translation: For this he received the triumphal regalia, and shortly after two priesthoods, besides the consulship, which he held for the last two months of the year.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: the being out of one's mind; insanity, madness; folly

examples.original: Quae ista dementia est malum suum antecedere?
examples.translation: What madness it is to anticipate one’s troubles!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Illud vero cuius dementiae est, credere, quarum rerum extra nostrum arbitrium posita principia sunt, earum nostri esse arbitrii terminos?
examples.translation: But what folly it is, when the beginnings of certain things are situated outside our control, to believe that their endings are within our control!
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: A dis quidem immortalibus quae potest homini maior esse poena furore atque dementia?
examples.translation: But what punishment could be visited upon a man by the immortal gods severer than madness and infatuation?
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: To present a thing in words, as fixed, firm, i. e. certain, true; to assert, maintain, aver, declare, asseverate, affirm
English: to drive out of its position or place; to stir up, rouse up, disturb.

examples.original: Nam illa tumultu gaudens non est industria, sed exagitatae mentis concursatio.
examples.translation: For love of bustle is not industry,—it is only the restlessness of a hunted mind.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Credula si fueris, aliae tua gaudia carpent, Et lepus hic aliis exagitatus erit.
examples.translation: If you are too trusting, other women will reap your joys, and that hare will be hunted by others.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Non videmus quam multa nos incommoda exagitent, quam male nobis conveniat hoc corpus?
examples.translation: Do we not see how many discomforts drive us wild, and how ill-assorted is our fellowship with the flesh?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: an opening in the wall to admit the light, a window
Latin: Foramen in muro quo foras perspicere potes. Vitrea, specularia

examples.original: Nec lucem in thalamos totis admitte fenestris;
examples.translation: And let not light into your room by all the windows;
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Si tibi per tutum planumque negabitur ire, Atque erit opposita ianua fulta sera, At tu per praeceps tecto delabere aperto: Det quoque furtivas alta fenestra vias.
examples.translation: If it is denied you to go by a safe and easy road, and if the door be held by a fastened bolt, yet slip down headlong through an opening in the roof;
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: the liver.—
Latin: Viscus maximum in dextra parte, sub praecordiis situm

examples.original: En cor Zenodoti, en iecur Cratetis.
examples.translation: Lo! Crates’ heart, mind of Zenodotus.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of Illustrious Men. Grammarians And Rhetoricians. Grammarians

examples.original: Cernit tabe iecur madidum, venasque minaces Hostili de parte videt.
examples.translation: He saw the liver flabby with corruption and with boding streaks in its hostile half.
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: rank, luxuriant, exuberant.

examples.original: Ergo et avarus erit, sed finite, et adulter, verum habebit modum, et luxuriosus eodem modo.
examples.translation: He will be a miser—within limits; an adulterer—in moderation;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nec non et ratibus temptatur regia, qua se Protulit in medios audaci margine fluctus Luxuriosa domus.
examples.translation: They assailed the palace also by means of ships, at the point where the splendid pile projected with bold frontage right over the water.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Observa te itaque, numquid vestis tua domusque dissentiant, numquid in te liberalis sis, in tuos sordidus, numquid cenes frugaliter, aedifices luxuriose.
examples.translation: Observe yourself, then, and see whether your dress and your house are inconsistent, whether you treat yourself lavishly and your family meanly, whether you eat frugal dinners and yet build luxurious houses.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: of or belonging to burden, transport, or carriage; that bears a burden, carries freight (class.)

examples.original: Huc accedebant xviii onerariae naves, quae ex eo loco ab milibus passuum octo vento tenebantur quo minus in eundem portum venire possent: has equitibus distribuit.
examples.translation: To the total stated eighteen transports should be added, which were detained eight miles off by the wind, and prevented from entering the port of concentration; these he allotted to the cavalry.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: a holding back, trop. *

examples.original: Non erat in hoc neque crimen ullum neque reprehensio.
examples.translation: There was no ground here for prosecution, or even for criticism.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: deaf.
Latin: Qui auditum caret, aut totum aut partim

examples.original: Surdum te amantissimis tuis praesta;
examples.translation: Be deaf to those who love you most of all;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Nec caelum servare licet: tonat augure surdo, Et laetae iurantur aves bubone sinistro.
examples.translation: It is not permitted to watch the sky: it thunders, but the augur is deaf;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: an eagerness for something (either lawful or unlawful), avidity, longing, vehement desire.

examples.original: Veri boni aviditas tuta est.
examples.translation: The real good may be coveted with safety.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: In castris tiro etiam tum propter nimiam vini aviditatem pro Tiberio ”Biberius,” pro Claudio ”Caldius,” pro Nerone ”Mero” vocabatur.
examples.translation: Even at the outset of his military career his excessive love of wine gave him the name of Biberius, instead of Tiberius, Caldius for Claudius, and Mero for Nero.
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Est ille plus quam capit, et ingenti aviditate onerat distentum ventrem ac desuetum iam ventris officio, ut maiore opera omnia egerat quam ingessit;
examples.translation: The master eats more than he can hold, and with monstrous greed loads his belly until it is stretched and at length ceases to do the work of a belly;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to be inflamed with anger, to be angry, irritated, enraged (class.; syn.: irascor, indignor).
English: That falls or has fallen, falling, fallen

examples.original: De homine dixi, fluvida materia et caduca et omnibus obnoxia causis;
examples.translation: So much for man,—a substance that flows away and falls, exposed to every influence;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Satorum vero animaliumque virtutes cum mortales sint, fragiles quoque caducaeque sunt et incertae.
examples.translation: But, since the virtues of plants and of animals are perishable, they are also frail and fleeting and uncertain.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: De divinis humanisque discendum est, de praeteritis de futuris, de caducis de aeternis, de tempore.
examples.translation: One must learn about things divine and human, the past and the future, the ephemeral and the eternal;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to scatter, strew something on something; or of liquids, to sprinkle, spatter over (syn.: adfundo, inicio; never in Ovid, but he often uses the simple spargo).
English: a slough, bog, morass, puddle.

examples.original: Census actus est, lustrum conditum.
examples.translation: The census was taken and the lustrum closed.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cum alter ex censoribus C. Iulius decessisset, in locum eius M. Cornelius suffectus est. Nec id postea factum est, quoniam eo lustro a Gallis Roma capta est.
examples.translation: On the death of one of the censors, Gaius Julius, Marcus Cornelius was chosen to fill out his term, but this was never afterwards done because in that five-year period Rome was taken.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Census deinde actus et conditum ab Quinctio lustrum.
examples.translation: The census was then taken and Quinctius solemnized the concluding purification.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: violence, vehemence, impetuosity, ferocity (class.)

examples.original: Timere relicta ab suis plebes violentiam patrum;
examples.translation: The plebeians, having been abandoned by their friends, feared violence at the hands of the senators;
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Simili superbia violentiaque ceteros tractavit ordines.
examples.translation: He treated the other orders with like insolence and cruelty.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

examples.original: Nec nominis homines tum pertaesum esse, quippe quo Iovem appellari fas sit, quo Romulum, conditorem urbis, deincepsque reges, quod sacris etiam ut sollemne retentum sit: superbiam violentiamque tum perosos regis.
examples.translation: Nor was it the name, said he, which had then disgusted men, since by this name Jupiter was duly called; and Romulus, the founder of the City: and the successive kings;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: poetic, poetical

examples.original: Natura sic ab iis investigata est ut nulla pars caelo, mari, terra (ut poetice loquar) praetermissa sit.
examples.translation: Natural Philosophy the Peripatetics have investigated so thoroughly that no region in sky or sea or land (to speak poetically) has been passed over.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Nam nec tu agitare et insequi poetas intermittis, et ego, cui desidiam advocationum obicis, cotidianum hoc patrocinium defendendae adversus te poeticae exerceo.
examples.translation: You on your part are never done assailing the poets with your invective, and I, whom you charge with neglect of professional duty, am daily retained to defend the art of poetry against you.
examples.author: Tacitus

definitions: English: to take the auspices.

examples.original: Quid alia quae auspicato agimus omnia fere intra pomerium, cui oblivioni aut cui neglegentiae damus?
examples.translation: What about the other matters nearly all of which we transact, after taking auspices, within the pomerium?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a pear-tree
English: wear away underneath; to rub, bruise, or grind to pieces
English: to become tired or wearied; to grow weary, faint; to be exhausted.

examples.original: Sed quia finem aliquam pariendi debet habere, destitit, ut mulier spatio defessa vetusto.
examples.translation: But because she must have some limit to her bearing, she ceased, like a woman worn out by old age.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Tandem vulneribus defessi et pedem referre et, quod mons suberat circiter mille passuum, eo se recipere coeperunt.
examples.translation: At length, worn out with wounds, they began to retreat, retiring towards a height about a mile away. They gained the height;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Valerius Catullus, consulari familia iuvenis, stupratum a se ac latera sibi contubernio eius defessa etiam vociferatus est.
examples.translation: Valerius Catullus, a young man of a consular family, bragged that he had penetrated the emperor and worn himself out in intercourse with him.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: a tuft on the head of animals; most freq. of the comb of a cock
English: these are hen-tracks
Latin: Femina galli

examples.original: Leporem et gallinam et anserem gustare fas non putant;
examples.translation: They account it wrong to eat of hare, fowl, and goose;
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

examples.original: Semper enim boni assiduique domini referta cella vinaria, olearia, etiam penaria est, villaque tota locuples est, abundat porco haedo agno gallina, lacte caseo melle.
examples.translation: For the provident and industrious proprietor always has his store-room and cellars well filled with oil and wine and provisions;
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: the infernal regions
Latin: locus mythologicus in medio Hade
Latin: flumen italicum in regionis Venetia et Langobardia

examples.original: Mox cetera cantu Explicat Haemonio penetratque in Tartara lingua;
examples.translation: The dog’s bark and the wolfs howl were in that voice;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Cerberus et Furiae iam vero et lucis egestas, Tartarus horriferos eructans faucibus aestus— qui neque sunt usquam nec possunt esse profecto.
examples.translation: Cerberusb also and the Furies and the with-holding of light, and Tartarus belching horrible fires from his throat—these neither exist anywhere nor in truth can exist.
examples.author: Lucretius

examples.original: Utque patrem Psamathes, condat te Phoebus in ima Tartara, quod natae fecerat ille suae.
examples.translation: And like Psamathe’s sire may Phoebus bury thee in lowest Tartarus, as he had done to his own daughter.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: thirty at a time, thirty each, thirty.
English: to hear, learn, esp. something secret (mostly ante-class. and in the tempp. perff.): quod ego inaudivi, accipite, Pac. ap.

examples.original: Quid est, quod quisquam aut illo dignum aut vobis novum aut cuiquam inauditum possit adferre?
examples.translation: What tribute can anyone pay other than what would be unworthy of him, stale to you and familiar to everybody?
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hoc vero tam inopinatum malum et paene inauditum non miror si sine metu fuit, cum esset sine exemplo.
examples.translation: I do not wonder, however, that he was free from apprehension touching an evil so unexpected and practically unheard of as this, since it is without precedent.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: to attack, trouble, molest, disturb, infest (mostly post-Aug.).

examples.original: Ab triumpho exercitum in agrum Vescinum, quia regio ea infesta ab Samnitibus erat, hibernatum duxit.
examples.translation: After triumphing, Papirius led his army into the country of the Vescini—a district infested by the Samnites—to pass the winter.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Rex Pharnaces magis discordiae nostrae fiducia quam suae virtutis infesto in Cappadociam agmine ruebat.
examples.translation: King Pharnaces, relying rather upon our internal feuds than upon his own valour, invaded Cappadocia with a hostile force.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Nec tamen expers insidiarum usque quaque permansit, sed et a singulis et per factionem et denique civili bello infestatus est.
examples.translation: Yet he did not remain throughout without experience of treachery, but he was attacked by individuals, by a conspiracy, and finally by a civil war.
examples.author: Suetonius

definitions: English: a foreigner, stranger, or alien; and

examples.original: Spernentibus Etruscis Lucumonem exsule advena ortum, ferre indignitatem non potuit oblitaque ingenitae erga patriam caritatis, dummodo virum honoratum videret, consilium migrandi ab Tarquiniis cepit.
examples.translation: She could not endure this indignity, and forgetting the love she owed her native land, if she could only see her husband honoured, she formed the project of emigrating from Tarquinii.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Alii proelio victum Latinum pacem cum Aenea, deinde affinitatem iunxisse tradunt: alii, cum instructae acies constitissent, priusquam signa canerent processisse Latinum inter primores ducemque advenarum evocasse ad conloquium;
examples.translation: Some say that Latinus, having been defeated in the battle, made a peace with Aeneas, and later an alliance of marriage.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a dispute, disputation, debate, discussion, disquisition.
English: name of a Roman gens.—
English: from there, from that place, thence (freq., but not in Ter., Caes., or Quint.).
Latin: post hac, tum, tempore sequenti, iam inde uti
Latin: ab hoc loco
English: repeatedly, several times, often, now and then, at intervals, ever and anon; continually, constantly, habitually (class.; cf.: subinde, interdum)
English: to lay the foundation of a thing, to begin, commence (syn. incipere; opp. absolvere, perficere; class.).
entries.grammaticalClass: v. a. and n.; āvi, ātum, 1

examples.original: Mater Antonia portentum eum hominis dictitabat, nec absolutum a natura, sed tantum incohatum;
examples.translation: His mother Antonia often called him ”a monster of a man, not finished but merely begun by Dame Nature”;
examples.author: Suetonius

examples.original: Incohavit autem aquae ductum regione Tiburti et amphitheatrum iuxta Saepta, quorum operum a successore eius Claudio alterum peractum, omissum alterum est.
examples.translation: He likewise began an aqueduct in the region near Tibur and an amphitheatre beside the Saepta, the former finished by his successor Claudius, while the latter was abandoned.
examples.author: Suetonius
examples.work: Lives Of The Caesars 4. Gaius Caligula

definitions: English: of or belonging to mid-day, mid-day-.
Latin: medio die
Latin: australis; meridionalis
English: of or belonging to the Peripatetic (Aristotelian) philosophy, Peripatetic

examples.original: Itaque haec cum illis est dissensio, cum Peripateticis nulla sane.
examples.translation: Here then I have a quarrel with the Stoics, but certainly none with the Peripatetics.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Hic quoque suus est, de summoque bono dissentiens dici vere Peripateticus non potest.
examples.translation: He too stands by himself; differing about the Chief Good he cannot correctly be called a Peripatetic.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Sed idem hoc omnes tibi ex omni domo conclamabunt, Peripatetici, Academici, Stoici, Cynici.
examples.translation: But this same watchword rings in your ears from every sect,—Peripatetic, Academic, Stoic, Cynic.
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: that has a passage through; hence

examples.original: Nam ab Saticula profectus Cornelius consul exercitum incaute in saltum cava valle pervium circaque insessum ab hoste induxit nec prius quam recipi tuto signa non poterant imminentem capiti hostem vidit.
examples.translation: For the consul Cornelius, marching from Saticula, had unwarily led his army into a forest which was penetrated by a deep defile, and was there beset on either hand by the enemy;
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a flat or even surface, level ground, a plain (class.)
Latin: Aequalitas loci, locus planus
Latin: planum, terra plana

examples.original: Planities erat magna et in ea tumulus terrenus satis grandis.
examples.translation: There was a large plain, and in it a mound of earth of considerable size.
examples.author: Gaius Iulius Caesar

definitions: English: to rain; constr.
English: to leap or spring forth, to spring up (class.).

examples.original: Quid ante signa feroces prosiluissent et alieno pugnarent loco?—his inter se vocibus concitati clamore renovato inferunt pedem et primum gradu moverunt hostem, deinde pepulerunt, postremo iam haud dubie avertunt;
examples.translation: What good had they done by dashing boldly out in front of the line and fighting in a place that belonged to others?
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: full of trouble or commotion.

examples.original: Illa igitur omnia Quinctiana iniqua, falsa, turbulenta, popularia, seditiosa iudicia fuerunt.
examples.translation: Then all those trials, Quinctius’s work, were the fruits of injustice, lies, violence, demagogy, and insurrection.
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Et quemadmodum temeritas et libido et ignavia semper animum excruciant et semper sollicitant turbulentaeque sunt, sic improbitas si cuius in mente consedit, hoc ipso quod adest turbulenta est;
examples.translation: And just as Rashness, Licence and Cowardice ever torment the mind, ever awaken trouble and discord, so Unrighteousness, when firmly rooted in the heart, causes restlessness by the mere fact of its presence;
examples.author: Cicero

examples.original: Consul educto in aestiva milite, dum quietos Samnites habebat, exercitum purgare missionibus turbulentorum hominum instituit, aliis emerita dicendo stipendia esse, alios graves iam aetate aut viribus parum validos.
examples.translation: The consul having led out his troops to the summer encampment, and finding the Samnites quiet, resolved to purge the army of its troublemakers by discharging them.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: the enclosed space between the entrance of a house and the street, a fore-court, entrance-court (cf. atrium).

examples.original: Certe, cum commotus ira se a vestibulo templi citato gradu proriperet, lapsus per gradus capite graviter offenso impactus imo ita est saxo ut sopiretur.
examples.translation: At all events, as he hurried, beside himself with rage, from the entrance of the temple, he slipped on the stairs, and struck his head so hard on the lowest stone that he lost consciousness.
examples.author: Livy

definitions: English: a wayfarer, traveller

examples.original: Quid mihi tunc animi est, ubi sumit tela viator Atque oculis plagae destinat ante locum?
examples.translation: What spirit have I then, when the traveller takes his weapons, and his eye picks out the spot for his blow?
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: of or belonging to a maiden or virgin, maidenly, virgin
English: a. [clamo], to cry out violently or aloud, to bawl out, vociferate (class., esp. freq. since the Aug. per.; in Cic. only twice; not in Quint.; usu. of human beings).

examples.original: Haec Volscio clamitante adeo concitati homines sunt ut haud multum afuerit quin impetu populi Caeso interiret.
examples.translation: As Volscius shouted out this story, men became so excited that Caeso had nearly perished by the fury of the people.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: T. Quinctius clamitat, cui rei capitalis dies dicta sit et de quo futurum propediem iudicium, eum indemnatum indicta causa non debere violari.
examples.translation: Titus Quinctius cried out that a man who had been charged with a capital crime and whose day of trial was at hand ought not to suffer violence, uncondemned and unheard.
examples.author: Livy

examples.original: Cuius tu tribus venditorem, et corruptorem, et sequestrem Plancium fuisse clamitas, eam tribum profecto, severissimorum praesertim hominum et gravissimorum, edere debuisti.
examples.translation: It was what we expected, and what would have been in keeping with your high principles.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: a false oath, perjury.
English: to urge, bring, or assemble together, by exciting or rousing, to collect

examples.original: Inde ruunt toto concita pericula mundo.
examples.translation: And now dangers, summoned from all the world, came rushing on.
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: Tum pectore curas Expulit armorum pacique intentus agebat, Quoque modo vanos populi conciret amores, Gnarus et irarum causas et summa favoris Annona momenta trahi.
examples.translation: At once he banished thoughts of battle from his mind, and passed his time over problems of peace and the means of winning the fickle favour of the populace;
examples.author: Lucan

examples.original: In nemus et saltus thalamo regina relicto Fertur, ut Aonio concita Baccha deo.
examples.translation: Leaving her bower the queen hies her to the woods and glens, like a Bacchanal sped by the Aonian god.
examples.author: Ovid

definitions: English: a sprout, shoot, offshoot, twig, spray
English: farthest, most remote, last

examples.original: Sed nec illo voluntario ad hostis suos reditu nec ultimo sive carceris seu crucis supplicio deformata maiestas;
examples.translation: His voluntary return to his enemies and his final sufferings, whether in prison or on the cross, in no way sullied his dignity;
examples.author: Florus

definitions: English: to join one in opinion, to agree with; hence, to assent to, give assent, to approve, give approval; with

examples.original: Ex quo efficitur id, quod ego magno quondam cum assensu omnium dixi, miseram esse senectutem quae se oratione defenderet.
examples.translation: Hence it follows—as I once said with the approval of all who heard it—that that old age is wretched which needs to defend itself with words.
examples.author: Cicero

definitions: English: unsoundness of mind.
English: to throw, cast, hurl.

examples.original: Et adversus mortem tu tam minuta iacularis?
examples.translation: Are you, then, hurling petty weapons like yours even against death?
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

examples.original: Hi iaculo pisces, illi capiuntur ab hamis: Hos cava contento retia fune trahunt.
examples.translation: These fish are caught with spears, those with hooks; these ones are dragged with taut ropes in bulging nets.
examples.author: Ovid

examples.original: Iam non excussis torquentur tela lacertis, Nec longinqua cadunt iaculato volnera ferro, Miscenturque manus.
examples.translation: No longer were weapons hurled from vigorous arms, no longer were the wounds of the hurtling steel inflicted at a distance;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a marking out, delineation, copy, transcript: in concreto.
Latin: Factum describendi; delineatio

examples.original: Ait utilem futuram et descriptionem cuiusque virtutis;
examples.translation: He remarks that it will also be useful to illustrate each particular virtue;
examples.author: Seneca The Younger

definitions: English: A wellknown river in Syria, which rises in Armenia, and, after its junction with the Tigris, empties into the Persian Gulf, now Frat

examples.original: Idem tunc Faesulae quod Carrhae nuper, idem nemus Aricinum quod Hercynius saltus, Fregellae quod Gesoriacum, Tiberis quod Euphrates.
examples.translation: Faesulae meant the same to us then as Carrhae lately meant; the Arician Wood corresponded to the Hercynian Forest, Fregellae to Gesoriacum, the Tiber to the Euphrates.
examples.author: Florus

examples.original: Dividit Euphrates ingentem gurgite mundum, Caspiaque inmensos seducunt claustra recessus, Et polus Assyrias alter noctesque diesque Vertit, et abruptum est nostro mare discolor unda Oceanusque suus.
examples.translation: The waters of the Euphrates shut off from us a mighty world, and the Caspian Gates hide boundless solitudes; in Assyria a different hemisphere makes the changes of night and day;
examples.author: Lucan

definitions: English: a., to be greatly afraid of, to fear greatly; to await with fear, to dread (class.).

examples.original: Nec nocuisse ulli et fortunam habuisse nocendi, Nec quemquam nervos extimuisse tuos?
examples.translation: To have harmed none, yet to have had the power to harm, and that none feared thy might?
examples.author: Ovid
